10057-the-secret-of-the-tower:
Anthony Hope's 1919 novel, from the author of The Prisoner of Zenda, opens with Doctor Mary's paying guest and a general who remembers. Mr. Saffron at home, professional etiquette, a familiar implement, and the odd story of Captain Duggle deepen the puzzle.

A gentlemanly stranger appears, Captain Alec raises his voice, and Doctor Mary gives her ultimatum. That magical word Morocco leads to the car behind the trees and the secret of the tower itself, with a scepter in the grave. Hope writes light, deft adventure. Readers get a Ruritanian-style romance with a mystery at its heart.
10073-the-century-vocabulary-builder:
Garland Greever and Joseph M. Bachelor wrote this Century handbook to help readers build a larger, more exact vocabulary. It opens with reasons for increasing your word stock, then warns of pitfalls when words combine: abstract against concrete, general against specific, literal against figurative, and connotation.

Later chapters teach mastery through translation, paraphrasing, discourse at first hand, and adapting talk to an audience, with individual words studied as verbal celibates. The book is practical, not theoretical. Students and writers get exercises for choosing words that say what they mean, and no more.
10080-mobilizing-woman-power:
Harriot Stanton Blatch's 1918 book, dedicated to the able and devoted women of Great Britain and France, calls them an unswerving second line of defense for liberty and civilization. Her frontispiece shows Jeanne d'Arc as the spirit of the women of the Allies.

Chapters treat the foe, winning the war, and mobilizing women in Britain, France, and Germany. They add women over the top in America, Eve's pay envelope, pooling brains, business as usual, a land army, and woman's part in saving civilization. Blatch, a suffrage leader, writes with force. Readers get feminism in wartime, practical and proud.
10110-the-postmaster-s-daughter:
Louis Tracy published this mystery novel in 1916, in the shadow of the First World War. John Menzies Grant, a young man of means, grows puzzled by a face at a window and by strange doings around a country house. Police, secrets, and family past soon pull him into a case that will not stay simple.

Scotland Yard takes a hand, suspects shift, and clues point toward heredity, blackmail, and old wrongs. The postmaster's daughter stands at the heart of the puzzle, though the truth comes out only late. Readers get a brisk, twist-filled detective tale with romance, village life, and wartime unease in the background.
10213-the-everlasting-whisper:
Jackson Gregory published this California wilderness novel in the early twentieth century, setting it in the high Sierra in June. Spring, summer, and winter touch across seventy miles, from burning lowlands to snow on peaks above seven thousand feet. The land itself, with pines, cedars, and bare rock ridges, shapes the tale.

A hero drawn by what Gregory calls the everlasting whisper of the wild must face the forest's beauty and its danger. Love, rivalry, and the lure of gold or hidden treasure drive the human plot. Readers get a sweeping, romantic western of mountains, pines, and the call of untamed country.
1024-the-wrecker:
Two young men in San Francisco buy a wrecked ship at auction and sail to find what she hid, chasing a fortune that may be real or a trap. Robert Louis Stevenson wrote this tale of trade and the sea with his stepson Lloyd Osbourne, drawing on Pacific ports, shady deals, and the lure of quick wealth.

The hunt leads through offices, docks, and island waters, where each clue twists the plot and tests the friends' nerve. Behind the wreck lies a scheme of fraud and murder that the pair must untangle. The novel blends sea yarn, mystery, and comedy, and it moves at a brisk clip from start to finish.
10267-the-outdoor-chums-or-the-first-tou:
Captain Quincy Allen published this boys' camp story in 1911, first in a series about the Rod, Gun and Camera Club. Four friends plan a tour, pick a camp site, and set out to fish, hunt, and take photographs. The book treats outdoor skill as a school for courage, care, and fair play.

Storms, a lost friend, a muskrat trapper, a bear's hollow, and an old mine shaft test the boys in turn. Clues, mishaps, and teamwork carry the plot from one camp crisis to the next. Readers get a wholesome, lively adventure of camping, woodcraft, and loyal friendship.
1027-the-lone-star-ranger-a-romance-of-t:
Buck Duane, a young Texan turned outlaw after a feud killing, rides the border country and slowly earns his way back by joining the Texas Rangers. Zane Grey sets the tale among rustlers, gunmen, and desert trails, where a man's word and his draw decide his fate.

Duane hunts the outlaw bands he once rode with, torn between old loyalties and new duty. Grey writes the West in broad, sunny strokes, with chases, sieges, and a love interest to soften the gun smoke. The novel helped fix the Ranger myth, and it remains a sturdy, fast western.
10324-bull-hunter:
Max Brand, a prolific western writer, opens this novel with men baffled by a great stump on a high mountainside, nine thousand feet above the sea. The taproot will not yield to hatchets, and the men tug, rest, and gaze down at spruce and fir below. The scene sets the hard, physical world of Brand's West.

The hero, known as Bull Hunter, must face wild land, stubborn work, and human foes with strength and grit. Brand's prose is brisk, vivid, and full of mountain detail. Readers get a tough, fast western of labor, landscape, and a man whose name fits his trade.
1033-rose-o-the-river:
Rose Wiley, a bright young woman who keeps house by a Maine river, wins the hearts of the lumbermen and river drivers who pass her door. Kate Douglas Wiggin sets this light romance among log drives, country dances, and small-town talk, with Rose at its warm center.

A handsome stranger and a steady local man both seek her hand, and Rose must weigh charm against worth. The tale moves through mishaps, jokes, and kind deeds to a happy close. Wiggin, famed for Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, writes here with the same sunny touch, and the book suits readers who like gentle, old-style romance.
10368-the-vizier-of-the-two-horned-alexa:
Frank R. Stockton published this fantasy novel in 1899, based on legends in the chronicles of the historian Tabari. Its hero is El Khoudr, vizier to a great monarch called the Two-Horned Alexander, whom Stockton carefully separates from Alexander the Great. The Two-Horned king belongs, in legend, to the time of Abraham.

El Khoudr's strange adventures furnish the motive for later tales of wonder, magic, and high civilization. Stockton tells them with humor and invention, in his own whimsical style. Readers get a charming, learned fantasy drawn from old Eastern legend, full of marvels and wit.
10371-the-cinema-murder:
E. Phillips Oppenheim published this crime novel in 1917, when cinema was still a new wonder. A young man steps off a London train at Detton Magna, a grim colliery town, and walks up into town with no coat against the rain. The scene sets a mood of damp, industry, and hidden purpose.

The plot turns on murder, a film, and a man who may use the new screen art to hide or to reveal guilt. Oppenheim builds suspense through towns, trains, and shadowed streets. Readers get a stylish, early thriller that links old crime plots to the new world of moving pictures.
10373-the-middle-temple-murder:
J. S. Fletcher published this detective novel in 1919, opening with a young newspaper man named Spargo leaving his office at two in the morning. A scrap of grey paper, a cap, and a body in the Middle Temple set Spargo on a trail through London hotels, stamp dealers, and old papers. Fletcher wrote many such puzzles with care.

Spargo follows Mr. Aylmore, a safe-deposit man, a leather box, and a silver ticket toward a hidden past and a proved identity. A coffin, a window-cleaner, and a final telegram bring the truth out. Readers get a classic, well-plotted mystery of London law, press, and old secrets.
10438-up-the-hill-and-over:
Isabel Ecclestone MacKay, author of The House of Windows, wrote this gentle novel of a road that runs back and runs on, scented with clover. A dusty, hot wayfarer singing his way from Wimbleton to Wombleton collapses on a green slope above a cool pool, where a small boy with school books lies stretched out. The scene sets a whimsical, pastoral tone.

The wayfarer and the boy trade questions about distance, and the road itself becomes a figure for life's ups and downs. MacKay writes with humor and tenderness about ordinary folk. Readers get a light, charming tale of travel, youth, and the next dawn over the hill.
10449-burnham-breaker:
Homer Greene, author of The Blind Brother, published this coal-country novel in 1887, inscribing it to his father at Honesdale, Pennsylvania. A breaker is a coal-breaking plant, and the story follows young lives, schemes, and courtroom trials around that hard industry. Greene writes with moral warmth and local detail.

A surprise in the screen room, a strange visitor, a brilliant scheme, and a search for a mother open the tale. Rhyming Joe, a friend in need, evidence in court, and gentlemen of the jury carry it on. Readers get a vivid, Victorian-era story of mining towns, family, and justice.
10452-peter-s-mother:
Mrs. Henry de la Pasture wrote this novel of a typical Englishwoman of a certain class, reissued in 1906 with her own introduction for American readers. Its heroine is Lady Mary Crewys, whose life is guarded, isolated, and circumscribed, yet full of content and kindness to those around her. The author defends narrow lives as worthy of art.

Peter, her son, and the world beyond her home test Mary's quiet strength and love. The novel follows duty, sacrifice, and the slow opening of a sheltered mind. Readers get a sincere, Edwardian portrait of an English mother, praised for truth to its type.
10496-red-masquerade-being-the-story-of-:
Louis Joseph Vance published this thriller in 1921, as the story of the Lone Wolf's daughter. It follows Alias the Lone Wolf. Vance admits the tale derives from his own invention for a 1919 film, The Lone Wolf's Daughter. He took liberties with the film version as freely as the film took with his original. The book stands alone.

Prince Victor, pain and reluctance in his gesture, opens a tale of masks, jewels, and daring. In it, the Lone Wolf's daughter must face her father's world. Vance writes with pace, romance, and style. Readers get a stylish, fast crime romance of a heroine caught between crime and honor.
10556-the-old-man-in-the-corner:
Baroness Orczy, creator of the Scarlet Pimpernel, published this detective book in 1908, dedicating it to her uncle and aunt in Transylvania. Its hero, the old man in the corner, sits in a tea shop and solves crimes by pure deduction, explaining each case to a lady journalist. The format is a string of short mysteries, each with a twist.

The Fenchurch Street mystery, a millionaire in the dock, a robbery in Phillimore Terrace, and mysteries in York, Liverpool, Edinburgh, and Dublin fill the set. Forgery, alibis, and conflicting evidence test the old man's logic. Readers get a classic, clever collection of armchair detection.
10601-the-rangeland-avenger:
Max Brand first published this western in 1922 in Western Story Magazine as Three Who Paid. He used the pen name George Owen Baxter. Then, in book form in 1924, it appeared as The Rangeland Avenger. Four men open the tale: Hal Sinclair, vital spirit; Quade, mighty arms; Lowrie, trail lore; and Sandersen, dreamy spirit of lost causes who hoped for gold until hope became belief.

Sandersen's hunches, fears, and superstitions drive the party, while Hal, still a boy at thirty, hums songs and talks softly to his horse. Failure and fear blight the spirit, yet Sinclair offers an antidote. Readers get a classic Brand western of mining, revenge, and the hard lore of the trail.
10778-the-prose-marmion-a-tale-of-the-sc:
Sara D. Jenkins adapted Scott's Marmion into prose in 1903 as The Prose Marmion, a tale of the Scottish border for young readers. Her introduction sketches Scott himself: born in Edinburgh, lame from his second year, raised for five years on his grandfather's farm at Sandyknowe, then schooled in Edinburgh. Portraits of the poet front the book.

The prose version keeps Scott's story of Flodden, love, and border warfare, freed from verse for school use. Jenkins, who had done the same for The Lady of the Lake, writes plainly and well. Readers get Scott's romance in accessible form, with a short life of its author.
10811-de-la-salle-fifth-reader:
The Brothers of the Christian Schools prepared the De La Salle Fifth Reader, revised in 1922, for Catholic schoolchildren. A portrait of President William McKinley fronts the book. Its contents mix hymns, history, and verse. Pieces include Columbus at the convent, the brook song of James Whitcomb Riley, work by Carlyle and Helen Hunt Jackson, and "My Old Kentucky Home." A guide to pronunciation and definitions aids the pupil.

The reader aims at clear speech, good morals, and love of country as well as letters. Its selections are short and varied for classroom use. Modern readers get a window onto Catholic schooling in 1920s America, and a sample of what children then read aloud.
10996-whig-against-tory-or-the-military-:
An 1851 children's tale of the American Revolution, told as a father, General P, answers his sons William, Henry, and John. The boys ask about battles, and their father instead tells of Enoch Crosby, a shoemaker who served as a spy, or informer, for the American cause. The story explains Whigs and Tories in simple terms: Tories backed the king, Whigs fought for liberty.

Crosby risks his life gathering news of Tory plans, asking only that, if he falls, his memory be cleared and his service known. The dialogue form lets children ask questions and hear answers in turn. The book teaches patriotism and the meaning of secret service, using one humble man's courage to make the Revolution vivid for young readers.
11051-the-cruise-of-the-dazzler:
Jack London wrote this 1902 boys' adventure about Joe, a bold San Francisco lad who leads his friends scorching through Golden Gate Park on bicycles. Joe chafes at school and home, then falls in with Frisco Kid and the bay pirates aboard the sloop Dazzler. French Pete commands the boat, and Joe must learn sailing while keeping his conscience.

Chapters follow Joe among oyster beds, in wild anchorages, and in perilous hours as he and Frisco Kid plan an escape. A ditty-box, a father's search, and a final reckoning with Joe's father close the story. London writes the bay with energy, and the novel shows a boy choosing honesty over the romance of piracy.
11122-choice-specimens-of-american-liter:
Professor Benjamin N. Martin of the University of the City of New York edited this 1874 literary reader, a supplement to Shaw's Choice Specimens of English Literature, enlarged in a second edition. Martin drew extracts directly from collected works, with help from the Society, Mercantile, and Astor libraries, giving larger space to Franklin, Jefferson, Calhoun, Webster, Irving, Cooper, Hawthorne, Bryant, Poe, Emerson, and Lowell.

Later writers join the older lists, and brief, fragmentary extracts give way to extended, coherent passages. A mid-book passage on Baron von Steuben drilling militia shows the method: history told through well-chosen prose. The reader served schools and general readers, offering a canon of American literature as the 1870s understood it, and it remains useful for tracing that canon's formation.
11270-a-practical-illustration-of-woman-:
Edited by Caroline H. Dall in 1860, this volume presents a letter from Marie E. Zakrzewska, a Berlin-trained woman physician, as a practical illustration of woman's right to labor. Dall explains that Zakrzewska's autobiography is subordinated and veiled by the title out of respect for her modesty, and dedicates the book to Samuel E. Sewall, a friend of the New-England Female Medical College. Epigraphs from Aurora Leigh frame the argument.

Zakrzewska's story shows a woman doing medical work competently despite opposition, and Dall uses it to answer doubters who claimed women could not labor gracefully. The book belongs to the early American women's rights movement, arguing by example rather than theory. Its evidence is one life, presented as proof of a principle.
11290-emilie-the-peacemaker:
Mrs. Thomas Geldart's Emilie the Peacemaker, published in 1851 with the text Blessed are the peacemakers. follows two girls gathering primroses on a May evening by the sea, then traces Emilie's efforts to soften quarrels at home and among friends. Chapters include The Soft Answer, Edith's Trials, Emilie's Trials, Better Things, Good for Evil, Fred a Peacemaker, and Joe's Christmas, ending with a new home and a last chapter.

Geldart, author of Truth Is Everything and Stories of England, writes moral fiction in which a gentle word prevents a breach. The book's seaside setting and domestic scenes keep its lessons concrete. For readers of Victorian children's literature, it is a clear example of peacemaking taught as a practical, daily virtue.
11508-reminiscences-of-a-pioneer:
Colonel William Thompson's 1912 Reminiscences of a Pioneer, edited at Alturas, California. traces a life from farewell to an old southern home through a first winter in the Willamette Valley, the Indian outbreak of 1855. canyon history, a first newspaper venture, Modoc history, the Ben Wright massacre, treaty and lava-bed battles, the peace commission, trailing fugitives, the Bannock War, snake uprisings, vigilantes, and the Lookout lynching. Photographs show Thompson, Captain Jack's cave, and lava-bed forts.

Thompson wonders whether modern palace-car travelers realize the hardships of Argonauts crossing three thousand miles of wilderness fifty-eight years earlier. His memoir mixes personal adventure with frontier journalism. For Pacific Northwest historians, it is a firsthand, partisan account of settlement and Indian wars.
11553-the-wonders-of-prayer:
Revised by D. W. Whittle in 1885, this volume gathers accounts of answered prayer told by George Muller, D. L. Moody, Charles Spurgeon, Martin Luther, John Knox, Abraham Lincoln, and many others. Its introduction insists every case was checked, and nothing doubtful was printed.

Stories follow one after another: a girl helped to a place, two dollars put to good use, and other small, plain incidents presented as proof of persevering faith. The book is a record of belief in action, not a work of argument, and it speaks to readers who already trust prayer.
1162-the-jacket-the-star-rover:
Jack London tells of Darrell Standing, a prisoner in San Quentin. Locked in a straitjacket for days, he learns to leave his body and live past lives: as a child, a sailor, a Roman, and more. The novel frames these lives with a protest against prison cruelty.

Standing's visions carry the book's sweep, from ancient battles to frontier trails, while the jacket scenes keep its anger sharp. London wrote from reports of real prison abuse. The novel blends adventure with a plea for mercy, and it remains one of his strangest and most heartfelt works.
11620-my-brilliant-career:
Miles Franklin's 1901 novel opens with a preface by Henry Lawson, who calls it a real yarn, not a romance or a novel in the usual sense. The narrator, Sybylla, says her sphere in life is not congenial, and she hates the living death that has swallowed her teens.

Tall gum trees, hardship, and bitter heartache frame her story, set in New South Wales. Later scenes bring uncle Julius, a devil of a Joe who should water horses, and a girl left to spoon with her lad on a holiday. The book is an Australian girl's fierce, funny account of farm life and thwarted ambition.
11772-narrative-of-a-voyage-to-senegal-i:
Written by surgeon J. B. Henry Savigny with Alexander Corréard, this narrative recounts the 1816 French voyage to Senegal and the wreck of the frigate Méduse. After the ship struck ground off West Africa, some 150 people were set adrift on a makeshift raft, and only fifteen were still alive thirteen days later.

Savigny describes thirst, delirium, and violence on the raft in plain, firsthand detail, then follows the survivors through the desert of Zaara to St. Louis and the camp at Daccard. Closing observations on farming along the coast from Cape Blanco to the Gambia give the book a second life as a report on West African agriculture.
11802-u-s-copyright-renewals-1950-july-d:
Covering renewals registered from July through December 1950, this Copyright Office catalog lists literature, art, and film alphabetically by title, with cross-references from essential names. Musical compositions are excluded, as in the other volumes of the series.

Most entries renew works first registered in 1922 and 1923, from Margaret Wilson's novel The Able McLaughlins to Chesterton and Lloyd Osbourne magazine stories. Each line gives the original registration and the renewal claimant and date, preserving a clear paper trail for books and stories entering their second copyright term. The alphabetical run also includes Jeffery Farnol's Peregrine's Progress, John Farrar's Bookman anthology of essays, a book of plays for children. Helena Smith Dayton's one-act Fashion Show, produced by the Shuberts.
11804-u-s-copyright-renewals-1951-july-d:
This catalog records Class A renewal registrations from July through December 1951, arranged alphabetically under author, editor, compiler, or title. Joint authors and editors appear through references leading to the main headings, and each entry carries both original and renewal details.

Works first copyrighted in 1923 and 1924 predominate, from Franklin P. Adams's So Much Velvet and Samuel Hopkins Adams's novels to textbooks on road building and edited collections of pre-Shakespearean drama. The volume is a working register, useful for settling who claimed a renewal and when, rather than for continuous reading.
11806-u-s-copyright-renewals-1952-july-d:
Renewals registered in the second half of 1952 fill this Class A catalog, arranged alphabetically under main headings of author, editor, compiler, or title. Cross-references guide readers from joint authors and variant names to the full entry, which states the original and renewal registrations.

Titles first published in 1924 and 1925 run through the list, including Conrad Aiken's stories and poems, textbooks on materials testing and organic chemistry, and the love letters of Abelard and Heloise. For each work the claimant and renewal date are given, preserving the legal record of a second copyright term.
11808-u-s-copyright-renewals-1953-july-d:
Renewals filed in the second half of 1953 are listed alphabetically in this Copyright Office volume, under author, issuing body, or title. Cross-references from claimants, joint authors, and variant names are included, and every entry carries the original registration beside the renewal.

Early entries include Achmed Abdullah's magazine story The Godless Man and a Columbia English test, both first registered in 1926. The alphabetical run stretches across books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical pieces, giving a single dated record of which 1920s works their owners chose to keep protected. Deeper in the alphabet come De Witt Eggleston's Auditing Procedure, Lillian Eichler's Well-bred English, Charles W. Eliot's biography edited by William Allan Neilson, and Ethel Cook Eliot's Storey Manor, serialized in Everygirl's.
11810-u-s-copyright-renewals-1954-july-d:
Alphabetical by author, issuing body, or title, this volume records renewal registrations from July to December 1954. Each entry joins an original registration, mostly from 1927, to a renewal number, claimant, and date, with references from joint authors interfiled.

Its opening pages move from a collection of Negro spirituals to Edith Abbott on the great painters and George Abbott's play Broadway, written with Philip Dunning. That spread, from music and art history to the stage, shows how the renewal catalog swept up nearly every kind of published work in a half-year.
11812-u-s-copyright-renewals-1955-july-d:
For the second half of 1955, this Copyright Office register lists renewal registrations alphabetically by author, issuing body, or title. Both the original and the renewal registration appear in each entry, so a reader can see a work's full copyright history at a glance.

Eleanor Hallowell Abbott's stories But Once a Year and Love and the Ladies open the run. Andy Adams's Log of a Cowboy follows in a new illustrated edition, with hymns and cantatas by Carrie B. Adams. The mix of fiction, textbooks, and church music reflects the ordinary breadth of American publishing in 1928, the year most of these works first appeared.
11814-u-s-copyright-renewals-1956-july-d:
Arranged by author or issuing body, with serials by title, this volume covers renewals from July through December 1956. Cross-references from claimants and joint authors are interfiled, and each entry states the original registration and the renewal claim.

Charles G. Abbot's revised book The Sun heads the alphabetical sequence. Later pages include Arthur Adair's Dinners, Long and Short and Eustace Adams's children's story The Runaway Airship. Most entries renew works from 1928 and 1929, a reminder that the catalog's half-year slices track publishing almost exactly twenty-eight years behind. The run also renews Edward Dreiser's Dreiser Looks at Russia and his Moods, Cadenced and Declaimed with symbols by Hugh Gray Lieber, alongside Marquis James's biography of Sam Houston, The Raven. Wanda Gag's Millions of Cats is renewed in the same run.
11816-u-s-copyright-renewals-1957-july-d:
This half-year volume lists renewal registrations from July to December 1957, alphabetically by author or issuing body, or by title for serials and certain other works. Original and renewal details sit together in each entry, with references from claimants and variant names interfiled.

Jane Abbott's novels Beggarman and Merridy Road open the sequence, both first registered in 1930. The run continues through legal digests, French studies, and school texts. For anyone checking whether a work from around 1930 remained in copyright, the volume gives the claimant, date, and renewal number in a single line.
11818-u-s-copyright-renewals-1958-july-d:
Renewals from the second half of 1958 appear here in alphabetical order by author, issuing body, or title for serials. As in the rest of the series, each entry pairs an original registration with its renewal. Cross-references from claimants, editors, and variant forms are woven in.

The volume's value lies in its completeness for the period rather than in any single entry: thousands of books, pamphlets. Periodical contributions, first published around 1930 and 1931, are reduced to one line each. Researchers use such a run to settle ownership questions that no single title's publishing history would answer on its own.
11820-u-s-copyright-renewals-1959-july-d:
Covering July through December 1959, this Copyright Office catalog arranges renewal registrations alphabetically by author or issuing body, or by title for serials and compendia. Information on both the original and the renewal registration appears in every entry, with references from claimants interfiled.

Most of the works renewed here first appeared in the early 1930s. The entries run from fiction and poetry to textbooks, plays, and magazine stories. Taken as a whole, the volume is a legal finding aid: it answers, in compact form, who renewed what, and when, during a single half-year.
11822-u-s-copyright-renewals-1960-july-d:
This volume records renewal registrations made from July to December 1960, in alphabetical order by author, issuing body, or title for serials. Each entry gives the original copyright date and number, the renewal claimant, and the renewal date and number.

The alphabetical run covers the full range of early-1930s publishing, from novels and histories to school books and periodical contributions. Because the catalog states both registrations together, a reader tracing a title need not consult two separate registers to learn whether its copyright was extended and by whom. Midway through the volume come Phyllis Bottome's novel The Advances of Harriet and Marquis James's Andrew Jackson, the Border Captain. Both were renewed by a widow or family claimant in the second half of 1960.
11824-u-s-copyright-renewals-1961-july-d:
Renewals registered in the second half of 1961 fill this alphabetical catalog of books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions. Original and renewal registrations are stated together, and references from renewal claimants, joint authors, and variant names are interfiled.

Works first published in the early 1930s dominate the run. The entries move steadily from A to Z without commentary, each line a small legal fact. That plainness is the point: the volume preserves, in one place, the renewal history of a half-year's worth of American publishing. Further entries include Charles Winfred Douglas's Kyrial with plainsong melodies, Aubrey Douglass's survey of the American school system, Paul Klapper's Teaching of Arithmetic, and Alma Sioux Scarberry's Penthouse Love.
11826-u-s-copyright-renewals-1962-july-d:
For July through December 1962, this Copyright Office volume lists renewal registrations alphabetically by author or issuing body, or by title for serials and certain other works. Each entry carries the original registration and the renewal claim, with claimant references interfiled.

The run covers books, pamphlets, and contributions to periodicals first published in the mid-1930s, and its steady alphabetical order makes any single title easy to find. As a reference work it is deliberately unadorned, offering dates, numbers, and names where a narrative history would offer argument. The 1962 run also carries Robert A. Davis's Psychology of Learning, Tech Davis's Terror at Compass Lake, Annette Kolb's Die Schaukel, and Platt and Munk coloring books such as Jumbo and Kitty and Doggie.
11828-u-s-copyright-renewals-1963-july-d:
This catalog lists renewal registrations from the second half of 1963, arranged alphabetically by author, issuing body, or title for serials. Both registrations appear in each entry, and references from claimants, joint authors, editors, and variant names are interfiled.

The works renewed here mostly date from the mid-1930s, and the entries span fiction, scholarship, textbooks, and magazine pieces without distinction of rank. For copyright research the volume's strength is its uniformity: every title, famous or forgotten, receives the same compact line of dates, numbers, and names. Warwick Deeping's No Hero, This, Charles David Kepner Jr.'s Banana Empire study of economic imperialism. Joseph Kessel's La Passante du Sans-Souci all appear among the 1963 renewals.
11830-u-s-copyright-renewals-1964-july-d:
Renewals from July through December 1964 are recorded here alphabetically by author or issuing body, or by title for serials and certain other works. Original and renewal registrations stand side by side in each entry, with claimant and variant-name references interfiled.

Titles first published in the mid-1930s make up most of the volume, from novels and plays to scientific works and school texts. The catalog does not judge its contents; it preserves the legal facts, so later readers can tell at a glance whether a given work's copyright was renewed and who claimed it.
11832-u-s-copyright-renewals-1965-july-d:
This volume catalogs renewal registrations from the second half of 1965, alphabetically by author or issuing body, or by title for serials and compendia. Each entry states the original registration and the renewal registration, with references from claimants and joint authors interfiled.

Works first published in the late 1930s fill the run. The alphabetical sequence treats a novel, a textbook, and a magazine story with the same brief formula. The result is a dense but navigable record, useful for tracing ownership of mid-century works that remained commercially or scholarly alive.
11834-u-s-copyright-renewals-1966-july-d:
Renewals registered from July to December 1966 appear in this alphabetical catalog of books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions. Arrangement follows author or issuing body, or title for serials, and every entry gives both the original and the renewal registration.

The period covered reaches back to works first published in the late 1930s, and the entries run without narrative or comment. For researchers, that restraint is an asset: dates, registration numbers. Claimant names are stated plainly, making it possible to verify a title's second-term copyright without guesswork. The volume also includes further parts of Craigie and Hulbert's Dictionary of American English on Historical Principles, Carleton Joeckel's Current Issues in Library Administration. Albert Johannsen's Descriptive Petrography of the Igneous Rocks also appears.
11836-u-s-copyright-renewals-1967-july-d:
Renewals from the second half of 1967 are cataloged here alphabetically by author or issuing body, or by title for serials and certain other works. Original and renewal registrations appear together in each entry, with references from claimants, joint authors, and variant names interfiled.

Most entries renew works first published around 1939 and 1940, from novels and plays to textbooks and magazine stories. The volume works best as a finding aid: a researcher can confirm, from a single line, the renewal date, number. Claimant for a title that might otherwise require searching several registers.
11838-u-s-copyright-renewals-1968-july-d:
This alphabetical catalog covers renewal registrations from July through December 1968, for books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions. Arrangement follows author or issuing body, or title for serials, and each entry states the original registration beside the renewal.

Works first published around 1940 and 1941 dominate, and the entries proceed without comment from A to Z. That plain presentation suits the catalog's purpose, which is legal rather than literary: to preserve, in compact form, who renewed a work, under what number, and on what date. Among its entries are D. Dwight Davis and Karl P. Schmidt's Field Book of Snakes of the United States and Canada, with colored plates, and Joseph Henry Jackson's Anybody's Gold, on the story of California's mining towns.
11840-u-s-copyright-renewals-1969-july-d:
Renewals registered in the second half of 1969 fill this alphabetical volume of books, pamphlets, serials, and contributions to periodicals. Each entry pairs an original registration with its renewal, and references from claimants and variant forms of names are interfiled.

The bulk of the titles first appeared around 1941 and 1942, and the catalog treats scholarly works, fiction, and popular writing alike. For anyone verifying the copyright status of a work from those years, the volume offers the essential facts in one place, without the need to chase separate records. The volume treats scholarly works, fiction, and popular writing with the same brief formula throughout.
11842-u-s-copyright-renewals-1970-july-d:
Covering renewals from July to December 1970, this catalog arranges books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions alphabetically by author or issuing body, or by title for serials. Original and renewal registrations are given together, with claimant references interfiled.

Most entries concern works first published around 1942 and 1943, and the volume's alphabetical run makes individual titles straightforward to locate. Like its predecessors, it serves researchers, publishers, and librarians who need a dated, authoritative record of second-term copyright claims. Walt Disney entries stand out in this half-year. They include a paint book and Pedro, the story of a little airplane, beside Edwin Lanham's Rider in the Red Coat from Esquire and a statistics textbook.
11844-u-s-copyright-renewals-1971-july-d:
This volume lists renewal registrations from the second half of 1971, alphabetically by author or issuing body, or by title for serials and certain other works. Each entry gives the original registration and the renewal claim, with references from claimants, joint authors, and variant names interfiled.

Works first published around 1943 and 1944 make up most of the run. The catalog's steady alphabetical order covers fiction, scholarship, and periodical writing without distinction. As a reference tool it answers a narrow but useful question: for a given title, who held the renewed copyright, and when was it recorded.
11846-u-s-copyright-renewals-1972-july-d:
Renewals from July through December 1972 are listed here alphabetically by author or issuing body, or by title for serials and certain other works. Original and renewal registrations stand together in each entry, and claimant references are interfiled throughout.

Most titles first appeared around 1944 and 1945, and the volume covers the same broad ground as its predecessors: books, pamphlets, serials, and magazine contributions. Its alphabetical arrangement and uniform entries make it a practical tool for settling who renewed a mid-1940s work and on what date. Gerhart Eisler's Lesson of Germany, Elliott's quick longhand course, Ernst Lothar's The Door Opens illustrated by Garth Williams. Volume 206 of the Louisiana Reports all appear in the 1972 second-half run.
11848-u-s-copyright-renewals-1973-july-d:
Unlike the alphabetical volumes, this 1973 catalog arranges renewals by registration number, in continuous sequence across all classes, so breaks appear where other classes intervene. It covers renewals registered in the second half of 1973, with original and renewal details in each entry.

Works first published around 1945 and 1946 predominate, and the number order mixes books, films, and periodical pieces in a single run. Readers used to alphabetical lists must search by number here, but the entries carry the same facts: original registration, renewal claimant, and renewal date. Numbered entries here include Lloyd Lewis's columns in the Chicago Sun from March and April 1946, a Siegel and Shuster Superman installment in the New York Post. Jesse Jackson's Call Me Charley, illustrated by Doris Spiegel.
11850-u-s-copyright-renewals-1974-july-d:
This volume arranges renewal registrations from the second half of 1974 by registration number, continuously across classes, with breaks for other types of material. Each entry states the original registration and the renewal claim, including claimant and date.

Titles first published around 1946 and 1947 fill the run, spanning books, pamphlets, and periodical contributions in number order. The arrangement suits a register kept by number rather than by name. It preserves the same legal facts as the alphabetical volumes in a different sequence. Albert Deutsch's PM Daily pieces on mental clinics and state aid for mental health show the run reaching into journalism. Irving Cheyette's BVC band show, with marching instructions for high-school cadets, shows it reaching into school music.
11852-u-s-copyright-renewals-1975-july-d:
Books and pamphlets renewed in the second half of 1975 make up this catalog, arranged by registration number with a number of non-renewal entries noted. Each entry gives the original registration, the renewal claimant, and the renewal date.

Opening entries include a Jessup-Redfield work on law and practice in New York surrogates' courts, first registered in 1947. The run continues through works first published in 1947 and 1948. The volume's number order, rather than alphabetical order, reflects how the Copyright Office filed these renewals, and it remains a compact record of second-term claims.
11854-u-s-copyright-renewals-1976-july-d:
Books and pamphlets renewed in the second half of 1976 appear here in registration-number order, with non-renewal entries noted. Each entry records the original registration, the renewal claimant, and the renewal date.

Early entries include an exhibition of original paintings by Christine Louise Richards and Smith's Bible Dictionary in a revised edition, both first registered in 1948. The run continues through works from 1948 and 1949, giving researchers a numbered sequence for checking second-term copyright claims from those years. Superman installments in the Lowell Sun from September 1948 recur through this numbered run, beside Maurice Bardèche's Nuremberg ou La Terre Promise and volume 1 of Patty's Industrial Hygiene and Toxicology.
11856-u-s-copyright-renewals-1977-july-d:
This final half-year volume in the sequence lists books and pamphlets renewed from July through December 1977, in registration-number order with a few non-renewal entries noted. Each entry states the original registration, the renewal claimant, and the renewal date.

Opening entries include a work on law, totalitarianism, and democracy by Sidney Post Simpson, Julius Stone, and M. Magdalena Schoch, and Cradle Rhymes by Gladys Horn and Rachel Taft Dixon, both first registered in 1949. The catalog closes the alphabetical and numbered runs with the same compact formula used since 1950.
1190-the-jolly-corner:
Henry James tells of Spencer Brydon, an American who returns after decades abroad to his old New York house and grows obsessed with the man he might have been. Night after night he stalks the empty rooms, sure his other self, the hard businessman, haunts them, until the two meet at last.

The tale is a ghost story where the ghost is a life unlived, and James writes it in his late, winding style. The final meeting is both terror and pity. The story stands among his finest short works, and it haunts readers who wonder what their own choices cost.
11915-the-adventures-of-mr-mocker:
Thornton W. Burgess's 1914 animal story, illustrated by Harrison Cady, follows Mr. Mocker, a mockingbird whose talent for imitation throws the Green Meadow into confusion. Sammy Jay grows indignant, then thinks he is going crazy, and stays up all night listening to a voice that sounds like his own.

Peter Rabbit sets out to solve the puzzle, hurrying across the meadows and up the Lone Little Path to the Laughing Brook before sunset. Burgess uses the mockingbird's tricks to teach young readers how birds sound and behave, wrapping natural history in a short, funny mystery about who is really making all that noise.
11945-essays-of-schopenhauer:
Essays of Schopenhauer, translated by Mrs. Rudolf Dircks with an introduction, gathers the German philosopher's shorter writings for English readers. Contents include essays on authorship and style, on noise, on education, on reading and books, and on the emptiness of existence.

Further pieces treat women, thinking for oneself, religion in dialogue form, psychological observations, the metaphysics of love, physiognomy. Suicide, with a short dialogue on the indestructibility of our true being by death. Schopenhauer's voice is sharp, aphoristic, and often contrarian, and the collection shows his philosophy at its most readable, applied to ordinary subjects rather than to systems alone.
11950-preliminary-report-of-the-commissi:
The Preliminary Report of the Commission appointed by the University of Pennsylvania to investigate modern spiritualism is known as the Seybert Commission report. It was issued in accordance with the request of the late Henry Seybert, with a foreword by H. H. Furness Jr. The report, dated 1887 and reissued in 1920, addresses the university's trustees.

Seybert, a believer in spiritualism, left funds for a scientific investigation, and the commission tested mediums, séances, and claimed phenomena under controlled conditions. Its preliminary findings became a landmark in the history of psychical research. They show a university willing to examine popular supernatural claims with the same rigor it applied to other subjects, whatever the result.
11959-a-brief-memoir-with-portions-of-th:
This 1869 memoir preserves the diary, letters, and other remains of Eliza Southall, late of Birmingham, England, wife of William Southall Jr. and daughter of John and Eliza Allen, born at Liskeard on the ninth of the sixth month, 1823. Its epigraph, from Philippians, declares that to live is Christ and to die is gain.

Southall's diary records spiritual struggle in plain Quaker language: seasons when she loses all sense of good for days. Days when things are placed more rightly in her heart. Entries from 1847 show her comforted by small acts that declare which side she is on, making the memoir a quiet record of nineteenth-century religious life rather than a public biography.
11961-the-lords-of-the-wild-a-story-of-t:
Joseph A. Altsheler's 1919 novel The Lords of the Wild returns to his French and Indian War series, with Robert Lennox, Tayoga the young Onondaga warrior, and the hunter David Willet among its characters. The opening chapter, The Blue Bird, finds Lennox kneeling to drink at a forest stream, noticing its silvery color and soft sighing over a pebbly bed.

Lennox, weary and in danger, still has an eye for beauty, and the brook's deep green setting speaks to him of comfort and hope. From that quiet opening the story moves into the old New York border country, where wilderness skill, loyalty. Sudden violence decide the fate of its young heroes.
1204-cabin-fever:
B. M. Bower, a prolific writer of westerns, tells of a gold prospector snowed into a lonely cabin with a stranger, where greed, suspicion, and cabin fever turn two partners against each other. The tale moves from the diggings to the long winter, with claims, lies, and a woman waiting in town.

Bower writes the West with brisk, plain prose and a sure sense of mining life. The novel is short, tense, and full of frontier color. It suits readers who like westerns with a psychological edge and a wintry bite.
12042-the-value-of-a-praying-mother:
Isabel C. Byrum's The Value of a Praying Mother was published by the Gospel Trumpet Company, with a first printing in 1911. Its preface announces its purpose: the book is sent forth as precious seed, with the prayer that it will fall into good soil in many hearts and bring forth a hundredfold.

Byrum writes for parents with natural affection who desire the best for their children and hope that from their home will go forth young people of faith and character. The book argues that a mother's prayers shape a household more deeply than advice or discipline alone, in the plain, earnest style of early twentieth-century evangelical publishing.
12071-the-torch-bearer:
The Torch-Bearer, a suffrage publication by Agnes E. Ryan, reprints material from the Woman's Journal and Suffrage News, a weekly founded in 1870 by Lucy Stone and Henry B. Blackwell and devoted to woman's educational, industrial, legal, and political equality, especially her right of suffrage. Alice Stone Blackwell served as editor-in-chief, with contributing editors including Mary Johnston, Stephen S. Wise, Josephine Peabody, Zona Gale, and Florence Kelley.

The volume's title fits its cause: carrying the torch for votes for women in the years before the Nineteenth Amendment. Its articles, news, and arguments show the suffrage movement's press at work, linking local campaigns to a national demand for equality before the law.
1224-sidney-lanier:
Edwin Mims writes a biography of Sidney Lanier, the Georgia poet, musician, and critic who died young in 1881. Mims follows Lanier from his youth through the Civil War, his work as a flautist, and his final years at Johns Hopkins. Mims, a professor at Vanderbilt, wrote Lanier's life from letters and family papers.

The life sets Lanier's poems beside his theory of verse as music, and his struggle with illness and poverty. Mims gives a sympathetic, readable life of a poet whose promise outran his years. Lanier's years at Johns Hopkins, teaching English, came just before his early death.
12248-the-king-s-cup-bearer:
Mrs. O. F. Walton wrote The King Cup-Bearer as a retelling of Nehemiah story for young readers, with chapters named for scenes in the Bible. Walton, known for Christie Old Organ, aimed to make scripture vivid for children.

The book opens in the city of lilies, at the king table, and follows Nehemiah from cup-bearer in a Persian court to builder of Jerusalem walls. Chapters on the sword and the trowel, the eighty-four seals, brave volunteers, and the holy city stress work, prayer, and courage under opposition. Walton adds simple lessons to each episode, in the manner of Victorian Sunday reading. The story endures as a clear, earnest Bible tale for the young.
12260-jonas-on-a-farm-in-winter:
Jonas on a Farm in Winter belongs to Jacob Abbott popular Jonas books for children, written in the mid-nineteenth century to teach industry and care through story. Jonas, a farm boy, works through the cold months with his younger companion Josey.

Episodes follow sled loads of rafters gathered in deep new snow. Chores must be done before sundown, and Jonas insists on thorough work. He wades about in the snow to be sure no rafter is left behind, though Josey urges haste. Abbott moral is plain and practical: do work completely, even when cold and dusk press. The book gives a detailed, if idealized, picture of winter farm labor for young readers of its day.
1229-select-poems-of-sidney-lanier:
Morgan Callaway edits a selection of Sidney Lanier's poems, choosing the lyrics that best show the Georgia poet's musical gift. Lanier believed poetry should be heard as song, and his rhythms carry that belief. Callaway, a scholar of Lanier, chose poems that show the poet's range.

The selection gathers nature poems, Southern lyrics, and experiments in sound, without the bulk of a complete works. Readers who want Lanier in brief will find here a sound introduction, edited with care. The selection, shorter than a complete works, suits readers who want Lanier's best first.
12346-a-roman-singer:
F. Marion Crawford published A Roman Singer in 1909, a novel narrated by Cornelio Grandi, a Roman professor of philosophy turned scribbler. Grandi tells his own story first: once rich, driven to sell his patrimony, a dear castello in the Sabines with corn land, vineyards, and olives.

The plot follows Nino, a young singer, and the intrigues around him, with a mid-book card naming Baron Ahasuerus Benoni, a man of unearthly freshness whom Nino described. Crawford writes with Roman local color, music, and old-family pride. The novel mixes love, ambition, and the decline of an ancient house. It shows Crawford at his most atmospheric, using Rome itself as a character.
12366-the-cost-of-shelter:
Ellen H. Richards, instructor in sanitary chemistry at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, published The Cost of Shelter in 1905. Richards, a founder of home economics, asks what a house truly costs a family in money, health, and life.

The book opens with reasons households exist: protection, child rearing, convenience, companionship, and independence. Later passages ask what a man with limited income can do when millionaires shirk taxes elsewhere. They also ask whether he has a moral right to bring unhappiness to wife and children by marrying poor. Richards treats housing as a social problem, not a private luxury. The book is an early work of domestic science with a reforming edge.
12403-fenwick-s-career:
Mrs. Humphry Ward's 1910 novel follows an artist, Fenwick, whose career gives the book its title. A prefatory word defends the artist's right to gather material from real life, so long as he does not steal another artist's minted phrases or conceptions. Ward insists that recorded life and observed life are both fair matter for story.

That principle shapes the novel that follows, in which artistic ambition meets love, reputation and the claims of other people. Fenwick's work, friendships and household decisions test what an artist owes to art and to those around him. Ward writes in her serious, moral manner, making a painter's life a study of conscience as well as of talent.
12406-kepler:
Walter W. Bryant of the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, wrote Kepler in 1920 for the Pioneers of Progress series, Men of Science, edited by S. Chapman. Bryant traces astronomy before Kepler, his early life, Tycho Brahe, their partnership, Kepler laws, and closing years.

The book explains why Kepler reforms mattered: he broke with circular orbits and found ellipses, areas, and periods that fit Tycho data. A mid-book passage follows Kepler off at a tangent on refraction, trying sets of ideas that reduced to absurdity before he found his laws. Bryant writes clearly for general readers, with dates, bibliography, and glossary. The biography is a compact introduction to the man who made modern astronomy possible.
1258-ten-years-later:
Alexandre Dumas carries his musketeers into the 1660s in this volume of the great cycle. D'Artagnan serves a young Louis XIV, Athos watches his son Raoul love and lose, and the court of the Sun King gleams with intrigue. The tale runs from the fall of Fouquet toward the mystery of the man in the iron mask.

The musketeers, older and graver now, face a France where politics has replaced swordplay, and loyalty costs more than ever. Dumas writes at his usual gallop, with duels, escapes, and court plots. The book is the hinge of the cycle, and it rewards readers who have ridden with the four friends.
12677-personality-plus-some-experiences-:
Edna Ferber's 1914 stories follow Emma McChesney, a travelling saleswoman, and her son Jock as he starts work in business. Emma's wit, grit, and salesman's charm have carried her far; now Jock must find his own way in offices, shops, and showrooms. Five linked tales track his blunders, boasts, and slow growth.

Ferber's theme is plain: charm helps, but only steady work and honest dealing make a career last. Jock learns that lesson through lost sales, sharp bosses, and his mother's frank advice. The stories are funny and warm, with a keen eye for American work life just before the First World War.
1273-the-autobiography-of-a-slander:
Edna Lyall lets a slander tell its own life story: born as a whisper, nursed by gossip, and grown into a lie that ruins a good name. The novel follows the slander from mouth to mouth, showing how careless talk, envy, and malice feed it, and how hard it is to kill once loose.

Lyall writes with a moralist's warmth and a novelist's eye for parish life. The device is bold and the lesson is plain: words wound like deeds. The book was a bestseller in its day, and it still speaks to any age of gossip and rumor.
1274-martin-hyde-the-duke-s-messenger:
John Masefield, later Poet Laureate, tells of Martin Hyde, a boy in the days of the Duke of Monmouth's rebellion. Martin becomes a messenger for the duke and rides through plots, pursuits, and battles in the west of England. The tale moves from inns to battlefields with a boy's-book pace.

Masefield writes the seventeenth century with color and a sailor's sense of action. Martin's courage and loyalty carry him through danger. The book suits young readers who like historical adventure and the romance of a lost cause. Masefield's boy hero earns his place among classic adventure tales.
12772-cowper:
Goldwin Smith's 1880 life of William Cowper places the poet between Alexander Pope and the Romantics who followed him. It follows Cowper from a troubled youth through Huntingdon and Olney, his friendships with the Unwin family and John Newton, and his bouts of deep religious gloom. Poetry, letters, and translation each get close attention.

Smith argues that Cowper helped pull English verse back toward nature and plain feeling, and that his faith shaped a new, tender moral voice. The Task and the shorter poems anchor the account, with the famous letters showing his humour and pain side by side. The book is a compact, humane guide to a poet both gentle and tormented.
12784-the-prose-works-of-jonathan-swift-:
Edited by Temple Scott, this sixth volume of Swift's prose works gathers the Drapier's Letters, Swift's famous Irish pamphlets. Writing as M. B. Drapier, Swift attacked William Wood's patent to coin copper money for Ireland, warning that debased halfpence would drain the kingdom's silver and gold. Portraits and facsimiles of Wood's coinage illustrate the edition.

Swift compares Wood's patent with earlier coinage patents under Charles II and James II, noting that older patentees had to take their coin back for gold or silver. The letters blend law, economics, and fierce irony. The volume remains essential for readers of Swift and of Irish history.
12832-said-the-observer:
Louis J. Stellmann's Said the Observer, published in San Francisco in 1903, gathers humorous city sketches under a watchful narrator. Dedicated to his mother on her fiftieth birthday, with verses on fifty years of gladness and tears, it turns to street life, manners, and human folly. Illustrations by Burnham and Forsythe add to the fun.

A piece on horse sense argues that the average horse, meeting another horse, swerves right without fuss, while men meeting in halls and doorways block each other with side-steps. Stellmann's observer loves such small, sharp contrasts. The book offers light, period humour from early San Francisco.
12863-campaign-of-the-indus-in-a-series-:
Campaign of the Indus, published in 1840 with an introduction by A. H. Holdsworth, prints letters from his son, an officer of the Bombay division. The army's march into Central Asia, the first European force there since Alexander, gives the letters their historic frame. Holdsworth printed only a few copies for friends, keeping the familiar family tone.

Marching detail fills the pages: strayed horses and camels seized by provost-marshals, exorbitant prices for replacements, and kit lost with health after. The letters honour British and Indian soldiers' patience under hardship. The book serves readers of the First Afghan War who want a young officer's own voice.
12891-running-water:
A. E. W. Mason's 1907 novel Running Water opens on the Geneva express leaving Paris by night, bound for Alpine country. Sylvia Thesiger, her mother, and a cast of climbers, guides, and card players move through hotels, passes, and ice slopes, with a house of running water at the story's heart. Fathers, secrets, and old passions complicate the climb.

A card game scene, where Barstow fetches two new packs from a landlord whose guests were put off by a death, shows Mason's social eye. The Brenva ridge and a night on an ice slope supply the thrills. The novel blends romance, mountain adventure, and drawing-room intrigue.
12919-a-texas-matchmaker:
Andy Adams wrote A Texas Matchmaker in 1904 about life on the Las Palomas ranch under Lance Lovelace. The narrator, not yet of age when hired, follows ranch years through Christmas, pigeon hunts, San Jacinto Day, drought, hide hunting, and Indian scares. Matchmaking itself waits until late in the book, after seasons of work.

Ranch labour fills the pages: mule teams ploughing and hauling rock, a water wagon travelling ten miles for camp and stock, and a tank built to raise cattle capacity. Letters from Frances Vaux and visits from Esther add romance. Adams writes ranch life with the authority of a man who lived it.
12935-the-song-of-the-blood-red-flower:
Johannes Linnankoski's Song of the Blood-Red Flower, first published in Finnish and in English in 1920, follows a young Finnish woodsman through love, work, and wandering. Chapters named for flowers and places, from Fairy of the Forest to Rapids, Camp-Fire, and Homecoming, trace his restless youth. The setting sun on wooded slopes opens the tale in lush prose.

A log-driving scene shows the hero's world: rivals praised on the bank, a log striking a rock, a red jacket vanishing in foam, then rising to swim on. Linnankoski blends nature poetry with a moral tale of passion and return. The novel is a classic of Finnish literature in translation.
12943-the-hilltop-boys-on-the-river:
Cyril Burleigh's Hilltop Boys on the River follows Jack and Dick as they take to the water in a new motor-boat. Jack refuses Dick's offer to buy him one, insisting he will have a boat of his own, though Dick's gilt-edged craft cost far more. A gold watch mystery, with rival claimants and a detective, soon tangles their summer.

A courtroom-style scene has a doctor defending a boy against a charge of theft, arguing that suspicion does him rank injustice. Prizes, poems, and river fun fill the later chapters. The book offers light schoolboy adventure with a detective thread.
12959-newton-forster:
Captain Frederick Marryat's Newton Forster, or the Merchant Service, first appeared in the Metropolitan Magazine in 1832. The novel follows a young merchant seaman through impressment, wreck, and service, in the vigorous style that invited comparison with Smollett. Jeffrey of the Edinburgh Review wrote warmly to Marryat's wife on reading it.

A mid-book scene finds Newton, wrecked and unarmed, signalling to Black sailors who crawl from a fore-scuttle with weapons, led by a grizzled chief. Marryat treats impressment with anger and humour alike. The novel remains a lively classic of early sea fiction.
12973-personal-recollections-of-pardee-b:
Personal Recollections of Pardee Butler, published at Cincinnati in 1889, gathers the life of a Kansas preacher and free-state man. His daughter Rosetta B. Hastings adds her own memories, since Butler kept no journal, seldom reported his meetings, and destroyed most of his old letters. Later chapters come from Elders John Boggs and J. B. McCleery, men who knew him well.

Border scenes give the book its color, as riders gallop into Atchison crying that Lane is coming, only to learn the alarm was a stray cow. Butler's preaching, baptisms, and stand for a free Kansas emerge through family memory and friends' witness rather than a formal life.
12977-black-beetles-in-amber:
Black Beetles in Amber, by Ambrose Bierce in 1892, is a book of satirical verse and short prose aimed at the public men of his day. Its contents list reads like a rogues' gallery, with pieces on statesmen, a lifted finger, a commuted sentence, Dennis Kearney, and Black Bart. Bierce spares neither politicians, clergy, nor the press.

One dialect poem shows an editor boasting that no one shapes his paper's course, while the amber of the title turns out to be blood from priestly wounds. The bite, the wordplay, and the sheer malice make the book a sharp sample of Bierce at his most savage.
13010-frank-mildmay-or-the-naval-officer:
Captain Frederick Marryat's Frank Mildmay, or the Naval Officer, was his first novel, and its preface begs indulgence for a first attempt's faults. The editors decline to review their own work, leaving praise or blame to literary friends, and note that reviewing one's own books is usually done sub rosa. Frank's naval career, loves, and scrapes follow.

A shore-leave scene shows the service's grip: a captain's note orders Keep that damned young scamp, Mildmay, on board, and a sergeant's charge would break orders just as much. Letters to Eugenia pass easily, but Frank stays aboard. The novel remains a lively early sea tale.
13047-daniel-webster:
Daniel Webster, by Henry Cabot Lodge in the American Statesmen series, follows the great orator from childhood to his last years. Lodge, working from printed sources alone, traces Webster's New Hampshire youth, his law practice, the Dartmouth College case, and his return to Congress. The tariff of 1828, the reply to Hayne, the fight with Jackson, and the rise of the Whigs follow.

Later chapters cover his time as secretary of state, the Ashburton Treaty, and the Seventh of March speech. A debate on the Cumberland road shows his creed, that Congress should act for all states united, not balance one region against another. The life remains a classic study of American statesmanship.
13049-reveries-of-a-schoolmaster:
Reveries of a Schoolmaster, by Francis B. Pearson, Ohio's state superintendent of public instruction, appeared in 1917. Pearson, author of books on the teacher and the high school, writes short chapters with titles like Brown, Balkings, Lanterns, Beefsteak, Freedom, and Rabbit Pedagogy. Each opens in medias res, straight at the heart of the matter, a phrase he borrows with pleasure from Horace.

A chapter on Brown turns on knowing the truth, as Pearson, lost among drug-store labels he cannot read, envies the clerk's freedom. The book charms teachers by tying small school scenes to large ideas about truth, habit, and the work of teaching.
13058-the-teeth-of-the-tiger:
Maurice Leblanc's 1914 adventure novel brings back Arsène Lupin, here under the name Don Luis Perenna, in a case of murder, inheritance, and terror. Chapters run from a dead man and a doomed man to a clouded turquoise, an iron curtain, and a devil's post-office. The prefect of police opens the tale, and Lupin soon takes the hunt in hand.

Perenna stalks a suspect through the Bois de Boulogne at dusk, urges his man Mazeroux to seize him by the throat, and races to free Marie Fauville and Sauverand from prison. Clues pile up around a hundred-million inheritance and a hater who works in secret. The novel is pure Lupin: fast, cunning, and full of disguise, chase, and last-minute rescue.
13139-lives-of-john-donne-henry-wotton-r:
Volume two of Izaak Walton's Lives, based on John Major's 1825 edition from a copy corrected by Walton's own pen, gives the lives of Richard Hooker, George Herbert, and Robert Sanderson. Austin Dobson read the text and added notes. Walton, the angler and biographer, writes with affection for churchmen he knew or admired.

Hooker's life opens with praise for his learned books on ecclesiastical polity. Herbert, on his deathbed, meditates angels and their blessed order, and wishes earth could share heaven's peace. He tells his wife and nieces he has passed a conflict with his last enemy and overcome by his Master's merits. Walton's lives are gentle, pious, and still read as classics of English biography.
13142-self-development-and-the-way-to-po:
L. W. Rogers's 1922 booklet Self-Development and the Way to Power, priced at twenty-five cents, claims happiness is man's natural right and suffering comes only from ignorance. Rogers opens with a motto: we may be suffering slaves of nature or happy masters of her laws. Wisdom, he says, ends suffering and brings unshadowed joy.

Rogers warns there is no magic rule to turn an ignoramus wise at once, though scores of incarnations may be needed for the full work. Will grows by desire and effort, even when a man rises only because his livelihood depends on it. The booklet is short, confident New Thought, promising power through cooperation with nature's forward push.
13155-james-fenimore-cooper:
Mary E. Phillips's 1913 life of James Fenimore Cooper, dedicated to the young of all ages from ten to ten times ten, follows the novelist from Burlington, New Jersey, to Europe and back. Illustrations show his birthplace, the Fenimore box, the Susquehanna, and Chingachgook on the trail. Phillips writes for young readers, but she does not skip Cooper's quarrels and travels.

She shows young Cooper at twenty-five, driving, riding, rowing, and playing the flute, with his mother delighting in flowers at Otsego Hall. Later, in Rome, a line in The Water Witch, that Rome survives only in fallen temples, gave offense and barred its printing there. The life is a friendly, well-illustrated introduction to the author of the Leatherstocking Tales.
13184-narrative-and-lyric-poems-first-se:
O. J. Stevenson, professor of English at Ontario Agricultural College, edited Narrative and Lyric Poems, first series, for lower schools in Toronto in 1912. Contents run from Moore's Meeting of the Waters and Scott's Jock o' Hazeldean to Macaulay's Horatius, Wordsworth's Solitary Reaper, and Harte's Dickens in Camp. Notes aid classroom reading.

Macaulay's Horatius marches Latian towns to war, with Mamilius in a red-gold helmet leading Aricia, Cora, and Tusculum. A later poem shows pilgrims marching north to Plymouth, giants in the mist, believing in God and the Bible. The anthology is a schoolbook of its time, chosen for story, music, and moral force in verse.
13196-quiet-talks-on-prayer:
S. D. Gordon's 1904 Quiet Talks on Prayer, published by Fleming H. Revell, treats prayer as the greatest outlet of power and the deciding factor in a spirit conflict. Gordon divides his talks into the meaning of prayer, its hindrances, how to pray, and Jesus' habits of prayer. His tone is plain, earnest, and made for quiet reading.

Gordon holds that God's kingdom and another kingdom cannot stand together, any more than Charles II and Cromwell could share London. Thy kingdom come, he says, means the other kingdom go, and the other prince go. A later tale shows Moody's meetings, where crowds rose in clumps and fifties to profess faith. The book is a devotional classic of its era, simple and direct.
13246-the-conqueror-being-the-true-and-r:
Gertrude Franklin Atherton's 1902 novel The Conqueror retells the life of Alexander Hamilton as true and romantic story. Atherton quotes Talleyrand, who ranked Napoleon, Fox, and Hamilton as the three great men of the age, and gave Hamilton first place. Her books run from Rachael Levine and Hamilton's West Indian youth to the little lion, Alexander the Great, and the last battle of the giants.

Hamilton vows his pledge with solemn humor, and friends warn him not to make it too strong. Later, Washington's levee is described in full dress: black velvet, diamond knee-buckles, hair in a bag, and a sword in a green scabbard. Atherton's Hamilton is brilliant, proud, and doomed, a founder cast as a romantic hero.
13290-martin-rattler:
R. M. Ballantyne's 1858 Martin Rattler follows a boy his aunt, Mrs. Dorothy Grumbit of Ashford, calls the bane of her existence and the torment of her life. Villagers agree with her, yet smile cheerfully on the child and greet him heartily as if he were the best boy in the place. Ballantyne writes boys' adventure with moral warmth.

Later, a hermit tells Barney how vampire bats killed two cows and a young horse, then applies herb poultices to Martin's bleeding toe and bandages it. The travelers then wind for many days through the Gapo, afloat on Amazon waters, creeping through small streams, lakes, and swamps, with a monkey riding dog-back like a limpet. The book is a classic tale of South American adventure.
1334-paul-kelver:
Jerome K. Jerome's long novel follows Paul Kelver from a drab East End London childhood into youth and adult life. As a boy he meets a cast of odd, kind, and severe grown-ups. Among them is the grave man in grey who shapes his early years, and he learns hard lessons about work, pride, and love.

Later books of the novel carry Paul through solitude, strange company, and a slow search for his own road, with a princess of golden locks haunting his hopes. The tale blends humour with sober feeling, and its chapter titles read like signposts on one young man's road to a settled self.
13487-the-ideal-bartender:
Tom Bullock of the St. Louis Country Club sets down the art of the bartender in 1917, after a quarter century of mixing, testing, and collecting recipes. He dedicates the book to those who enjoy snug club rooms and want to prepare good drinks for themselves, calling bartending an art that borders on magic.

Recipes fill the pages in working order: mint muddled for a julep, brandy punch over shaved ice, fruit shrubs bottled with brandy, and cocktails such as the Deronda. A St. Louis Post-Dispatch editorial on Colonel Roosevelt's julep admission opens the book. Bullock writes with pride in craft, measurements, and the club-room manners of his time.
13514-tales-of-a-traveller:
Washington Irving's Tales of a Traveller divides into four parts: strange stories by a nervous gentleman, Buckthorne and his friends, the Italian banditti, and a final miscellany. A hunting dinner, an uncle, an aunt, a bold dragoon, a German student, a mysterious picture, and a young Italian open the book.

Buckthorne, a young man of great expectations, dreams of Paternoster Row, where printers' devils will repeat his name and Amen Corner echo it back. At Terracina, a Roman surgeon, poet by choice and improvisatore by gift, tells an Englishman about banditti with fluency and pleasure. Irving mixes ghost story, literary satire, and Italian adventure with the ease of a traveller telling tales after dinner.
13542-left-tackle-thayer:
Ralph Henry Barbour's 1915 school story Left Tackle Thayer follows Clint and his friends at Brimfield through football, mystery, and a broken fiddle. Chapters run from a new boy and an old one, Captain Innes receives, and Amy airs his views, to a runaway wheel, a mysterious auto, buried treasure, and Brimfield meets defeat.

A small man winks across a room as Mike tells of a safe blown and nearly a thousand dollars' worth of stuff taken. With an automobile seen near the Baptist church at three in the morning without lights. Penny finds a violin out of its case and struck, perhaps deliberately, over a table corner. Barbour mixes gridiron action with schoolboy detection in his usual brisk style.
13561-browning-as-a-philosophical-and-re:
Henry Jones, professor of philosophy at Glasgow, reads Robert Browning as a philosophical and religious teacher. Chapters take up the need for a philosophy of life, Browning's place in English poetry, his optimism. Its clash with ethics, his treatment of love, his idealism, his solution of evil, and the failure of knowledge.

Jones stresses Browning's interest in man as a moral agent, quoting the Sordello preface: his stress lay on incidents in the development of a soul, little else worth study. Evolution, in Jones's reading, gathers all being into one self-centred totality, with God immanent in all things, first in potency though last in time. The book makes Browning a thinker for readers who want poetry with a system.
13651-alphabetical-catalogue-of-books-in:
Chatto and Windus, a London publisher, issued this trade catalogue in September 1905. It lists fiction and general books in alphabetical order by author and title. Each entry gives format, price, and a short note on contents. Popular novels sit beside drama guides, travel books, and works of history.

Browsing it reveals what a large Edwardian firm thought readers would buy. Cheap reprints appear next to new novels, and series titles cluster under familiar names. Prices range from sixpenny editions to larger fine-paper volumes. For book historians, the list is a snapshot of taste, marketing, and publishing practice. For general readers, it is a guide to forgotten titles worth hunting down.
13730-the-amateur-poacher:
Richard Jefferies wrote this memoir of boyhood poaching in the Wiltshire countryside. It opens with an old flintlock gun kept in a garret beside a stuffed fox. Jefferies recalls pheasant stalking, matchlock against breech-loader, and nights spent watching game. Country boys, keepers, and farmers people the tales.

The book is less a manual than a record of feeling for fields, woods, and seasons. Jefferies notes the east wind, leaf colour, and the habits of birds with close care. Poaching appears as daring and mischief, not crime for gain. His prose loves nature in all its detail. Readers of country writing will find here an early classic of the genre.
13782-lady-rose-s-daughter:
Mrs. Humphry Ward published Lady Rose's Daughter in 1903, with illustrations by Howard Chandler Christy. Julie Le Breton, daughter of the late Lady Rose, enters London society under Lady Henry's wing. Sir Wilfrid, Mr. Montresor, and other suitors watch her with interest. Julie listens, charms, and hides a past she fears will condemn her.

Ward studies reputation, class, and the double standard for women. Julie must choose between a brilliant marriage and an honest life. Lady Henry listens eagerly to gossip while guarding her charge. The novel moves through drawing rooms, the Foreign Office, and country houses. It remains one of Ward's most readable social novels.
13853-new-national-first-reader:
Charles J. Barnes, with Harlan H. Ballard and S. Proctor Thayer, wrote this first reader in 1888. It teaches beginners by the word method, holding that words stand for things and actions, while bare letters mean little to a child. Short lessons introduce new words with pictures and simple sentences. Counting rhymes and animal lines make early reading fun.

Lessons progress from one dog and two cats to longer sentences about dolls, hats, and home life. Each lesson lists new words before the reading passage. The American Book Company published the volume for schools across the country. The reader shows late Victorian ideas about teaching. It also preserves charming period illustrations and rhymes.
1387-mother:
Owen Wister tells a short story through Richard Field, a handsome young man. When his turn comes to tell a tale, he offers not invention but a page of truth from his own life, about his mother. The story follows a son's memory of love, pride, and loss.

Wister writes the tale with warmth and restraint, and its frame gives it the feel of a story told among friends. The piece, first printed anonymously in a shared volume, stands as a small gem of his art. It suits readers who like short fiction with feeling.
13879-the-death-of-balder:
Johannes Ewald wrote this Danish tragedy in 1773, and George Borrow translated it in 1889. The play tells the Norse myth of Balder, god of light, whose death brings grief to gods and men. Nanna mourns him, while Loke, in the shape of an old woman, refuses pity. Borrow's edition was limited to two hundred and fifty copies.

A preface praises Ewald's works in Denmark, ranking this tragedy with his opera The Fishermen. Borrow stresses fidelity to the Danish original. The verse moves between lament, taunt, and fate. Readers of Norse myth and Romantic drama will find it striking. The play also shows Borrow's skill beyond his travel books.
13898-don-strong-patrol-leader:
William Heyliger wrote Don Strong, Patrol Leader in 1918 as a Boy Scout story. Don leads the Wolf Patrol, elected by his fellows at the start. Chapters follow a first clash, Danger Mountain, a plea on the road, and a fight in the woods. Tim stands by Don, while rivals test his leadership. James E. West, Chief Scout Executive, fronts the book.

Scouts learn knots, hikes, and fair play through action, not lectures. A baseball scene opens the tale, with scouts halting under a maple after a hike. Don learns that staying in the lead counts more than gaining it. The story stresses loyalty, courage, and teamwork. It suits young readers and fans of early Scout fiction.
13937-the-mysterious-rider:
Zane Grey published The Mysterious Rider in 1921, a Western novel of ranch rivalry and love. A round-up shows a loss of one hundred head of stock, and rancher Belllounds roars at the news. Columbine, his daughter, watches a cowboy ride toward her while thoughts whirl. A club-footed cowboy named Moore and a suitor called Buster Jack complicate her choices.

Wade, the mysterious rider, rides into a feud over cattle, land, and honour. Grey fills the tale with round-ups, rides, and desert colour. Columbine must judge men by deeds, not by talk. The novel follows Grey's popular formula with pace and feeling. Western fans will recognise his best-known strengths here.
14014-dangers-on-the-ice-off-the-coast-o:
