A registered letter and a man from Grunau who must explain his connection with John Siders give Muller his next case. Muller, the modest Austrian detective, listens to the engineer's story and weighs it against the paper trail.

The novel follows Muller's method: let the witness talk, note the small slip, and follow the letter to its sender. Readers who have met Muller in the lamp and diary cases will recognize the same quiet procedure. The book stands alone as well, a compact mystery in which a postal form becomes the hinge of a crime.
18342-the-answer:
H. Beam Piper wrote this short story for Fantastic Universe Science Fiction in December 1959. It opens with Lee Richardson waking from a vivid dream as a screen door snaps. In the dream he sees a slim woman with graying blonde hair. She plays with a little dachshund among new-fallen leaves on a lawn. He strains to hold the picture before it fades.

Alexis Pitov wakes him, speaking German instead of Spanish as the two men always do between themselves. A countdown stands at minus three hours, and Pitov has phoned the launching site for a jeep. The story thus joins a private dream to a public launch, and asks what answer a man finds when his past and his mission meet at the same hour.
1837-the-prince-and-the-pauper:
Edward, Prince of Wales, and Tom Canty, a pauper boy, change clothes in Tudor London, and each must survive in the other's world. The prince and the pauper swap clothes and swap lives, and each must then get by in the other's world.

The prince learns hunger, beatings, and the cruelty of the law, while Tom learns the weight of the Great Seal and the loneliness of a throne. Twain writes the swap as both adventure and protest. The book's famous scenes — the crowd crying 'tis another prince in disguise, the horse-pond, the coronation — have kept it a children's classic with a sharp edge.
18394-cheerfulness-as-a-life-power:
Orison Swett Marden, author of Pushing to the Front and editor of Success, published this booklet in 1899 with Thomas Y. Crowell of New York. Marden wrote against the soul-consuming, friction-wearing hurry of a grasping, competing age. Cheerfulness, he says, has a lubricating power: it lengthens the life of human machinery, as oil lengthens the life of inert machinery.

The book urges readers not to fret all week and hope to make it up on Sunday or a holiday, but to enjoy each day as they go. It is not mirth alone, Marden says, but a habit: pleasant words, a sunny side, and a little time each day for others. Readers get a classic of American self-help, short and direct, on keeping temper and spirits in a hard-working world.
18434-a-melody-in-silver:
Keene Abbott published this short-story volume with Houghton Mifflin in 1911, after an April release from the Riverside Press in Cambridge. Fourteen stories fill its pages, each named in the contents, from The Lost Cause to Sky Blossoms.

The opening tale follows a boy named David, who suspects his mother thinks him a good little boy and his friend Mitchell a bad one. Other stories carry titles of guilt, loss, and light, and the book reads as a set of quiet, gentle American tales about children, faults, and small acts of grace.
1844-the-scholemaster:
Tudor schoolboys were beaten into Latin, and this treatise argues they would learn faster by praise, patience, and double translation. Ascham argues for learning by double translation — turning a passage into English and back again. And against beating boys into study, holding that praise and patience teach faster than fear.

The book also gives Ascham's famous account of court life, with its four ways to win grace: to laugh, to lie, to flatter, and to face. It remains a landmark in the history of education, and a window into Elizabethan England, where a schoolmaster to a princess could write about teaching as a moral art.
18445-bohemians-of-the-latin-quarter:
Henry Murger wrote this book of Paris bohemian life, first published in 1851, here in the 1888 Vizetelly edition in London. It became the source of two operas called La Bohème, one by Puccini in 1896 and one by Leoncavallo in 1897.

The opening chapter tells how the bohemian club was formed, starting on the morning of April 8, when painter and musician Alexander Schaunard wakes to a cock's crow. The book follows young artists in the Latin Quarter through poverty, friendship, love, and daily work, giving the full life that later operas made famous.
18478-john-ward-preacher:
Margaret Deland wrote this novel, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, with copyright in 1888 by Houghton, Mifflin. Deland, author of The Old Garden, dedicated the book to Lorin Deland, and its epigraph from Omar Khayyám sends the soul through the invisible to spell some letter of the after-life.

The story opens on the evening before Helen Jeffrey's wedding day, when the household at the rectory comes out into the garden, full of suppressed excitement. Dr. Howe smiles at his niece as the family breathes the garden air, and the novel goes on to weigh faith, doubt, and marriage through the life of its preacher.
1848-montezuma-s-daughter:
H. Rider Haggard tells this tale through Thomas Wingfield, an Englishman who sails to the New World and falls in love with the daughter of Montezuma. The chapters follow his parentage, the coming of the Spaniard, his oath, and his farewell to his sweetheart, as gold and conquest reorder every bond around him.

Wingfield's love must survive the fall of an empire. On one day, great is the power of gold and there is no more talk of her marrying any man except himself. On the next, empires and armies decide otherwise. Haggard writes the conquest of Mexico as romance and tragedy together, and the novel's sweep — from England to Tenochtitlan — carries the reader with it.
18480-boulogne-sur-mer:
Rev. William Canon Fleming, rector of St. Mary's, Moorfields, London, wrote this history of Boulogne-sur-Mer as St. Patrick's native town, published by R. and T. Washbourne in London and Benziger Brothers in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago in 1907. The book carries a nihil obstat and imprimatur, and is dedicated to Bishop Patrick Fenton.

Fleming opens with the many bewildering and contradictory theories about St. Patrick's native country, found in books, pamphlets, and reviews. The frontispiece marks the ruins of fortifications built round Caligula's tower by Henry VIII, and the book argues the case for Boulogne as the saint's home town.
18496-big-brother:
Annie Fellows-Johnston wrote this children's story in the Cosy Corner Series, published by Joseph Knight in Boston in 1894, with copyright in 1893. The illustrations list a barefoot girl in a sunbonnet, a little white cottage in New Jersey, and a boy named Robin who follows his brother everywhere.

The story follows a big brother and the younger children who look up to him. Small home adventures follow: a black dancing bear put to bed, and a ball of yarn rolled after a white kitten. Scraps of history overheard from Mrs. Estel fill the rest. It is a warm tale of family care, told for young readers who know what a big brother means.
18538-i-married-a-ranger:
Dama Margaret Smith, known as Mrs. White Mountain, published this memoir with Stanford University Press in 1930. It tells how she came to the Grand Canyon in 1921, when no woman had yet held a park clerk post there, and became the first woman government worker at the Canyon. She later married a ranger, and the book follows their pioneer life in the park.

Chapters range from Navajo land and a Grand Canyon Christmas to a badger fight, floods, dynamite work, and visits from famous guests. Park official Arno Cammerer praises the book in a foreword for its humor and grit. Readers get a lively, personal view of early national park life.
18603-what-social-classes-owe-to-each-ot:
William Graham Sumner first published this short work in 1883, at a time when Americans argued over rich and poor, aid, and reform. He starts from a puzzle: people deny that America has classes, yet talk daily of the poor, the weak, and the workers as fixed groups. His chapters then test slogans about wealth, poverty, and duty one by one.

Sumner defends self-help, warns against plans that take from one person to aid another, and points to the forgotten man who pays the cost of such plans. The closing chapters urge plain dealing and minding one's own business. The book is still read as a sharp statement of laissez-faire views.
18615-hugh-memoirs-of-a-brother:
Arthur Christopher Benson wrote this memoir of his brother Robert Hugh Benson, printed at New York in 1916. It traces Robert from childhood and Eton through Cambridge, work at Llandaff, the Eton Mission in Hackney, and the Mirfield community. The heart of the book is his break with Anglican life and his reception into the Catholic Church at Rome.

Later chapters cover his writing life, his failing health, his last illness, and his burial, closing with notes on his temper and gifts. Benson writes as a loving brother, not a distant biographer. The memoir gives a close view of a gifted priest and writer of the early 1900s.
18677-the-ghost-of-jerry-bundler:
W. W. Jacobs and Charles Rock adapted this play from Jacobs's story Jerry Bundler, published by Samuel French at New York and London in 1908, after a Haymarket Theatre run opening September 9, 1902. The cast lists Hirst, Penfold, Malcolm, Somers, Beldon, Dr. Leek, and George the waiter, with Penfold, Malcolm, and Beldon drawn as three types of commercial traveler. Cyril Maude led the Haymarket company.

French's edition warns that reading the book gives no right to perform it, with amateur royalty set at five dollars a show and programs required to credit the arrangement. The play text itself offers a compact ghost tale for the stage. The edition is a neat relic of Edwardian theatre business.
18757-prince-henry-the-navigator-the-her:
C. Raymond Beazley, fellow of Merton College, Oxford, wrote this life of Prince Henry the Navigator for Putnam's Heroes of the Nations series. Henry lived from 1394 to 1460, and the book pairs his story with an account of geographical progress through the Middle Ages as preparation for his work. A gateway at Belem, with Henry's statue in armor, fronts the volume.

Beazley traces how maps, travel tales, and sea lore built toward Portugal's age of discovery, with Henry at the center. The series also holds lives of Nelson, Gustavus Adolphus, Pericles, and Lincoln, priced at a dollar and a half in cloth. The book is a solid, old-style hero biography with a scholarly frame.
18781-hero-and-leander:
Christopher Marlowe's poem opens its first sestiad on the Hellespont, where two cities stand in view of each other, Abydos and Sestos, divided by Neptune's might. At Sestos dwells Hero the fair, whom Apollo courted for her hair, dressed in lawn, purple silk, and green sleeves bordered with a grove.

Hero, Venus's nun, wears a myrtle wreath and a veil of artificial flowers, with buskins of shells silvered to the knee, so lovely that Nature weeps at what she took from her. Across the strait at Abydos dwells amorous Leander, beautiful and young, whose tresses and straight body draw the praise of gods and mortals. The poem's opening leaves them an arm of sea apart.
1882-the-young-forester:
Zane Grey's Young Forester follows Ken, a boy who loves outdoor life and hunting. Ken must explain forestry to a brother who teases him for reading dime novels about grizzlies. Ken chooses a profession his family doubts, and the novel follows his training in the woods.

Grey writes the forest as a workplace: fire, timber, and the men who guard them, with a villain named Buell whose bills and searching eyes test Ken's temper. The book is a boys' story of vocation, arguing that a life outdoors can be serious work, and it carries Grey's usual love of open country.
18847-the-white-sister:
F. Marion Crawford published this novel in 1909, in a Macmillan edition, after an earlier copyright in 1908. The story is set in Italy and centers on a young woman whose life is pulled between love and a religious vocation. The title points to the white habit of a nun, and the plot turns on vows, loss, and a lover whose fate is uncertain.

Crawford, known for Italian romances like Saracinesca, writes with close attention to Rome, its churches, and its social world. Feeling and duty contend throughout, and the heroine's choice carries the novel's weight. Readers get a romantic melodrama of the old school, earnest in tone and rich in Italian setting, from a writer at the height of his popularity.
1887-the-life-of-the-spider:
Jean-Henri Fabre's Life of the Spider opens with the black-bellied tarantula and a defence of an animal most people hasten to crush underfoot. Against the verdict that the spider is odious and noxious, Fabre sets her industry, her talent as a weaver, her wiliness in the chase, and her tragic nuptials.

Fabre watches spiders in artificial burrows, heaping soil layer by layer around a central reed. He records their hunting, mating, and building with the patience of a man who spent a lifetime outdoors. The book is natural history written as literature, and it turns a feared creature into a subject of wonder without ever softening the facts.
18872-the-field-of-clover:
Laurence Housman's fairy tales, first published by Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner in 1898 and reprinted by Dover in 1968, open with The Bound Princess in six parts. The tale begins with the wisest man in the world, his head crammed with all earthly knowledge, seeking a wife as wise as himself.

Their only child proves a simpleton, small-headed and large-limbed, whom his parents name Noodle and leave to fend for himself. Fire-eaters, a galloping plough, a thirsty well, a princess Melilot, a burning rose, and a camphor worm carry Noodle's story on. Shorter tales follow, among them The Crown's Warranty, The Wishing-Pot, and The Passionate Puppets, all engraved by Clemence Housman.
1891-a-plea-for-old-cap-collier:
Irvin S. Cobb's Plea for Old Cap Collier, dedicated to Will H. Hogg, defends the dime-novel detective against the charge of absurdity. Cobb says he carried the idea around for years, loose and unformed, until it jelled: the old heroes, judged by modern standards, look like idiots or liars. They taught a generation to read.

Cobb argues with humor and affection, recalling schoolbook classics and scenes that physically could never have occurred, and asking what the critics miss. The plea is really for the pleasures of boyhood reading, and for a hero who, for all his impossibilities, stood for courage, loyalty, and a straight shot.
18965-the-substitute-prisoner:
Max Marcin wrote this 1911 novel of crime and mistaken identity in New York. It opens with a woman's visit that leaves a man torn between fear and hope, and the plot turns on a prisoner who takes another man's place. Theatre crowds, late streets, and city contrasts set the scene.

Whitmore walks Broadway and Seventh Avenue by night, weighing guilt, love, and escape while others watch and scheme around him. The story moves through homes, offices, and dark side streets toward a reckoning. Readers get a tense city melodrama about who pays for a crime and who walks free.
19023-a-daughter-of-the-sioux-a-tale-of-:
General Charles King published this frontier novel in New York in 1903, with illustrations by Frederic Remington and Edwin Willard Deming. King, a soldier-author, wrote many tales of army life on the plains. The chapters move from foreshadowed events and absence from duty through night encounters, the sign of the bar shoe, and a grave discovery.

First sight of the foe, blood will tell, and bad news from the front carry the story toward its climax among soldiers and Sioux people. The novel reflects its era's view of the frontier wars, told from the army's side. Readers get a period military romance, vivid on cavalry detail, and a reminder of how the Indian wars were retold for popular readers.
19055-steve-yeager:
William MacLeod Raine wrote this 1915 western about Steve Yeager, a cow puncher who lands in trouble with a film company in Mexico. Steve makes a mistake early, tells too much truth, and crosses Chad Harrison, a bully actor who is also a fine fighter. Desert trips and night visits follow.

Camera men and actors argue over Harrison's temper, while Steve must prove his grit without losing his job or his honour. Gabriel Pasquale and other border figures add danger. Readers get a brisk range tale of pride, pluck, and a working cowboy among movie folk.
19070-both-sides-the-border-a-tale-of-ho:
G. A. Henty wrote this historical tale of Hotspur and Glendower on the Anglo-Scottish and Welsh borders. A border hold, Alnwick, Ludlow Castle, and the Welsh rising frame a story of raids, jousts, missions, and battles, including Homildon Hill and Shrewsbury. Ralph Peacock drew the pictures.

A border lord returns wounded, arm in sling and helmet cleft, after a cattle raid turned fight with the Bairds, losing Long Hal, Rob Finch, and Smedley. His wife Mary greets him at the steps with fear and relief. Young readers get stirring history fiction on loyalty, war, and life on a restless frontier.
19079-the-adventures-of-lightfoot-the-de:
Thornton W. Burgess wrote this 1921 animal tale for children, with pictures by Harrison Cady. Lightfoot is a handsome deer in the Green Forest who meets Peter Rabbit and other wood folk while learning the ways of deer life. The book also pleads for care toward wild creatures.

Lightfoot tells how his new antlers grow soft and tender, then harden and shed their skin, and why he hides while they are sore. Hunters, dogs, and forest friends test his speed and sense through the seasons. Young readers get a kind, nature-wise story about growth, caution, and life in the woods.
19083-the-border-boys-across-the-frontie:
Fremont B. Deering wrote this 1911 boys' tale, one of his Border Boys books. A group of lads rides with a cow puncher named Pete toward the frontier, where a haunted mesa, desert trails, and a coming sand storm test their nerve. The story opens on open range under a strange, hazy sky.

Sand, heat, and night alarms push the boys to act as a team, and each chapter adds a fresh scrape or chase. Pete's dry talk steadies the younger riders when fear rises. Young readers get a lively western tale of friendship, grit, and life on the trail near the Mexican border.
19090-star-hunter:
Andre Norton wrote this 1961 science fiction novel about Ras Hume, a man with a grudge, on the planet Nahuatl. Two moons cross a cloudless sky above a pleasure house terrace, where scented flowers mimic an off-world jungle. Hume, who neither forgets nor forgives, plots against Wass, the serpent of many worlds.

Wass needs a youth with taped memories of Jumala, made by expert techs who slipped past the law. Three or four months of research and tapes must come first. Readers get a tense Norton tale of memory, revenge, and a hunter who may become the hunted.
19092-the-adventures-of-paddy-beaver:
Thornton W. Burgess wrote this 1917 animal tale for children, with pictures by Harrison Cady. Paddy Beaver comes down from the North to the Green Forest, where he fells trees, plans a pond, and builds a house. Peter Rabbit, Sammy Jay, and Farmer Brown's boy watch his work with mixed feelings.

Sammy Jay scolds Paddy as a thief, but Paddy answers with good humour and keeps at his dam and lodge. Each chapter shows a new step in beaver work and a new visitor to the pond. Young readers get a cheerful nature story about skill, patience, and making a home in the wild.
19107-an-arkansas-planter:
Opie Read wrote this novel about an Arkansas planter whose land lies along the river below Little Rock. The old planter race, come mostly from Virginia with whisky from Kentucky, grew cotton for Liverpool and prized their daughters' fame. Their country was new, yet they held themselves as lordly as medieval lords.

A major argues with Louise, who insists she will marry another man, while memories of a moonlight steamboat dance and a daughter saved from the river haunt him. Pride, love, and family honour drive the plot. Readers get a Southern novel of planter life, talk, and the stubborn wills of fathers and daughters.
19173-the-cow-puncher:
Robert J. C. Stead wrote this 1918 Canadian novel, The Cow Puncher. It was published in Toronto. A boy who handles a lasso better than a scrubbing brush leads a girl into an old ranch house. The house is musty with flies. They lay a stretcher down and ride forty miles for a doctor. His father lies hurt, and the girl Irene must cook and wait.

The boy promises to burn the trail and return by morning. He leaves grub and hope that her father's leg will not hurt much. Ranch work, love, and prairie hardship follow. Readers get a warm western Canadian tale of youth, duty, and life on the range.
19190-men-called-him-master:
Elwyn Allen Smith wrote this 1948 life of Jesus for young readers. It is called Men Called Him Master, published by Westminster Press. Chapters move from a voice in the wilderness to fishers of men. Later come a man of authority, God is now king, and who is this carpenter. The style is plain and direct, aimed at youth.

John the Baptist tells a tax gatherer to turn his life toward God. He must never force unjust payment. John tells soldiers to shun blackmail. He bids all who own two garments to share with those who have none. Pharisees hear hard words on repentance. Young readers get a clear Gospel retelling in modern, simple speech.
19194-rebel-raider:
H. Beam Piper wrote this tale, Rebel Raider, first printed in True magazine in December 1950. It opens near midnight on January 2, 1863, at a party for General J. E. B. Stuart at the Ratcliffe home in Union-held Fairfax County. Stuart, raiding from Culpeper, shot up outposts, stole horses, and burned forage for a merry Christmas.

After Stuart rides south, John Mosby leads six men over Bull Run Mountain toward Middleburg, scatters them to farms, and returns alone to gather contacts. On January 10 he leads them through Aldie Gap. Readers get a sharp Civil War tale of guerrilla strategy, where uproar in the rear may tip a future battle.
19222-modern-english-books-of-power:
George Hamlin Fitch wrote this study of modern English books of power, opening with Dickens reading The Chimes in 1844. He argues that great writers earn power through sorrow, each passing through a Gethsemane before moving hearts. Milton's line on books as the life-blood of a master spirit sets the theme.

Lamb's Dream Children aches for a lonely man who gave up happiness for his sister, while Thackeray writes on family love from a heart clouded by loss. Each essay links life to work. Readers get warm, earnest literary criticism on why certain English books still move readers across years.
19246-the-young-pitcher:
Zane Grey wrote this 1911 school and baseball novel, The Young Pitcher. Its hero is Ken Ward at a big university. Ken, a freshman, longs most, after his diploma, to make the varsity baseball team. Yet his first days bring a class battle. In it he slugs the sophomore president, who is also varsity captain. His luck seems miserable.

Ken wakes in a corridor among torn, bruised freshmen, laughing despite hurt. Then he lies a week in his room, marked by freshmen for honour. Sophomores mark him for revenge. A great arm and a call for candidates follow. Young readers get a lively college tale of sport, rivalry, and pluck.
19257-michael-mcgrath-postmaster:
Ralph Connor wrote this 1900 story, Michael McGrath, Postmaster, about old Michael and a traveller's first meeting with him. The narrator rides all day with a pack pony, photograph kit, and tent, dodging trees, pushing brush, and wading Sixty-mile Creek toward the Pacific Coast. Weariness gives way to welcome.

As afternoon wears on, the trail leaves the creek, winds up a mountain slope, and meets side trails from valleys, hinting that somewhere lies ahead. Michael's post office and mountain life anchor the tale. Readers get a warm Canadian frontier sketch of a postmaster, a traveller, and a hard, beautiful land.
19303-raftmates-a-story-of-the-great-riv:
Kirk Munroe wrote this 1893 river tale, Raftmates, about boys on the great Mississippi. Winn Caspar, sixteen, joins the crew of the Venture, while his father the Major weighs his traits: ambitious and persevering, yet impulsive, impatient of control, and full of self-conceit. His mother fears for him with love.

Winn dashes away with the speed of a deer in the front piece scene, and Billy Brackett starts down river as the voyage begins. Rafts, snags, and river folk test the boys. Young readers get a stirring river adventure on work, courage, and the lessons that curb a proud boy.
19309-the-reminiscences-of-an-astronomer:
Simon Newcomb wrote these reminiscences in 1903, tracing a life from a world of cold and darkness to sweetness and light at observatories. Chapters cover ancestry, a long walk to Dr. Foshay, Harvard at mid-century, the Naval Observatory in 1861, and trips to Manitoba and up the Saskatchewan. The tone is modest and reflective.

Newcomb's father, a wandering country teacher in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, scorned rote learning and praised Cobbett's grammar, while his mother, deeply religious and gifted, shaped his mind. Readers get a classic scientific memoir on learning, work, and the growth of American astronomy.
1931-the-zeppelin-s-passenger:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's Zeppelin's Passenger opens with afternoon callers admitting they never heard a sound, and with Miss Fairclough pouring tea in a low chair. The novel follows a German agent who escapes by Zeppelin, and the English men and women who must stop him, through country houses and London rooms.

Griffiths' suspicions vanish with a second glass of port, though his manner grows no more genial, and Philippa asks whether her companion is almost too daring. Oppenheim writes the wartime thriller with polish. The Zeppelin itself — silent, huge, and out of reach — gives the book its image of a war fought in the sky as well as on the ground.
19329-the-sunny-side-of-ireland-how-to-s:
John O'Mahony wrote this guide to seeing the south and west of Ireland by the Great Southern and Western Railway, in a second edition that was rewritten and enlarged. It maps routes out of Cork and Dublin to places such as Kenmare, Glengarriff, and the lakes of Killarney, with maps and many pictures.

A chapter by R. Lloyd Praeger adds the natural history of the region, so the book serves walkers and plant lovers as well as rail travelers. It still reads as a window on Irish travel before the car, when the train set the pace of a holiday.
19330-an-apache-princess-a-tale-of-the-i:
General Charles King wrote this 1903 frontier tale, An Apache Princess, with pictures by Frederic Remington and Edwin Willard Deming. It follows soldiers, agents, and Apache people in Arizona, where a young lieutenant, Blakely, takes charge of a reservation, falls ill with mountain fever, and meets Angela Wren, his captain's only child.

Blakely's fancy duty angers his senior, while the agent's wife and Lola, daughter of the interpreter and his Apache-Yuma wife, nurse him back to health. A fight in a canyon fronts the book. Readers get a romantic army tale of the Southwest, told in the attitudes of its time.
19338-the-keeper:
H. Beam Piper wrote this science fiction tale, The Keeper, first printed in Venture in July 1957. Raud, keeper of an ancient crown, sets out with his deer rifle and great dog Brave to catch thieves who stole his treasure before they reach the Starfolk. Negatron pistols mean little to a man of his post.

Raud tracks deer through brush, reads snow for morning hunting, and guards a crypt where dogs lie on a stone slab over a bearskin bundle. Traders from the Warm Seas brought his story to a Space Navy base on Dremna. Readers get a haunting tale of a lonely guardian, old relics, and a world after empire.
19358-war-rhymes-by-wayfarer:
Wayfarer wrote this book of war rhymes from the First World War, opening with Modern Diplomacy, or How the War Started, in August 1914. Limericks give each power a voice: Austria scolds the murderous Serb, Serbia calls on uncle the Czar, the Kaiser vows to teach him his place, and the Czar answers his cousin. The verse is satiric and topical.

Later rhymes mock Jack Canuck, who lets British brothers take front seats while he parades with his lodge, and a German speaker wondering where the Kaiser stays while bullets whiz. Readers get wartime comic verse, sharp, partisan, and full of the slang of its day.
19389-child-songs-of-cheer:
Evaleen Stein wrote this book of songs and verses for children, published in Boston in the late nineteen teens with pictures by Antoinette Inglis. Dandelions, fairy ships, Easter eggs, and moonlight all appear, sung in simple rhymes meant to be read aloud or set to music.

The opening verses liken the little words to a flock of birds brought to sing for children, foolish at times and glad at others. The book's aim is cheer itself: short poems that lift a child's day and give families verses to share. A pop-corn poem turns popping kernels into fluffy white puffs, with a chorus children can shout along.
19401-the-plunderer:
Henry Oyen wrote this novel of business and the West, under a New York imprint in the early nineteen twenties. Roger Payne, a young manufacturers' agent, and his partner Jim Tibbetts are drawn from office figures into a rougher world of dams, cattlemen, and knives drawn in seeming jest.

One scene turns on a clasp knife opened in a pocket while its owner feigns injury, a neat image of the book's theme: plunder wearing a friendly face. Oyen mixes office comedy with western danger, and the result is a brisk tale of trust tested by greed.
19404-life-of-abraham-lincoln-little-blu:
John Hugh Bowers wrote this 1922 short Life of Abraham Lincoln, Little Blue Book number 324 in the ten-cent pocket series edited by E. Haldeman-Julius. The story follows one American rising by honest effort from the humblest beginning to the highest station of honour. Log cabin, rail splitting, pine-knot study, and flatboat trips frame the rise.

Lincoln, postmaster of New Salem, kept the very coins he collected and never borrowed them, though he sorely needed a loan, then served as deputy surveyor and won election in 1834. Ann Rutledge's death left deep despondency. Readers get a compact, admiring Lincoln life for pocket reading.
19412-set-in-silver:
C. N. Williamson and A. M. Williamson wrote this romance of a motor tour through England, published in the early nineteen hundreds. A young woman tells the story in her own voice, with her father close by and a new suitor soon in view. The road, the inns, and the English countryside frame the whole tale.

Much of the charm lies in small scenes: talk in cars, stops in towns, and the slow growth of trust between two people. The book pairs travel writing with a love plot, so readers get both a tour of the land and a courtship told with light humor.
19438-the-hero-of-esthonia-and-other-stu:
W. F. Kirby compiled this two-volume study of Estonian romantic literature from Estonian and German sources, published in London in the late eighteen hundreds. Its center is the Kalevipoeg, the national epic of the hero Kalev's son, retold canto by canto with notes on its sources and meanings.

Around the epic, Kirby gathers folk tales in prose, ballads, short poems, and a sketch of Estonian mythology, with a map of the country. The volumes brought a little-known literature to English readers, and they remain a useful door into the songs and stories that fed Estonian national feeling.
19495-tom-slade-motorcycle-dispatch-bear:
Percy K. Fitzhugh wrote this wartime Boy Scout tale, released by a New York publisher in the late nineteen teens with pictures by R. Emmett Owen. Tom Slade rides a motorcycle as a dispatch bearer in France, turning his searchlight on a hatless, coatless German soldier in the frontispiece scene.

Later Tom watches German speakers gather gear in a pit, noting who knows the place and who fears the officer in charge. The book mixes scout pluck with war service, and it shows how boy heroes were drafted into the Great War's story.
19500-can-you-forgive-her:
Anthony Trollope wrote this novel of love, money, and marriage, first issued in monthly parts in the mid eighteen sixties. Its heroine must choose between suitors and face what forgiveness means when a promise is broken. Country houses, London rooms, and debt all press on her choice.

Around her move figures such as a captain who boasts of Inkerman while his creditors doubt every word. Trollope's great strength is moral talk made vivid: long, fair debates in which no party is quite right. The novel remains one of his most searching studies of a woman's lot.
19509-the-opinions-of-a-philosopher:
Robert Grant wrote this gentle novel of a man turned philosopher at forty, appearing from a New York press in the mid eighteen nineties with an etching by W. H. Hyde. His wife Josephine says he has grown philosophical in old age, and he admits a touch of grey and a slower step.

Opinions on marriage, beauty, and society follow, told with humor: a daughter who escapes being homely by smile and hair, and a father who boils when his wife is compared to her. Grant's book is a kind, witty record of middle age thinking itself through.
19597-national-character:
N. C. Burt, pastor of Franklin Street Presbyterian Church in Baltimore, preached this Thanksgiving discourse on national character in mid-November of eighteen fifty-five. Parishioners at once asked for a copy for publication, and it was printed in Baltimore the same year.

Burt argues that civil rule rests on religious citizens, and that America is blessed so long as pure Christianity guides public life. The sermon is a window on antebellum pulpit patriotism, earnest, moral, and sure of its nation's calling. Burt preached to Baltimore listeners, and his hearers asked at once for print. Burt argues that true religion among citizens is of the highest advantage to the State itself.
19615-the-dairyman-s-daughter:
Legh Richmond wrote this tale of the dairyman's daughter, printed in Edinburgh as a separate tract from his Annals of the Poor. It traces divine grace in a poor girl's life, where mercy beams on a heart unencumbered by riches, rank, or polished society.

Richmond contrasts her simple faith with the hindrances wealth and fashion lay in the way of true religion. The tale, long used in Sunday schools and missions, made its heroine famous as a model of humble, sincere piety. Richmond contrasts simple faith with the hindrances of wealth and fashion. The narrator parts from the family with blessings exchanged all round, his returning meditations sweet and hopeful.
19721-the-literary-world-seventh-reader:
John Calvin Metcalf, Sarah Withers, and Hetty S. Browne compiled this seventh reader for schools, published in Richmond in the late nineteen teens. Legends of the land open the book, with Irving's Rip Van Winkle first, followed by poems, tales, and speeches for classroom reading.

A ballad of Lochinvar, wooing his lost love with a cup of wine, shows the anthology's taste for stirring verse. The reader was made to build taste and memory in older pupils, and it preserves the canon schools taught a century ago. Study helps quiz readers on Ariel's dance preparations and on Mamie Pike's character, with reasons required.
19815-roy-blakeley-pathfinder:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh wrote the Roy Blakeley books about a Boy Scout troop. Roy Blakeley, Pathfinder, from 1920, is all about a hike. Roy warns that it starts and ends on Bridge Street. The hike begins at a soda fountain in Catskill, New York. It ends at a candy store soda fountain in Bridgeboro, New Jersey. Between fountains lies a full scout adventure.

Roy narrates in a slangy, digressing, funny voice. Fitzhugh let him wander off the trail in talk as in fact. The Bridgeboro troop's hikes made the series beloved. Scouts of the 1920s read Roy as one of their own. The books preserve early Scouting's ideals and jokes. Pathfinder shows the formula at full stride.
19852-the-gipsies-advocate-or-observatio:
The Gipsies' Advocate pleads the cause of Britain's Romani people. Its full title promises observations on their origin, character, and habits. The author adds facts from his own immediate notice. Travellers and other writers on this people fill the appendix list. The dedication is respectful and sincere. James Crabb, a Southampton philanthropist, wrote it in the 1830s.

Gypsies, as they were then called, faced scorn and harsh laws. Crabb campaigned for their schooling and Christian instruction. His observations record Romani life as outsiders rarely saw it. The book mixes sympathy with missionary purpose. Both attitudes mark early Romani studies in Britain. It remains a source for the people's history.
1993-told-after-supper:
Jerome K. Jerome gathers ghost stories told after supper, in the cosy, comic manner of his humorous tales. Friends round a fire swap tales of haunted houses, strange visitors, and things that go bump in the night. Jerome wrote Told After Supper in 1891, as a Christmas-style ghost book.

Jerome keeps the horror light, letting humour undercut fear, and the stories suit reading aloud on a winter evening. The collection shows a lighter side of the ghost story, before horror turned grim. The supper frame, with friends swapping tales, keeps the ghosts friendly rather than grim.
19970-son-of-power:
Will Levington Comfort and Zamin Ki Dost wrote Son of Power in 1920, a novel of India. Its hero Skag returns to the zoo day after day. For three days he stays from opening to closing time. He falls into deep absorption before the tigers and monkeys. He does not hear what goes on around him. Skag's gift is an uncanny bond with animals. India will give that gift its true field.

Comfort wrote popular novels of the East and of animal life. Son of Power blends both into one adventure. Zamin Ki Dost was his Indian collaborator and friend. The zoo scenes tune the hero before the jungle takes him. Kipling's shadow lies over every such tale. Comfort's version adds an American seeker's mysticism.
19994-the-aesop-for-children-with-pictur:
The Aesop for Children, dated 1919, retells Aesop's fables with pictures by Milo Winter. One fable stars a little Kid whose horns are growing. The horns make him think himself a grown-up Billy Goat. He can take care of himself now, he believes. One evening the flock starts home and his mother calls. The Kid's confidence meets the coming dark. Winter's pictures give the fable its charm.

Winter illustrated many classics for Rand McNally's list. His Aesop became a standard school and home edition. Short fables, each with its moral, suit beginning readers. The pictures carry animals with real personality and weight. Generations met the fox, the crow, and the tortoise here. This edition is a landmark of American children's publishing.
20040-the-call-of-the-beaver-patrol-or-a:
Capt. V. T. Sherman wrote The Call of the Beaver Patrol, also called A Break in the Glacier. Four lads of seventeen wear the khaki of the Boy Scouts of America. They sit in the dim, empty office of the Labyrinth mine. There, caretaker Case Canfield speaks with them at the start.

Boy Scout tales of this era mix camp craft, mines, ice, and brave deeds. The patrol faces wild country and sudden risk far from home. Readers get a period view of scouting as training for grit and teamwork. The mine office hints at wealth, danger, and secrets ahead.
2014-the-lodger:
Marie Belloc Lowndes builds a slow-burning thriller around a London couple, Robert and Ellen Bunting, who take in a lodger to pay the rent. The stranger is polite and quiet, yet his night walks and odd habits alarm them. Lowndes based the Avenger on Jack the Ripper, whose murders in 1888 still haunted London memory.

Outside, a killer known as the Avenger stalks the foggy streets, and the Buntings begin to fear the man under their own roof. Lowndes, drawing on the Jack the Ripper murders, keeps the horror in suggestion and doubt rather than gore. The Buntings' need for rent money makes their fear sharper, since they cannot simply turn the lodger out.
20364-notes-and-queries-number-189-june-:
Notes and Queries, number 189, for June 11, 1853, shares literary finds by post. One note settles where Thomas Moore's first poem appeared in print. It was entrusted to Anthologia Hibernica, a monthly Irish magazine. That magazine ran from January 1793 to December 1794 in Dublin.

It is now a storehouse of Ireland's spirited efforts at periodical writing. Notes and Queries built knowledge from hundreds of such small answers. Antiquaries, editors, and keen readers all traded facts in its pages. This number shows Victorian scholars at their most helpful and exact. Literary men, artists, and gentlemen formed its core circle of writers.
20368-notes-and-queries-number-191-june-:
Number 191 of Notes and Queries came out on June 25, 1853. The journal worked as a meeting place where readers sent in questions, answers, and short notes on history, books, and old customs. Scholars and keen amateurs all wrote in to share what they knew.

Its pages carry an account of witchcraft beliefs still held in parts of Somersetshire. A clergyman reports that two children near his house were said to be bewitched, and his inquiries showed such beliefs were far from rare. The issue gives a direct look at the folklore debates of Victorian England.
20369-notes-and-queries-number-190-june-:
Dated June 18, 1853, number 190 of Notes and Queries gathers short notes and replies from readers across Britain. The journal's pages mix church history, old books, word lore, and family records. Each item is brief, and many answer questions raised in earlier issues.

One note quotes a Latin passage on the evil of sermons that run too long. It tells how the early church fathers fixed preaching at about an hour, and kept to that limit themselves. The issue shows how the journal's readers traded exact facts and sharp quotations on small but curious points.
20381-the-village-by-the-river:
H. Louisa Bedford set her novel The Village by the River in a country parish where the church and churchyard anchor daily life. Villagers speak in broad local dialect, and great events arrive from the world beyond the lanes. The story keeps close to ordinary people and their talk.

One early scene describes a grand funeral coming from the station. A shining black hearse carries a score of plumes. Fine horses step with manes and tails near the ground, and men with silk hatbands walk alongside. The scene shows how death, pride, and village custom meet in the book.
20432-young-captain-jack-or-the-son-of-a:
Horatio Alger, Jr. wrote Young Captain Jack, published in 1901, as a boys' novel of the Civil War years. Jack is raised by a foster mother who thinks the world of him. A surgeon appears and claims to be the boy's true father.

Jack refuses to believe the claim, and he will not leave his foster mother. Many complications arise as the claim is tested. In the end, the truth about the youth's birth is uncovered, and all ends happily for the young son of a soldier. The tale follows Alger's beloved pattern of pluck rewarded.
2046-clotel-or-the-president-s-daughter:
William Wells Brown published Clotel in 1853, one of the first novels by an African American author. It tells of Clotel, said to be the daughter of President Thomas Jefferson and an enslaved woman. The novel follows her family through sale and escape. Brown published Clotel in London in 1853, since American publishers feared its theme.

Brown, himself born enslaved, uses the tale to indict slavery and the men who profited from it. Clotel remains a landmark of African American literature, and a powerful early protest novel. The president's daughter title, pointing at Jefferson, made the novel a political charge.
20460-the-citizen-soldier:
The Citizen-Soldier: Memoirs of a Volunteer tells the Civil War as one ordinary volunteer lived it. The author wrote for readers who wanted more than generals and battle maps. He promises the everyday life of the common soldier in the wars that founded the republic's second birth.

How were their days spent, he asks, and among what surroundings? What were their thoughts, fears, hopes, and acts? Who were their comrades, and on which side did they stand? The memoir answers with marches, camps, hunger, jokes, and battles, in the voice of a man who carried a rifle through them.
20471-grace-harlowe-s-golden-summer:
Grace Harlowe's Golden Summer, published in 1917, belongs to the long Grace Harlowe series of girls' books. Grace and her friends, the Eight Originals, spend a summer of outings and good works. Hippy Wingate supplies much of the comedy with his teasing speeches.

In one scene Hippy beams at his victim and demands a confession of ignorance. Either you or I know very little, he says, so which of us is a know-nothing? The friends laugh their way through such sparring. The series followed Grace from high school to college and beyond, and readers grew up with her.
20525-isabel-leicester:
Isabel Leicester, billed as a romance, follows a young woman thrown on the kindness of others. Mrs. Arnold is the widow of a clergyman, with a very limited income. Isabel is unwilling to burden a woman whose means she knows are so small.

Yet she has no alternative at the time. She trusts the stay will not be long. From that uneasy start, the novel builds its tale of love, pride, and dependence in a quiet household. It shows the tight choices open to a gentlewoman without money in the world the book describes.
20610-the-complete-prose-works-of-martin:
Martin Farquhar Tupper's Complete Prose Works gathers the writings of the man whose Proverbial Philosophy was a Victorian household book. Tupper's moral verses and prose sold in huge numbers. Demand for his work stayed strong for decades, and publishers moved to meet it.

Earlier editions, the publishers admit, were of rather indifferent character in their making. The demand still shown for them has led the present publishers to collect the entire works of Mr. Tupper. They printed the set in stereotype, in a style worthy of its fame. The volume shows popular Victorian wisdom in its full dress.
20619-general-gordon-saint-and-soldier:
J. Wardle's General Gordon: Saint and Soldier tells the life of Charles George Gordon, the British general who died at Khartoum. Wardle presents Gordon as a hero of faith as much as of war. The title's two words frame every chapter.

It has been said, Wardle begins, that the most interesting study for mankind is man. Surely one of the grandest objects for thought is a noble character. A lofty type of a truly great and good man, he writes, is humanity's richest heritage. From China to the Sudan, the biography follows Gordon's strange, devoted career.
20622-the-kentucky-ranger:
Edward T. Curnick's The Kentucky Ranger, published in 1922, is a novel of the Kentucky backwoods and its camp meetings. Two young men and a young woman come riding through the woods from a camp meeting. They travel in a smart spring wagon drawn by two good horses, singing as they go.

The young man who is not driving keeps falling into song and talk by turns. Curnick, a minister himself, fills the tale with revival scenes, rangers, and frontier courtship. The book preserves the speech and faith of the Kentucky hills as he knew them.
20630-the-borough-treasurer:
The Borough Treasurer is a novel of a small English borough caught up in a building boom. Materials pour in from every corner of the kingdom. Here is slate from Wales, there marble from Aberdeen, and there cement from Portland.

The old chambers of the grey buildings are filled to overflowing with all the things that go toward making a house. Ironwork, zinc, lead, and tiles crowd every store. Behind the borough's new prosperity stands its treasurer and his accounts. The novel turns civic pride and public money into a story of temptation and detection.
20663-the-american-practical-brewer-and-: The American Practical Brewer and Tanner is an early American manual for two needful trades. It teaches brewers to make beer, ale, and porter, and tanners to turn hides into leather. Its recipes were written for working masters, not gentlemen. Such manuals passed trade knowledge from shop to shop, in an age when few schools taught such trades.
20694-an-inquiry-into-the-nature-of-peac:
An Inquiry into the Nature of Peace and the Terms of Its Perpetuation asks how wars can end for good. Written in the shadow of a great war, it argues that peace is not a mere pause between fights. Its terms must be built into the life of nations before the guns stop.

The writer weighs how nations rally for war. The spiritual forces of any Christian nation, he says, may be mobilized by two pleas. One is the defense of the community's material interests, real or fancied. The other is the vindication of the national honor. Peace, the inquiry argues, must answer both.
20695-the-spirit-of-sweetwater:
The Spirit of Sweetwater, published in 1898, is a Western romance set at a desert health resort. Sweetwater Springs was a village in a canyon, out of which rose two wonderful springs of water. The virtues of those waters were known throughout the land, and the sick came far to drink and bathe.

The village was wedged in the canyon, which ran to the mighty breast of the Mogollon mountains like a fold in a garment. Among the invalids, cowboys, and schemers at the springs, the novel works out its story of love and cure under the hard desert sky.
20727-the-cosmic-computer:
H. Beam Piper published The Cosmic Computer in 1963, near the end of a long run of future-history tales. Conn Maxwell stands at the glass front of a ship and watches land rush past far below. He feels like sand draining from an hourglass, and time presses on him from the start.

Piper builds a poor colony world that pins its hopes on a lost war machine. Young Conn must weigh hope against hard facts his elders would rather ignore. The novel blends space travel, politics, and a search story. It remains a clear case of Piper's lean, smart style of science fiction.
20731-quiet-talks-on-power:
S. D. Gordon wrote plain talks on Christian life, and Quiet Talks on Power turns on one sharp point. A woman in the text says many church members lack real power in their lives. Gordon takes that gap between form and force as his theme.

Short talks urge readers toward prayer, trust, and daily faith with real effect. Gordon writes in a warm, direct voice, using talks and small scenes. The book belongs to his famed Quiet Talks set, read widely in its day. The talks were meant for daily life, not for study alone.
2082-memoirs-of-the-comtesse-du-barry-wi:
Baron Etienne Leon Lamothe-Langon wrote these memoirs as if by Madame du Barry herself, favourite of Louis XV, though the work is pseudonymous. The narrator tells her career in her own voice, beginning and ending in the middle of events. Lamothe-Langon wrote many such memoirs, inventing voices for famous women of the past.

She claims to tell truth as she sees it, while the reader sees how seldom that truth matches fact. The result is a piquant, gossipy tour of the French court, best read as vivid fiction dressed as a journal. Du Barry's rise from shop girl to royal favourite made her a perfect subject for gossip and romance.
20859-wandl-the-invader:
Early summer 2070 finds stargazers baffled by a strange thing in the sky. Ray Cummings sets Wandl the Invader just after a wild trip to the Moon. Johnny Grantline's radiactive treasure, and lives as well, had hung in the balance there.

A body from deep space nears Earth, and its aims look far from kind. Cummings, a pulp master of ray and atom tales, keeps the peril brisk. Heroes race to read the invader's plan and strike first. The book shows 1930s science fiction at full stretch: bold science talk, vast menace, and Earth itself at stake.
20954-notes-and-queries-number-179-april:
Why does John Bull call so much by his own pet name of Jack? Notes and Queries, number 179, from April 2, 1853, puts that plea to students of mankind. Jack Tar, Jack Frost, and a host of Jacks crowd the query's mind.

Notes and Queries served as a medium where scholars swapped facts and lore. Each weekly number brims with short pleas, replies, and curious finds. Genealogy, proverbs, books, and customs share its dense small print. One number like this shows Victorian learning as a vast, friendly letter trade among strangers bound by curiosity alone.
21062-the-cruise-of-the-nonsuch-buccanee:
In 1569, young George St. Leger comes home to Plymouth from a cruise and learns bad news in Harry Collingwood's buccaneer tale. His brother has been captured by the Spaniards somewhere in the West Indies. A friendly local shipbuilder has a fast new vessel, the Nonsuch, nearly ready to sail.

The builder agrees to fund a rescue voyage in return for half the proceeds of the cruise. George sails with a crew of Devon men, speaking in strong local dialect, before the government can seize the ship. Battles follow, plus a grim look at the Spanish Inquisition, before the brother is found barely alive.
21079-the-trawler:
James B. Connolly, a writer of Gloucester fishing stories, published The Trawler with Scribner's in New York in 1914. On the night the tale opens, Saul Haverick brings word to John Snow's home. Arthur Snow has been washed from Hugh Glynn's vessel and lost at sea. Saul still wears his sea clothes as he tells it.

Pride runs through the loss: Arthur would never be first to take in sail or let another vessel lead. Connolly knew Gloucester and its fleet at first hand, and wrote books like Out of Gloucester. The story honours the skill and stubborn courage of working fishermen.
21218-mayfair-belgravia-and-bayswater:
G. E. Mitton and others wrote this volume of The Fascination of London, edited by Sir Walter Besant and published in 1903. Besant's plan was a full survey of London, district by district, each parish complete in itself. This number walks Mayfair, Belgravia, and Bayswater, the fashionable west of the city.

Hyde Park Corner fronts the book, and maps and pictures support the walk. Streets, squares, great houses, and the people who built and lived in them get their histories. Companion volumes cover the Strand, Westminster, Chelsea, and Kensington in the same way. The series remains a handy Edwardian guide to London's past street by street.
21220-notes-and-queries-number-180-april:
Number 180 of Notes and Queries, dated Saturday, April 9, 1853, calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, borrowed from Captain Cuttle in Dickens, runs: when found, make a note of. Readers wrote in with finds and questions.

This issue prints Rigby correspondence and notes on the Isthmus of Darien and misunderstood words. Folklore covers drills presaging death and Beltane fires in Devonshire. Queries ask about wolves nursing children and the Luneburg table. Book lovers still know the format: a public notebook where small facts wait for answers from strangers.
21234-the-gold-that-glitters-the-mistake:
Jenny Lavender is sixteen and lives on a farm just after Charles I's execution. Colonel Lane's household has lately hidden the young king in an oak tree. Emily Sarah Holt tells how Jenny, at odds with her parents, decides to leave home. She takes a place as lady's maid with the Lanes.

In the servants' hierarchy Jenny ranks so low she may not speak at meals, a snub she must learn to handle. Slowly she comes to enjoy the work. Then the Lanes must flee to France, and Jenny loses her place, a mistake-filled road that leads her home again to a glad welcome.
21249-clayhanger:
Edwin Clayhanger stands on a canal bridge between Bursley and Hillport as Arnold Bennett's novel opens. Pitheads, chimneys, and kilns rise east through the smoke of the Five Towns. Edwin is leaving school for his father's printing business. His father is a martinet, and Edwin's working life begins under a hard rule.

Bennett, himself a son of the Staffordshire Potteries, follows Edwin through childhood, youth, and early manhood until he inherits the firm. Canals, chapels, and printing offices give the novel its ground. Clayhanger is the first of Bennett's Clayhanger family novels, praised for the truth of their picture of provincial industry.
21258-devil-worship-in-france-or-the-que:
Arthur Edward Waite published this study in London in 1896, subtitled a record of things seen and heard in the secret societies according to initiates. He asks whether the devil worship then being reported in France was real. His contents promise chapters on Satanism in the nineteenth century and the mask of Masonry.

Waite, who also translated Eliphas Levi's work on high magic, sorts the witnesses for Lucifer one by one. He begins from the opposite suspicion: there is, he suggests, no modern diabolism of the kind advertised. The book became a key source on the French occult hoaxes and panics of the 1890s.
2126-the-quest-of-the-sacred-slipper:
Sax Rohmer sends his heroes after a sacred slipper, a relic whose theft sets off a chase through London museums, safes, and midnight streets. A girl with violet eyes, Hassan of Aleppo, and a phantom scimitar open the mystery. Rohmer wrote the quest tale after his Fu Manchu successes, keeping the same exotic machinery.

Attempts on a safe, a shrivelled hand, a dwarf, and a woman with a basket pile up, while the Hashishin watch from the dark. Rohmer writes exotic thriller prose at full stretch, and the quest holds its secrets to the end. The slipper, a holy relic, gives thieves and holy men alike a reason to kill and to chase.
21285-the-story-of-a-dark-plot-or-tyrann:
The author, signing only A. L. O. C., published this temperance tale in Boston in 1903, with Canadian roots in Sutton, Quebec. Its preface admits the book will not revolutionise society: it is one more line and precept for the temperance cause. The writer hopes it helps show the colours on the right side.

A dark plot of tyranny on the frontier carries the argument, with drink behind the wrongs done to frontier families. The preface notes how tales of attempted murder pass us by when we do not know the people involved. This story works to make its victims known, so the lesson lands at home.
21299-blue-jackets-the-log-of-the-teaser:
HMS Teaser, a clipper gunboat, lies up the Nyho River off a Chinese city, hunting pirates in the China Seas. Nathaniel Herrick, one of three young midshipmen aboard, tells the story and keeps the log of the title. Ching, the Chinese interpreter who longs to be more important than he is, steers much of the trouble.

The boys beg Ching to take them to a Chinese theatre. They find themselves instead at the public beheading of pirates the Teaser brought to justice. Walking out might cost their own heads, so they sit tight. George Manville Fenn loads the cruise with close calls, river patrols, and uneasy cross-cultural scenes.
213-the-man-from-snowy-river:
Andrew Barton Paterson's title poem tells of a mountain horseman who rides where others dare not. The Man from Snowy River and Other Verses, in its second edition, gathers Paterson's bush ballads from the Bulletin years. Clancy, the drovers, and the mountain chase fill its pages.

Paterson answered Henry Lawson's city-bushman verses with In Defence of the Bush, included here. His riders, shearers, and pioneers speak in galloping rhythm. The book, first published in 1902, made Paterson a national figure. Its title ride became Australia's best-known poem. Paterson's ride has been recited, filmed, and celebrated as Australian legend.
21302-charge-a-story-of-briton-and-boer:
Val Moray farms in South Africa with his father John and brother Bob in George Manville Fenn's story of Briton and Boer. An Irish agitator named Moriarty stirs the Dutch Boer farmers to rebel against British rule. Moriarty demands that Val be handed over to fight the British.

Val goes, escapes, and reaches the place where Joeboy, the family's worker and a hero of the tale, waits for him. They join a British Light Horse unit, where Val meets his old friend Denham. Skirmishes follow, with wounds, capture, and escape helped by Bob and John. Fenn keeps loyalties tangled: the enemy are neighbours, not strangers.
21309-fitz-the-filibuster:
Fitzgerald Burnett, always called Fitz, is a young midshipman aboard a gunboat on Channel patrol in George Manville Fenn's nautical tale. His captain scolds him for stammering reports instead of speaking out sharp and business-like. The patrol is hunting a smuggler running arms to a small Central American republic.

The gunboat's crew are drawn into that republic's struggle, with small fights and tense landings following. Fenn draws the old seamen around Fitz with particular care. Filibuster, in the period sense, means a freebooting adventurer in Latin America. Fitz earns the title before his cruise ends, despite his captain's drilling in proper naval speech.
21327-the-works-of-guy-de-maupassant-vol:
Volume One of Maupassant's works in English was published in New York in 1909. It opens with Boule de Suif, his first famous story, about travellers in a coach during the Franco-Prussian War. Miss Harriet and Francesca and Carlotta Rondoli follow. The tales show Maupassant's range from the start: war, peasants, clerks, and kept women.

Later stories include The Umbrella, The Little Cask, and How He Got the Legion of Honor. The Horla also appears, his tale of an unseen presence driving a man toward madness. Love, drawn from a sportsman's book, and The Devil close the selection. An introduction weighs his gift for painting outward things in few, exact strokes.
21332-charles-dickens-as-a-reader:
Charles Kent, who knew Dickens well, published this memorial of Dickens's public readings in 1872, two years after the novelist's death. Dickens gave his farewell reading at St James's Hall on March 15, 1870. He wrote to Kent approving this record and offering his marked reading copies and statistics for it. John Forster, Dickens's biographer, receives the dedication.

Kent traces the readings from their beginning to their close: the tours, the audiences, the famous performances from his own books. He writes from intimate knowledge, having watched the career throughout. The book preserves how the most popular author of the age became a performer of his own work before thousands.
21335-the-moving-finger:
Mary Gaunt gathers Australian bush stories under a title taken from the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam: the moving finger writes and moves on. The opening tale, A Trotting Cob, stops at a lonely change station on the stock route between Hay and Deniliquin. The night coach takes news, letters, and tobacco to isolated folk there. A ghost walks the road there, they say.

Other stories cover Christmas Eve at Warwingie, the loss of the Vanity, a digger's Christmas, and the Yanyilla steeplechase. Gaunt wrote from long travel in the outback. Heat, distance, and sudden death shape these tales of station life and the people who endured it.
21445-notes-and-queries-number-181-april:
Number 181 of Notes and Queries, dated Saturday, April 16, 1853, opens with the Shepherd of Banbury's weather rules. Those rules, first printed in 1670, long guided farmers and country folk. W. B. Rye's note treats how far such lore can be trusted.

The journal styled itself a medium for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and family historians. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, was to make a note of things when found. Each weekly number mixed short notes, queries, and replies on odd points. This single issue shows Victorian scholars trading small facts in public, fourpence at a time.
21474-peter-the-whaler:
Peter, son of an Irish country vicar, falls into poaching in W. H. G. Kingston's Peter the Whaler. His father warns that his conduct will bring ruin and shame on the family. Peter steals back his seized gun, goes out by night, and is caught by gamekeepers.

The magistrate frees him to his father, who takes him to Liverpool. For fifteen pounds, Captain Swales of the Black Swan agrees to teach him seamanship on a Canada run. The ship proves a brutal, ill-run emigrant carrier, and fire strikes her. Rescue by the Mary, then service on the Foam, opens Peter's whaling life.
21475-peter-trawl-or-the-adventures-of-a:
Peter Trawl grows up in a Portsmouth wherryman's family in W. H. G. Kingston's Peter Trawl. His brother Jack shoulders a seaman's bag while his father carries oars and sails. Then a bank failure wipes out the family's savings, as often happened around 1830.

A freak storm kills the father on a harbour trip, and sickness takes the mother. A kind Quaker shipowner, Mr Gray, shelters the orphans and gives Peter a berth. Mishaps follow at sea, and Peter and his friend Jim reach Shetland by hard roads. Whaling adventure grows from this sad, true-feeling start.
21479-the-south-sea-whaler:
A whaling captain takes his two children on his last voyage in W. H. G. Kingston's The South Sea Whaler. Their mother died during his prior three-year trip, so the boy and girl sail with him. Some crewmen, above all the boatswain, mean no good.

Whale hunts of mixed luck fill the outward run to the Pacific. Then mutiny breaks out, the ship catches fire, and boats and rafts scatter. The children drift with two officers and a kind sailor, losing and finding each other. Their father turns up at last, and joy closes all but the villains' tale.
21554-frank-mildmay-or-the-naval-officer:
Frank Mildmay owns at the start that he was a coward and a boaster as a child. Captain Marryat's Frank Mildmay, published in 1829, was his first book, written at sea. Its full title adds Scenes and Adventures of a Naval Officer.

Marryat argues that what folk call cowardice in a child is often a sharper sense of danger. Pride teaches us to hide fear, and habit dulls us to risk. Mildmay's career tests that claim through cruises, fights, and scrapes. Writing the book helped Marryat choose the pen over the service for good.
21578-rattlin-the-reefer:
Edward Howard wrote Rattlin the Reefer, and Captain Marryat polished it for print in 1838. A post-chaise with four horses races to the Crown Inn at Reading on a February night. Sleet and rain drive every soul indoors as the tale begins.

Howard's language runs more flowery than Marryat's usual plain style, with long and curious words. The tale tracks young Rattlin through school and sea service in the old navy. Marryat counts it as the twelfth book from his pen, though the draft was another sailor's. Sea humour, hardship, and tall talk fill its pages.
2158-the-prime-minister:
Anthony Trollope's The Prime Minister follows Plantagenet Palliser, Duke of Omnium, as he takes the highest office, and his wife Glencora, whose social ambitions complicate his rule. Ferdinand Lopez, a doubtful financier, threads through the plot. Trollope wrote The Prime Minister as the fifth Palliser novel, after Phineas Finn.

Trollope, in the Palliser series, studies politics, marriage, and reputation with his usual breadth. The novel, first serialised in 1875 and 1876, remains a masterly portrait of Victorian government and society. Palliser's honest, awkward rule contrasts with Lopez's flashy fraud, a pairing Trollope loved.
2160-the-expedition-of-humphry-clinker:
Tobias Smollett tells a comic expedition through Britain in letters, as Matthew Bramble and his family travel to spas, baths, and country houses. Humphry Clinker, a poor servant, joins the party and gives the book its name. Smollett published Humphry Clinker in 1771, the year of his death, as his last novel.

Each letter writer sees the same journey differently, and Smollett uses the clash for satire on health cures, manners, and national character. The novel remains Smollett's most readable work, and a classic of the epistolary form. The letter form, with five voices telling one journey, gives the comedy its variety.
21619-the-tale-of-nimble-deer:
Nimble, a spotted fawn, seems too frail for life in Arthur Scott Bailey's Tale of Nimble Deer. His mother doubts she can raise so tiny and delicate a child. The tale, copyrighted in 1922, is one of Bailey's Sleepy-Time Tales, drawn by Harry L. Smith.

Nimble grows up on wooded ridges and in tangled swamps under Blue Mountain. He tells everybody he meets his news, as the front picture shows. Short chapters give one small scrape or lesson at a time. Bailey's Pleasant Valley folk, from Cuffy Bear to Timothy Turtle, share the woods around him.
21622-architects-of-fate-or-steps-to-suc:
Orison Swett Marden urges youth to build character in Architects of Fate, copyrighted in 1895. The full title adds Steps to Success and Power, aimed at self-culture and noble deeds. Sixteen portraits of eminent persons, fronted by Phillips Brooks, grace the book.

Marden's Pushing to the Front had run through a dozen editions in its first year. This companion volume tells tales of men and women who brought great things to pass. Such themes, he says, are as old as the race, yet ever new to the young. A Longfellow line supplies the title: all are architects of fate.
21632-fame-and-fortune-or-the-progress-o:
Horatio Alger continues Ragged Dick's rise in Fame and Fortune, entered for copyright in 1868. Richard Hunter, the reformed bootblack of Ragged Dick, now climbs in earnest. The tale first ran as a serial in the Schoolmate, a Boston magazine for the young.

Alger aimed the series at the friendless and poor boys of the cities. Publishers offered free sets to any Newsboys' Lodge that applied, to spread the tale. Alger dedicated the book to his father, his constant backer in letters. Honest work, luck, and good patrons carry Dick upward, in the pattern Alger made famous.
21648-westminster:
Sir Walter Besant and G. E. Mitton survey Westminster in the Fascination of London series, issued in 1902. Whitehall in 1775 fronts the booklet, and a chapter on the Abbey comes from Mrs A. Murray Smith. Besant died with the great survey still in hand.

The work, he said, fascinated him more than anything else he had done. His wider history of London, finished to the end of the eighteenth century, made dry bones live. This part treats the seat of Parliament, courts, and kings. Streets, palaces, and the Abbey itself carry tales of power and faith across a thousand years.
21713-the-young-trawler:
North Sea fishing life fills this Ballantyne novel, which opens off the danger sands near the port of Yarmouth. Skipper David Bright is getting his smack, the Evening Star, ready for sea on a wild October morning. At home in one of Yarmouth's narrow Rows, he snaps at his gentle wife over their missing son.

The boy is the young trawler of the title, caught between a rough father and the hard trade that waits for him. Ballantyne had gone out with the fishing fleet to learn its work before writing. The book shows the boats, the weather, the homes, and the faith of the fishing families in close detail.
21718-the-big-otter:
Two friends hunt the snowy backwoods of North America in this Ballantyne tale told by George Maxby, called Max. His chum Jack Lumley loves warmth and ease, yet swears nothing beats a night slept in a snow bed. The pair spend their holidays from their outpost on long hunting trips together.

Snowshoes carry them through drifts four feet deep, and cold shapes every plan they make. Ballantyne writes the winter woods from his own Canadian years, and the detail feels earned. The hunt for the big otter gives the story its drive. Along the way readers get a close look at backwoods travel, camps, and game.
21728-the-dog-crusoe-and-his-master:
A dog takes the hero's place in this Ballantyne tale of the western plains and the backwoods. Crusoe starts life as a fat, blind pup, and Ballantyne lingers over his hard puppyhood before the real story starts. Grown, he is strong and grand, the loyal partner of a young hunter on the frontier.

Their world is the wide country where the Pawnee, Sioux, Delaware, Crow, and Blackfeet peoples still roam. White settlers press in year by year, cutting trees and driving game west toward the Rockies. Ballantyne tells the pair's hunts and dangers from close to the ground. The bond between boy and dog carries the tale, in his warmest storyteller's voice.
21750-martin-rattler:
Martin Rattler is a very bad boy, at least by his aunt Dorothy Grumbit's account, in this Ballantyne favorite. Yet the whole village smiles when Martin passes, and the old vicar calls him full of mischief but sure to improve. His rosy cheeks and quick grin win friends wherever he goes. Aunt Dorothy, who keeps him, sees only the torment of her life.

The tale sends Martin far from his quiet English village, to sea and to Brazil. There his mischief turns to courage among new friends and real dangers. Ballantyne's second great boys' book made his name beside The Coral Island. It still reads as warm, funny, and full of motion.
21808-the-house-an-episode-in-the-lives-:
Building a house becomes a comic war in this 1896 tale by Eugene Field, told as the story of Reuben Baker and his wife Alice. Alice's honeymoon wish was simple: someday to be rich enough to build a dear little house of their own. The chapters follow the wish into hard fact: buying a place, signing a bargain, and raising a mortgage.

Then come the vandals, as Field calls the workmen: plumbers, painters, and sellers of things the Bakers never knew they needed. Neighbors, dogs, taxes, and insurance each get a chapter of grief and fun. Field, a newspaper humorist, writes from the wallet outward. Anyone who has built or mended a house will know every pain in it, and laugh.
21830-the-little-mixer:
Hannah, a Jewish girl of seven, wants Christmas to come down her chimney like her friend Virginia's in this 1922 novel by Lillian Nicholson Shearon. A kimono from Cousin Carrie is a fine gift, Hannah grants, but Santa Claus brings Virginia's gifts in person. Her mother argues the merits of Chanukah while dressing her before a mirror. The child, lovely as a flower, sags with disappointment all the same.

The little mixer of the title is Hannah herself, set between two faiths and two holidays in one American street. Shearon writes the child's logic with a straight face and a kind heart. The book is a gentle period tale of neighbors, festivals, and a small girl trying to have both worlds at once.
21910-mitch-miller:
Two boys in a small Illinois town live inside books in Edgar Lee Masters's Mitch Miller, published in 1920 with drawings by John Sloan. The narrator opens half-asleep, hearing talk that means nothing, while the room blurs into squares of light and dark. That dreamy voice tells the tale of Mitch, a boy who takes Tom Sawyer as his scripture and the river as his church.

Masters, famed for Spoon River Anthology, writes boyhood from inside its own haze. Mitch's schemes, talk, and early death give the novel its ache. Dedicated to the author's little daughters, it is a tender book. Readers meet the prairie town through a boy's eyes, where play and grief share the same streets and the same long summer days.
2192-the-dark-flower:
John Galsworthy's novel follows one man's loves across three stages of life, from youth to middle age and beyond. The Dark Flower traces how passion changes its shape: first love's fire, then a quieter bond, then a late affection that tests loyalty and honor. Galsworthy sets these turns against English country and town life.

The writing is reflective rather than sensational, interested in what people owe each other when feeling and duty pull apart. Each section stands as its own story while adding to a single life's pattern. Readers who like a thoughtful novel of love and time will find it subtle and moving.
2197-the-gambler:
Fyodor Dostoyevsky wrote The Gambler at speed, and its fever shows on every page. A young tutor in a German spa town falls under the spell of roulette while tangled in love, debt, and the whims of a ruined Russian family. The wheel turns, fortunes rise and crash, and reason keeps losing to the urge for one more spin.

The novel's power lies in its portrait of addiction: the gambler's logic, his excuses, and the brief, wild hope of each bet. Around the tables, Dostoyevsky sketches a whole society living on credit and chance. It is short, intense, and uncomfortably honest about how desire can rule a life.
21977-the-narrative-of-a-blockade-runner:
Running the Union blockade is told by a man who did it in J. Wilkinson's Narrative of a Blockade-Runner, published at New York in 1877. Wilkinson, a captain in the late Confederate States Navy, says literary friends chose his plain title. He also gives a full account of the passage of the forts below New Orleans by the United States fleet. Commodore Mitchell's unpublished official report backs his version of that fight.

Wilkinson pauses to praise the kind treatment of prisoners at Fort Warren, where he himself was held. His scope runs wider than blockade runs alone, to the war at sea in full. The narrative is careful, firsthand, and meant to settle arguments about who took New Orleans. It remains a standard source for the Confederacy's sea war.
220-the-secret-sharer:
A young captain takes command of a ship anchored off a tropical coast and finds a stowaway. Joseph Conrad's Secret Sharer follows the captain as he hides Leggatt, a fugitive mate who killed a man in a storm. The two men, strangers, mirror each other.

Conrad sets fishing stakes, barren islets, and a still sea around their secret talks. The captain risks his authority and his ship to help Leggatt escape. The tale probes guilt, loyalty, and the double self. It ranks among Conrad's most perfect short stories. Conrad's tale is often taught as a study in conscience and command.
22061-the-carpenter-s-daughter:
The Carpenter's Daughter came from the authors of The Wide, Wide World, the Warner sisters whose religious tales sold by the hundred thousand. Nettie, the carpenter's girl, comforts her mother in the book's frontispiece scene. The family draws water at a spring with a little tin dipper, for the water is too shallow for a pail. They fill their pails in silence while the spring sings, then climb the path home together.

Poverty, sickness, and faith shape the tale that follows. The Warners wrote for children and cottage readers who wanted story and sermon in one. Their carpenter's household endures its trials by patience and prayer. The book is a small, tender piece of the vast Warner output.
22129-wee-tim-rous-beasties-studies-of-a:
Douglas English, a naturalist and photographer, borrowed Burns's famous phrase for Wee Tim'rous Beasties. His subtitle promises studies of animal life and character. English writes from the field, not the library. One passage freezes a walker who finds a yard of snake at his side, its eyes cold and its mouth too full to strike.

Stoats, snakes, birds, and small mammals pass through his pages. Each study rests on watching one creature closely at a time. English had a pioneer's skill with a camera among wild things. The book belongs to the great age of British nature writing, when patient amateurs taught the public to look at hedgerow life.
22196-little-miss-grouch-a-narrative-bas:
Samuel Hopkins Adams built Little Miss Grouch on the real log of Alexander M. Reynolds, an ocean passenger. Its narrator, the Tyro, boards a great liner for his maiden voyage.
