Anyone missing that hour counts as lost, and great seas of snow and ice sweep toward each other since Earth reversed on its axis in a catastrophe a millennium before. Summer and winter alike bring paralyzing gales, and sleety snow holds the tracks of skin-clad feet. Guldran, a trained anthropologist, ponders two men found nearly frozen days before. One died at once, one speaking in primitive signs of cave dwellers to the west.
30349-the-peace-of-roaring-river:
George Van Schaick sets a wilderness novel in the country around Roaring River. A scorned woman, a lost telegram, and a journey into rough terrain open the action. Copyrighted in 1918, the book follows Madge and the men around her through gunpowder, doubt, flight, and rescue, with the settlement of Carcajou at the center of local loyalties.

Chapters move from a widening horizon to a final hoisting and a hard-won peace, as Stefan runs, help arrives late, and reputations are tested. Van Schaick pairs frontier adventure with a love story, using rivers, camps, and winter travel to press his characters toward plain choices about honor, courage, and home.
30353-the-smiler:
Albert Hernhunter opens a science fiction story at an inquest, where literary agent Martin Cole faces a coroner, a six-man jury, police officers, and a scattering of onlookers. Sanford Smith was discovered dead beside Cole's house, a firearm beside him and a fatal head wound, and suicide is the first theory offered.

Cole, who sells science fiction to magazines and book publishers, dismisses that theory as a weak cover story and calmly admits that he killed Smith. His thin, mirthless smile unsettles the room as the coroner probes the claim. The tale turns on motive, confession, and the gap between a neat official story and a stranger truth.
3038-the-armies-of-labor-a-chronicle-of-:
Samuel Orth wrote The Armies of Labor, volume forty of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. Chapters move from background and formative years through transition, amalgamation, and federation to the trade union, railway brotherhoods, issues and warfare, the Industrial Workers of the World, and labor and politics. Orth treats organized labor as an army with generals and campaigns.

Samuel Gompers dominates the later chapters, jumping into every fray where a federation union faced attack, whether strike, boycott, debate, maneuver, or foreign pilgrimage. Orth notes Gompers's zealot limits and partisan dogmatism, yet credits his rare record of emerging unhumiliated. The book gives a clear early history of American unions for general readers.
30434-occasion-for-disaster:
Mark Phillips builds a science fiction serial around a small fault with very large results, first printed in Analog across November 1960 to February 1961. Its opening frames the theme with a chain of past scares, from enemy aliens in 1914 and Wobblies in 1930 to fellow travelers in 1957 and insane telepaths in 1971.

By 1973, FBI director Andrew J. Burris faces a threat no one can name, and a single flawed part threatens a costly missile program. The story follows officials, agents, and ordinary people caught between fear, blame, and the search for a cause. Phillips uses that pressure to ask how a society picks its villains when the real danger stays unseen.
30446-the-bountiful-lady-or-how-mary-was:
Thomas Cobb writes The Bountiful Lady, subtitled How Mary Was Changed from a Very Miserable Little Girl to a Very Happy One, published in London in 1900. Twelve chapters follow Mary Brown. She finds herself in a different place, sees her fairy godmother, and learns what magic counters can do.

Later scenes add a discontented boy and a magician, plus wings and other wonderful things. They also show a little girl with a dog and a doll, and a prince with a blue bird and a cage. Evangeline gives Mary magic counters, then says goodbye. Cobb insists the wonderful thing was not a dream, and the tale turns misery into joy through kindness and wonder.
30480-the-humors-of-falconbridge-a-colle:
This collection gathers the humors of Falconbridge, a set of humorous and evergreen pieces in the American comic tradition, preserved here with careful transcriber notes on spelling and punctuation. The notes record small fixes, from cantankerous and velocipeding to governor and knowledge, and note the change of pointing-hand symbols to angle marks in end advertisements.

Falconbridge's sketches mix stage humor, dialect, and everyday mishaps, offering short comic scenes that once filled parlors and theaters. The volume reads as a sampler of nineteenth-century American wit, brisk, broad, and fond of wordplay. For modern readers, it preserves a popular comic voice in a clean, readable text.
30485-the-rustler-of-wind-river:
G. W. Ogden sets a western novel in Wind River country, published in March 1917 with a frontispiece by Frank E. Schoonover. Twenty-five chapters move from strange bargainings and beef day to a ranch house by the river, a man in plaid, and a bold civilian.

Later scenes add throwing a scare, travel afoot and alone, and the cry of the rustlers. A trail at dawn, friends parting, boots and saddles, love and death, and tears in the night carry the plot toward its close. Ogden pairs cattle work with gunplay and loyalty, giving readers a brisk ranch tale of theft, honor, and the open range.
30500-the-passenger:
Kenneth Harmon writes The Passenger, a science fiction tale about Lenore aboard a transport on the last leg of a long journey to Sol, past Centaurus. No flash or roar marks the ship's sweep across space. Silent as a ghost and quiet as a puff of moonlight, it rides gravitational fields like tangled, invisible spider webs between stars.

Inside, a faint, persistent vibration from field generators stirs the air. It pulses through passageways lined with closed stateroom doors, up stairways to bridge and navigational decks, and down into echoing holds filled with strange cargo. Lenore relaxes on her couch, bathing in the pulse as it flows through her. Harmon opens a tale of travel, desire, and alien cargo.
30511-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
Birds Illustrated by Color Photography, volume two, number three, for September, opens with a poem on bird song and a note from Thoreau. Thoreau calls some birds poets who sing all summer, true singers who sing for love of music rather than for mates alone.

The editors say their selections for the month include some of those poet birds, led by the ruby-throated hummingbird. Rich in color and sun sparkle, it shines like the polished gem that gives it its name. The issue pairs color photographs with short, popular text, aiming to teach bird life to families and young naturalists.
30539-the-terrible-answer:
Arthur G. Hill writes The Terrible Answer, a Mars story in which seven men come seeking the stuff of empire and meet a grim reply. Larkin had secured an edge, a copy of the Primary Report, so his party lands ahead of the rest in a flash of orange tail-fire.

Each man glows with greed for empire, though their looks vary. Evans marvels at the Martians' green shade, and Cleve, the psychologist, dismisses color as mere pigmentation, proof that God loves variety. Cleve notes their grins prove nothing, since they were born with them and will die with them. Larkin exudes the most power, and his role drives the tale toward empire's price.
30559-eighth-reader:
James Baldwin and Ida C. Bender write the Eighth Reader, part of an eight-book series from the American Book Company, copyrighted in 1911. Baldwin, author of School Reading by Grades and Harper's Readers, joins Bender, supervisor of primary grades in Buffalo, New York, for a volume titled Reading with Expression.

An illustration shows David Copperfield at Salem House, pointing to the literary selections inside. The reader gathers prose and verse meant to be read aloud with feeling, building skill through graded practice. It serves schools and home learners who want classic passages, clear guidance, and steady progress in expressive reading.
30641-notes-and-queries-number-232-april:
Notes and Queries, number two hundred thirty-two, dated Saturday 8 April 1854, serves as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, genealogists, and others. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of.

Contents open with Arabian tales and their sources by J. W. Thomas, La Rochefoucauld by J. Macray, a Shropshire ballad, and a work on the benefit of the death of Christ by Aonio Paleario. Minor notes add stone chisels, acrostics, Simmels, Ogborne's history of Essex, fleas and bugs, and a cure for hydrophobia. Queries follow, in the weekly's familiar mix of scholarship and curiosity.
30644-notes-and-queries-number-233-april:
Notes and Queries, number two hundred thirty-three, dated Saturday 15 April 1854, serves as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, genealogists, and others. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of.

Contents open with palindrome verses, children crying at their birth, and an unpublished letter of Lord Nelson by E. G. Bass. Folk lore follows, with Devonshire superstitions, quacks, and burning a tooth with salt, plus parallel passages by H. L. Temple and Cuthbert Bede. Minor notes close the named items, in the weekly's familiar mix of scholarship and curiosity.
30683-the-unthinking-destroyer:
Rog Phillips wrote this short science fiction tale about two men in a garden who argue over what counts as intelligent life. Gordon Marlow, a doctor of philosophy, is working among carrots, cabbages, and cauliflower when Harold Harper, a student, brings a newspaper. Its headline tells of a robot rocket ship to Mars, and the talk turns to whether explorers would know alien minds if they saw them.

Harold says artifacts would give the game away, since only minds make pots, houses, and machines. Gordon pushes back, asking whether a mind without hands or legs must still build things to count as a mind. The story's title points to its warning: humans may destroy a thinking thing simply by failing to see it. It is a short, sharp debate in story form.
30713-captain-pott-s-minister:
Francis L. Cooper writes Captain Pott's Minister, illustrated by John Goss and copyrighted in 1922 by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard of Boston, dedicated to Betty. Illustrations show a frontispiece line, then let me hear you say you love me, plus scenes of Beth pretending, money enough, and Miss Pipkin disturbed by noise.

Chapter one opens with voices arresting Captain Pott's fork in mid-air, a morsel of salt mackerel dangling from dingy tines as he turns to face the open door. Cooper blends seafaring humor, romance, and village life in a tale where a captain, a minister, and a love story meet. The novel suits readers of light, character-driven fiction.
30732-the-son-of-his-mother:
Clara Viebig wrote this German novel in an authorized translation by H. Raahauge, published by John Lane in London and New York in 1913. Its opening couple are literary, well off, and well liked: he writes a little, she paints, and they once played and sang duets together. Now they go to concerts and the opera instead, and they are called charming people wherever they go.

Yet something is missing from their happiness, for they have no children, and after years of marriage a child seems very unlikely. The husband sighs at his desk and on rides through villages in the Brandenburg March, near Berlin, where he goes for his health. Viebig follows the longing for a child, and what a son means to a mother and father, with quiet realism and close feeling for German middle-class life.
30811-the-moving-finger:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this 1911 novel, published in Boston by Little, Brown, with pictures by J. V. McFall. Its title points to a quatrain printed at the front, on fate writing a line that no piety, wit, or tears can lure back or wash out. The contents run from a prologue called The Dreamer through a letter, old friends, and a puzzling Mr. Saton.

Chapters follow Pauline Marrabel, Lady Marrabel, Rochester, and a spa town called Naudheim, with talk of occultism, obligation, and a growing trouble that ends in first blood. Oppenheim mixes society romance with mystery and a hint of the uncanny, as past acts catch up with his people. Readers who enjoy Edwardian thrillers will find a smooth, tense tale of secrets that cannot be undone.
30813-notes-and-queries-number-234-april:
Number 234 of Notes and Queries, dated Saturday, April 22, 1854, and priced at fourpence, shows a Victorian weekly at work. The paper called itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, and it invited readers to send notes and ask questions. No single author stands behind it; its strength lay in its many contributors.

This issue mixes notes on Whitefield and Kennington Common, anachronisms, epitaphs, and the Rigby correspondence with queries on Genesis, Roland the Brave, and clay tobacco pipes. Minor notes touch tippets, Arthuriana, and Lady Jane Grey. For modern readers it is a lively scrapbook of 1850s antiquarian talk, where a small query could draw an answer from a stranger across Britain.
30901-fee-of-the-frontier:
H. B. Fyfe wrote this science fiction story, printed in Amazing Stories in August 1960, with pictures by Emsh. Its tagline frames the theme: the settlers did not think of themselves as pioneers, but simply had a job to do. Money, power, love, or life counted as part of that frontier price when settlers had to surrender them. Fyfe tells the tale from inside a Mars dome, where Deimos and Phobos shine in the night sky.

Outside, past the developed strip around the dome, the desert lies chilled and brittle as it did for ages before Earthmen reached Mars. A walker pulls furs around his nose and checks his oxygen mask. Early on, every supply arrived by rocket from Earth, until chemistry learned to convert crops grown on Mars into food. It is a nostalgic story of the men who opened Mars, told by one who knew them.
30902-expediter:
Mack Reynolds wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog in May 1963, about a man whose assignment is to get things done. He does so, though not quite in the way intended. Josip Pekic hears a knock at his door late in the middle of the night, as he always thought he would. He was only four when a knock first came, and three large men gave his father only minutes to dress and go with them.

The days of the police state are said to be over, the cult of personality past, the five-year and seven-year plans finished, and a new constitution guaranteeing personal liberties. So they tell you, Reynolds says, but fears die hard, above all fears learned in childhood. The story follows Pekic through a state that promises freedom while its old habits linger, with dry irony throughout.
30907-rosemary-in-search-of-a-father:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote this 1907 novel for McClure, Phillips in New York, with pictures by William Hatherell and decorations by Thomas Maitland Cleland. It is dedicated to Minda, and its frontispiece shows Evelyn and Rosemary climbing hand in hand while Hugh carries two huge baskets. The story's title gives its quest: Rosemary in search of a father.

Nine chapters move from the white girl on the terrace and the rose girl at the casino, through the rose girl's little story, dogs and fathers, and fairy fathers who must vanish. They end with a white figure at the door and the last word of Mademoiselle. The Williamsons mix romance, travel, and mystery, with a light, theatrical touch. Readers who enjoy Edwardian popular fiction will find a sweet, lively tale of a girl seeking her past.
30960-the-people-of-the-crater:
Andrew North wrote this complete novelette about a hidden land and a prophecy, with Garin as its hero. Its tagline sets Garin three tasks: send the Black Throne to dust, conquer the Black Ones, and bring the Daughter from the Caves of Darkness. Those tasks fulfill the prophecy of the Ancient Ones and settle his destiny. The tale opens six months and three days after a Peace of Shanghai ended a great war of 1965 to 1970.

In New York a young man, trained only to fly a fighting plane, sits on a park bench in worn shoes, his search for civilian work having cost him health and ambition. A stranger, compact and alert despite middle age, recognizes him as Captain Garin Featherstone and shows a clipping from his wartime service. North follows Garin from that bench into a crater world of ancient powers, in a brisk adventure of fate and courage.
30964-the-ethical-engineer:
Harry Harrison wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog Science Fact and Fiction in July and August 1963, with pictures by John Schoenherr. Its opening question asks whether mores are strictly a matter of local custom, and whether ethics is pure opinion also, with times for murder, theft, and slavery. Its epigraph, from Alexander Pope's Essay on Man, says all nature is but art unknown to thee, and all partial evil, universal good.

The story opens with Jason dinAlt looking unhappily at two stretchers carried by, asking if they are at it again. Brucco nods, his scowl permanently ingrained on his hawklike face, thankful only that so far they have not used weapons on each other. Jason, seeing shredded clothing, crushed flesh, and broken bones, doubts that bare hands could do such damage. It is a sharp story about ethics, custom, and violence on an alien world.
30972-take-the-reason-prisoner:
John J. McGuire wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog Science Fact and Fiction in November 1963, with pictures by George Schelling. Its tagline warns that no process is perfect, though some men always feel unalterably convinced that their system is the be-all and end-all. Psychology now, it says, should make prisons absolutely escape-proof and cure all aberrations. The story tests that confidence.

Its hero is Major General, retired, James J. Bennington, who feels both deep professional admiration and personal distaste. It is a sharp story about prisons, psychology, and power.
30981-the-real-latin-quarter:
F. Berkeley Smith wrote this 1901 book on the real Latin Quarter of Paris, published by Funk and Wagnalls in New York in November 1901. It has pictures by the author and an introduction and frontispiece by F. Hopkinson Smith. A front watercolor shows the gardens of the Luxembourg, drawn by Hopkinson Smith in Paris in 1901. Berkeley Smith writes as a visitor who knows the quarter's streets, cafés, and studios.

Ten chapters move from the Rue Vaugirard and the Boulevard St. Michel through the Bal Bullier and the Bal des Quat'z Arts to a déjeuner at Lavenue's, Marcel Legay's, Pochard, the Luxembourg Gardens, the ragged edge of the quarter, and exile. It is a lively, first-hand sketch of student Paris at the turn of the century, full of artists, dancers, and the daily life of the Left Bank.
31024-mine-pumping-in-agricola-s-time-an:
Robert P. Multhauf, curator of science and technology at the Museum of History and Technology in the Smithsonian's United States National Museum, wrote this paper on mine pumping in Agricola's time and later. It appeared as Contributions from the Museum of History and Technology, paper 7. Elaborately detailed mining landscapes on sixteenth-century German coins in the National Museum, found by the curator of numismatics, led Multhauf to this study of early mine-pumping devices.

Multhauf argues that heavy reliance on a single source has drastically over-simplified the history of medieval and Renaissance mining techniques in Europe. That condition still appears in recent accounts by Parsons, Wolf, and Bromehead. Preoccupation with Agricola, well known in English since the Hoovers' translation of 1912, has inhibited study of the machines he describes so elegantly. It is a sharp revision of a familiar story, grounded in coins and machines.
3110-the-american-newspaper:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote The American Newspaper as an address on the press and its place in American life. Warner notes that everybody is interested in newspapers, and that although many cannot pay for one, he never heard of anybody unable to edit one. The theme has many points of view, but his hour allows one only, a philosophical inquiry into the press's relations to complex modern life. Warner contrasts instant telegraph news of an assassination in India or a landslide in Switzerland.

Slow reporting of vast movements such as the Wahabee revival, which may change provinces, yet never reaches the wires, forms the other half. The daily paper, he argues, favors event over movement. The address remains a prescient critique of news values, still quoted by media historians.
31101-spenser:
R. W. Church, Dean of St. Paul's, wrote this 1879 life of Edmund Spenser for Macmillan's English Men of Letters series, drawing on state papers on Ireland, the Carew manuscripts, and Arber's reprints. Six chapters follow Spenser from early life between 1552 and 1579 through the Shepherd's Calendar of 1579 and his years in Ireland from 1580. They continue through the two parts of The Faery Queene, down to his last years in the 1590s.

Church writes without footnotes, as the series required, but with the care of a scholar who had mined the archives. The result is a compact, readable life of England's great allegorical poet, balancing the poetry against the Irish service that shaped and shadowed his career.
31223-infinite-intruder:
Alan E. Nourse's story, printed in Space Science Fiction in July 1953, follows Roger Strang, an engineer on the Barrier Base, whose son David keeps narrowly escaping death. The first monowheel crash looks like a boy's accident, and David's claim that he never left the slow lane sounds like a fib. Then Roger himself watches the second attempt and sees with horrible clarity that someone is trying to kill his son.

As diplomatic relations with the Eurasian Combine worsen and Barrier work reaches a critical stage, Strang's investigation of the attacks turns into an investigation of his own life. Tense and twist-driven, the story asks what a father does when the danger to his child comes from a past he has not faced.
3125-the-complete-essays-of-charles-dudl:
This 1904 Backlog Edition volume gathers Warner's essays in full. Its contents run from As We Were Saying and Rose and Chrysanthemum to The Red Bonnet and The Loss in Civilization. Social Screaming, Does Refinement Kill Individuality, and The Directoire Gown follow. The Clothes of Fiction, A Chew of Gum, Women in Congress, and Shall Women Propose sit among them.

Frocks and the Stage, Altruism, Social Clearing-House, Dinner-Table Talk, and Art of Governing round out the range. Together the pieces show Warner as a critic of manners at ease with large themes and small ones. One page weighs a gown, the next weighs government, and the same clear voice carries both.
31279-a-review-of-hoffman-s-race-traits-:
Kelly Miller's 1897 review, number one in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, answers Frederick L. Hoffman's Race Traits and Tendencies of the American Negro, published in August 1896 under the American Economic Association. Hoffman, statistician to the Prudential Insurance Company, had spent ten years in laborious investigation and claimed that his German birth freed him from personal bias.

Miller grants the work's thoroughness, calling it the most important statistical utterance on the subject since Uncle Tom's Cabin stirred sentiment. He argues that freedom from conscious bias does not save an author from partiality to his own opinions beyond their warrant. The review is a landmark of Black scholarly criticism, meeting statistics with statistics.
31359-notes-and-queries-number-235-april:
Number 235 of Notes and Queries, dated Saturday, April 29, 1854 and priced fourpence, continues the journal's work as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Notes in this issue cover a curious old pamphlet, errata in printed Bibles, impossibilities of history, unregistered proverbs, Mr. Justice Talfourd, the screw propeller, ancient chattel-property in Ireland, and Bishop Atterbury.

Minor notes, queries, queries with answers, and replies follow, with photographic correspondence on collodion, printing positives, and photographic excursions. As always, the issue's motto from Captain Cuttle applies: when found, make a note of it. The number is a window into mid-Victorian antiquarian conversation.
31367-the-training-of-a-forester:
Gifford Pinchot's 1914 book, published by Lippincott in Philadelphia and London with eight illustrations and dedicated to Overton W. Price, explains what a forester is and how one is trained. Forestry, Pinchot writes, is the knowledge of the forest. More exactly, it means managing a forest to supply any needed service, saw logs, telegraph poles, or anything else, while keeping the forest itself undamaged and productive.

Chapters cover the forest and the nation, the forester's point of view, the establishment of forestry, the Forest Service and its supervisors, and personal equipment. They go on to state forest work, the service in Washington, private forestry, forest schools, and training itself. Written by the first chief of the Forest Service, the book is both a career guide and a statement of conservation's founding creed.
31391-an-isle-in-the-water:
Katharine Tynan, writing as Mrs. H. A. Hinkson, published An Isle in the Water in London and New York in 1896, dedicating it to Jane Barlow. The collection's contents include "The First Wife," "The Story of Father Anthony O'Toole," "The Unlawful Mother," "A Rich Woman," and "How Mary Came Home." Each story stands alone, yet together they form a portrait of a community told through its women, priests, and families.

Tynan's stories mix tenderness with moral seriousness, and their titles hint at the domestic dramas within: marriages, mothers, and homecomings. Readers of late Victorian short fiction will find the author's characteristic sympathy for ordinary people. The book is a quiet, humane collection, rooted in the world Tynan knew best.
3146-two-on-a-tower:
Hardy sets this love story on a lonely tower where the stars are watched night after night. Swithin St Cleeve, a young astronomer, meets Lady Constantine, and their shared vigils under the sky turn into affection. A quotation from Crashaw on love's horoscope stands at the head of the book, and a map of Wessex marks its country.

The tower itself shapes the plot: a place apart, high above parish talk, where science and feeling meet. Class, marriage law, and a young man's hopes for his work press on the pair from below. Fate here works through small choices, not grand crimes, and tenderness carries more weight than villainy.
31470-john-march-southerner:
George W. Cable's novel John March, Southerner, published by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York in 1894, follows its title character through a Southern life. Its contents open with "Suez," "To a Good Boy," and "Two Friends," then follow the judge's son as he makes two lifelong acquaintances and is offered a third. Later chapters bring the master's homecoming, trouble, exodus, seven years of sunshine, Launcelot Halliday, Fannie, and a bleeding heart.

Cable, a leading Southern novelist of his generation, writes of a South remaking itself after the Civil War, with old loyalties and new choices in tension. John March stands at the center of that world, as son, friend, and citizen. Readers of American regional fiction will find a long, humane novel of character and place, told with Cable's ear for Southern speech and society.
31526-life-of-wagner:
Louis Nohl's Life of Wagner, translated from the German by George P. Upton, was published in Chicago by Jansen, McClurg and Company in 1884, as part of the Biographies of Musicians series. The series also offered lives of Mozart, Beethoven, and Haydn, each from Nohl's German, at one dollar and twenty-five cents. Nohl's Wagner volume follows the composer from youth to fame, through the operas that remade German music.

Upton's translation brings Nohl's clear, popular biography to American readers. The book treats Wagner as poet and musician together, with attention to his theories as well as his works. Readers seeking a short nineteenth-century life of Wagner will find this volume a useful starting point, written before the composer's legend hardened into myth.
3162-the-enchanted-typewriter:
John Kendrick Bangs explains this book with a strange fact he cannot account for. Over six months, between midnight and four in the morning, pages evolved themselves from a typewriting machine, though he does not claim to romance. The machine, it seems, took dictation from the shades, and Bangs merely found the copy in the morning.

The typewriter's ghosts supply the tales that follow, in Bangs's light, witty manner. The device lets a living author lend his machine to the dead, and the dead prove chatty. Readers who enjoy A House-Boat on the Styx will feel at home: the same comic underworld, now reached through an office machine after dark.
31635-the-silent-barrier:
Louis Tracy's novel The Silent Barrier, illustrated by J. V. McFall, was published at New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with copyright in 1908 and 1911 by Edward J. Clode. Its first chapter, The Wish, opens at a letter window, where a clerk sorts a batch of correspondence for a man who gives his name as Charles K. Spencer. The second chapter is called The Fulfillment of the Wish.

Tracy's novel builds on that opening, as a wish made in the first chapter works itself out in the chapters that follow. The book is a romance of its period, and its frontispiece shows a man asking a Miss Wynton to spare him one moment.
31735-the-psilent-partner:
Edward S. Staub and John Victor Peterson's short story was printed in Fantastic Universe in March 1954. It follows a probing mind with strange powers, one of the widely talented psis, espers, and telepaths of science-fiction forecast. Its hero casts his consciousness far, floating high above New York and seeing the thin crescent of a waning moon.

The tale's playful title points to its Wall Street turn: a mind that crosses state lines, seas, and sky to bring something new to the market. Readers get a light story of mental powers used for speculation, afraid of subway tunnels yet bold enough to dream of the moon.
31736-star-performer:
Robert J. Shea's Star Performer, illustrated by Dick Francis, appeared in If for September 1960. Its tagline boasts Blue Boy's high rating and fans loyal to the death, anyone's death. The story opens as Gavir gingerly fits the round opening of a silvery globe over his hairless blue skull, feeling tiny filaments touch his scalp, cold at their tips.

The moderator announces that Dreaming Through the Universe tonight brings Gavir of the Desert Men, the first native Martian on the dreamwaves, with Dr. Malcomb Rice, his guardian and a noted anthropologist. Shea's story turns a Martian dream broadcast into a star turn, with loyal fans and a nervous performer.
31745-wau-nan-gee-or-the-massacre-at-chi:
Major Richardson's Wau-Nan-Gee, or The Massacre at Chicago, a romance of the American Revolution, was published at New York by H. Long and Brother, entered in 1852. Richardson was already the author of Wacousta, Hardscrabble, Ecarte, Jack Brag in Spain, and Tecumseh. His prefatory inscription says the text stays so close to historical fact that only Maria Heywood is strictly invented.

The novel joins the Chicago massacre to a romance of the revolutionary age, in Richardson's manner of history close told. It is a tale of frontier violence and personal fate, written by a soldier-novelist who knew the border country he described.
31765-my-lady-of-the-chimney-corner:
Alexander Irvine's My Lady of the Chimney Corner was published in August 1913 by The Century Company. Dedicated to Lady Gregory and the players of the Abbey Theatre, Dublin, it is subtitled a story of love and poverty in Irish peasant life. Its ten chapters include Love Is Enough, The Wolf and the Carpenter, Rehearsing for the Show, and Sunday in Pogue's Entry.

The opening finds old Bridget McGrady and Mrs. Tierney on a doorstep after early mass, watching Mrs. Gilmore pass with five-year-old Anna, a favorite child in a pink dress with a blue ribbon. Readers get a tender portrait of a County Antrim farm family, hardworking and poor, held together by faith, talk, and love.
31767-the-peacemaker:
Alfred Coppel's short story The Peacemaker tells, as its headnote puts it, the true story of Jaq Merril, the pirate benefactor of mankind. It sets that story against the legends that made him a one-dimensional figure of folklore. Coppel opens by arguing that humans are a strange breed, unique among the races met among the stars, because only human beings thrive on deliberate self-delusion.

Legends, he says, are our strength, and they will drive a man to the rim of the galaxy and across the gulfs toward the suns of Andromeda. Readers get a space adventure that plays legend against history, following a pirate whose real deeds were stranger than the myths that daubed him with rouge.
31772-si-klegg-book-2-thru-the-stone-riv:
John McElroy's second Si Klegg book appeared in its second edition of 1910. It follows the raw recruit Si Klegg and his partner Shorty through the Stone River campaign and winter quarters at Murfreesboro. The 200th Indiana marches south from Nashville through mud and rain after Christmas 1862, expecting a battle that will end the war.

Twenty-two chapters carry the pair from the march and the battle of Stone River to victory, winter quarters, and the arrival of Deacon Klegg, whose blunders add comedy to camp life. Readers get a Civil War tale that mixes battle narrative with humor about green soldiers learning army ways.
31776-si-klegg-book-6-si-and-shorty-with:
John McElroy's sixth Si Klegg book, in its second edition of 1915, puts Si and Shorty in charge of boy recruits entering the Atlanta campaign. Shorty begins by acting as a father to Pete Skidmore, and the partners nearly lose their boys before getting back to their regiment at last.

Twenty chapters follow drills, marches, skirmishes, foraging lessons, and the fighting around Buzzard Roost, ending with the pair under arrest and Shorty before a court-martial. Readers get a Civil War story that pairs battle narrative with the comedy and worry of older soldiers training raw young recruits.
31782-the-poniard-s-hilt-or-karadeucq-an:
Eugene Sue's tale of Bagauders is part of the series The Mysteries of the People, or History of a Proletarian Family Across the Ages. It follows the age when Clovis invaded Gaul and feudalism began to take hold in France. Its four parts are The Korrigans, The Vagres, The Burg of Neroweg, and Ghilde, with an epilogue.

Chapters move from fairies and hobgoblins and a peddler named Hevin to bishops and counts, vagres in judgment, a treasure chamber, and the death of Chram. Readers get a sweeping historical romance that uses one family's story to trace how a whole social order was born.
31791-training-the-teacher:
Training the Teacher, copyrighted in 1908 by the Sunday School Times Company and approved as a first standard course by the International Sunday School Association, was written by A. F. Schauffler, Antoinette Abernethy Lamoreaux, Martin G. Brumbaugh, and Marion Lawrance, with supplementary chapters by Charles A. Oliver and Ira Maurice Price. It organizes and conducts a teacher-training class.

Its sections cover the book, how the Bible came to us, the gist of the books, and the pupil. They also cover the teacher, with lesson questions on patriarchal, Mosaic, and later periods of Bible history. Readers get a practical Sunday-school training manual, built for classes that needed both Bible knowledge and teaching method.
31816-the-history-of-the-medical-departm:
Doctor Robert Peter's History of the Medical Department of Transylvania University was prepared for publication by his daughter Johanna Peter. Published at Louisville in 1905 as Filson Club Publication Number 20, it traces a famous Kentucky medical school. Its illustrations portray Peter himself and professors Samuel Brown, Benjamin W. Dudley, James Overton, Daniel Drake, and Charles Caldwell.

The narrative sets the school against Kentucky's struggle for railroads, where hill and valley, streams, and hard rock made building expensive. Lexington, though it had the first railroad in the West, saw it run only to Frankfort for years. Readers get an institutional history of medicine in the Ohio Valley, from rise and success to decline and disappearance.
31837-little-wolf-a-tale-of-the-western-:
Mrs. M. A. Cornelius's Little Wolf, a tale of the western frontier entered for copyright in 1872 and published at Cincinnati, opens on a long-ago midsummer morning in a quiet New England home. The mistress oversees the table with mingled interest and abstraction. Her maid of more than twenty years, adept in the kitchen if not in affairs of the heart, tries a word of comfort.

Chapters follow the Sherman family, a sad breakfast and a parting, Pendleton and a revelation at the saloon, Bloody Jim, and Little Wolf's allies preparing for defense. Readers get a frontier melodrama of family trouble, highwaymen, and defense, written in the sentimental manner of its day.
31841-the-water-eater:
Win Marks's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in June 1953, is narrated by a beer-truck driver who has just lost a weekend and is not too anxious to find it. He had planned to go fishing with McCarthy and the boys, but by almost noon Monday he has not turned a wheel.

Instead of fishing, bowling, poker, or taking the children to the amusement park, he has lost sleep over an experiment. His friends at the Elks' Club say he has an inquiring mind. Readers get a comic science-fiction tale, told in a working man's voice, about an experiment that worked too well, as its headnote warns.
31869-the-lamplighter:
Maria S. Cummins's novel The Lamplighter, published in New York by A. L. Burt, opens on a chilly November evening in the city, where dusk has already fallen in the streets, though the open country would stay light half an hour more. On the wooden doorstep of a low-roofed, dark, unwholesome house sits a little girl, gazing earnestly up the street.

The girl is clad in the poorest garments, her hair long, thick, and uncombed, her face thin and sallow. Her fine dark eyes are large against her puny face, and no one in the world cares for her. Readers get a beloved American sentimental novel, whose first chapter, Light in Darkness, promises that a lamplighter will bring light to a neglected child.
31950-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This volume of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica covers the alphabetical range from Columbus to Condottieri. Its transcriber's notes point to an article on Stapleton Cotton, Lord Combermere, who in 1852 succeeded Wellington as constable of the Tower and lord lieutenant of the Tower Hamlets.

Its pages also discuss the compass, the magnetized needle floated on cork, the Italian name calamita, and the simple water-compass used by Koreans into the middle of the eighteenth century. Readers get a volume of the great encyclopedia where exploration, science, and biography sit side by side in alphabetical order.
32028-the-battle-of-stone-river:
Major Henry M. Kendall of the United States Army prepared this paper on the Battle of Stone River for the Military Order of the Loyal Legion. It appeared as War Paper number 49 of the Commandery of the District of Columbia, and Kendall read it at its stated meeting on November 4, 1903. Like other Loyal Legion papers, it is a veteran's staff-style account, written for fellow officers rather than for a general audience.

Kendall begins after the Battle of Perryville on October 8, 1862, with a leisurely Union pursuit of Bragg's retreating forces toward Cumberland Gap. No engagement followed, and it soon became clear that Bragg would withdraw into Tennessee, join the force left watching Nashville, and concentrate near that city. General Buell therefore broke off the pursuit and turned toward Nashville. Readers get a careful, movement-by-movement lead-up to the Stone River fighting.
32039-the-third-day-at-stone-s-river:
Lieutenant-Colonel Gilbert C. Kniffin of the United States Volunteers prepared this paper on the third day at Stone's River for the Military Order of the Loyal Legion. It appeared as War Paper number 69 of the Commandery of the District of Columbia, and Kniffin read it at its stated meeting on May 1, 1907. Like its companion papers, it speaks from inside the Union army's experience, with officers' names and movements given in full.

Kniffin opens by recalling the first day's fight, when the Union commander hurled hard-hitting brigades of the left and centre against Hardee's advance. He praises Thomas, calm and brave, superintending every move like a tower of strength, and Crittenden, cheerful even amid carnage, bringing regiment after regiment to the threatened point. Readers who follow the Stone River papers in order will find this one the close of the sequence, focused on the battle's final day.
32042-captain-macedoine-s-daughter:
William McFee's 1920 novel Captain Macedoine's Daughter, published by Doubleday, Page and Company in Garden City, opens aboard H. M. S. Sycorax, patrolling the Aegean Archipelago under convoy escort. None of the men in deck chairs are surprised to hear the Chief say he had known Ipsilon in peace-time. He alone had truly wandered the face of the waters.

Its epigraph, from Mr. Spenlove, calls it an amiable but disastrous illusion of the western nations that they have created a monopoly in freedom and truth and the right conduct of life. Readers get a sea novel of the eastern Mediterranean, war patrols, and a captain's daughter, by the author of Casuals of the Sea.
32043-army-of-the-cumberland-and-the-bat:
Lieutenant-Colonel Gilbert C. Kniffin of the United States Volunteers prepared this companion paper to his account of the third day at Stone's River. It appeared as War Paper number 68 of the Commandery of the District of Columbia, Military Order of the Loyal Legion. Kniffin read it at its stated meeting on April 3, 1907. Where the later paper focuses on one day, this one gives the army's background and the campaign that led to the battle.

Kniffin follows the Army of the Ohio through the summer of 1862. In six weeks, it crowded in more hard marching and fighting than any other American army that season. By the last of October, it lay encamped near Bowling Green, Kentucky. Bragg and Kirby Smith had invaded Kentucky, threatened Louisville, and then slipped away through Cumberland Gap after Perryville. Readers get the strategic frame for Stone River, told by a veteran officer.
32087-the-executioner:
Frank Riley's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in April 1956, makes public execution a popular spectacle. Its hero is Sir Jacques de Carougne, Lord High Executioner for the Seventh Judicial District. A vote has gone three to two for death, and Jacques, a public servant with a duty, has no choice. Reports promise more than a hundred thousand spectators by court time, with all unreserved tent space sold out for days.

Jacques travels by single-seater rocket and misses his vidcasts during a vacation, but after a thousand executions, he says, everything is instinct and reflex. Some condemned die hard, and some die easy. Some fall to their knees, too paralysed with fear to fire their own shots, while others fight daringly. The story's chill lies in that routine: death as entertainment, handled by a professional who treats it as ordinary work.
32166-thomas-andrews-shipbuilder:
Shan F. Bullock's Thomas Andrews, Shipbuilder, with an introduction by Sir Horace Plunkett, was published in Dublin and London by Maunsel and Company in 1912. First and second editions both date from October 1912. Bullock dedicates his brief story of Andrews's life to the men with whom Andrews worked, who knew and loved him. A Wordsworth epigraph speaks of those summoned to the deep, to keep an incommunicable sleep.

Its illustrations follow Andrews from Ardara, Comber, through Harland and Wolff's turbine erecting shop and turning shop. They continue to the Titanic and Olympic building in the largest gantry in the world, and the Titanic leaving Belfast. The opening chapter notes six generations of the Andrews family. Readers get a short, affectionate life of the Belfast shipbuilder behind the Titanic and Olympic, written by a friend of his workmates.
32230-wainer:
Michael Shaara's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in April 1954, is told by the oldest man alive to beings who are not human. Its sidenote holds that life has a meaning, though sometimes it takes a lifetime to learn what it is. The man in the purple robe is too old to walk or stand. He is wheeled on a purple bench into a room, where beings not human, called They in the story, have gathered and waited.

The old man commands respect, but he is nervous before Them, speaking apologetically, sometimes irritably, because he cannot understand what They are thinking. No one anywhere is as old, the story notes. An old man's worth lies less in lessons learned than in people known. This old man had known Wainer, and so he speaks, telling Them both what he knew and what he had guessed.
32236-the-story-of-the-trapper:
A. C. Laut's The Story of the Trapper, in the Story of the West series edited by Ripley Hitchcock and published by D. Appleton and Company in New York, tells the trapper's part in opening the West. Laut, author of Heralds of Empire, joins companion volumes. They cover the railroad by Cy Warman, the cowboy by E. Hough, the mine by Charles Howard Shinn, the Indian by George Bird Grinnell, and the soldier by George A. Forsyth.

Its frontispiece shows a trapper with eye and ear alert, paddling silently on. Readers get the fur trapper's world: canoes, traplines, and the wilderness trade that preceded settlement. The series format, illustrated and uniform at a dollar and a quarter net, presents each western figure in turn. The trapper's volume stands as the wilderness scout of the set, silent, watchful, and alone on the water.
32249-the-princess-and-joe-potter:
James Otis's The Princess and Joe Potter was illustrated by Violet Oakley and published in Boston by Estes and Lauriat in 1898. It is a children's adventure of a boy, a lost little girl, and a detective. Its contents run from A Ruined Merchant and The Princess through An Advertisement and Joe's Flight. They continue to In the City, Dan the Detective, Aunt Dorcas, and A Hungry Detective. A Fugitive, The Journey, A Bribe, and A Struggle in the Night lead to A Confession. A Ray of Light and The Reward close the book.

The frontispiece shows Joe finding the princess, and later pictures show him feeding the little maid, Dan pointing to an advertisement, and Joe pointing to a tiny cottage. Readers get a late Victorian boys' adventure, where a runaway boy shelters a child, a detective hunts them, and kindness, flight, and confession drive the plot toward a reward.
32309-practical-high-school-speller:
Tobias O. Chew's Practical High School Speller, compiled by the superintendent of city schools at Washburn, Wisconsin, was published by Allyn and Bacon in Boston, New York, and Chicago in 1914. It is a spelling textbook for high-school pupils. Chew dedicates it to superintendents, principals, and teachers whose cooperation made the book possible. Its opening rules are few, meant to be learned by heart.

When ei and ie sound like long e, Chew explains, c is followed by ei and all other letters by ie. Examples are ceiling, receive, siege, and believe, with exceptions leisure, seize, and weird. The word slice helps pupils remember. It gives i after l and e after c, in believe and receive. A final y after a consonant turns to i before most suffixes, except those beginning with i, as busy to business and dry to dried. Readers get a school speller, rule by rule.
32327-the-seventh-order:
Jerry Sohl's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in March 1952, brings an invincible conqueror from space to an Earth pasture. Its sidenote says history is filled with invincible conquerors, and this one from space was genuinely omnipotent, but that never keeps humanity from resisting. A silver needle moves with fantastic speed, slows near the air shell around Earth, then glides noiselessly through the atmosphere.

It settles gently to the ground near a wood and lies silent and still for a long time, a lifeless silver cylinder, streamlined, eight feet long and three feet across. Eventually the cap end opens and a creature of bright blue metal slides out and stands upright, a man's figure except that it is not human. A bird's sound turns its shiny blue head toward the wood, and its eyes begin glowing. Readers get an invasion tale, where omnipotence meets resistance.
32353-the-mind-digger:
Winston Marks's story, printed in Imagination in April 1958, follows a playwright whose scripts are smash hits because they are real. Its sidenote says his scripts were smash hits because they had realism: he was reliving every scene and emotion in them. The narrator, producer, needs a play, when every playwright is in France, Hollywood, or a slump.

He asks Ellie to bring the unknown to his office with a contract ready. When she announces him, his door bangs open and a youngster in jeans, a sweatshirt, and a stubbly crew cut pops in like a wayward champagne cork. The producer tries to send him away, saying he has an interview now and they are not casting yet. I am your interview, the youngster announces: I am Hillary Hardy, and your girl said you would see me. Readers get a story of a playwright who relives his plays.
3238-poems-of-cheer:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox gathers her cheerful verse in this 1914 Gay and Hancock volume. The book holds the poems published as Poems of Life, all but about half a dozen, which appear in her other volumes. A few new verses join them. Wilcox notes that any edition of her poems published in Great Britain should follow this text.

The poems preach courage, hope, and good humor in plain, musical lines. Wilcox, famous for Laugh and the world laughs with you, writes for readers who want verse to lift a day rather than darken it. The collection's long popularity testifies to its audience: ordinary readers who kept her books by the bedside and quoted them to friends.
32394-the-torch-bearer:
Reina Melcher Marquis's novel, published in New York and London in 1914, opens at the Shadyville Seminary for Young Ladies on a Friday afternoon in April. Peter Burnett, a poor young schoolmaster and a Burnett of Kentucky, closes the seminary door with relief, glad to be freed from his bread-winning duties for the weekend. Though he values scholarship deeply, he has never duly valued his post as instructor to Shadyville's feminine youth.

Dressed in a much-darned shirt, Peter descends the broad white steps with an air of leisure and arrogance, ready to spread his wings for his own inclinations. From that opening, the novel follows a young teacher torn between duty, pride, and the wider world he longs to enter. Marquis writes with wit about southern manners, school life, and a young man's search for a calling.
32407-fair-and-warmer:
E. G. Von Wald's tale, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in July 1954, follows Tensor, an alien whose spells of melancholy threaten the whole citizenry. When Tensor gazes at mist falling from a hazy, violet sky, his administrator Ruut protests that lichens and other growths will soon cover the Prime's fine landscapes. Tensor cannot control the spells, and his distress is treated as a public nuisance rather than a private mood.

The remedy, the story suggests, is to let Tensor investigate the peculiar aliens who have stirred his curiosity until he is fully satisfied. Only inquiry, not scolding, can cure him, and the cure may teach him more than he bargained for. Von Wald turns a comic alien ailment into a fable about curiosity, mood, and the cost of keeping feelings tidy.
32428-the-brightener:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson's novel The Brightener, published in Garden City and Toronto in 1921, opens with a note from A. M. Williamson explaining why she keeps her late husband's initials on the title page. She feels he helps her work even more now than in life, having given her his notes from their motor tours and his advice. The firm name, she writes, could not be dropped without loss.

Book One, The Yacht, begins with chapters titled Down and Out, Up and In, and Thunderbolt Six, promising motor, sea, and society adventure. The Williamsons, known for motor-tour romances, mix travel, romance, and light mystery. Readers who enjoy early motoring fiction and bright, upper-class heroines will find this volume in their familiar, entertaining manner.
32457-pioneer:
William Hardy's tale, printed in Imagination in February 1953, is narrated by a dog trained by a man named Max. The story opens on a nervous morning when Max fastens broad leather straps over the dog's body, his hand trembling at the buckles. After breakfast and a bath, Max loads the dog into a car, even letting him stick his head out the window, before a large brick building full of strange smells swallows them.

Inside, a doctor pokes the dog's mouth, shines light in his eyes, and prods his body, while women in white uniforms fuss over his eighty pounds of blue-grey bulk. Hardy frames the tale with a monument raised a few years hence to a brave deed, inviting readers to guess what deed a dog could do. The story's humour comes from a proud, grumbling narrator facing honours he never sought.
32461-the-scarlet-banner:
Felix Dahn's novel The Scarlet Banner, translated from German by Mary J. Safford and published in Chicago in 1903, opens before the war with a letter to Cornelius Cethegus Caesarius, a friend. The narrator sends notes rather than to any other man, partly because he does not know where Cethegus is, so the letter will probably be lost. That loss, he jokes, might spare the reader these pages, while suiting the writer just as well.

Dedicated to Karl Hase of Jena, the novel takes epigraphs from Sallust on kingdoms kept only by the virtues that founded them, and from Hamlet on a noble mind overthrown. Book One, Before the War, sets up a Roman world of loyalty, ambition, and coming conflict. Dahn writes with the same grand historical sweep as in his other translated novels.
32506-notes-and-queries-number-228-march:
Notes and Queries, number two hundred and twenty-eight, dated Saturday, March 11, 1854, served as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Priced fourpence, with a stamped edition at fivepence, it opens by asking where wills are to be deposited. Notes follow on J. R. of Cork, marmortinto or sand-painting, and a soldier's discipline from a broadside of 1642.

Minor notes treat materials for a history of Druidism and domestic chapels. They also cover Thom's Irish Almanac for 1854, the antiquity of the word snub, Charles I at Little Woolford, and a feather in your cap. Queries ask about domestic architecture and licences to crenellate, Dixon of Beeston, the Atherstone family, and classic authors and the Jews. The issue offers a compact sample of mid-Victorian scholarly correspondence.
32555-the-club-at-crow-s-corner:
James Otis's Club at Crow's Corner, published in Philadelphia in 1915 with illustrations by Isabel W. Caley, follows animal neighbours who form a club in the big woods. Chapter one introduces Mr. Crow and Mr. Turtle beside a brook winding among alders to a very large, very old oak, whose branches roost feathered inhabitants and shade warm days for all.

Later chapters bring Cheeko in danger, Bunny Rabbit's efforts, Sonny Bunny's peril, a meeting of the club, and Mr. Man's boy Tommy. Cheeko's curiosity, Jimmy Hedgehog's escape, fooling Mr. Fox, Bobby Coon's trick, and Towser and the senator follow, with folly not bravery, disciplining Jimmy, Mr. Crow's plot, and trouble in the club. Otis writes gentle animal tales with clear morals for young readers.
32574-the-telenizer:
Don Thompson's tale, printed in Galaxy in March 1954, opens with a narrator who knows someone has a telenosis beam on him when he sees blood dripping from a bathtub tap. For days he wondered if he was cracking up. He saw visions of a bearded man with a halo, dreamed of a perfect world, felt intense loyalties to undefined ideals, and acted on sudden impulses, cruel and kind. The beam's overplay, he thinks, proves he is not going insane.

If the unseen sender had kept a slow, subtle pace, the narrator admits, he would soon have been won over for whatever purpose was intended. Now he knows something is happening, though not who does it, why, or whether he can stand it even knowing. Thompson builds a tense story of mind control, paranoia, and relief, as a victim names his tormentor's weapon and still cannot escape it.
32637-the-envoy-her:
H. B. Fyfe's The Envoy, Her, printed in Planet Stories in March 1951, opens with an emperor landing on Klo, second moon of Jursa. Despite concentrated patrol defenses, the emperor's space yacht slips down without incident, for the Jursan agitators for a scientific renaissance have at last been beaten to their knees.

Lord Vyrtl, viceroy for Terra and emperor of Pollux and its fourteen planets, comes to a transparent dome built on the airless satellite for his convenience. Weary and cynical beneath his titles, he demands transport and quarters while the rebels on Jursa come to their senses, and Fyfe sets diplomacy against rebellion.
32684-the-invader:
Alfred Coppel tells of a Triomed scout, a scientist of a dying race that needs warm-blooded hosts to live. His tiny craft lands unseen on Earth, and he creeps toward a sleeping man in a dark cell, eager for the rapport and command a host can give.

Earth's native viruses prove primitive, far below his own ancient kin, so the scout presses on and takes over his host. At first the invasion seems easy, but streets, crowds, weapons, and searchlights soon turn the hunter into prey, and the scout must climb for his life.
32702-the-romance-of-the-reaper:
Herbert N. Casson tells the true story of the harvester, dedicated to the farmers of the United States. He calls it a fairy tale of American life, yet every wonder in it rests on iron, work, and trade. The old hand-sickle took three hours of a man's life for each bushel of wheat.

Five chapters follow Cyrus Hall McCormick and William Deering, then the International Harvester Company they helped build. Casson traces American machines abroad, from Siberia to Argentina, and shows how the reaper changed the farmer's day. The book ends as a praise of energy, invention, and honest sale.
32810-the-soldier-turned-farmer:
This Portland primer, published by Bailey and Noyes, teaches children their letters through the world of a farm. Each letter brings a picture and a plain description. A globe almost round like the earth comes first, then a mortar for pounding spice, boots and shoes, and a black hat of wool and fur. A wool sack and a great tree on the Common follow.

Horses, a barrel of cider, a house, a sheep, a chest of tea, and a cow follow in turn. The book closes with the story of a boy who would be a soldier. At four years old he scorned his letters and longed for the drum, dressed fine every day, until farm life claimed him instead.
32835-geraldine-farrar-the-story-of-an-a:
Geraldine Farrar tells her own story as an American singer, published by Houghton Mifflin in March 1916. She offers sketches, not a formal life, jotted in her library, on trains, and under California skies, and dedicates the volume to her mother.

Fourteen chapters move from childhood and the dramatic impulse to her resolve to sing Carmen, her refusal to sing at the Metropolitan, Paris, and Germany as the turning point. In September 1899 she sailed from Boston on the cattle boat Armenian to Liverpool and on to Paris. Later chapters follow imperial encouragement, tours, Berlin, her first New York appearance, and the days she now enjoys.
3285-the-deerslayer:
James Fenimore Cooper opens The Deerslayer with a Byron epigraph from Childe Harold. There is pleasure in the pathless woods, the lines say, and rapture on the lonely shore, with society where none intrudes. The young Natty Bumppo, not yet Hawkeye, steps into that world of lake and forest, among Delaware, Huron, and the white settlers pressing west.

The novel is the first in time of the Leatherstocking Tales, though written last. Deerslayer's code, his first love, and his first killing shape a hero defined by restraint. Cooper writes the frontier as a moral place, where the woods test character daily. Readers meeting Leatherstocking here get his origin: a youth learning to shoot straight and to live straight with it.
32864-bedside-manner:
William Morrison tells of a woman who wakes broken after a spaceship crash, in this story from Galaxy Science Fiction of May 1954, illustrated by Vidmer. At first there is only pain and a feeling of life although she should be dead.

Then she learns the silence is complete because she is deaf, and the blackness deep because she is blind. She cannot move her arms and legs because she has none, and her pains are phantom pains from nerve endings. Fred, her companion, must surely have been killed when an asteroid struck without warning. She must trust an alien doctor, who has never seen a human before, to restore her body and mind.
32866-beyond-the-thunder:
H. B. Hickey opens with the destruction of a city, in a story from Amazing Stories of December 1948. Ten thousand persons in New York look skyward at a rumble, and a flash sears them where they stand; the rest die slowly among rubble. Case Damon knows nothing of it, riding in San Francisco with thoughts of Karin.

A Washington code call pulls him back: a blinding force has come out of a hole in the sky. Case flies his ship at a closing crack in the void, praying his speed will carry him through before it shuts. Beyond the thunder he drops into light, his altimeter reading ninety thousand feet over rolling country. With Burnine he must rig a permanent end to the installation from a tank of atomic fuel, and reach a ship in a hangar beyond the last tower.
32936-an-unknown-lover:
Mrs George de Horne Vaizey opens at a breakfast table in a dim, brown, oak-panelled room, where Katrine Beverley, twenty-six, sits behind the coffee urn in rich blue. Martin, thirty-three, eats his unvarying breakfast of porridge with sugar, bacon and eggs, and marmalade and toast. Katrine nibbles fruit and cream, deep in a fruitarian craze.

The two are not man and wife, though they share the house: Martin is Katrine's brother, and Grizel, the sweetest and kindliest of women in Martin's eyes, completes the household. Grizel insists that Katrine, only just beginning to grow, will become a sweet woman, and asks who Katrine thinks of when she sits smiling into space. Captain Bedford, with his cricket and his 1882 tale of Arabi in Egypt, drifts through their circle. The unknown lover of the title is the question behind Katrine's distant smile.
32980-confessions-of-an-opera-singer:
Kathleen Howard's Confessions of an Opera Singer, published by Alfred A. Knopf in September 1918, tells how a young American singer made her way in European opera. Early chapters cover how it all happened, a struggle and a solution, Paris at last, and pension personalities. They then turn to operatic France versus operatic Germany, preparing roles in Berlin, and her first operatic contract. Later chapters treat her debut, stage delights, and the makings of a small municipal opera house.

Howard writes with humor and candor about salaries, a tenor's genius, misplaced moisture, human passions, smallpox, and discouragements that led to a court theatre. Her confessions give the backstage life of opera, not only its glamour, and they show a woman building a career across languages and borders during a tense period. The book remains a lively memoir for lovers of singing and theater history.
33-the-scarlet-letter:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's 1850 novel opens with a woman on a scaffold in Puritan Boston. Hester Prynne bears a scarlet letter A for adultery and refuses to name her partner. A long custom-house introduction frames the tale as a found manuscript.

Her daughter Pearl grows wild and watchful beside her. Minister Arthur Dimmesdale hides his guilt while Hester's husband, Chillingworth, plots revenge in disguise. The novel weighs sin, shame, and mercy in a closed community. Its letter became a lasting symbol of public judgment. Generations of readers have argued whether Hester's letter marks shame, strength, or both at once.
33004-the-red-rat-s-daughter:
Guy Boothby's Red Rat's Daughter, published in London in 1899 and illustrated by Henry Austin, opens with John Grantham Browne, a man given to cynical wit toward his friends. Browne is worth one hundred and twenty thousand pounds a year, ten thousand a month. His wealth, the narrator suggests, may excuse a little skepticism about other people's motives and a distrust of the world in general. His father, Old Brown, looms behind the fortune.

From that portrait of money and mistrust, Boothby, author of Doctor Nikola and Pharos the Egyptian, builds a sensational romance of the period. The romance has a heroine tied to the red rat of the title and a plot of danger, disguise, and pursuit. The novel moves at the pace of popular melodrama, and its frontispiece shows a rescue at last. It is a period thriller for readers who enjoy Victorian sensation fiction at full tilt.
331-the-mucker:
Edgar Rice Burroughs pairs two serial tales in this volume: The Mucker from 1914 and its sequel, The Return of the Mucker, from 1916. Chicago street tough Billy Byrne starts as a gang hand who knows saloons and police by first name. A chain of crimes and flights then pulls him far from the alleys where he grew up.

Byrne is shanghaied, wrecked, and tested among strangers who judge him by his fists and his nerve. Slowly he learns steadier loyalties and a code beyond the gang. Burroughs keeps the pace fast, with fights, escapes, and last-minute turns, while tracing one rough man toward a harder, better self.
33103-helena-brett-s-career:
Desmond Coke's Helena Brett's Career is billed by its author as an unromantic comedy of married life. It was published in New York in 1913 and dedicated to Arthur Waugh, critic, publisher, and friend. Coke's prefatory postscript warns thin-skinned readers that his author, publisher, and artist do not represent real people. Insisting that such self-centered authors, unscrupulous publishers, and vulgar-minded artists have existed and will exist again, and that a paragon makes poor food for fiction.

Helena Brett's career, then, is the story of a woman navigating a literary world of egos, bargains, and marriages, where talent and temper collide. Coke writes with wit and a touch of malice, and his comedy targets the publishing trade he knew. The novel suits readers who enjoy a sharp, period satire of authors and the people who live off them, told with polish and a raised eyebrow.
33139-gen-cowdin-and-the-first-massachus:
General Cowdin and the First Massachusetts Regiment of Volunteers, printed in Boston in 1864, gives the general's own statement about treatment he received from high officials of Massachusetts. In a preface dated October 1864, Cowdin says friends repeatedly urged him to publish, and he wishes only to state facts simply. He leaves the public to judge whether a man who sacrificed business, home comforts, and friends for his country's defense deserved unkind and ungenerous usage. He signs himself R. C.

Cowdin's account opens in the days just after Sumter fell, with the capital apparently under threat and Cowdin presenting himself to Governor Andrew with an offer of service. The pamphlet is both a regimental record and a personal defense, written while the war was still being fought. For Civil War historians, it preserves a commander's grievances in his own words, and a glimpse of the politics behind a volunteer regiment.
33293-the-great-miss-driver:
Anthony Hope's novel, copyrighted in 1908, centers on the great Miss Driver, a young woman whose looks, wit, and will stir all around her. Its chapters ask what she is like, then follow scrapes, amends, a secret treaty, and a flick of the whip, as suitors and friends try to read her heart. Hope, famed for Tristram of Blent, writes with the light, ironic touch of his best romances.

The tale moves between country houses and open sea, where rapiers and clubs give way to frank talk and sudden turns. Miss Driver herself dominates every scene, by turns charming, proud, and hard to pin down. For readers who enjoy Edwardian comedy of manners with a dash of adventure, the novel offers a bright, well-turned story.
33353-patricia-brent-spinster:
Herbert Jenkins's novel, published in 1918 in a fifteenth printing, follows Patricia Brent, spinster, through indiscretion, revenge, and a lord's promises. Its chapters move from Patricia's indiscretion and the Bonsor-Triggs household to an adventure at the Quadrant Grill-Room, the madness of Lord Peter Bowen, and the intervention of Aunt Adelaide. Lady Tanagra takes a hand before the tale's close.

Jenkins writes with light, comic verve, turning a spinster's life into a romance of wit and nerve. Patricia herself, sharp and spirited, carries every scene. For readers who enjoy Edwardian comedy of manners, Patricia Brent, Spinster offers a bright, fast-moving story, whose many printings show how widely it was loved.
33384-the-story-of-a-red-deer:
J. W. Fortescue's Story of a Red Deer, published in 1897, tells the life of a stag from a deer's own point of view. Its chapters follow the animal through seasons, herds, and hunts, with an epistle dedicatory to a friend that frames the tale. Fortescue, writing for readers who love the countryside, gives the deer a voice that is both natural and touching.

The book's charm lies in its blend of natural history and story, as the red deer faces dogs, guns, and the changing year. Its prose is clear and vivid, suited to young readers and adults alike. For lovers of animal tales, it is a classic of its kind, a short, moving life of a wild creature in a human world.
33425-the-crimson-sweater:
Ralph Henry Barbour's Crimson Sweater, published in 1905, is a school story of sport, loyalty, and fair play. Barbour, a master of boys' school tales, writes of a hero whose crimson sweater marks him on the field, where games test character as much as skill. The book belongs to a long shelf of Barbour school novels, loved by generations of young readers.

The story's charm lies in its vivid school life, its football scenes, and its lessons on teamwork and honor. Its tone is wholesome and brisk, suited to boys and to adults who remember school days. For fans of classic school fiction, The Crimson Sweater offers a bright, old-fashioned tale of a boy earning his colors.
33437-cyclopedia-of-telephony-and-telegr:
The Cyclopedia of Telephony and Telegraphy, volume two, is a general reference work on phones, stations, party lines, safety, switchboards, auto systems, power plants, and telegraphy, and wireless. Prepared by a corps of experts for the American School of Correspondence, it opens with a portrait of Thomas A. Edison, pioneer electrical investigator. Its copyright dates run 1911 and 1912.

The volume suits readers of early phone history, offering detailed guidance on systems now long replaced. Its tone is practical, aimed at students and workers in the field. For historians of phones and wires, it is a rich source on how phones and wires were built, run, and fixed a century ago.
33466-the-social-gangster:
Arthur B. Reeve's Social Gangster, in the Craig Kennedy series and copyrighted in 1916, pits the scientific detective against crime in high society. Its frontispiece shows a telegram read in haste and stuffed into a riding habit pocket, just before a departure, a scene that sets the book's tone of secrets and haste. Reeve, famed for Kennedy's use of science to solve crime, writes with brisk, popular verve.

The novel's appeal lies in its mix of society life and detection, as Kennedy applies new methods to old motives like greed and revenge. Its chapters move quickly through clues, labs, and confrontations. For readers who enjoy early scientific mysteries, The Social Gangster offers a bright, fast tale of a detective who trusts evidence over gossip.
33492-the-christian-use-of-the-psalter:
The Reverend A. R. Whitham, principal of Culham Training College, explains how Christians can pray the Psalms with understanding. His short book, published in 1909 as part of the English Churchman's Library, argues that the Christian use of the Psalter is as old as Christianity itself.

Three lectures take up general principles and difficulties, the presence of Christ in the Psalms, and the church's voice within them. An appendix then gives brief suggestions for the use of each psalm in turn, with notes and an index of psalms referred to. The book suits clergy, choir members, and lay readers who want to move beyond reciting the psalms toward praying them thoughtfully.
33546-the-missioner:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's 1907 novel opens with the lady of Thorpe bored by leases and repairs, then widens into a story of agents, hunters, evictions, and London's night side. Book One follows mistress and agent, a hunter and his quarry, summer lightning, a still figure in a chair, and the baying of hounds. Book Two moves to Paris, Mayfair, and a king of the Apaches.

The missioner of the title enters this world of money, crime, and fashion as a figure of conscience and possible salvation. Oppenheim balances melodrama with social observation, and the novel's two books build from country-house intrigue toward a confrontation between preacher and underworld. Fans of Edwardian popular fiction will enjoy its pace and its large, colorful cast.
33570-bill-the-minder:
W. Heath Robinson both wrote and illustrated this 1912 storybook, dedicated to the good children of Chloe and Crispin and to a roll call of young names from Chad to Boadicea. Bill the Minder narrates their ever-wonderful adventures in a series of whimsical tales. These include the King of Troy, the Ancient Mariner, the Triplets, Good Aunt Galladia, the Doctor, the Respectable Gentleman, and the Sicilian char-woman.

Later stories add a real soldier, a wild man, a musician, a lost grocer, a merchant's wife, camp followers, and a siege of Troy. The book mixes fairy-tale invention with gentle jokes about grown-up institutions. Young readers and lovers of classic illustration will enjoy its imagination and its warm, teasing tone.
33604-tony-butler:
Charles James Lever sets this long novel beside the Giant's Causeway on the north coast of Ireland. The opening cottage stands in a cleft between grassy hills, above a coast from the White Rocks to the Causeway. Sandy bays lie between pillared rock walls, with Dunluce in ruin, the fairy bridge of Carrig-a-Rede, and Staffa visible on clear days. Cutting North Sea winds and light sandy soil favor fern and foxglove over trees.

From that cottage, Tony Butler's story unfolds through Lever's characteristic mix of humor, adventure, and social observation. The novel follows its hero through Irish society, soldiering, and romance, with Lever's eye for landscape and character. Readers of Victorian Irish fiction will enjoy its breadth, its coastal scenery, and its leisurely, good-humored storytelling.
33740-ti-ti-pu-a-boy-of-red-river:
J. Macdonald Oxley writes a Canadian frontier adventure in this 1900 Toronto book. The story begins with Thomas Douglas, Earl of Selkirk, persuading fellow countrymen to leave hillside farms and voyage with their families to the rich hunting grounds of the Hudson's Bay Company. Among the emigrants are Andrew Macrae, his wife Kirstie, sturdy son Hector, bonnie daughter Ailie, and two splendid sheepdogs, Dour and Dandy.

Twelve chapters follow the family from the old world to the new, through a bear encounter, a cold plunge, Hector entrapped and searched for, a buffalo hunt, being lost on the prairie. Oxley writes sturdy boys' adventure with attention to settler life. Young readers will enjoy its dogs, hunts, and prairie dangers.
33859-the-old-riddle-and-the-newest-answ:
John Gerard, a Jesuit writer, published this defense of faith against the new science in a fourth edition in 1907. Gerard takes up the old riddle of how the world began and what came before it, and he answers with reason as well as with science. Chapters weigh the principles of reasoning, the scope of science, and the law of evolution.

Later chapters treat laws of nature, the law of substance, and seven enigmas that Gerard says evolution leaves unexplained. He writes as a Catholic thinker engaging Darwin's age on its own terms. The book gives a clear view of the faith-and-science debate at the turn of the century.
3386-the-editor-s-relations-with-the-you:
William Dean Howells takes up the editor and the young contributor in this essay from Literature and Life. One of the trustiest jokes of the humorous paragrapher, he writes, is that the editor lives in great and constant dread of the young contributor. Neither Howells's experience nor his observation bears out that theory of the case, and he says so plainly.

Of course one must not encourage a young person to abandon an honest industry, he adds, in the vain hope of earning a living by writing. That caution frames the essay's kindness: editors welcome new writers, but they will not lie about the odds. A humane corrective to a durable newsroom joke, from an editor who welcomed newcomers without lying about the odds.
33884-alec-lloyd-cowpuncher:
Eleanor Gates wrote this western tale, first called Cupid: The Cowpunch, published in New York in 1907 with pictures by Allen True. Alec Lloyd, a singing cowpuncher, tells his own story in lively slang. Chapters turn on Rose Andrews, a gasoline bronc, a sheriff and a little widow, a round-up in Central Park, and a boom that busts.

Gates writes Alec's voice with humor and heart, letting love and ranch work tangle together. The tale moves from range to city and back, with jokes on every page. It remains a cheerful sample of the popular western humor of its day.
33888-aesop-dress-d-or-a-collection-of-f:
Bernard Mandeville turned Aesop's fables into familiar verse in 1704, in this reprint with an introduction by John S. Shea, published by the Augustan Reprint Society in 1966. Mandeville speaks plainly, saying outright what La Fontaine left implied. His grasshopper and ant, for one, contrast an idle singer with a provident worker in blunt terms.

Shea's introduction sets Mandeville's verse beside its French models and notes its plainspoken force. The fables read as short, sharp lessons in verse. The book serves readers of early English satire and of Aesop in a lively, period dress.
33901-the-little-minister:
J. M. Barrie wrote this novel of a Scottish village, first copyrighted in 1891. Its hero is a young minister in Thrums, a weaver's town, and its heroine is a mysterious young woman the town calls Egyptian. Soldiers, weavers, and church folk watch as the minister's sermons against women give way to love.
