Barrie's chapters mix humor with tenderness: night watchers, a military cloak, a mud house tragedy, and a dance to a woman's piping. The minister must face his own pride and his flock's gossip. The novel endures as a warm, comic portrait of a small town and a man caught between duty and heart.
33952-what-you-can-do-with-your-will-pow:
Russell H. Conwell wrote this book on will power, copyrighted in 1917 by Harper and Brothers as volume one of a National Extension University set. Conwell, a lecturer and preacher for more than fifty years, tells young men and women that success holds no hidden secret. Will, he says, is the voice crying in the marketplace and the wilderness.

The future, Conwell argues, stands like a block of unwrought marble, to be shaped by firm, driving determination, health, and intelligence. Neither birth nor surroundings need bar the way. The book offers a classic American gospel of effort and resolve.
33967-descriptions-of-new-hylid-frogs-fr:
William E. Duellman published this 1968 study of new tree frogs in the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series. No fewer than nineteen new species of hylid frogs had been found and named in Mexico and Central America in the past decade. Most lowland kinds were long known, so most novelties came from the less easy highlands.

Duellman studied hylid frogs across the region in the spring and summer of 1966, with close work on Hyla and related genera. The paper describes the new kinds with plates and measures. It serves frog students who need exact, first-hand accounts of these small-range species.
33985-manslaughter:
Alice Duer Miller wrote this novel of New York society, published in 1921 with pictures from the Paramount photoplay. Its heroine, Lydia, faces temptation, a theft, and an investigation by O'Bannon, while a bracelet she has seen and shrunk from haunts the plot. Scenes of sobbing, dread, and a firm hand on a shoulder mark the tale.

Miller, author of Come Out of the Kitchen, writes of wealth, law, and a woman's name at stake. The novel asks how far a rich young woman can go before the law catches her. It remains a brisk, dramatic tale of the Jazz Age's bright surface and hard edge.
34023-the-bread-line-a-story-of-a-paper:
Albert Bigelow Paine wrote this story of a newspaper, published in New York in 1900 by the Century Company, with copyrights in 1899 and 1900. Paine dedicates the book to those who have started papers, thought of starting papers, or are thinking of starting papers. Chapters open with a first dinner and Frisby's scheme.

Letters between Truman Livingstone of New York and Dorothy Castle of Cleveland carry much of the tale. Premiums, cash for names, the sanctum, and the gentle art of advertising fill the way. An hour of dark foreboding, final straws, and the end of the rainbow close the arc. The book offers a lively tale of paper-making.
3403-the-register:
William Dean Howells sets this short farce in an upper room of a Boston boarding house in Melanchthon Place. A plain young lady, newly arrived, puts small touches of decoration around her room while she talks with a friend in the next room. The friend, Ethel Reed, teases her about a young man and about country places with fanciful names.

The comedy turns on gossip, vanity, and the small wars of boarding house life. Howells builds the scene from voices heard through a doorway, so much of the fun lies in what is overheard and half understood. Like his other farces, the piece is short, dialogue driven, and best read as a play for the ear.
34069-a-kut-prisoner:
H. C. W. Bishop wrote this account of a Kut prisoner, published in London and New York in 1920 by John Lane, the Bodley Head, in the On Active Service series. Bishop dedicates the book to the memory of all British and Indian officers and men of the Kut garrison who suffered and died in captivity. Pictures show Kastamuni and its castle rock.

Chapters run from Ctesiphon and Kut through the march to Kastamuni, life there, escape, the first night, hills, slow progress, bluffing peasants, and reaching the coast. Recapture, rescue, hiding with Turks, delays, three days on the Black Sea, and the Crimea and home close the tale. The book offers a vivid prisoner-of-war story.
3410-the-american-spirit-in-literature-a:
Bliss Perry traces American writing from its first settlements to the early twentieth century in this volume of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1918. Chapters move through the pioneers, first colonial literature, later colonial generations, the Revolution, and the Knickerbocker group of New York writers.

Perry asks what holds American literature together across such change. He follows the shift from sermons and colonial pamphlets to a national voice shaped by war, growth, and new wealth. The book works as a short history for general readers, giving names, periods, and themes without demanding prior study of each author.
34100-lefty-locke-pitcher-manager:
Burt L. Standish's 1916 baseball novel follows Lefty Locke, a pitcher who is offered a manager's post. The offer comes with tangled deals, a shadowy backer named Weegman, and a mystery player whose true aims stay hidden for much of the book.

Thirty-seven chapters carry Lefty from the mound to the manager's bench, through tests of nerve, temptation, and games where one bad call can undo a season. Young readers get both a sports tale and a puzzle, as Lefty must judge men as sharply as he judges pitches. Standish had already told Lefty's tale in earlier books of the bush and the big league.
3412-the-golden-chersonese-and-the-way-t:
Isabella Bird records a trip across the Malay Peninsula in this travel book, whose old name for the region gives the title. The Golden Chersonese was the ancient Greek name for the peninsula, and Bird describes the route to reach it as well as the place itself. She travels by river and road through settlements, forests, and towns that few British readers then knew at first hand.

Bird writes as a keen observer of people, houses, markets, and local rule. She notes Malay customs, Chinese and Indian settlers, and the work of tin mines and plantations. The book remains valuable as a first hand account of Southeast Asia in the late nineteenth century, written by one of the great women travelers of her age.
34195-notes-and-queries-number-229-march:
Notes and Queries, number 229, came out on Saturday, March 18, 1854, at fourpence. The journal calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, and genealogists. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, urges readers to make a note of what they find. Contents open with notes on gossiping history and on works on bells. An inedited letter of Lord Nelson stands in the notes as well.

Folk lore from Herefordshire, a Greenock fair, dragons' blood, and a charm for the ague follow. Hebrew music and the psalms for the chief musician get a note by Buckton. Minor notes touch Swift, Dean of St Patrick's, and an anecdote of George the Fourth. Queries ask about anonymous works, blind mackerel, old Scotch airs, and royal salutes. The number shows Victorian scholars at their shared desk work of small facts.
3422-the-life-of-the-fly-with-which-are-:
Jean Henri Fabre studies flies and their kin in this volume of natural history essays, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. The chapters move from the harmas, Fabre's stony field laboratory in Provence, to the anthrax fly, the greenbottles, the gray flesh flies, and the bluebottle in its egg and grub stages. Two chapters pause for the author's memories of school and of mathematics.

Fabre watches living insects with patience, noting how parasites lay eggs in maggots and how larvae change form. He explains his terms in plain language and adds notes where a name might puzzle a reader. The book suits anyone curious about insects, field observation, and a scientist who wrote with the eye of a storyteller.
34227-her-letter-his-answer-her-last-let:
An illustrated gift book of three poems by Bret Harte. Houghton, Mifflin and Company published it at Boston in 1905. Arthur I Keller drew the many designs, several in colour. The first two poems had been favourites since about 1870. Harte wrote the third near the end of his life. A publishers' note explains the grouping.

Her Letter opens by a fireside after a dance. The writer sits alone, still dressed from the ball. She teases a distant lover about her partners and her taste. His Answer speaks in the voice of a mining-camp man. Sandy McGee's shooting colours its stanzas. Her Last Letter rounds the romance out at last. The poems trade sentiment and slang between East and West.
34355-marching-on-niagara-or-the-soldier:
Marching on Niagara, or The Soldier Boys of the Old Frontier, is a boys' tale by Edward Stratemeyer. It was put out at Boston with rights held in nineteen hundred and two. It stands in a set of tales of the first years of the land. His past sets are named on the title leaf. They run from a life of a great chief to tales of lost men and far towns. Plates are by a named hand.

The list of parts is a war log of the old march lands. In the woods heads the run. Deer and the first folk, a find and a chase, and the burn of a hut come next. A rise of the first folk, the loss of a boy, and a two fold warn fill the first run.
34377-the-preaching-tours-and-missionary:
Mrs Müller wrote this account of her husband George Müller's preaching tours and mission work. Nisbet printed it in London in 1883. Müller of Bristol was famed for his orphan homes, run on prayer and gifts alone, with no begging.

The book could be had at the Bible and Tract Warehouse in Park Street, Bristol. That house served the Scriptural Knowledge Institution for Home and Abroad, Müller's own base. His tours took the gospel across Britain and far lands in his old age. His wife sets down the roads, the halls, and the fruit of the work. Readers who knew the orphan homes' tale got its mate here: the preacher abroad.
34380-the-call-of-the-wildflower:
Henry S Salt wrote The Call of the Wildflower, essays on hunting wild blooms in their home ground. George Allen and Unwin issued the book in London, first in nineteen hundred twenty two. Salt owned his debt to Jack London for the title. Parts first ran in the Daily News and other papers.

Garden charm is strong, Salt grants, but wild charm pulls harder. Sussex shingles, ditches, and dikes start his walks. Open downland and a Surrey chalk pit come next in turn. Derbyshire dales and limestone coasts each earn a chapter. April in Snowdonia and the coves of Helvellyn close the climbs. Salt roams as a lover, not a picker, and says so. His plea runs through the book: leave wild flowers their free ground.
34425-johnstone-of-the-border:
Johnstone of the Border, by Harold Bindloss, was copyrighted in 1916 and published in England under the title The Borderer. Thirty-one chapters run from The Summons to Unexpected Happiness, through signals, wrecks, lost papers, and a whammel boat. Front matter lists some two dozen earlier Bindloss tales of the Canadian North-West and the prairie.

The opening chapter sets Sable Lake among ragged pines, where a new transcontinental railroad is cutting through the silent woods. Ballast cars and gravel plows sound for a mile or two before the forest swallows them. Stokes issued the book at New York with a frontispiece in color.
34460-the-court-jester:
Cornelia Baker tells a tale of a court fool and a brave princess for young readers in a Bobbs-Merrill volume held under rights from 1906. Margaret Ely Webb and Margaret H Deveneau drew the plates. Baker names past books at the front, among them The Queen's Page.

Le Glorieux, jester to the late Charles the Bold, turns handsprings behind the chair of the old duchess as she talks of the past. Such tricks pleased his late master but grate on the querulous widow, Baker notes with care. Thirteen chapters move through a festival at an inn, broken promises, and a moonstone pendant of Lady Clotilde. A royal alchemist, a midnight adventure, and the egg-dance close a tale set at the Spanish court.
34467-in-camp-with-a-tin-soldier:
In Camp with a Tin Soldier, a children’s tale by John Kendrick Bangs, was copyrighted in 1892 and issued at New York. Pictures by Ashe go with the fun. The first chapter is called The Start, and it opens with a drum. Rub a dub dub rolls off the page in Bangs’s comic hand.

What’s that, cries Jimmieboy, rising from his nursery couch in wonder. His mother sits near at hand, knitting a pair of socks. Bangs was a famed American humorist of his day. His nursery tales let toys march, talk, and camp like soldiers. A tin soldier leads the small battalion of the playroom. Children of the nineties met his jokes at bedtime, with pictures to match.
34481-the-prime-minister:
An unnamed novelist, living long in Portugal, built this tale of fiction on that country. The times of the Marquis of Pombal struck the author as a good subject, untouched by any other writer. For a long while the work waited, almost in despair of finding the needed materials, the preface confesses.

Letters to Lisbon brought information at last for the writer's design. Portuguese friends put family documents at the author's disposal, from which the work was composed, the preface says. Free access to the public library at Oporto, with its many thousand volumes in all languages, and help from Senhor Gandra, its chief librarian, completed the research.
34551-witch-winnie-the-story-of-a-king-s:
Witch Winnie, the story of a King's Daughter, by Elizabeth Champney, was copyrighted in 1889 and published in New York by Dodd, Mead. Champney dedicates the book to her little witch Marie, with a verse portrait. The poem calls Marie tricksy and elfish, busy keeper of the house, with helpful fairy fingers. Yet her heart is tender, and she is a gentle angel-nurse.

The tale follows Winnie through boarding-school scrapes and the affair of Guinevere's gown. The King's Daughters were a real church society of girls pledged to service in the King's name. Champney builds her story on that badge: a lively, mischievous heroine whose pranks keep running into errands of mercy. The book mixes schoolgirl fun with the earnest tone of its decade's girls' fiction.
34591-clue-of-the-silken-ladder:
Mildred Wirt wrote Clue of the Silken Ladder, a Penny Parker mystery, copyrighted in 1941. The series list runs from Tale of the Witch Doll through The Cry at Midnight, sixteen titles of large cloth volumes. Contents open with Double Trouble, then A Rope of Silk.

Society routine, a turn of fortune, and the man in gray follow. An apartment burglary, the mark of the iron hook, and psychic signs build the case. Mrs Weems' inheritance, ouija board wisdom, and the celestial temple come next, with a message for Mrs Weems and Cousin David's ghost. Readers get a girl reporter-sleuth working a medium-and-money mystery in wartime America.
34619-the-gateless-barrier:
Lucas Malet wrote The Gateless Barrier, published by Dodd, Mead and Company at New York in 1900. A preface quotes Lafcadio Hearn on the book that gives the novel its name. Mu-Mon-Kwan, in the Japanese reading, means the gateless barrier. The Zen sect studies that book of questions. Its texts do not explain; they only suggest. The student must think out the answers himself, and not write them down.

The tale opens at sea on a great ship at night. Laurence leans on the bulwark rail as the water hisses away below. Foam patterns lace the side, lit green, violet, and amber from the port lights. The funnels' smoke streams off and turns in a following wind. The ship lifts like a horse at a fence. Malet sets a story of belief and doubt under a Zen title.
34673-the-chief-engineer:
Chief Engineer is a story by Henry Abbott, published at New York in 1920 under his copyright. It opens on a dark July night with no moon and clouds hiding the stars. A camp fire group sits while Bige kicks the burning logs into a shower of sparks. That fireside frame sets up a tale told in the dark by the men.

North woods camps and the men who run camps and works form Abbott usual ground. A chief engineer stands at the centre of the yarn the frame introduces here. Talk by firelight, memory, and a past job give the story its forward pull. Readers get a short, plain told tale of work, risk, and character.
34775-the-boss-of-wind-river:
Boss of Wind River is a lumber camp novel by A M Chisholm, copyright nineteen eleven. A picture at the front shows a girl clutching the hero's arm as a log drive breaks away. Other picture captions promise fights and a line drawn against McCane's crew. Chapter one opens as young Joe Kent enters the office of the Kent Lumber Company at nine in the morning.

A sudden pause falls over the morning's work as he enters, the tale says. Every eye fixes on him with an interest he never excited before. Respect is mixed with misgivings in that look, he feels. A dubious weighing, a sizing up, runs through the room. A thick set, grizzled man named Wright comes forward and shakes his hand.
3478-legends-of-vancouver:
Pauline Johnson, whose Mohawk name was Tekahionwake, retells Coast Salish legends of the Vancouver region in this book. Johnson was the daughter of George Johnson, head chief of the Six Nations, and his English born wife Emily. A friend's preface notes that a poet has arisen to cast her art over the grey mountains, trails, and shores of British Columbia.

The legends explain peaks, inlets, and landmarks through stories of chiefs, spirits, and transformations. Johnson heard many of them from local storytellers and shaped them in graceful English prose. The book remains a treasured bridge between Indigenous oral tradition and Canadian literature, and it suits readers who love place based tales.
34830-little-frankie-and-his-mother: Little Frankie and His Mother is a children's book by Baker, who wrote as Mrs Leslie. It belongs to the Little Frankie series. The opening pages of the hosted copy are the publisher's catalogue of Mrs Leslie's books for little children. The catalogue lists her Sabbath school books, among them Tim the Scissors Grinder, Prairie Flower, The Bound Boy and The Bound Girl. It also lists question books on the Sermon on the Mount, for children, youth and adults. Frankie's own story lies past these pages.
34852-moonshine-clover:
Laurence Housman wrote fairy tales, engraved by his sister Clemence, here selected and reprinted at New York from four out-of-print volumes of the eighteen-nineties and after. A motto over a woodcut gives the title its spell: shine, moon, grow clover, when my day is over. Eighteen tales fill the contents.

The first, The Prince with the Nine Sorrows, opens with a rhyme of eight white peahens. Then come a king and queen whose only son is nursed by the forester's wife beside her own daughter. The queen dreams the prince at twenty, dead of a wound over the heart, his foster-sister crowned and holding his bleeding heart. A family fairy is summoned to read the dream. Literary fairy tale in the Arts and Crafts manner is the book.
349-the-harvester:
David Langston, a harvester of the woods, lives by Thoreau's ideals in a modern age. Gene Stratton-Porter's Harvester follows David from Belshazzar's decision through forest harvests to a quest for a dream girl. Ruth Jameson, a city girl, and Granny Moreland join his story.

Chapters cover demonstrated courtship, snow wings, and love invading science. David's cleanliness, poetic temper, and mental force mirror Thoreau, as the book's dedication claims. Stratton-Porter's nature lore fills every chapter. The novel closes her Limberlost-era romances. Stratton-Porter's harvester closes her series of nature romances.
35047-little-robins-love-one-to-another:
Madeline Leslie wrote 'Little Robins' Love One to Another' for children, in her Robin Redbreast series, published at Boston in 1860. Chapter One, 'Jack Robin's Offence,' opens on a lovely May morning. Under the old elm tree, Symmes stands in the shed churning butter, and Fred calls the chickens with a pail of dough. Annie follows her grandfather to the barn with a pan of warm milk.

The milk is for Whiteface, the lamb, and the barn yard gate has been left open, so the lamb bounds forward to meet Annie. After a chase round the old tree, Annie turns to feed her robin family. Jack, without waiting for invitation, hops into the entry, flies upon the set table, and walks among the dishes. Standing on one leg, he turns his head archly, as if to say he hopes he does not intrude, and Annie laughs till she cries.
35049-spotted-deer:
Elmer Russell Gregor wrote a boys' tale of the frontier, printed at New York in 1924. Gregor's White Wolf and War Trail are named on the title page. Twenty chapters carry the tale. Heads promise the cry of the loon, a night of worry, and a capture.

A wily captive, the Shawnee camp, and a hard ordeal follow. Then come a mystery woman, an alarm, and a hunt. Councils of war, a strange ally, an easy win, and a bold ruse lead to Spotted Deer's freedom. The tale opens in early autumn. The young Delaware hunter paddles home with a fat buck, geese and grouse in his canoe, singing thanks to the Great One.
35082-saboteurs-on-the-river:
Saboteurs on the River, by Mildred Wirt, is a Penny Parker mystery, copyrighted in 1943 and published in New York by Cupples and Leon. Twenty-five chapters run from Trouble Afloat through a test blackout, a drifting barge, a stolen boat, and a message in the bottle, to A Bow in the Cloud. Wartime sabotage on an American river drives the plot.

Chapter one sends a girl in blue slacks, a woolen sweater, and tennis shoes along the creaking boards of a dark river dock. A big white cotton bag hangs slung over one shoulder. Penny Parker, girl reporter, soon faces suspicion, a missing Jerry, and men who mean harm to river traffic. Wirt mixes newsroom hustle with patriotic danger in a brisk wartime tale for girls.
35096-no-surrender:
Werner wrote No Surrender in German, and Christina Tyrrell turned it into English for a London printing in 1881. Werner was the pen name of Elisabeth Burstenbinder, as a front note states. Sun fills the first scene: a broad lake shines like glass and mirrors a town on its shore, with snow peaks sharp in the far view.

A small villa suburb lines the shore, and one modest house stands out for its neat garden, white walls, and green shutters. Two men pace a vine draped veranda in cool shade at noon and talk as they walk. The elder, near fifty, bears a bent frame and grey hair, with furrowed face and bitter mouth that speak of long strife. Fire in his eye still burns, and sets the tone for a tale of will.
35104-over-here-impressions-of-america-b: Over Here, impressions of America by a British officer, is a war time book of an English soldier's sight of the United States. Its front pages are filled with notices for kindred war books. One such, a guide to life at the front by a British artillery officer, is pressed on every American reader. Send it to your son, brother, or friend in arms, the notice urges. The impressions themselves belong to the years when British officers crossed to train and visit the new American army of the Great War.
35148-here-and-hereafter:
Here and Hereafter is a collection of short stories by Barry Pain, first published by Methuen in London in 1911. Pain had earlier written Lindley Kays, The Gifted Family, and The Exiles of Faloo. Twenty stories make up the contents.

Titles hint at quiet unease. The Feast and the Reckoning, Post-Mortem, The Unfinished Game, and The Four-Fingered Hand stand among them. The first story, Mala, opens on a Saturday night in a doctor's surgery. A fair-haired man in a frayed mustard-coloured suit waits with a broken straw hat in his hand. His face and hands show an outdoor working life. Pain builds his effects from such plain, closely seen detail. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
35178-ben-pepper:
Ben Pepper is a children's novel by Margaret Sidney, printed at Boston by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard. Copyright stands in the name of Harriett Lothrop in 1905, and the printing was the twentieth thousand. Sidney was the author of Five Little Peppers and Their Friends. Eugenie Wireman illustrated the book. The Pepper trade mark is registered on the title page.

The Pepper children fill the contents: Ben, Polly, Joel and the rest, with Jasper King and Mother Fisher. The Christmas shopping expedition opens the story, and Ben's plan follows. Where's Pip, what a home-coming, and the big box come in the middle. The postponed Christmas morning and around the Christmas tree close the book, with Jasper and Ben at the last. Sidney's Pepper books taught thrift and cheerfulness to generations of American children.
35194-the-niagara-river:
The Niagara River by Archer Butler Hulbert, professor of American history at Marietta College, was published by Putnam of New York and London in 1908 with maps and illustrations. Hulbert had already written The Ohio River and the Historic Highways of America series, and he edited the Crown Collection of American Maps.

In his author's note Hulbert admits the difficulty of gathering into one volume the many interests centring in a single short river. He calls Niagara the geologic wonder of a continent and the commercial marvel of the present century, and ranks its historic interest with that of any American river. He names his chief debts: the historical writings of Peter Porter, Severance's Old Trails of the Niagara Frontier, and The Niagara Book. The volume is dedicated to Henry Carlton Hulbert, in thanks for encouragement and friendship.
35195-the-fatal-cord-and-the-falcon-rove:
The Fatal Cord and The Falcon Rover are two frontier tales by Captain Mayne Reid, in an edition issued at London in 1872. The first tale opens with a bivouac of boy hunters. Its first chapter sets the camp under the shade of a Mississippian forest. The trees stand unthinned by any woodman's axe, the narrator says.

The spot lies on the Arkansas side of the great river, not far from the town of Helena. A small glade is ringed by tall cottonwood trees, two of them blazed to mark a trace of travel. That trace leads toward a settlement on the forks of two rivers. The time is a quarter of a century back, the tale adds, when the district held a mixed and rough population. Reid's boy hunters and backwoodsmen were the school of many a British and American lad.
35206-brother-against-brother-or-the-war:
Oliver Optic wrote a Civil War tale for boys dated 1894, one of the Blue and the Gray Army set. The tale opens in Kentucky, a border state torn in the first days of the war. A northern family at Riverlawn, the Lyons, faces kin and neighbors split by the great fight.

Chapter heads trace a night trip on the creek, a cave by Bar Creek, and the rise of Fort Bedford. Arms moved in secret, a Union talk at Big Bend, and rude men thrown out raise the heat. Hostile force draws near as this part ends, with kin set hard against kin in arms.
35217-the-oyster:
A Peer wrote a novel called The Oyster, first published in 1914. John Long Limited issued the book from Norris Street in London's Haymarket. Other tales by the same hand, such as Theo and The Hard Way, are listed at the front. Rights were fully held by the house.

The tale opens in a trim small flat dressed to ape grand town luxury. Sheraton chairs, rich cloth, fine linen, and good silver crowd the small rooms. Strawberries, cream, and hot bread mark a rich early meal. Class, show, and want sit close in this bright shell, and the plot turns on what the shell hides.
35282-fra-ulein-schmidt-and-mr-anstruthe:
Fraulein Schmidt and Mr Anstruther is a novel in letters by the author of Elizabeth and Her German Garden. Scribner published the book at New York in 1907. The writer's name is withheld on the title page, as with her earlier garden book. The story is set at Jena in Germany.

The first letter is dated the sixth of November and addressed to Roger. The writer, a young German woman, confesses that she loves him. She jokes that her sober greeting hides warmer words she chose not to use. Only a day before, the two stood on stiff, polite terms. He had lodged a whole year in her family's house, practising his German on her. She never saw a sign that he cared for her beyond her help with meals and mending. Then, in one hour at parting, he became the dear Roger of her letter.
35356-betty-grier:
Joseph Waugh wrote this Scottish tale, first printed by Chambers in November 1915. A frontispiece by Kerr, of the Royal Scottish Academy, illustrates Betty's story. Waugh had written 'Robbie Doo' and talks with that character before this book, his author line notes.

When I look round my little bedroom, the narrator begins in chapter one. Fourteen years have come and gone since he last slept in the small truckle-bed there, he says. Everything stands exactly as he left it, and the familiar things wake a feeling of homeliness that opens a story of homecoming and Betty Grier herself.
35365-philip-massinger:
Cruickshank wrote this study of the playwright Philip Massinger, printed at Oxford in 1920. Cruickshank had been a scholar and fellow of New College, Oxford, and taught Greek and classical literature at Durham. He inscribes the book to Frederic Kenyon, in memory of a friendship of forty-four years. A portrait of Massinger fronts the study.

The contents list twenty appendices on hard points in the plays. They treat the plays Massinger wrote with others, the mark of Shakespeare on his work, and the authorship of The Virgin Martyr and The Fatal Dowry. Cruickshank says he read Massinger again to test the judgments of his youth. His first task was to number the lines of the plays for easy reference.
354-the-story-of-a-pioneer:
Anna Howard Shaw tells her own life in this memoir, written with Elizabeth Jordan. Shaw recalls first memories, a hard youth in the Michigan woods, and school and college days that led her to preach and to practice medicine. The book then follows her into the long fight for votes for women.

Chapters name the work plainly: the wolf at the door, a divided flock, Cape Cod summers, and years with Susan B. Anthony, called Aunt Susan here. Shaw later led the national suffrage group and built homes of her own. The memoir reads as a pioneer's plain record, proud yet free of boasting.
35400-presidential-candidates-containing:
D W Bartlett gathered these sketches of the prominent men named for the presidency in 1860, published in New York in 1859. The contents list twenty-one names, from William Seward and Stephen Douglas through Salmon Chase, John Bell, Jefferson Davis, and John Fremont.

In his preface Bartlett admits the sketches vary in length, since a few subjects were too cautious to let their private history out. He passed over Buchanan and Pierce as men the people already know, and aimed at the new men instead. Each sketch gives the candidate's stand on the issues of the day plus personal detail meant to show character. Readers get a campaign-year portrait gallery.
35431-a-modern-buccaneer:
A Modern Buccaneer is a South Seas tale by Rolf Boldrewood. Boldrewood had won fame with Robbery Under Arms before this book. Macmillan brought it out in London and New York in 1894. Three volumes made the first edition, then one volume followed that year. Louis Becke lent help for the South Sea Island part, he owns.

One chapter rests on his late father's whaling cruise diary instead. Seventeen chapters run from my first voyage to Jack come home. Samoa, the brig Leonora, and Captain Ben Peese fill the early list. Cruising among the Carolines and poisoned arrows come in the mid part. Murder and shipwreck, a king and queen, and the Rosario follow. Norfolk Island stands as an Arcadia near the end of the tale. A swim for life tests the teller in the late chapters here. His father had sailed every sea from India to the Pole.
35436-mr-claghorn-s-daughter:
Hilary Trent wrote this novel, copyrighted in 1903 by Ogilvie of New York. Chapter one pairs a philosopher and a marchioness as its opening scene. Chapter two sets two pagans talking of fish, Paris and the higher criticism, in the witty manner the contents promise.

A cousin in the coils of the great serpent and the diversions of the Claghorns follow. A pagan philosopher enters the service of the church in chapter five. Art, diplomacy and love, a conference of spinsters about a runaway damsel, and the devil walking in Hampton fill a contents list rich in talk and satire.
35510-the-preparation-of-plantation-rubb:
Sidney Morgan's The Preparation of Plantation Rubber, from Constable at London in 1922, is a working manual for estates in the East. Morgan writes as visiting agent for estates, formerly senior scientific officer and now honorary adviser to the Rubber Growers' Association in Malaya. Henry Stevens, the Association's consulting chemist in London, adds a preface and a chapter on vulcanization.

An earlier book by the Association in 1914 had already made Morgan's name on the subject. The volume treats the whole making of the crop, from the early collection of latex and its transport to the factory, through tapping cuts to the weighing of crepe lengths. Transcriber notes record the original's care with terms, down to the V-shaped cut used in tapping.
35545-sanders-of-the-river:
Sanders of the River is a set of tales of West Africa by Edgar Wallace, from Ward and Lock. Wallace lists his many novels on its pages, Bones and Bosambo among them. Commissioner Sanders rules a river district of a quarter million people in the tales. Thirteen chapters and a last piece called Dogs of War fill the volume.

The first chapter, The Education of the King, shows how Sanders learned his ground. He came to his own land by slow stages through all southern Africa. Basuto, Zulu, Fingo, Pondo, and Matabele taught him the small gaps between peoples. That gap, he holds, lies in character more than in colour of skin. His code trusts each people up to one point, as one trusts children. Bosambo of Monrovia and the dancing stones follow in the contents.
35597-a-treatise-on-the-brewing-of-beer:
Hughes, a practical brewer, published this treatise at Uxbridge in 1796, in a second edition sold by Lake there and Newbery in London. Its promise stands on the title page. One bushel of malt will produce a gallon of beer more than another bushel of equal strength, though both malts be made of one sort of barley. A saving of twenty per cent is the headline claim. The different experiments, Hughes says, come from twenty years of practice.

The book gives directions to maltsters and improvements in the brew-house and its utensils. It shows what makes beer hard and sour, and how to keep it from turning sour or foxed even in the warmest season. Cleansing, cellar management, and the choice of hops follow, with proof that hops are useful after they have been used in brewing. A closing section admonishes the publican who retails common brewer's beer.
35670-no-quarter:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote No Quarter, a tale of England’s great civil war. Hurst and Company issued this form in New York in eighteen hundred ninety. Its prologue hails the decade from sixteen hundred forty to fifty. No age outshines it in England’s whole tale, Reid boasts at once.

The Long Parliament sat rich in statesmen and patriots then, he holds. They shrank not from a crowned traitor’s block in the realm’s cause. Queen Henrietta opens the tale in Whitehall’s bright gardens. Give your island churls a taste of French kingship, she urges Charles. Magna Charta has gone to their heads like a craze, he sighs back. I would waste the land with fire and sword first, she cries in rage. Dissolve the pack and rule without them, she bids her husband. Money is the chain that binds his hands, the king owns in grief.
35671-the-messenger:
The Messenger, by Elizabeth Robins, is a novel of talk and intrigue printed in New York in 1919. The Century Company issued it that September, with plates by George Giguére. Robins had written Come and Find Me before it.

The plate captions promise the plot in glimpses: a finger-print demanded, a cry for Gavan to save me. A cabin placed at a lady's disposal, and the name of a man in the War Office. The first talk sets the hero up: Gavan Napier is of the governing class at sight. Eton and Balliol stand behind him, and he serves as unpaid private secretary to a minister. His friend Julian warns him not to carry his notions past reason. Gavan flashes back that he may chance to be honest in his scheme of social justice.
35746-the-pearl-of-peace-or-the-little-p:
The Pearl of Peace, or The Little Peacemaker, is a moral tale for girls by Madeline Leslie, published at Boston in 1868. It is volume six of her Bible Pearls series for girls, each named for a virtue: faith, diligence, meekness, forgiveness, contentment, and peace. A matching series for boys runs from love to patience. The book's motto is the blessing on the peacemakers from the Gospel of Matthew.

The opening chapter is called The Quarrel. Matilda has been repeating, with some stretching, the remarks of Cynthia Manning about another girl's dress. She did not mean to stir up so much anger, and Sallie's warmth at the report nearly frightens her. From such small sparks the story teaches its lesson on making peace among schoolgirls. The volume is dedicated to five named children of a New York family, in the custom of the series.
35781-the-deemster:
Hall Caine wrote The Deemster, a Manx novel in his best books edition printed at New York. Contents open with the death of old Ewan, a man child born, the christening of young Ewan, the Deemster of Man, and the Manxman's bishop. A cosy nest at Bishop's Court, Danny the madcap, and passing the love of women follow.

A service on the shore, the first night with the herrings, a herring breakfast, Dan's penance, and Ewan mourning for his wife fill the middle. The lie Ewan told, a plowing match, a blind woman's second sight, blind passion and pain, and a voice in the night raise the storm. Alone on a wide sea follows. Manx melodrama readers get Caine.
35836-the-bail-jumper:
The Bail Jumper is a prairie novel by Robert Stead, first published at London by Fisher Unwin in 1914. A verse epigraph from a poem called Prairie Born praises races hardened by winter, blizzards, and country dances.

Chapter titles trace the arc: a friend and an enemy, Crotton's Crossing, under suspicion, the arm of the law, only a Barnardo boy, and a fugitive. Later chapters bring love or law, the sacrifice of silence, the homestead line, and the light at last. The story opens at the end of a short winter day, five-o'clock twilight gathering around a frost-shrouded team and a farm sleigh. On the road, a neighbour is greeted roughly and warned home out of the cold.
36044-white-otter:
White Otter is a boys' novel of the Sioux by Elmer Gregor. Appleton issued it, with copyright in 1917. It belongs to Gregor's Western Indian Series. Twenty chapters carry the young hero through one season. Riders of the night open the tale. A war party and a trail in the dark follow. White Otter is grandson of Wolf Robe, a famed Ogalala chief. He rides to visit the Minneconjou camp.

His friends Sun Bird and Little Raven wait there. A great buffalo drive fills the middle chapters. The Pawnee camp is spied upon near the end. A splendid victory closes the hunt and war. The crown of eagle plumes ends the book. Gregor wrote many such tales of the plains.
36057-the-boy-grew-older:
The Boy Grew Older is a novel by the sport scribe Heywood Broun. It came out in 1922 and was printed six times in five months. The tale starts with a phone call to a card room at night. Peter Neale learns that his son has just been born to him.

Peter does not rush off at once, to the reader's dry shame. He stays to end the hand and pay his loss at the cards. The joke is sad, and it sets the stamp of the man. The book is given to a news chief who was Broun's own boss. What grows in the tale is the boy, and his flawed sire as well. The style is light on its face and grave at its heart.
36121-the-snow-burner:
The Snow-Burner is a novel by Henry Oyen, author of The Man-Trail, printed at New York in 1916. Its frontispiece shows the Snow-Burner toppled face downward on the ground. The book is built in two parts: The Natural Man and The Super Man. Part one opens with a cry of help, a girl, and Toppy getting a job.

The Hell-Camp Reivers, the Snow-Burner's creed, and a duel begin the action. A court at Hell-Camp, the tightening of screws, and Tilly's warning fill the middle chapters. The end of the boss closes the first part. Part two turns to the cheating of the river, gold, and the trail of fortune. The Snow-Burner hunts, the squaw-man appears, and the scorn of a pure woman follows. Later chapters bring a bargain, a test of the bottle, and a fight that was a fight.
36168-rosemary-and-rue-by-amber:
Amber, a Chicago newspaper writer, left prose and verse gathered under the title Rosemary and Rue, published at Chicago and New York in 1896 with a preface by Opie Read. He remembers her as an individual of no society and no creed, holding all form in good-humoured contempt and revering all simple things, the constant victim of her own generosity.

Her column, he says, held not the news of the day but the news of the heart, and her reward was letters from invalids' bedsides. The book opens with a poem of wondering, asking whether a friend hearing of her death tomorrow would mourn. Read insists she found her own hard place and maintained it alone. A memorial garland for a beloved columnist is the volume.
36170-the-son-of-his-father:
A western novel by Ridgwell Cullum, published at Philadelphia by George W Jacobs. The copyright dates to 1915, and this printing is March 1917. Douglas Duer drew the illustrations. Cullum also wrote The Night-Riders and The Watchers of the Plains. The dedication thanks G Ralph Hall-Caine for loyal friendship. Twenty-six chapters carry the story.

The opening scene is a reckoning at a desk. James Carbhoy totals his son's bill with a smile. Wine, women, and gambling at twenty-four cost one hundred thousand dollars. Gordon, lounging opposite, knows the iron will behind the smile. That will built a railroad fortune in America's hardest arena. The contents send Gordon west to Snake's Fall. Hazel Mallinsbee, a code book, and a boom await him there.
36202-nan-sherwood-on-the-mexican-border:
Annie Roe Carr wrote a Nan Sherwood girls' novel published in 1937 by the World Syndicate Publishing Company of Cleveland and New York. Unexpected guests open the contents. You're going with me, trouble at the border, and Adair Mackenzie speaks up follow. Tell us about the hacienda and something about Mexico teach the setting. Bess smells a romance by chapter seven.

Trouble for Rhoda, resolutions, and a first Mexican experience build the middle. A legend and Linda Riggs's turning up follow. Nan turns photographer later in the list. The Nan Sherwood series sent its heroine traveling widely. Border adventure gave 1930s girls an exotic but safe Mexico.
36220-my-little-sister:
Elizabeth Robins wrote My Little Sister, a tale of two sisters told by the elder. Dodd, Mead and Company issued the book in New York in January nineteen hundred thirteen. Robins had written The Magnetic North and Votes for Women. Bettina, the fair young sister, stands at the tale’s bright heart.

She is white and golden, and brings a shine where she goes. The teller slips between was and seems as she writes her. That slip, she owns, is the sum of her whole story. Both girls were small when they came to Duncombe to live. A dim ship and dark faces hint at an India birth. A mother’s vow, a storm, and a cloud mark their young years. Eric, a first ball, and a yachting party crowd their prime. Where is Bettina, one stark chapter asks at the core.
3624-chaucer:
Adolphus William Ward writes a short critical life of Geoffrey Chaucer in this volume of the English Men of Letters series. Ward builds the life partly from public records, such as the Royal Wardrobe Book, the Exchequer Issue Rolls, and the Customs Rolls, and partly from the poems themselves. He also leans on the work of the Chaucer Society, above all its director Frederick Furnivall.

The book traces Chaucer from court and customs work to the Canterbury Tales, explaining his language, his sources, and his humor for general readers. Ward differs at times from other scholars, including Fleay, and he notes those doubts with care. The volume suits readers who want a compact, scholarly introduction to England's first great poet.
36298-amenities-of-literature-consisting:
Amenities of Literature, by Isaac Disraeli, holds sketches and characters of English literature. This new edition was edited by his son, the Earl of Beaconsfield. Frederick Warne issued it in London. In his preface Disraeli says the history of our home literature filled his studies for years. He refused a dry list of books and authors. Instead he traced the steps of the human mind through time.

He links books to public opinion and to great events in the nation's story. Authors, he says, make opinion or reflect it. The great form an age, while the many mirror it. Curious topics that arose in his research fill these pages. The work mixes literary history with a philosophy of books and their sway over a people.
3633-jezebel-s-daughter:
Wilkie Collins writes a sensation novel that he presents as a standalone work, not a sequel to his previous novel The Fallen Leaves. In his preface he explains that The Fallen Leaves had reached only a limited class of readers in England. That was due to the forms of publication used so far, and a cheap reprint would come later. This new novel therefore stands on its own, with its own heroine and mystery.

The story follows a young woman caught between a powerful mother figure and a secret from the past, in Collins's familiar mix of romance, villainy, and legal intrigue. Readers who enjoy his sensation fiction will find a brisk plot and a heroine who must fight for her name. The book suits those who like Collins without needing his earlier novel first.
3634-the-guilty-river:
Wilkie Collins writes a short mystery novel set beside a river, where a moth collector's quiet hobby turns strange. The narrator, snaring moths in the woods, reaches for a large specimen and meets an apparition that changes his summer. Later chapters introduce a deaf lodger, a portfolio that returns, a game played by Mrs Roylake, repeated warnings, and a claret jug that holds a clue.

The river itself becomes a character, carrying secrets and bodies of evidence. Collins builds suspense from small details and half understood meetings. The book suits readers who enjoy his shorter sensation tales, with a compact plot, a vivid riverside setting, and a mystery that unfolds by hints.
36355-the-salamander:
Owen Johnson wrote The Salamander, a novel of New York stage life issued at Indianapolis in 1914 with art by Everett Shinn. Johnson had won fame with Stover at Yale. The tale opens at one in the afternoon on a Thursday in late October, in a huge dim room on the third floor of a boarding house on lower Madison Avenue.

Two of the room's four windows are blinded by a new brick wall that crowds in and steals the air. Trunks lie open and ransacked, flowers crowd the vases, and cards and photos stuff a great gilt mirror. The room is a young stage girl's base, and its mix of glamour and shabbiness sets the key for a tale of girls who play with fire in the theatre world.
36384-the-squire-s-daughter:
Silas Hocking wrote The Squire's Daughter, issued in a fourth edition at London and New York in 1906 with original illustrations by Arthur Twidle. Hocking also wrote Pioneers and The Flaming Sword. A frontispiece line begs: if you can only say yes, I will make you the happiest woman in the world.

Thirty-two chapters open with an imperious maiden, apprehensions, and a new sensation. David, Ralph, and Dorothy each speak their minds in turn. Storm clouds gather and burst, Sir John gets angry, and a big house, a confession, and a red-letter day follow. Readers get a popular melodrama of love, family pride, and fortune.
36390-erskine-dale-pioneer:
Erskine Dale Pioneer is a border tale by John Fox, out from Scribner in nineteen twenty. Fox wrote famed Kentucky tales of hill and pine in the same years. Draw work by Yohn lines the book with war and chase scenes. A wild dawn opens the tale in the deep woods of the old west. A cougar springs and a deer flees a worse foe in the gloom.

A boy with bow and scalp lock runs a buffalo trail in flight. Three foes grunt on his track prints not far at his back. A fenced camp in a clear space lets out three dim forms at dawn. Sword clash cuts and a hand kiss plate mark the plate list. The tale hails Dale as a first man of the raw new land.
36480-the-sweep-winner:
Nat Gould opens this racing novel under a blazing Australian sun, along the rabbit-proof fence between New South Wales and Queensland. A keeper on horseback shades his eyes along hundreds of miles of glittering wire, which dances with sparks and blinds the eyes. His horse is skin and bone, yet strong and enduring. The man snatches his hand back from the hot wire with an oath against the cursed country.

Gould dedicates the book to the memory of his son, killed in action on the Western Front in August 1918. The contents run through a glittering wire, a hut, and a face in the water to the Chinaman's shop and an accusation. Leigh hears strange things, and sweep money and Flemington build to the finish. Man and horse lay side by side before the sweep winner's home.
36501-olive-leaves-or-sketches-of-charac:
Sigourney published Olive Leaves, or Sketches of Character, with Gall and Inglis of London and Edinburgh. Her preface explains the title from the Flood. An olive leaf was the first gift of the earth after the deluge, borne by the dove over the surging waters to the survivors in the ark.

The plant so honored, she writes, has long been a consecrated emblem of peace. It brought tidings of a home once more upon the green earth. Her sketches offer the leaf in the same spirit: character studies meant to reconcile and console. Sigourney was the famous American woman poet of her generation, the sweet singer of Hartford, whose annuals and gift books reached every parlor. A frontispiece of an Indian chief promises sketches beyond the parlor, and her moralizing travels, as it did, in the dress of observation.
36552-york-minster:
A P Purey-Cust, Dean of York, wrote York Minster as a fond guide to his own great church. Isbister and Company issued the book in London in eighteen hundred ninety seven. Alexander Ansted drew the pictures. A Latin line on its walls calls it a rose among houses.

Cust grants that zeal, war, and poor taste have marred the church. Much old art has passed away for good, he owns. Yet the house still stands a thing of beauty and awe. He traces how it grew from a small start, age by age. Each school of stone craft left its mark in turn. Kings, saints, and workmen share its long tale. His aim is thanks for the chance to pray in such a place.
36592-the-fire-trumpet-a-romance-of-the-:
The Fire Trumpet, a romance of the Cape frontier by Bertram Mitford, was published by Spencer Blackett of London, with this edition dated 1889. The novel opens in a solicitor's office, where a will is being read to Arthur Claverton.

Claverton learns that his friend Spalding has left him nine thousand pounds, a sum far beyond the keepsake he expected. The lawyer reminds him that he once saved Spalding's life, a rescue Claverton shrugs off as a swim that did him good. Claverton is a man of about thirty, with a handsome, refined face and a look of firmness mixed with recklessness. A legacy of that size, in a frontier romance, is the engine that carries an Englishman toward adventure in South Africa, where Mitford set much of his fiction.
36605-the-sirdar-s-oath-a-tale-of-the-no:
The Sirdar's Oath is a tale of the North-West Frontier by Bertram Mitford. White of London published it, in an edition of 1904. Its first chapter is called The Stranger Within Thy Gates. The scene is London on Mafeking night. Crowds pack the space before the Mansion House. A tall Oriental in a frock coat draws their stares. His beard and fine face recall President Kruger.

Mocking cries of Kroojer rise around the stranger. Lamps flare and hats fly as the news is cheered. Mitford sets his Eastern hero amid that roaring crowd. The oath of the title binds the tale's course. Frontier honour and Empire pride drive the plot. Mitford wrote of Africa and India by long habit. His tales favour soldiers, chiefs, and hard bargains.
36615-the-life-of-a-celebrated-buccaneer:
Richard Clynton wrote a tale for the children of his day, issued in London in 1889. He frames it as a page of past history, told in a once upon a time style. His buccaneer lives on a rock-bound island, cut off from the main land of Europe by a streak of sea.

The island's caves, bays, and creeks make a safe den for plunder, and soon wharves and stores must be built to hold it. Towns rise, ships crowd the bays, and wives and children thrive on the shore. Yet the wealth came, the tale admits, as goods seized by force in a rough age. Young readers get a stern, sly lesson in how such gains were made.
3669-a-woman-hater:
Charles Reade writes a novel that opens at the Golden Star hotel in Homburg, a modest house used by travelers rather than gay gamblers. At two o'clock on a fine June day, two strangers sit at small tables far apart in the dining room, absorbed in their own thoughts. One is a sharp faced, middle aged man of business, Joseph Ashmead, an operatic and theatrical agent who scribbles hasty letters.

The story follows a man who calls himself a woman hater and the women who prove him wrong, through theater, business, and romance. Reade writes with energy and strong feeling, as in his other sensation novels. The book suits readers who enjoy Victorian melodrama with a hero whose prejudice must yield to love.
36732-charlie-newcomer:
Charlie Newcomer is a short religious biography by Wilbur Stover, published in Ohio in 1894. Stover knew and loved the boy whose life he tells. Charlie belonged to the Missionary Reading Circle's circle of readers. The preface says Stover had told the story often from the pulpit. He wrote it in the family's home at Ringgold. The parents allowed the facts to be told, though with hesitation.

Charlie joined the church while still a child. His example, Stover hopes, will lead other children to do the same. A bright future seemed to lie before the boy. His heart's desire was to become a missionary. The first chapter opens at the Ringgold school at noon. Schoolmates call Charlie to hurry to baseball after dinner. The sketch presents a model child for young readers.
36770-sun-and-saddle-leather:
Badger Clark's Sun and Saddle Leather, a book of cowboy poems from the Gorham Press at Boston, is here in its third edition, with photographs by Huffman. Clark dedicates it to his father, who seldom noticed a man's rough exterior or missed his obscurest virtue. The first poem, Ridin', sets the terms: some like the city, but for him it is horse and saddle every day, and a desert sun blazing on a hundred miles of range.

The contents run through the cowboy's year: A Cowboy's Prayer, The Christmas Trail, A Border Affair, The Bunk-House Orchestra, The Legend of Boastful Bill, The Tied Maverick, and A Roundup Lullaby. Clark writes in the cowboy's own tongue, with the spelling to match. The frontispiece poem looks ahead to the last free trail becoming a fenced lane, and to sons who will never love the young land as its first riders did.
36790-a-book-about-the-theater:
Brander Matthews, professor of dramatic literature at Columbia University, gathered these essays on the stage for publication in 1916. His opening letter to Augustus Thomas explains the aim with candor. Rather than stay with Sophocles, Shakspere, Moliere, and Ibsen, he turns to the lesser arts of the theatre. Dance, acrobats, conjurers, minstrels, pantomime, and scene painting all get his attention.

Readers get a critic who treats side paths as worth the walk. Matthews argues that such detours can teach as much as the main road of high drama. The tone stays warm and plain, even when the topics are small or half forgotten. Anyone curious about how plays were made, staged, and watched will find close, humane comment here.
36846-blue-robin-the-girl-pioneer:
Blue Robin, the Girl Pioneer is a girls' story by Rena I Halsey. It came out in March 1917. The book is dedicated to Lina Beard, who founded the Girl Pioneers of America.

A note at the front tells what the Girl Pioneers stand for. The group held its first public meeting at Flushing, New York, in February 1912. Its aim is to breed in girls the strong traits of the first pioneer women. It seeks to stir a wish for a happy, broad and useful life. Blue Robin's tale shows that aim at work in story form. Nana French Bickford drew the pictures for the tale.
36968-william-de-colchester-abbot-of-wes:
William de Colchester, Abbot of Westminster is a short life by Pearce, a canon of Westminster. It was published in London in 1915 by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. The book grew from a Friday evening discourse at the Royal Institution on the archives of Westminster Abbey. Pearce chose one man whose record had never been written.

Chapters follow the abbot from a novice from Essex to a man of affairs. He serves as a proctor at Rome and as an archdeacon before ruling the abbey. Later chapters show him at home and abroad. The book draws on the abbey's own records to rebuild a medieval churchman's career.
36970-the-confessions-of-a-poacher:
John Watson edited The Confessions of a Poacher, the life tale of an old game thief. The Leadenhall Press issued the book in London in eighteen hundred ninety. James West drew its plates of keepers and night work. Watson had written Nature and Woodcraft before this set.

Old Phil, the poacher, is no made up man, Watson swears. All in the book came from Phil’s own long life of craft. At eighty his back stays straight and his eyes keep fire. Nature made him poacher, sportsman, and nature lover at once. Dogs and children fell for his charm at first sight, Watson adds. First steps in wood craft lead his boyhood chapters. Partridge, hare, and pheasant runs fill the mid book in turn. Salmon, grouse, and rabbit work close his trade schooling.
36974-old-trails-on-the-niagara-frontier:
Old Trails on the Niagara Frontier is a local history by Frank Severance, printed at Buffalo in 1899. A frontispiece shows the vision of Brébeuf, drawn by Green. Severance inscribes the studies to the young people of the schools of Buffalo. Many of them, he says, had accompanied him in school-room talks over the old trails of their home region.

The contents open with the Cross Bearers, the Jesuit missionaries of the frontier. The Paschal of the Great Pinch and With Bolton at Fort Niagara follow. What befell David Ogden, a Fort Niagara centennial, and the journals of an early Buffalo merchant fill the middle. The value of such local history, Severance writes, depends on its relation to the general history of the country.
37012-the-recruiting-officer:
The Recruiting Officer is a comedy in five acts by George Farquhar, printed here from the prompt book of the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden. The edition carries remarks by Mrs Inchbald, the actress and critic. She judges that if the last two acts matched the first three, the play would rank foremost among Farquhar's works. Those first acts she calls brilliant in wit, humour, character, and incident.

Inchbald notes that Farquhar was himself a recruiting officer. He likely gathered the play's materials on the very spot where he set its scene, Shrewsbury. He dedicated the piece to all friends round the Wrekin, the local hill. She praises the country folk he drew: Rose, her brother, and the two recruits. The remarks also touch on the old stage custom of women in men's dress. The volume is a classic acting edition of the best-known English recruiting comedy.
37100-the-backwoodsman-or-life-on-the-in:
Backwoodsman, or Life on the Indian Frontier, is a frontier narrative edited by Lascelles Wraxall. Ward, Lock and Tyler published the book in London from Warwick House, Paternoster Row. A frontispiece shows a fight with grizzly bears at page 290 of the tale. Contents list the chapters of a settler life on the border.

My Settlement and The Comanches open the narrative in order of the chapters. A Fight with the Weicos and Hunting Adventures follow in the list. The Naturalist and the fate of Mr Kreger fill the next shown chapters of the book. The tale belongs to the shelf of Texas and border narratives that London publishers reprinted for British readers. Wraxall, a translator and editor of such works, presents a first hand life among hunters, settlers, and the peoples of the plains in the years before the Civil War remade the frontier.
37102-cedric-the-forester:
Bernard Marshall tells a tale of old England in Cedric the Forester, issued by D Appleton and Company, copyrighted in 1921. The contents open with the siege of Castle Mountjoy and a tapping on the dungeon wall, then name the hero in chapter three. A festival of the archers, outlaws of Blackpool, and the fortress of the monk-slayer follow.

Later chapters bring an iron collar and end on the road to Runnymede, planting the tale in King John's England. Plates show Cedric claiming victory, stones hurled by Alan the Armorer into a moat, and a shot by old Marvin's crossbow. Boys get archery and honor.
37109-health-through-will-power:
Health Through Will Power is a book on the mind and the frame by Walsh, a man of the heal craft with charge of a school of the lore of man. It was put out at Boston in nineteen nineteen. Its list of parts gives the path of the work. The will in life heads the run. Dreads, habits, and warm care come next.

Self pity stands past them in the list. Then come the shun of the willed use of the will, and what the will can do. Pain and the will, the will and air and sport, and the will to eat fill the mid run. The place of the will in the great lung ill stands near the end. The first words own a long truth of the heal craft.
37149-fritz-to-the-front-or-the-ventrilo:
Fritz to the Front, or the Ventriloquist Scamp Hunter, is a dime novel by Wheeler, author of a run of boy sleuth tales and of famed west tales. Its rights were set in law in the early eighteen eighties by a great house of cheap books. A print at its front shows its hero struck with dread at a sight.

Its parts open with a girl, then a strange wed tale. A bluff house, a grim relic, and a pals tale of the place fill the first run. The form is plain from its title: a lad who can throw his voice hunts rogues and solves crimes with that gift, in the loud cheap print of its day.
37178-cecil-castlemaine-s-gage-lady-mara:
Cecil Castlemaine's Gage, Lady Marabout's Troubles, and Other Stories gathers tales by Ouida. Lippincott published the volume at Philadelphia in 1900, under an arrangement with the author. A publisher's note says the pieces first appeared in leading European journals. Ouida had lately gathered and revised them herself for book form.

The title tale turns on a broidered shield and a famed beauty of an old county family. Cecil Castlemaine is praised as the handsomest woman of her race and age. A second tale treats a Maltese peerage, and a third follows the worries of a chaperone through three seasons. Shorter studies in period dress close the contents. The publisher warns that rival American editions break the courtesies of the trade. Another volume of Ouida tales was in press at the same time.
37189-the-return-of-the-soldier:
Rebecca West published a short novel in 1918 about a soldier who comes home changed. It opens in a nursery kept bright and gay though the child of the house is dead. Kitty waits there for word from her husband, who is somewhere in France. She tells herself that no news for a fortnight is no cause for fuss.

The narrator watches a home strained by war, loss, and long silence. Spring light fills the room while dread sits under each calm word. West uses a small house and a few people to show what war does off the field. The book is brief, tense, and closely observed.
37243-jane-oglander:
Jane Oglander is a novel by Mrs Belloc Lowndes, printed at New York by Scribner in 1911. An epigraph sets its key: something more imperious than reason warns us that life's secret lies not in slow adaptation, but in costly victories and splendid defeats. A French line heads the prologue: she was born to please noble souls.

Jane Oglander is walking across Westminster Bridge on a late September day. It is a little after four, on the bridge perhaps the quietest hour of the working day. Yet a ceaseless stream of human beings ebbs past her. A human being, and especially a woman, the narrator remarks, may be described in many ways. It was fortunate, for the tale, that on this eventful afternoon Miss Oglander attracted a certain attention. Lowndes, later famous for thrillers, here writes a society novel with a psychological edge.
37255-the-young-dragoon-every-day-life-o:
The Young Dragoon: Every Day Life of a Soldier is a novel by A W Drayson, published at London by Ward, Lock and Tyler, with illustrations by Richard Huttula. Its narrator introduces himself at once: I am a soldier, Frederick Trenchard, at your service. The prospect before him in his early days was to follow the plough, not the drum.

His father was a farmer in the Midland counties, and his grandfather, uncle, and cousins were farmers too. He is the only one of a numerous family who ever took the Queen's Shilling. Soldiers, in the popular opinion of his family, were utter outcasts, vultures in red coats and pipeclay. A certain young Meadows in the village had gone for a soldier, and the wiseacres shook their heads at any youngster's frolic. Drayson's tale follows a ploughboy into the ranks and through a dragoon's daily life.
37355-pray-you-sir-whose-daughter:
Helen H Gardener wrote Pray You, Sir, Whose Daughter, issued in New York by R F Fenno and Company in eighteen ninety two. The book opens with a dream in which Life holds out Love in one hand and Freedom in the other. The dreamer picks Freedom. Gardener gave the book to her husband, whom she praises for his faith in equal rights for women.

The preface says the tale shows what want and dependence do to the heart and mind. Three girls from three ranks in life each face a hard test. Each test shows the need for self reliance and self support for women. A rich home in the tale holds a strong wife worn down to a mere echo of her husband. The novel speaks for change in home and law.
37389-chlorination-of-water:
Joseph Race wrote Chlorination of Water, published by John Wiley and Sons. The publisher's notice states the book's intent directly. In it, the various aspects and methods of chlorination are discussed. The aim is to stimulate research work in this field of science. Race also wrote the Examination of Milk for Public Health Purposes for the same house. That handbook serves those engaged in examining milk.

The milk book runs to two hundred and twenty-four pages, with four diagrams, at a dollar seventy-five. Chlorination was then a young art in water supply, spreading from emergency dosing toward routine treatment. A chemist who examined milk for towns was well placed to argue water disinfection to them. Wiley's list presents both books as working tools for the new profession of public health analyst.
37392-green-balls-the-adventures-of-a-ni:
Green Balls, the adventures of a night-bomber, is a war memoir by Paul Bewsher, printed at Edinburgh and London in 1919. Bewsher dedicates the book to his faithful friend, the night sky, which guarded him from the enemy and a thousand times saved his life. In the preface he owns that the personal pronoun works hard in his pages.

He explains that the public who did not fly in the war would rather hear one man's own tale than a dry record of events. So he sets down his feelings, his strange fears, and his spells of fearlessness. He was a desk-bound London youth pitchforked in a moment into war and into a new trade, bombing at night from the air. Verses at the chapter heads come from his own poems, The Bombing of Bruges and The Dawn Patrol.
37482-the-postmaster:
Joseph Lincoln's The Postmaster was published in April 1912, with copyright in Appleton's name and pictures by Howard Heath. Lincoln had written Cap'n Eri and The Depot Master before it. The tale is told in the first person by Cap'n Zeb, a schooner skipper just retired from the sea.

Mr Pike, his owner, is sorry to lose him, and asks what he will do back in Ostable. Nothing at all, says Zeb, prompt as a shot. The chapter heads promise a livelier rest than that: two bets made, a venture into politics, a clam chowder with results, a trap, a cousin Lemuel, and a letter to Ichabod. The talk is salt-water talk from the first page.
37501-in-answer-to-prayer:
In Answer to Prayer holds essays on prayer by ten church men, first written for the Sunday Magazine and printed in book form in New York in 1899. The writers hold the Bishop of Ripon, Dr. Cuyler of New York, and Dr. John Watson, who wrote as Ian Maclaren. Canon Knox Little and William Quarrier of Glasgow also wrote pieces.

Each writer treats prayer from his own life and work in the church or in care for the poor. The note at the front says Watsons piece stands apart in kind, yet fits as a bridge to the seen world. The Dean of Salisbury and Dr. Horton are among the rest. Readers of faith get plain, warm counsel on what prayer can do, drawn from real lives of service.
37557-open-water:
Arthur Stringer wrote this book of poems, Open Water, printed at New York, London, and Toronto in 1914. Stringer also wrote The Woman in the Rain and a book of Irish poems. A contents page lists some sixty lyrics, from Milkweed and Home Thoughts to Sappho's Tomb, At Notre Dame, The Steel Workers, The Wild Geese, and April on the Rialto.

A foreword warns the casual reader what to expect. These lyrics, Stringer says, are written without end-rhyme, and it may be claimed they are without rhythm too, so that they may seem a revolt against two chief assets of modern verse-making. Yet poetry, he argues, must honour its ancestry even while the artist's soul wars against the forms that wall it in, as painting, music, sculpture, and the drama have lately done.
37674-some-account-of-the-public-life-of:
An account of the public life of Lieutenant General Sir George Prevost was published to answer his critics, particularly a Quarterly Review article of October 1822. Prevost had governed the Canadas during the War of 1812. A Shakespeare motto heads the title page: let him be testified in his own bringings forth, and he shall appear a statesman and a soldier. The strictures on his military character are the target.

Prevost's recall and death left his reputation contested. Supporters printed this defense of his Canadian services. The book belongs to the pamphlet wars that followed controversial commands. It argues from his own dispatches and acts. Prevost commanded at Plattsburgh, the campaign that drew the harshest criticism.
37709-leo-xiii-the-great-leader:
Doyle wrote a warm tribute to Pope Leo the Thirteenth for the Catholic World in August 1903, just after the pope died. Leo died at four in the afternoon on July 20, past ninety years of age. Doyle says the world watched the deathbed for two weeks.

The piece opens with words from Leo on the need to return to Christ as the way, the truth, and the life. Doyle holds that a land heals when that spirit grows in it, for folk and for the state alike. He calls Leo the great man of his age and says a full praise must wait, since we stand too close to so large a life.
37711-astronomical-lore-in-chaucer:
Florence Grimm wrote Astronomical Lore in Chaucer as number two of the University of Nebraska studies in language, literature, and criticism, published at Lincoln in 1919. The study asks how much of the old astronomy lives in Chaucer's poetry, and why.

Grimm begins with astronomy in the Middle Ages, when the names astronomy and astrology covered one subject and ordinary people read the heavens without clocks or almanacs. In a universe centred on the Earth, the planets governed more than light and seasons. Venus ruled love, Mars war, and the Sun power and honour, and each planet bore on parts of the body. Chapters then measure Chaucer's scientific knowledge, his cosmology, and his astrological lore in detail. The book reads a poet through the science of his century.
3782-huntingtower:
John Buchan sends Dickson McCunn, a retired Glasgow grocer, on a walking holiday that turns into a rescue tale. McCunn, a decent and bookish man, wanders into a Galloway village where a captive princess and foreign plotters hide behind quiet walls. A bachelor's den, with red paper, a fire, and a whisky decanter, becomes one unlikely council chamber as local allies gather.

Buchan writes with a light hand for a thriller, letting an ordinary hero grow brave by steps rather than by bluster. The Scottish countryside, its speech, and its stubborn folk carry much of the charm. Readers who like adventure with humor will find Huntingtower a fine entry to Buchan, with suspense that never quite loses its smile.
37824-the-wireless-officer:
The Wireless Officer, a sea novel for boys by Percy Westerman, was published by Blackie at London and Glasgow in 1922. Wigfull drew the pictures. Its front plate shows lascars bundling bodies into a lifeboat. Westerman wrote scores of such tales, and the list at the front names dozens: The Third Officer, Sea Scouts All, and many Standish adventures among them.

Chapter titles from the tale promise the old man disturbed, Mostyn to the rescue, and a decoy wireless message. The difference of a dot, in Morse, turns one plot point, and an eventful river trip follows. A night of horror, repairs and renewals, and a fight to a finish close the voyage. Westerman served at sea and wrote from knowledge. His wireless officer stands at the key where the war and the wireless age met, in a story built for boys who dreamed of the sea.
37829-little-man-s-family-dine-ya-zhi-ba:
Little Man's Family is a bilingual pre-primer for Navaho children. The Bureau of Indian Affairs issued it through the Phoenix Indian School Print Shop. J B Enochs wrote the book, and Gerald Nailor drew the pictures. This third edition of September 1953 ran to 5,000 copies. A single copy cost 20 cents.

Each page pairs a short English sentence with its Navaho translation. A Navaho boy introduces his family one by one. His mother, father, baby brother, big sister, and little sister appear in turn. The hogan, the sweathouse, the sheep, and the corral follow. His mother cleans, cards, and spins wool at her loom. She weaves a rug, and the family sells it. An appendix explains the Navaho alphabet and its vowel sounds for English speakers.
37837-peter-and-polly-in-winter:
Peter and Polly in Winter is a children's school reader by Rose Lucia. The American Book Company published it in 1914. Lucia had been principal of a primary school in Montpelier, Vermont. Peter and Polly volumes for the other three seasons precede this one. The contents list more than thirty short winter pieces. Peter and Polly and a birds' game of tag open the book. The Stone-Wall Post Office and Playing in the Leaves follow. The Bonfire and The Hen That Helped Peter come early.

The First Ice, The Three Guesses, and The First Snowstorm mark the season. Cutting the Christmas Tree and Christmas Morning give holiday pieces. The Snow House and The Fall of the Igloo continue the snow play. Fishing through the ice and making molasses candy close the list. The reader teaches winter through two children's days.
37908-adeline-mowbray-or-the-mother-and-:
Adeline Mowbray, or the Mother and Daughter, is a novel by Opie, opening in an old family mansion on a Gloucestershire estate called Rosevalley. There reside Mowbray and Adeline, her only child.

The first chapter reaches back to the grandmother, Editha Woodville, whose father married the sole daughter of an opulent London merchant, her large dower paying off mortgages on the Woodville estates. Editha, an only child and probable heiress of great possessions, became the idol of her parents. One of her first lessons was egotism: that all who approached her should study the gratification of her whims. Yet she had a taste above those enjoyments, a decided passion for literature caught from an aunt raised among literary characters.
38072-wind-and-weather:
Alexander McAdie wrote Wind and Weather, a book on winds and storms that came out in 1922. McAdie taught at Harvard and ran the Blue Hill weather post in his state. The book opens with the old Tower of the Winds at Athens. That tower once told the hour and the turn of the year.

Each wind then gets its own short part, named for the Greek gods of old tales. Boreas is the north wind, and Zephyros is the west wind. Charts show the paths of high and low air, and how storms form and move. Photos show the Blue Hill post in ice. The book suits readers who want the science of weather told in clear words.
38254-bart-keene-s-hunting-days-or-the-d:
Bart Keene's Hunting Days, or the Darewell Chums in a Winter Camp, is a boys' tale by Allen Chapman. Cupples and Leon held the rights from 1911, and Goldsmith printed it. The tale opens with a midnight trip and a missing diamond bracelet. A fruitless search and a shooting gallery scene fill the early chapters. Thirty chapters carry the chums from home to camp and back.

An odd letter, a railroad wreck, and tents going up fill the road part. A place of turtles, a mud volcano, and Bart's first shot follow in camp. Fenn falls in, Frank makes pancakes, and a wildcat trees the boys. Lost in the woods and a night of misery test the camp crew. Christmas comes in camp, then footprints in the snow raise alarm. Bart's best shot and the bracelet close the long winter hunt.
3828-simon-the-jester:
William Locke opens this comic novel at a London club, where the knowing Renniker answers every question, from trimming a puppy's tail to the mind of any European potentate. Asked for the most God forsaken spot in England, Renniker names Murglebed-on-Sea, a south coast watering place in the fine flower of November desolation. The narrator sends his man Rogers to inspect it, and Rogers returns like a servant who expected a pantry and found a desert.

Later scenes bring Colonel Bunnion, a genial red faced man with a moustache too big for his body. A small figure in a devil of a top hat butts him in the stomach and bounds off like a football. Locke writes with light irony throughout. Readers who like Edwardian comedy will find a tale of odd places and odder people, told with a smile.
38283-schopenhauer:
Thomas Whittaker wrote Schopenhauer, a short primer in the Philosophies Ancient and Modern series from Constable. The series grew from the success of a like set on religions of old and new times. Each book is a neat shilling volume, with a brief preface, a list of dates, and chief sources. The aim is to give the wide public the chief points of each school. Greece, Rome, the middle ages, and modern Europe all fall in the plan.
