Arthur Schopenhauer may be called, says the book's own note of him, the greatest philosophic writer of his century. Whittaker sets out the marks of that thought in small compass. The primer serves readers who want a sound first map of a hard thinker, with dates and books to guide them on.
3831-the-secret-power:
Marie Corelli sets this mystical romance in the hills of Southern California, above the Sierra Madre. A bearded man lives in a roughly built hut with papers and books neatly piled, reading through the heat while a great cloud sails overhead like foam on a sea wave. He claims a discovery given by a Supreme Intelligence, a power meant to rid the earth of mischief, disease, and sorrow.

His friend Gwent questions him, asking why man should not leave such work to the Supreme Intelligence itself. The hermit answers that man exists to help the scheme of the universe, not hinder it, and must destroy hindrance wherever it stands. Corelli writes with earnest grandeur throughout. Readers who like spiritual romance will find a tale of faith, science, and high purpose.
38367-knowledge-is-power:
Charles Knight's Knowledge Is Power views the productive forces of modern society and the results of labour, capital, and skill. The second edition, from John Murray in London in 1859, adds twenty-four woodcuts of manufacturing processes. Knight inscribes the book to Neil Arnott, in admiration of his devotion of scientific knowledge to the public good.

An extract from the introduction states the method. The book will not take the formal shape of a treatise on political economy. Knight conveys the broad parts of that science in a somewhat desultory manner, though not devoid of logical arrangement. He wishes especially to be understood by the young, on whose grasp of the principles governing society much of the coming security and happiness depends. Chapter one measures the feeble resources of civilized man alone in a desert; chapter two makes society a system of exchanges.
38418-from-manassas-to-appomattox-memoir:
James Longstreet's From Manassas to Appomattox, memoirs of the Civil War in America, was published by Lippincott at Philadelphia in 1896. Longstreet, lieutenant-general in the Confederate army, dedicated the work to the officers and soldiers of the First Corps. The preface explains why the book came thirty years after the surrender. General Lee had meant to write the campaigns of the Army of Northern Virginia himself.

Lee asked Longstreet for reports, despatches, and letters whose originals were lost, and Longstreet sent what he had. Lee gave up the work, and his death closed the hope of the story from its commander. Longstreet says he is glad to write late, when softened feeling lets the tale be read in its own spirit. Gratitude that the Liberty Bell is welcomed in Atlanta and Charleston closes the preface.
38424-notes-of-a-son-and-brother:
Henry James published an autobiographical volume at New York in March 1914, a sequel to A Small Boy and Others. A pencil portrait of William James, drawn by himself about 1866, forms the frontispiece. Illustrations include a portrait of Katherine Temple from 1861 and a leaf from a quoted letter. James writes as son of his father and brother of William.

The memoir recalls the James family's travels, schooling, and Civil War years. Henry James shaped the record with a novelist's care for scene and consciousness. Critics treat the two autobiographies as works of art in themselves. Scribner's issued the book with illustrations from family papers.
38447-adventures-in-swaziland-the-story-:
Adventures in Swaziland is the tale of a Boer of South Africa by Owen Rowe O'Neil. It was put out at New York in nineteen twenty one. Plates from light prints stand thick in it. The book is sworn to the sire of the hand. That sire is named there as guide, farm man, and war man. The list of parts is writ in long, full heads.

The first head tells how the house of O'Neil came to the north land. Boers with Irish names are its theme. A great chief's no to the buy of a bay, the break of the Boers for free state, and their red fights with the wild tribes fill it. The great trek and the foul play of a Zulu king stand past them.
38458-the-enemies-of-women-los-enemigos-:
The Enemies of Women, a novel by Vicente Blasco Ibáñez, was turned from the Spanish by Irving Brown and issued at New York in 1918. Dutton published the book in the flood of his war era fame. The author list names The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse first. Mare Nostrum, Blood and Sand, and La Bodega follow among his works.

The Spanish title, Los Enemigos de la Mujer, is kept on the title page. Ibáñez wrote of love, war, and the Riviera world of rich idlers. His novels sold across the world in translation in those years. This tale belongs to that run of success after the Four Horsemen. English readers met a Spain of passion and sharp social sight. The book is a sample of the first great wave of his fame abroad.
38463-a-selection-from-the-works-of-fred:
Frederick Locker's light verse fills this 1865 selection in the Moxon's Miniature Poets series, with pictures by Richard Doyle and Millais. Many pieces had appeared in London Lyrics, which ran through two editions, in 1857 and 1862. A few are restored here to the reading of the first edition. A dedicatory poem to Charlotte opens the book, dated from Rome in May 1862.

The contents mix wit and tenderness, from The Jester's Moral and The Widow's Mite to A Human Skull and To My Grandmother. Piccadilly and The Pilgrims of Pall Mall give the London scenes, while The Housemaid, The Old Government Clerk, and The Victoria Cross follow. The manner stays polished and gently sad by turns. It is verse from a man of the world writing for readers who knew the London he describes.
38535-the-great-illusion-a-study-of-the-:
Norman Angell wrote The Great Illusion, a study of how military power bears on national advantage. Putnam put out this fourth, revised and enlarged edition at New York and London. Rights were held in 1910, 1911, and 1913, and the book first came out in November 1909. Editions for sale abroad cover much of the world. Heinemann sold it in Britain, Hachette in France, and houses in Germany, Italy, Spain, and Japan.

Angell asks what motives explain the rivalry of armaments in Europe, above all the Anglo-German race. Each nation pleads the need for defence against attack, he notes. His study tests whether great fleets and armies still buy a nation wealth or safety. The title names the error he attacks: the belief that force secures trade and gain. Few books of its season were reprinted so often or read so wide.
38542-a-century-of-sail-and-steam-on-the:
Barlow Cumberland wrote a local history of boats on the Niagara River, put out in Toronto in 1913 by The Musson Book Company. The book came out about two months after his death, with all final proofs passed by his own hand. It treats only craft that served ports on that river, not all of Lake Ontario.

Cumberland traces sail giving way to steam, the fame of the Frontenac and the Ontario, and hard trade wars on the route. Railways then cut the traffic down to one boat. The last thirty five years tell of the Niagara Navigation Company, which brought the route back to full and bright success.
38602-the-monk-and-the-hangman-s-daughte:
Danziger de Castro and Ambrose Bierce stand as authors of The Monk and the Hangman's Daughter, in 1911. A note tells the strange history of the tale. Danziger wrote it in 1889, founded on a German tale, with a tragic plot. He gave it a happy ending, then asked Bierce to revise the story. Bierce urged that the tragic part be kept, and revised it so. The book came out, and the publishing house failed.

In 1900 a publisher wanted the tale, if a happy ending were restored. Bierce wrote in August 1900 that it would not do. The book is almost perfect as written, he said, and his own part pleased him least. A happy ending, he held, is the shallowest of devices, a schoolgirl desire. Benedicta, her secret love, and the monk Ambrosius stand at the heart of the quarrel over the close.
38627-queen-victoria-as-i-knew-her:
Theodore Martin wrote these memories of Queen Victoria for private circulation in 1901. Blackwood of Edinburgh and London printed the small tribute that year. A sonnet at the front bids the reader stifle the throbbing of a haunting pain at her death.

She is not dead, the sonnet insists, for still in our hearts she lives. Martin, her biographer of Prince Albert and a knight of her household orders, knew her long. His pages recall audiences, letters and kindnesses from a reign of sixty-four years, written in the first grief of 1901 for friends rather than the market.
38629-charles-darwin-his-life-told-in-an:
Francis Darwin edited this life of his father from Charles Darwin's own autobiographical chapter and a selected series of his published letters. John Murray published the book at London in 1908, with a portrait. The contents trace the whole arc. They cover the Darwins, the autobiography, religion, Cambridge life, and the appointment to the Beagle. Then come the voyage of 1831 to 1836 and the settling at Down.

The later chapters are the history of a book. They trace the foundations, growth, writing, and publication of the Origin of Species in 1859. Then come the reviews and attacks of 1860, and the spread of evolution in the decade after. Further chapters treat the fertilisation of flowers, climbing and insectivorous plants. Francis inscribed the volume to Holland of St Moritz, where he had worked at it, in token of friendship.
38645-minstrel-weather:
Minstrel Weather is a book of poems by Marian Storm, issued at New York and London in November 1920, with pictures and decorations by Clinton Balmer. A Greek tag from Euripides stands at the front: knowledge, we are not foes, though the world blows with a great wind not of thee. Storm dedicates the book to Amy Loveman. Its keynote poem names the minstrel's making in a string of hours and seasons.

Dewfall, moonrise, high sweet clover, and chimney swifts at their twilight play open the list. Quail call, owl hoot, and a moth hovering stand before midnight pales at the step of day. Star wane, cobweb, and brown bracken turn the wheel toward morning laughing with frost in flower. Duck flight, hound cry, and wild grapes blackening close the round. The poems sing the turning year in that minstrel key.
38762-how-we-are-fed-a-geographical-read:
James Franklin Chamberlain wrote a school reader on where our food comes from. The book came out in New York in 1912. Chamberlain taught land lore at a state school in Los Angeles. The book sits in the Home and World series for the young. It was first put out in 1903 and oft reprinted since.

A tale of a loaf of bread starts the lessons. Meat, milk, fruit, and spice get the same world tour. Each food is traced from far farms to the home table. Maps of trade and land tie the tales as one. Young readers learn how wide the world feeds one house.
38775-the-first-easter:
Willard's First Easter came from the Henry Altemus Company at Philadelphia with a 1906 copyright. It belongs to Altemus' Beautiful Stories Series. Sibling volumes tell the first Christmas, the story of Ruth, and the story of Solomon. Willard reviews the blessed life of Jesus so children can grasp the day's significance. Jesus, he writes, used his powers only for the good of others.

Shepherds led by angels witnessed the birth, and the boyhood passed at Nazareth without sin. John baptized Jesus, who resisted temptation and began his public ministry. The ministry wandered through Galilee, to Capernaum several times and Jerusalem twice. At Cana he turned water into wine at a wedding feast. At Capernaum he healed all the sick who surrounded him. The narrative moves from these works toward the resurrection morning.
38822-the-genius-of-scotland-or-sketches:
The Genius of Scotland, or Sketches of Scottish Scenery, Literature and Religion, by the Reverend Robert Turnbull, was printed in New York by Robert Carter in 1848, in a fourth edition. Rights were entered in 1847. Turnbull was born and schooled in Scotland.

In his preface Turnbull says his birth and training gave him means to give Americans a just idea of his native land. His plan joins views of scenery with literary and life sketches, portraits of social and church character, travel events, and thoughts on local and general themes. He leaves out much that a mere tourist would note, and puts sketches of lasting interest in its place. Heads treat the Highlands, the Lowlands, and Burns Genius of Scotland. American readers of 1848 got a Scot case for his homeland.
38845-stories-of-the-scottish-border:
Stories of the Scottish Border, by Mr and Mrs William Platt, was first published by Harrap in December 1910 and reprinted into 1929. Sixteen full-page illustrations by Meredith Williams accompany the tales. Three opening essays treat the character of the Borders, a brief history of the Border, and what the Border names tell us. Then forty-nine story chapters follow, from Bamburgh and its coast onward.

The tales draw on ballad, legend, and history. Sir Patrick Spens, Black Agnes of Dunbar, and the Young Tamlane stand beside Otterbourne and Chevy Chase. Alnwick Castle and the Percies, the battle of Flodden Field, and the raid of the Kers fill the middle. The last chapters reach the Civil War, Montrose, and the Jacobites.
38873-the-gentle-reader:
Samuel McChord Crothers gathers a dozen literary essays in The Gentle Reader, published at Boston and New York in 1904. The pieces range over the enjoyment of poetry, the mission of humor, quixotism, Thoreau, and the pleasures of a bookish life, closing with chapters on doubt, cheerfulness and the growth of ideals. Each essay speaks in a relaxed, companionable voice rather than a scholarly one.

The opening essay mourns the passing of the Gentle Reader, once addressed in Tom Jones by Henry Fielding, and replaced in modern publishing by the Intelligent Reading Public. Crothers still writes for the older figure, the reader who takes a book to the fireside for company.
38932-steel-the-diary-of-a-furnace-worke:
Steel is the diary of a furnace worker by Charles Rumford Walker. The Atlantic Monthly Press published it in Boston in 1922. Walker kept the diary while working in the steel trade. The contents trace his path through the mills. Chapters move from an army camp to the open-hearth furnace.

The opening chapter finds troops coming home from war. Men on the ferry talk of lost jobs and strikes. Walker then takes work in a Pennsylvania steel town. Later chapters cover night shifts and the twenty-four-hour shift. One treats a blast-furnace apprenticeship. Another is named Dust, Heat, and Comradeship. The diary aims to show mill life from inside the work itself.
38945-canute-the-great-995-circa-1035-an:
Canute the Great, by Laurence Marcellus Larson, tells the life of the Danish king who ruled England and built a northern empire in the Viking Age. Larson taught history at the University of Illinois. Putnam published the book in 1912 in the Heroes of the Nations series.

Chapters follow Canute from his heritage through the conquest of England and the hard struggle with Edmund Ironside. His rule over the Danes in England and his ties to the English Church come next. Larson then traces the beginnings of empire, the fight with Norway, and the battle of Holy River. The pilgrimage to Rome and the conquest of Norway crown the story. A chapter on northern culture in Canute's days precedes the last years and the collapse of the empire after his death in 1035.
38948-four-years-a-scout-and-spy-general:
Four Years a Scout and Spy tells of General Bunker, one of Lieutenant General Grant most daring and successful scouts. The book was written by Downs, a major of the Twentieth Ohio Veteran Volunteer Infantry, and published at Zanesville, Ohio, in 1866.

The full title promises a narrative of thrilling adventures, narrow escapes, noble daring, and amusing incidents. They come from the experience of Corporal Ruggles, during four years service as scout and spy for the Federal Army. His services for twelve of the most distinguished generals in the United States Army are embraced. A dedication to Grant praises his energy, valour, and generalship. Readers get a Civil War spy memoir, published the year after the war ended.
38959-comparative-ecology-of-pinyon-mice:
Comparative Ecology of Pinyon Mice and Deer Mice in Mesa Verde National Park, Colorado, by Charles Douglas, appeared in August 1969 in the University of Kansas museum series. The study runs from page 421 to 504. Contents cover the land and plants of Mesa Verde, trap sites, home range, habitat choice, nesting, breeding, growth, food habits, water use, parasites, and predators.

Douglas sets the scene first: Mesa Verde spans about two hundred square miles of plateau and canyon. Trapping records ground each claim, with home range worked out by boundary strip methods and distances between captures. The paper compares two like mice sharing one park, showing how each fits its niche in pinyon and juniper country.
38978-mildred-s-new-daughter:
Martha Finley's Mildred's New Daughter was published in New York by Burt, under a copyright of 1894 held by Dodd, Mead. Finley, who also wrote as Martha Farquharson, was the author of the famous Elsie books. A verse from Mrs Hale on a sweet, heartlifting cheerfulness heads the title page.

Chapter one opens at six in the morning as a mantel clock wakes Ethel and Blanche Eldon, two little sisters in one bed. Their mother comes in smiling: their father, ill for weeks, has slept unusually well and seems easier and brighter, and has asked to see his children after breakfast. The girls' joy is plain, and Ethel's hope with it: that papa will soon be well enough for the family to go back to their own home, and to grandma and grandpa.
39002-herbert-spencer:
Herbert Spencer, by J Arthur Thomson, stands in the English Men of Science line shaped by J Reynolds Green. Dent printed it in London in 1906, with Dutton in New York. Thomson was a professor of natural history at the University of Aberdeen.

Early chapters treat Spencer birth, nurture, and years of practical work. Later parts trace how he thought out his Synthetic Philosophy, his grand plan to join all knowledge under evolution. Thomson sorts Spencer gifts of body and mind, then his heart and morals. Long parts weigh Spencer as a biologist and as champion of the evolution idea. The close runs through mind, society, and the population question. Readers get a clear life of a huge, shy thinker.
39237-the-conquest-the-story-of-a-negro-:
The Conquest, The Story of a Negro Pioneer, was writ by the pioneer himself and issued at Lincoln, Nebraska, in 1913. The book is given to Booker T Washington. A short note calls it a true tale of a Black man who was discontented. What came of that feeling is the tale, the note says.

Prints show a man who became number one in the opening of new land. One print shows folk come from miles round to mark a day. One shows his vow to build a town. Grain and alfalfa land, sand hills, and the Missouri River set the scenes. Late prints show two hundred and eighty acres under crops and folk in autos. The tale tracks a town built from raw land.
39238-the-homesteader:
Oscar Micheaux copyrighted his novel The Homesteader in 1917 with the Western Book Supply Company. Sioux City, Iowa published it, with pictures by Farrow from paintings. A note to readers owns the tale draws more on fact than most novels. Micheaux, born in southern Illinois thirty-three years back, homesteaded in South Dakota himself.

He bought a relinquishment at twenty and owned good lands five years later in full. A clash in his twenty-sixth year turned him from ranching to writing for good. Jean Baptiste carries that lived story under a changed name in the novel. Agnes, a sod house, a town shot up, and a railroad's coming fill early chapters. A Black pioneer's own West fills the pages.
39396-a-population-study-of-the-prairie-:
Edwin Martin studied the population of the prairie vole in northeastern Kansas for the University of Kansas museum series. The paper came out in Lawrence in April 1956 with nineteen figures. Contents run from introduction and general methods to habitat and population structure. Martin trapped voles with a trap described by Fitch in 1950, after other types proved less sure.

Tests showed that model easy to set, proof against springing empty, and kind to the captured animal. Chapters give population density, home range, and life history. Reproduction, litter size and weight, growth rates, food habits, runways and nests, and activity fill the life history part. Predation and mammalian associates close the study with a summary and cited literature.
39432-the-house-round-the-corner:
The House Round the Corner is a mystery novel by Gordon Holmes, the author of A Mysterious Disappearance. It was copyrighted in 1919 and issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. The chapter heads promise a haunted house handled as a puzzle.

A new tenant takes the house in the first chapter. A midnight seance follows in the third. Explanations, the fifth chapter warns, do not always explain. The tenant, Percy Whittaker, proves himself a man of action. A case is stated by a man named Armathwaite, and preparations for battle follow. The last chapter is called The Laying of the Ghost. The tale opens on a small train crawling up a valley. A traveller with fishing rods gets out at Nuttonby, a place of three thousand souls, and heads for the house.
39465-eleven-years-in-the-rocky-mountain:
Eleven Years in the Rocky Mountains and Life on the Frontier is a western history by Frances Victor. Victor also adds a history of the Sioux War and a life of General Custer. The volume was sold by subscription only, from Hartford in eighteen seventy seven. Its pictures are engravings, with maps of the country it describes.

The introduction opens with the author reading Irving's Astoria in a New York study. No hint then foretold her own knowledge of those far western scenes. Astoria, Fort Vancouver, and Walla Walla later became familiar ground to her. She notes the railroad now crossing plains where fur traders once wore trails. Steamboats ply rivers where mountain men once set their beaver traps. Cities rise where hunters once chased buffalo for winter food stores.
39466-reading-the-weather:
T Morris Longstreth wrote Reading the Weather for the Outing Publishing Company at New York in 1915, as Outing Handbook number forty-three. Photographs by Richard F Warren show clouds and storms, with a shower behind Valley Forge as front plate. Longstreth dedicated the book to his grandmother, herself responsible for so much sunshine.

Chapters treat the clear day, the storm cycle, and sky signs for campers. Clouds, winds, temperatures, rain and snow, dew and frost each get a section. The thunderstorm, tornado, hurricane, and cloudburst follow, then the barometer and the seasons. A weather bureau chapter and a chapter of explosions close the main run. Short lists at the back give signs of fair weather, storm, and clearing.
396-the-lady-or-the-tiger:
Frank Stockton poses a famed riddle in this short tale of a semi-barbaric king and his arena of poetic justice. Accused men must pick one of two doors: behind one waits a fair lady, behind the other a hungry tiger. When the king's daughter loves a young courtier, her lover faces the same cruel choice.

Stockton ends without telling which door the youth picks, leaving readers to weigh love, jealousy, and pride. The tale's fame rests on that open end, which has sparked debate for generations. Brief and polished, it shows how a simple puzzle can outlive whole novels.
39615-the-life-and-adventures-of-bruce-t:
Major Sir Francis B Head writes The Life and Adventures of Bruce, the African Traveller, here in a New York edition from Harper and Brothers, 1840, taken from the last London edition. An advertisement praises Bruce's heroic fortitude, constancy and perseverance under trials few travellers have matched. His subject is James Bruce, whose journeys into Abyssinia long met groundless distrust.

Head's abridgement keeps whatever is most interesting in Bruce's larger work, in a familiar and lively style. The advertisement stresses Abyssinia's singular position: an ancient Christian country cut off from other Christian states and ringed by pagan and Mohammedan nations.
39646-shaggycoat-the-biography-of-a-beav:
Shaggycoat, the Biography of a Beaver, is Clarence Hawkes's animal biography, published at Philadelphia by the Macrae Smith Company under a copyright of 1906. Hawkes had written Black Bruin, the biography of a bear, and Shovelhorns, the biography of a moose, in the same vein. Charles Copeland supplied the illustrations.

The dedication addresses the beaver himself as a little brother. Living in a house of his own making, ringed by a moat of his own device, the beaver heads a large family in a goodly community. He is more like man in his mode of life than any other creature. Verses of the dam on the quiet pond, where Pau-Puk-Keewis stood and the beaver rose from the bottom, open the tale. Hawkes tells a wild animal's whole life from inside its own world, the manner he made popular.
39647-the-spanish-american-reader:
Ernesto Nelson, once a professor at the University of La Plata in Argentina, made this Spanish reader for Heath in 1916. Full notes and a vocabulary support the texts. Nelson had served as an education commissioner from Argentina to the Panama Pacific International Exposition.

In his foreword Nelson notes the fast-growing interest in Spanish in American high schools and colleges. Many students, he found, took the language for the sake of Spanish America itself. He calls that region a fair and fruitful field for work and trade, and shapes his readings to serve both language study and knowledge of the lands.
39870-bert-wilson-marathon-winner:
Bert Wilson, Marathon Winner, by J W Duffield, was held under a 1914 copyright by Sully and Kleinteich and reprinted at Racine, Wisconsin, in 1924. Duffield wrote Bert Wilson at the Wheel, Bert Wilson Wireless Operator, and Bert Wilson Fadeaway Ball. Seventeen chapters fill the book.

The tale opens with a thundering cheer from ten thousand throats as three athletes run. Field events crowd the day, pole vault, hammer throw, and broad and high jumps, all hotly fought. Chapter heads name a deadly rattler, a run for life, a floating race track, and the first marathon. A liner path, a man overboard, crooked work, and a dynamite ship pace the mid tale. A fearful waking and a glorious victory close the run. Boys of the day got track thrills with sea peril mixed in.
39956-the-expositor-s-bible-ezra-nehemia:
Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther is a volume of the Expositor's Bible by Walter Adeney. Funk and Wagnalls published the authorized edition in New York in 1900. Robertson Nicoll edited the twenty five volume series. Adeney was professor at New College, London, in New Testament and church history. His volume treats three books of the Old Testament in turn. The contents run to twenty six chapters or more.

Cyrus and his royal edict open the historical account. The second exodus and the new temple follow. Ezra the scribe gets chapters on his mission and his expedition. Foreign marriages and the cost of an idealist's success mark the Ezra section. Nehemiah the patriot then takes the stage. His prayer, midnight ride, and wall building fill the middle chapters. Usury, the reading of the law, and the joy of the Lord come later.
40008-the-autobiography-of-a-cornish-smu:
John Cornish edited The Autobiography of a Cornish Smuggler, Captain Harry Carter of Prussia Cove, in a second edition printed in London in 1900. Carter lived from 1749 to 1809 and wrote his own life in Cornish dialect. The manuscript stayed with the Carter family at Helston for many years.

Cornish learned of the memoir by chance talk with a distant relative of the writer's family. A Wesleyan magazine memoir of 1831 had drawn on the manuscript and on family knowledge of the captain. The tale centres on the coast between Marazion and Helston, a classic smuggling shore of Cornwall. Readers get a rare first-hand smuggler's life, with landing scenes and narrow escapes.
40016-the-last-rose-of-summer:
The Last Rose of Summer is a novel by Rupert Hughes. Harper issued it in New York and London in 1914. The tale opens in the town of Carthage. Mrs Shillaber throws her dining room into the parlour. Folding doors and a rug over the register do the work. Guests fill every seat in the house. Camp-stools are borrowed from Crankshaw, the undertaker.

Those stools are a standing joke of the town. One will surely collapse under some guest. A solemn man will fail to open his at all. Funerals gain a light touch from the peril. Deborah at her dressing table fronts the book. Hughes writes small-town life with warm comedy. Music and young love are his usual fare.
40017-the-stampeder:
S A White wrote a tale of the gold fields printed at Toronto in 1910, with pictures. The front picture shows Rex Britton pushed to the brink of a crack in the ice by a wild eyed Corsican. Other pictures show dog teams racing neck and neck, and raw gold flashing in an Indian's palm.

The tale opens in an Algerian port, where Britton's steam yacht runs down a coasting ship in the dark. Rex is thrown from his berth and polishes the passage with his face. He clutches the stairs and climbs on deck in his night clothes. White's tale then moves north, where men stampeded for gold in the far cold country.
40211-church-reform-the-only-means-to-th:
Church Reform, a letter to Sir Robert Peel by Richard Carlile, argues for change in the church. Carlile printed and published it himself at 62 Fleet Street in London. A correspondence with the Bishop of London in 1833 is prefaced to the letter. Carlile opens that correspondence with a letter dated November 18, 1833.

He has long thought the state of the country and the church calls on him, he writes. He offers to wait on the bishop as his diocesan for an interview on the matter. There the bishop may hear what he advances against the present state of the church. And what he proposes as a necessary and proper reform follows in that plea. A famed radical publisher presses a prime minister on the established church.
40254-bert-wilson-s-twin-cylinder-racer:
J W Duffield wrote Bert Wilson Twin Cylinder Racer, a tale for boys held by rights from 1914. The book was printed again in 1924 at Racine, in Wisconsin. Duffield had told past tales of Bert at the wheel and at sea. The tale opens at a train stop on a bright June day.

A shout warns that a train is on the loose with no crew in its cab. The great engine picks up speed as the crowd stands spellbound. That rush sets the pace for the whole book. Bert and his Blue Streak bike race from coast to coast in the next parts. A lost hut, a burst dam, a feud, and a forged wire add risk. A fire in the woods and a race with a sky ship close the run to a win in a fight.
40277-the-little-indian-weaver:
Madeline Brandeis wrote The Little Indian Weaver, put out by Grosset and Dunlap at New York in 1928. Brandeis made motion pictures of the same name, and took the photos for the book herself. It is given to each child of each land, in hope that all learn to love each other. Bah, age five, is a small Navajo girl on the reservation in Arizona. Her sole doll is made from a corn ear, the sole kind she has ever known.

Bah lives with her mother in a hogan of mud and sticks. Her mother weaves fine blankets and sells them, and Bah learns the craft each day. Chapters take her to a trading post, show a prayer stick, and ask who wins a radio. Young readers get daily Navajo life in plain, warm terms.
40369-the-silent-readers-sixth-reader:
The Silent Readers Sixth Reader trains school children to read in silence. William D Lewis, Albert Lindsay Rowland, and Ethel H Maltby Gehres made the book. The John C Winston Company issued it in nineteen hundred twenty. Frederick Richardson and Edwin J Prittie drew its bright plates.

Speed drills with a watch open the teacher’s part of the book. All pupils start at one sign and raise a hand at the end. The teacher marks each child’s time in half minutes on a sheet. Mode and median are taught from one class of twenty names. Five minutes stands as both mode and median in that class. Lewis had served Pennsylvania schools as a chief of instruction. Rowland trained teachers for that same state school system. Silent speed with clear grasp was the new creed of the day.
40450-violet-forster-s-lover:
Violet Forster's Lover is a novel by Richard Marsh, printed in 1912. Cassell brought the book out in London, New York, and Toronto. Hodgson drew the colour frontispiece of Sydney's glad discovery scene. Marsh had writ Twin Sisters and The Lovely Mrs Blake before this. Thirty-four chapters run from the card on the floor to letters and a telegram.

While the groom waited and stop thief fill the early intrigue here. The good Samaritan, dreaming, and his wife come next in the list. Among thieves, the sandwich-man, and the drapery crowd the middle chapters. The lacquered club, sleepers awakened, and the two women follow on. The leather bag, an envelope, and the countess and Violet come later. A game of billiards and an irregular visitor raise the late stakes. Tickell turned his cards at the opening: a straight, he shows.
40497-the-prairie-schooner:
William Hooker wrote these tales of the prairie schooner and bull trains. Saul Brothers printed the book in Chicago in 1918. Hooker gives it to his wife, a Dakota valley pioneer. Contents open with letters between old pards of the trail.

Trains that run without rails and bull train magnates follow next. Guarding a freight outfit, rattlesnakes, and redskins fill the mid chapters. Bill Hickok as city marshal and young Cheyenne stand among them. A lost Indian, a she bear, and trousers tales close the set. One eyed Ed fate and a Christmas dinner grace fill two more chapters of trail life.
40520-the-soul-stealer:
C Ranger-Gull wrote The Soul Stealer, published at London in 1906. His other books listed include The Serf, The Harvest of Love, and The Price of Pity. Twenty-six chapters open with Mr Eustace Charliewood, man about town. An unexpected entrance of two ladies follows.

News of a revolution, the second lover's arrival, and a conspiracy of scientists build the plot. Will you walk into my parlour, England's great sensation, and the chivalrous baronet keep the pace. Beef tea and a phosphate solution, the tomb-bound man, and Lord Malvin deepen the strangeness. A death-warrant presented to a prisoner leads toward two final pictures. Readers get an Edwardian scientific romance of villainy and exchanged souls.
4053-nuttie-s-father:
Charlotte M. Yonge's novel follows Nuttie, a girl in a fresh Holland Sunday dress worked with wild strawberries by her mother's hands. In a small drawing room, nearly pushed in by Mr. Dutton, she meets a lady on the sofa through a daze of tears.

A chapter heading from King Lear frames the scene: a father wonders if the lady before him is truly his child. Yonge builds the story from family duty, faith, and the slow repair of broken ties. Readers who like Victorian domestic novels will find a gentle tale of a daughter, a father, and a home learning to hold together.
40592-the-little-spanish-dancer:
Madeline Brandeis wrote The Little Spanish Dancer, held in 1936 and issued at New York by Grosset and Dunlap by leave of A Flanagan Company. Photos by the author, taken in Spain, illustrate the book. Pilar Herrera of Seville plays the lead girl in the photos. A street in Seville forms a front print. Fifteen chapters and a pronouncing word list fill the book.

The Magic Castanets leads the chapters. An Old Red Cape and tales of old Cadiz follow. Souvenirs speak and old Granada legends fill the middle. A fiesta, a young prince mystery, and a stout sweetheart build the plot. Dance of the Six and a bullfight in Madrid are castanet legends in turn. Where Is Pilar and a stranger's arrival close the tale. Brandeis gives the book to her sister and kin with an international jest.
40664-the-wee-scotch-piper:
Madeline Brandeis writes The Wee Scotch Piper for Grosset and Dunlap in New York, copyrighted by the Flanagan Company in 1929. Brandeis produced motion pictures of the same tales, and her own photographs made in Scotland illustrate the book. A dedication in verse addresses every child of every land.

Eleven chapters run from The Craig Family through Scotland with Sandy to the title chapter. Chapter one sets Aberfoyle in Perthshire, where shepherd Alan Craig keeps sheep among bluebells and shady trees. A tattered piper marches up and down the village hoping for pennies, and Brandeis jokes that bagpipes may have begun as sheep bleating in chorus. Craig's sheep still roam the hills in heavy wool, lambs hiding under their mothers, while his dog Roy watches beside him.
4070-the-master-builder:
Henrik Ibsen's play follows Halvard Solness, a master builder who fears the young, above all Ragnar, and schemes to keep a talented young woman in his office. If he could get her into the office, he thinks, then Ragnar too would stay where he is.

Solness tells Dr. Herdal how he stood, looked, and wished intently, speaking to her in a friendly way about one thing and another before she went away. Ibsen turns that wish into a study of ambition, guilt, and the price of building high. Readers who like serious modern drama will find a tense, symbolic play about power and fall.
40732-liverpool-a-few-years-since-by-an-:
Liverpool a Few Years Since, by An Old Stager, reached a third edition at Liverpool in 1885. The writer looks back some fifty years to the town he knew. Chapter heads start with the Goree warehouses, the docks, and ships bound for sea. War, press gangs, convoys, and privateers come next. Named captains, merchants, and town officers fill page after page.

Later heads treat clubs, dinners, practical jokes, and the old Corporation. Roscoe, Sir John Gladstone, and Dr Currie appear among the local worthies. Watchmen, pigtails, and hair powder mark a vanished street life. The book is a store of tales and sketches of persons, kept for readers who knew the port in its earlier days.
40746-first-impressions-on-a-tour-upon-t:
First Impressions on a Tour upon the Continent in the Summer of 1818 is a travel book by Marianne Baillie, printed at London in 1819. The tour runs through parts of France, Italy, Switzerland, the borders of Germany, and French Flanders. Baillie gives the book to John Trevor, a valued friend of her earliest years, and a Swiss cottage faces the title.

In her preface Baillie says the pages began as private writing for a few close friends, not for print. She calls the work a sketch only, and begs pardon for its faults. She warns that readers must not look for fine writing from a novice, nor for the full history of every place from a woman travelling for pleasure so soon after the wars.
40783-the-minute-man-on-the-frontier:
Puddefoot, field secretary of the Home Missionary Society, sketches frontier life in The Minute Man on the Frontier for Crowell in 1895. Crowell published the book in New York and Boston, and a signed portrait of the author fronts it. Twelve chapters run from the frontier's place in the world to out of the way places.

His preface says he prints the sketches at friends' urging, before a fast vanishing frontier life disappears for good. Set pieces gleaned from diaries, he argues, can show a country's life more truly than great formal histories. Chapters cover early memories, immigrants, frontier oddities, and lights and shadows. A Saturday afternoon in the South, springtime in the South, and the North-West all get their own sketches.
4082-the-barrier:
A northern adventure novel opens with a song in dialect, as Poleon Doret sings of two brown eyes that changed everything for him. Clouds lift from the sky, winter feels like spring, and his pack grows light on the trail.

He sings of walking forty miles in a night to hear one song, and of making a fortune to marry the girl he loves. The Barrier, by Rex Beach, sets love and gold-seeking against the hard country of the far North. Readers who enjoy frontier romance will find a brisk tale of trails, traders, and stubborn hope.
40878-turner:
Cosmo Monkhouse wrote a life of Joseph Mallord William Turner for the Illustrated Biographies of the Great Artists series. Monkhouse had earlier written Studies of Sir E Landseer. The series list in front names lives of Titian, Rembrandt, Raphael, Van Dyck and Hals, Holbein, and Tintoretto, each from recent authorities. Turner, a Royal Academician, is the subject. The small volume aims at students and general readers.

Monkhouse traces Turner from a London barber son to the greatest landscape painter of his age. Early water colours, the Royal Academy rise, and continental tours fill the tale. The Liber Studiorum, the late sea pieces, and the bequest to the nation close it. Ruskin championship of Turner stands in the background. Art lovers get a compact Victorian life of a titan, with plates of the works.
40908-jane-allen-center:
Jane Allen plays center, and Edith Bancroft's 1920 series book keeps her at the heart of the team. Clouds pile over the prairie as Jane muses that sunshine waits behind each storm. She will not fret, she vows, over the trip back to Wellington school.

The table of chapters mixes court and campus: telltale tidings, a lost girl, election night, and the woes of Alias Helen. Madam Nalasky and the boy Stanislaus bring a mystery thread. Saalfield printed the set for girls who liked their heroines in the game. Bancroft's Jane stays cool, kind, and first to the ball. Games, votes, and lessons share the school year.
40939-under-cover:
Under Cover is the novel form of Roi Cooper Megrue's stage play, novelized by Wyndham Martyn and published by Little, Brown of Boston in 1914. Illustrations by William Kirkpatrick include a frontispiece of a gun found under a man's nose. The story opens in Paris in early spring.

An editor's note warns that the chapters jump from five to seven, with no chapter six in the original book. The plot turns on smuggling and secret service work, to judge by its scenes of arrest and payoff. Amy and Denby and Dick move through a world of customs men and undercover agents. Novelized plays were a steady trade of the day, letting theatre successes reach readers who never saw the stage. Megrue's hit made the crossing in the year of its first production.
41000-her-majesty-s-minister:
William Le Queux wrote the spy novel Her Majesty's Minister, a tale of secret state work in Paris. The narrator, Ingram, serves Lord Barmouth, the British ambassador to France. A planned move against Britain's foes has failed, and a secret has been sold by some unknown hand. Talk at the start turns on Yolande, a woman Ingram knows from Rome and trusts.

Lord Barmouth does not share that trust, since Yolande was seen with Hartmann, a man no friend to Britain. Ingram must find who sold the secret while court balls and quiet talks hide real risk. The book gives readers a close look at embassy life, coded talk, and the fear of a leak at the top.
41078-the-hunchback-of-westminster:
The Hunchback of Westminster is a novel by William Le Queux, in an edition dated 1904 from Methuen of London. Le Queux opens with a word before reading, in which he tells of his own odd hobby. For years he gathered rare and choice papers from the past.

His hunt for old parchments led him through France, Italy, Russia, Germany, and Belgium, and all over England. He says the hobby of old handwriting gave him his most magic hours and some real danger. From such papers, he hints, this strange tale grew. A young man named Jose Casteno came to his rooms with a grave charge in his second year as a private detective. Readers get mystery tied to old records, scandal, and peril.
41086-randolph-caldecott-a-personal-memo:
Henry Blackburn, editor of Academy Notes, wrote this personal memoir of Randolph Caldecott's early art career in 1886, the year of the artist's death at forty. One hundred and seventy-two illustrations fill the book, for Caldecott is known to the world chiefly by his picture books.

Blackburn prints letters and the sketches that accompanied them, sent to his own family and lent by friends. They show the artist before fame: the bank clerk from Chester teaching himself to draw the hunting field and the farmyard. Caldecott's toy books, John Gilpin and The House that Jack Built among them, reinvented the picture book with line that moves. The memoir preserves the charm his friends knew, in the year the children's world lost him.
41089-the-sign-of-the-stranger:
The Sign of the Stranger is a novel by William Le Queux, in an edition dated 1913 from Ward, Lock of London. Chapter one, The Advent of the Stranger, opens in the tap room of a village inn. A shabby stranger seats himself by the wide open chimney and asks for cold meat or bread and cheese, and a glass of beer.

Warr, the publican, scans the man keenly and moves slowly, until a handful of money speeds the meal. The stranger, tall, thin, and near forty, says he has come ten or eleven thousand miles and is glad of green English fields. He speaks as though he knows Sibberton, then denies it too fast, and the narrator detects the lie in his keen dark eyes.
41159-the-red-battle-flyer:
Manfred von Richthofen, the German air ace known as the Red Baron, wrote his own account of his war flying, here in English in 1918. Ellis Barker translated it, and Grey, editor of The Aeroplane, added a preface and notes. The frontispiece shows the captain in uniform.

Richthofen begins with his family, landed folk near Breslau and Striegau who had taken small part in wars. He goes on to the outbreak of war, boredom before Verdun, and his first solo flight. Chapters tell of bombing in Russia, his first English victim, and the day he won the Ordre Pour le Mérite. Few enemy accounts of the air war reached Allied readers so soon.
41191-jenifer-s-prayer:
Oliver Crane wrote 'Jenifer's Prayer,' a tale in three parts first printed in The Catholic World and in The Literary Workman. It opens in a room at an inn in Hull, where a young woman weeps like a child while an older man watches her in silence. He has spoken because he dreads the influence of the house they are going to, and of the people she will meet there.

She kneels, prays, and sleeps, while he walks the night streets of Hull at a quick pace, hands clenched, memory surging over him. The narrator then fills in the pair: she is beautiful and English, he is Scotch born and bred, strong and ruddy. What binds them, and what the dreaded house holds, drives the parts that follow.
41210-the-life-of-isambard-kingdom-brune:
Isambard Brunel wrote The Life of Isambard Kingdom Brunel, Civil Engineer, printed in London in 1870, with a portrait painted by Horsley and engraved by Barlow. The son follows his father's life in order only to the close of 1835, when the act for the Great Western Railway was obtained by Parliament.

Later chapters group the works: railways, the broad gauge fight, the atmospheric system on the South Devon line, bridges, docks, and ocean steam navigation. The Great Western steamship, the Saltash Bridge, and the Great Eastern all reached completion by his death in 1859. Staff engineers and friends supplied chapters and letters for the record. Engineering historians get a family monument.
41265-the-ocean-wireless-boys-and-the-lo:
The Ocean Wireless Boys and the Lost Liner, by Captain Wilbur Lawton, was copyright in 1914, with pictures by Charles L Wrenn. Lawton had written the Boy Aviators and Dreadnought Boys sets. A front plate shows a flash of blue fire fill the wireless room.

The liner Tropic Queen plunges south through green seas east of Hatteras, bound for the West Indies. In a steel hut on the boat deck sits Sam Smalley, a schoolboy who serves as aid wireless man. His chum Jack Ready is head operator of the ship. Forty chapters bring strange pleas, code notes, and a call of SOS. A lost craft of the skies, a leap for life, and a theft follow. Boys get a fast sea tale built on the new wireless art.
41323-the-mosstrooper-a-legend-of-the-sc:
The Mosstrooper is a tale of the Scottish edge lands by Robert Scott Fittis. It came out in nineteen six as a stone book past his death, with a life sketch past a friend. His wife tells in her front note that he wrote the tale when he was but past sixteen years old. Two verse quotes head it, both on the stark moss men of old.

The life sketch calls Fittis a man of writ of a kind fast lost in his land. He loved that land with a deep fire and set its heroes past his folk as marks to ape. He was read in all fields and held a store of rare lore. His work was long out of print and hard to get when his friends urged this book.
41328-may-iverson-s-career:
May Iverson's Career, by Elizabeth Jordan, author of May Iverson: Her Book and Many Kingdoms, was published by Harper. Twelve chapters follow May from her first assignment to the rise of the curtain, through cases, rehearsals, and rescues. A front plate shows May herself, and the book is dedicated with memories of the wistful Adriatic.

Chapter one opens as commencement ends at the school of Catharine, and the assembly hall breathes relief. Classmates shine in set pieces: one welcomes parents in a speech rehearsed for weeks, another forgets her address at the vital point. May steps from schoolgirl fame into newspaper work, and Jordan tells her cases with warmth and comedy, in the voice of a young woman finding her trade.
41388-the-modern-american-pistol-and-rev:
The Modern American Pistol and Revolver, by A C Gould, editor of The Rifle, was published by A C Gould and Company of Boston in 1888. A photograph of Mr F E Bennett, expert pistol and revolver shot, stands at the front. The title page promises a description of modern pistols and revolvers of American make, the ammunition used in them, the results accomplished, and the shooting rules followed by American marksmen.

Gould's preface tells how the book grew. For years he shared the common belief that fine shooting with a pistol past a few yards was impossible. He arranged trials by the most skilful marksmen to be found, and rivalry did the rest. The results, the makers told him, beat what anyone had thought the arms could do. Smith and Wesson, Colt, and the cartridge companies all lent their help.
41397-uncle-walt-walt-mason-the-poet-phi:
Uncle Walt is a verse book by Walt Mason, called the poet philosopher in its title. A Chicago house, George Matthew Adams, brought it out in nineteen ten. Short rhymes on daily life fill the book from first page to last. A few heads show the range at a glance: Longfellow, The Flag, and Home Life.

The verse works in brief, plain lines that turn a small thought into a homespun motto. Mason writes in the newspaper verse philosopher manner, close to home and plain speech. Creed pieces stand beside light rhymes, each kept short, clear, and firm in tone. No long tale holds the page; the point lands fast and stays in mind.
414-the-pageant-of-summer:
Richard Jefferies celebrates one English summer in this short prose poem of fields and lanes. Green rushes, hawthorn, angelica, and wild parsnip fill the opening pages, each plant noted for scent, sap, and shape. Birds, pollen, and ditch water join the slow march of heat and growth.

Jefferies writes with a naturalist's eye and a poet's ear, letting small sights carry large feeling. No plot disturbs the pageant; the season itself is the hero. The book endures as a classic of nature prose, best read slowly, like a walk through high summer grass.
41453-the-mysterious-mr-miller:
The Mysterious Mr Miller, a novel by William Le Queux, was published by Hodder and Stoughton of London in 1906. Le Queux wrote many tales of intrigue and secret service. The tale is told by Godfrey, a young man living in a boarding house at Shepherd's Bush in London.

It opens on a death. A stranger lodging in the house dies in a shabby bedroom as Godfrey and Doctor Tulloch watch. The man was strong and athletic, but a morphia habit had wrecked his health. He had told Godfrey almost nothing, and seemed set on hiding who he was. The search of his things promises the first clue to the mystery.
41460-the-king-of-alsander:
The King of Alsander is a romance by James Elroy Flecker, published by George Allen and Unwin of London in 1915. Flecker dedicated the book to Mavrogordato, who, he says, never despaired of the romance in the rough. Its chapters mix whimsy with adventure in an invented kingdom.

The story begins in the English village of Blaindon, whose hero's modest and pathetic ideal Flecker praises against city life. Norman Price is then knighted, joins a Society for the Advancement of Alsander, and fails a qualifying examination for the post of King of Alsander, for which failure he is whipped. A president tells a tale and debates the advantages of murder. Princess Ianthe and a priest enter the plot, counter conspiracy follows, and a battle looms. Flecker's comic Ruritania was written by a poet better known for The Golden Journey to Samarkand.
41492-whistler:
Wood wrote a small life of the painter Whistler for a series of masterpieces in colour. Jack of London and Stokes of New York sold the book. Eight colour plates go with the text. The frontispiece shows Old Battersea Bridge, a night piece now in the National Gallery.

That canvas, Wood notes, was brought out in court at the famed trial of Whistler against Ruskin. Other plates show a night view of Venice, the artist's studio, and the portrait of his mother, kept at the Luxembourg in Paris. Wood opens in Chelsea, where Rossetti and his circle gathered. Before Whistler, he says, night in painting was a dull, closed thing. Whistler showed its stillness lit by man's own silver and gold.
41562-the-hanging-stranger:
Philip K Dick wrote The Hanging Stranger, printed in Science Fiction Adventures Magazine for December 1953. Ed Loyce, a practical man of forty, runs a television sales store. The tale opens at five o'clock as he washes up and drives across town to the shop. His back aches from digging out his own basement. His wife Janet will get a new vase with the money saved.

Passing the little town park, he sees something hanging from the single lamppost. A shapeless dark bundle swings a little in the wind. The Chamber of Commerce sometimes puts displays in the square, he thinks. He turns the car around for a closer look. No one else on the street seems to see anything wrong. Dick builds his tale on a hanged stranger in plain view, and a town that will not notice.
41570-the-asteroids-or-minor-planets-bet:
The Asteroids, or Minor Planets Between Mars and Jupiter is an astronomical essay by Daniel Kirkwood. J B Lippincott published it in Philadelphia in 1888, copyrighted 1887. Kirkwood was professor emeritus at the University of Indiana. His preface cites the zone's claims on attention. Discovery there was progressing rapidly, and the orbits showed anomalous forms.

Part one gives the history in popular form. It tells how Ceres, Pallas, Juno, Vesta, and Astraea were found. Tables list every asteroid in order of discovery. Discoverers are credited with their totals, and elements are tabulated. Part two turns theoretical. It asks after the cluster's origin and the elimination of members. The law of gap formation gets a chapter. Commensurability of periods with Jupiter's is examined closely. Very eccentric orbits, Kirkwood argues, are weeded out. The elements come from the Paris Annuaire for 1887 and recent Berlin circulars.
41603-toto-s-merry-winter:
Laura Richards wrote this second and last book of Toto adventures for children. Roberts Brothers printed it in Boston in 1887. Richards gives the book to blind children of the Perkins Institution. They had heard the first Toto story read aloud with joy.

Chapter one sets a good old winter evening, cold out and warm in. Snow falls soft, caps the pump, and taps at cottage windows. Flakes peer in at brass, tin, and a great soup kettle. A crackling fire makes the kitchen glow bright for the tale start. The book is the second and last part of Toto's adventures.
41734-du-rer:
Herbert E A Furst wrote the Dürer volume in the Masterpieces in Colour series, edited by T Leman Hare. The series paired each artist with a writer, from Velazquez to Whistler. Furst says he has known and loved Dürer for many a year.

Albrecht Dürer lived from fourteen seventy-one to fifteen twenty-eight. Furst writes in a warm, chatty way, hoping to make readers love the master too. Colour plates show the great prints and paintings, starting with a portrait of Hieronymus Holzschuher. The book gives a plain path into the work of the famed German artist. Short text and fine plates suit new readers.
41777-blazing-arrow-a-tale-of-the-fronti:
Edward Ellis wrote Blazing Arrow, a tale of the frontier, number two of the War Chief Series, printed at Philadelphia in 1900. Ellis had written the Boy Pioneer, Deerfoot, and Log Cabin series. A plate shows a plunge over the falls. Thirty-three chapters carry the tale: Larry and Wharton, on the brink, and over the falls. Blazing Arrow himself comes fourth, then through the woods and a miscalculation.

A check, a chat, turning back, and groping in the dark fill the next heads. In a corner, reversing positions, and a blunder lead on. The detour, by the lake, and the strange sight follow. Across the gorge and Arqu-wao come in turn. Red Crow, good news, and all together lead to the last halt and the close. The first chapter opens on a bear hunt. Two youths have spied an enormous bear lumbering into the canebrake.
41791-the-house-by-the-river:
A P Herbert wrote The House by the River, a novel issued by Alfred A Knopf in New York in nineteen hundred twenty one. The scene is Hammerton Chase, a short road by the Thames. Old houses, trees, and small gardens line its bank. An island of young willows lies across the road.

The Whittakers hold an open house each Wednesday on the Chase. All the road goes, since no one else keeps a set day. Folk there know each plan and grief of each house. They lend wine glasses, tools, and boat anchors as kin do. Herbert sets this snug world apart from cold Kensington. There, he says, no one knows the folk next door at all.
41826-wild-heather:
Wild Heather is a girls' novel by Meade, published by Cassell in 1911. A colour frontispiece and three plates illustrate it. Heather Grayson, the heroine, tells her own story. She looks back on the first things of childhood. Her big thing, she says, arrived when she was eight years old. That year she came home with her father from India. Major Grayson doted on his little daughter aboard ship.

Heather was petted so much that she gave herself airs. Her father laughed and pressed her to his heart. He told her she would be a fascinating woman when she grew up. The voyage ends at Southampton, with a big hotel for the night. Plates promise later scenes: a captain refused by a stepmother, and talks on the heather. The novel follows an Anglo-Indian child into English life.
41859-the-terms-of-surrender:
The Terms of Surrender is a novel by Louis Tracy, published by Clode in New York in 1913. A long list of Tracy's earlier tales stands at the front of the book. The story opens far from his usual sea coasts. Its first scene is a store and saloon in the American West.

John Darien Power, the hero, rides in on a mustang gone lame. Colorado sunshine blazes on the June scene as the tale begins. Chapters trace the sudden rise of Peter MacGonigal and Power's travels east. A meeting, forty steps, and a step that counted build the middle. Nancy decides, and Power comes home, before darkness turns to light. A settlement and the passing of the storm close the long arc.
41935-the-adventures-of-ulysses-the-wand:
C Ranger-Gull retold The Adventures of Ulysses the Wanderer, an old story, published at London in 1902 with illustrations by W G Mein. He dedicates the book to Herbert Beerbohm Tree, in memory of the first night of Hamlet at Manchester. A frontispiece shows the Cyclops staring with his single eye.

A foreword and a brief account of the Odyssey's main characters come first. The episodes then run in order: how they blinded the son of Poseidon, the adventure of the palace in the wood, and how Ulysses walked in Hell. Readers get Homer's wanderer reshaped as an Edwardian storybook hero, episode by famous episode.
41947-boucher:
Haldane Macfall's Boucher, in the Masterpieces in Colour series edited by Leman Hare, treats the painter Francois Boucher, whose dates, 1703 to 1770, stand on the title page. The series gives each artist a small book of colour plates with a life and study by a named writer. Macfall also wrote the Fragonard volume.

The frontispiece is Boucher's Madame de Pompadour, held by the National Gallery of Scotland. Edinburgh, the note says, is fortunate to hold one of the world-famous examples of his portrait work, and that he painted the lady more than once with rare charm. The series list at the front shows the company Boucher keeps: Bellini, Botticelli, Da Vinci, Raphael, Rembrandt, and Turner among them.
42006-notes-and-queries-number-230-march:
Notes and Queries, No. 230, came out on Saturday, March 25, 1854, at fourpence a copy. The weekly called itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Captain Cuttle's line, 'When found, make a note of,' served as its motto.

The notes in this number print old English royal letters to the Grand Masters of Malta and a letter from the Countess of Blessington. Writers ask about Welsh consonants, the Consolato del Mare, and a drama called The Innocents. Replies take up the electric telegraph in 1753, false pedigrees, and leave to build with towers. A photo column closes the number, true to the new art's rise.
42039-notes-and-queries-number-137-june-:
Notes and Queries, number 137, dated Saturday, 12 June 1852, is a weekly number of the journal that called itself a medium of inter-communication. It is volume five, priced at fourpence, or fivepence stamped. Its readers were literary men, artists, antiquaries, and family historians, and its motto bids them make a note of what they find.

The leading note tells how John Goodwin's six booksellers were nonsuited, by James Crossley. A passage in As You Like It, tied to Collier's folio Shakespeare, follows, with notes on Laurence Humphrey of Magdalen College. Small notes bring a singular epitaph and the meaning of largesse. Queries ask about a boy bishop at Eton and the massacre of the Welsh bards. Answers fill the back pages.
42117-the-pirates-of-the-prairies-advent:
Gustave Aimard wrote The Pirates of the Prairies, a tale of adventure in the American desert, issued at London by Ward and Lock in 1862. Aimard had already written The Trail Hunter, The Tiger Slayer, and The Indian Chief. The story takes up the Trail Hunter's party two months on, in the heart of the desert, where boundless prairies roll out like oceans of green.

Thirty six chapters carry the hunt through ambush, grotto, and flight. Red Cedar, the Apaches and Comanches, a scalp dance, and a torture stand among the chapter heads, with Ellen and Doña Clara on the other side of the tale. Aimard wrote the Far West for European readers as a land at once grand and terrible, and this sequel keeps that pitch throughout.
42155-tom-slade-on-the-river:
Percy Fitzhugh sends Tom Slade and the Bridgeboro scouts to camp in this 1917 Grosset and Dunlap volume, published with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. Walter Rogers drew the pictures. The opening chapter seats the old scout Jeb Rushmore on a log with a small boy, swapping tales. Jeb tells how he backed a grizzly against a ledge in Devil's Pass with one bullet, and how General Custer once took his advice about a Sioux ambush.

The boy trusts Jeb wholly and is almost sorry the troop is coming. The contents promise Roy's campfire yarn, an old trail, a rescue party, and a mountain shelter. Jeffrey Waring, a new kind of first aid, Pee-wee's triumph, and a cruise in the Honor Scout follow. Lost scouts and a tragic adventure close the nineteen chapters.
42170-summer:
Summer is a nature book by Dallas Lore Sharp, illustrated by Robert Bruce Horsfall and issued as part of a named nature series. Sharp had written on the seasons before, with books on fall, winter, and spring named on the title page. This volume completes that round of the year. He dedicates it to Horsfall, the friend and artist of all four books.

The contents open with the summer afield and the wild animals at play. Two chapters list things to see and things to hear in the season, as a field guide in essay form. A coyote of a named point, a trip from a wharf to a playing field, and the home of the sea birds follow. A front picture shows night herons on a summer evening. The mother bird named at the contents' edge closes the sample of summer life.
42190-out-of-the-hurly-burly-or-life-in-:
Out of the Hurly-Burly, or Life in an Odd Corner, is a book of humour by Max Adeler, the pen name of Charles Heber Clark. It was entered in 1874 and issued by David McKay of Philadelphia with nearly four hundred illustrations. Arthur Frost, Fred Schell, and others supplied the pictures. Adeler's dedication is itself a joke, aimed at a humorist who has had too little fame.

That humorist is the intelligent compositor, the typesetter whose happy blunders gave the author laughter worth a hundred groans. Adeler instances one of his own articles, which remarked that filtration is sometimes accomplished with the assistance of albumen. The compositor turned it into flirtation accomplished with the same assistance. A scrap preserved in the copy mocks another talent: the idea that a count slept in the haymow in a traveling shirt.
42195-seventy-years-on-the-frontier:
Seventy Years on the Frontier presents Alexander Majors' memoirs of a lifetime on the border, edited by Colonel Prentiss Ingraham. The book was published in Chicago and New York in 1893, with a preface by Buffalo Bill Cody. Majors dedicates the work to Cody, his friend for forty years, in warm terms.

Chapters recall wild Missouri, a silver trip, the Mormons, the war with Mexico, and Doniphan's march. Later parts cover the overland mail, the Pony Express and its riders, the gold rush, early Denver, and mining. Trap and hunt tales, talks with Kit Carson, and notes on Kansas City give a broad, first-hand view of the old West.
42199-winter:
Dallas Lore Sharp catches the spirit of the cold season in sketches and tales for boys and girls. Houghton Mifflin issued the book at Boston in 1905. Robert Bruce Horsfall drew the pictures. Sharp dedicates it to four small boys on Mullein Hill.

His preface names his aim. He wants the large, free, fierce soul of winter itself. Chapters open with hunting the snow and a turkey drive. White-Foot the mouse gets a tale. Christmas in the woods follows. A chickadee, a peculiar possum, and a February freshet fill the middle. Lists of things to see, do, and hear in winter guide young walkers. The frontispiece shows fox sparrows at their bath. Sharp taught a generation to read tracks, weather, and birds.
42240-the-paston-letters-a-d-1422-1509-v:
The Gairdner edition of the Paston Letters, the great Norfolk family's correspondence of 1422 to 1509, closes with its sixth volume. It is given here in its first part: the letters themselves, with the index reserved for a companion text. The transcriber's notes explain the edition's conventions in detail.

Brackets, parenthetical question marks, and marks of doubt are all in the original, the notes insist, and series of dots show damaged text. The spelling Jhon is not an error, readers are warned, and Gresham and Tresham are different people. The year of each letter ran in a sidenote at the page head, here merged with the letter's own heading. Fifteenth-century gentry writing home, edited to the standard of a national archive, is the volume.
42254-beyond-the-black-river:
Beyond the Black River is a Conan story by Robert Howard, first published in the magazine Weird Tales in May and June 1935. The opening chapter is titled Conan Loses His Ax. Howard sets the tale on a forest frontier beyond Thunder River.

A young settler walks the trail in the first scene, dressed in a coarse tunic and buckskin boots, a short heavy sword at his belt. The last settler's cabin lies miles behind him. Each step takes him nearer the peril that hangs over the ancient forest like a shadow. Conan himself enters the danger zone the chapter builds. The story is among the best known of Howard's frontier pieces. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
42273-the-expositor-s-bible-the-epistles:
Rawson Lumby wrote the volume on the Epistles of St Peter for the Expositor's Bible, a series of commentaries issued at London in 1893. Robertson Nicoll, editor of The Expositor, edited the whole series. Each volume sold in crown octavo, cloth, at a uniform price.

The series list printed in front shows its sweep: Maclaren took Colossians and the Psalms, and Dods took Genesis and the Gospel of John. Findlay took Galatians and Ephesians, and many more follow across five series. Lumby's Peter takes its place among them, a passage-by-passage reading for preachers and students. The Expositor's Bible aimed to put sound commentary within reach of the ordinary minister's shelf.
42351-the-cruise-of-a-schooner:
Albert Harris wrote The Cruise of a Schooner, privately printed at Chicago in 1911. Photographs illustrate the book. Harris gives the tale to his friend Doctor Lancaster. The schooner of the title is a prairie schooner, a wagon under canvas.

Fifteen chapters map the drive: the Mojave Desert, Kelso, the Dixie country of Utah, and Salina Canyon. The party crosses to Grand Junction, then the mountains and plains of Colorado. Harris notes how overland driving differs from rail travel: no time tables, no bookings, and few living men to ask for advice. The party shrinks as the road runs on, toward Denver and a last anchorage.
42362-caleb-west-master-diver:
F Hopkinson Smith wrote Caleb West, Master Diver. Houghton, Mifflin and Company issued it in 1898. Malcolm Fraser and Arthur I Keller drew its plates. Twenty-six chapters carry the tale. The Cape Ann Sloop opens the action. A Morning's Mail follows at once.

Captain Brandt at the Throttle comes third. Blackfish and tomcods fill a fishing chapter. Betty's First Patient and Aunty Bell's Kitchen soften the middle. The Equinoctial Gale storms at chapter eighteen. From the Lantern Deck and At the Pines follow it. Caleb Trims His Lights closes the book. A front quote shows Caleb mild in blame of a wife. Sea-coast fiction of divers and light work, the tale joins hard trade craft to a tender home plot.
42392-the-jumble-book-of-rhymes-recited-:
The Jumble Book of Rhymes, recited by the Jumbler, is a book of light verse by Frank Heine, with illustrations by Cobb. Hackney and Moale of Asheville, North Carolina, published it in 1919 at a dollar. Heine's motto is that many people read a song who will not read a sermon.

The dedication gives the book its purpose. Heine offers the rhymes to the boys who found the old War Horse a dangerous animal and came to cropper in the Big Muss. They are now, he says, assigned to bunk fatigue in the hospitals at Kenilworth and Oteen. The verses, which the author admits limp and stumble at times, were meant to rout serious and sombre thoughts for wounded soldiers. A New Year greeting from the Jumbler opens the collection.
42417-the-air-patrol-a-story-of-the-nort:
Herbert Strang wrote The Air Patrol, a story of the North-West Frontier, for Hodder and Stoughton in 1913. Cyrus Cuneo drew the plates. The tale opens on a summer afternoon in wild borderlands of northern India. Sun leaves a deep, wide valley among the hills as night comes on. Chapters start at a ruined rest-house and move beyond the pale. A mine owned by Appleton and the arrival of an aeroplane set the plot in motion.

Nurla Bai, a key figure, vanishes, is held at bay, and slips a noose in turn. A flight by night, a fight at a bridge, and a revolt of Kalmuck miners raise the pace. Pathans rally, a gun is taken, and a death trap waits near the end. Strang gives a fast tale where the new air arm meets old border war.
42469-convenient-houses-with-fifty-plans:
Convenient Houses is a house-planning book by Louis Gibson, an architect, published at New York in 1889. Its full title promises fifty plans for the housekeeper, a walk through the house room by room, sound house building for the owner, and advice on how to pay for a home. Gibson wrote in a housekeeping spirit, with ease of use, strength, and beauty in mind.

The book first weighs how building bears on good, cheap housekeeping. A tour then goes from the porch through each room, weighing details. After that, fifty house plans are drawn and described, most of them houses already built. Business points in building and ways to pay close the work.
42536-yonder:
Yonder is a novel by Emily Hilda Young. George Doran published it in New York in 1912. The story opens on a September morning in the country. A boy stands at the edge of a pool, ready to dive. The flat stone is warm under his feet from yesterday's sun.

The boy is Alexander, at home among woods and water. He swims, dresses, and watches the low water with care. Drought has shrunk the stream to a trickle. The bracken has dried before its time. He whistles as he walks home across the fields. His mother answers from the house. Bacon is in the pan for breakfast. The Blue Hill tops the mist beyond the garden wall.
42653-full-back-foster:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote a school football novel copyrighted in 1919, drawn by E C Caswell. Barbour had written Left End Edwards and Left Guard Gilbert in the same vein. A front picture caption reads that he felt he was being discussed. The title names the hero by his position on the team.

Full back is a key carrying and kicking role in the football of that era. Barbour's school stories follow boys through practice, rivalry, and big games. Foster's story sits among his many tales of prep school sport. The books stress pluck, loyalty, and fair play. Readers who followed Barbour's left end and left guard can meet the backfield here.
42768-much-ado-about-peter:
Much Ado About Peter is a comic novel by Jean Webster, the author of Daddy Long-Legs. Its chapters first appeared in magazines from 1905 on, and Doubleday, Page brought the book out in March 1909. The scene is Willowbrook, a country house where Peter and Billy serve as upper grooms.

The opening chapter brings Mrs Carter into the carriage house to inspect the washed phaeton and scold Peter for the wet floor. Ten chapters follow the stable yard and the house through small storms of love, pride, and money. Titles along the way include The Ruffled Frock, Dignity and the Elephant, The Rise of Vittorio, and Held for Ransom. George Washington's Understudy and A Parable for Husbands close the set. The tone stays light, with servants' talk set against the manners of their employers.
42779-notes-and-queries-number-138-june-:
The hosted text is number 138 of Notes and Queries, volume five, dated Saturday, June 19, 1852. The paper calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and students of family history. It cost fourpence. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, is: when found, make a note of.

The notes open with a piece by James Crossley on a pamphlet of Defoe about the Septennial Bill. Pieces on Arthur O'Connor and on verse never before printed follow. Folk lore notes take up a Lancashire May-day custom and the weather signs of oak and ash. The queries ask after old music, the unicorn, and a work on the round towers of Ireland. Replies settle the sons adopted by Ben Jonson and the seal of Shakspeare, among much else.
42780-notes-and-queries-number-139-june-:
Notes and Queries number 139, volume five, for Saturday, June 26, 1852, is one weekly number of the London journal for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Captain Cuttle saying, when found, make a note of, stands as its motto. A stamped copy cost fivepence.

The notes open with Popular Stories of the English Peasantry, number five, by T Sternberg. Dr Thomas Morell copy of the Stephens Aeschylus of 1557, with manuscript notes, follows. A passage in the Merchant of Venice, act three, scene two, and an episode of the French Revolution stand next. Milton indebted to Tacitus fills a note by Thomas H Gill. Minor notes treat a Warton note on Aristotle Poetics, a mislaid quotation, and vellum bound books. Queries ask on Thomas Gill, the blind man of St Edmundsbury, and on bronze medals.
42790-notes-and-queries-number-175-march:
Notes and Queries number 175 came out on Saturday, March 5 in 1853, at fourpence a copy. The weekly calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto runs: when found, make a note of.

Notes in this number treat Cowper and tobacco smoking, a ballad on Shakespeare in the shades, and Swedish words current in England. Minor notes take up unlucky days, the pancake bell, and quoits. Queries ask after wild plants and their names, popular sayings, playbills, the Iron Mask, and Mary Queen of Scots. Replies sort out picnics, regimental names, and smock marriages. A new photographic column shows the age: scholars and hobbyists built knowledge by post, note by note.
42791-notes-and-queries-number-176-march:
Notes and Queries, number 176, dated Saturday, March 12, 1853, again offers itself as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, price fourpence. The number's notes treat Marlowe's Lust's Dominion, Dover Castle, and Dean Swift's autographs in books.

Thomas Keightley contributes Shakespeare elucidations, and a note derives the words lad and lass. Queries ask after national portraits, the descendants of Sir Humphrey Gilbert, and Boston matters. Photographic notes and queries close the number, a sign of the new art's rise. Notes, queries, and replies together show the journal's readers working as a scattered antiquarian society, pooling small facts week by week.
42792-notes-and-queries-number-177-march:
Notes and Queries, number 177, was dated Saturday, March 19, 1853, priced fourpence, or fivepence stamped. The weekly called itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of. Contents fill pages 277 onward.

Notes print fresh letters of General Green and of Washington, a passage on domestic architecture, and surnames, with a piece on Coleridge. Folk-lore items treat well-flowering, devil's marks in swine, and Saint Valentine. Queries ask about the Corbet peerage and whether Wellington was a marshal of France. Replies debate epitaphs, throwing old shoes for luck, and Owen Glyndwr. The issue is a fair sample of the famed question-and-answer journal.
42795-notes-and-queries-number-178-march:
Notes and Queries, number one hundred and seventy-eight, is one weeks print of a sheet for men of letters. It is dated the last Saturday of March in eighteen fifty-three.
