Its mast line calls it a path of talk past lore men, art men, and men of old things and blood lines. A sea chiefs words, when found make a note of it, stand as its motto.

Heads in this print ask if a great war chief wrote verse and weigh two new word books of old lore. Small notes treat a famed ball of the war year. Queries ask past ghost horse men and a line of a poet. Replies take up old age terms, the wrap of dead church men, and the new art of light prints.
42819-notes-and-queries-number-241-june-:
Notes and Queries, a medium of inter-communication for literary men and antiquaries, reaches number 241 with this issue, dated Saturday, June 10, 1854. The price is fourpence, and the motto, from Captain Cuttle, bids the reader make a note of what he finds. Page numbers run in the five hundreds, deep in a bound volume.

The notes open with stone pillar worship and Somersetshire folk lore. Irish records, by Ferguson, and the derivation of curious botanic names follow. Minor notes carry forensic jokes, Cromwellian gloves, and a progress of the war then running in the Crimea. Queries ask after sepulchral monuments, a phrase from school Latin, and a digest of critical readings in Shakespeare. A Bristol compliment and a church-tower columbarium wait among the minor queries. The issue is the republic of letters at its weekly market, small change and all.
42820-notes-and-queries-number-242-june-:
Notes and Queries, number 242, dated Saturday, June 17, 1854, calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, at fourpence the stamped edition fivepence. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, is: when found, make a note of.

The number's notes cover political predictions, the derivation of the word bigot, and Professor De Morgan's Book of Almanacs. Queries ask after a Rubens picture and the pax pennies of William the Conqueror. Replies treat early German coloured engravings, the bellman at Newgate, and Herbert's Church Porch. Readers across the country wrote in with notes and answers of their own, which is the journal's whole design.
42821-notes-and-queries-number-243-june-:
Number 243 of Notes and Queries appeared on Saturday, June 24, 1854, priced at fourpence. Its subtitle calls it a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. The motto, borrowed from Captain Cuttle, urges readers to make a note when they find a fact. Contents divide into notes, queries, replies, and letters on photographs.

Items in this number range from the Memoirs of Grammont and Bohn's Junius to Cranmer's martyrdom and Coleridge manuscripts. Shorter replies settle points on bell inscriptions, pedigrees, refuge in a church porch, and the Duke of Parma. Minor queries get brief answers in bulk. Readers see Victorian scholarship done by post, one small fact at a time.
4284-the-window-gazer:
Isabel Ecclestone Mackay wrote this novel around Professor Spence, who begins the story perched on an upturned keg in a foggy coast city. No one warned him about the fog, and its swift arrival leaves him shivering and out of sorts. He is a reasonable man, but the day has turned strange in fifteen minutes.

The title points to the book's theme: people who watch life from outside, like gazers at a window, rather than buying what pleases them within. Mackay follows Spence and his circle through letters and encounters, mixing humor with a study of loneliness, learning, and the wish to belong.
42845-the-sea-la-mer:
The Sea is a prose study of the ocean by Michelet, the French historian. Rudd and Carleton issued the translation in New York in 1861. It was rendered from the latest Paris edition. The title page lists his kindred books. Love, Woman, The Child, The Insect, and The Bird are named. A London review extract opens the volume. It calls the book half science and half fancy.

The reviewer pictures Michelet with the seas in his hands. He summons their monsters and their finny droves. He sails with Behemoth in northern waters. Chapters treat sands, cliffs, beaches, and waves. Tempests and the kinship of air and water follow. The sea's fecundity fills a later chapter. Michelet wrote nature as a living, feeling whole. His sea is a person as much as a place.
42916-memoirs-of-robert-houdin-ambassado:
Robert-Houdin wrote these memoirs himself, and Shelton Mackenzie edited the translation issued by Evans at Philadelphia in 1859 from Houdin's French memoirs. The editor calls Houdin the greatest artist in what is called conjuring, and his book a work the world will not willingly let die.

From the editor's sketch, Houdin was born at Blois on December 6, 1805, the son of a watchmaker, and educated at the College of Orleans. His bent for juggling made him averse to his father's trade, and his gift for mechanical invention won him a medal at the Paris Exhibition of 1844 for his automata. He opened his own theatre in the Palais Royal, where his fantastic evenings drew crowds, and in 1848 he brought his performances to London.
42958-ulster:
Ulster is a travel volume described by Stephen Gwynn and pictured by Alexander Williams, printed by Blackie in 1911. It belongs to the Beautiful Ireland series, uniform with volumes on Leinster, Munster, and Connaught. A frontispiece shows Muckross Bay at Killybegs in Donegal. The contents open at the Gap of the North.

The Black North and the Maiden City follow, then Tirconnell. The illustrations tour the province: Narrow Water Castle, Cave Hill above Belfast, Carrickfergus Castle, the Giants' Causeway, and Fair Head. Londonderry is seen from the Waterside, and Mount Errigal from the Gweedore River. Gwynn writes with a homecomer's heart. When he thinks long for Ireland, he says, his thought goes back to Ulster: to the homely ways and quaint speech of northern folk, hard yet kind. The book is a love letter with a camera's help.
43021-baseball-joe-on-the-giants-or-maki:
Lester Chadwick wrote this Baseball Joe tale, published by Cupples and Leon in New York. A plate shows Joe catching a ball square on the end of the bat at the front. The Baseball Joe series sold at 60 cents per volume, postpaid, its list at the front announces.

Joe Matson joins the New York Giants in this volume of the long series. Making good as a ball twirler in the metropolis is the subtitle's plain promise to boy readers. Chadwick had sent Joe through school, Yale and the central league before the big league, and the College Sports series stands beside it in the publisher's list.
4303-denzil-quarrier:
George Gissing opened this novel in a silent room at dusk, where Lilian sits with a large open volume she is not truly reading. The cat sleeps on the hearthrug, the fire has sunk to a red glow, and the cold autumn light thickens outside. Lilian's pose, an old childhood habit, invites reverie as a way of passing long, solitary hours.

From that quiet opening the story follows Denzil Quarrier and the woman at its center through love, doubt, and social pressure. Gissing's interest lies in inward life: what people think while they seem idle, and how silence shapes a marriage. The novel is slower than his London panoramas, and more intimate.
43064-the-criminal-imbecile-an-analysis-:
Henry Herbert Goddard wrote The Criminal Imbecile, an analysis of three remarkable murder cases, printed at New York in 1915. Goddard directed research at the Vineland Training School in New Jersey. Portraits show the three young defendants whose cases fill the book: Gianini, Pennington, and Tronson.

The Gianini case opens with a jury verdict of not guilty on the ground of criminal imbecility at trial. Goddard then treats responsibility and the punishment fit for criminal imbeciles as a class of offenders. Defence and prosecution questions from the Gianini trial fill long appendices for lawyers and doctors. The book is a period landmark in debates over mental testing, crime, and the law.
4308-the-town-traveller:
George Gissing wrote this comic novel around Mr. Gammon, who breakfasts in bed and sets out on a London quest. The contents promise a missing uncle, a china shop, Polly and Mr. Parish, a head waiter at Chaffey's, and a lord's will. Gammon's craft, Polly's wrath and defiance, and a pursuit of a brougham keep the plot busy.

Unlike Gissing's grimmer London novels, this one leans toward farce. Wills, names, and mistaken identities drive the action toward a double event and New Year's Eve. Readers who know Gissing only as a novelist of poverty will enjoy his lighter touch here, with London streets and shops as the stage.
43085-meissonier:
Meissonier, a volume in the Masterpieces in Colour series, treats the French painter of that name. The series was edited by Henry Roujon for readers of art books. Meissonier lived from 1815 to 1891, as the title page gives his dates. Reynolds, Rubens, Velazquez, and Holbein stand in the same series list of painters.

Greuze, Burne-Jones, Turner, and Botticelli fill out that roll of colour plate volumes. Chardin, Romney, Millet, and Rembrandt stand further down the list of the series. Raeburn, Bellini, Sargent, and Fra Angelico share the shelf in the advertisement. Colour plates of the master small scale battle and genre scenes fill such a volume. Meissonier fame for finish and detail made him a giant of French art in his day.
43096-leinster:
Leinster is a travel volume in the Beautiful Ireland series, described by Stephen Gwynn and pictured by Alexander Williams. Blackie and Son published it in London in 1911. Sister volumes cover Ulster, Munster and Connaught, and a parallel series describes beautiful England.

Gwynn calls Leinster the richest of Irish provinces and the heart of Ireland. For beauty, he says, it can challenge any of its sisters in one respect only lacking: it has no wildness. The plates show the Bay of Dublin from Howth Cliffs, Killiney Bay, the Port of Dublin, a hawthorn glade in Phoenix Park, and Glendalough. Other views follow the Boyne at Trim and the Slaney at Ballintemple. The text plans its tour from the county of Dublin, touching Kildare, and then through the Wicklow Mountains, choosing what best shows the province.
431-the-fortune-hunter:
David Graham Phillips follows a handsome, penniless German actor named Feuerstein through New York society in this novel. Feuerstein, down to a ten-cent piece, lives by looks, nerve, and unpaid tailors. He hunts a rich wife with bold charm, and each conquest brings fresh risk.

Phillips tracks his hero through salons, quarrels, and a bold dash that ends in disaster. Love, pride, and hunger for rank tangle at every turn. The novel reads as a sharp study of a man who sells himself for fortune, and of a city eager to buy the act.
43128-jasper:
Jasper is a children's novel by Mrs Molesworth, in an edition dated 1906. Macmillan issued the book with pictures by Gertrude Hammond. The first chapter is titled Stockings. It opens on Chrissie Fortescue, a girl of ten. She sits in winter cold with bare, freezing toes. Her nurse will not dress her, by her mother's order. The child must learn to do it herself.

The scene sets the book's gentle method of lessons. Chrissie's cross face meets a firm, kind refusal. The nurse holds to a promise made to the mother. Trouble in the house hangs over the morning. Molesworth wrote many such tales of home life. Her stories taught conduct through small daily trials. Jasper's own part grows from this nursery opening. The book speaks to children in a direct, fond voice.
43154-an-interloper:
Frances Peard's novel, published by Harper and Brothers in 1894, opens with Raoul making a ceremonial round of his French estates by carriage. Tenants greet him warmly, and white-capped women bring their children out to see him pass.

The land is rich and glowing: vineyards, orchards, and a broad river bordered with poplars. When Raoul points down a narrow path and orders the carriage that way, the driver protests that Madame de Beaudrillart expressly forbade it. Three times the one word comes back: there. The driver yields, sighing, knowing the risk of being crushed between strong wills. The driver Jean had lived long at Poissy and knew how hard two such wills were to reconcile.
4316-the-romance-of-the-colorado-river:
Frederick S. Dellenbaugh, a member of the United States Colorado River Expedition of 1871 and 1872, wrote this history of the river's discovery and exploration. He begins with Ulloa in 1539 and Alarcon's ascent, then follows Onate, the trappers, Fremont, and Lieutenant Ives toward the great canyons.

The heart of the book is John Wesley Powell, the one-armed knight who attacked the canyons by boat, faced cataracts and short rations, and returned for a second voyage. Dellenbaugh tells the story with maps, pictures, and a member's knowledge. It remains a readable history of how the Colorado and the Grand Canyon became known.
43301-wizard-will-the-wonder-worker:
Wizard Will, the Wonder Worker is a penny tale of adventure for boys. The Aldine firm issued it in London as number 77 of its Tip-Top Tales. The story runs to twenty-four chapters. Chapter titles promise oaths, raids, and secret service. A grave on the prairie appears near the end.

The contents sketch the hero's path. Will begins as a boy messenger. He becomes a boy protector and then a boy captive. He serves as a guide and joins a raid. One chapter turns on a lost gold piece. Another turns on a reward offered for a convict. The Aldine list bound into the volume advertises dozens of kindred tales. Buffalo Bill heads that list.
43318-tarnished-silver:
Tarnished Silver is a novel by Mary Frances Outram, illustrated by Stanley Wood and published in London by the Religious Tract Society in 1914. Outram had written The Story of a Log-house and The Mystery of the Ash Tree. A Bible line heads the book: the eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.

Twenty chapters carry the tale. Mister Field lays down the law, and forbidden fruit follows. Judge Simmons, Timothy's three friends, and a thief in the night open the plot. That terrible eye and the mysterious packets deepen it. A tramp, a flash of lightning, and the treacherous shore bring death and the tide. Alive from the dead, well-founded fears, and revelations lead to good hope at the close. The Tract Society's tales joined adventure to a moral watched by heaven, for the Sunday reading of the young.
43447-the-tale-of-reddy-woodpecker:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote The Tale of Reddy Woodpecker for the Tuck-Me-In Tales series. Grosset and Dunlap of New York published the book in 1922. Harry Smith drew the pictures. The story belongs to Bailey's farmyard world around Farmer Green.

The tale opens on a May day full of twittering and squawking. News spreads that a handsome stranger has arrived in the orchard. Jolly Robin's wife praises his elegant dress to everyone. Her husband asks a sharper question about his manners. She admits the stranger is noisy and may be quarrelsome. Later chapters bring morning tattoos, a very short fight, and a hunting party. The redcaps, beechnuts, and the winter store carry the year along.
43450-the-settler:
The Settler is a novel of the north west plains by Herman Whitaker. Past books by his hand tell of a barranca riddle and a planter. Rights date the work to the year nineteen six. Its first scene is the park lands of the wild north frontier.

An axe clip scares a heron off a reed lake as the tale opens in calm. Claims, a deputation, the trail, and a coyote snap fill the first parts. Frost, a break, a red team man, and hard birth mark the grim mid course. Sin wages, hunts, and a mock rite of shame crowd the late list in turn. A strike, a bluff, and fire close the long tale of claim and soil.
43594-the-bright-messenger:
Algernon Blackwood wrote The Bright Messenger, a novel. E P Dutton and Company issued it in 1922. Blackwood had written Julius LeVallon before this. John Silence and The Empty House stand his too. The book goes simply To the Unstable. Edward Fillery stands at its center from page one.

Fillery takes a detached view of life, Blackwood opens. He is thirty-eight and still a spectator of men. The planet is his stage in that figure. Humanity fills both stage and seats there. His parents' fierce, illicit passion bore him, he knows. It cost him an honorable seat in life. He learned that truth at twenty years old. First shock past, he bore it with charity. Wonder and tolerance mark his strange calm. Blackwood's occult novel of a gifted outsider asks what a man outside the human family can see in it.
43723-a-burlesque-translation-of-homer:
A Burlesque Translation of Homer is a jest turn of the Greek bard by Thomas Bridges. A Robinson house of London brought out this fourth print in seventeen ninety seven. Two books make the set, and this is book one of the pair. A front cut shows Homer cast pearls ere swine in jest form. Book one of the Iliad heads the scheme with a jest tale brief.

Atrides takes parson Chrysis by the nose in that brief jest start. Apollo backs his parson tooth and nail, as gods do for their own. A dire row breaks twixt Pelides and the king of men from that grab. A lost fair wench costs Achilles dear in that row of the brief. Jove and wife fall out till Vulcan steps in to part them there.
43807-little-bessie-the-careless-girl-or:
Josephine Franklin wrote this tale for children in her Martin and Nelly line. Brown and Taggard printed Little Bessie at Boston in 1861. A plate shows children creeping close to a squirrel, who lets them come near.

Going Nutting opens the book, then the Ride Home and Water-Cresses. Bessie, the careless girl of the title, learns her lessons in the woods and fields. Franklin had written Nelly and Her Friends and Nelly's First School-Days before this. Ten small books fill the line's list, from Nelly's Visit to Martin and the Miller. Plain morals in bright country scenes made the set a New England nursery stand-by.
43921-one-irish-summer:
William Eleroy Curtis reports a season in One Irish Summer, published by Duffield of New York in 1909 with many pictures. Thirty-two chapters roam the island: Dublin's cathedrals and Dean Swift, how Ireland is governed, Dublin Castle, and the old and new universities. Tara, Saint Patrick, and the Sinn Fein movement get chapters of their own.

The road runs on through Belfast and Derry, Cork and Blarney Castle, Glengariff, and the Lakes of Killarney. Landlords and the landless, Irish emigration, and the work of the Congested Districts Board ground the travel in hard questions. A full Edwardian survey results.
43925-the-prairie-flower-a-tale-of-the-i:
The Prairie Flower is a frontier novel by Gustave Aimard, published in London by Charles Henry Clarke in 1874. Aimard also wrote The Indian Scout, Trappers of Arkansas, and Trail Hunter. The subtitle calls it a tale of the Indian border.

Twenty-eight chapters move from a hunting encampment through emigrants, a grizzly bear, and the defence of a camp. An Indian chief, a massacre, a great council, and a spy carry the middle of the book. Fort Mackenzie and the camp of the Blackfeet appear near the close. The first chapter opens with praise of America's gigantic scale, its mountains and rivers carved on a sublime pattern. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
43961-the-life-savers-a-story-of-the-uni:
James Otis wrote The Life Savers: A Story of the United States Life-Saving Service for E P Dutton at New York, copyrighted in 1899. Otis also wrote An Amateur Fireman. A front plate is set at page 185, in the surf. Nineteen chapters run from an introduction to a final decision.

The opening chapter traces the service back nearly a century, to the Massachusetts Humane Society of 1786. Huts for the shipwrecked rose on the coast, and the first life-boat station opened at Cohasset in 1807. Voluntary crews did the early work, with state and federal aid coming slowly. The tale then follows a boy and a dog, Benny's story, patrol duty, and rescues from the Amazonia and a stranded steamer. Fluff the dog becomes a hero.
44032-thirty-years-on-the-frontier:
Thirty Years on the Frontier is a memoir by Robert McReynolds, issued at Colorado Springs in nineteen oh six. McReynolds is billed as author of several other books, of fact and fancy. A picture shows a party crossing the Gila river at flood tide. Contents run to twenty six chapters, from In Days of Innocence to When the West Was New.

Chapter heads promise Black Hills days and the Custer massacre. A shadow scout, an Indian fight in Colorado, and a cow boy duel follow. Capturing wild horses and an expedition that failed take their turns. Outlawry in Oklahoma and tales told round the camp fire fill the middle. The opening chapter looks back to the author's boyhood. His grandfather's plantation in Kentucky, opposite an Indiana town, was as much his home as his mother's, he says.
44046-munster:
Munster is an illustrated guide to the south of Ireland, written by Stephen Gwynn with pictures by Alexander Williams. It was published in London in nineteen twelve as part of a series on Ireland and England. The frontispiece shows the old clock tower at Youghal. A list of pictures maps the tour that follows.

Towns, rivers, and castles of Munster are shown page by page. Blarney Castle, the Blackwater at Dromana, and Shandon Steeple at Cork all appear in the picture list. The book pairs a travel account with plates, so readers can see each place as it is described. It belongs to a uniform series covering all four Irish provinces.
44227-the-flying-reporter:
The Flying Reporter, by Lewis Theiss, is a boys aviation novel. Wilcox and Follett issued it at Chicago, with rights held from 1930. Jimmy Donnelly flies a plane for the New York Morning Press daily. A scorched bit of parachute in the mail scents his first story here.

Chapters send Jimmy on a long flight to a fire and blind flying. A forced landing in fog and a saved boyhood friend follow in turn. He covers a great flood by airplane and visits a lightship offshore. Bootleggers, marooned islanders, and a rival named Rand crowd the plot ahead. Joining the Caterpillar Club marks his parachute jump chapter near the end.
44234-ypres-1914-an-official-account-pub:
Ypres 1914 is an official account published by order of the German General Staff, translated and printed at London in 1919. The Historical Section of the Committee of Imperial Defence added an introduction and notes. Contents open with preliminary remarks, the theatre of operations, and the advance of the Fourth Army.

Operations of the Fourth Army from October 20 to 31, the attempt to break through south of Ypres, and operations to November 9 follow. Companion advertisements praise Mons and the Retreat, the Marne Campaign, and French's own 1914 volume. The Evening News called the companion the true history of amazing and heroic days, briefly and clearly told. War historians get the enemy's official version.
44367-the-mentor-walter-scott-vol-4-num-:
The Mentor for September 15, 1916, serial number 115, volume 4, number 15, is devoted to Walter Scott. Hamilton Mabie writes the number for the Department of Literature, at fifteen cents a copy. The opening essay, headed The Wizard of the North, praises Scott's goodness of heart and the cheer of his works. A passage from William Winter's Over the Border is quoted on his freedom of genius.

The number then retells the novels in short form for daily reading, under the magazine's motto, Learn One Thing Every Day. Waverley comes first: Edward Waverley, a captain of dragoons, visits Baron Bradwardine in Scotland. Highlanders drive off the Baron's cattle, and Waverley falls in love with Flora MacIvor. The rising of 1745 follows, and Waverley is dismissed from his regiment on a false charge of desertion and treason. Further Scott tales receive the same condensed treatment.
44530-hugh-miller:
Hugh Miller, by Keith Leask, tells the life of the Scots stone mason turned writer and man of science. The book forms part of the Famous Scots series. It was printed in Edinburgh and London. Chapter one treats his early days in Cromarty. Chapter two moves to Edinburgh and the Cromarty bank. A long chapter then covers the Scottish Church from 1560 to 1843 and his paper, the Witness.

Later chapters treat his last years in Edinburgh and his work in science. A bibliography fills an appendix. Leask opens with the town of Cromarty on its firth. He notes its links to Sir Thomas Urquhart as well as to Miller. The life shows a working man who rose by study of rocks, faith, and print.
44604-how-to-become-an-engineer:
Frank Tousey issued a guide for boys who want to drive a locomotive, entered at Washington in 1898. The writer calls himself an old engineer on the New York Central Railroad. Full directions claim to cover all a driver should know, with many pictures.

Early pages tell how steam power grew, from the Marquis of Worcester in 1663 to Watt and his patent of 1769. The writer gives dates for the first boats and roads, then turns to the parts of a locomotive. Later parts list the steps to the cab, the duties of the post, the way to run a train, and the way to build a small model engine.
44748-the-witch-hypnotizer:
Zena Maher wrote The Witch Hypnotizer, published for the author in San Francisco in 1892. The tale runs to twenty-six chapters and opens with lines from Genesis and Matthew about light. Its central figure is a woman who lives alone in a small cottage at the edge of a large American city.

She keeps a dog and several cages of canaries, a new choice of pets for a witch, the teller notes. Neighbors respect her, yet some of the more fearful ones take her for a kind of good witch. Nothing in her looks sets her apart. Her power lies in a strange hold over other minds, bending them toward her will, and even firm habits give way near her.
44879-up-terrapin-river:
Up Terrapin River is Opie Read's novel of the backwoods of northern Arkansas. Rand, McNally published it at Chicago and New York. Terrapin River winds among hills above and below the farms. Its clear water, the opening says, seems the blended flow of countless dewdrops. Wild hogs fill the cane-brakes, and deer kill rattlesnakes on the hillsides.

No steam-whistle has yet broken the blue jay's noon nap. The people speak rough, and prize strength of mind by roughness of tongue. Schools sit empty outside winter, since children old enough to study are old enough to work the crops. One afternoon a boy of about sixteen plows corn with sadness under his sunburn. Local tales say Andrew Jackson whipped the whole outside world.
4493-the-case-of-general-ople-and-lady-c:
George Meredith wrote this comedy around General Ople, a retired officer who hires a pony-carriage for an excursion beyond London's suburbs. He crosses a famous common, falls in love with it at once, then exchanges his heart for a lofty highway along a park's borders. Gradually he comes within a stone's throw of the riverside.

There he determines to bestow himself near Lady Camper, and the case of the general and the lady unfolds as a comedy of courtship, neighborhood, and military manners. Meredith treats an old soldier's second campaign, for a home and a wife, with gentle irony. The tale is short, witty, and characteristic of his lighter manner.
44949-james-frederick-ferrier:
A brief life of James Frederick Ferrier stands in the Famous Scots set. That set's list names Carlyle, Knox, Burns, and Hume. Macpherson, Smeaton, Leask, and Setoun wrote those mate books. Each life is short, clear, and made for home shelves. Ferrier takes his due place in that proud Scots row.

Ferrier was a thinker whose work dealt with mind and truth. His life is told year by year with his books in place. Scot thought in his age had few more keen names in it. The set aimed to keep such names warm for new Scots. Brief lives in plain prose serve that aim well here. Fans of Scot past get a neat, firm sketch.
45021-jack-the-giant-killer:
Percival Leigh wrote Jack the Giant Killer in verse, with pictures by John Leech, in eighteen fifty-three. Leigh had written The Comic Latin Grammar. The poem opens with an argument that sings the deeds of famous Jack.

In King Arthur's days, Leigh says, every cave held its giant, and griffins flew thick as bats. No knight thought much of himself till he had slain his dragon. Jack won fame, a lady, money, and thanks by his pranks. A chapter on giants in general shows them huge, shaggy, and very stupid. Their mouths, like sharks' mouths, mark them as man-eaters. Broad humour rules.
45098-boris-the-bear-hunter:
Fred Whishaw wrote Boris the Bear-Hunter for Thomas Nelson and Sons of London, Edinburgh, and New York. The frontispiece shows the huge brute in full pursuit of the hero's young wife.

The contents run to more than twenty chapters. Boris is hunted, finds a new friend, changes masters, and goes a-sailing. Peter the Great is knocked over, and Boris tastes the knout. A race for life, a night ambush, and one sword against five follow. He is taken prisoner, escapes, sails for England, and throws a big Dutchman overboard. Nelson's boys' books carried Russia to the schoolroom as pure adventure. The chase on the frontispiece is the book in one image.
45339-the-practical-ostrich-feather-dyer:
Alexander Paul wrote a shop book of dye plans for ostrich plumes. A fixed form by Frank came out in Philadelphia in 1888. Frank's wife put the book out from the Textile Colorist house. Ads at the front sell French dye stuffs for plume and silk work. A plate shows a group of the great birds at rest.

Paul's front words state his aim in plain terms. He gives plans for each hue and shade men know. Speed, truth, and work-day use rule each plan he prints. Bath mixes, times, and care steps fill the pages. Plume dyers of that gay age get a full kit.
45390-winter:
Winter, or Old Age, the Winter of Life, is a small tract printed and sold by Samuel Wood and Sons in 1816. Wood cuts grace the short pages. The tract reads the cold months as a picture of man's last age, stern and closing.

The birds are mute and the trees are stripped of green, it starts. Days shrink, nights lengthen, and keen winds and frosts pinch. Yet the season has its own beauty and gifts, the tract holds. New snow caps the hills in white folds. Frost turns each branch to a shining crystal at sunrise. Hard air clears the sick fumes of still pools and gives health and spring to the mind.
45416-gods-and-heroes-or-the-kingdom-of-:
Francillon wrote Gods and Heroes, or The Kingdom of Jupiter, copyrighted in 1894. The book retells the old myths for young people. A pronouncing vocabulary at the end helps with the hard names of gods and heroes.

In his preface Francillon says he follows the old fashioned plan, going to Ovid as the chief source. He does not split the gods of Greece from those of Rome. Scholars may learn the science of myth later, he argues. First the poetry of the tales must come, as the makers of literature knew them. The book was begun for a boy named Francis Felix.
45598-love-and-the-ironmonger:
F J Randall wrote Love and the Ironmonger, published at London in 1908. Twenty-three chapters open with What Came to George Early through a Keyhole. A young man in search of bad habits and George Early proving that knowledge is power follow.

Three worms that turned, a new lodger in Leytonstone, and lamb chops and tomato sauce fill the early chapters. An erring husband improves against his will, and Cupid takes a hand. An ironmonger in love, a fortnight's holiday, Aunt Phoebe surprising her nephew, and George Early and the giant Alcohol carry the fun on. Readers get an Edwardian comic novel of shop life and courtship.
45619-history-of-the-prophet-joseph-by-h:
Lucy Smith, mother of Joseph Smith, dictated the History of the Prophet Joseph by His Mother. Martha Jane Knowlton Coray wrote it down from her words and memoranda. The Improvement Era printed this revised text at Salt Lake City in 1902.

The introduction tells a tangled tale. Orson Pratt took a copy to Liverpool and printed it in 1853, unrevised and without leave. Errors were found, and Brigham Young suppressed the edition in 1865. A committee under George Smith and Elias Smith, cousins of the prophet, later revised the text. Lucy Smith had died near Nauvoo in 1855, the year after her son's death she wrote about.
45627-wings-over-the-rockies-or-jack-ral:
Ambrose Newcomb wrote Wings over the Rockies, or Jack Ralston New Cloud Chaser, issued at Chicago by the Goldsmith Publishing Company with copyright in nineteen thirty. Newcomb had earlier written The Sky Detectives. Thirty chapters fill the book. Chapter one is Waiting for Orders. Jack Ralston and his pal Perk fly the air mail over the mountains. Dialect talk opens the tale at full throttle.

Hot ziggetty dog, Perk cries, we have put the new cloud chaser through every trick up our sleeves. They have flopped her over on her back, done nose dives and Immelmann turns, he boasts. Perk Grows Suspicious and The Hold Up follow. A Chance Clue and When a Cog Slipped fill the early chapters. They Are Off and The Threatening Crash deepen the peril. In the Colorado Canyon Country and A Stranded Plane close the middle. Boys get air mail adventure in the high Rockies.
45652-jack-ballington-forester:
Jack Ballington, Forester is a tale by John Trotwood Moore, put out in nineteen eleven. Moore was known for a shelf of south tales. The book is given to twin girls of his house. Its form is in four parts, each with its own run of parts, that trace one life from heir to full growth.

The front word speaks in the voice of the child of all time, born of fire and star dust. It thanks the past and trusts that what comes will be yet more. Part names run past soil dreams, a wood flame, war in far isles, and the sick tree. Love, land, and war all mark the path the parts lay out.
45685-mr-poskitt-s-nightcaps-stories-of-:
Fletcher's Poskitt's Nightcaps, stories of a Yorkshire farmer retold by him, was published at Toronto by Copp Clark in 1911. The introduction, signed at London in May 1910, paints the scene of telling. After a Poskitt high tea of tender chickens and home-fed hams, the parlour fire is stirred and the curtains drawn. Decanters, cigars, and a quaint leaden tobacco box come out under the shaded lamp. Poskitt then tells the story of the evening, always before his ten o'clock retirement.

Fourteen stories stand in the contents, from The Guardian of High Elms Farm to The Chief Magistrate. A stranger in Arcady, the man who was nobody, and little Miss Partridge come early. William Henry and the dairymaid, an Arcadian courtship, and brothers in affliction fill the middle. Fletcher says Poskitt knows the countryside's joys, sorrows, and humours from seventy years of watching.
45699-the-last-american-frontier:
Frederic Logan Paxson, junior professor of American history at Michigan, tells the closing of the frontier in this volume. Macmillan published it in New York in 1910 in the Stories from American History series. His chapters begin with the westward movement and the Indian frontier.

The Santa Fe and Oregon trails follow, then the overland journey of the Mormons and the forty-niners in California. Pike's Peak or bust, the overland mail, and the Union Pacific Railroad carry the story through the Civil War plains. The Cheyenne and Sioux wars and the peace commission lead to the last stand of Chief Joseph and Sitting Bull. A chapter on letting in the population ends the history.
45746-learning-to-be-a-schoolmaster:
Thomas R Cole, superintendent of schools at Seattle, tells how a young man learns the schoolmaster's trade. The Macmillan Company issued his book at New York in 1922. His earlier posts run from village schools to a state office.

Cole opens with a confession. He never meant to teach. His college mates planned law, engineering, or commerce. They counted teaching creditable only as a fill-in job. Graduation left him with a diploma and no definite place. The chapters that follow teach the craft step by step. Getting a position, teachers' meetings, and the school board come first. The janitor gets a chapter of his own. Cole then shows how the principal can help the teacher. Many associates of fifteen years back, he admits, entered the profession as sideways as he did.
45754-abc-butter-making-a-hand-book-for-:
F S Burch wrote ABC Butter Making, a hand-book for the beginner. The C S Burch Publishing Company issued it at Chicago in 1888. Burch edited The Dairy World. A Jersey cow, Matilda the Fourth, fronts the book. The contents begin at the cow: milking first. Washing the udder, kicking cows, and the stool and pail get their lines. The care of milk follows.

Cooling, deep setting, and when to skim fill that section. Churning at sixty degrees, starting slow, and stopping at the proper time are prescribed. Working the butter, getting the buttermilk out, and the rule for salting follow. Marketing and packing close the book. Burch teaches the farm dairy from udder to market in short lessons.
45896-the-world-of-homer:
Andrew Lang wrote The World of Homer, published at London in 1910 with illustrations. A frontispiece shows a moulded pithos from Sparta illustrating seventh and sixth century armour. Contents open with Homer's world and the four ages.

Homeric lands and peoples, Homeric polity and its over-lord, and Homer's world in peace follow. Men and women, the world in war, and Homeric tactics fill the middle. Dress, armour, bronze and iron, burial and the future life, and religion in Greece come next. Homer and Ionia, Attic against Achaean traditions, Homer and the saga, and the story of Palamedes close it. Readers get Lang's case that the poems picture one real, early world, argued from the ground up.
45917-origin-of-cultivated-plants-the-in:
Alphonse de Candolle wrote a study of the origin of cultivated plants, here in a New York edition of 1908. He had first treated the question in a work on the geography of plants in 1855. Since then, travellers and diggers had brought much new fact to light.

Rather than reprint, he made a new and larger work, covering near twice the species, from both tropics and temperate zones. For each plant he seeks its state and home before men grew it. He charges that three of four of Linnaeus' marks of origin are wrong or short. Farmers, botanists, and historians all, he says, have cause to care.
45931-wounded-and-a-prisoner-of-war-by-a:
Wounded and a Prisoner of War is a Great War tale told firsthand. The writer gives no name, but that of a swapped man of arms. It came out in Edinburgh and London in the year 1916. Plates show the towns and wards of his time in the foe's hands.

The first ten days of the war and the great walk back fill the start. A town in France where he was held gives the third part its name. His ward, the one six, gives the next two parts their tales and name. The road then runs from that town to a town deep in the foe's land. Life in the camp there fills the long part of the book in the midst. The last part brings him home to England by the swap of men. The tale is plain, brave, and full of the small facts of war.
45942-manpower:
Manpower is a book on managing men by Lincoln Andrews. Dutton published it in New York in 1920. Andrews also wrote Military Manpower on training psychology. That earlier book applied psychology to training men and raising effectiveness. A dedication honours the civilians who qualified as military leaders in the war. It is addressed to officers and non commissioned officers of civil life. They are charged with directing the work of others, it says. They are responsible for results through other men, it continues.

The war had turned civilians into leaders of soldiers overnight. Andrews writes for that class of leader in peace as in war. His cavalry and training experience stands behind the counsel. The book carries military lessons into civil management. It belongs to the first wave of manpower thinking after the war.
45960-a-naval-venture-the-war-story-of-a:
A Naval Venture, the war story of an armoured cruiser, was written by Jeans, a fleet surgeon in the Royal Navy. Blackie published it at London in 1917. In his preface Jeans calls it a gun room tale. It aims to give a general impression of the navy's part in the Dardanelles operations, and of gun room life under those conditions.

Shipmates helped him, from officers to men, with tales of work on shore and in steamboats, tugs, and lighters. Two officers of his ship read the manuscript as it grew and corrected its errors. Chapters bombard at Suvla Bay, labour at Mudros, and stand in dugouts at Cape Helles. The tale runs through both evacuations, of Suvla and of Helles, to the ship's return to Malta. It mixes fiction with a surgeon's eyewitness view of the Gallipoli sea war.
46028-leaves-from-my-journal-third-book-:
Leaves from My Journal is the memoir of President Woodruff of the Latter-day Saints, printed at Salt Lake City in 1882. It is the third book of the Faith-Promoting Series. The title page says it is designed for the instruction and encouragement of young Latter-day Saints. The first chapter tells of the strict blue laws of Connecticut and of an old prophet named Mason. Mason's vision and prophecy point the young Woodruff to the gospel. He visits Kirtland and sees Joseph Smith.

The Camp of Zion and its march fill the next chapters. Woodruff is sent on a mission to Arkansas. His journal tells of a voyage down the Arkansas River by canoe. He sleeps in a deserted tavern, walks swamps knee-deep in mud, and is left alone in an alligator swamp. Healed in answer to prayer, he reaches Memphis to preach.
46095-private-journal-of-henry-francis-b:
Henry Francis Brooke kept a lone journal of his war months in Afghanistan. Brooke led the 2nd Infantry Brigade of the Kandahar Field Force. His notes run from April 22 to August 16, 1880. The book was for lone spread only, its title page says. It came out in Dublin in that same war time.

Day by day, Brooke sets down marches, camps, and foe moves. Notes on names like Gholam and Wali stand in its side marks. He weighs where the foe throw up works as he rides. Heat, dust, and short food mark the hard south road. War past fans get a chief's own hand, untrimmed.
46125-pablo-de-segovia-the-spanish-sharp:
Pablo de Segovia, the Spanish Sharper, is the picaresque novel of Francisco de Quevedo-Villegas in English dress. Fisher Unwin printed it in London in 1892, with one hundred and ten drawings by Daniel Vierge. Joseph Pennell comments on the drawings, and Henry Edward Watts contributes an essay on the life and writings of Quevedo.

The contents follow Pablo from his parentage and schooling into service with Don Diego Coronel. University life at Alcala, the road to Madrid and a gang of sharpers fill the middle chapters. Prison, a whipping for the old woman of the gang and Pablo's release on bail lead on to his later turns, including a spell as a player.
46156-the-maid-of-sker:
The Maid of Sker is a novel by Blackmore, the author of Lorna Doone, Clara Vaughan, and Craddock Nowell. A new edition with a frontispiece was issued at Edinburgh and London in 1893. The front plate shows all that a wreck left: captain, crew, and cargo summed in one helpless child. The first chapter calls its teller Fisherman Davy, a fish out of water.

Hunger drives Davy a fishing, and the fish prove as hungry as he is. Then he lands an unexpected fish: a little orphan mermaid, a child cast up by the sea. She finds a home of some sort among the sandhills folk. Chapters proceed through wreckers wrecked, a coroner and a coronet, and a verdict on the jury. Blackmore sets the tale on the wild coast by Sker, among fishermen, gentry, and smugglers. It is one of his strong regional novels of the west country.
46160-malaeska-the-indian-wife-of-the-wh:
Ann Stephens wrote the first of Beadle's dime novels, entered at New York in 1860 and sold for one dime. The cover calls it the choicest work of a most popular author. Fourteen chapters make up the tale. A poem on the red man's stealthy tread opens the first chapter.

The scene is Catskill, on the Hudson river. A creek washes one side of the village there. A heavy stone house stands alone on a green point of meadow. Its quiet stands out against the busy town across the water. Stephens's tale of an Indian wife and a white hunter launched the whole dime novel trade in America, as number one of the famous orange covered line.
46189-while-i-remember:
While I Remember is a memoir by Stephen McKenna, printed at New York by Doran in 1921. The front matter lists his novels: The Sensationalists, Sonia, Midas and Son, and Ninety-Six Hours' Leave among them. Their author steps out of fiction here to set down his own times. He dedicates the book, pointedly, to those who may forget.

A long passage from Carlyle stands at the threshold. Two men I honour, it runs, and no third: first, the toil-worn craftsman who conquers the earth with his hard hand. The rugged face, weather-tanned and besoiled, is venerable for its rude intelligence. McKenna takes that text as his standard for a life. His memories run through the London of clubs, letters, and war work that his novels drew on, told by a man who had stood close to the governing world.
4622-trials-and-confessions-of-a-houseke:
T. S. Arthur published Trials and Confessions of a Housekeeper at Philadelphia in 1859. Part of the matter had already appeared as Confessions of a Housekeeper, but the book is now considerably increased. Its range covers the grave and instructive as well as the agreeable and amusing. Arthur is sure no lady reader familiar with housekeeping trials will fail to recognise her own experiences, since nearly every picture is drawn from life.

Chapters include a speculation in china ware, something about cooks, light on the subject, and cheap furniture. They go on to ask whether it is economy, to living at a convenient distance, a picked-up dinner, and who is Kriss Kringle. Later chapters cover shirt buttons, pavement washing in winter, regard for the poor, house cleaning, and broiling a lobster. Readers get a lively, practical Victorian housekeeping book, full of humour and hard-won sense.
46260-up-the-country-letters-written-to-:
Up the Country gathers Emily Eden's letters from the upper provinces of India. Eden wrote them to her sister. She travelled with the Governor-General's party in 1838. Bentley published this new edition in London in 1867. A dedication letter, dated May 1866, frames the volume. Eden says not a word was added to the letters.

She warns that the world they show is vanishing. Railroads are falling on India like a curse. The Taj may become a monster hotel, she jokes. The Governor-General will shrink to a first-class passenger. The first letter dates from October 1837. Eden writes aboard a river flat called the Megna. Eighteen months of steamers, tents, and mountains lie ahead. Public grandeur and private discomfort fill the pages.
46343-the-man-with-the-black-feather:
The Man with the Black Feather is a mystery tale by Gaston Leroux. Edgar Jepson turned the French tale into English for this printing. Small, Maynard of Boston held the rights in the year 1912. Relyea drew the pictures that stand through the strange account here. Leroux had writ The Mystery of the Yellow Room and The Phantom.

An historical preface called The Sandalwood Box opens the whole tale. A man in black sat three hours in the waiting-room of Le Matin. A sandalwood box inlaid with polished steel rested on his knees. His friend Theophrastus Longuet had charged him to bring it to Leroux. The box stands locked and its key lost, the bearer owns flatly. Leroux must break it open to learn what waits inside it. In horror, one picture shows, he knew his own handwriting there.
46365-our-schools-in-war-time-and-after:
Arthur Dean's Our Schools in War Time, and After was published by Ginn in 1918. Dean was professor of vocational education at Teachers College, Columbia University, and supervising officer of the Bureau of Vocational Training for New York State's Military Training Commission. Twelve chapters set out what war should make of American schools.

Bringing the war into the schools comes first, then war and community uses of schools, the field for industrial and trade schools, and colleges and technical institutes. Later chapters take the opportunity for manual and household arts, the work impulses of youth, organized boy power against military drill. Then Red Cross and other community work, and the re-education of the disabled. Chapter one recalls the summer of 1917, when America learned the war would not be won by army and navy alone. Wilson's proclamation called the whole nation to mobilize its industry, education, and woman power.
46579-my-experiences-as-an-executioner:
My Experiences as an Executioner is a memoir by James Berry, told in his own voice. A man named Ward shaped the text for print as its editor. Berry held the post of hangman for the crown in his day. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

Parts tell how he came to the post and of his first grim task at the rope. Counts, drops, and tools of the trade get plain and cold report. Two dire mishaps and the ways men die fill the mid parts in turn. A part gives the view of the doomed man from his own cell side. Last parts weigh the death law and the press hunt for tales.
46677-an-introduction-to-psychology-tran:
Wilhelm Wundt, professor of philosophy at Leipzig, wrote An Introduction to Psychology, translated from the second German edition by Rudolf Pintner. George Allen and Unwin published the book in London in 1912. Wundt founded the first laboratory of experimental psychology, and this small book sums up his view of the new science.

His preface sets the limits. The book will not survey all research or argue the philosophy of the field. It introduces the main thoughts behind present-day experimental psychology, using only a few results of the first importance. Experiments must be mentioned, he says, but the complex instruments behind them can be left out. Readers who want more are sent to his larger Outline of Psychology.
4670-lightfoot-the-deer:
Thornton W. Burgess tells Lightfoot the Deer for children, opening with Peter Rabbit meeting Lightfoot. Later chapters follow Lightfoot's new antlers, and Lightfoot telling how his antlers grew, with the spirit of fear, Sammy Jay bringing word, and a game of hide and seek. The merry little breezes help Lightfoot, wit meets wit, and Lightfoot grows uncertain before a clever trick turns the tables.

The hunted watches the hunter, Lightfoot visits Paddy the Beaver, and the two become partners, with Paddy warning Lightfoot of danger. Three watchers, visitors to Paddy's pond, a hunter losing his temper, a dreadful sound, hounds got rid of, and a long swim follow. The hunting season ends, a mystery is solved, and a surprising discovery closes the tale. Readers get a gentle woodland adventure about fear, wit, and friendship.
4674-tennessee-s-partner:
Bret Harte's Tennessee's Partner appears here as Western Classic number three, with an introduction by William Dallam Armes. Its epigraph calls both men fearless types of a civilisation that in the seventeenth century would have been called heroic, but in the nineteenth was simply called reckless. Armes sets the tale in California after Marshall's discovery brought thousands of adventurers from almost every class and country.

Government in California then stood at its worst, Armes says, with an unpopular Mexican system and law practically unknown, until Congress made other provision. Free and slave states stood equal in number, California would turn the scale, and the congresses of 1848 and 1849 left the battle unsettled. Yet the worst elements did not win, and a de facto government was accepted. Readers get a classic Harte tale of gold-rush friendship, loyalty, and rough justice.
4677-our-world-or-the-slaveholder-s-daug:
Our World, or The Slaveholder's Daughter, published at New York and Auburn in 1855, presents itself as an honest tale plainly told. Its preface expects charges of misrepresenting Southern society and misconstruing facts, and it urges champions of things as they are to read and digest what follows. The authors believe readers will find truth stranger than fiction, and they aim to give a true picture of Southern society in its various aspects.

Slavery, they argue, is directly chargeable with the moral, social, and political evils detailed in the book. They offer the work as an incentive to those, North or South, who would rid the country of its darkest, foulest blot. Contents open on Marston's plantation, a night spent there, and things not so bright as they seem. Readers get a strong anti-slavery novel of its day, plain in style and urgent in purpose.
46789-rubber:
Rubber is a small volume in the Peeps at Industries series, written by Edith Browne. The hosted copy is the second edition of 1920, from the London house of A and C Black. Each book in the series gives a short, clear look at one trade, with pages of photographs. Press praise quoted inside calls this one free from hard terms and heartily recommended.

A front picture shows wild rubber being smoked on a paddle in the Brazilian forest. The series aimed to cure the wide ignorance of how the goods of daily life are made. Sugar, tea, and cocoa stand beside rubber on its list.
46830-the-roadmender:
Michael Fairless wrote The Roadmender, a set of quiet essays first praised in the years before this 1922 New York printing. Twenty photographs by Will F. Taylor show downs, gates, and country roads. The book holds three pieces: The Roadmender, Out of the Shadow, and At the White Gate.

The narrator has found his ideal as a roadmender, mending stone by the roadside under a hedge. He lacks nothing and has nothing over, and he serves all who pass. Fairless turns small sights, a white gate, a pool, a plough team, into thoughts on life, work, and death. The three pieces share one voice, calm and glad, rooted in the soil he tends.
46905-the-kentucky-warbler:
The Kentucky Warbler is a tale by James Lane Allen, with a front plate that shows the bird at the heart of its hunt. A note at the front tells where a form with that plate can be had, and where page scans of the first print rest. The book came out as the war years closed.

A quote at its head dreams of a day far ahead for the west republic. When its folk have spread to each acre fit for a home, that voice says, no bird will flit through the brush with its name, notes, and ways not known to all. Each will live in the sayings and town songs of the land. The tale weds that love of bird lore to a human plot in the fields of Kentucky.
4699-we-of-the-never-never:
Jeanie Gunn, Mrs. Aeneas Gunn, wrote We of the Never-Never, dedicated to the bush folk of the Never-Never. Its prelude introduces the people of an Australian cattle station. They include the Maluka, the Little Missus, the Sanguine Scot, the Head Stockman, the Dandy, the Quiet Stockman, the Fizzer, Mine Host, and the Wag. Guests, a few Black boys and lubras, dogs, Tam-o'-Shanter, Happy Dick, Sam Lee, and Cheon follow.

Cheon, crudely recorded on station books as cook and gardener, is ever mirthful, ever helpful, and irrepressible. Behind the main figures moves a medley of Whites, Blacks, and Chinese, travellers, overlanders, and billabongers passing through. Gunn writes the Northern Territory with warmth, humour, and close observation. Readers get a classic Australian station memoir, full of bush life, hardship, and affection for a remote world.
47012-dick-darling-s-money-or-the-rise-o:
Number 801 of Fame and Fortune Weekly came out at New York on February 4, 1921, at seven cents a copy. Its banner calls it a paper of stories of boys that make money. The lead tale, by a writer who signs himself A Self-Made Man, tells of Dick Darling. Dick is a fifteen year old office boy, bright and good looking, still in knickerbockers.

He works for Roger Bacon, a wholesale dealer in watches, jewelry, and silverware on John Street. The first chapter is called The Office Boy's Peril. Later chapters bring a missing diamond, a fortune told, and a hidden treasure. The same number holds a second tale of a lawyer at nineteen who fights a fraud. News, jokes, and short items fill the rest. The paper fed boys a steady diet of pluck, luck, and rise in the world.
47071-motor-matt-s-century-run-or-the-go:
Stanley Matthews spins a dime tale in Motor Matt's Century Run, or The Governor's Courier. It is number 3 of Motor Stories, dated March 13, 1909, from Street and Smith of New York. The price is five cents, and the line runs each week.

A cover plate shows Matt brought face to face with sudden peril as a man yells to loose Bolivar. Sixteen heads map the ride. A dangerous mission, a red roadster, and smoke signals fill the first half. Potter's Gap, Joe Bascomb, and the road on to Phoenix fill the rest. Matt King heads the cast, a lad ringed by mystery, the cast list says. Matt reports to the governor at the end.
47136-schopenhauer:
Schopenhauer is Margrieta Beer's short study of the philosopher, published in London by T C and E C Jack and in New York by Dodge. Four chapters carry it: the life, pessimism, art, and virtue.

Beer begins by granting that the outer life was uneventful: a scholar's seclusion untouched by the great movements of European history. Schopenhauer himself mocked readers who study a philosopher's frame instead of his picture. Yet of no thinker, she argues, is thought so much the expression of character. Arthur Schopenhauer was born at Dantzig on February 22, 1788, of Dutch descent. His father, Heinrich Floris, raised his merchant firm to the first position, read Voltaire, and admired English life. His mother Johanna, married at eighteen, became in widowhood a well-known authoress in Germany. The unhappy marriage and the family temper set the stage for the pessimism.
47139-stories-from-wagner:
Stories from Wagner by J Walker McSpadden, published by George G Harrap in London in 1912, retells the tales behind Wagner's operas for general readers. The contents open with The Ring of the Curse, in four parts from The Rhine-Gold to The Downfall of the Gods. They continue through Parsifal, Lohengrin, Tannhäuser, The Master Singers, Rienzi, The Flying Dutchman, and Tristan and Isolde. Illustrations include Wotan's farewell to Brunhilde as the frontispiece.

McSpadden's introduction traces the legends to camp-fire tellings centuries before writing, when people believed in giants, dwarfs, and gods. He also wrote Stories of Robin Hood and Stories from Dickens and Chaucer.
47144-over-the-brazier:
Robert Graves wrote Over the Brazier, a book of poems first printed in nineteen sixteen and reprinted in nineteen twenty by the Poetry Bookshop of London. Graves had gone on to Fairies and Fusiliers and Country Sentiment by the time of this printing, and he signs the book from Harlech in North Wales. A first poem, the Poet in the Nursery, tells of a small boy who steals a thin green book of verse.

The boy hides the book down his neck, takes it to bed, and learns the grand lines by heart. Jam and grease mark the cover in months of secret reading. Part one holds poems mostly written at Charterhouse from nineteen ten to fourteen. Star-Talk, its first piece, lets the twin stars, the Pleiads, and Orion speak on a frosty night.
47168-the-forest-schoolmaster:
Peter Rosegger's The Forest Schoolmaster, in Frances Skinner's authorised translation, was published in 1901 by Putnam of New York and London, under the translator's copyright of 1900. A preface, borrowed from the author's Leipzig publisher, sketches Rosegger's life, and it is a life worth the novel.

Born in Steiermark, Austria, in a lonely mountain region, Rosegger lived as a forest peasant till eighteen. Then he served four years with a travelling peasant tailor, and four more as charity scholar in the commercial school at Graz. Long before print, the boy had made books for himself. No fewer than twenty-four volumes were written out by hand at home, ink made from soot. The pictures were drawn in pencil and painted with a brush of his own hair. He wrote, the sketch says, to make two out of one, a comrade for his loneliness.
47271-the-second-dandy-chater:
The Second Dandy Chater is a tale by Tom Gallon, out in nineteen hundred. Gallon was known for past tales named at the front. Past twenty parts fill the book, with names of dread and chase. A corpse from a stream, a plea for a dead man, and a who slew this wife all stand in that list.

The tale opens on a gust eve of March in a flat marsh tract north of the great stream. That tract is named the most drear spot in the wide world on such a night. All winds of heaven seem to meet there to box with all that stands. The sun sinks in a sulk, and the few way folk are surly. One lone man, wrapt to the eyes, fights the winds on his way to a small town, to his own great cost of calm.
47359-the-ashtabula-disaster:
Stephen D Peet of Ashtabula, Ohio, wrote The Ashtabula Disaster, published at Chicago in 1877, as the narrative of the greatest railroad disaster on record. Peet had unusual means of knowing it: he observed the wreck on the night itself and examined it before removal in the morning. He also helped identify bodies and search for relics.

His preface thanks the coroner's jury, the reporters of the press, and the artist Frederick Blakeslee for pictures of the wreck. Peet leaves the public argument over the cause to the railroad papers and the engineers, whose debate over iron bridges the disaster had set running across the country.
47363-the-life-of-james-mcneill-whistler:
Joseph Pennell and Elizabeth Robins Pennell wrote this life of the artist James McNeill Whistler. Lippincott at Philadelphia and Heinemann at London issued it in a new and revised sixth edition, with a preface dated at Washington on July 4, 1919. The book is illustrated throughout and opens with a portrait of the artist by himself.

The contents run year by year from Whistler's birth in 1834. Boyhood in Russia follows, where his father served and he began art study at the Imperial Academy, then schooldays at Pomfret after the family's return. West Point comes next, where the cadet failed and left stories behind him, and then a draughtsman's post in the Coast Survey at Washington. Paris student days in the Latin Quarter and the beginnings in London close the part of the life shown in these opening chapters.
47436-the-american-journal-of-science-an:
Volume fifty of The American Journal of Science and Arts is the general index to the forty-nine volumes before it. The journal was conducted by Professor Silliman of Yale and Benjamin Silliman the younger, and printed at New Haven by Hamlen, printer to Yale College. A portrait of the elder Silliman, professor of chemistry, pharmacy, mineralogy, and geology, fronts the volume.

The preface tells the journal's founding. Colonel Gibbs proposed it in November 1817, aboard the steamboat Fulton in Long Island Sound. Dr Archibald Bruce's American Mineralogical Journal, the first purely scientific journal in the country, had stopped at one volume as his health failed. Silliman took up the work with diffidence, and the new journal first appeared in July 1818. Thirty years on, he calls the editorship an affair for life.
47443-henner:
Roujon ran a set of small art books on the great painters in color. Henner, who lived from 1829 to 1905, is this book's man. The set's list names Reynolds, Turner, Raphael, and Da Vinci. Their books stand in one row of cheap, fine art guides. Plate one shows a small girl with a blue band in her hair.

That plate is from Henner's first years as a painter, the note says. Its hues are fine and its charm is soft, the book holds. More plates show his grave, calm nudes and heads in turn. A short life and a keen judge of his art fill the text. Art fans get a loved French hand in brief. Color does half the work.
4759-the-romance-of-rubber:
The Romance of Rubber, edited by John Martin, editor of John Martin's Book, The Child's Magazine, was published by the United States Rubber Company as a booklet for young readers. Its contents cover The Discovery, Charles Goodyear, The Hevea Tree, and Wickham's Idea, then Plantation Development, Plantation Life, and Harvesting the Rubber, closing with A Last Word. An introductory note explains why the company printed it.

The company, as the largest rubber manufacturer in the world, wanted coming generations to understand rubber's importance in everyday life. It hoped to interest and inform young readers, believing the rubber industry would be better off if future citizens knew more about it. Chapter one asks what Columbus discovered in 1492, then turns to what he found on his second voyage, a discovery less easy to name. Readers get a clear, company-published primer on how rubber is grown, gathered, and made useful.
47654-the-monster:
Edgar Saltus wrote this novel of a bride and her yacht owning husband. Pulitzer printed The Monster in New York in 1913. A clergyman has just left as the tale opens at a window. Open sea, brine scent, lilies, and far mandolins fill the air.

Scarlet geranium heaps glow in the garden below the window glass. A white yacht rides on the Caprian blue of San Diego Bay. He is fair, resolute, and frankly material in the contrast drawn. Leilah, dark and all soul, seems of an alien race beside him.
47749-letters-from-a-su-fi-teacher:
Baijnâth Singh turned letters of a Sufi teacher from Persian into English, issued by the Theosophical Publishing Society. The teacher was Shaikh Sharfuddîn Manerî, also called Makhdûm-ul-Mulk. He was born at Maner, a village near Patnâ in Behâr, and showed a love of learning from his youth.

The foreword tells how he left home after a son was born and was taken as a pupil near Dehli. He then lived long in the woods of Bihiâ and the Râjgiri Hills before he settled at Bihâr. One set of his letters holds a hundred pieces, and a second set holds twenty-eight replies to a senior pupil.
4784-brother-and-sister:
Josephine Lawrence, author of Brother and Sister's Schooldays and Holidays, opens Brother and Sister with the Morrisons. The series runs from Brother and Sister, through Schooldays, to Holidays. This first volume introduces a brother and sister whose daily life fills its chapters. Contents include Grandma Hastings, Sister in Mischief, and party preparations, with Dick's buttons, Ralph's present, and more presents.

A party, time out in the barn, a haunted house, and Jimmie's surprise follow, with a little shopping and a big disappointment. Two in trouble, trouble again, and Miss Putnam complaining lead to making up with Jimmie and Mickey Gaffney. A very sick doll, plans for Mickey, a call paid by brother and sister, and Mickey owning up close the book. Chapter one has Mother Morrison urging Brother to drink his milk before leaving the table. Readers get a gentle children's story of siblings, neighbours, and small adventures.
47887-sir-charles-napier:
Sir Charles Napier is a biography by Butler in the English Men of Action series, published by Macmillan in 1890. Napier was the soldier who conquered Scinde and later commanded in India. The chapters follow the career in order: the Irish home at Celbridge, the Peninsula and Corunna, Cephalonia, the war in Scinde, the battle of Meanee, and the last command.

Butler begins with the place and the parents. Celbridge, ten miles west of Dublin, took its name from a hermit's church by a bridge. There in 1785 settled Colonel George Napier and his wife Lady Sarah Lennox, once courted by George the Third himself. From that remarkable pair came a family of soldiers, Charles the most famous. The biography is a Victorian life of action: brisk, admiring, and built on the campaigns that made Napier a household name.
47895-the-gunner-s-examiner:
Harold Cloke, a captain of the Coast Artillery Corps, prepared The Gunner's Examiner, printed by Wiley at New York in 1908. The third edition runs 206 pages with 109 figures. A front plate shows results of long range firing in Boston Harbor.

Cloke compiled the book because a student of gunnery could not easily gather the scattered orders and pamphlets he needed. The text follows General Orders 141 of 1904, which set the tests for first and second class gunners. Later editions add the range board and deflection board, newer guns, and the planting and care of submarine mines.
47902-the-romance-of-leonardo-da-vinci-t:
Dmitri Merejkowski wrote a novel about Leonardo da Vinci and his age. Herbert Trench made the English form of the book. The head calls Leonardo the forerunner and links him to a rebirth of the gods. A front plate shows Leonardo from the famed Uffizi portrait. The novel is part of a set on Christ and the anti-Christ.

Inside, art, faith, and power clash in the courts of Italy. Leonardo paints, builds, and thinks while dukes and priests press round him. The tale treats him as a man caught between two worlds. Readers get a rich, grave view of his time.
47934-an-old-man-s-prayer:
Old Man Prayer is a story poem by George Baker, issued by Lee and Shepard in 1868. Hammatt Billings drew the illustrations, engraved by Kilburn for the Boston edition. Baker dedicates the simple story to his wife in a front note of thanks. Many in New England, he says, will know it from his own reciting of it.

Frequent requests to put the piece in shape for preservation emboldened him to print. He owns its defects as a literary work with plain, touching candour. A frontispiece note quotes a line about a goblet raised high in the tale. Parlour recitation pieces of the age survive in such keepsake printings.
47974-for-the-honor-of-the-school-a-stor:
For the Honor of the School is a school story by Ralph Henry Barbour. D Appleton published it in New York, with a copyright of 1900. C M Relyea illustrated it. Barbour dedicates it to that school, wherever it may be, whose athletics are purest. The setting is Hillton Academy, whose crimson H the runners wear. Sport and school honour drive every chapter.

The first chapter is a cross-country race. Hillton's captain briefs his ten boys at the grand stand. House and Beaming of St Eustace are the men to beat. Save strength for the last three quarters, he orders. Take the water jump carefully, and check your shoes. The contents continue through a boys' revolt against the principal. A football game, a mysterious skater, and a faculty race vary the terms. The interscholastic meet and a win at the finish close the book.
48128-the-affable-stranger:
The Affable Stranger, by Peter McArthur, is a book of essays printed at Toronto in 1920. Thomas Allen held the Canadian issue, with Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York. Twenty-three pieces run from the title essay to an epilogue.

The scheme of the first piece sets the tone: an observation car, Montreal to Boston, twelve hours of talk. No one knew a fellow rider's name or trade, so speech ran free. McArthur steered the talk with a remark here and there, and printed what he heard. He had been warned that American pride in winning the war would grate. Grasping the nettle, registering reform, and a burden of farmers follow. Prince Kropotkin's cow, the ward leader, and the shivering Texan come in turn. The Soul of Canada and A Land of Upper Berths close the homeward run.
48134-electric-transmission-of-water-pow:
Electric Transmission of Water Power is an engineering manual by Alton D Adams, published by the McGraw Publishing Company of New York in 1906. Adams belonged to the American Institute of Electrical Engineers. His subject is the young art of sending water power to cities as electric current.

The first chapter counts more than fifty North American cities already supplied this way. Some lines ran over two hundred miles. Chapters price the conductors and weigh direct against alternating current. Others treat the design of power stations, alternators, and transformers. Switches, fuses, circuit-breakers, and lightning arresters get full studies. Pole lines, insulators, pins, and steel towers close the book. Adams wrote for engineers building real systems, not for the curious. The manual catches hydroelectric power at the moment it became big business.
48232-the-robinson-telegraphic-cipher:
S L Robinson sells grain men a telegraph code in a revised edition issued at Chicago, copyright 1897. Grain and Feed Journals Consolidated handled his account books and grain tables from 332 South La Salle Street.

Telegraph tolls were charged by the word, so code words saved money. One cipher word could carry a whole printed phrase. Where blanks occur, the filler words follow in order. The example reads: Revelation, Alkali, Chicago, meaning quote price number 2 corn laid down in Chicago. The revised edition keeps every old word and phrase in place. Fifteen new pages stand printed in italics. Grain grades, new railroads, and fresh freight lines forced the changes. Robinson warns that safe cipher words must not be easily misread on the wire.
48265-daughters-of-the-dominion-a-story-:
Bessie Marchant set her novel Daughters of the Dominion on the Canadian frontier, with illustrations by William Rainey. The Toronto edition opens with praise for Canada as a mother with room for all who will work. Chapter one places Nell, or Eleanor Hamblyn, in the lone house at Blue Bird Ridge with her grandfather Doss Umpey.

Nell climbs down from the loft to tend Pip, a dog mauled in a fight. From that spare start, chapter titles promise a strange welcome, a new vocation, Camp's Gulch, a rescue, and a woman of business. Marchant writes brisk frontier adventure for younger readers. Hard work, danger, and family secrets carry Nell toward a larger life.
48270-the-motor-rangers-cloud-cruiser:
Marvin West wrote a boys book printed at New York in 1912, drawn by Charles Wrenn. West had written The Motor Rangers' Lost Mine, Through the Sierras, and On Blue Water. In a flash Nat's strong arm was about him, the frontispiece says. The magnetic island opens the contents, then Nat to the rescue and the islands vanish.

Professor Grigg and Mr Tubbs, trouble with a hat, and what would you say to a voyage in the air follow. A strange sail appears, trapped by two rascals, and some strategy fill the middle. Ding dong bells and a queer sort of gun lead to an involuntary passenger. All our lives depend on it, feathered aeroplanes, a serious accident, and overboard, 1950 feet up, close the list. The ranger boys take their machine into the sky.
48337-her-lord-and-master:
Her Lord and Master, by Martha Morton, is a play turned into a novel by the playwright's sister, Victoria Morton. The play had run for over one hundred nights at the Manhattan Theatre in the spring of 1902. This novel version appeared the same year, with pictures by Howard Chandler Christy.

The foreword explains the double birth of the story. It had met great success on the stage in New York and was touring the chief cities as the book came out. The first chapter, A Reunion, opens at the Waldorf Hotel. A tall, broad-shouldered Westerner named Stillwater greets the clerk and registers in a quick, bold hand. A dark, distinguished stranger reads the register after him with interest. Chapters move to a model farm, a camp in Indiana, an escapade, and an awakening.
48372-a-canadian-farm-mystery-or-pam-the:
Bessie Marchant wrote A Canadian Farm Mystery, or Pam the Pioneer, printed in London and Glasgow with pictures by Cyrus Cuneo. Marchant had written The Unknown Island and A Girl and a Caravan. Contents open with her great idea, business enterprise, and the surprise party. What they found, the next day, and where has he gone follow. Searching, the first snow, and making the best of it come next.

Someone's desperate plight, sugaring, and just a doubt fill the middle heads. Pam's big adventure, what Reggie suspects, met on the trail, and the stranger's errand lead on. Wedding plans, how it was done, good news, and the mystery cleared close the tale. The first chapter opens with a crash. Pam comes dashing down the stairs with a wonderful new plan, straight into Barbara, the little maid, who is toiling up with a soup tureen and plates on a tray.
48442-a-pioneer-mother:
Hamlin Garland honors his mother in A Pioneer Mother, a monograph printed for The Bookfellows of Chicago in 1922. Five hundred small paper copies and twenty-five tall paper copies made up this first edition. Garland opens with a claim: she was neither witty, nor learned in books, nor wise in the ways of the world, but her life was noble.

Her first home was a rude three-room cabin in Greene's Coolly, in La Crosse County, Wisconsin. There she lived alone through two years of the Civil War while her husband served in the Army of the Tennessee. She played the violin, sang in the schoolhouse, and taught her son to read.
48453-the-abandoned-farmer:
The Abandoned Farmer is a novel by Sydney Preston, published by Scribner's in 1901. It opens with a doctor's quiet verdict in a city parlour. A small boy, Paul, needs to be turned loose in the country. His mother Marion fears the worst for his lungs. The parents hide the visit's purpose from the child, who dreads parting from them. From that tense start the family takes the plunge into farm life.

Fifteen chapters follow their country education. Peter Waydean is found wanting early on. Chapters treat chickens, a cow and a calf, and the harvest. A wedding day, a fairy well, and a pastoral call fill the middle. Names like Griggs, William Wedder, and Uncle Benny mark the cast. The exit of William Wedder comes before the close. The novel treats a city family's remaking on the land.
48484-narrative-and-lyric-poems-second-s:
Narrative and Lyric Poems, second series, was printed at Toronto in 1914. Copp and Clark issued the book for use in the lower school. Stevenson, professor of English at the Ontario Agricultural College, wrote the notes. The poems were set by the Ontario Department of Education. They served exams for public school diplomas and high school entrance. Order follows the official list, split between junior and senior sets. Notes clear the chief hard points in each poem.

Tennyson's Enoch Arden and Morte D'Arthur open the junior set. Byron's Prisoner of Chillon and Gray's Elegy follow. Scott's Lochinvar and Shelley's Skylark close that half. The senior set adds Tennyson's Enid and his ode on Wellington. Where later editions changed words in poems still under copyright, the notes flag the older readings.
48500-sir-wilfrid-laurier:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier is a life sketch of the great Canadian chief by Peter McArthur. A front print shows him in speech at a town in his home shire. A dirge verse on a broke staff heads the front of the book. The book came out in the year nineteen nineteen.

The gift page owns, in jest, that the book is built of thefts from the press. Near fifty years in state life mark the span of the mans long road. Thirty years as head of his party and fifteen as chief crown the tale. The author jokes that more time would have let him steal yet more. Warm praise and press lore fill the brief, bright life in print.
48501-katy-gaumer:
Katy Gaumer is a tale by Elsie Singmaster, put out at Boston and New York in nineteen fifteen. The first rights in the tale were held in nineteen ten. Her past books are list at the front. One is a tale of a great fight town of the war of the states. Two are of a girl named Sarah at school and in a day of need. Plates stand in this book.
