The list of parts gives the life of the hero in brief. The great news heads the run. A Yule guest of the wild kind, a great man, and two Yule days come next. A school of a small town, a bee cure, and a charge made for the last time fill the mid run.
48555-the-history-of-the-most-noble-orde:
History of the Most Noble Order of the Garter is an old heraldic history of the order and its seat. A frontispiece shows George Augustus, Prince of Wales, as a knight of the order in the plate. The full title joins the several orders of knighthood extant in Europe to the Garter history. Its contents open with the antiquity of the town, castle, chapel, and college of Windsor.

 Windsor chapel and college are the theatre of the Garter feasts and stall plates of the knights. Histories of this kind recount the founders, the statutes, and the ceremonies of the order in full. The Garter, oldest of the British orders, gathered such histories as naturally as its chapel gathered banners. This volume belongs to that shelf of heraldic record, where chivalry is kept as archive rather than as romance for its readers.
48568-the-gate-of-remembrance-the-story-:
The Gate of Remembrance tells how the Edgar Chapel at Glastonbury was found, in a 1920 third edition. Frederick Bligh Bond, director of excavations at the abbey, wrote it. Marshall Jones published the Boston edition. The chapel's discovery came through what Bond calls a psychological experiment. Scripts obtained by automatic writing from a friend pointed the diggers. A note by Sir William Barrett vouches for the record's genuineness.

Barrett testifies that Bond kept scrupulous fidelity to the scripts. The archaeological knowledge available before digging is set beside them. Later scripts concerned the Loretto Chapel, found in 1919. Societies were asked to read those scripts before new digging began. The excavation could then test the scripts' statements fairly. The book mixes abbey archaeology with psychical research in earnest.
48615-the-shogun-s-daughter:
Robert Ames Bennet wrote The Shogun's Daughter, published by A C McClurg and Company at Chicago in 1910. W D Goldbeck painted its five pictures in color. The Princess Azai serves as frontispiece. Thirty-four chapters fill the tale. Eastern Seas opens it, and Kagoshima Bay follows. The gentleman with two swords enters early. Yoritomo's betrothed comes next.

On the Tokaido, the geisha, and the Princess Azai herself carry the middle. The rout of the ronins and an escort to the princess raise the pace. Before the Shogun and requital follow. The pit of torment, the shadow of death, and the garden of Azai come late. Hara-kiri and high treason close toward the end. The narrator is a young American midshipman on his first cruise, set down in feudal Japan.
48791-project-gutenberg-newsletters-1999:
Michael Hart wrote the Project Gutenberg Newsletters collected here, thirteen letters from December 1998 through December 1999. Hart founded Project Gutenberg to give away free electronic books to the world. A contents list maps each monthly newsletter of the year for volunteers and readers of the young digital library.

The December 1998 letter, posted early in response to new United States copyright laws, claims the biggest newsletter of all time. More electronic texts than ever, more schedule progress, and more volunteer contacts fill the hectic report from Hart. His father, who died on December 10 nine years before, is remembered as the project's initial supporter. Internet historians get a primary record.
48849-frank-armstrong-drop-kicker:
Matthew Colton wrote Frank Armstrong, Drop Kicker, printed in New York in 1912. Colton had written Frank Armstrong's Vacation and other books of the line. Four halftone plates by Arthur Scott go with the tale. A front plate shows Frank whispering: listen, what was that? Contents run to twenty-three chapters. A new enterprise opens the book.

Failure and a happy rescue follow. Queen's Transportation Company and Burton's arrival come next. The water carnival and an old rival's trick fill the early heads. A swim for life, saved, and profits of Queen's Ferry lead on. The hazers' Waterloo and class nines stand in the list. Frank's football schooling, the Warwick game, and Frank saves the game fill the middle. Saved by the wires and the end of Gamma Tau close the book. The first chapter opens at the summer resort of Seawall, where a trim sloop rides at anchor.
48877-the-alberta-public-school-speller-:
The Alberta Public School Speller, from the Copp, Clark Company of Toronto in 1910, was authorized by the Minister of Education for Alberta. It is a complete spelling course for the public schools of the province.

The book is graded by standards, from the first two grades up through grade eight, with reviews of hard words closing each stage. Rules for spelling and syllabication, lists of words often mispronounced, and sections on prefixes, suffixes, and English, Latin, and Greek roots fill the back. Its stated features are careful choice of words, grouping by pattern so pupils see law and order in spelling, phonic lessons, dictation exercises, and frequent reviews. A sample dictation runs a boy named Jack through a string of rhyming words.
48972-boots-and-saddles-or-life-in-dakot:
Boots and Saddles, or Life in Dakota with General Custer, by Elizabeth B Custer, was published by Harper and Brothers at New York in 1885, with portrait and map. Custer dedicates the book to her husband, the echo of whose voice, she writes, has been her inspiration.

Her preface aims to give civilians a glimpse of garrison and camp life, about which they know little, especially for the cavalry on the extreme frontier. Chapters promise a change of station, a blizzard, western hospitality, cavalry on the march, and camping among the Sioux.
48998-in-the-village-of-viger:
Duncan Campbell Scott wrote In the Village of Viger, a story collection printed at Boston in 1896, given to his daughter Elizabeth. A verse dedication crowds robins, bobolinks, shore-larks, rye-fields, ferns, bloodroot, and violets into praise of one sweet girl. Scribner's permitted reprinting of several tales from their magazine.

An opening poem addresses whoever has put into ports of idleness from toil and stress, watching thistledown wheel in soft air. Perch in amber pools, basswood trees booming with bees, and fisherman's lore fill the idyll. Scott, a Confederation poet and civil servant, set his tales in a French-Canadian village on the Saint Lawrence shore. Canadian literature readers get his prose.
49089-recollections-of-a-pioneer:
Recollections of a Pioneer, by Watt Gibson, is a memoir of plains travel and war. The Nelson-Hanne press printed it at Saint Joseph, Missouri. Gibson dates his foreword there in August 1912, and a portrait of him fronts the book.

He says plainly the pages come from memory alone, with no notes kept. Friends urged him to set them down before the period passed out of living recall. He warns that places and distances may err, the plains having had few maps and fewer lines. The chapters run from early days in Buchanan County to a first trip to California. Gold mining in 1849 and 1850 and cattle drives follow. A bear hunt and a trip home by Panama lighten the middle. War chapters close the book: Lexington, Arkansas, and a plains crossing in 1865.
49330-the-stingy-receiver:
Eleanor Hallowell Abbott published The Stingy Receiver with the Century Company of New York in 1917, with illustrations by Fanny Munsell. The novel opens in a hotel room, where a young doctor talks with a woman of fifty who has lost nearly all power of movement.

The patient keeps only her pocketbook and her sense of humour, and the doctor urges her to spend her one wish rather than make a will. She fences with him, asking how many years he can give her, then how many he can sell her. Abbott builds the tale on this sharp talk between the brisk doctor and the woman who bargains for time. The frontispiece shows a tall blond girl of Norse looks, one of the figures drawn into the patient's narrow world.
49340-joseph-haydn-servant-and-master:
Herbert F Peyser wrote Joseph Haydn, Servant and Master, for the radio members of the Philharmonic Symphony Society of New York. The society holds copyright in nineteen fifty. A portrait shows Haydn at thirty three, in the gold embroidered uniform of the Eszterházys. The essay opens with Mendelssohn. When Mendelssohn first heard Haydn Grand Organ Mass, he found it scandalously merry, Peyser says.

The work, composed at Eszterháza in seventeen sixty six, was by no means a mature effort, Peyser notes. But Haydn did not outgrow a joyfulness rooted in optimism of soul, he holds. His heart preserved the serene geniality of his youth, he says. Even his later masses show that merriment, he notes. I do not know how to do it otherwise, Haydn told the poet Carpani, he quotes. Music lovers get a warm short life.
4948-love-the-fiddler:
Frank, a young man deeply in love with Florence Fenacre, finds his neighbors already treating the match as settled, in this romance of courtship. Every old lady within three miles regards the wedding as good as arranged, and Frank looks forward to it as the dearest thing fate could give him.

Florence, however, has never said no and has not yet been prevailed upon to say yes, preferring to leave matters as they are and forestalling any set proposal. The catalog record gives no author name. Readers get a light comedy of wooing, where the comedy lies in a suitor's certainty meeting a heroine's determination to decide in her own time.
49492-under-orders-the-story-of-a-young-:
Kirk Munroe published 'Under Orders: The Story of a Young Reporter' with Putnam's Sons in 1890 and dedicated it to John Bogart, for many years city editor of the New York Sun. Munroe calls Bogart the ideal city editor and credits him with helping him win a literary foothold. The frontispiece shows young Van Cleef asking a police sergeant whether anything is going on tonight.

The reporter hero, Myles, begins by trying to become a reporter and beginning a new life. Chapters carry him through a fight and a mistake, a trap, and a strike in which the strikers capture a train. A safe robbery then turns the tale: Myles is reinstated and arrested, collects evidence for the defence, and stands a day of trial before a triumphant acquittal.
49495-recollections-of-thomas-d-duncan-a:
Recollections of Thomas Duncan is a Confederate soldier's memoir. The McQuiddy Printing Company published it at Nashville in 1922. Duncan copyrighted the book himself in that year. A dedication addresses his two grandsons by name. He hopes the story teaches them two great truths. The old South and its gray armies deserve their devotion, he writes. The reunited nation is inseparable and eternal, he also holds. The contents list his war in chapter order. The Tocsin of War and Mobilization open the memoir.

Henry and Donelson give the first campaigns as chapters. Shiloh fills a long chapter at the centre of the book. Corinth after Shiloh and the Battle of Rienzi follow. Murfreesboro, the Kentucky campaign, and Chickamauga come in turn. Pursuit of the Streight Raiders gives a chase story. Duncan writes as an old soldier for his grandsons' generation.
49497-tuscan-folk-lore-and-sketches-toge:
Isabella Anderton gathered this book of Tuscan folk-lore and sketches, printed in London in 1905 and edited by her brothers, who add a life note. The folk tales lead the contents. A Tuscan Snow-White and the dwarfs comes first, then Monte Rochettino and a Tuscan Bluebeard. Padre Ulivo, the snake's boudoir, and Pomo and the goblin horse stand in the list.

Sketches of a Tuscan countryside, a wedding, olive-oil making, and the Florentine game of calcio follow the tales. A month in Elba, translations from Ada Negri, and studies of Carducci and Pascoli fill the back. Anderton says the tales were told her by peasants during a summer in the Apennines above Pistoia, as an old woman nursed her through illness.
495-amy-foster:
Joseph Conrad tells of a shipwrecked stranger in an English seaside village in this short story, narrated by a country doctor named Kennedy. A man cast ashore near Colebrook, speaking no English, finds shelter and work, then marries Amy Foster, a plain servant girl. Her pity turns to love, then to fear as his strangeness grows.

Conrad writes in slow, grave prose, tracking exile, speech, and the gap between kindness and understanding. The tale ends in lonely grief. It stands as a compact study of the outsider, and of how a village can take a man in yet never truly take him home.
49577-beleaguered-in-pekin-the-boxer-s-w:
Robert Coltman, Jr., a doctor serving in Peking, wrote Beleaguered in Peking, published at Philadelphia in 1901 with seventy-seven photo-engravings. Coltman taught surgery at the Imperial University and held posts with the customs and the Chinese railways. His book bears the subtitle The Boxer's War Against the Foreigner.

Early chapters trace the Boxer rise, Governor Yu Hsien, and why converts drew such hate. Coltman's own diary then runs from June 1, 1900, through the siege of the legations, joined by his son's diary. Separate chapters tally the siege work of Russians, Americans, and Austro-Hungarians, and print the edicts the Empress issued while the guns fired.
49580-wallace-or-the-life-and-acts-of-si:
Wallace, or the life and acts of Sir William Wallace of Ellerslie, is an old Scots poem by Henry the Minstrel. This Glasgow edition of 1869 prints it from a manuscript dated 1488. Notes and opening remarks are by John Jamieson, a fellow of learned societies in Edinburgh and America. The volume pairs the poem with The Bruce, from two old manuscripts.

Jamieson's remarks treat the life of the author and the character of the work. So little is known of Henry the Minstrel, he warns, that he can add almost nothing new. The poem itself tells the deeds of Wallace, the Scots hero, in verse. A glossary and biographical sketches help readers with the old tongue. The new edition of 1869 made the pair of national poems widely available in print.
4959-the-life-and-adventures-of-maj-roge:
Major Roger Sherman Potter, a Cape Cod man, narrates his own life and adventures in this comic history, opening with a defense of his bleak native home. Cape Cod, he insists, is the birthplace of the most celebrated critics, though critics acknowledge her only with reluctance, and her poets and novelists set their romances elsewhere.

One solitary poet was even punished for singing to her sands, Potter complains, setting the satirical tone. The major's adventures follow in the same boastful, digressive voice. No byline appears in the catalog record. Readers get a tall-tale autobiography that pokes fun at literary fame, regional pride, and the hero himself.
49657-bosambo-of-the-river:
Edgar Wallace, already known for Sanders of the River and People of the River, returns to the same West African coast in a set of linked tales. Ward, Lock and Company published the book in London and Melbourne in 1914.

The tales include Arachi the Borrower, The Tax Resisters, The Rise of the Emperor, The Fall of the Emperor, The Killing of Olandi, and The Pedometer. Later stories cover The Chair of the N'Gombi, The Child of Sacrifice, and Guns in the Akasava. The opening chapter tells how Bosambo, a Kroo sentenced to penal servitude for life, killed Captain Peter Cole with his axe and escaped. A reward of two hundred and fifty dollars was claimed for the wrong man, and Sanders later found no proof against the new Ochori chief.
49672-father-clark-or-the-pioneer-preach:
An old pioneer wrote Father Clark, or The Pioneer Preacher, published at New York in eighteen fifty-five. The book sketches the life of the Reverend John Clark, a preacher of the Mississippi valley. Clark was the first preacher, the writer says, to carry the gospel into the Spanish lands west of the great river.

The writer knew Clark well for many years and drew on his spoken tales. Clark began his own life story, but his weak hand failed early. Frontier manners, hard travel, and works of faith fill the pages. The book was meant as the first of a set of pioneer books for families.
49674-the-stolen-cruiser:
The Stolen Cruiser is a naval adventure by Percy Westerman, author of The Sea Monarch and The Flying Submarine. Jarrold printed it in London, with illustrations by Charles Norman and Walton. The frontispiece shows a shell striking the base of a funnel and reducing it to atoms.

Chapter one opens at half past eight on a May morning, with Spithead wrapped in sea fog. Aboard the torpedo boat destroyer Frome, Lieutenant Commander Douglas Drake waits with Sub Lieutenant Paul Fielding after a night of firing practice spoiled by haze. The contents promise an outrage on the high seas, a trapped crew holding the conning tower, hydro aeroplanes, hostages, a mutiny, and the recapture of the Independencia.
49715-your-affectionate-godmother:
Elinor Glyn advises a young bride in Your Affectionate Godmother, printed in New York and London in 1914. Appleton made the book, with plates by Grace Hart. The letters first ran in Harper's Bazaar in 1912 and 1913. In England the book was called Letters to Caroline.

Plate lines give the tone of the counsel. Never ask your husband questions, one warns. A great position will count more than the romantic part of love, one holds. Marriage is the aim and end of all sensible girls, one states flat. Play your golf and tennis, one bids, but make your partner feel his ends come first. Society readers get a cool, worldly code for wed life.
49785-scouting-dave-the-trail-hunter:
Scouting Dave, the Trail Hunter, is a western tale by James Jackson. Chapter one is named David Barring. The scene opens in the Far West, in a forest where the evening gloom already settles.

Here and there, through some narrow vista, a rich ray of sunlight pours its golden flood into the shadowy depths. The place is lonely and drear, yet wild and grand. Advancing settlement had driven out the red man, while his place was not yet filled by the spreading white. Deep silence reigns, broken only by the sounds of animal and insect life. Stealing cautiously along, with a tread as light as that of a shade, comes one of the famed border scouts. Born to danger and inured to hardship, they embody bravery, endurance, strategy, and recklessness. West tale fans get dime novel scouting.
4990-the-adventures-of-a-boy-reporter:
Harry Steele Morrison's Adventures of a Boy Reporter follows Archie from country life and school, where the Hut Club forms, to a longing for change that carries him to New York. A trip to the city with his uncle settles it: Archie will leave home at night, work on a farm for money, endure cruel treatment, and sleep among ruins and tramps' campfires.

Stealing a ride, kicked out by a brakeman, a night in a lodging house, dishwashing in a Bowery restaurant, and a police station all precede his kindly reception at a newspaper office. There Archie becomes the boy reporter of the title. Readers get a rags-to-newsroom tale about a boy earning his place in the city.
4993-a-texas-ranger:
William MacLeod Raine's Texas Ranger opens with a girl crouched in bear-grass, listening to wheels crunch over broken granite as a trap dips into a draw. Desperation spurs her courage. A pair of bays hitched to an open rig rounds the bend. A young man drives them, draws up, and looks down into a valley glowing golden.

The ranger's arrival sets a western tale of pursuit, danger, and rescue in motion. Raine writes the desert country with a rider's knowledge of draws, granite, and distance. Readers get a brisk Texas western, where a chance meeting on a winding road becomes a fight for a life.
5006-harriet-and-the-piper:
Richard Carter called his estate Crownlands, not to please himself or his wife, but for his mother's newly born family pride. The place had belonged to a Carter. Tradition held it a grant of the first George to the first of the name in America. Madame Carter adopted the unknown owner into vague cousinship. She told old friends Crownlands had always been in the family.

Harriet, the heroine, and the piper of the title move through this world of invented ancestry and real feeling. An author name is absent from the record. Readers get a domestic novel about family pride, property, and love, where a house's name matters almost as much as the people inside it.
50104-jessica-s-first-prayer-and-jessica:
Jessica's First Prayer and Jessica's Mother, by Hesba Stretton, are two tales in one volume. Caldwell printed the volume in New York. A frontispiece carries a line: Lord, these are the lambs of thy flock.

The tale runs ten chapters, from the coffee-stall and its keeper to the shadow of death. Jessica's temptation, an old friend in a new dress, and peeps into fairy-land follow. A new world opens, the first prayer is prayed, and hard questions come after. An unexpected visitor leads to the prayer answered. The opening scene is a London coffee-stall under a railway bridge. From five in the morning the keeper serves workmen thronging into the city. Two tin cans boil over charcoal fires on his trestle board. He is a spare, solemn man, and no one knows his name.
50265-the-battle-of-the-falkland-islands:
Commander Spencer-Cooper wrote The Battle of the Falkland Islands, Before and After, for Cassell, with ten maps and charts and a colored frontispiece. The frontispiece shows the Cornwall engaging the Leipzig on December 8, 1914, from a drawing by a naval officer who was there.

The battle was the sequel to Coronel, where a German squadron under Spee had destroyed a British force in November. Sturdee's battle cruisers crossed the Atlantic, coaled at Port Stanley, and were caught at anchor when Spee arrived. By evening the German squadron was on the bottom, the Scharnhorst, Gneisenau, Leipzig, and Nürnberg sunk, and Britain's honor repaired. Before and after is the book's plan: the cruise out, the day of battle, and the reckoning. Cassell published the sea war's narratives while it ran, and this one had a victory to sell.
50394-boy-the-wandering-dog-adventures-o:
Marshall Saunders, who wrote Beautiful Joe, tells it in Boy's own voice; Boy is an open-faced, wire-haired fox-terrier. Grosset and Dunlap published it at New York under a 1916 copyright. Boy opens with a challenge: name one friend who never criticises you, lives for you, fights for you, would die for you. A million dogs, Boy says, do that. The book is dedicated to his members of the American Humane Association.

Two books divide the life: my life in the city, and my life in the country. Boy seeks and finds a friend, loses him, and finds a second. There are masters kind and cruel, a lady gay cat, and Amarilla the spaniel next door. In the country come twins, showman's dogs, and Sir Edward Medlington. Saunders wrote autobiography as moral argument, and Boy's wandering is her case that kindness is owed to creatures who give it first.
50422-history-of-the-thirty-sixth-regime:
A group of men of the unit wrote the History of the Thirty-Sixth Regiment of Massachusetts Volunteers. The book came out at Boston in 1884 and spans the war years 1862 to 1865. The group gives the book to their mates of the unit, as a record of a shared past. A poem by William Cullen Bryant heads the gift page.

A plan for such a book rose just past the close of the war. It lay still for years, while parts were read at the meets of the old unit. At the meet at Worcester in September 1876, the wish for a full book grew strong. Five men, White, Ranlett, Burrage, Hodgkins, and Noyes, were picked to run the work. They were told to have the book ready for the next meet of the unit.
50512-mr-wayt-s-wife-s-sister:
Wayt's Wife's Sister is a novel by Marion Harland of America. Harland was Mary Virginia Terhune, famed for Common Sense in the Household. Cassell published the novel in New York with rights in 1894. Contents add two tales, A Social Success and The Articles of Separation. Chapter one opens one breezy May day on a New Jersey ferry.

The ferry car boat runs so late that the 12:30 train leaves her. Passengers rush through the station to find egress barred by an official. His stentorian tones roar the next train's name and stopping places. A hazel eyed figure stands foremost in that pell mell run for home. Domestic comedy and a tangled kinship by marriage drive the tale.
50532-jacquard-machines-instruction-pape:
Jacquard Machines is an instruction paper prepared by William Nelson, head of the weaving department at the Lowell Textile School, for the American School of Correspondence at Chicago, copyright 1909. A cross-border double-lift machine by Thomas Halton's Sons is pictured at the front. The paper teaches the shedding machinery behind figured weaving, for students learning by post.

Jacquard weaving, the paper opens, covers harness weaving above the range of harness shafts. The machine is a shedding motion that can form a great variety of sheds, and its range grows with its lifting hooks, which run from a hundred to twenty-six hundred. The principles have held while the working parts changed. Four classes are set out: single action, double-lift single cylinder, double action, and rise and fall machines, with special machines besides.
50542-the-women-who-came-in-the-mayflowe:
The Women Who Came in the Mayflower is a history by Annie Russell Marble, printed at Boston with copyright in 1920. The Pilgrim Press issued it. Four chapters and an index fill a short book. An errata leaf at the front corrects names and numbers throughout, down to reading eighty for ninety years.

Marble opens with endurance and adventure, the voyage and the landing. She then shows communal and family life in Plymouth from 1621 to 1623. Matrons and maidens of the Mayflower get their own chapter. Companions who arrived in the Fortune and the Ann close the story. The book restores the women of the colony to the record.
50551-history-of-brighthelmston-or-brigh:
John Ackerson Erredge wrote this local history, History of Brighthelmston, or Brighton as I View It and Others Knew It. Brighton printers issued it in 1862, with a table of local events by date. A preface tells a sad publishing story. The history had run through ten monthly numbers with gratifying success when its author died, suddenly and at his desk.

His sons finished the last pages from his materials, the preface says, and any faults there should be pardoned. Contents begin with the Romans at Brighton, then the town's situation, soil, geology, and climate. Early history, the book of ancient customs, the workhouse, a French attack in 1545, the town's defences, and the sea's inroads follow. The parish church and its old churchyard get chapters of their own.
50561-the-dark-other:
Fantasy Publishing of Los Angeles issued The Dark Other in 1950. It is a posthumous novel of Stanley Weinbaum, the writer whose Martian Odyssey had reset science fiction in 1934 and who died the following year. The contents promise a case history in horror: pure horror is the first chapter's title.

Science of mind, psychiatrics of genius, and the transfiguration follow. The red eyes return, a gateway to evil opens, and the descent into Avernus leads to a rescue from Abaddon. A letter from Lucifer, a modern Hyde, possession, and the question man or monster carry the second half. Weinbaum wrote the novel early, before his fame, and it waited fifteen years for print. It is a possession story told as psychiatry, by a writer who would soon make aliens sympathetic and left this human monster in a drawer.
50602-the-boy-scouts-at-the-canadian-bor:
The Boy Scouts at the Canadian Border is a boys' adventure by Lieutenant Howard Payson, printed at New York by the Burt Company with copyright of 1918. Payson wrote a long shelf of Scout books, from the Eagle Patrol to the Boy Scouts with the Allies in France. The patrol here is Rob's: Andy Bowles, Tubby, Zeb and the rest. The story is a wartime one, set on the northern border while America is in the Great War.

Twenty-six chapters mix hiking with espionage. A glimpse over into Canada opens the book, and rumblings of coming trouble follow. Tubby has his adventure, and a man outside the camp is watched. In swift pursuit and everybody satisfied close the tale. Payson's Scouts do their duty against saboteurs in the north woods.
50658-the-feather:
The Feather is a fairy tale for children by Ford Madox Hueffer, issued in London in eighteen ninety two. It belongs to a Children's Library series of tales and story books. Its picture plate carries the words that the eagle had the best of it after all. Hueffer had already published The Brown Owl in that same series.

A prose poem from Shakespeare's Romeo stands at the head of the tale. It tells of a hidden king's land of green dales, groves of oak, and sweet rivers. Steep waterfalls and rugged passes guard the only road into that quiet country. Its king's daughter, self willed and motherless, defies her old nurse one summer evening. She asks what lies beyond the western hills at sunset time. The nurse speaks of a fiery serpent and a cliff near three miles deep.
5071-the-philanderer:
George Bernard Shaw's Philanderer opens in a room furnished for argument. The room is not quite square. One back corner is cut diagonally by a doorway. The opposite corner is rounded by a turret window filled with flowers around a statue of Shakespeare. A fireplace and armchair stand on the right. A small round table holds a yellow-backed French novel, open. A grand piano stands open on the left.

The play's philanderer moves through this world of actresses, critics, and new ideas, with Bernhardt, Jones, Pinero, and Grundy invoked as the theatrical background. Shaw's comedy of love and modern womanhood unfolds in drawing-room debate. Readers get an early Shaw play, witty about courtship and the new woman alike.
50723-the-demon-cruiser:
The Demon Cruiser, a sea tale by Wheeler, was copyrighted in 1909 and published at Cleveland by the Arthur Westbrook company. Eighteen chapters run from A Dark Deed through Lashed and Adrift, The Fire-Chasm, and Walled In, to the conclusion. A ship, an island, a vision, and a capture fill out the heads.

Chapter one sets the ship Maxwell, Captain Roberts, homeward bound from Australia to New York under full sail. The night is dark, lit only by phosphor gleam and two lanterns. Her one passenger, William Manton, has made a fortune in Australia and sails home to a daughter in New York. In an iron box he carries gold pieces amounting to five hundred thousand dollars, locked in a chest with a patent lock. His care over the box hangs over the voyage.
50775-twenty-years-experience-as-a-ghost:
Twenty Years' Experience as a Ghost Hunter is a book of haunting cases by Elliot O'Donnell. O'Donnell also wrote The Sorcery Club and Werwolves. Heath Cranton published it in London, first in November 1916. A second edition followed in February 1917. Campbell and Bevan-Petman supplied the illustrations. An author's note explains that names have been changed. Fictitious names shield real persons and houses from libel actions.

The contents list cases across Ireland, Scotland, and North America. O'Donnell begins his investigations in Dublin in chapter one. Phantom footsteps pursue him in the next chapter. He ghost hunts in San Francisco, Denver, and Saint Louis. Haunted offices, woods, and quarries in Canada follow. Cases in the East End of London close the early list. The book is a memoir of a professional hunter of ghosts.
50884-today-is-forever:
Today is Forever is a science fiction story by Roger Dee, taken from Galaxy Science Fiction for September 1952. Emsh illustrated it. Its hook warns that Boyle knew there was an angle behind the aliens' generosity, but he had one of his own.

Two Alcorians, Fermiirig and Santikh, have been on Earth a month, kept close by the government combine called AL&O. Their offer to the Administrative Council is a longevity process that can be repeated: in effect, immortality, for the rulers only. David Locke of the Social Body bursts in on Boyle at Moira's apartment to protest. This is tyranny, he says: the Weal cannot let three councillors take forever and deny it to the populace. Boyle hears him out with hot attention and private delight. The secret has come in his time, and no combine will keep it from him.
50923-the-serpent-river:
Don Wilcox published The Serpent River in Other Worlds in May 1957. The magazine's blurb states the Code: no fraternization with the peoples of other planets. Earth wanted no shotgun weddings of the worlds of space.

Split Campbell and the narrator land on a naked rock a mile wide. Through the telescope they study the strange thing they came to see. Eighteen or twenty miles off, a long silvery serpent crawls over the planet's surface. It might be a river of bluish-gray dough shaped into a great cable. If it were a hollow tube, cities could flow through it. Wilcox builds the tale on that single vast sighting.
5093-the-little-minister:
J. M. Barrie's Little Minister opens long ago in Thrums, when caged blackbirds whistled impudently at a king's soldier to come over the water to Charlie. A minister of Thrums was to be married. Then something happened, and he remained a bachelor. In old age he passed the lady who was to have been his wife. Her hair was white, but she, too, was still unmarried.

Only a weaver witnessed the meeting. He said solemnly afterward that they did not speak, but gave one another a look, and he saw the love-light in their eyes. No more is remembered of the two. Readers get Barrie's Scottish romance of love deferred, tender, whimsical, and quietly heartbreaking.
50939-the-high-hander:
William Turner's The High Hander was published in New York by Ace Books under a copyright of 1963. Hard rock makes hard men, the opening page declares. Jack Tesno is a troubleshooter, hired by a railroad construction company to see that nobody interferes with the tunnel it is digging through a frontier mountain.

A cast list sets out the players. Tesno carries his own law, the law of the six-gun and the firm high hand. Willie Silverknife is a half-breed kid with a stutter and nothing but his courage. Persia Parker is blonde, beautiful, and a lady. Ben Vickers has staked everything he owns on the contract, Pete Madrid is a trained killer wearing a marshal's badge, and Mr Jay wants the contract any way he can get it. Chapter one rides Tesno into the Cascade Mountains at dawn.
50980-the-freelancer:
The Freelancer is a tale of the far days by Robert Zacks. It first ran in a press sheet of star tales in September of nineteen fifty-five. A front line warns that past the pass of such laws, all past times were the good old days. The tale is set in a world of state desks that grade and place each soul.

Jeb, a free lance watch man, is shaken from bed by his wife, who cuts the heat and bids him earn or be stamped. To be sent to set work by the state is a jail of dull days, he fears. He picks a suit of a smog test man from his rack of false garbs. A call from the wed desk cheers that his wifes spite score rose past five points. The jest of that world lands at once.
50990-spanish-and-portuguese-south-ameri:
Robert Grant Watson wrote a two volume history of Spanish and Portuguese South America in the colonial period, published at London in 1884. Watson had edited Murray's Handbook of Greece. Verse from Byron's Childe Harold heads the title page: fallen nations gaze on Spain, and Columbia's ease repairs Quito's wrongs. Volume one is dedicated to Sir James Hudson.

Hudson is praised as the reign's most distinguished British diplomatist. He helped end the slave trade with Brazil and aided Italian unification, the dedication says. Watson's preface begins an account of the colonial centuries. The work surveys conquest, rule, and the wars of independence for Victorian readers of imperial history.
51027-jaywalker:
Jaywalker, a science fiction story by Ross Rocklynne, was printed in Galaxy in December 1950. Its headnote warns that women may oppose progress because it brings new kinds of widowhood, such as space widowhood. Marcia McHenry is at last on the gangplank, entering the mouth of a spaceship, and nothing can stop her now. Nothing, unless she breaks down before all the Moon bound passengers.

Two kind ladies show her she blocks the way, and a smiling stewardess leads her to her seat. Her azure tipped fingers clutch the chair arm, and she yearns for her house at Toluca Lake, its comfort, safety, and sanity. Then the stewardess holds out a hand for her card. Marcia stiffens: the pink card she holds bears Nellie Foster's name, not her own. Rocklynne builds a tale of a wife stealing a ride to the Moon, and of what drives her to it.
51054-the-wolf-leader:
Alexandre Dumas wrote this tale, The Wolf-Leader, in a new rendering by Alfred Allinson, said on its title page never before to have been turned into English. Three coloured pictures by Frank Adams illustrate it, and the frontispiece shows an immense wolf entering a room, walking on its hind legs. Twenty-four chapters and an introduction carry the story.

The introduction tells who Mocquet was, and how the tale came to the narrator. Chapter heads then name the matter: the grand master of the wolf hounds, a sabot maker, the black wolf, a pact with Satan, bedevilled hair, and Thibault's wishes. A village wedding, a death and resurrection, the genius of evil, a last wish, and the hunting down of the were-wolf close the roll.
51067-living-too-fast-or-the-confessions:
William Adams, writing as Oliver Optic, published this cautionary novel at Boston in 1876. Its full title is Living Too Fast, or the Confessions of a Bank Officer, and the preface states the moral outright.

The story records a bank officer living too fast, in the downward career of crime. Adams admits the career ought to have ended in the state prison, but punishes his defaulter another way, and runs an honest young man's life alongside for contrast. The contents follow the fall: getting a situation, going to housekeeping, a shadow of suspicion, over the precipice, a crash in coppers, and at last a confession. The hero, Paley Glasswood, competes with his friend Tom Flynn for a clerk's place. Boys get a sermon in story form.
51076-aaron-rodd-diviner:
Phillips Oppenheim deals in crime and plots in Aaron Rodd, Diviner, printed in London in 1920. The contents promise a run of linked tales with bold heads. Thieves form an alliance, a strange aide appears, and a yellow eye gleams.

The first tale is The Cunning of Harvey Grimm. It opens in the Embankment Gardens as a streak of sun breaks a pall of cloud and mist. A tall, gaunt young man stares at the light in shock. A young lady in deep black smiles and cries out at sun in London in January. Later heads name Paul Brodie, Jack Lovejoy, Rosa Letchowiski, and the end of Jeremiah Sands.
51089-did-betsey-ross-design-the-flag-of:
Franklin Hanford read this paper before the Scottsville Literary Society on January 22, 1917. It appeared as number seven in the society's publications, printed at Scottsville, New York. His question is the famous one of whether Betsey Ross designed the flag of the United States.

Hanford opens with the resolution Congress adopted on June 14, 1777 in Philadelphia. It set thirteen stripes, alternate red and white, and thirteen stars in a blue field, he quotes. The Journal of Congress is silent on who brought the resolution in, he notes, and silent on any debate, which leaves the Ross story to be weighed on its evidence.
5113-the-confessions-of-a-beachcomber:
Edmund James Banfield spent years living on a small island off the tropical coast of Queensland. These linked sketches record what he saw there day by day. Birds, fish, turtles, coral gardens, and the changing moods of sea and weather fill the pages, alongside notes on the island's early history and its neighbours.

Banfield writes as a close watcher rather than a distant naturalist, naming the creatures he meets and describing their habits in plain detail. Readers get a slow, vivid portrait of island life at the turn of the century. A beach walk could turn up a shark, a rare bird, or a story from the people who lived nearby.
51226-connecticut-wide-awake-songster:
The Connecticut Wide-Awake Songster is a campaign song book of the election of 1860, edited by John Hutchinson of the Hutchinson Family of Singers. Benjamin Jepson helped him. It was published in New York in 1860. The Wide-Awakes were the marching clubs of the Republican party.

The contents are songs for the canvass. The Republican platform stands near the front, set to be sung. Lincoln and Victory, Strike for the Right, and Hurrah for Abe Lincoln follow. Lincoln and Liberty is the best known of the set. The People's Nominee and Flag of the Brave fill the early pages. Such cheap songsters went into every pocket of the cause. They gave the marching companies words for the road, the rally, and the torchlight parade.
51296-the-sense-of-wonder:
The Sense of Wonder is a tale of the far worlds by Milton Lesser, first put out in a sheet of such tales in the ninth month of nineteen fifty one. Drawings by Harry Rosenbaum stand with the text. A hook line stands at its head. When no one on a ship can call to mind where the ship is bound, the line asks, how can they tell when it has come there?

For a week past, Rikud has come each day to the view port to watch the great still sweep of space. He can not quite say what the sense in him is. It feels strange and not of his kind.
51311-make-me-an-offer:
Con Blomberg wrote a short tale in the form of memos twixt city managers. The tale ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in August 1957. Ross Ro, New York's city manager, writes to his peers for help. He has just won a new four-year term at his post. He wants a gift act to thank the voters of his town.

His plea deals with gelatin molds, of all things. A glib aide named Charlie Tight stands at his side in the tale. The memo tone hides a sly joke on town rule and red tape. Each new note adds a fresh twist to the ask. Readers get light satire dressed as office mail.
51331-swenson-dispatcher:
Miller's story ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in April 1956, with illustrations by Francis. On October 15, 2177, Swenson staggered into Acme Interplanetary Express and demanded work as dispatcher. They threw him out, and forgot to lock the door. The next time they locked the door and forgot the window, and Swenson came in through it. Acme's board decided it had an unusual kind of determined drunk.

The dispatcher had been fired that morning, leaving the schedule in a muddle. Ship Number 7 lay grounded at Luna City until a demurrage bill was paid. Swenson's first act was to order a case of beer; his second, to look at the dispatch sheet. There were no vacuums in Space Regulations, the headnote says, and Swenson knew how to plot courses through sub-ether legality. The comedy runs on one drunk, one rulebook, and the solar system to schedule.
51361-birds-of-a-feather:
Robert Silverberg wrote this science fiction tale for Galaxy Magazine, where it ran in November 1958. The narrator, Corrigan, runs an interstellar zoo, the Corrigan Institute of Morphological Science, and has come to the planet Ghryne to recruit. Aliens line up for hundreds of feet, in every shape and colour, all keen for a contract and a trip to Earth.

Corrigan's posters promise good pay, short hours, and the thrills of show business on Terra, and they always bring a crowd. His three staff men feed the applicants in one at a time for interviews. Getting specimens was never the hard part, he says; the trouble starts when a display threatens to make a monkey of him.
51433-hunt-the-hunter:
Kris Neville's Hunt the Hunter appeared in Galaxy Science Fiction in June 1951, with pictures by Elizabeth MacIntyre. Its teaser warns that live bait is the best way to lure dangerous alien animals, unless you turn out to be the bait. The hunter Extrone has landed on the wrong side of a ridge and presses two local men into service as guides.

The guides, Ri and Mia, blame the pilot, who they think dislikes the Hunting Club and set them down wrong on purpose. Then a coughing roar sounds ahead: a farn beast, close by. Extrone orders camp pitched on the spot and the hunt set for tomorrow, while his unwilling guides count what he pays them.
51478-dumbwaiter:
Dumbwaiter is a science fiction story by James Stamers. The Project Gutenberg text was taken from Galaxy Magazine for February 1960. Its headnote warns that the divers of Antimony Nine cannot be seen, and have nothing in mind when one of them is near you.

Sol Jones stands in line at the customs hall of Philadelphia International. The man ahead of him tried to smuggle a dragon in a thermos, and the inspectors are singed and short-tempered. They belong to Lamavic, the customs service for livestock, animals, minerals, and vegetables. Jones declares that he carries no livestock and no banned article. The big black record book is opened on him. It names him a four-star offender, with twenty-four small fines for bringing banned livestock onto various planets. Worse cases, numbered one to seventy-six, hang over his name.
51482-perfect-answer:
Perfect Answer is a science fiction story by Stecher, with pictures, printed in a galaxy magazine in June 1958. Its head note turns on travel and survival. Getting there may be half the fun, it says, but it is also all of a society's chance of staying alive. The tale opens in talk on an alien shore, between two spacemen in godlike guise.

As one god to another, let us go home, Jack Bates said. Bill Farnum raised a space gloved hand in lazy answer to a kneeling native, and shook his head. Let us try one more star almost in line on the way back, he urged, and then call it quits. Bates wanted to hurry home and make profit of their find. The galaxy is full of men like themselves, he cried; they had hit the jackpot on the first trip out.
51530-the-last-letter:
The Last Letter, a science fiction tale by Fritz Lieber with drawings by Dillon, ran in Galaxy in June 1958. Far ahead, on the first day of the tenth month in the year 2457, a robot mail sorter in NewNew York gulps ten thousand letters at nine in the morning, Federation time. The meal does not agree with the machine.

Black Sorter shakes, glows blue, and spits one envelope back over his shoulder. The rest blast out as chewed confetti. The saved letter passes from Red Subsorter to Yellow Rerouter, Green Rerouter, Brown Study, and at last Pink Wastebasket, a delicate and intuitive machine. Lieber builds a droll fable of fate, junk mail, and one letter that will not die.
51570-cry-snooker:
Andrew Fetler wrote this short story, printed in Galaxy Magazine in October 1960 with art by Dick Francis. George and Rosy are newly wed, and the tale opens in a storm of small scoldings. George begs Rosy to cap her perfume bottles, since the Chanel cost twelve bucks. He blames her for the flooded basement washer and the power mower left running.

Rosy answers each charge in kind, cool and quick. The magazine billed her as a wife out of this world: pretty, smart, and a cook beyond compare. At breakfast next day they trade gifts, a diamond cocktail ring for him and a self-winding watch for her, bought on long credit. Love and nagging share the same small house.
51622-extracts-from-the-galactick-almana:
Extracts from the Galactick Almanack is a humorous science fiction piece by Harris. Don Martin drew the illustrations. It appeared in a magazine called Galaxy in June 1959. The extracts cover the music section of a future almanack. Dates are converted to the Terran calendar. A warning heads the piece. Music will hold more than meets the ear.

The first entry honours a child prodigy of Dubhe. Freem Freem gave his first concert at four years old. Critics refused to believe his age. A sworn statement from a truthful Sirian convinced them. He concertised across the galaxy for eight years. His single composition was called Memories of Old Age. At twelve the prodigy was dead. Other races felt the loss more than Terrans did.
51654-gillingwater-s-history-of-lowestof:
Gillingwater's History of Lowestoft was reprinted in 1897. Murton added a chapter of more recent events. The reprint was made at Lowestoft itself. Section one treats the island of Lothingland. It sits at the most eastern point of Great Britain, in Suffolk. The German Ocean bounds it east, the Yare north, and the Waveney west. Lake Lothing lies to the south. A narrow neck of land makes it a peninsula in strict terms. Sixteen parishes fill its ten miles by six.

Lowestoft stands as the chief place and only market town. In Saxon times the island formed part of the East Angles' kingdom. An act of 1764 joined its half-hundred with Mutford's. A house of industry for the poor came with that act. The old history mixes bounds, parishes, and church rule.
5166-the-poetaster:
Ben Jonson's comedy The Poetaster, or His Arraignment, is set in ancient Rome and stages a literary war. Ovid, Tibullus, and Gallus mix with the poetasters Crispinus and Demetrius. Jonson uses the Roman scene to answer his own rivals, putting bad poets on trial before Augustus in a final arraignment.

The play is Jonson's sharpest satire on the theatre world of his day, full of classical allusion and personal score-settling. Readers interested in Shakespeare's contemporaries will find a lively, combative comedy. It opens a window into how Jacobean playwrights fought their battles in verse on the public stage.
51707-the-ontario-readers-third-reader:
Ontario set its Third Reader for use in the public schools of the province. Gage of Toronto published it, entered in 1885. The preface says its plan is that of the Second Reader, with two changes. A few lessons in history are added, and two that open the way to natural science.

Each lesson should be talked over before reading, during it, and after. The teacher should draw out what the pupils know, mend their wrong notions, and throw them back on their own eyes. For the nature lessons, pupils should fetch the very things described and judge for themselves. The poems are chosen as good writing that children can grasp, with old favourites kept for their proven worth.
51736-star-crossed-lover:
William W Stuart wrote Star-Crossed Lover, a tale of a wife with spare bodies. Galaxy Magazine ran the story in its April nineteen sixty two issue. Ritter drew the pictures that spice its wild first pages. Its blurb warns: sweet wife, but she litters the house with used bodies.

The teller swears he is no fiend, no mad scientist, no Bluebeard. Front pages brand him a butcher of women by the garage, he protests. Those buried bodies are an illusion of sorts, he insists stoutly. His seat in the electric chair may prove an illusion too, he hopes. A plain, friendly, upper middle sort of man is all he claims. One good deed landed him in this bloody mess, he owns. An old lady stood lost at York and Grand Avenue one fall day. Her green, glowing eyes in a ruined face begged his arm across.
5174-allan-and-the-holy-flower:
H. Rider Haggard's Allan Quatermain novel, first published in 1915, sends the famous hunter after a rare orchid rather than gold. Brother John, an auction room, and a slave road lead Quatermain and his companions into the African interior, where a king, a magic mirror. A people called the Motombo guard the home of the holy flower.

Haggard mixes adventure with African legend and lost-world wonder, as Quatermain faces a sentence of death and a battle for the flower itself. Readers of his earlier African romances will find the same blend of danger, mystery, and vivid landscape, told in Quatermain's dry, first-person voice.
51767-death-s-wisher:
Jim Wannamaker wrote this science fiction tale for Galaxy, where it ran in February 1960, with plates by Dick Francis. Its head note turns on bombs: the one way to disarm one is to stay a step ahead of it. But what if the bomb stays a step ahead of you?

Flinn is hauled from his California flat to Washington with no word of why. The state needs him, he is told, and that is all. Jackson Wilmer, a tall, dark nuclear physicist, waits in a small room of a vast block. Five hours on a plane have left Flinn restless and full of questions. The tale sets a plain man against a thinking bomb.
51797-to-the-highest-bidder:
To the Highest Bidder is a novel by Florence Morse Kingsley. Kingsley also wrote The Singular Miss Smith and The Glass House. Dodd, Mead published it in New York in 1911. John Rae illustrated the volume. The story first ran in The Christian Herald in 1910. The contents list twenty three chapters of the tale. The opening scene sits in a village post office. Abram Hewett and his son distribute the mail there.

They work behind a high tier of numbered glass boxes. The frontispiece shows a spring time moment in David Whitcomb's love. That picture is keyed to a page deep in the book. Kingsley wrote wholesome popular fiction with a Christian bent. Her market was the family reading public of her day.
51799-farmer:
Farmer is a science fiction story by Mack Reynolds, printed in Galaxy Magazine in June 1961. The scene is the Sahara Project, a vast scheme to make the desert bloom. Johnny McCord runs a station there, in khaki shorts and Moroccan slippers. He checks auto-copters, feeds reports into a card-punch, and drinks forbidden iced beer against the heat.

Someone out there hates trees, the opening warns, and means to wreck the project. Murder is part of the plan. Reynolds mixes office routine, sand-clogged machinery, and sabotage into a working future. The story shows his trademark interest in economics and labor, dressed here as a desert mystery with the fate of a green Sahara at stake.
51852-founding-father:
Founding Father is a science fiction story by J F Bone, first printed in Galaxy Magazine in April 1962. Its creatures are huge, hairy, and surly, and the males are always chasing the females. But what else, the heading asks, could you expect of mammals? The narrator and his mate Ven have landed on a world of rocks and vegetation.

They need data, for the animate life collected so far is of a low order. Nothing here shows intelligence, Ven says, yet the creatures are obviously related to their own race. They could not have built the artifacts seen on the way down, nor made communications gear or airboats. The narrator glared at her and she flushed a delicate lavender. He had not wanted to land in this isolated spot: less than two vards of useful fuel were left when he cut the drives.
51917-the-revolt-of-the-oyster:
Don Marquis wrote The Revolt of the Oyster, a set of comic tales published in nineteen twenty-two. Marquis opens with a quote from a famed man of science: our remote forebear was probably a tree dweller. The first tale takes that line and runs with it.

Probably Arboreal lazes in his tree-top hut and watches folk fish in the sea below. His neighbour, Slightly Simian, argues with his wife about how to raise the children. She will slap the boy's feet when he picks things up with them. He calls foot use natural and fair. Marquis turns the dawn of man into sharp, fond satire.
51958-the-mountain-school-teacher:
The Mountain School Teacher, a novel by Melville Davisson Post, was issued at New York and London by Appleton in 1922. The tale opens on a lost path along the backbone of a mountain. The wilderness has nearly wiped that path away. Wind, leaves, and rain have packed it back into the ridge.

Great hickories shoot up sixty feet without a branch in that forest. The open way runs down the gentle slope to the mountain road. Post sets his scene in the primeval woods of the high country. A school teacher in such a land faces more than lessons, his books promise. Post was a master of the mystery tale, and place broods over his first page. The ridge, the road, and the vanished path frame the human drama to come.
51976-the-first-quarter-century-of-steam:
The First Quarter-Century of Steam Locomotives in North America is a museum study by Smith Hempstone Oliver, of the United States National Museum. More than eighty illustrations go with the text. A photograph at the front shows a replica of the Lafayette, an engine of the 1830s. In the fall of 1955 it was dressed as an other engine for a film. The film told the tale of the famous Civil War locomotive General. The study proper covers the years from the first engines to about 1855.

Oliver traces the forms the young locomotive took on this continent. Wood burners, balloon stacks, and cowcatchers mark the age. The models in the national store are his base of fact. The book belongs to the Smithsonian's bulletin line on the history of technology. It serves the rail fan and the scholar alike.
51993-the-mentor-russian-music-vol-4-num:
Henry Finck, a music critic, wrote the November 1, 1916 number of a learn a day sheet on Russian music. Plain asks and replies open the piece, on the size of Russia and the youth of its art. Less than a dozen famed names in Russian music is one frank count the sheet gives.

Notes hold that song and tale in Russia share one root in the songs of the folk. Catherine the Great gave an early push, but true home school waits for Glinka and his opera of 1836. Vast land, harsh rule, and few hubs of light kept the art late, the sheet argues in plain terms.
51996-my-pretty-maid-or-liane-lester:
McVeigh Miller wrote a dime tale sold for fifteen cents in a New York series, with rights of 1898 and 1899. Her other tales in the same line are named at the front. They hold titles such as Sweet Violet, The Pearl and the Ruby, and The Senator's Bride.

Contents promise a hot line of love and wrong. A lost chance, secret love, and a crime come early. Then a broken troth, love at first sight, and a beauty show. A cruel forgery, a dying mother, and a strand of ruddy hair lead on. The tale opens on a young wife dying, who clings to her husband's hands as a river roars in her ears.
52017-a-boy-s-fortune-or-the-strange-adv:
Horatio Alger Jr wrote A Boy's Fortune, or The Strange Adventures of Ben Baker, copyrighted in 1898. The John C Winston Company issued the book at Philadelphia, Chicago, and Toronto. The front picture shows a boy fallen asleep. The chapters open at Oliver Hitchcock's lunch-room and a lodging in St Mark's Place. A merchant's secret and a mock philanthropist follow. Ben gets into trouble, and a strange adventure comes early.

Later chapters take Ben to the office of a lawyer named Codicil and the home of poverty. A surprising announcement and a farewell call lead to a voyage on board the Parthia. The Beauforts fall into trouble, and brighter prospects open. A midnight escape, Ben's flight, and a wanderer in France carry the tale abroad. A maison de fous and a trap at Geneva's lake close the run.
52026-matthew-calbraith-perry-a-typical-:
Matthew Calbraith Perry: A Typical American Naval Officer is a biography by William Elliot Griffis, published in Boston by Cupples and Hurd in 1887. Griffis had written The Mikado's Empire and other books on Japan and Korea. His subject is the commodore whose squadron opened Japan to American trade.

Griffis dedicates the book to his father and grandfather. Both were merchant navigators who carried the flag to the ends of the earth. The choice of Perry as the typical officer is itself the argument. Perry's career joined seamanship, diplomacy, and naval reform in one life. Griffis wrote from personal knowledge of Japan, where he had lived and taught. The biography thus doubles as a celebration of the old merchant marine from which the author's family came.
52044-the-wide-awake-third-reader:
Clara Murray wrote The Wide Awake Third Reader, issued in Boston by Little, Brown, and Company in nineteen twelve. Copyright rests from nineteen eight. The Wide Awake series ran from a primer at thirty cents to this third reader at forty cents. A frontispiece shows Dutch children scrubbing their wooden shoes. Lessons mix stories, poems, and nature pieces for the third school year.

All the Children of All the World opens the lessons. The Song Sparrow Work by Etta Austin Blaisdell and Dutch Children follow. A Little Dutch Girl by Edith Colby Banfield and The Great Feast by Laura E Richards come next. Little Folk Land and A Strange Milk Wagon fill the early pages. How the Corn Grew and The Little Plant teach nature. A Rose by Emily Dickinson and Robin Redbreast by William Allingham give short poems. Teachers get a period third grade reader.
52071-the-book-of-the-otter:
Richard Clapham writes a manual on the otter for sportsmen and naturalists, with photos by himself and others. William Thompson adds an introduction to the London volume. Clapham had already written on fox-hunting on the Lakeland fells and on rough shooting.

The first chapter places the British otter, Lutra vulgaris, in the weasel family and describes it as a water-going marten fed chiefly on fish. Later chapters treat the otter's haunts and habits, then otter-hunting past and present. Hounds and terriers get a chapter of their own, with famed packs pictured at work. A closing set of memories rounds out the book. Readers get both the natural history of a shy river beast and the lore of the hunt that pursued it.
52121-recollections-of-a-confederate-sta:
Moxley Sorrel wrote Recollections of a Confederate Staff Officer, first held in print in nineteen five. Sorrel served as chief of staff to Longstreet in the First Corps of Lee's army, and later he led his own brigade under Hill. His wife urged him to write while he lay ill, and he thanks her in the front of the book.

The parts run from Manassas in eighteen sixty-one to the siege of Petersburg, and Sorrel tells of Seven Pines, Gettysburg, Chickamauga, and the wild woods fight of eighteen sixty-four. He gives sketches of men, horses, and staff life along with the battles. The book is a staff man's view from close to command, not a full history of the war.
52207-dick-kent-fur-trader:
Milton Richards wrote Dick Kent, Fur Trader, published by the Saalfield Publishing Company in 1927. Richards sent his hero through a whole series: with the Mounted Police, in the far north, with the Eskimos, and with the malemute mail. This adventure finds Dick at Fort Good Faith, a trading post in the Canadian north.

The first chapter, Blind Man's Pass, opens in the trading room of Factor MacClaren. Dick, bronzed by wind and sun, listens as Murky Nichols, a prospector, talks with the factor. Chapters promise spying, an ambuscade, a first prisoner, and the outlaws' cabin. Dick follows a pack-train, goes to a rescue, and hears Murky's confession before the party returns to the fort. The book is a brisk northern tale for boys.
52208-new-books-new-editions-published-b:
New Books and New Editions, published by Ward, Lock, and Tyler, is a trade catalogue. The firm listed its books from Warwick House, Paternoster Row, in London. Beeton publications for family reading and reference head the catalogue pages. A one hundred and forty fourth thousand edition leads that Beeton list in the front.

Mrs Beeton Book of Household Management stands there at seven shillings and sixpence. It aims to cover household duties in every grade of life, the notice says. From the mistress to the maid of all work, its counsel runs in that account. Coloured plates show dishes as they ought to look when ready for the table. Victorian publishers sold whole home libraries through catalogues just like this.
52246-boswell-the-biographer:
George Mallory wrote a life of James Boswell, the famed Scot who wrote the life of Samuel Johnson, issued in London in 1912. A portrait of Boswell from a drawing by George Dance fronts the book. A full list at the start names the books on Boswell that Mallory used for his work.

That list traces Boswell's own pen, from early poems and his tale Dorando to his Account of Corsica and his essays in the London Magazine. Mallory then tells the tale of a man known best as the shadow of a greater mind. The book asks what Boswell was in his own right: a keen watcher, a frank self writer, and a tireless keeper of talk.
52252-spanish-and-portuguese-south-ameri:
Spanish and Portuguese South America during the Colonial Period, by Robert Grant Watson, fills two volumes, printed in London in 1884. Watson edited Murray's Handbook of Greece. This second volume opens in Brazil with the Dutch war of 1623 to 1637. Chapters follow Count Maurice of Nassau's government, the rising of the Portuguese, and the war's close in 1661.

Later chapters treat Jesuit missions in northern Brazil and the French foothold in South America. Peru, New Granada, and Chili get their own surveys of growth. The discovery of mines and of the diamond district follows, then the growth of Buenos Ayres. The expulsion of the Jesuits from Brazil and from Paraguay closes the main line. Watson writes a dense, dated political history of empire.
52264-trial-of-william-palmer:
Trial of William Palmer stands in the Notable English Trials set, shaped by George H Knott, a barrister, and printed at Edinburgh and London by William Hodge and Company in 1912. A drawing of Palmer by Joseph Simpson stands at the front. Twin volumes treat other famed trials.

Knott gives the book to Sir Harry Bodkin Poland, who bears the name of one of the chief counsel in the trial. Poland was for many years the standing figure in the court where that trial was held. In his preface Knott says the chief trouble in telling a trial of more than half a century back is to find a true account from the time. State trials are easy to find, but a copy of a mere crime trial is rare. Crime fans get the famed Rugeley poison case in full.
52285-mungo-park-and-the-niger:
Joseph Thomson wrote Mungo Park and the Niger, for Dodd, Mead at New York. Thomson had written Through Masai Land before this life. The book stands in a series of the world's great explorers. Keltie, Mackinder, and Ravenstein edited that series for its house. An editors' preface opens the volume on the lure of exploration.

The story of the world's exploration is always attractive, they hold. Men take a keen interest in those who forced the unknown, they say. Such men unveiled the face of mother earth to the rest. Interest in exploration runs strong and widespread in recent years, they add. Each volume of the series treats mainly one leading explorer. The man himself is brought out prominently in each, they promise. Thomson gives Park's Niger journeys and his death in that cause.
52311-the-little-navajo-herder:
Little Navajo Herder, by Ann Clark with drawings by Hoke Denetsosie, was issued by the United States Indian Service at Haskell Institute. The single-volume English edition of September 1951 joins four short books first made for classroom use in federal Indian schools. The price on the title page is .25.

Short prose poems follow a young Navajo girl through a full year with her sheep and goats. Scenes cover the hogan, the night corral, the cornfield, wool work, weaving, the trading post, and dry and flood weather. The simple lines and pictures give young readers a warm, close view of home, work, and care for animals on Navajo land.
52438-imperfectly-proper:
Peter Donovan, signing as P O'D, gathered his sketches Imperfectly Proper for McClelland and Stewart at Toronto. A first edition of November 1920 sold into a second by February 1921. Johnston drew the pictures, starting with Algie's motor boat in trouble. The preface owns the pieces ran first in Toronto Saturday Night.

Contents promise light war on daily life in the city and suburbs. Motor boats, tea, cosmetics, clerks, ventilation, chickens, porters, and fur coats title the early fun. Moving day, tennis without a lawn, first drives, furnaces, dogs, and tools follow in kind. Donovan dedicates the set to Constant Reader and Old Subscriber with thanks. Canadian magazine humor of its day fills a slim, genial book.
52491-the-theatrical-primer:
Harold Acton Vivian wrote a mock primer that jokes about the stage. The book came out in New York in 1904. Francis Sagerson drew the pictures. Each short page speaks to the reader as if to a child in school. Short, prim lines hide sharp jokes for grown readers.

Pages greet the theatre, the press agent, and the man in charge. Vivian mocks high prices, free passes, and stars who act badly. He notes that crowds rush in but rush out just as fast. Stage folk and fans get a light, sly look at their own world. Each page is short, so the joke lands fast and then gives way to the next.
52656-ten-months-in-a-german-raider:
Captain John Stanley Cameron wrote Ten Months in a German Raider, a war tale put out in New York in 1918. Cameron was master of the American bark Beluga. A plate at the front shows him with his daughter Nita. Plates show the German ship Wolf, its torpedo tube, and its port side gun.

Cameron sailed from San Francisco on May 15, 1917, bound for Sydney. His load was 15,000 cases of benzine, a rich prize for a war ship at sea. He thought the trip would take two months and end in that far port. It took ten months and ended in Denmark, on the far side of the world. Plates show the last dive of a Japanese ship and the grave rite for a lost mate. He calls his tale an escape from the jaws of hell, as a held man of war.
52674-how-to-become-a-successful-singer:
Four famous voices advise beginners in How to Become a Successful Singer, published at London by George Newnes. Madame Clara Butt opens with the question of how to sing a song, naming four factors: the voice, the singer, the master and the song. Madame Melba writes on the gift of song and voice culture, Enrico Caruso gives hints on cultivating the voice, and Ben Davies tells how to attain success.

Butt insists that a singer is born, not made, and distrusts throat operations. She refused tonsil cutting in the operating chair at the Royal College of Music, recalling a soprano who lost her tuning after the operation.
527-the-end-of-the-tether:
Joseph Conrad follows Captain Whalley, an old master going blind, in this sea novella. Whalley commands the steamer Sofala on a Malay coast run, hiding his failing sight from owners, crew, and himself. A Malay serang, a low swamp coast, and a river estuary mark his last voyages.

Conrad writes with grave, slow power, tracking pride, duty, and the end of a working life. Whalley must choose between honor and ruin as the tether runs out. The tale stands as a somber study of age at sea, where a captain's nerve outlasts his eyes.
52790-history-of-a-six-weeks-tour-throug:
A young party's six-week tour of Europe was set in print in London in 1817. The book tells of trips through France, Switzerland, Germany, and Holland. It adds letters on a sail round Lake Geneva. It also tells of the ice fields at Chamouni. The front note calls the book plain and free of pride.

The writers grant that the scenes were well known by then. They built the book from a thin journal and a few home letters. Lakes, passes, and ice hills give the tour its charm. Youth and awe mark each stop on the road. Readers get an early taste of Alps travel in print.
52844-the-long-remembered-thunder:
Keith Laumer wrote a science fiction story for Worlds of Tomorrow of April 1963. Its headnote promises a man as ancient as time, fighting a frightful battle against incredible odds. It opens in a small-town hotel, where Tremaine opens his luggage, takes out a tool kit, and fits a tiny cylinder inside the telephone.

He dials Washington and asks Fred to put the buzzer on; the scrambler hums. An unauthorized transmitter is interfering with the top-secret hyperwave program, and General Margrave, its project officer, wants someone to hang. Tremaine, who calls hyperwave his baby, insists on working his own way as a leg-man. Fred warns him that certain quarters are pressing. Espionage with a technical hero is the manner.
52962-hugh-gwyeth-a-roundhead-cavalier:
Beulah Marie Dix wrote Hugh Gwyeth, a Roundhead cavalier, first published by Macmillan in 1899 and reprinted many times, including in 1913. The novel is set in England during the Civil War between King Charles and Parliament. Its hero bears the crossed loyalties of the subtitle: a gentleman bred in a cavalier world who rides with the Roundheads.

Early chapters bring tidings out of the north and send Hugh to seek his fortune on the road to Nottingham. He rides to war and into the trail of battle, finds comrades in arms, and falls under the king's displeasure. The life of Edmund Burley and the honor of the Gwyeth family carry the middle of the book. Dix closes with a call out of Kingsford, a riding of Arrow Water, and life after the victory.
52963-cuchulain-the-hound-of-ulster:
Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster, retold by Eleanor Hull, retells old Irish tales for general readers. Hull had written on the Cuchulain saga in Irish literature before. Stephen Reid drew the eight plates. A motto in Irish and English gives the hero's own words. He would trade a long life for lasting fame. Contents list thirty chapters, plus notes on sources.

Early chapters tell how Conor became king of Ulster. Readers learn how the boy Cuchulain got his name and took arms. Queen Meave demands the Brown Bull of Cooley and is refused. That refusal starts the great war of the tales. Later chapters bring the fight with Ferdia, Deirdre's sad end, and the hero's last stand.
5302-the-land-of-the-blue-flower:
Frances Hodgson Burnett's Land of the Blue Flower is a fairy tale of a kingdom once called King Mordreth's Land, after a fierce and cruel king. The tall, strong, beautiful King Amor descends from his mountain castle. He begins to reign. The land takes its new name, and the story follows his rule.

Burnett, author of The Secret Garden, writes a parable of kingship, kindness, and the power of love to change a country. The book offers young readers a gentle allegory, illustrated in the original, in which a good king remakes a gloomy land into a place of blue flowers.
53028-the-hampdenshire-wonder:
The Hampdenshire Wonder is a novel by Beresford, printed in London in 1911. Sidgwick and Jackson put the book out from Adam Street that year. Beresford had written The Early History of Jacob Stahl before this tale. He gives the book to his friend and critic Arthur Scott Craven. Three parts and an epilogue shape the long, strange life story here.

Part one traces the teller's early ties with Ginger Stott in youth. Part two turns to the childhood of the Wonder and his odd birth. The boy passes through a prison of knowledge, tests, and flight. Part three brings the teller back to the Wonder as a grown man. Subjection to the Wonder grows, eases, and lifts in those late chapters. An epilogue on the uses of mystery closes the whole strange tale. The first scene opens on a train with Bergson in hand.
53044-devlin-the-barber:
Devlin the Barber is a mystery novel by B L Farjeon, printed at London in 1888 in its fourth edition. Farjeon also wrote The Nine of Hearts and Great Porter Square. An introduction refers to a strange, unfathomable being, through whose instrumentality an awful mystery was solved. The first chapter gives an account of the good fortune which befell Mr Melladew.

Terrible news reaches the narrator, and a shoal of visitors follows, then another mystery. Richard Portland makes a singular proposition. The narrator visits Mrs Lemon and is haunted by three evil-looking objects in her room. Fanny Lemon relates how she resolved to let her second floor front. Devlin the barber takes her first floor front instead. He performs wonderful tricks, fascinates Mr Lemon, and strikes terror to Fanny's soul. Her husband, growing better acquainted with Devlin, seemed haunted by shadows and spirits.
53134-the-admiral-s-daughter:
Admiral Daughter is a novel by Margaret Stuart Lane, set in the West Country. Humphrey Milford and Oxford University Press issued the book at London. This printing is a nineteen twenty seven reprint made at Edinburgh. Twenty six chapters run from The Fair Return to Sumer Is A Comen In.

Garth House, a letter from Kensington, and Roger Trevannion open the tale. A lady in waiting, Simone Leblanc, and a haunted cove follow in turn. Exeter, a signal, a gaol yard, and Zacchary quest build the middle acts. Spring comes to the West Country in the first page primroses and lambs. Sailor boys watch the rising tide in the harbour as it opens.
53164-the-standard-bearer:
Crockett wrote a tale of old Scotland, issued at New York in 1898 and dedicated to the folk of his native parish of Balmaghie. He calls it a rendering of strange happenings among their forebears, of which they have not yet quite lost the memory. The foreword warns that the book is iron-grey and chill.

It tells of times when the passions of men still worked like a yeasty sea after the storms of the Great Killing. In those days, he says, the things of the spirit had lost their old authority without gaining a new graciousness. Crockett had won his readers with The Lilac Sunbonnet and Cleg Kelly; this darker Galloway story asks for a different patience.
53179-sea-plunder:
H De Vere Stacpoole wrote Sea Plunder for John Lane at New York in 1917, from a Street and Smith copyright of 1916. Stacpoole also wrote The Gold Trail and The Pearl Fishers, priced on the title page at $1.30 net each. Part one, The Buccaneers, follows Captain Blood and the ship Penguin.

Captain Blood walks McGinnis' wharf at San Francisco each afternoon, an Irishman of black hair and grey eyes with Spanish blood from Armada days. Chapters bring the sailing of the Penguin, a cable message, and the crew's share of the spoils. The last of the Penguin ends part one. Part two ships a new captain aboard the Heart of Ireland, with a cargo of champagne and a big haul.
53213-marjorie-dean-marvelous-manager:
Pauline Lester's novel for girls, copyrighted in 1925 by the Burt Company in New York, belongs to the Marjorie Dean Post-Graduate Series. The series was meant for girls of twelve to eighteen, and this volume follows Marjorie at college after the high school and college books. Jerry Macy, her roommate, shares the opening scene.

Marjorie holds a letter and debates going home for Thanksgiving against staying for the dormitory girls. Jerry parodies Hamlet on the question and proposes the way out: organize the new Travelers' sorority. The new Travelers, well chosen by their elders, can see the dormitory girls through the holiday, and the older pair can go home free.
53252-the-boy-apprenticed-to-an-enchante:
The Boy Apprenticed to an Enchanter is a tale for young readers by Padraic Colum, printed at New York in 1920. Dugald Stuart Walker drew the pictures. Colum gave the book to Ella Young, in memory of the many stories she had told him, and its shape honors that gift of told tales.

A prologue tells of the horses of King Manus and a youth bound for death at sunrise. The tale then splits into parts: Eean the fisherman's son, Bird-of-Gold the bramble gatherer's daughter, and the two enchanters. Magic, quests, and old Irish story craft run through the whole, in prose a child can follow and a grown reader can savor.
53277-the-every-day-book-and-table-book-:
Volume three of William Hone's Every-Day Book and Table Book completes his everlasting calendar of popular amusements, sports, pastimes, ceremonies, manners, customs, and events. There is one for each of the three hundred and sixty-five days. The whole forms a history of the year, months, and seasons, and a perpetual key to the almanac.

The title page promises the calendar's range: accounts of the weather and rules for health and conduct.
