Then come remarkable anecdotes and facts in chronology, antiquities, topography, biography, natural history, art, and science. Hone's own couplet leads his telling: festivals and fairs and plays, merriment and bonfire blaze, Christmas mummings and twelfth-night king and queen. A frontispiece of Petrarch's inkstand, in Miss Edgeworth's possession, carries her verses on the poet's Cupid, welcoming the arch suppliant to his favourite isle.
53320-the-motor-boys-in-the-army-or-ned-:
The Motor Boys in the Army, or Ned, Bob and Jerry as Volunteers, is a boys' adventure novel by Clarence Young, published by Cupples and Leon in 1918. It is one of the long Motor Boys series, with more than twenty companion volumes. This time the boys' world is overtaken by the First World War.

The contents sketch the plot: a fire alarm, a runaway engine, the call for volunteers, and off to Camp Dixton. Later chapters bring camp life, a stab in the back, an accusation, a minstrel show, a hand grenade and a round-up. The opening has the three friends thrilled that the President has asked Congress to defy Germany. It is wartime series fiction, selling enlistment as the boys' greatest adventure.
53396-practical-talks-by-an-astronomer:
Harold Jacoby gave plain talks on the sky for home readers. Jacoby taught the science of the sky at Columbia University. His book came out in New York in 1902. A photo of the moon at first quarter fronts the book. Each talk takes one clear theme and keeps to plain words.

Talks deal with sailing by the stars and with the Pole Star. Star crowds, clouds in space, and brief new stars come next. Galileo, sun dials, and sky photos fill the mid part. Time rules round the world and the rings of Saturn close the set. New sky fans get a kind, firm guide.
53422-free-trapper-s-pass-or-the-gold-se:
Free Trapper's Pass, or The Gold-Seeker's Daughter, is a penny novel from Jackson's Novels. James Jackson published it in Fleet Street, London, at one penny. It is number two in that cheap series. The first chapter is called The Raid of the Blackfeet. The story opens on a tributary of the Yellowstone River. A cabin stood near the Bighorn Mountains at its opening. Roughly built, it still had an air of nicety and comfort. Its walls were smooth outside from axe work, not the plane.

Inside, the walls seemed plastered with stiff brown clay. A chimney of the same substance vented the fire's smoke. A fair girl stood in the shadow of the rude doorway. Golden hair floated in soft ringlets over her shoulders. The penny dreadful trade carried frontier romance to London readers. Trappers, raids, and a gold seeker's daughter are its stock.
53499-martin-luther:
Koppenhaver's Martin Luther, a short life printed by Muhlenberg Press of Philadelphia in 1953, follows Luther from the copper mines to the Augsburg Confession. Luther was born on November 10, 1483, at Eisleben, son of Hans and Margarethe, and baptized the next morning in the church of Saint Peter. The family moved to Mansfeld, where Hans scraped school fees, and the boy earned his board singing from door to door.

The chapters are grouped in scenes: the miner's son, the professor, the collision with Rome over indulgences and the Ninety-five Theses, and the breach widening through his writings. Then comes the monk standing firm at the Diet of Worms, the Wartburg, marriage, and a church reborn. A chronology closes the book. Koppenhaver writes plainly for the general reader, presenting Luther as a man of common sense who came to trust in God's love and mercy rather than fear.
53519-horace-walpole-and-his-world-selec:
Seeley picked and shaped these extracts from the letters of Horace Walpole for an eighteen eighty-four book. Walpole, son of a prime minister, built the famed house Strawberry Hill and wrote through much of the late seventeen hundreds. Seeley groups the extracts by theme and adds a long first part on Walpole's life and work.

Readers meet court balls, garden parties, and trips to Paris and Bath, and Walpole writes on kings, wars with America, riots in London, and deaths of friends. He gossips about dress, food, books, and art with a light, sharp pen. The extracts show why his letters are still read as a record of his age's talk and taste.
53522-ann-and-her-mother:
O Douglas writes a novel of a mother and daughter in a Doran volume from New York held under rights from 1922. Douglas had written The Setons and Penny Plain before this quiet tale. A Goldsmith quote on the charm of a country fireside heads the book at the start.

Mrs Douglas and her daughter Ann sit in their living room on a November night as chapter one opens. The room glows soft and warm, spare of trinkets, with each chair and picture of worth in its place. The mother knits a stocking as she reads, loath to waste a spare hour of her day. Ann pores over a seedsman's catalogue by the fire, puzzled over what will grow best with them at home. Rose names in that list, Queen Mary and Mr Asquith among them, draw her dry wit at once.
53604-the-touch-of-abner:
The Touch of Abner is a comic tale by Cody, printed in Toronto in 1919. McClelland and Stewart put the book out, with Doran holding the rights. Cody had writ The Frontiersman, The Long Patrol, and The Fourth Watch. A verse from the Biglow Papers heads the front of the book. Cody gives the tale to the various tribes of Zeb with love.

Thirty chapters run from brains, gall, and luck to the heart-touch. Ten-centers, society pigs, and a flea in the ear fill the early list. Beating the movies, a dump scheme, and town rats come in turn. Bottled devils, a joy-ride, and in the klink crowd the mid chapters. A sermon with a punch and a hold-up raise the late stakes. Counsel for the defense sets up the closing heart-touch of all. The tale opens as a man drawls out a thousand-dollar pledge.
53831-christmas-at-punkin-holler:
Elizabeth Guptill wrote a Christmas piece for a place called Punkin Holler. The Paine house in Dayton, Ohio, put the book out. Bright songs for shows frame the front of the book. Those songs, by Edna Randolph Worrell, were sold as sheet music. Their ads claim tunes that children love at first hear.

The main piece gives a home or school a ready Christmas show. Song, speech, and fun in a country set fill the bill. Such books let small towns stage a feast night with ease. Each part is short and built to please a crowd. Groups in search of a warm show get one here.
53942-letters-from-a-landscape-painter:
Charles Lanman, author of 'Essays for Summer Hours,' wrote these letters, published at Boston in 1845. A line from Izaak Walton stands at the front, warning readers not to let prejudice prepossess them. Lanman confesses his discourse will prove calm and quiet, like his own recreation of painting.

Critical notices of his earlier essays fill the opening pages of the copy. John Neal praises a book of some twenty essays on pilgrimages there, in the quoted notice. Woods and city, morning and evening, mirth and sadness fill Lanman's letters from the road, written by a painter who fished, walked and sketched across America.
5401-old-rose-and-silver:
Myrtle Reed wrote Old Rose and Silver as a romance of music, memory, and second chances. The novel opens with an author's note about its songs, including an unpublished piano arrangement of Wilson G. Smith's Entreaty, and then follows its characters through chapters titled A Falling Star, The Voice of the Violin, and The Crosby Twins. Music threads through the household scenes.

As the story moves from welcome-home gatherings to an enchanted hour and a thirtieth of June, old affections resurface and new ones form. Reed writes in a gentle, old-fashioned style, letting violins, letters, and summer afternoons carry the feeling. Readers get a warm, sentimental romance from the early twentieth century.
54028-three-heroines-of-new-england-roma:
Three Heroines of New England Romance sets forth true stories by Harriet Prescott Spofford, Louise Imogen Guiney, and Alice Brown, printed at Boston in 1894 with many drawings by Edmund Garrett. Priscilla, by Spofford, opens the set; Agnes Surriage, by Brown, follows; Martha Hilton, by Guiney, closes the tales.

Drawings show Priscilla at her spinning wheel, Miles Standish, John Alden, and a wedding procession in the colony. Marblehead streets, old graveyards, azaleas, and merchant ships fill the Surriage plates of town life. Martha Hilton wears sweeping brocades with a cushion towering on her powdered head in the frontispiece. Readers get romance rooted in colonial fact.
54049-sailor-jack-the-trader:
Harry Castlemon wrote this war tale of Sailor Jack, the trader. Porter and Coates printed it at Philadelphia, copyright 1893. Four plates by George White show scenes, the last of the Louisiana. Contents open with Tom Randolph, a conscript, in chapter one.

Lambert signal fire, tales carried, and phantom bushwhackers follow in line. Cotton thieves and Sailor Jack in action fill the mid chapters. Bad news from Marcy, a Williamston jail, and a prison pen come. The dead line and Sailor Jack trading close the war tale. Castlemon Gunboat and Rocky Mountain tales stand named on the title page of this one.
54125-beyond-the-old-frontier-adventures:
Beyond the Old Frontier, by George Bird Grinnell, tells of Indian fighters, hunters, and fur traders for Scribner in 1913, at net $1.50 in its series. Seven tales make the book, from An Early Fur Trader to The Council at Fort Benton. One follows the days when beaver skins were money; another puts a boy in Indian camps.

Plates show a buffalo herd, a Cheyenne camp, Kit Carson, and the plan of Bent's Old Fort. A map of the frontier country faces the first tale. Grinnell had earlier written Trails of the Pathfinders and Blackfeet Indian Stories. The series mates it with boys' lives of Drake, Hakluyt, and Pike.
5422-the-masquerader:
Katherine Cecil Thurston sets this novel in London on a foggy January night, when two events collide: a border rising against the Persian government and a strange case of mistaken identity. A man who looks exactly like a rising politician becomes entangled in the politician's life, and the resemblance soon shapes both men's fates. Parliament gossip and street fog set the opening mood.

The plot turns on doubling, disguise, and political intrigue, as the substitute is drawn deeper into public life and private danger. Thurston keeps the tension between the two look-alikes at the center, asking what happens when appearance replaces identity. Readers get an Edwardian thriller with romance, politics, and a steady sense of menace.
54284-william-dampier:
William Clark Russell wrote a life of William Dampier for the English Men of Action series, first issued in 1889 and reprinted in 1894. The book opens with the buccaneers of Hispaniola and with what sea life and navigation were like in the seventeenth century. It then takes Dampier from his early years and the Campeche coast into the ranks of the buccaneers he sailed with from 1681 on.

Later chapters trace his first voyage round the world, the Roebuck voyage of 1699 to 1701, and the Saint George voyage that followed. The last sea years came with Woodes Rogers, from 1708 to 1711. Russell gives a clear short life of a sailor whose name still stands for bold and rough voyaging.
54289-three-days-on-the-ohio-river:
Three Days on the Ohio River is a river travel book by a writer who signs himself Father William. Carlton and Phillips published it at New York in 1854 for the Sunday-School Union. A western steamboat stands as the front picture. The first chapter owns that the writer, once in Cincinnati, wished to reach Pittsburg by the river.

It was not the nearest, swiftest, or cheapest way. He longed to see the country the river runs through, having read much of the Ohio in histories and in tales of the Indian wars. Fifteen chapters cover the steamboat, Maysville, the cabin, four Indians, and the coal country. Blennerhasset's Island, the ancient mounds, a suspension bridge, and Logan the Mingo chief follow, ending with arrival at Pittsburg and reflections.
54340-the-art-of-architectural-modelling:
The Art of Architectural Modelling in Paper, by the architect Richardson, was published in London in eighteen fifty nine. Its preface calls it the first work ever printed on this practical art. Models, the author argues, let clients grasp a design as words and drawings cannot. A client can see faults in a model and have them fixed at the start.

Chapters cover first the stuffs a modeller needs, paper, glue, and other supplies. Next come the tools, from cutting boards and presses to knives and compass gear. The main part then walks through building a model step by step. Plans, window frames, doors, cornices, and roofs each get their own treatment in turn. A greenhouse and a full house serve as worked examples for the learner.
54413-bill-bolton-and-hidden-danger:
Bill Bolton and Hidden Danger, by Noel Sainsbury, is an adventure for boys. The Goldsmith company printed it at Chicago in 1933. Sainsbury had sent Bill out before, in Winged Cartwheels and as a flying midshipman.

The book is given to Bo King, in hope he keeps singing Bill's praises. Seventeen chapters run from a shot in the night to the close. Strange doings at Turner's, watchers in the trees, and a mysterious trio fill the middle. An offer and a threat, another intruder, and Pig Island again raise the stakes. The opening is alarm: bangs wake Bill in a storm. A bullet pings the rainpipe, and the next shot smashes his window pane. A copper jar crashes from the mantel as Bill drops to the floor. The shooter, he guesses, is perched in a maple.
54572-the-chronic-loafer:
Nelson Lloyd loiters in print in The Chronic Loafer, printed in New York in 1900. Taylor made the book, with copyright the same year. Twenty two chapters of village tales fill it, from The Reunion to A Piece in the Paper.

Heads name the village round: a spelling bee, Absalom Bunkel, the missus, and the awfullest thing. A wrestling match, a tramp's romance, and an argument on ambition stand in the run. A bass horn, a mule courtship, and a haunted store vary the humour. Chapter one sets the stage in the heart of Pennsylvania. In the center of one of the most picturesque valleys lies the village, he writes. At one end of its single street stands the store. On its broad porch a long oak bench, hacked in countless places by the knives of many generations of loungers, faces the meadows.
54718-india-impressions-with-some-notes-:
India Impressions, with some notes of Ceylon, by Walter Crane, records a winter tour of 1906 to 1907. Macmillan published it at New York in 1907 with the author own sketches. A colour frontispiece and many other illustrations come from his hand. He inscribes the record to his wife, his travelling companion on the tour.

The voyage opens the contents, and Bombay with the caves of Ellora follows. Ahmedabad, Chitorgarh, Udaipur, and Jaipur fill the road north in the contents. Agra, Gwalior, Delhi, and Amritsar with Lahore carry the tour on in the list. Lucknow, Benares, Calcutta with Darjeeling, and Madras close the Indian chapters. An artist of the arts and crafts world looks at India with a sketch book.
54737-out-for-business-or-robert-frost-s:
Out for Business, or Robert Frost's Strange Career is a boys' novel begun by Horatio Alger and finished by Arthur Winfield. Copyrighted in 1900, it was issued by Grosset and Dunlap of New York. The preface calls it a complete tale in itself and the first of two companion stories, the second being Falling in with Fortune.

The tale follows a sturdy country youth of high moral aim. Driven out by the harsh acts of his step-father, he goes to make his way in the world. The frontispiece shows Robert overhearing an important talk. The publishers note that these two stories were the last tales Alger began, and that his books sold in the hundreds of thousands.
54820-brief-account-of-the-english-chara:
Brief Account of the English Character is a short tract, shown here side by side in English and in Chinese. A note by the man who put this form in order tells its odd past. Charles Marjoribanks first drew it up in English for the China coast. He led the choice group of the East India Company at Canton.

Robert Morrison, a church man and a scholar of Chinese, put the tract into that tongue. He printed scores of copies at his Anglo-Chinese College in Malacca. In 1832 two men bore cases of the tract on a sea trip up the coast of China. That trip broke the law of the land, and its aim was trade. It sought to learn how far the north ports could be pried open to British goods.
54836-the-trial-of-peter-zenger:
Vincent Buranelli edited the trial of Peter Zenger in a volume printed at New York in 1957, with an introduction and notes. The liberty of the press is a subject of the greatest importance, the New York Weekly Journal of November 12, 1733, is quoted at the front. The front page of Zenger's journal of February 18, 1733, is pictured whole.

Without freedom of thought, there can be no such thing as wisdom, and no public liberty without freedom of speech, the Cato letter in that issue runs. It is the right of every man, so far as he does not hurt the right of another. Whoever would overthrow the liberty of a nation must begin by subduing the freeness of speech. Zenger, a printer jailed for his paper's attacks on the governor, was acquitted by a jury. Buranelli sets the great press trial in its papers.
54862-humphry-davy-poet-and-philosopher:
Humphry Davy, Poet and Philosopher is T E Thorpe's life of the chemist, in the Century Science Series edited by Sir Henry E Roscoe. Macmillan and Company of New York published it in 1896; its author was principal chemist of the government laboratories.

Davy was born on December 17, 1778, eldest son of Carver Robert Davy and Grace Millett. The chapters follow the career: Penzance to 1798, then the Pneumatic Institution at Bristol. The Royal Institution and its laboratory come next, then the isolation of the metals of the alkalis and the work on chlorine. Marriage, knighthood, and the Elements of Chemical Philosophy fill the middle. Davy and Faraday, the iodine work, and the safety lamp follow. The Royal Society years and his last days close a life the title insists was a poet's as well as a philosopher's.
54872-the-life-story-of-an-otter:
The Life Story of an Otter follows one animal from birth to death. Tregarthen wrote the book. John Murray published it in London in 1909. The author had earlier written a life story of a fox. Illustrations show the otter at the creek and on the coast.

The contents map the animal's career. Chapters move from the nursery to early training. A first trek and life at the creek follow. Sea and marsh broaden the range. The family breaks up midway. Frost and famine test the otter in winter. Hounds track him in a later chapter. The first chapter opens in a morass among the foothills. A mother otter lines a nest with reed down for two cubs.
54915-the-bears-of-blue-river:
Bears of Blue River is a boys frontier tale by Charles Major, published at New York in 1908. The Macmillan Company issued this edition, first copyrighted in 1900 and 1901. Major is named as author of When Knighthood Was in Flower on the title page. Frost and others drew the illustrations for the volume of tales.

A frontispiece note shows the boy Balser giving a bear a mortal wound with his aim. The scene is the Blue River country of Indiana in the pioneer years of that state. Major tales, told by an old man of his youth among the bears and the woods, belong to the wave of frontier boy books after the closing of the West. They keep the speech, hunts, and alarms of the Indiana backwoods in a form young readers could take up.
54916-a-prince-to-order:
Charles Stokes Wayne wrote a novel of a man woke to find a prince's life. The book came out in New York and London in 1905. Its rights date to 1904 and 1905 in two claims. Wayne gave the tale to his wife as its first spark and spur. Grey's wake is slow as a grey dawn in the first page's words.

Dreams and true things mix as he comes back to his flesh in bed. His hands clutch a silk spread in that slow first dawn. He turns on his side to a cool cloth case for his cheek. Pale blue drapes hang round the shut bed where he lies in hush. A prince to order is the odd fate that waits for Grey. Court plots build fast.
54989-the-young-emperor-william-ii-of-ge:
The Young Emperor William the Second of Germany is a study of the growth of a cast of mind on a throne, by Frederic. He was the author of past tales of a vale and of a girl of the law. Prints of faces fill the book, put out at New York in the early eighteen nineties.

Its gift word makes it out to his sheet chief, and still more to his friend. Its first part takes the high place of the kings house. In the summer of the year the young king took the throne, it says, a host of work men toiled in Paris on the base of a great worlds fair. That fair would mark the year count of the death by force of the God given right of kings.
55089-little-miss-grasshopper:
Little Miss Grasshopper, by Johanna Spyri, is a story for children by the Swiss author of Heidi, here in the English version by Helen B Dole. This edition was published in New York in 1918.

The heroine is Rita Feland of Dresden, a lively little girl whose skill at jumping earns her the grasshopper name from her father. Her quiet sister Ella stands in contrast, waiting politely for a morning greeting while Rita springs onto her father's knee. Five chapters carry the family from home on a journey over the Gemmi Pass in the Swiss Alps. New acquaintances, a terrible night, and the next morning follow. Spyri's list of books at the front names Heidi, Moni the Goat Boy, and other tales of Swiss children.
55099-the-federal-reserve-monster:
Jim Jam Jems of Bismarck, North Dakota, issued 'The Federal Reserve Monster' in 1922, by Sam Clark and Wallace Campbell, priced at two dollars with carriage prepaid. The editor's foreword begins with charity toward all and malice toward none, then indites a volume of criticism of the Federal Reserve 'Bunking' System as practiced in America. The editors are not posing as a David and do not depend on one stone.

Their volley of rocks aims not to kill and not to reform, for a thing needing reform needs an axe. They want to awaken public sentiment against the Federal Reserve Octopus until the people force the system to be born anew. Touters for the system, they say, behave like a mother duck at hatching time, flapping along to draw attention from the nest they are feathering. Two years of monthly bombardment are here collected under one cover.
55312-the-rainbow-feather:
Fergus Hume's The Rainbow Feather, copyrighted in 1898 by G W Dillingham Company of New York, opens on a gorse-covered common in July. An old gipsy, Gran Jimboy, takes Miss Lester's hand to read it, then flings it back with a startled look, mortal feared to tell what the lines show.

The young man with the girl, Mr Lovel, catches the gipsy by the arm and demands she earn her shilling. She holds that the hand is easy reading, yet she would not freeze the blood of the maid by speaking. The contents carry the prophecy through a sermon, an inquest, a society of the Rainbow Feather, and a trial, to the truth at last.
55330-a-biography-of-rev-henry-ward-beec:
Wm C Beecher and Samuel Scoville wrote a Biography of Henry Ward Beecher. Charles L Webster and Company issued it in 1888. Mrs Henry Ward Beecher aided the life's making. The book goes to the authors' mother in love. Her patient devotion comforted their father, it says. She blessed him in prosperity as in trouble.

Chapter One treats the Beecher ancestry in full. Ward and Foote lines join that telling. The Anvil and the great Oak stand as heads there. Lyman Beecher's courtship of Roxana Foote fills it. Their home at East Hampton, Long Island follows. Removal to Litchfield, Connecticut closes the chapter. A portrait of Henry Ward Beecher fronts the life. A family's own life of America's most famous preacher carries love and loyalty into every page of his rise.
55399-the-rhymer:
Allan McAulay wrote a tale printed at New York in 1900 and given to Mary and Jeanie. It opens in Perthshire in the year 1787. Mr Graham of The Mains holds few acres and a modest purse. Yet he has seven daughters, and a son newly born.

On an autumn market day a fellow laird stops him in the dusk. A rich friend from Fife, Jimmy Cheape, lodges with the neighbour. The man seeks a wife, and the neighbour has promised him a meeting at The Mains. Graham pricks up his ears at the news. A house with seven lasses, the friend jokes, is the very shop for such a search.
55484-lucian-the-dreamer:
Lucian the Dreamer, a novel by J S Fletcher, was published by W Collins Sons and Company of London. Fletcher dedicates the book to Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, in thanks for a kindly service. A note at the front calls the book the study of an artistic temperament in the generation that fought in the Boer War. Lucian is a thinker rather than a doer.

The tale follows Lucian from his arrival at a little village station to a final tragic scene in the dry bed of a South African river. He lives under the care of an uncle and aunt in the country village of Wellsby. Its simple rustic beauties please him, and his many love affairs fill the middle of the book. The station serves Wellsby, Meadhope, and Simonstower, three villages hidden in the woods.
55553-the-last-frontier:
The Last Frontier is a travel and war book on Africa by Alexander Powell. Scribner issued it in New York, with copyright in 1912. Its subtitle calls it the white man's war for civilisation in Africa. Powell had served in the American consular service in Egypt. Sixteen full-page illustrations and a map accompany the text. A plate shows a sandstorm passing over Khartoum.

Powell thanks many magazines for pieces reused here. Collier's, The Outlook, and Scribner's are named among them. He also thanks Bryce for South African material. The book is dedicated to his wife. She is praised as his comrade on the long African trail. Powell wrote a shelf of such expedition books. Gentlemen Rovers and Fighting in Flanders are its mates. The tone is that of the colonial age in full voice.
55590-jim-mortimer:
Jim Mortimer is a novel by Warren Bell, printed at London by Adam and Charles Black in 1908. Bell also wrote Tales of Greyhouse. Sixteen full page illustrations by Gordon Browne accompany the text. The story turns on a telephone wire.

The wire, the narrator insists, was fraught with interest. It had paid for itself scores of times over. Messages of life and death passed across it constantly. Instructions in emergencies saved the time of walking the three hundred yards, for doctors do not often run. Reprimands were roared across it, bulletins despatched, dietary altered and medicine prescribed. Bell builds a country practice novel around the wire, where every call may bring a case, a secret or a fee.
55596-life-of-robert-stevenson-civil-eng:
David Stevenson wrote the life of his father Robert Stevenson, the great lighthouse engineer, published at Edinburgh in 1878. Robert Stevenson was engineer to the Commissioners of Northern Lighthouses, and the bust from which the frontispiece is taken stands in the library of his Bell Rock Lighthouse. The contents show the range of his practice: ferry engineering, railways, harbours and rivers, the preservation of timber, and stone and suspension bridges.

Later chapters treat the Wolf Rock Lighthouse, the Carr Rock beacon, cranes, fisheries, and marine surveying. Stevenson advised on everything from cathedral ruins to night signal lamps, and corresponded with George Stephenson on railways. David, himself an engineer of the next generation, made the book both a memoir and a record of Scottish engineering in its heroic age.
55624-the-young-train-dispatcher:
The Young Train Dispatcher is a boys' novel by Burton Stevenson, published in Boston in 1907 by the Page Company. It belongs to the Boys' Story of the Railroad series, alongside volumes about a young section-hand, a young train master, and a young apprentice. The book is illustrated, and four printings in three years show its reach.

The frontispiece gives a taste of the action promised inside. Its caption describes something hurling itself across a waiting room and out the door to safety, and points the reader to page 271. The series title makes the plan plain. Each book puts a young hero inside one job on the railroad and builds adventure from the real work of that trade. In this volume the job is the dispatcher's desk, where trains are guided by wire and order.
55680-transmission-or-variation-of-chara:
Georgiana Kirby wrote Transmission, or Variation of Character Through the Mother, issued in a revised and enlarged edition by Fowler and Wells in New York in 1882. Kirby argues that the mother holds the greater power to shape her unborn children, for good or ill. With that power, she says, comes grave responsibility.

She lays down a few plain propositions and supports them with cases seen in nearly forty years of watching. Names and places are changed in each case. Kirby attacks the common view that the mother merely nourishes what the father gives. She blames false modesty for keeping women ignorant of how a mother's mind and body during pregnancy may mark a child. The book reflects a wide Victorian belief in prenatal influence.
55695-pioneer-saturn-encounter:
Pioneer Saturn Encounter is a NASA booklet published in September 1979 by the Ames Research Center. It reports the Pioneer 11 spacecraft's flyby of Saturn. Contents run from a foreword and introduction through Saturn images, science highlights, and an outward bound section.

The spacecraft began its journey on April 5, 1973, as Pioneer 11. It reached Jupiter in December 1974, passing close above the cloud tops and photographing the polar regions. Jupiter's gravity then swung it back across the solar system toward Saturn. The booklet presents the first close view of the ringed planet and its moons. Artist's drawings stand in where the craft's speed kept cameras from the closest moments. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
55831-the-spider:
The Spider, a mystery novel by Fergus Hume, was printed in London in 1910 by Ward, Lock and Company. Hume had won fame with The Mystery of a Hansom Cab years before. The tale opens in The Athenian Club on Pall Mall, a house built like a Roman villa.

Inside, the rooms bear Latin names, and their use is strictly enforced on members. Hume jokes that the club, like Saint Paul, is all things to all men. The contents promise a possible partnership, a trap set and sprung, and grief for a girl named Ida. Lady Corsoon makes an appeal in one chapter, and witchcraft is named in the next. Later chapters run to Bowderstyke and Gerby Hall before justice closes the tale.
55880-the-young-train-master:
Burton Stevenson wrote a railroad tale for boys, issued at Boston in 1909 and priced at $1.50. It follows his Young Section-Hand and Young Train Dispatcher, and shares their hero. The contents open with old friends and new duties, and a chapter called The Miracle at Greenfield.

Allan, the young hero, takes charge at Wadsworth as a strike begins, in chapters that promise a threat from a Mr Nixon and a declaration of war. A derelict train, an old stone house, and a bomb fill out the perils. The downfall of Bassett and a chapter named Nemesis lead to the last, where Allan earns the title of young train master. Railroad boys were the natural readers.
55923-carl-the-trailer:
Harry Castlemon wrote a boys western tale printed in Philadelphia in 1899. Castlemon was known for his Gunboat and Rocky Mountain tales. His hero Carl earns the name of the trailer, a scout who can follow a trail. A front picture shows Carl finding Indian horse thieves.

The tale builds toward the end of Sitting Bull and the battle of Wounded Knee. The ghost dance, a solitary horseman, couriers with dispatches, and an Indian policeman fill the mid chapters. A trip to Saint Louis and a hard fight test Carl and his friend Claude. Castlemon mixes army life, scouting craft, and the last Sioux war into a fast tale for boys.
55962-kate-meredith-financier:
C J Cutcliffe Hyne wrote Kate Meredith, Financier. A Hamburger and Sons brought out a special edition in 1906. Frank Parker painted its pictures in water colors. Hyne also wrote the Captain Kettle books. Twenty-three chapters fill the contents list. A West Coast welcome opens the tale.

Miss Laura Slade enters in chapter two. A king who stopped the roads follows. Events at Malla-Nulla and the coming of the Okky-Men build the middle. The head of the firm appears twice in the list. Tin Hill's mine, a cablegram from Kate, and a song of speed close the book. Its front plate shows men claiming to be the chief ju-ju men of all Africa. West African trade and risk drive this business romance.
55965-air-monster:
Edwin Green wrote Air Monster, a boys' tale of flight and spies issued at New York in 1932. Its chapters run from secret duty through a mystery plane, a night alarm, and trial flight to rescue work in far seas. The tale opens at midnight in Kratz, the capital of Rubania, where lights burn in the tower room of the Gerka, the secret police. Such a late meeting can mean only pressing business.

Rubania is a free state east of Prussia, formed after the World War. Alex Reikoff, a harsh ruler with a lust for world power, has crushed all who stood against him and built up fleets of submarines and airplanes. He trusts air power as a tool of war above all. Green's tale pits young airmen against this watching state, in the fast style of boys' adventure books.
55975-voyager-encounters-jupiter:
Voyager Encounters Jupiter is a picture book put out by NASA in July 1979, after the Voyager craft flew by the giant planet. A cover view joins ten color images from Voyager 1 into one full turn of Jupiter air. A second view shows the planet from below its south pole.

Parts hold images of Jupiter and its moons, the story of the Voyager mission, and the chief science results. Named moons hold Amalthea, Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. A Titan Centaur rocket launched Voyager, the last planned use of that type before the shuttle age. Robert A Frosch led NASA at the time. Space fans get the first close look at Jupiter in rich color, with dates and distances for each frame.
56058-lost-in-the-atlantic-valley-or-fra:
Lost in the Atlantic Valley is a Frank Reade adventure from the Frank Reade Weekly Magazine, number 35, dated the twenty-sixth of June 1903 and priced at five cents. The story, signed Noname, sends Frank Reade Junior under the sea in his new submarine boat, the Dart. The contents promise a sunken wreck, an earthquake and a sunken city.

The opening chapter introduces Readestown, a flourishing city that owes its founding to the Reade family of inventors. Frank, the latest of the line, is a household word for machines that travel in air, under water or anywhere else. His new submarine, built with a famous scientist, is to explore the great Atlantic valley beneath the ocean. The party is soon imprisoned in a wreck and buried under the sea, in the best dime-novel manner. The number is a complete specimen of the Tousey invention story.
5611-the-satyricon-of-petronius-arbiter:
Petronius Arbiter wrote the Satyricon, a Roman satire surviving in fragments, here translated by William Burnaby with an introduction by C. K. Scott Moncrieff. The introduction opens as an open letter to a young gentleman, beginning on high ground above St. Andrews, looking seaward for the Inchcape Rock, where at first nothing shows and then a speck of whiteness lasts no longer than a wave.

The novel itself follows Encolpius, Giton, and Ascyltos through feasts, quarrels, and escapades in Nero's Rome, with the famous dinner of Trimalchio at its center. Readers get ancient satire at its most vivid: comic, frank, and full of Roman daily life.
56191-the-cruel-murder-of-mina-miller:
Kenkouwsky, also called Kettler, wrote a pamphlet on the cruel murder of Mina Miller. Barclay and Company issued it at Philadelphia, with rights held in 1881. Bold heads call it the Guttenberg-Hoboken tragedy and claim the only life of Mina Miller in print. The case is tied to the same spot as the famed Mary Rodgers killing.

A body was found on a path near Bull's Ferry on Friday, May 13. Coroner Wiggins of Hoboken found deep wounds made, it seemed, by a stone. The dead woman was named as Philomena Muller, wed just an hour, it is said. True crime fans of the time got stark facts and high drama.
56216-rodney-the-overseer:
Harry Castlemon wrote Rodney, the Overseer, a Civil War tale for boys printed at Philadelphia in 1892, with four illustrations by White. Castlemon wrote the Gunboat Series and many other boys war and frontier series. The tale opens with Captain Tom Randolph dressing down his Home Guards in sharp terms.

Randolph charges his men with firing on an unarmed boat without orders and warns that citizens of Baton Rouge might lynch them. Chapters bring conscripts, hounds on a trail, escaped prisoners, and lost boys of the Union army. Rodney keeps a promise and passes inspection by the close of the long tale. Boys got war adventure with a Southern setting and strong moral stakes.
56221-backwater:
Dorothy Richardson's Backwater was first published in London in 1916 by Duckworth and Company. Richardson had already written Pointed Roofs, and Backwater follows the same heroine, Miriam Henderson. The book opens inside Miriam's head, in a quiet drawing-room full of old things.

Miriam sits with her mother while three sisters who keep a school lay out their needs in soft, broken phrases. They want help with the lower school, the children from six to eight, in the mornings and afternoons. In the evenings Miriam would watch over the four older girls. All the while her thoughts drift to the tapestry screen, the ferns, the trams jingling past, and the row of poplars beyond the fence.
56223-oat-meal-the-war-winner:
Grieve, a Scot who served as an army surgeon with United States troops in 1865, sang the praise of oatmeal in a ten cent pamphlet of the great war years. Its sub title calls the pages glimpses and tales of Scotland and its people. An opening note owns the book's faults. Its verse quotes run loose, and no proof reader, it seems, was ever called in.

At a time when all are urged to save food, he owns his shock that so little backs oatmeal. Facts, not theories, are his pledge. His father farmed in Perthshire with big ploughmen. Their breakfast, he asks, fed men who shouldered four bushel sacks up warehouse stairs. The answer is the pamphlet's whole case.
56278-frank-merriwell-s-endurance-or-a-s: Frank Merriwell Endurance, or A Square Shooter, is one tale in the Merriwell series of stories for young men. The series list at the front names Frank and Dick Merriwell as its heroes. Its stories, priced at fifteen cents, are billed as tales of athletics. The publisher boasts of half a million followers of the brothers and of the high moral tone of the adventures. Frank, the older brother, is the pattern of the series, and endurance is the virtue this number tests.
56365-history-of-the-transformer:
History of the Transformer, by Uppenborn, was translated from the German and published in London and New York in 1889. Uppenborn edited a German journal of electrical work, and led a testing station in Munich. In his preface he explains why he wrote a short notice of this invention now.

The use of alternating current transformers, he says, has lately grown large, and become of great weight. They are called to play a striking part in electric lighting from central stations. Yet many distorted versions of the invention and its priority have found place in the trade journals. He was not put off by reading a large number of patents. Readers get an early history of a device that made modern power supply possible, by an engineer close to the work.
5638-an-adventure-with-a-genius-recollec:
Alleyne Ireland wrote An Adventure with a Genius as recollections of Joseph Pulitzer, dedicated by permission to Mrs. Joseph Pulitzer. Ireland says his wanderings through life's labyrinth brought a new adventure around every corner, rich in experience for a mature and reflective mind even when lacking vivid action. His Pulitzer adventure proves the point.

Chapters run from In a Casting Net and Meeting Joseph Pulitzer through life at Cap Martin. Yachting in the Mediterranean, getting to know Pulitzer, Wiesbaden and an Atlantic voyage follow, ending at Bar Harbor and the last cruise. Readers get an intimate portrait of the press lord in private life.
56408-the-mail-carrier:
Harry Castlemon wrote The Mail Carrier for his Boy Trapper series, and Porter and Coates of Philadelphia held the copyright from 1879. A front plate shows Dave, the mail carrier. Castlemon also wrote the Frank Nelson, Gunboat, and Sportsman's Club series for boys.

Chapter titles follow Bob, Lester, Don, and Godfrey through hunts, cabin visits, and river work. Bob faces a runaway, serves as a cub pilot, and George takes the wheel. The burning of the Sam Kendall forms a late high point. A lost pocket-book and a discovery by Dan lead into the close. Woods, traps, and steamboats give the tale its ground, in the brisk style Castlemon used across his many series.
56465-an-act-in-a-backwater:
An Act in a Backwater, by Benson, was copyright 1903 and published in New York that November.

Chapter one opens at half past five on a June afternoon. In consequence, Colonel Raymond was approaching the Wroxton County Club. He was a man of method, a retired colonel of volunteers. Thus he left his house, christened Lammermoor by his wife, with great regularity. In summer he left at a quarter past five, in winter at a quarter past four. He marched rather than walked, with an inflated chest and a gallant bearing. The colonel, even at fifty six, remained one of those harmless figures the narrator teases at once. Readers get a Benson novel of English county society, all club, lawn, and quiet intrigue.
56551-the-newspaper: The Newspaper is a volume of the Home University Library of Modern Knowledge, a series of specially written books edited by Gilbert Murray, Fisher, Thomson, and Brewster. The front matter of this copy is given over to the series catalogue. It lists volumes on history, religion, and philosophy, from Belloc on the French Revolution to Russell on the problems of philosophy. Each volume ran to 256 pages in cloth. The series aimed to put modern knowledge within reach of general readers.
56686-tom-temple-s-career:
Horatio Alger wrote this boys' novel, printed at New York under copyright in 1888. Its hero, Tom Temple, loses his father, Stephen Temple, and is left in the care of Nathan Middleton of Plympton. Middleton, an insurance agent, is a famous miser who saved his first penny at five and married late, after long sums, to a wife as thrifty as himself.

Into that stiff, saving household comes a lively boy with no money and no mother to speak for him. Alger builds the tale on the clash between the miser's tight purse and the boy's open hand and good heart. Like his other books, it promises that honesty, pluck, and hard work will carry a poor boy upward in the world.
56746-airplane-boys-at-platinum-river:
Craine wrote Airplane Boys at Platinum River, for the World Syndicate in 1931. It is the fifth book of the Airplane Boys, the front pages say. In it, Jim and Bob risk their lives for a worthy family. Their aim is to help that family out of its difficulties. The Cleveland and New York house holds the rights from that year.

Contents open with an old enemy and a delayed return. An unidentified trouble and a distress call follow in the list. Platinum River itself, a capture, and a flight through space come next. An air battle, a ride taken by force, and shivering rocks fill the middle. Treasure and a gross exaggeration close the tale's chapters. One boy jokes in big medical words to his step-brother at the start. Craine gives young fliers danger, loyalty, and a northern river prize.
56846-what-every-mother-should-know-or-h:
What Every Mother Should Know, by Margaret Sanger, teaches mothers how to tell children the truth about birth. The Rabelais Press issued the book in New York in 1914. Sanger gives it to Stuart, her first born, whose coming led her into motherhood.

The preface explains the method: the facts are put in story form for the mother to use. The child should soak up the knowledge without knowing he has had a lesson on sex. Chapters begin with flowers and a pair called the Buttercups in the story frame. Toads and frogs follow, then birds and their families. Mammals and their children come next, and a chapter on man's development closes the course. Sanger argues that parents ignore the body's most vital powers while teaching all the rest.
56869-the-art-of-being-happy-in-a-series:
Timothy Flint prepared The Art of Being Happy for American readers, published at Boston in 1832 by Carter and Hendee. The book rests on a French work by Droz, cast as letters from a father to his children. Flint added his own observations and comments. His advertisement warns that the text is no literal translation. Droz writes in a strongly idiomatic French, sometimes laconic to the point of obscurity.

Flint therefore expands where the English reader would stumble. About seventy notes stand at the back of the book. The subject is conduct: how a person may be happy through the ordering of daily life, work, and feeling. Books of this kind crossed the Atlantic often in the early republic, and Flint, a western writer himself, reshaped a French moralist for American families. The result is half translation and half commentary, a father's counsel twice over.
5696-a-yankee-girl-at-fort-sumter:
This children's story opens with two schoolgirls, Sylvia Fulton and Grace Waite, walking to school and talking about a song that holds Sylvia's name. Grace, nearly eleven and a year older than Sylvia, explains with proper pride that the song praises Sylvia's spelling, and Sylvia, delighted, plans to tell her mother. The scene sets a warm, everyday tone before the story's larger setting, Fort Sumter and the coming Civil War, enters the girls' lives.

We follow a young Yankee girl as ordinary friendship, school, and family life meet a national crisis. The book is written for young readers, with clear scenes and gentle humor, and it uses a child's view to make a distant war feel near. It suits families reading about American history together, and children who enjoy stories where a young heroine watches her world change.
56976-the-bondman-a-story-of-the-times-o:
Bondman is a tale of the times of Wat Tyler, in the Library of Romance series of 1833. Smith, Elder and Company published the volume in London from Cornhill that year. Leitch Ritchie edited the series in which the tale appears as volume five. An advertisement at the front explains how the idea of the tale arose for its author.

The idea was suggested by the first volume of Robertson Charles the Fifth, in its pages. Robertson treatment of the feudal policy of Germany gave the author his starting point there.  The bondman of the title is the serf of that order in England. Wat Tyler rising of 1381 gives the tale its storm, in which the claims of the unfree are tried by fire in the manner of the historical romance.
56988-franciscus-columna-the-last-novell:
Franciscus Columna is presented as the last novella of Charles Nodier, the French writer who lived from 1780 to 1844. The tale opens by recalling a friend, Abbot Lowrich, met in Ragusa, Spalato, Vienna, Munich, Pisa, Bologna, and Lausanne.

Lowrich is excellent and most knowledgeable, but he knows many things others would happily forget: the printer of a bad book, the birth year of a fool. His glory is discovering the real name of a forgotten scholar who wrote verses on fleas. Yet he is witty, obliging, and gifted with a lively, singular imagination. Readers get a bibliophile's novella where learning itself becomes the comedy.
57039-prince-rupert-the-buccaneer:
Prince Rupert the Buccaneer is a sea romance by Cutcliffe Hyne. Methuen of London first issued it in April nineteen o one. This third edition dates from May nineteen o seven by the title page. Grenville Manton drew the eight illustrations for the buccaneer tale.

Eight chapters run from The Pawning of the Fleet to The Regaining of the Fleet. Admission to the brotherhood and the rape of the Spanish pearls follow first. The ransoming of Caraccas and the passage money fill the middle acts. The mermaid and the act of faith and the galley chapter come next. Chapter one opens on Tortuga, where engagés are the genteel word for slaves.
57041-observations-upon-the-town-of-crom:
Edmund Bartell wrote these observations upon the town of Cromer, printed in 1800. His title page sets out the plan: Cromer considered as a watering place, and the fine scenery in its neighbourhood. A picture of the sea shore at Cromer stands at the front of the book.

The preface asks a plain question. Bathing places draw crowds all summer for health or pleasure, yet who has written up the smaller ones, away from Weymouth, Brighthelmstone, and Ramsgate? Bartell lived on the spot, and his work as a surgeon took him daily among the scenes he describes, in every weather and light. In a place with no public rooms, he argues, walks and rides are the chief pleasure, and worth pointing out.
57164-warwick-the-kingmaker:
Charles Oman wrote this life of Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick and Salisbury, for the English Men of Action series, first published by Macmillan in 1891 and reprinted many times through 1916. A portrait from the Rous Roll faces the title. Oman opens by calling Warwick probably the least known of all the great men of action who have guided English policy since the Conquest.

For ten years, Oman says, the Kingmaker was the first subject of the English crown, yet most readers know him only through Shakespeare's Henry the Sixth or Lytton's Last of the Barons. Seventeen chapters trace the house of Neville, Warwick's youth, and the cause of York, through the first battle of St Albans, his captaincy of Calais, and exile. Towton Field, the triumph of King Edward, and the fatal quarrel between earl and king follow, ending at Barnet, where the Kingmaker fell.
57178-the-life-of-a-fossil-hunter:
The Life of a Fossil Hunter is the life tale of Charles Sternberg, writ by him self. Osborn, a great man of the field, wrote its first words. It was put out at New York in nineteen hundred and nine. It stands in a set of books on the wild world. The front plate shows the hand in his years of work. The list of parts is a log of trips west.

First days and work in a young rock bed of the west head the run. A first trip to the chalk of Kansas in eighteen seventy six comes next. A trip with a great teach man to the bad lands of the same age stands past it. More work in that chalk, and the find of a new bed in Kansas, fill the first run.
57190-seeing-the-west-suggestions-for-th:
Seeing the West, suggestions for the westbound traveller, is a guidebook by K E M Dumbell, printed at New York in 1920. Its frontispiece shows the Yosemite Valley. The author's note thanks publishers and others for leave to quote from their books. Special thanks go to Robert Sterling Yard of the National Parks Association, who let her quote freely from his Book of National Parks.

The guide was made for travellers heading west in the age of the railroad and the new national parks. It gathers extracts from many publications into one handy volume. The front matter carries verses by Robert Service on the lure of the timeless things. Dumbell wrote for tourists who wanted to plan a western trip with sound advice. The book belongs to the years when the parks drew their first great wave of visitors from the east.
572-the-great-big-treasury-of-beatrix-po:
Beatrix Potter's best-loved tales gather in one large treasury, from Peter Rabbit and Benjamin Bunny to Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle, Jemima Puddle-Duck, and Mr. Tod. The book opens with four little rabbits in a sand bank under a fir tree. Potter wrote and drew the tales between 1902 and 1913, starting with Peter Rabbit.

Potter's stories pair small animals with precise country detail, and her pictures, in the original books, made the tales famous. This treasury lets young readers meet the whole company in one volume, story after story. Her precise natural detail, learned from years of sketching, gives the animals their truth.
57229-mark-tidd-manufacturer:
Mark Tidd Manufacturer is a boys trade tale by Clarence Budington Kelland. A Harper house of New York brought it out in nineteen eighteen. Three lads wait on the front porch while Mark ends his supper in peace. Mark full name runs Marcus Aurelius Fortunatus Tidd in the tale jest. His supper takes an hour, since his great frame needs much fuel to run.

Not Grant nor Napoleon at his door would speed that meal one mite. The scheme of plates hints at a dam fight in the tale course. You will not get our dam till we say so, one plate line warns. Mark long chain of books spans Egypt, Italy, woods, and trade posts. A hand creeps close in the front plate of the book.
57249-my-queen-a-weekly-journal-for-youn:
Grace Shirley opens a story paper for young women in the first number of My Queen, dated September 29, 1900. Street and Smith issued the weekly at New York for five cents a number. The first tale, From Farm to Fortune, carries the subtitle Only a Farmer's Daughter.

Marion Marlowe, seventeen and handsome, walks a dusty road making a daisy chain of wishes. From her father's hill she looks down on scorched pastures and the Poor Farm, which she calls a blot on the view. She asks why she had to be born a farmer's daughter and sickens of country life. Her twin sister is fairer and more childish, and the small station below links their world to Boston and New York. Readers get the first chapter of a dime weekly tale of ambition and escape.
57298-scott-burton-forester:
Edward Cheyney's Scott Burton, Forester came out from Appleton in New York and London in 1917, with pictures by Norman Rockwell. Cheyney dedicates the novel to his brother, whose broad views shaped his life. A front plate shows a shot praised by a friend named Morgan.

Chapter one finds Scott telling Dick Bradshaw that he has chosen the western forest school over nearer ones. His parents feared the distance, but extra credits from high school and summer terms may cut the course to two or three years. The boys grew up together in a New England village, sharing books, studies, and long walks in woods and fields. Dick, who stays home, dreads a parting of four years.
57384-the-one-dog-and-the-others-a-study:
Frances Slaughter's study of canine character, The One Dog and the Others, came from Longmans, Green in 1907. Augusta Guest and Vernon Stokes drew the illustrations, alongside photographs, and the book is dedicated to the memory of the One.

A sonnet at the front sets the tone, praising a faithful soul that loved one person only and was true. The first book gives life histories of five dogs, each under a character name: the Child of the House, the Diplomatist, the Professor, the Soldier of Fortune, and the Artistic Thief. A second book of studies and stories follows. Slaughter treats each dog as a person with a temper, habits, and a history worth telling in full.
57396-the-dreadnought-boys-aboard-a-dest:
The Dreadnought Boys Aboard a Destroyer is a boys' naval novel by Captain Wilbur Lawton, printed at New York with copyright in 1911. Hurst issued it. Lawton also wrote the Boy Aviators series and other Dreadnought Boys tales. Twenty-two chapters run from The Foreign Agent to the sea fight off Santa Anna.

Ned Strong and Herc Taylor halt in the shadow of the Brooklyn Navy Yard wall. A dark-skinned speaker greets them as brave sailors bound for the destroyer Beale. The contents promise a man overboard, the secret of a derelict, and an insult to the flag. A drum-head court-martial and a bombardment follow. Lawton gives his boy sailors the full navy adventure of their day.
57428-peter-vischer:
Cecil Headlam wrote this life of the Nuremberg bronze founder Peter Vischer for the Handbooks of the Great Craftsmen series, published by George Bell and Sons in 1901. Headlam had already written The Story of Nuremberg. The book opens with Hermann Vischer and the early German bronze-work of the family foundry. Peter's life follows, then his early works.

The shrine of Saint Sebald gets a chapter of its own, as the foundry's masterpiece. The tomb of Maximilian, the Tucher monument, and the Nuremberg Madonna come next. Minor works of Peter Vischer the younger, the tomb of Elector Frederick the Wise, and the Rathaus railing follow. The fall of the house of Vischer and the importance of the Vischers' work close the study, with a catalogue of their works and an index.
57444-gypsy-and-ginger:
Eleanor Farjeon wrote Gypsy and Ginger, published in New York in 1920. The book follows a young married couple known by nicknames. His hair was not quite black enough for a true gypsy's. Hers was every spice color at once, from mace to cayenne, with one hair pure vermilion. Their real names, grand ones, are set aside in the first pages.

The contents follow the pair through married life in London: a honeymoon, talks on ways and means, housekeeping, work, and at last a party and two moves. Chapters in between introduce their friends one by one — a pavement artist, a taxi-man, a balloon woman, a night watchman, a groundsel man, a policeman, and the Piccadilly flower-girls. One chapter even has the couple reform London. Readers get a warm, playful portrait of two cheerful people and the street folk they gather round them.
57475-experience-of-a-confederate-states:
An officer of the Confederate States Army kept a daily record that became Experience of a Confederate States Prisoner, issued in Richmond in 1862. The preface says paper was scarce in the South, since it could serve for cartridges. Still, the writer set down plain facts so others could learn what prison life was like. He hoped readers could learn without the pain of being held by Yankees.

Dated notes start in May 1862, with a hard march and a win at McDowell on the eighth day. General Jackson drove Generals Milroy and Schenck back twenty-five miles and took arms and stores. The writer then fell ill with typhoid fever at Front Royal. Doctor Brown, the town doctor, cared for him there.
57532-passages-from-the-life-of-a-philos:
Passages from the Life of a Philosopher is the memoir of Charles Babbage, the deviser of the calculating engine. A plate shows a small portion of his Difference Engine Number One. That engine was begun in 1823, and the portion shown was put together in 1833. The construction was abandoned in 1842, the caption records.

The portion of the engine rests in the museum at South Kensington. It was shown in the Exhibition of 1862, as the plate notes. Babbage fills his life story with engines, society, and sharp opinion. He quarrels, invents, and observes in page after page. The book is the self portrait of a man ahead of his age. Computing begins, in a real sense, in these passages.
57537-index-for-works-of-harold-frederic:
David Widger compiled this index to the works of Harold Frederic for Project Gutenberg, with links to each chapter of each book. The list runs from The Damnation of Theron Ware and The Market-Place to Gloria Mundi, March Hares, and In the Valley. It also covers The Young Emperor, a life of William the Second of Germany, and story sets such as The Deserter and Other Stories.

Each title opens into its own table of contents, chapter by chapter. A reader can jump from this one page to any part of any listed work. It serves as a map and a reading guide to the full set of Frederic texts held in the project, novels, tales, and history alike.
57538-index-for-works-of-rudyard-kipling:
David Widger compiled this Index for Works of Rudyard Kipling, a hyperlinked guide to the Gutenberg Kipling texts. Its contents list the volumes it indexes: The Jungle Book and The Second Jungle Book, the verses, Rewards and Fairies, American Notes, Plain Tales from the Hills, and Captains Courageous. Soldiers Three, The Light That Failed, Stalky and Co, Life's Handicap, Kim, and The Bridge Builders stand among the rest.

Under each volume the index prints its full table of contents: Mowgli's Brothers and Rikki-Tikki-Tavi under the Jungle Book, Gunga Din and Mandalay under the ballads. A reader can jump from this page to any chapter of any indexed work. The file is a finding aid, not a Kipling text, and its value is exactly that: one door into the scattered shelf of Gutenberg's Kipling.
57543-the-health-master:
The Health Master, by Samuel Hopkins Adams, was published at Boston and New York in 1913. Adams was an associate fellow of the American Medical Association. He gives the book to George Goler, a health official of Rochester, praised as courageous, unselfish, and far sighted.

Contents open with the Chinese plan physician, then in time of peace, repairing Bettina, and the corner drug store. The magic lens, the remade lady, and the red placard follow. A besieged city and plain talk close the set. In an introductory note Adams warns that dogmatising on medical practice invites controversy. The highest wisdom of today may be refuted by tomorrow discovery. His simple principles of disease prevention, he claims, represent only the progressive thought of modern medical science. Readers get health teaching in story form.
57568-peter:
Benson wrote this novel Peter of a London flat and tea table scene. Cassell printed it first in 1922 in London and New York. Chapter one seats two who mattered in a low window seat. Lower panes stand pushed up for air on a sultry day.

Little cool air comes, yet Green Park currents stir her hair now. London seems far remote, as from a ship at sea there. Inside, four sit round the tea table with the hostess mother. Mrs Alston waves a bitten sandwich like a baton, unheard by all.
57574-sir-edwin-landseer:
Frederick Stephens wrote this life of Sir Edwin Landseer for the Illustrated Biographies of the Great Artists, published at London in 1880. The preface says the text, twice revised, now continues the story to the artist's death.

The contents follow the painter from his family's origin and his first studio through early etchings and his first Royal Academy picture. Later chapters take in Chevy Chase, the making of a Royal Academician, and the famous dog pictures: Dignity and Impudence, The Shepherd's Chief Mourner, and The Sanctuary. Stephens aims to show the course of the studies behind a success he calls extraordinary. The volume carries many engravings after the works. Art lovers get the Victorian animal painter whole.
57584-the-book-of-the-homeless-le-livre-:
The Book of the Homeless, edited by Edith Wharton, appeared in 1916. Scribner published it in New York and London. Its French title is Le Livre des Sans-Foyer. The book was sold for two war charities. The American Hostels for Refugees gained by it, with the Foyer Franco-Belge. The Children of Flanders Rescue Committee shared the benefit. A letter from General Joffre fronts the volume, in French and in translation. It is dated August 18, 1915. America, he writes, has not forgotten the French blood in its first page. Now it brings France aid and solace in her struggle.

Writers and musicians fill the contents. Binyon sings the orphans of Flanders; Brooke offers a dance song. Claudel, Cocteau, and Conrad write in prose and verse. Bernhardt and Duse lend famous names.
57595-my-crochet-sampler:
Miss Lambert wrote My Crochet Sampler, printed in New York in 1847 with numerous illustrations. Lambert had written the Hand-Book of Needlework and My Knitting Book. A preface says the pages hold a choice of patterns fitted to almost every purpose of crochet, useful or decorative. Many designs were composed expressly for this little treatise. Others were chosen from the Hand-Book's chapter on crochet, and re-engraved.

In the directions, Lambert follows the plan of her knitting books: simplicity, and as few words as clearness allows. The warm reception of My Knitting Book led her to think a distinct work on the sister art might please as well. A German rendering of this very volume had already appeared, she notes, in the country that claims the invention of the art. Contents open with an introduction, terms, and the plain and open stitches.
57684-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Irving Bacheller maps one author’s shelf. David Widger built the guide to Bacheller’s books in that free store. Each work in the set stands with its own table of contents. Eben Holden, a tale of the North Country, leads the long roll.

The Master of Silence, a romance, stands second in the guide’s list. The Light in the Clearing threads candle and compass through its parts. In the Days of Poor Richard takes the reader to young Franklin’s age. A Man for the Ages gives Lincoln his place in Bacheller’s world. Silas Strong, Emperor of the Woods, heads a North Country name. Keeping Up with William and The Marryers show his lighter vein. Charge It and The Prodigal Village round the full author shelf. Chapter lists let the reader pick a road through each tale.
57703-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of the works of Vaughan Kester, gathered for readers of his books in electronic form. Its contents page lists five novels: The Prodigal Judge, The Just and the Unjust, The Manager of the B and A, The Fortune of the Landrays, and The Hand of the Mighty.

Full tables of contents follow for the novels. The Prodigal Judge alone runs to thirty-six chapters. Its heads trace the story in shorthand: a boy at the barony, then trouble at Scratch Hill. Law at a cross-roads follows, with a fight at a tavern. A judge breaks jail, prisoners are taken, a duel is fought, and a crisis comes at the court-house. The Just and the Unjust, with pictures by Bracker, opens with fighting Shrimplin and the price of folly.
57740-kingsford-quarter:
Kingsford, Quarter, by Ralph Henry Barbour, came out at New York in 1910, with pictures by C M Relyea. Barbour had written The Crimson Sweater and Captain Chub. Evan, a strong lad of fifteen, drags a heavy bag up the stairs at his new school at Riverport, late and tired.

The bag holds books and boots, and Evan holds one clear aim, to try for the football team. Chapters bring hazing, a climb in fog, and a football meeting. A band of boys forms a team of their own, the Independents, and plays the school second team. A last game with Adams ends the term. School boys get a brisk tale of pluck, codes, and the great game.
57744-a-woman-rice-planter:
Patience Pennington wrote this record, A Woman Rice Planter, printed at New York in 1913 with an introduction by Owen Wister and pictures by Alice Smith. Parts of it had been copyrighted over the years 1904 to 1907. She dedicates the fragments, as she calls them, to her father, on the anniversary of his birth, at Chicora Wood.

A list of pictures shows the world the book lives in. Sheaves are beaten with flails in the frontispiece. Each rice field has its small flood-gate, and hands tote the rice into flatboats. Women shuffle the grain about with their feet until it is clayed. A girl picks her usual thirty-five pounds alone. Neighbours fish by a bridge, and a mother sends for something to stop bleeding.
57836-jinny-the-carrier:
Jinny the Carrier, a novel by Israel Zangwill published in London by William Heinemann, grew from a short play set in rural Essex. In a long opening letter Zangwill says the book was drawn from twenty years of watching the land, people, and speech near an Essex home he calls Bassetts. He calls it his first novel of the new century.

Zangwill warns that his Little Bradmarsh is a made-up blend, not a copy of one real village. He admits the speech is shaped rather than copied word for word. That care sets up a warm rural tale built on carriers' carts, small hamlets, sea marshes, and the slow rhythms of country life and talk.
579-the-poems-of-sidney-lanier:
Sidney Lanier, the Georgia poet and musician, writes verse that tries to make English poetry sing like music. His poems draw on the South, on nature, and on the sound of words themselves. Lanier died in 1881, at thirty-nine, after years of illness and hard work.

Lanier, who played the flute in an orchestra and wrote on the science of verse, believed rhythm carried meaning. The collection gathers his best-known lyrics, and it remains the standard way to meet a poet who heard poetry as song. His Marshes of Glynn, among his finest poems, shows his musical theory in full flower.
58078-observations-on-the-sermons-of-eli:
Observations on the Sermons of Elias Hicks is a set of letters to the Quaker preacher Elias Hicks, signed by a writer who calls himself a Demi-Quaker. Robert Waln's name stands on the title page. It was printed at Philadelphia in 1826, addressed to the junior members of the Society of Friends.

The introduction tells young Friends that the Society's late situation must have caught every member's eye. Two mottoes frame the argument, one from Burgh on the arrogance of expecting to know God's economy as plainly as our own duty, and one from Dryden on reason's dim light. The letters then take up Hicks's sermons one by one. Students of American religion get a front-row paper from the Quaker quarrel that split the Society just after this book.
58106-a-second-letter-to-the-bishop-of-e:
Second Letter to the Bishop of Exeter is a church tract by a layman. Joseph Masters printed it in London in 1851 for private circulation. The writer tells the bishop that both men have long been mistaken. At stake is the judgment of the Privy Council in the Gorham Case. The layman holds that no church rule was breached by that judgment.

Much of the letter turns on a suit called Duplex Querela in form. That suit ran in the Archbishop's Court, the writer now grants. Old authorities show how archbishops of Canterbury once claimed wide rights. They curbed comprovincial bishops who strayed from their set bounds. Readers get a close, lawyerly case on crown rights in church law.
58120-go-to-cromer:
Go to Cromer is a seaside guide by a Rural Rector, printed at Norwich by Agas Goose in 1889. Its title takes its text from Jane Austen. In Emma, a family doctor is quoted in praise of Cromer: he held it the best of all sea-bathing places, with a fine open sea and very pure air. The rector, like that doctor in the novel, recommends a visit of fair length.

He joins the stay to mild expeditions in the neighbourhood, by sea and land. The opening chapter asks when the dog-days begin, and corrects the almanacs by the star Sirius itself. The dog star, he notes, has of late withheld its full downpour of heat until the end of July. The book is a parson's brief for a Norfolk resort, full of weather, bathing, and local walks.
58195-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Edna Ferber was compiled by David Widger. It is a finding list rather than a narrative. For each of Ferber's books held by the project, it prints the book's own table of contents. A reader can see at a glance what any volume holds.

Ten works are indexed. Fanny Herself stands first, its nineteen chapters named by number alone. Buttered Side Down follows, twelve stories from The Frog and the Puddle to Where the Car Turns at 18th. Emma McChesney & Co., One Basket with its thirty-one short stories, and Dawn O'Hara, the Girl Who Laughed, fill the middle. Roast Beef, Medium, Cheerful by Request, Personality Plus, Half Portions, and Gigolo complete the list.
58198-pic-the-weapon-maker:
George Langford wrote and drew a novel of early man, published in 1920, with a foreword name of Henry Fairfield Osborn on the title page. Pic lives in the Dordogne region of France under a hard glacial winter. Snow hides the grass while bison, moose, stag, and ox gather below a limestone ridge. The picture list shows a mammoth, cave lions, and flint workers on the Seine.

Pic learns by trial, from beating rocks together to finding the use of a bone tool. Langford mixes story with care for how tools and hunts may have worked. Young readers get both adventure and a picture of Ice Age life.
58232-the-american-prisoner:
The American Prisoner is a Dartmoor novel by Eden Phillpotts. Methuen of London brought the book out in the year 1904. A front view shows the war prison near Tor Royal on the moor. That prison held ten thousand men, with barracks for two thousand more. Phillpotts gives the book with hearty greeting to Jeannette Gilder.

Four books divide the tale: Fox Tor Farm, the Seven, and more. Cater's Beam, the Malherb amphora, and beside Exe open the farm part. The war prison stands named in the seventh chapter of book one. Book two's Seven fail, hangman's hollow yawns, and snowstorms strike hard. Under the Earth, book three, turns on a tunnel growing in secret. Stars and Stripes, hue and cry, and the first through fill that part. The Peace closes the tale as hope wakes and dies by turns.
58307-the-military-adventures-of-charles:
The Military Adventures of Charles O'Neil tells the wars of a rank-and-file soldier under Wellington. O'Neil served in the Peninsular War and the campaigns of 1811 to 1815. Livermore printed the book at Worcester in 1851, for the author, with six engravings.

The title page promises full histories of the battle of Barossa and the siege of Badajos. A graphic account of Waterloo closes the campaigns, ending with the overthrow of Napoleon. One plate shows a whipping at Gibraltar, a taste of army discipline. The preface turns from generals to the men who did the deeds. Generals, it quotes, often reckon men as blocks of wood or machines. Each nameless soldier, O'Neil argues, feels suffering and honour as keenly as his chiefs.
58350-the-chinese-opium-smoker:
The Chinese Opium-Smoker is a sixpenny tract issued in London by S W Partridge and Company of Paternoster Row. Twelve illustrations, reproduced from the Chinese, show the ruin which the opium trade with China is bringing upon that country. The pictures carry the argument, each with its letterpress beneath.

The sequence begins with the incipient smoker reclining in his mansion while a companion smokes tobacco through a water pipe. Next the smoker, still portly and well dressed, is entreated on bended knees by his wife to give up the habit. Their child runs off with the dreaded pipe, and the aged grandmother leans on her staff to add her tears. Later sections compare opium-smoking in China with the drinking habits of England and weigh England's responsibility for the trade.
58422-seth-jones-or-the-captives-of-the-:
Seth Jones, or the Captives of the Frontier, is a Beadle dime novel. Beadle printed it in New York, entered in the year 1863. Front ads hail a Kentucky tale of the year 1800 as next. Jo Daviess client, courting in Kentucky, fills that coming number.

Mrs Victor wrote the Daviess tale, of gold hunters and Maum Guinea fame. Her people are drawn true to life, the ad contends. Seth Jones stands as number tale of frontier captives and peril. Beadle dime novels sold at William Street and Paternoster Row shops. Edward Ellis wrote the tale for Beadle readers.
58462-the-story-of-valentine-and-his-bro:
Oliphant published 'The Story of Valentine and His Brother' with William Blackwood and Sons in 1876, in a stereotype edition of a tale first printed in Blackwood's Magazine. She dedicates the book to her Eton boys. The opening scene is a great dim drawing-room at Rosscraig House, high above the brawling Esk, lit only by fits of firelight while a March storm dashes rain against the windows.

Two ladies sit by the fire, one a strong prevailing voice, the other answering in soft monosyllables of assent or wonder. The stronger voice warns that Richard's story cannot be supposed interesting to any but themselves, and the other reproaches her for calling the interest curiosity. From that fireside frame the brothers' story begins to unfold, told between intimates on a wild night.
5847-the-heart-of-rome-a-tale-of-the-los:
The Heart of Rome, subtitled A Tale of the Lost Water, opens with the Baroness Volterra driving to the Palazzo Conti in the heart of Rome at nine in the morning. She hopes to find Donna Clementina at home, having tried twice to telephone the previous afternoon, only to hear that communication was interrupted. Her anxiety to see Clementina at once sets a Roman mystery in motion.

Readers follow aristocratic Rome through palaces, telephones, and old water rights, as a lost water supply becomes a matter of love, money, and honor. The novel favors atmosphere and intrigue over action, with Rome itself as a character. It suits readers of Italian historical romance, and fans of novels where a city secret drives a family's fate.
58513-mary-louise-adopts-a-soldier:
Edith Van Dyne wrote Mary Louise Adopts a Soldier, published by Reilly and Lee in Chicago in 1919. The book belongs to the Bluebird Books and continues the Mary Louise series. Earlier volumes had taken Mary Louise through a mystery and through the war work of the Liberty Girls. This story opens in May, as the Dorfield Regiment comes home from the war.

Mary Louise talks it over with Grandpa Jim at the breakfast table. A young soldier named Danny Dexter soon stands at the centre of the plot. Chapters bring a mysterious disappearance, a telegram, and the arrival of Josie O'Gorman. An empty room, a desert bungalow, and a nest of conspirators follow. Van Dyne wrote wholesome mysteries for girls; here the war's end gives her heroine a soldier to help and a plot to untangle.
58551-lodrix-the-little-lake-dweller:
Lodrix the Little Lake Dweller is a children's story by Belle Wiley and Grace Willard Edick, published in New York by Appleton in 1905. It is dedicated to the children. The tale is set among the prehistoric lake dwellers of Switzerland and France, whose houses stood on piles over the water.

The first chapter describes the people. Many years ago, in the high regions among the lakes, they lived not on land but on the water, hidden by forests from the land folk. Lodrix is the chief's son, a brave boy of twelve. The chapters follow his people: their home, their watch for the enemy, and time on shore. Then Lodrix is lost, captured, and carries a message. He stays with the bear people and returns at last. Books of this kind taught children the new science of prehistory by dressing it as adventure.
58609-buried-treasure-of-casco-bay-a-gui:
Kennedy of South Portland, Maine, wrote Buried Treasure of Casco Bay as a guide for the modern hunter, and the book reached a third printing after its 1963 copyright. He dedicates it to his father, who loved Casco Bay very much, and thanks islanders and Portland men who helped him.

The contents read like a chart of the bay: how treasure was buried, Fort Gorges, Fort Scammell, Peaks Island, Cushing's Island, Willard Beach, Portland Head Light, Cliff Island, and Richmond's Island. Pirate gold and wartime caches are the lure, but the book works as local history too, one island legend at a time. Treasure guides of this kind sold the search as much as the gold.
58647-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
