David Widger compiled this index of Winston Churchill works on Gutenberg. The River War heads the list, the Sudan reconquest account. The Malakand Field Force and London to Ladysmith follow in order. Liberalism and the Social Problem and Ian Hamilton March appear.

Lord Randolph Churchill, My African Journey, and Savrola close the list. The River War contents run from the Mahdi rebellion onward here. The fate of the envoy and the Dervish empire take chapters. Firket, Dongola recovery, and the desert railway fill the middle. The battle of the Atbara and the grand advance fill the later River War chapters.
58672-westminster:
Walter Besant wrote Westminster, a portrait of London's great quarter. Frederick A Stokes Company issued it at New York. Copyright dates run 1894 and 1895. One hundred thirty pictures aid the text. William Patten drew many of those plates. The papers first ran in the Pall Mall Magazine.

Three Abbey chapters grew for the book form. Besant wrote a famed book called London before this. He claims no full history of Westminster here, he warns. Stanley, Loftie, and Dart tell the Abbey's story, he says. Parliament's history belongs to the nation, he adds. His aim runs against received opinion, he hints. The volume goes to Mrs William Patten in thanks. Her walks with her husband adorned these pages, he writes. A novelist's stroll through abbey and parliament streets made deep history read like a friend's guided walk.
58750-superstition-and-force-essays-on-t:
Henry Lea wrote these essays on old law tests of truth and guilt. Lea Brothers printed the fourth revised edition in Philadelphia in 1892. Essays treat the wager of law, wager of battle, ordeal, and torture. A Cicero line on old law in the Twelve Tables leads.

Lea opens by calling law history the history of civilization itself. Lawgiver work shows the manners and deep beliefs of an age. He traces how forebears sought hid truth in disputes of fact. Chronicler records fill in the details of his broad picture. Wager of law, wager of battle, and ordeal fill its essays.
58757-chats-on-old-silver:
Chats on Old Silver, by Arthur Hayden, belongs to a long series of chats for collectors. Unwin issued the set in London, with Stokes in New York. A coffee-pot of the George the Second period, dated 1741 and made by Peter Archambo, serves as frontispiece.

Ninety-nine full-page plates go with Hayden's text in this volume. Sister chats treat old china, furniture, prints, lace, pewter, and coins, most of them by Hayden himself. The opening argues that silver is in the Englishman's blood in a way china is not. A taste for old china or furniture is often acquired, he says. But a man will brood by instinct over his old plate and its hall-marks. The marks of the assay offices, and what they prove of age and maker, are the heart of the collector's lore here.
58795-memoir-of-a-brother:
Memoir of a Brother, by Thomas Hughes, was published at Boston in eighteen seventy-three by James R Osgood and Company. Hughes had written Tom Brown's Schooldays. His brother is drawn in an engraving by C H Jeens after G F Watts. The preface explains the book's private origin with unusual frankness.

Hughes wrote the memoir for near relatives and intimate friends, not for the public. His brother was a home-loving country gentleman of ability who shunned fame entirely. Publication followed because Hughes saw a public lesson in the private life. England, he argues, rests on thousands of such quiet men of culture, courage, and principle. They bring up families in the love of God and neighbour, far from the daily press. In a noisy time, Hughes offers one unnoticed life as ballast for the nation.
58870-the-midlander:
Booth Tarkington writes a novel of a changing city in The Midlander, copyrighted in 1923 and published at Garden City by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1924. The book is dedicated to S K T. Its first chapter contrasts the two Oliphant brothers: Harlan looks as if he lived in the Oliphants' house, but Dan does not.

The house stands in a row of great yards at the upper end of National Avenue, built when bricklayers worked for a dollar a day and the workman's day was ten hours. Tarkington calls such houses stately, and sets their spaciousness against the city's growth, named Progress.
58912-the-earth-quarter:
Damon Knight published his story The Earth Quarter in Worlds of If Science Fiction in January 1955. Laszlo Cudyk looks from his garret at an alien city that glows frost-blue against a black sky. Below him spreads the Earth Quarter, sixteen square blocks of squalor.

The Niori let Earth refugees live in the cramped ghetto on one condition: that they keep the peace. Two thousand three hundred humans of three races and eighteen nations form the last human remnant near Capella. Fanatics such as Harkway and Rack stir trouble, the headnote warns. Cudyk feels the city press on the Quarter like prison walls. Exile and pride drive the tale.
58915-voyage-to-jupiter:
Voyage to Jupiter is a NASA book by David Morrison and Jane Samz, dated 1980. The Scientific and Technical Information Branch issued it as NASA SP 439 in Washington. A colour reconstruction shows the volcano Loki erupting on Io, from Voyager one. Edward Stone, Voyager project scientist, signs the front matter of the report book.

Contents open with the Jovian system, the giant planet and its family of moons. Voyager flybys of 1979 had just remade Jupiter science when the book appeared. Rings, spots, storms, and volcanic moons fill the mission account in plain language. Space history keeps the volume as the public record of a great voyage.
59024-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled an index of the Project Gutenberg works of Arthur Schopenhauer, listing the philosopher's books in English and the tables of contents of each volume. The main list runs from The Art of Literature through Counsels and Maxims, The Art of Controversy, and Studies in Pessimism.

On Human Nature, The Wisdom of Life, and Religion, a Dialogue follow. The World as Will and Idea appears in three volumes, then The Basis of Morality and the works on sufficient reason and the will in nature. Sample contents show the essays' shape: on authorship, on style, on thinking for oneself, on genius. Readers get a doorway into Schopenhauer in the standard Saunders translations.
59069-young-crow-raider:
Young Crow Raider, by Francis Lynde Kroll, was copyrighted in 1954 by Lantern Press and issued at New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with drawings by Charles Geer. Bent Arrow, a Crow boy of thirteen summers, runs a foot race on a leg once hurt, and will not let the pain excuse him. He beats Sly Fox and Laughing Deer to the line.

His uncle Flying Arrow tells him he is proud, not ashamed, and that the older boys who won are a summer ahead of him. Eleven chapters carry the boy toward a raider's life. Pictures show him at the buffalo hunt and creeping on a hilltop with a fellow Crow.
59183-psychology-and-pedagogy-of-anger:
The Psychology and Pedagogy of Anger, by Roy Franklin Richardson, professor of education at the University of Maine, is a study of one emotion and its schooling. Warwick and York published it at Baltimore in 1918. It is number nineteen in a series of monographs on educational psychology, edited by Bell. Five chapters and a bibliography make the book.

The first chapter treats the mental situation that stirs anger up. Then come the behaviour of consciousness under it, and the way anger disappears. Its after effects on the mind follow, and a last chapter asks what anger is for in education. Richardson holds that an emotion's stimulus is a whole mental situation, not a single blow. Anger, slow to develop, lends itself well to such study, he says. The book joins laboratory psychology to the classroom, in the earnest manner of its day.
59199-the-desert-healer:
The Desert Healer is a desert romance by Hull, author of The Sheik, published in Toronto by McClelland and Stewart in 1923. The setting is Algeria. The first chapter opens on a spur of the Little Atlas Mountains in afternoon sun.

Three horses stand tethered by a clump of olive trees. Ten miles west lies Blidah, Europeanised and noisy, while here the desert keeps its deep stillness. Pigeons coo and voices murmur low. A man lies on the soft ground out in the full sunshine, apparently asleep, his face almost hidden by a sun helmet. The scene sets the stillness that the title's healer will enter. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
59223-flower-and-jewel-or-daisy-forrest-:
Mrs Alex McVeigh Miller wrote Flower and Jewel, or Daisy Forrest's Daughter, a novel in fifty-four short chapters. Miller was a writer of popular tales for the story papers. The tale opens in a darkened, rich bedroom.

Young Mrs Fielding wakes from a drugged sleep and calls her nurse. The old woman, beaming, tells her she is the mother of two beautiful twins. Both are girls, one with blue eyes like her husband, one with dark eyes like her own. The mother sighs that she wanted a boy, then rallies in delight. From this birth the fortunes of the twins unfold.
59303-a-vagabond-s-odyssey-being-further:
A Vagabond's Odyssey is a book of travel memories by Safroni-Middleton, printed at New York in 1916 with sixteen pictures from photographs. It bills itself as further tales of a wandering sailor-troubadour in many lands, and follows his earlier Sailor and Beachcomber. The writer gives the book to the memory of his comrade Omar, buried in the Australian bush, and to friends in Samoa.

The contents roam wide: Boston, military music, and selling bug powder in America; Samoa and its changes; talks of Robert Louis Stevenson; Honolulu, Yokohama, and Bombay. A chapter lists his many professions, and the whole reads as a life spent drifting, singing, and looking back.
59320-the-aswa-n-obelisk-with-some-remar:
Engelbach studies a giant stone in The Aswan Obelisk, with remarks on ancient engineering, printed at Cairo in 1922. The Antiquities Service of Egypt stands behind the book. Engelbach was chief inspector in that service. Plates and a tight table map a quarry study.

First heads give the size of the obelisk and the account of its clearance. They treat the burning and wedging that freed the top rock layers. They treat test shafts, cracks, and the flattening of the face. One head treats the trench, the dolerite pounders, and the ranks of workmen. Time sums for the trench work show how the old Egyptians planned a vast task.
59347-circe-s-daughter:
Priscilla Craven, author of A Lighted Candle and The School of Love, wrote this novel. Duffield and Company published it at New York under a 1913 copyright. A French saying serves as its motto: life is an instrument one always begins by playing out of tune. The contents run through two parts and titles like The Game, A Toy Mother, and Love Is the Only Convention.

The opening chapter belongs to Richards, the well-trained manservant of the Currey family, setting a room for guests on a warm May night. He heats it well because Carey Image is coming, home from five years on the frontier of India and liable to feel a chill. Richards remembers that Image, godfather to the rooms' owner, prophesied at the christening thirty-two years before that the baby would grow into a remarkable man. He wonders whether the prophecy is coming true.
59369-murder-in-black-letter:
Murder in Black Letter is a mystery novel by Poul Anderson, published in New York in nineteen sixty. Anderson, famed for science fiction, here writes a crime tale with a rare book at its heart, as the title's black letter hints. Black letter is the old Gothic type of early printed books. A killing tied to such a book gives scholars and collectors a motive pool.

The Macmillan imprint and its offices across America and abroad fill the title page in the grand manner of the day. A note states that no renewal of the book's copyright was found by later searchers. Anderson's crisp style serves detection as well as it served space opera. Bibliophiles get a mystery in their own world.
59393-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of the works of Herbert Spencer, gathered for readers of his books in electronic form. A contents page lists the volumes on offer. Essays on education stand first, then three volumes of essays scientific, political, and speculative. The Right to Ignore the State, The Data of Ethics, and First Principles follow, with the first volume of a work on biology.

Full tables of contents follow for the chief books. An essay on the philosophy of style is set out part by part, on the economy of the reader's energies and feelings. The first essay volume opens with a piece on the development hypothesis and one on progress, its law and cause. The second runs from the genesis of science and the sorting of the sciences to a piece asking what electricity is.
59397-santa-fe-sketch-book-history-and-s:
The Santa Fe Sketch Book gives a history and sketches of the city different, published by Ewen Enterprises at Santa Fe Plaza. During the sixteen hundreds, the Santa Fe Plaza extended to the position of the present Cathedral, it says. All official, religious, and military functions took place there.

Government buildings, the jail, and the customs house stood around it, the book notes. The centre was a market place and the scene of fiestas and cock fights, it adds. The public stock and flogging post stood there too. Governor Martinez de Lejanza erected a wooden bullring in the Plaza in sixteen eighty four. The Pueblo Indians revolted in the Plaza in sixteen eighty, it says. The Cathedral of St Francis, long a dream of Archbishop John B Lamy, follows. Tourists get a picture history of old Santa Fe.
59415-to-pay-the-piper:
James Blish wrote a tale of the world after plague for Worlds of If in February 1956. Its headnote says that schooling man's brain would not fit him to live on the plague ridden surface. Schooling his body might, but the process was very long.

Samuel Carson, medical head of a re-education project, waits at its door while a scanner checks him over. A sound bomb shakes the deep halls and sets the scanner back to the start. Inside, the colonel in command reads a press sheet. A speech by a man named Hamelin has fired the public cry to re-educate civilians ahead of soldiers. Carson warns that the outcry may lose the war.
59446-under-the-big-dipper:
Dery published a first book in New York in 1916, dedicated to his wife, whose faith he credits for its existence. A front picture shows a woman named Helène. Book one opens not with a scene but with a sweeping portrait of India, the land the tale takes as its stage.

India, Dery writes, has drawn Assyrian and Greek, Mongol and Parsee, Portuguese rover, Dutch trader, and English merchant prince. All fought and schemed for her gold and for rule over her people. The result, he says, is a land of palaces and hovels, of caste, plague, famine, and unfulfilled desires. Yet he calls India the cradle of humanity, whose people pray to Brahma, Shiva, Buddha, and the fire of Zoroaster. Readers meet a young author's grand, sorrowful canvas before the story proper begins.
59504-a-matter-of-order:
A Matter of Order, by Fox Holden, ran in Worlds of If Science Fiction in August 1956. A note above the tale poses its theme: balance is a basic law of order. Can integrity cancel such a law, it asks, even when mankind's future demands it? The story opens in a colony of artists. Tharn, tall and thin, sweats over a strange sight in the sky. A slim, stylus-shaped object circles above, catching the sun. It will land at the colony's edge, and both men know it.

Angelo, Dean of Masters, rises from his easel with a smile. Tharn, in a paint-spattered smock, strikes a pose like Mark Antony. Angelo warns against alarm: panic would upset the young for weeks. Another Realist period, he fears, could follow. Holden builds his tale on art, law, and fear of change.
59511-sarah-bernhardt-as-i-knew-her:
Madame Pierre Berton told her memories of Sarah Bernhardt to Basil Woon, who shaped them into a book printed in London in 1923. Nineteen pictures go with the text, led by a 1921 photo of Bernhardt in her dressing room. Thirty one chapters, none named, carry the life story in order.

Photos show Bernhardts birth record from 1846, an early view of her, and her in plays such as La Tosca and Hamlet. Her husband Pierre Berton was one of Bernhardts first close friends, the list notes, and played with her in La Tosca. A sketch of Madame Berton herself from 1881 and a letter from Sardou also appear.
5957-the-art-of-the-story-teller:
Marie L. Shedlock sets out to defend storytelling as an art rather than a set of rules. Her preface contrasts a coming science of education with the living work of teachers who keep a direct sense of childhood. She argues that wise teachers still need artists who can read a tale with feeling and restraint.

The praise quoted in the preface points to her range across Daudet, Grimm, and deeper world philosophy. Shedlock is shown at home in wit, folk wisdom, and grave thought alike, always within the limits of the craft. The volume offers her papers on how stories should be chosen, shaped, and told aloud.
59581-brain-teaser:
Tom Godwin wrote Brain Teaser, a science fiction story printed in Worlds of If in October 1956. A riddle stands at the head: how can a ship travel forward and backward and sideways in two directions, go twice as fast as light, and still be completely motionless?

Carl Engle watches the flight crew file out of the starship Argosy's airlock in the Arizona sun. Barnes, fat and bald, reports the drives checked and counterchecked. Ground Control warns that a Slug cruiser still circles 700 miles out, and the Slugs suspect something. Barnes calls the enemy damned centipedes and swears they are telepathic. Zero hour stands 26 minutes away. Aboard, the physicist Harding waits by the space warp shuttle, the new device that must fool the Slugs or leave the Argosy a target. Godwin opens his tale on a countdown, with the riddle as the mission plan.
59648-the-jester:
Leslie Moore published this novel with Putnam in New York and London in 1915. A front plate shows a man who would have given his soul at a word from a woman. Chapter one, 'Cap and Bells,' brings in the fool of the title, and 'The Fool's Entry' follows as the second chapter.

Balda the witch, a council at Sangdieu and a casting of the net come early in the contents. Later chapters name a quest, a sage, a moon ritual and devil worship, then Easter eve and Easter morning. Romance, faith and outcast wandering shape a tale set in a half-legendary world.
59671-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of the Project Gutenberg works of Bram Stoker, gathering the tables of contents of Stoker's books in one file. Dracula stands first, in two forms, and its contents show the tale's odd build: the journals of Jonathan and Mina Harker, letters, and Dr Seward's diary entries. Eight works are listed in all.

The White Worm, The Man, and The Lady of the Shroud follow, then The Jewel of Seven Stars and Dracula's Guest. The Mystery of the Sea and Famous Impostors close the list, the last a work of fact among the tales. For a reader new to Stoker, the index maps where to start and what each book holds inside.
59712-the-floater:
The Floater, a short science fiction tale by Kenneth O'Hara, ran in Worlds of If in February 1957. Barton is a watchman alone on a man-made watching post floating far out among the planets. His two jobs are simple to state and hard to do: keep the watch, and keep his sanity.

The gear mostly runs itself, and Barton need only report if an alarm sounds. Staying sane is the true strain. A doctor named Von Ulrich visits in a space boat to test and question him, and warns that most watchmen crack in a week and none last past six months. Barton has lasted near a year. The hook is that he stays calm by bending time itself.
5977-bound-to-rise-or-up-the-ladder:
Horatio Alger Jr. writes for boys about rising by honest effort, and the sketch that opens this volume recalls his life among New York street boys. He mingled with them, gained their trust, showed concern for their affairs, and urged them toward honest and useful living. Over seventy stories followed his first.

The novel itself follows a boy climbing, step by step, from small beginnings toward a better place. Alger's formula pairs hard work with a fair chance and a helping hand. Readers meet a hero whose pluck matters more than his purse, in a tale built to encourage young strivers.
59802-census-statistics-of-the-negro-a-p:
Census Statistics of the Negro is a paper by Walter F Willcox, reprinted from the Yale Review of November nineteen hundred four. Willcox opens with a claim about race and records in the United States. No leading country has race relations as important as America's, he states. For that reason none has so highly developed a study of race in its statistics, he argues.

Census counts of Black Americans reach back across a long span in those records. Willcox tests what the numbers can and cannot show about growth, movement, and condition after slavery. Europe, he notes, does not class its people by race in the same way. The paper is a period landmark in American demographic study, with period limits.
5990-rosamond-or-the-youthful-error-a-ta:
Mary J. Holmes opens her Riverside tale on a rainy September day, with a young man gazing at a glowing grate while rain beats the windows. His thoughts lie elsewhere than wind or weather, and the story that follows traces Rosamond Leyton, her education, and a brother and sister bound by old ties.

Chapters on Ben's visit, Marie Porter, making love, a guest at Riverside, and the end frame the main tale. Shorter pieces follow, among them Diamonds, Bad Spelling, Maggie Lee, and The Answered Prayer. Holmes writes domestic romance with a steady, sentimental hand, centered on home and heart.
5991-the-solitary-summer:
Elizabeth von Arnim writes in diary form, opening on 2 May with a wish to be alone for a whole summer and get to the very dregs of life. She plans to be idle so her soul may grow, to invite nobody, and to spend months in garden, plain, and forest, watching where she has made mistakes.

On wet days she will seek the driest pine woods, and in sun she will lie on the heath watching broom flare against the clouds. The Man of Wrath answers only, mind she does not get her feet damp. The book finds peace in silence, and humor in a solitude that others keep interrupting.
59940-rhymes-of-the-survey-and-frontier:
George Blackstone Field wrote these rhymes of the men who surveyed the Canadian West. William Briggs published the book at Toronto in 1911. Its epigraph is Cecil Rhodes on the pioneers of civilization who penetrate savage countries to survey and open up the land. Field's poems speak for the survey crews themselves. To You Who Will Understand opens the book, addressed to the men who conquered the wilderness and are building the land.

The titles map the life: Men of the Line, The Breaker of the Trail, The Rodman's Dream, The Coming of the Line, and The Price of the Line. Wooden Mike, Sunny Limited, and My Pal give the camp its characters. The Home Trail and L'Envoi close the round. Field writes of wandering days by the camp-fire's blaze, of comrades left by the way, and of a land peopled and loved as a home to come.
60021-conference-of-officers-in-charge-o:
Government hospital officers met at Washington in January 1922, and their full proceedings make up this conference volume. The meeting ran from January 17 to 21, in the auditorium of the Department of the Interior. The officers in charge of hospitals serving veterans of the World War took part. Eight working sessions fill the five days of the record.

The conference sat under the auspices of the United States veterans service of the day. Its business was the care of former soldiers in state hospitals. Officers compared practice on wards, records, and the needs of sick veterans. The volume prints the sessions in order, from the opening on Tuesday to the close on Friday. As a source, it shows how the young veterans hospital system was built. It holds the words of the men who ran those wards.
60039-the-secret-of-heroism-a-memoir-of-:
Mackenzie King wrote a life tale of Henry Albert Harper, his lost friend. The book came out in 1906 in a second form of the work. A plate shows Harper's face at the book's front in full. King gave the book to his mother with an Arnold verse on souls. O strong soul, by what shore do you wait now, that verse asks.

The Secret of Heroism heads the list, then home's force in him. School and past school years take the next full part in line. The day's work, fields, books, and love of men fill the mid. His town and state dreams and life's aim close King's scheme. A stone by the folk marks him in the crown town. Warm love rules it.
60045-the-golden-wheel-dream-book-and-fo:
The Golden Wheel Dream Book and Fortune Teller is a cheap popular guide. Books of its kind sold by post across the United States. Its front pages carry the publisher’s own gay trade list. Dick’s One Hundred Amusements for Evening Parties leads that list.

Games, tricks, puzzles, and comic illusions crowd those ads. The Flexible Giant, a startling trick sight, fronts one of them. The Art and Etiquette of Making Love fills the next bright page. Bashfulness cured, courtship opened, and the question popped fill its scope. Love letters for all chances stand ready in its back part. A quadrille call book and ball room prompter share the list. Paper covers at thirty cents, boards at fifty, price the whole set. The dream book’s own art reads dreams and tells fates by old signs.
60059-the-lunarian-professor-and-his-rem:
Lunarian Professor and His Remarkable Revelations is a speculative work by James Alexander. Alexander published it at Minneapolis in 1909 and held its rights. He also wrote The Dynamic Theory and The Soul and Its Bearings. The title page joins moon lore to a cruise tale of the Sally Ann. Contents move from an outing and an old stake to the professor himself.

Middle chapters treat the moon and its people, with life on and in the moon. Forecasts for Earth follow: single tax, seizure of lands, purchase of railways. Money, socialism, women's rights, marriage, and divorce each get a hearing. Flying machines, sun power, and crowding of the Earth close the survey.
60179-the-prime-minister:
The Prime Minister is a life of David Lloyd George by Harold Spender. Doran published it in New York, with a 1920 copyright. A frontispiece photograph was taken specially for this book. It shows Lloyd George at 10 Downing Street in October 1917. A Wordsworth passage on the Happy Warrior fronts the title page. A foreword thanks Lloyd George himself for help with the book. Spender drew on twenty seven years of unbroken friendship. The prime minister's wife and only brother also helped.

His secretaries and his former law partner gave memories too. Board of Trade and munitions officials helped with certain chapters. The book is a friendly portrait written from inside the circle. It presents the war premier to American readers at his height. Spender writes as an intimate, not a critic, throughout.
60248-the-messiah-of-the-cylinder:
Victor Rousseau wrote this novel, printed at Chicago in October 1917 with pictures by Joseph Clement Coll. It opens over coffee cups, moves to a great experiment and a cellar, then takes the road to London. A strangers' house, hidden things, and a chapter called How the World Was Made Over set the scale of the tale.

Later come a domed building, a goddess of the temple, lords of misrule, and the story of the cylinders. A figure named Sanson defies his captors and will not drink, and the book moves through a chapel underground, a messiah's annunciation, and the coming of the cross. Rousseau mixes future war, secret power, and religion into a strange, fervent romance of a world remade.
60258-new-lands-within-the-arctic-circle:
New Lands Within the Arctic Circle tells of the Austrian ship Tegetthoff's finds. Julius Payer, one of the expedition's commanders, wrote the narrative himself. Appleton of New York printed this English form in the year 1877. The German text was turned with the author's own leave for this copy. Maps and many pictures from Payer's drawings fill the two-year tale.

The ship lay locked in ice through the years 1872 to 1874. Payer praises his colleague Weyprecht in the preface at some length. Weyprecht fought to free the ship and led the hard retreat south. Order held on the march over the frozen ocean by his skill. Sledging and survey work fell to Payer's own separate command then. Brosch and Orel win praise for self-denial and sharp observing work. The crew's rescue ends the tale of the far northern land.
60305-the-last-brave-invader:
Charles Fontenay wrote The Last Brave Invader, a science fiction tale from Worlds of If in August 1957. In youth Lauria was beautiful, proud, unattainable, but autumn changed her code and lowered her defense, the blurb says. Lauria sweeps down the spiral staircase in regal dignity, wishing someone witnessed her entrance on Pamplin.

She straps a holstered pistol over her evening dress skirt and checks the mirror by the framed Constitution of Pamplin. Its red letters proclaim no government the best government, a man's home his castle, women's rights equal, and only the brave deserving the fair. Slack jaw and hollow cheek get paint, powder, and artful repair work. Science fiction readers get Fontenay.
60312-the-germ-growers-an-australian-sto:
Robert Easterley and John Wilbraham's The Germ Growers, an Australian story of adventure and mystery, was published in 1892 by Melville, Mullen & Slade of Melbourne, with Hutchinson in London. Eleven chapters and a conclusion tell the tale: Disappearances, The Red Sickness, At Sea, Overland, Among the Blacks, Left Alone, The Cars, Signor Davelli, and The Seed Beds among them.

A preliminary chapter sets the frame. Years before, the narrator had witnessed strange things near Kimberley, in north-west Australia, without then knowing the place. At a hotel in Gippsland, on a pleasure tour with Jack Wilbraham, talk of Kimberley's geography brings the recognition back. The business part of the trip had been left behind at Bairnsdale; the two men were riding and sea-bathing by the lakes when the old adventure resurfaced.
60419-a-treatise-on-fever:
Southwood Smith wrote a cure book on fever from his own ward work. Smith was cure man to the London Fever Hospital. The book came out in London in 1830. He gave it to the Duke of Somerset and that house's board. Their care and thrift for the sick win his warm praise in front.

The book is of work use through all its parts, he says. Its aim is to fix what fever is and how it acts. Ward facts, not high thought, ground each claim he sets down. Heat, pulse, skin, and gut signs fill his close watch lists. Cure steps and food for the sick take their due turns. Cure men of that age prized a clear hand book. This one came from the wards.
60460-the-raider:
The Raider is a science fiction story by Don Berry, taken from Worlds of If for April 1958. A slim ship drops a lone man on the night side of a colony planet, thirty miles from Thanlar, the capital. Rising again, the ship is caught by the city's defence screens and burns in the sky.

The raider sleeps, and dreams of Mayne Landing, Earth Commissioner to the Colony Planets. Landing rules a hundred colony worlds with a fist of steel. In the raider's dreams he is marked as a victim. At dawn the man caches his gear and washes in a cold stream. Dressed as a local farmer, he walks down toward the village and the towers beyond. The magazine's blurb calls him a hunter with a cause above all law. Now, it asks, can the cause forgive him his service?
60461-teddy-and-the-mystery-deer:
Teddy and the Mystery Deer, by Howard Garis, author of the Buddy books, the Curlytops, and the Uncle Wiggily books, was copyrighted by Cupples and Leon of New York in 1940. It stands in the Teddy series of mystery stories of boys and animals, beside the mystery dog, monkey, cat, parrot, and pony. Twenty one chapters run from Lost to Caught.

A publisher's note explains the type: it matches the school books of its young readers. Chapter one finds Teddy Benson twisting the propeller of his toy model airplane. His chum Dick Kelly warns him not to wind the rubber bands too tight. Teddy wets a finger and tests the wind: it blows almost directly east. Mason's meadow, then, is the place for the test, with room to start on the far side, away from the woods. The mystery deer of the title appears by chapter three.
60507-the-super-opener:
The Super Opener, by Michael Zuroy, is a short science fiction story from Worlds of If, August 1958. Kalvin Feetch, chief engineer at the Piltdon Opener Company, faces a furious boss who wants a faster can opener in four months. Rival openers cut cans in about three to four seconds and one even plays Home Sweet Home in chimes, while Piltdon's takes nearly nine.

Feetch pleads for more staff and time to dream at the drawing board, and gets threats instead. The tale is a sharp joke about bosses who demand research on a deadline and starve the lab that must do it. Its humor still lands in any modern office.
60521-short-snorter:
Short Snorter is a science fiction story by Charles Einstein, first published in Worlds of If in August 1958. A short snorter was a banknote signed by fellow travellers; the story's visitor, Mr Steariot from Venus, is parked in a resort hotel lobby while his saucer sits in the woods. Newlyweds Fred and Alice Daniels find the saucer first.

Walking the unmarked third path from their hotel, the honeymooners spot a glint of red in a clearing. The craft is a gaudy red plastic disc some fifteen yards across, ringed like a wedding cake, with small windows between its rings. Fred peers in and reports, hollowly, that it has a steering wheel and dials. The couple's flat disbelief, and their question of who one tells about such a thing, open a comedy of first contact played at the level of a summer resort.
60561-mushroom-and-toadstools-how-to-dis:
Worthington Smith's Mushrooms and Toadstools, how to distinguish easily the differences between edible and poisonous fungi, is kept here in its third edition, published by Hardwicke and Bogue of London in 1876. The book works with two sheets of drawings: figures of twenty-nine edible and thirty-one poisonous species, drawn from nature by Smith himself.

His preface is a challenge and a boast: the proof of the fungus is in the eating. He has constantly eaten every species figured on the edible sheet, and many more besides. The poisonous sheet he has not eaten; its kinds bear such names as gloomy, fiery, satanical, and inflaming. Years ago, guideless, he made personal acquaintance with one or two dangerous species, as the book records. With the sheets, he promises, no one need fear a mistake. An index to popular names keys each figure to its sheet.
60580-the-big-blue-soldier:
The Big Blue Soldier, by Grace Livingston Hill, was published in Philadelphia and London in 1923 by Lippincott, from magazine copyrights of 1920 and 1921. A list of Hill's other romances names The City of Fire, Cloudy Jewel, Marcia Schuyler, and The Girl from Montana. She called them, in the publisher's phrase, charming and wholesome romances.

Chapter one opens in a farmhouse kitchen with a pie dispute. Marilla Chadwick turns from the window to ask Mary Amber a pressing question: ought she to have had lemon custard with the pumpkin, instead of the mince? Mince is better, Mary rules; all men like mince-pie, it is so comprehensive. The soldier is due in sight around the bend in about three minutes. All through the war, Marilla has knit and bandaged with a wistful look, waiting. Hill sets a home-front romance of return.
60837-matchmaker:
Charles Fontenay's story, printed in Worlds of If in May 1960, supposes a Calculator that holds punched cards on every man, woman, and child in the civilized world. No one living can solve the problem put to it, so the machine looks to the second generation and names the most likely father: Lao Protik, a psycho-artist living in Nuyork. The mother is the puzzle, since the fifty likeliest women jibe with none of the fifty likeliest men.

The best match proves to be Grida Mattin, a language teacher in Southgate, Tennessee, whose own rating is close to zero but whose rating with Lao is very high. Jasso and Tern, the officials in charge, must arrange a marriage between two strangers. Fontenay plays the bureaucratic matchmaking for quiet comedy and a sting of unease.
60881-the-last-trespasser:
Jim Harmon wrote The Last Trespasser as a science fiction tale, printed in Worlds of If in July 1960. Malloy lies in a padded cell, held as a mad man who walks in his mind from Peoria to Detroit. He has not left the cell for three years, and he trusts his inner trip more than the room around him.

Guards take him out for a sanity hearing, a thing he thought long past. He faces Doctor Heirson, whom he knows, and a lean young stranger at a broad desk. Heirson asks for the truth, and Malloy says he can lie if it helps him. Mind travel, doubt, and a sly clash of wits drive the short tale.
60961-the-book-of-shells-containing-the-:
The Book of Shells appeared in London in 1837, in a second edition published under the direction of the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. Its full title promises the classes Mollusca, Conchifera, Cirrhipeda, Annulata, and Crustacea. The little volume forms part of a natural history set. Companion volumes on the backboned animals followed the system of Cuvier. This one, covering creatures without backbones, follows Lamarck instead.

The preface is honest about that choice. Since Lamarck published, parts of his system had been revised with the sanction of high names. Still, as a whole it remained unrivalled, the writer holds. A young naturalist could add newer findings from later authors. An introductory chapter leads into the molluscs, beginning with the glassy heteropods. Books of this kind put orderly science into the hands of children and general readers across the country.
60999-the-seeder:
Max Williams wrote this science fiction tale, The Seeder, taken from a magazine of March 1961. A headnote gives its rogue in one line: being just plain Pop was not enough for him; he was out for all-fatherhood.

The teller took less than three thousand years to catch up with Pop, which, all things weighed, was good going. He comes out of overdrive in orbit over an ugly planet and finds Pop's ship below. He slams his cruiser down hard beside it, annoyed at the trouble the old man has caused. Pop stands sheepish, helmet off, breathing the foul air as if it were health gas, his gills bluing in the fumes. A weapon stays trained on him: Pop has given the security division trouble before, and the teller's orders are strict.
61017-tales-of-a-vanishing-river:
Earl Reed wrote Tales of a Vanishing River, published by John Lane in New York and London in 1920. Reed, who also wrote The Dune Country, illustrated the book himself. A Kankakee bayou serves as frontispiece. The river of the title winds through a great swampland some fifty miles east of the southern end of Lake Michigan.

French explorers, Reed writes, found the river's beginning there: a thread of current creeping through oozy bogs, pools, and rank grass. The tales gather the people of that country. Tipton Posey keeps a store, Muskrat Hyatt wins redemption, and Colonel Peets falls into predicaments. A brass-bound box and a family record book called a wether book carry other stories. Reed preserves a wet, wild landscape that drainage was already ending.
61045-a-montessori-mother:
Dorothy Canfield Fisher wrote A Montessori Mother, published at New York in October 1912. Fisher had written The Squirrel-Cage. She gives the book, by permission, to Maria Montessori herself. Photographs show the doctor and her schoolrooms in Rome.

Chapters spend a day in a Casa dei Bambini, the children's house, and explain its tools: buttoning frames, sandpaper letters, stairs, and color boxes. Fisher asks how the method and its gear can serve in an American home. Discipline, obedience, and moral training get chapters of their own. Montessori's life and the origin of her schools close the book.
61092-nat-the-navigator-a-life-of-nathan:
Nat the Navigator tells the life of Nathaniel Bowditch for young readers. The book came out at Boston in 1870. One of Bowditch's own children wrote the life.

The writer first told the tale to pupils of the Warren Street Chapel. That talk came on the Sunday after the father's death. Yet the heart of the teller held joy more than grief that day. His father's life had been active and good, and his death calm. The book shares that bright view with the young. It shows how a poor boy's love of numbers made him a famed guide for sailors. Bowditch's great book on navigation made his name known at sea worldwide.
61094-pee-wee-harris-fixer:
Pee-Wee Harris: Fixer is a boys' novel by Percy Keese Fitzhugh, printed at New York in 1924. It appeared with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. Fitzhugh also wrote the Tom Slade and Roy Blakeley books. Barbour drew the pictures.

A verse at the front sums up the hero. His middle name is hunter's stew, and when a thing goes all askew, he fixes it. The chapters bring a solemn vow, a safety patrol, and a parade. Pee-wee declares himself the law and takes up missionary work. A real Emerson, a night in the woods, and a Robin Hood turn fill out the fun. The book is scout comedy at full tilt, with its small, loud hero mending every muddle he meets or makes.
61107-tom-slade-picks-a-winner:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh wrote this Tom Slade book for boys, printed at New York under copyright in 1924 with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. It opens in suspense, with a sick boy laid back in a big chair while his mother bathes his forehead. His sister watches the street for the doctor, and every passing car raises and dashes their hope.

Tom Slade, Fitzhugh's scout hero, befriends the boy and picks him as a winner worth backing. The chapter titles run on baseball terms, from Strike Two and Strike Three to The Home Run and Tom's Big Day. Between them come camp-fire talks, old acquaintances, and shattered dreams rebuilt. The tale is scout teaching in story form, about grit when the game looks lost.
61335-i-executioner:
Ted White and Terry Carr wrote the tale I, Executioner. Worlds of If ran it in March 1963. I am the executioner of the law, the blurb cries. Terrible in my majesty, it adds. The doomed felon is myself, it ends. The teller shakes after each Arena visit.

This time knots of pain grip his stomach. Salt sweat stings his fresh-shaved neck there. He feels strangely empty after the killing. Careful boredom fills the Arena's air, he says. Business as usual rules the other citizens. Ozone and fear reach his nose in that crowd. Nine hundred ninety-nine citizens share Execution Duty. His notice came after months of waiting, he tells. Two years had passed since his last service. Rotation runs about every fourteen months, he says. A grim civic rite in future dress makes every citizen take turns at the death machine.
61414-threlkeld-s-daughter:
Threlkeld's Daughter is a science fiction story by James Bell. It first reached print in a magazine of science fiction in September nineteen sixty three, the hosted note says. Its headnote jokes that she was only a space captain's daughter. All she wanted was a human to call her own, it adds.

Night was a diamond studded dream where the pair sat, the tale opens. Threlkeld and his daughter ride in a pod shaped craft toward a green and purple planet. Their bodies are shaped out of all proportion to the craft, the text says. The father calls them perhaps the most unique imitation of humans the galaxy has produced. His whole career with the inter star patrol rides on this little mission, he tells her. She has taken on all the attributes of a beautiful Earth girl.
61497-the-eagles-gather:
The Eagles Gather is a science fiction story by Joseph Kelleam. It appeared in Astounding Science-Fiction in April 1942. A head note states the premise in broken lines. The mercenaries of the war lords had fought their last paying fight. The war lords themselves and civilization were bankrupt. The opening scene shows a ruined landing field at night. A huge bonfire lights it with dancing shadows. Broken towers look down with forlorn, hollow eyes. One battered space boat stands by the flames.

In a rickety tower's shadow a man tends a bubbling pot. He is lean and broad shouldered, with yellow curls. His tattered uniform takes a trim look from its wearer. He stirs the stew and glances at the dark sky. The night waits threateningly beyond the fire. Kelleam builds a fallen world of grounded spacemen.
61521-the-modern-traveller:
The Modern Traveller, a comic poem issued in London in 1898, came from the same hands as the Bad Child's Book of Beasts. The verse is light, brisk, and full of dry jokes at the cost of famed explorers. A journalist from the Daily Menace calls on a traveller just back from Africa.

The great man sits in a room strewn with shields, spears, and small savage gods. He claims to hate fame and grants only a few remarks, not a formal talk. He tells of a burnt fetish tree, a lost store of shot, and a hard retreat to the coast. Commander Sin, a wild youth grown into a flawed hero, stands at the heart of the tale. Drawings fill the pages.
61551-the-push-of-a-finger:
The Push of a Finger, by Alfred Bester, is a science fiction story from Astounding of May 1942. A tagline heads it: a push of a finger, or a careless word, can wreck the universe. The narrator opens by mocking the stock plots.

Mad scientists who want to change the world, dictators who want to rule it, alien planets that want to wreck it: he would burn the lot. His tale inverts the pattern, one man against the Earth. A whole world, he says, hunted a man to change his life, and to destroy him if it had to. The seat of it is a place in Manhattan City, a pivot of the universe. Shakes that rock the world come out of it, sent to head off worse ones. It looks like a block, ten stories tall, an abandoned hospital.
61590-this-and-that-and-the-other:
This and That and the Other is a volume of essays by Belloc, published in New York in 1912. The pieces range from an open letter to a young diplomatist to essays on inns, lying and fame.

The opening letter sets the tone. Writing to the son of an old diplomat friend, Belloc promises to reveal the trade's mysteries. He warns him, in swelling periods, of the destinies in his hands: lives, fortunes and the honour of his country will hang on his judgment. The grandeur is the joke, and the essay that follows punctures it with practical, worldly advice. Throughout, Belloc mixes the sermon and the squib in his most characteristic manner.
61595-jack-straw-lighthouse-builder:
Irving Crump wrote Jack Straw, Lighthouse Builder, a boys book published in New York in 1915 with pictures by Leslie Crump. Crump had already sent Jack Straw to Mexico in an earlier tale. A front picture shows Jack and Big O'Brien first to ride the aerial cable down to the lighthouse site.

The boys sail for Hood Island after a telegram starts the story. A runaway, an arrest, and lobster pirates keep the middle chapters busy. Then come a raid, a chase, and a find by Ray, before the reef takes its toll. The last chapter turns to football and a new full-back. Young readers got building, boats, and sport in one package. The lighthouse rises through it all, chapter by chapter, toward its first lighting.
6165-cowboy-dave-or-the-round-up-at-roll:
Frank V. Webster sends Cowboy Dave to the round-up at Rolling River, opening with stray cattle, a taunt, a confession, and a small stampede. Treachery, a cry for help, a rescue, Mr. Bellmore, and Dave meeting Len follow, with Dave wondering, hazardous work, and a fight.

Webster, author of farm boys, telephone boys, newsboy partners, and boy pilots, writes brisk western adventure for boys. Dave's round-up tests riding, nerve, and loyalty among cattle, rivals, and rough country. The chapters promise news, danger, and a round-up brought home through pluck and teamwork.
6173-the-note-books-of-samuel-butler:
Samuel Butler began early to carry a notebook, writing down anything he wanted to remember, whether heard from others or said by himself. His reason, in one note, was that thoughts fly so fast one must shoot them, since trying to put salt on their tails is no use.

He bagged as many as he could hit and preserved them, rewritten on loose sheets, as a museum of wise, beautiful, and strange creatures winging across his vision's field. Henry Festing Jones arranged and edited these selections, with a photogravure portrait from an 1898 photograph. The notebooks show Butler thinking aloud.
61771-the-double-search-studies-in-atone:
Rufus Jones, professor of philosophy in Haverford College, published 'The Double Search' in 1906 as studies in atonement and prayer. His earlier books, listed at the front, include lives of Eli and Sybil Jones and a work on social law in the spiritual world. The introduction opens with the myth in Plato's Symposium of round people cut in two by Zeus, each half seeking its lost other half.

Jones argues that love in Plato points higher, toward the eternal from which the soul has come. The search, he says, is double: the Divine Other whom we seek is also seeking us. Three chapters then take up the historical and inward Christ, the atonement, and prayer, turning the old myth into a frame for Christian teaching.
61852-kittens-and-cats-a-first-reader:
Kittens and Cats is a first reader for small children, by Eulalie Osgood Grover, copyrighted in 1911. Grover had written The Sunbonnet Babies’ Primer and The Overall Boys. Houghton Mifflin issued the book at Boston, New York, and Chicago. A first picture shows a cat who says, I am the queen.

First readers taught reading by short lines and bright pictures. Cats and kittens give this one its soft subject for beginners. A child meets pets on the page while learning her letters. The pictures were copyrighted by a photo company of the day. Grover built a small empire of primers on charm and ease. This volume starts readers off in the company of cats. It shows the gentle method of the reading lesson of its age.
61867-the-deep-sea-hunters-adventures-on:
Hyatt Verrill wrote a boys' tale of adventures on a whaler, issued in New York in 1922. Jim Lathrop dashes in to tell his chum Tom that the old bark Hector is being fitted out for a cruise. Tom laughs at the news, for the ship has lain on the mud flat for years.

Grass grew from her seams, and she seemed as fixed as the village church beside the dead whaling docks. But the news is true, and the boys ship out. Chapters promise a whale sighted, a narrow escape, an island out of the world, and a strange message. Verrill knew the sea well, and boys trusted his yarns for that reason.
61890-the-dragon-queen-of-jupiter:
Leigh Brackett's The Dragon-Queen of Jupiter appeared in Planet Stories in the summer of 1941. Its teaser ranks the winged dragon-queen and her white Legions of Doom above the green snakes and red beetles of that outpost of Earth Empire. Tex, a Texan serving at new Fort Washington on Jupiter, keeps watch on the parapet beside the Martian Breska.

The dawn attack of the swamp-dwellers is overdue, supplies run low and the relief has not come. Captain John Smith of the Volunteer Legion walks the catwalk as calmly as if he discussed cricket scores. Then a scream rises from the compound, where a tiny green snake on a man's wrist is growing by the second.
61900-the-educational-writings-of-richar:
Educational Writings of Richard Mulcaster gathers the Elizabethan schoolmaster texts. James Oliphant abridged and arranged them with a critical estimate in nineteen o three. MacLehose of Glasgow, publishers to the University, issued the volume that year. Mulcaster lived from fifteen thirty two to sixteen eleven in Tudor England.

Oliphant preface grants that some apology is owed for the abridged form. Three centuries had passed with Mulcaster works unread as literature, he notes. Yet Mulcaster ranks among our most interesting and important educationists still. His neglect is the puzzle this volume sets out to repair for readers. Mulcaster taught at Merchant Taylors and Saint Paul schools in London.
61935-outdoor-pastimes-of-an-american-hu:
Theodore Roosevelt wrote Outdoor Pastimes of an American Hunter, in a new and larger form printed at New York in 1908. Roosevelt loved the woods and fields, from farm land to wild country. He gave the book to John Burroughs, the famed nature writer.

Roosevelt praises Burroughs for his fight against false nature writing that fakes animal tales. The essays share hunts, camps, and close watch of birds and beasts from his own time outdoors. Clear views on fair sport and true field notes run through the work. Hunters and general readers alike get a vivid record of American outdoor life.
62036-the-unforgiving-offender:
John Reed Scott published the novel The Unforgiving Offender in 1913. His earlier fiction included The Colonel of the Red Huzzars and The Woman in Question. Clarence Underwood drew the color pictures. Scott dedicated the book, with a joke, to the knockers he used to lunch with at the Pittsburgh Club, calling himself the one who never knocked.

The story opens in the grill-room of the Otranto Country Club on a Saturday afternoon, where Montague Pendleton and the younger members gather after tennis and golf. Chapter titles trace what follows: the return of the offender, a ride on the bridle-path, an offer and an answer, a summons, and at last an arrest. Talk of clothes and guests fills the middle chapters before the truth comes out by persuasion. Readers get a society novel with a wrong at its center that no one will forgive.
62057-buffalo-bill-s-boy-bugler:
Colonel Prentiss Ingraham wrote a Buffalo Bill tale of a boy bugler and an Indian ring. Street and Smith held the rights in New York in 1909. A front note honors William F Cody, born in Scott County, Iowa, in 1846. Ingraham and Ned Buntline wrote the Bill tales from talks with Cody himself.

Young Cody rode the pony express in 1860 and scouted through the Civil War. Hunting buffalo for rail crews in 1867 won him his famed name. Sheridan made him chief of scouts for the Sioux and Cheyenne wars. Western fans get dime-novel thrills built on a scout's real, wild life.
62170-the-star-master:
Ray Cummings's story, printed in Planet Stories in the summer of 1942, is narrated by Arthur Frane, a rich young man of twenty-six. Frane keeps an income of ten thousand decimars and calls his money a disadvantage. In July 2003 he goes hunting in the Adirondac forest with Jim Gregg, an old college friend now in the Crime Prevention Bureau.

The two hold a one-day permit for twenty square miles of government preserve, with pencil-ray flash guns for the hunt. A rustling up the slope sounds like a deer, and Frane fires through the underbrush at it. A girl bursts from a thicket three feet from the burned swath, and the tale of Venta, and of a docile Venus marked for empire, begins.
62176-the-wrecking-master:
Ralph D Paine wrote The Wrecking Master, published in New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in nineteen eleven. George Varian drew the pictures. Paine had earlier written A Cadet of the Black Star Line and The Head Coach. Ten chapters carry a sea tale of salvage work. Dan Frazier is the young man at its center.

A Skipper in Bad Company opens the book. The Resolute Fathoms the Plo and The Race for the Kenilworth follow. Wicked Mr Pringle in Collision and All Hands Abandon Ship raise the danger. Dan Frazier's Predicament and A Fat Engineer to the Rescue fill the middle. A Fog of Suspicions and The Broken Hawser lead to Dan's Dreams Come True. Boys get a wrecking tale of races to stranded ships and work in bad weather.
62181-arnold-s-tempter:
Arnold's Tempter is a historical novel by Benjamin Comfort, printed at Boston in 1908. Illustrations show Mollie Greydon, girls seeking wild strawberries on the banks of the Wingohocking, and Captain Risk engaging two seamen with cutlass and pistol. The scene is Philadelphia in the days of the Revolution.

Roderick Barclugh has arrived with credentials from Franklin to the Secretary of Congress, influence at the French court, and bills of exchange for twenty thousand pounds. He is invited to dine with the FitzMaurices, where Benedict Arnold and his bride Peggy Shippen will meet him. Judge Shippen, Colonel Hamilton, clergy, lawyers, and financiers fill a house where schemes for independence mix with dreams of aristocracy.
62194-indian-summer:
Indian Summer is a novel by Emily Grant Hutchings, published by Alfred A Knopf of New York in 1922. The story is laid in Bromfield, a rusty old village in New York state. It is built in three books named Spring, Summer, and Belated Frost.

Lavinia Larimore, called Vine, is the handsomest girl in Bromfield. She has worn Calvin Stone's ring for three endless years. The prologue opens on her fear: Calvin now rides often to Rochester and does not stop. David, Vine Cottage, and a wedding enter the design. Later chapters carry names like A Web in the Moonlight and Red Dawn. The book moves toward a crisis of the heart, named Katharsis in the contents. Consummation and The Greater Love close it. Hutchings writes a romance of second chances, where love ripens late like the season of the title.
62529-the-life-of-col-james-gardiner:
Colonel James Gardiner's life is told in a short tract issued by the Religious Tract Society in London. Gardiner was the son of Captain Patrick Gardiner, who served under King William and Queen Anne and died abroad. His mother lost a husband, a brother, and her eldest son in war, and raised him in strict faith.

Inside, the account follows Gardiner from school at Linlithgow to an ensign's post in Dutch service at age fourteen. He fought at Ramilies at nineteen and bore a cheek scar from a boyhood duel for life. The tract stresses his later change of heart, when he refused a duel by saying he feared sin, not fighting.
62532-bennie-and-the-tiger:
Bennie and the Tiger is one of Dean's Illustrated Farthing Books, issued at London by Dean and Son at Ludgate Hill. A fair little English boy sleeps in the shady verandah of his Indian home as the tale opens. The servant left with him is unfaithful to her trust. She wanders away in search of pleasure while he sleeps.

A treacherous tiger prowls for a pig or a lamb for his supper. The village is quiet, with English gentlemen absent and most natives at work in the rice fields. White ladies rest in the heat, little dreaming how careless their nurses are. The tiger creeps past deserted homes and spies the sweet sleeper. He springs, grasps the white robe in his teeth, and darts to his native jungle. There he plays with the child as a kitten plays with a mouse. Bennie shows a brave heart and no alarm.
62569-the-monster-maker:
Ray Bradbury wrote this tale of the worlds of space, first printed in a journal of such tales in the spring of 1944. A note at its head gives the plot in brief. The word from the chiefs said: Get Gunther. It was a jest, the note says. For Click and Irish were stuck on the rock of a sea thief, with one gun and a reel of film twixt them for arms. The tale opens in the thick of a flight.

All at once the thing was there. There was no time to blink, to speak, or to fear. Click Hathaway's reel ran in his hands, and he knew he was set to get a fine roll of all that took place. Marnagan hunched huge at the board of the ship, tore at the levers, and jammed the studs with his thick fists.
62619-the-avenger:
The Avenger is a science tale by Fleming, first set in a pulp sheet in the mid war years. A head note sets its trap: a man made a super man to fight the weird great beasts that had burst in on Earth. But he lost sight of one wee thing, it warns. Like calls to like.

A note tells that no proof was found its rights were made new in law. Its first scene is a room of great machines and a dead man. He had been dead for some time, the text says in slanted lines. Dark blood yet oozed from the crushed wreck of his face. It ran down to his wet sleeve and fell, drop by slow drop, from his fin tips to the floor.
62632-canada-the-spellbinder:
Lilian Whiting wrote a rave tour book on Canada as a land of spell. Her book came out in London and Toronto in 1917. Plates in hue and in shade fill its bright pages. A front plate shows salmon sport at Moricetown in the far west. She gave the book to Charles Melville Hays with warm praise.

His sight and grit raised Canada's rail road, that page says in full. He spread its lines from sea to sea in his bold years. New fair lands lay bare by his work for folk to come. His death in the Titanic's wreck on April 15, 1912, left a breach. Whiting sings the land his roads laid wide for all guests.
62676-sewage-disposal-on-the-farm-and-pr:
Theobald Smith wrote a farmers' bulletin on sewage disposal on the farm and the protection of drinking water. It came out in 1896 as Farmers' Bulletin number 43 from the United States Department of Agriculture. Smith taught at Harvard University and served as pathologist to the Massachusetts State Board of Health.

Smith argues that farm health rests largely in the hands of each household, unlike city health, which rests on public systems. He treats the privy, the cesspool, the dry-earth closet, and the water closet in turn. Later pages cover liquid sewage, irrigation, kitchen slops, and garbage. A final section shows how wells get fouled and how to build them safely. Farm readers of the day got plain, practical rules for keeping waste away from the water they drank.
62744-the-glebe-1913-12-vol-1-no-3-the-a:
The Glebe, volume one number three, is an issue of a little magazine from December 1913. Each issue of The Glebe was given to one author alone. Its sole policy was absolute freedom of expression. Merit was the only test for print, its editors say. This number holds The Azure Adder by Charles Demuth. The price of the issue was thirty-five cents. Albert and Charles Boni published it in New York.

The Azure Adder is a play set in an artist's studio. Vivian's rooms are white on white, with little furniture. He enters in Greek dress, damp from the bath. Demuth is now famed as a painter of the modern school. His early play shows the same spare, sharp taste. The Glebe gave young writers room to show a full hand. Kreymborg and Abbott stood among its editors.
62959-the-horse-and-his-rider:
Sir Francis B. Head writes about horses and riding in a second edition issued in London in 1861. Head warns readers at the start that he never bred, raced, or bet on horses and never moved in the sporting world. His case rests on long use instead, on roads, on duty, and at times to save his life.

Inside, the book treats the bond between horse and rider as a skill that can be learned by care and feel. Head draws on years of hard riding to explain how a horse should be handled, kept, and trusted. Readers get plain advice from a man who rode far and often, not from the race course or the ring.
62979-the-ivory-tower:
Henry James wrote The Ivory Tower, published in New York in 1917 after his death, with his working notes for the novel printed after it. Percy Lubbock saw the book through the press. The story was never finished, and the notes show where it was meant to go.

Book First opens with a large young woman crossing an avenue under a vast pale-green parasol. Her white, voluminous draperies make her resemble a ship held back from speed with its canvas spread. She is bound for the gate of Betterman, a neighbor across the way, in a seaside place in the August light. James builds a world of money and watching out of such small crossings. The fragment is among the most famous unfinished novels in English. Readers get his late manner, and the notes as a second story.
6300-the-project-gutenberg-complete-work:
A single vast file gathers Parker's novels, tales, and poems, from The Judgment House and Pierre and His People through Romany of the Snows, Northern Lights, and Mrs. Falchion, to Valmond, The Trail of the Sword, and the Canadian and Egyptian books. The Trespasser, Seats of the Mighty, Battle of the Strong, Lane That Had No Turning, Right of Way, and Weavers all stand inside, with Embers and A Lover's Diary for verse.

The file opens, fittingly, in an opera house, where a singer named Al'mah makes Manassa the musical feast of the year at Covent Garden, while three watchers resist her spell. That scene comes from The Judgment House, first in the contents. As an omnibus it is a library in one place, for a reader who wants Parker's whole range, from prairie towns to Paris courts, without hunting volume by volume.
63017-dress-and-look-slender:
Dress and Look Slender, by Jane Warren Wells, was copyrighted in 1924 and published at Scranton, Pennsylvania. Contents open with why women want to look slender. When fashion demands slenderness and youthfulness, and business and social life make them a need, are early heads. Making the most of your good points follows.

Chapter two gives the real secret of dressing to look slender. Optical illusions head it: seeing is believing. Lines that slenderize, and lines that do not, are set out. A simple trick takes off twenty pounds, one head promises, and other heads treat tunics and height. Chapter three turns to little things that make big differences: posture, shoes and stockings chosen with care, necklines, jewelry, collars, purses, fans, and cosmetics. Chapter four covers foundations, corsets, and how to know a fit. Readers get a 1924 dress guide written wholly around one aim.
63046-mr-meek-musketeer:
Clifford Simak wrote the story of Oliver Meek, a musketeer of the space age, printed in Planet Stories in the summer of 1944. The blurb says adventure flamed in Meek's timorous heart. With a rocket ship for his steed and a ray gun for his sword, he sallies forth to carry cavalier justice to the stars.

Meek is a clerk at Lunar Exports, and he opens the tale by resigning. His boss, Belmont, offers him a leave of absence instead. He assumes Meek means one of the safe system tours. Meek corrects him: he has a ship of his own. For over thirty years he saved for the ship and the gear, until the plan became an obsession. Simak builds a gentle comedy on the meekest of men chasing the boldest of dreams.
63059-trains-of-recollection-drawn-from-:
Trains of Recollection gathers fifty years of railway service in Scotland and Canada, told by Hanna, first president of the Canadian National Railways, to Arthur Hawkes. Chapters begin with a Presbyterian background of Scottish migration.

Hanna recalls early service at stations near the Clyde, Van Horne and the Canadian Pacific challenge, and the Canadian Northern's start as a pioneer line with a staff of thirteen. Later chapters tell of prairie lines, midwinter work in empty country, and the Great War's destruction of the Canadian Northern. The dedication honors the men who served beside him. Portraits include Sir Donald Mann, Sir William Mackenzie, and Sir William Van Horne.
6307-the-story-of-a-bold-tin-soldier:
Attention is the word of command heard in a toy department at night, after customers and clerks have gone home. A Calico Clown peers round building blocks, a Candy Rabbit asks if the Sawdust Doll has returned, and a Monkey on a Stick reports no old friends in sight. Then the Bold Tin Soldier calls his men again, and the toys of Laura Lee Hope's make believe world stir into life.

Ten chapters follow the soldier through a make believe fight, saving the clown, a boy's purchase, a bean battle, a captain and a lamb, and a sad accident. A bunch of sweetness, a return to the store, and a rabbit close the tale. Hope writes for young children, with toys that talk, march, and care for one another when the shop lights go out.
63077-how-to-build-a-20-foot-bi-plane-gl:
How to Build a 20-Foot Bi-Plane Glider is a practical handbook by Alfred Powell Morgan. Spon and Chamberlain published the revised edition at New York in 1912, from rights dated 1909. Morgan edited the mechanical side of a boys' magazine. The book promises a first step into flying, with the principles made plain.

The text starts with the frame: beams held three feet apart by six struts. Each strut is cut to size, with notches at the ends for the joints. Brass clamps, bent from sheet strips, bind the frame and shield the beams. Two dozen clamps are needed for the whole machine. Figures mark each part and its place in the frame. Morgan wrote for lads with tools and a yard. The glider he describes could be built at home.
63083-the-marquis-de-villemer:
George Sand wrote this novel of a proud house and a sister's sacrifice. Ralph Keeler turned it into English, and Osgood printed it at Boston in 1871. The Marquis de Villemer opens as a letter, written on the road.

Do not worry, dear sister, the writer tells Camille: here I am at Paris, safe and not tired. A few hours' sleep and a cup of coffee have set her up. She will take a carriage to Madame d'Arglade's, who will present her to Madame de Villemer. The solemn interview's fruit she will write that night. Take courage with me, she begs: she could not sit with folded hands while Camille rears four children alone. Sand spins love and rank from that errand.
63164-nameless-river:
Nameless River is a west tale by Vingie Roe, out from Duffield in nineteen twenty three. Spring in the Deep Heart land opens the tale in wide word paint. Pine song, maple shake, and cotton wood flash fill the hill slopes. Great canyons cut the ridges in red, brown, and gold stone hues. Deer browse the hid vales while wolves prey and big cats cry at night.

Gold eagles rear their young on a crag crown of Mystery Ridge. Rich grass makes sleek beef herds on the slopes by the stream. Part names name a home claim on Nameless and a Sky Line iron hand. Brand fairs, gold spell, and a cliff lip mark mid part names. A face in a pack and the fight line at last close the scheme.
63166-growing-crimson-clover:
Growing Crimson Clover is Farmers' Bulletin 1142 of the United States Department of Agriculture, issued at Washington in August 1920. Kephart, a worker in forage-crop studies, wrote it. The bulletin revises an earlier one on crimson clover by Westgate. Crimson clover, it opens, is a handsome fall-planted annual, widely grown in the Middle Atlantic and Southeastern States. Farmers use it for forage, as a cover crop, and as green manure.

It is commonly sown in corn at the last working of the crop. It grows on poorer soil than most clovers and needs little lime, so it restores worn-out land. The chief trouble is the killing of young stands by drought. A fine, moist, firmly packed seed bed guards against it. August and September are the best months for sowing. Its only severe disease is the stem-rot, or wilt.
63180-letters-to-a-young-housekeeper:
Letters to a Young Housekeeper is a household manual by Jane Prince, published in Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin in 1917. Prince wrote the letters at her sister's suggestion, for young friends setting up house. The sister receives the dedication.

The contents lay out the young housekeeper's whole problem. Economy in the household and the budget come first. Servants fill two chapters, with their duties spelled out late in the book. Weekly cleaning, family meals, and a behind-the-scenes view of a dinner follow. In 1917 a mistress still managed a house through hired help, and this book taught the management kindly, in letters. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
63211-a-year-with-a-whaler:
A Year with a Whaler is a sea narrative by Walter Noble Burns, printed at New York by the Outing Publishing Company in 1913. Photographs illustrate it. A frontispiece shows the cutting out of a whale. The ship is the Alexander, and Burns sailed in her forecastle. Once outside the Golden Gate, he says, he felt blue water swing under him for the first time.

The contents run the whole cruise. The lure of the outfitter and the men of the Alexander open it. The A, B, C of whales teaches the trade's grammar. Through the Roaring Forties the ship works into the ice. Cross-country whaling, cutting in, and trying out follow. The crew shakes hands with Siberia, goes on strike in the person of Slim, and enters the Arctic. Blubber and song, a narrow pinch, and bears for a change lead to the stranded whale and home.
63261-be-kind-to-one-another:
Be Kind to One Another is a tiny illustrated story book for children, issued in London by Dean and Son. It belongs to a series called Dean's Illustrated Farthing Books, priced for the cheapest market. The tale follows three little girls who are near neighbours and dear friends. Lily Stuart and Ellie Graham head the cast.

Ellie's younger sister May joins the two in all their plays, the opening explains. The sisters are so seldom apart that to see one is to expect all three. School, play, and small acts of kindness between the girls carry the lesson of the title. Farthing books put moral tales, with pictures, within reach of poor children.
63407-linda-carlton-s-perilous-summer:
Edith Lavell wrote a girls' adventure in her Linda Carlton series, copyrighted in 1932. Linda is presented as the first girl in America to fly from New York to Paris alone. The tale opens at Green Falls, at the summer bungalow of her Aunt Emily, where Linda asks for a picnic lunch.

Her aunt looks grave at the flying suit, for the lunch means a flight in the Ladybug, Linda's autogiro, with her friend Dot. In June she had flown it south to Georgia and been kidnaped by thieves and stranded on an island. Chapters ahead promise a treasure hunt, a haunted house, and a ghost in the tower. A rescue closes the summer's perils.
63486-preacher-and-prayer:
E M Bounds wrote this call to prayer for preachers, printed at Chicago with a 1907 copyright. Luther's saying heads the book: three things make a divine, prayer, meditation, and temptation. Lines from McCheyne urge the preacher to get his text, thoughts, and words from God. They warn that a man laid aside from ministry may be taught prayer by the loss.

Richard Baxter asks whether a doctor in plague time may take more rest than his life needs, while souls gasp around him. Bounds's own voice drives the same point: a sermon's life is an hour or two, but the preacher's life preaches all week. If Satan can make a minister covet praise, pleasure, or good eating, the ministry is ruined.
63622-the-black-panther:
John Hall Wheelock offers verse in The Black Panther, a book of poems printed in New York in 1922. Scribner holds the copyright. Many poems first ran in magazines, from The Century and Harper's to Poetry and The Dial, as the thanks page lists.

The title poem leads, then a part called Dim Wisdoms. Its heads run from Night Has Its Fear to The Sorrowful Masquerade and October Moonlight. The Flesh and the Dream, a poem on 1914, and The Beloved stand in the run. Proud Doom, The Secret One, and Haunted Earth keep the grave tone. A poem on the fifth symphony of Tchaikovsky shows his range past love and night.
63645-the-last-monster:
The Last Monster is a science fiction story by Gardner Fox, taken from Planet Stories for Fall 1945. Its hero is Irgi, the last of his monster race. He is guardian of a dead planet and master of the secret of immortality. Four men from Earth must conquer him to gain that secret, though he is a tentacled being whom Earthly weapons cannot touch.

Irgi has dwelt alone for hundreds and hundreds of years in the marble halls of an eon-ancient city. He has lost count of time. Golden drapes that never wither hang along white marble walls, and black floors shine below. Opalescent mists bathe the city and destroy dust and germs. Irgi discovered the mist years ago, too late to save his kind. He flung a vast globe of transparent metal above the greatest city of the Urg and filled it with the mist.
63657-venusian-invader:
Larry Sternig wrote this science fiction tale for Planet Stories, where it ran in the winter of 1945. On Callisto, Mart Wells works as a rocketport dispatcher at Comprotown, the one town on a bleak moon. He is in love with Leah Barrow, whose father directs the town and looks down on any man with fewer than six stars.

A flash of metal in the hills turns out to be a small spaceship where none should be. Behind it stands Tar Norn, a Venusian pirate, who has sworn that Leah will die unless he is set free. Her father must hold him, though the price may be his daughter's life, and Wells is caught in the middle of the threat.
63696-the-vanisher:
The Vanisher is a science tale by Shaara, first set in a pulp sheet in the mid nineteen fifties. A head note sets its hero: he was of no great price, this young chief with the strange blood. So he was sent out to space, where he saw the bare stars.

There he met the bare thing of the void, that note says, and grew the first man in past tale to die more than once. A note tells that no proof was found its rights were made new in law. Its first scene is of two girls who stay to see a film a next time. Past the mid of night they come out to rain, and no cab can be had.
63759-the-brain-sinner:
Alan Nourse wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Planet Stories in spring 1955. An invisible network of human minds lay across the country, tuned and waiting for first contact with a telepathic alien. The tale opens as a ship skims down like a shadow and settles in tangled brush on a hill above a river bend.

Scorched leaves hiss and a small trapped animal pipes, then silence falls. The alien waits with open mind for any flicker of surprise, wonder, or fear from the dark hills. None comes, and he grunts with relief at the care taken in landing. In his cabin an image of light and shadow builds a full three dimensional form as his work begins.
63798-the-water-colours-of-j-m-w-turner:
W G Rawlinson and A J Finberg wrote the text for The Water-Colours of J M W Turner, a book from The Studio in 1909. The book came out in London, Paris, and New York at once. Sir Charles Holroyd wrote the first words. A set of rich owners lent their prized sheets for the plates.

Holroyd says the plates are the best copies of the true sheets he has yet seen. He holds that more such copies will spread the fame of the master. Rawlinson writes on the drawn work of Turner as a whole. Finberg writes on the sheets held in the great state rooms in London. Plates show a palace at Lambeth, the mouth of the Avon, and a great church. Views of Dover, Lichfield, and Edinburgh round out the first set.
63918-bob-hazard-dam-builder:
Carl Brandt wrote Bob Hazard, Dam Builder, issued in Chicago by the Reilly and Britton Company with copyright in nineteen sixteen. Herbert Morton Stoops illustrated the book. Twenty chapters fill the tale. A frontispiece shows Bob climbing through space a second later, faster than a rocket. Chapter one is Father and Son. So you would rather be an engineer than a lawyer, Bob, the father asks to open it.

Yes, sir, an engineer rather than anything else, Bob answers. The speakers sat on a bench in the park around the old Virginia State House in Richmond, the tale says.
