Father and son they were certainly, the likeness unmistakable, it notes. U S R S and When the Chief Was Away follow. The Labyrinth, Jerry Story, and The End of the Labyrinth come next. Boys get a reclamation dam adventure.
63965-monster:
William Morrison wrote Monster, a science fiction tale first printed in Planet Stories in July 1951. A headnote states the trouble: settling Mars was hell because of one thing, large hungry beasts. They flew, crawled, snarled, howled, burrowed up under the floors, and chewed at doors and windows. Then, to make things worse, came the Monster. The tale opens with a faint scratching at a door.

Alice Kidd has been listening in fear for just that sound, and up close she can no longer doubt it. She feels the bolt behind the door once more, and checks the shutters. Her small son, five years old, asks if it can get in. She carries him into the next room, bolts the joining door, and calls her husband. Anthony tells her not to worry: the thing cannot get in for a couple of hours. He is coming.
63989-halftripper:
Halftripper, a science fiction tale by Mack Reynolds, ran in Planet Stories in November 1951. A blurb at the head sets its world in a few stark lines. Mars is strewn with the human wrecks of halftrippers, terrorized cowards of space travel. The saddest and most fearful of them is an immortal space bum called Micheal.

The narrator knows Mars well after a long stay on the planet. This part of New Santa Fe lies off his beaten track, he admits at the start. He sits in a plain tavern called Sam Bar, drinking Martian brandy with little joy. A spaceport trip in a few hours holds no charm for him that day. An old man takes the stool next to him and orders from Sam. A chance bar talk opens the tale of the halftrippers and their dread.
64109-the-christmas-reindeer:
The Christmas Reindeer, by Thornton Burgess with pictures by Rhoda Chase, was copyrighted in 1926 and published in New York in 1929 by the Book League of America. Burgess dedicates the little volume to the beautiful faith of childhood and the keeping of a charming fable. Twenty-three chapters follow Tuktu, a small Inuit girl whose name means caribou, and her brother Aklak.

Chapters run from Kringle Valley through Whitefoot Goes Astray and Lost in the Fog to The Great Mill, The Chosen Deer, and the round-up. Tuktu tells her story; the deer people appear; wolves attack near the close. A front plate shows Whitefoot astray, and other plates show Tuktu with Santa Claus. Burgess, famed for his animal tales, here builds a Christmas story on the choosing of Santa's reindeer team.
64136-history-of-early-steamboat-navigat:
Hiram Martin Chittenden, a captain of engineers, wrote this history of early steamboat navigation on the Missouri River. It was published at New York in 1903 in a limited edition, by the author of a history of the Yellowstone. It doubles as the life and adventures of Joseph La Barge.

Chittenden met the venerable pilot at St Louis in 1896 while gathering material on the fur trade, and found his knowledge of early western history remarkably accurate. The contents follow La Barge from ancestry and childhood into the fur trade, through cholera on the Yellowstone, years at Cabanné's, and rivalry in opposition. Later chapters treat the river itself, its boats, and the voyages of 1843 and 1844. Western historians get the Missouri's commerce in one pilot's lifetime.
64137-history-of-early-steamboat-navigat:
History of Early Steamboat Navigation on the Missouri River, volume two, by Hiram Martin Chittenden, was printed in New York by Francis P Harper in 1903. Chittenden was a captain in the Corps of Engineers. The book tells the life and adventures of Joseph La Barge, pioneer navigator and Indian trader.

A portrait of Kennett McKenzie stands at the front. Chapters in this volume treat the Civil War on the river, gold in Montana, and river events of 1862 to 1867. The voyage of 1863 and the Tobacco Garden massacre follow. The Blackfoot annuities, La Barge in Montana, and La Barge in Washington fill the late chapters. The last treats the Indian of the Missouri Valley. River fans get fifty years of commerce told through one great pilot.
64147-a-stolen-name-or-the-man-who-defie:
Nicholas Carter stands behind this Nick Carter tale in the New Magnet Library. A Stolen Name, or The Man Who Defied Nick Carter, gives the plot in its two heads. The line's puff is plain: Nick Carter stands for a gripping detective tale.

The list at the front boasts that no book in the line is dull. Each tale is by Nicholas Carter, house name of the line's many hands. A stolen name sets the case: a man bold enough to defy the great detective himself. Cheap, fast, and full of turns, such tales fed the news-stands of their day by the million. Carter's cool nerve and sharp eye form the draw in every one.
64149-in-the-christmas-woods-being-the-i:
In the Christmas Woods is a nature essay by Adeline Knapp, printed at San Francisco in 1899. The Stanley-Taylor Company published it with a picture by William Keith. It introduces a series of observations of nature through the year. Knapp had written Upland Pastures before it. A poem, Rain up the Mountain, opens the pamphlet. White mist creeps along the serried slopes and through oak fringed canyons.

A passage on beauty from Marcus Aurelius follows the poem. Even things that follow nature's products hold something pleasing, it argues. Bending corn ears and the foam on a boar's mouth please the mind. Then the essay turns to a Christmas rainstorm in California. Nature sends no niggardly shower for her Christmas gift, Knapp writes. Redwoods, laurels, and manzanita stand in the rain.
64181-rocket-summer:
Rocket Summer is a science fiction story by Ray Bradbury, taken from Planet Stories for spring 1947. A blurb calls it the first great rocket flight into space, bearing pioneers to the Moon. Public joy flared into red mob hate when President Stanley canceled the flight.

The tale opens on a cold gray morning, as a crowd gathers with a curious noise before the scheduled Birth. Folk arrive in scarlet tumble bugs and yellow plastic beetles, yawning and singing. William Stanley stands alone at his high office window, head of the company that owns the field in the Jersey mists. He watches with sad impatience in his gray eyes. His firm built the rocket, and the day weighs on him. Readers get Bradbury early fire on space and crowds.
64190-purple-forever:
Purple Forever is a science fiction tale by Jack Lewis, taken from Planet Stories for November 1953. Its blurb shows three men on Venus in shirt sleeves, breathing chlorine and ammonia air that should kill in thirty seconds. The pictures lied, it says, and inquisitive Carl Keating found the true answer stranger still.

Major Carl Keating, retired as of last Tuesday at thirty-six, opens an envelope. A special delivery stamp marks fifty years since Harvey's first landing on Mars. Inside, one typewritten sheet asks him to come at once, signed Norman Hamlin. The phone rings as he reads. Hamlin leans into the view-plate and asks if he is the right man. Lewis starts his mystery with a summons.
64210-types-of-prose-narratives-a-text-b:
Types of Prose Narratives is a textbook for story writers by Harriott Fansler. Row, Peterson issued it in Chicago in 1911. Fansler taught English at Western Reserve and in the Philippines. The book sorts tales of imagined events by kind. Part one treats the primitive and religious group. Myth, legend, and fairy tale head the chapters.

Each kind is defined and then shown by examples. Lists of gods from many lands support the myth chapter. Greek, Roman, Egyptian, Hindu, and Norse names appear. Fairy lore is sorted by country in the same way. The nursery saga follows, with the Grimm brothers as guides. Working definitions close each treatment. Student writers of the day learned craft from such schemes. The book joins classroom order to the wild old tales.
6428-the-surgeon-s-daughter:
Walter Scott's Surgeon's Daughter, from the second series of Chronicles of the Canongate in 1827, was separated from the Highland Widow tales and deferred to this collection's close, for printers' reasons. An 1831 introduction explains the move, which hardly interests general readers. Johnson's verse on Levett, the village doctor whose useful care never mocked a summons with cold delay, opens the tale's praise of rural medicine.

Gideon Gray, Scott's surgeon, stands for village doctors from whom Scotland reaps more benefit than gratitude, schoolmasters excepted. Such a man serves a pretty borough or village as his practice's centre, day and night at the service of cases the village affords and beyond. Scott writes a tale of a surgeon's daughter caught between duty, love, and a father's calling, in a Scotland where medicine is also ministry.
64280-two-ways-of-becoming-a-hunter:
Two Ways of Becoming a Hunter, by Harry Castlemon, author of the Gunboat and Rocky Mountain sets, was copyrighted in 1892 and published at Philadelphia by Porter and Coates. A front plate shows a college president with a young taxidermist. Twenty-nine chapters follow schoolboys Frank and Oscar through truancy, bushwhackers, a duck hunt, an island camp, a black fox, and a voice from a snow-drift.

Chapter one, Playing Truant, opens near nine in the morning. One boy declares it time they were off and wishes school-houses had never been invented. His friend answers flatly: he is not going to school today. He means to take French leave. Castlemon spins a boys' tale of the woods, where hunting is learned by practice, trouble, and a taxidermist's craft.
64341-moon-of-danger:
Albert de Pina's story, printed in Planet Stories in the summer of 1947, opens on a dying Mars. A red plague of metallic dust has eaten most of the planet's people and their cities, and the ionization towers that held it back are failing. Dar Mihelson, the stern leader of the survivors, tells his people by televise that their great ship, the Valiant, is their last chance. Venus is denied them, Mercury has barred its skies, and only Earth has offered sanctuary.

Earth, though, fears the deadly spores the refugees might carry, and a faction has risen against their coming. Ric Martin hurtles out to intercept the space-giant as the greatest minds of Earth gather at Mount Palomar to watch a world in its death-throes. The Valiant, Mihelson warns, is a fully equipped fighting ship, and will be used as one if it must.
64406-in-camp-with-l-company-second-regi:
Corporal George Petty wrote a record of his militia company, printed in New York and Albany. Company L of the Second Regiment, New Jersey Volunteer Infantry, was mustered into state service on June 22, 1893. Its headquarters stood at Paterson. Petty gives the book to his officers, his comrades in the ranks, and the memory of the dead.

Addison Ely led the company as captain, with Bookstaver and Blake as lieutenants. From its first season at rifle practice the company stood high in state records. One year it ranked near the top of fifty six companies. Drills, camps, inspections, and range work fill a proud small history of citizen soldiers in peace time.
64410-the-story-of-a-great-schoolmaster:
The Story of a Great Schoolmaster, by Wells, was published in New York in 1924. Macmillan issued the life in January of that year. Its subject is Sanderson, for many years headmaster of Oundle School. Eight chapters are listed at the front. Sanderson the man comes first. The modernisation of Oundle School follows. Competition replaced by group work, and school tied back to reality, take two chapters. His growth is traced in his sermons and scripture lessons.

The war and his propaganda of reconstruction take a chapter. The house of vision and the school chapel close the list. Wells says in his opening that of all the men he has met, one only stirred him to write a life. Sanderson was that man. The book is a famous writer's tribute to a teacher who remade a school.
64435-first-base-faulkner:
Christy Mathewson, the famous pitcher, wrote First Base Faulkner, a baseball novel for boys published in 1916. Charles Relyea drew the pictures. The hero is Joe Faulkner, who steps off a train in Amesville, Ohio, on a cold January morning with little luck to his name.

Joe looks for work, finds a friend, and forms a partnership before he ever reaches the ball field. Later chapters put him in the batting cage, at outdoor practice, and at a try-out for first base. A loan, a pursuit, and a trip west raise the stakes before the last games. Young readers of the day got sport, work, and pluck in one story, told by a man who had played the game at its highest level.
64446-buffalo-bill-peacemaker:
Buffalo Bill, Peacemaker, or On a Troublesome Trail, is a frontier tale by Colonel Prentiss Ingraham, printed by Street and Smith with a 1910 copyright. Ingraham was a friend of William Cody, and an opening appreciation tells Cody's life. Cody was born in Scott County, Iowa, on February 26, 1846, and moved to Kansas while still in his teens.

When his father was killed in the Kansas border war, young Bill became his family's breadwinner. Through 1860 he rode the pony express, and he served as a government scout and guide through the Civil War. The thirty chapters that follow open with a prisoner in a dugout and a game of freeze out. They run through flush days in Texas and a sky pilot taking a hand. A fiendish plot and peace on the Brazos come later.
64458-a-silent-singer:
A Silent Singer is a book of short stories by Clara Morris, the actress. Brentano's of New York published it in 1899. Morris dedicated the stories to the small public of her very own, her mother and her husband, who had listened to her, criticised gently and encouraged heartily.

The contents list eleven tales: the title story, An Old Hulk, The Gentleman Who Was Going To Die, Old Myra's Waiting, Two Buds, and others. One title is simply Dinah, and another is Life's Aftermath. The title story opens on a hot day, as a country minister brings the narrator and her mother from the city to his country home in an ancient buggy. Morris jokes that country ministers alone can find that breed of buggy, which rattles on for years past its seeming end, carrying people and merchandise alike.
64561-the-berserker:
The Berserker, by Charles de Vet, ran in Planet Stories in March 1953. The tale is set on an other-dimensional world where men run large and strong. Big Jim Ostby stands six feet four and weighs two hundred and thirty-five pounds, yet he draws no special notice there.

Ostby lights a cigar on the street while his eyes sweep every face that passes. The police are after a killer called the Berserker, and word spreads that they have him cornered in the Flats. A net is drawn round the district that a fly could not slip through, men say. Street gamblers still give odds of two to one that he makes his escape. Ostby keeps out of the shadows and waits for an opening.
64635-frank-merriwell-s-first-job-or-at-:
Frank Merriwell's First Job, or At the Foot of the Ladder, is a boys' novel by Standish. The contents list thirty six chapters of railroad adventure. A Blow by Fate and Farewell to Yale open the tale. The reward of wrongdoing and a man who worked the wires follow. Captured by Whitecaps stands among the early chapters. Frank's strange friend and work for his enemy come next. The Bully of the Roundhouse gives a chapter its name.

Striking a Job and The First Foreenoon start Frank's working life. Frank discovers a break and captures a wild engine later. Firing a freight engine and a fight on the engine raise the pace. Merriwell's Generosity and an ungrateful man test his character. On Time, At Last closes the contents with a railroad triumph. The tale sends the Yale hero to the bottom rung of work.
64690-the-dead-star-rover:
The Dead-Star Rover, by Robert Abernathy, was produced from Planet Stories for winter 1949. A head summary sets the stakes: only savage engines roamed that arid world, charging one another with snarling guns beneath grinding treads. Two puny, machine less humans should die quickly there.

That Torcred and Ladna suddenly become the most dangerous things alive must be some dead god joke, the blurb adds. The tale opens with a terrapin travelling eighty miles an hour, far too fast for such uneven country. The wiry driver was furiously impatient, two hours behind his troop. Readers get a pulp tale of men against war machines on a dead world.
647-the-dynamiter:
Robert Louis Stevenson and Fanny Van de Grift Stevenson write a tale of anarchists and bombs in this 1885 volume, subtitled More New Arabian Nights. The Cigar Divan in Soho frames the stories. Prince Florizel, dethroned and now a tobacconist, hears tales of the Squire of Dames, the Superfluous Mansion, the Brown Box, and Zero's explosive bomb.

The Stevensons write with wit and adventure, mixing crime, comedy, and political horror. A dedication to police officers Cole and Cox sets the tone: crime is ugly even under sounding names. The book endures as a lively sequel, where London plots and Paris bombs meet in a cigar shop.
64783-mortal-summer:
Mark Van Doren wrote Mortal Summer in verse. The Prairie Press of Iowa City printed it in 1953. The poem opens in a cave on Mount Olympus. Seven gods wake there from a sleep of centuries. Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael fly toward a ship. All ten will sail on it, the lines say.

Athene's grey eyes question Hermes at the start. Hermes denies that he woke the rest. Apollo, Ares, and Aphrodite rose at one instant. Artemis and Hephaestus woke with them too. A mortal summer, not endless death, called them back. The lame smith admires the bright gods around him. Van Doren sets old gods loose in a brief, strange season. The poem asks what such beings do with one short span of life on earth.
64815-trips-in-the-life-of-a-locomotive-:
Trips in the Life of a Locomotive Engineer is a set of sketches by a working engineer, printed at New York in 1863 and entered for copyright in 1860. The author names himself only as one who shared the dangerous lot of railroad men, and he dedicates the book to them as a class he ever found generous and brave. His preface argues their case at length.

Railroad men, he writes, have been blamed for every disaster while their skill, bravery, and presence of mind went unsung. He holds that their gathered deeds would rank with those of any class that copes with disaster. The sketches aim to show the dangers passed by those who drive the iron horse, and to give the men of the footplate a chronicler at last.
64831-deeds-barn-and-the-self-starter:
Deeds Barn and the Self-Starter is a museum pamphlet about a famous Dayton, Ohio workshop. The barn was the birthplace of the modern ignition system for automobiles and of the electric self-starter. A 1912 Cadillac, the first car commercially equipped with a self-starter, stands as the central exhibit.

The original barn stood on Central Avenue in Dayton, and an exact replica stands in Carillon Park. Portraits show Kettering and Deeds, the men behind the invention, from about the time their Delco firm was founded. The text compares the starter's growth to the cash register's. A factory room forty by eighty feet, with thirteen people, grew into an industry on which the sun never set. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
64871-gene-stratton-porter-best-seller:
Staff of the Public Library of Fort Wayne and Allen County prepared a life of Gene Stratton Porter in April 1953. At Sylvan Lake she met a Geneva druggist, Charles Darwin Porter, and married him in 1886. They lived a year near the court house in Decatur, then settled in Geneva. Her husband rose in the local bank and gained from land that later yielded oil.

After visiting the 1893 exposition, the couple designed a fourteen room house called Limberlost Cabin. It was their home for twenty six years. Porter led a bucket brigade at a Geneva fire and was badly burned. The Limberlost Swamp, rich in wildlife, drew her deepest interest.
64888-in-trust-the-story-of-a-lady-and-h:
M O W Oliphant wrote In Trust, the story of a lady and her lover, in a new edition published at London in 1883. Oliphant is named as author of The Chronicles of Carlingford. Thirty-five chapters open with Father and Daughter, then The Rest of the Family and The Game.

Under the beeches, explanations, and a good-bye follow. The Meadowlands party, Cosmo, family counsels, and projects of marriage fill the early middle. A catastrophe, the will, and Heathcote's proposal drive the plot on. The heiress's trial and the rector satisfied appear near the close. Readers get a Victorian novel of property, trust, and a love tested by family manoeuvre.
64991-the-story-of-alexander:
Robert Steele retold The Story of Alexander, published by David Nutt in London in 1894 with drawings by Fred Mason. The book begins with an open letter to a young reader named Gracie. Steele explains that most fairy tales had already been well told by his friend Joseph Jacobs and others. He turned instead to the tales people loved hundreds of years ago.

In old English halls, he writes, families gathered round the fire to hear of a brave knight and a wicked enchanter. Travelling tale-tellers brought the newest stories from France and Italy. Steele chose the medieval Alexander romance for his retelling: the life and wonders of Alexander the Great as the Middle Ages imagined them. The book offers young readers a story from the age of castles, told plainly and pictured throughout, in the spirit of the winter evenings when such tales were first enjoyed.
65000-familiar-studies-in-homer:
Agnes M Clerke wrote Familiar Studies in Homer, issued by Longmans, Green and Company in London and New York in eighteen ninety two. A Latin motto heads the book, From Homer every beginning. A preface states the change in Homeric study. Homeric archaeology has left the groove of purely academic discussion, she says. It advances along a new route laid down by practical methods, she adds.

Excavations in Greece, Egypt, and Asia Minor have changed the aspect of the Homeric problem, Clerke holds. They promise a satisfactory solution, she says. The results imply a reconstruction of the Hellenic past, she argues. They make the Homeric world an historical reality, not a poetical creation alone, she adds. Yet few beyond scholars have realized their value, she laments. General readers get Schliemann age Homer in plain essays.
65047-the-british-campaign-in-france-and:
Arthur Conan Doyle closes his war history with the last drive in France and Flanders, from July to November 1918. Hodder and Stoughton issued the London volume as part of a set that starts with Mons and the Marne in 1914. Maps, plans, and charts walk with the text through each phase of the push.

Chapter heads track the turn of the tide after the French stroke of July 18 and the attack at Amiens on August 8. Rawlinson's Fourth Army and Byng's Third Army then press on past Albert and the old Somme field. Doyle names the Scots, Canadian, and Australian troops who bore hard fights at Buzancy, Chipilly, and Mont St Quentin. The road leads at last to the Hindenburg Line.
65085-the-barrier:
Bryce Walton spins a tale of a test pilot and a pardon in a story from Imagination for February 1951. Stevens can win a pardon on Earth if he crosses the high-speed barrier at the edge of space. Ten or fifteen people watch him go in gray rain, and none of them cheers.

Major Kanin wishes him luck without belief, having sent too many men on one-way trips. Mechanics shove Stevens headfirst into a torpedo-like craft his crew calls the Coffin. The cockpit is a tube barely larger than his body, with two inches between his helmet plate and the panel. No one knows why none of the earlier pilots came back. Readers get a stark tale of speed, guilt, and a bargain with death.
65101-maid-to-order:
Maid—to Order is a science fiction story by Hal Annas, printed in Imagination magazine in February 1951. Herb Cornith does not mind marrying, the headnote says, so long as the girl answers his strict specifications, which amount to a superwoman.

At the bureau, the willowy blonde clerk insists that Cornith himself fits Lucy Hollowell's specifications perfectly, since she specified a man very exacting, meticulous, and choosy. Cornith quibbles anyway: the sheet errs by an ounce in her weight and by an inch in his height, and he doubts he is handsome. The clerk corrects the typographical error, promises a second sheet tomorrow, and assures him the corrected copy is coming, while Cornith keeps finding fault.
65115-power-through-prayer:
Power Through Prayer, by EM Bounds, is a short book urging ministers and church members to give prayer the first place in their work. The copy here is the twelfth edition, with opening words by the Reverend AC Dixon and Albert A Head.

Dixon tells how the book reached him twice as a gift before he read it. One line stayed with him: the church looks for better methods, while God looks for better men. Bounds argues that preaching, study, and church plans all fail without long, earnest prayer behind them. He draws on the lives of noted praying men of the past to show what such prayer achieves. The book's call is plain: power in prayer, desire for prayer, and time set apart for prayer.
65125-a-journey-of-a-jayhawker:
A Journey of a Jayhawker is a travel book by Morgan of Hutchinson, Kansas, printed at Topeka in 1905 with illustrations by Albert Reid. The chapters are letters Morgan wrote for the Hutchinson Daily News on a European tour, printed without revision. His preface refuses excuses: any mistakes are the printer's, and any good grammar likewise.

The tour runs from Boston across the Atlantic to Ireland, Paris, Rome, Venice, the Alps, the Rhine, Holland, Belgium and England, ending at King Edward's house and the Tower. The first letter jokes about the traveller's self-importance: a man bound for Europe imagines every passerby saying so, while the other fellow only wonders whether he will be repaid his two dollars. The Jayhawker's eye is a Kansas newspaper eye: democratic, dry and determined to find Europe both wonderful and faintly absurd.
65130-the-power-of-sexual-surrender:
Marie Robinson wrote The Power of Sexual Surrender, for Doubleday in 1959. She was a psychiatrist, and author of a book on the drug addict. The library card number and the rights stand in the front matter. Her preface opens on the misery she sees in her profession. Destructive misunderstanding between men and women fills her days, she writes.

Contents fall in four sections, opening with paradise lost. The normal woman is the first section's theme, with the normal response. The psychology of frigidity fills the long second section. What frigidity is, and the war between men and women, stand there. Case histories of the fear of love fill the third section. Total and partial frigidity and the masculine woman take chapters. The bridge to womanhood and the nature of surrender close the book. Robinson argues a woman's fulfilment in yielded love.
65162-the-vagaries-of-tod-and-peter:
Allen Harker wrote The Vagaries of Tod and Peter, a set of tales printed at New York in 1923. Harker gives the book to Margaret Gwenelin Watson with love and high hopes. Contents split the tales three ways: boys first, then children of the last century, then children of this one.

Twins Tod and Peter star in the lead tale. Neighbours call them those dreadful twins, school staff call them far worse, and schoolfellows admire them as the most sly and surplus naughty boys they know. Their mother laughs, loves them, and trusts they will mend, as her six older sons turned out well in the world. Heads promise Tony, a square peg, a small event, and the surrender of Lady Grizell across warm, witty family tales.
6521-the-king-of-the-dark-chamber:
Tagore opens his play on a street where strangers ask a guard the way to a great feast, and learn that any road will lead them there. The talk is light at first, yet it points to the play's core riddle: a king who rules unseen, and a people who must trust a voice they cannot see. From that street scene, the drama moves inward, toward faith and doubt.

The king stays hidden in a dark chamber while queens, guards, and common folk weigh rumor, hope, and fear. Tagore, who made his own English version, lets the verse-like speech carry both story and symbol. The King of the Dark Chamber is a short, strange play about seeking a ruler who will not show his face.
65220-the-answer:
Emil Petaja wrote a dark tale that ran in Imagination in September 1951. John Reeve has strangled his wife Lisa many times in dreams. Each time, as she dies, the phone rings. The story asks whether he dares pick it up and answer the call.

Reeve stands in a dark room where the blinds are shut tight. He cannot see the bed or his own tall form in the mirror. He can hear Lisa breathing and smell her perfume in the hot, still air. He has forgotten who he is and how he got into her flat. Petaja builds dread from memory loss and a ringing phone.
65232-the-shadow-eater:
The Shadow Eater is a book of poems by Benjamin De Casseres, copyrighted in 1915 and issued at New York in 1917. The poems are dedicated to a man who was first to understand, value, and feel with them, the dedication says. This first edition ran to six hundred fifty copies. One hundred fifty were printed on hand made paper and signed by the author, the front pages boast.

The contents open with the protagonist, then a poem whose title is a trumpet call twice over. The tongueless one, a shrine in the mist, and my comic perspective follow. The peeper, a circle that looks like a line, and my divine hate fill the early list. The rotted ideal, a vision of evil, dying, and the dead who live come in one dark run. A cynic of Nazareth and a poem on a marriage close the visible heads.
65264-discipline-in-school-and-cloister:
Discipline in School and Cloister, by Jacobus X, was printed at Paris by Isidore Liseux in 1902 in five hundred copies for subscribers. The study traces the birch rod and the whip through schools and religious houses across the ages. It asks whether beating truly mends vicious or unruly children, or risks harm of another kind.

The text quotes Father Debreyne, priest and doctor, urging that the practice be cast out of homes and schools as harmful to morals. Sparta and Athens supply early cases from the old world. Plutarch stands out as an ancient voice against ruling children by blows.
65313-the-sublime-jester:
Ezra Brudno wrote this novel, The Sublime Jester, printed in New York in 1924. A line from Also Sprach Zarathustra heads the book, on a soul calm as mountains in the morning. The tale runs in three parts: a poet in the making, a fighter in the making, and a cynic in the making. Women named Hedwiga, Hilda, Eugenie, Miriam, and Marguerite mark the stages.

In a note Brudno says his hero, Albert Zorn, follows the life and career of Heinrich Heine. He chose Heine as a symbol of the spirit of his age and his people. The tale opens in Gunsdorf, where young Albert dreams on his way to school. Word has come from Amsterdam that a kinsman has died and left his father's small shop a fortune.
65314-little-joe-otter:
A children's nature story by Thornton W Burgess. Grosset and Dunlap published it at New York in 1925. Harrison Cady drew the illustrations. The book belongs to the Smiling Pool series. Its neighbours are Billy Mink and Jerry Muskrat at Home. Burgess lists his many series on the opening pages. Peter Rabbit threads through them all as the curious listener.

Little Joe Otter springs a surprise in chapter one. Peter Rabbit goes looking for his home soon after. Swimming lessons and a slippery slide give the young otters glory. Farmer Brown's Boy sets traps and lurks as the danger. Yowler the Bobcat follows the family on a journey. Burgess taught animal habits through these gentle adventures. Generations of children learned natural history from his storybooks.
65323-a-first-reader:
Spaulding and Bryce wrote a first book for children who learn to read. The book came out in New York in 1906. Both held school chief posts in Minneapolis in that day. Margaret Ely Webb drew its many plates for the young. It sits in the Aldine Readers set for grade schools.

With the Birds leads the book, and Out of Doors comes next. The Wind, the Leaves, and the Snow give short, plain reads. Small Birdie and the squirrel tales add song and fun. In Summer Time heads the next set of wee lessons. Each piece is brief, with words a new reader can sound. Bright plates hold young eyes.
65348-barnstormer:
Barnstormer is a short tale of a rocket man by Tom Harris. It first ran in a fiction magazine in October of nineteen fifty seven. Murph, its pilot, owns a silver ship and a pass to the stars. A boy named Pete longs for one ride in that bright ship.

The ship stands in a farm field, slim and black like a tall flask. Pete slips past brush to beg his ride ere the ship leaves town. His gran and his mother hate the ship as an ill sign in glass. To them its beauty makes the threat worse, not less, in their eyes. Longing and fear clash round the craft in the brief tale.
65380-washington-the-soldier:
Henry Carrington wrote this life, Washington the Soldier, printed at New York in 1899 with pictures, maps, a dated index, and appendices. Carrington also wrote Battles of the American Revolution and works on the Indian wars of the plains. He dedicates the book to the sons and daughters of liberty everywhere.

His watchword for Washington stands in the dedication: for the sake of God and country. Contents march through the whole war. Early promise gives way to the ferment of American liberty and its outbreak. Armed America needs a soldier, and Washington takes command. Boston is taken, the war is put on a system, and Howe invades New York. Long Island, Harlem Heights, White Plains, Trenton, and Princeton follow in order.
65381-on-translating-homer:
On Translating Homer collects Matthew Arnold's famous lectures on how Homer should be turned into English. This edition, from Routledge in London and Dutton in New York, binds the whole quarrel in one volume. Arnold's three lectures come first, then Newman's reply, then Arnold's Last Words in answer.

Arnold begins by explaining himself. It had more than once been suggested that he should translate Homer. That, he says, is a task for which he has neither the time nor the courage. But the suggestion set him studying Homer closely for a year or two. Though the study of classical literature declines, he argues, Homer will draw more readers as instruction spreads. His lectures name the qualities a translator must keep: rapidity, plainness of thought and nobility. Newman's Homeric Translation in Theory and Practice defends the ballad measure Arnold attacked.
65390-the-three-choirs-a-handbook-to-the:
Richard I King guides visitors in The Three Choirs, a handbook to the cathedrals of Gloucester, Hereford, and Worcester, from John Murray of London in 1866. The title page promises a complete description of the buildings, a history of each diocese, and biographical notices of the bishops. King was of Exeter College, Oxford.

Gloucester comes first, with sixteen illustrations. Its contents walk the south porch, nave, transepts, choir, and Lady Chapel, then the monuments, including that of Edward the Second, and the cloisters. A second part gives the history of the see, from King Lucius to the martyr Hooper and the bishops since.
65438-the-moon-maker:
The Moon Maker is a science fiction novel by Arthur Train and Robert Wood. A small press at Hamburg, New York, issued this edition in 1958. The printing was limited to five hundred copies. Frank McSherry drew the illustrations for the volume.

The story is told in five parts, from asteroid to moon. A summary at the front sets out the strange events behind it. During the world war, wireless messages signed Pax reached Washington's Naval Observatory. The sender claimed command over the forces of nature themselves. A craft called the Flying Ring then appeared in the heavens. Its lavender ray broke mountains in northern Africa and flooded the Sahara. Pax threatened to shift the earth's axis unless the nations made peace. Professor Benjamin Hooker sets out to find him.
65507-grandma-s-recipes-for-mother-and-d:
Grandma’s Recipes for Mother and Daughter is a free cook book from a molasses maker. The American Molasses Company issued it in New York in nineteen hundred fifty. Its plant stood at One Hundred Twenty Wall Street in that town. Breads, meats, cakes, cookies, and desserts fill its short list.

Grandma’s Unsulphured Molasses is the star of each dish here. No sulphur or guard drug taints the blend, the book boasts. Cane juice from the British West Indies feeds its best grades. New England has kept a molasses jug by the salt since old days. Buyers blend and age the grades for a smooth, rich taste. Waffles, bread, and milk take it at the plain board. Morn fruit through rich last course all call for its pour. The book sells the jar by giving the cook her week’s plan.
65521-guardians-of-the-tower:
Randall Garrett wrote this fantasy story, first printed in Imagination in April 1957. Jon is a guardsman of the Tower, one of many who for centuries have held swords against the Wild Ones, though he does not know why.

No one knows what the Tower is; it has stood by the sea as long as the Free People remember, sacred and always attacked. Jon, twenty-three, has fought in near twenty defenses. The story opens at dawn roll-call, then an enemy boat approaches, led by a giant over seven feet tall. Readers get a lean tale that asks what men defend when the reason is older than memory.
6563-the-blunderer:
Molière's early comedy, first played at Lyons in 1653 and in Paris five years later, turns on a servant whose eager help wrecks every plan. Mascarille, drawn from an Italian play by Nicolo Barbieri, means well but bungles each step, and his master's love plot keeps falling apart at his hands. The note that opens the text traces these debts with care.

A boasting soldier, sharp talk, and a string of counterplots keep the five acts in brisk motion. Molière changes the Italian ending to one he judged better, and adds scenes from other old comedies as he goes. The Blunderer is a lively early work, full of the mischief that would mark his later stage.
65634-a-nine-days-wonder:
A Nine Days' Wonder is a novel by Croker, published in London by Methuen in 1905. Croker wrote Anglo-Indian novels, among them Diana Barrington, Peggy of the Bartons, and The Cat's-Paw, as the list records. A French motto heads the tale: it takes greater virtue to bear good fortune than bad.

The first chapter opens at the Rag, the Army and Navy Club, on a wet October afternoon. A tall grey-haired soldier with a straight back stands at an upper window, his hands in his pockets and his face in medieval gloom. Colonel Doran makes no effort to hide his feelings. He has lived too long among a primitive race, and club life bores him after the East. Other men seem content. A nine days' wonder is a sensation that passes; Croker's title promises one among soldiers home from India.
65652-joyce-kilmer:
Joyce Kilmer collects the poems, essays, and letters of the American poet Joyce Kilmer, edited with a memoir by Robert Cortes Holliday. Doran Company published the set in New York, and this file holds volume one, the memoir and poems. Kilmer died in the First World War, and the book opens with a portrait of him at age thirty.

The poems fall into groups written in France and at home. War pieces stand beside verse on houses, roofs, snowmen, and small city scenes. The famous poem Trees appears here, along with the Rosary, Memorial Day, and a poem in memory of Rupert Brooke. Holliday's memoir frames the work of a poet whose short life and early death shaped how readers received him.
65656-roughriders-of-the-pampas-a-tale-o:
Captain Brereton wrote Roughriders of the Pampas, a tale of ranch life in South America under copyright in 1908, with pictures by Stanley Wood. Brereton had written many boys' adventure books, from How Canada Was Won to With Roberts to Candahar. This one sends a young Englishman across the ocean to a ranch, or rancho, on the grass plains.

The first chapter, Outward Bound, opens in a ship's saloon in the Bay of Biscay gales. A tall, kind passenger orders soup for Dudley Compton, a pale youth knocked flat by seasickness, and makes him eat it to feel a man again. The contents carry Dudley to the home on the pampas, where he shows his mettle, leads the gauchos against an Indian invasion, and fights white brigands. A front picture shows Dudley escaping with his prisoner. Readers get a fast ranch adventure of horsemen, raids, and tight corners.
65671-the-time-snatcher:
Randall Garrett wrote The Time Snatcher, a science fiction story first printed in Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy in February 1957. Its hero, Brek Halliday, works for the Time Patrol. He carries a pair of six-guns on a mission into the American past.

A man named Sagginer has forced a patrol operator to send him back in time, and taken her with him. If he changes history in a big way, the time-stream cannot smooth it out. Meter readings pin him to the old United States, somewhere between 1880 and 1895. The kidnapped operator is Dori Clayton, which makes the job personal for Brek. Garrett mixes western gunplay with time-travel rules in a fast pulp tale.
65686-henry-more-smith-the-mysterious-st:
Walter Bates, sheriff of Kings County, wrote the authentic account of Henry More Smith, the mysterious stranger. Bowes of Saint John printed this edition in 1910. Bates calls Smith the most noted road agent who ever pestered the authorities of New Brunswick.

Smith arrived at Windsor in Nova Scotia, obtained employment, professed religion, and married. Suspected of theft, he crossed into New Brunswick and was lodged in Kingston gaol. Before his trial a strange disease attacked him, baffling the physicians. Supposed to be dying, he escaped. Smith's escapes became legend: the dying man who rose, the prisoner no gaol could hold. The sheriff who hunted him wrote the book, which is why it reads as both a charge sheet and a marvel tale.
65730-world-of-the-hunter:
World of the Hunter, by C H Thames, is a short science fiction tale from the October 1956 issue of Imagination. Mulveen has come to Earth for a big game thrill. Gilbert, his guide, must supply that thrill, even if he must let himself be stalked.

The hunt opens in a swamp, and fast. A huge saurian, a thirty ton beast, splashes out with a high cry. Gilbert hands Mulveen an old Earth rifle that fires atomic shells. He stands bare of arms while the beast rears and falls. The set up hints that this hunt will not stay safe or fair for long.
65741-run-little-monster:
Chester Geier wrote this story, printed in Imagination in January 1952. Fran had heard about the monsters men hunted down and killed, but she had never seen one, until the night Sammy looked at her and screamed. The story opens with the girl running like the hunted thing she was.

Her bare feet flash over spring grass as she sobs for breath, her slight body trembling under a ragged dress. Two boys race after her, yelling threats. Davey Becker is hulking and dull-eyed; his brother Sammy, two years older and smaller, leads by cunning. Readers get a short tale that turns the word monster back on the hunters.
65753-earl-russell-and-the-slave-power:
Earl Russell and the Slave Power was put out at Manchester in 1863 by the Union and Emancipation Society, from its rooms at 51 Piccadilly. The front pages print the society's full roll, a roll of weight. Thomas Bayley Potter heads it as president. Mayors, members of Parliament, and dons stand as vice-presidents: John Stuart Mill, Goldwin Smith, and F W Newman among them. Churchmen, lawyers, and mill men of the north crowd the list.

The tract takes its name from its mark: the foreign chief of a land at war with itself over bondage. In the year of the great decree of freedom, such a body spoke for the North and for the slave. Record fans get a sharp leaf from the war of words that ran beside the war of arms.
65770-the-killer:
Oliver wrote The Killer, a crime tale printed in Imagination, Stories of Science and Fantasy, in March 1952. The head line gives the premise cold: Smith made a profitable business out of murder. He killed a man, then disposed of the body forever.

The sign on the door says Ernest Smith, Private Investigator. A brunette in a yellow dress walks in. She is Wilma Rogers, and she was recommended to him. Smith tests her card with red liquid from a desk drawer, and secret words rise: okay for any service. Then she says, pleasantly, that she wants her husband killed. He is stingy, and he will leave roughly two hundred thousand. Smith turns to his typewriter and asks what time would suit. She shrugs: any time. Pulp readers get murder run like a booking office.
65800-the-interloper:
The Interloper is a novel of Scotland by Violet Jacob, author of The Sheep-Stealers. Heinemann published the book at London in 1904. Jacob opens with an author's note dated 1903. She begs pardon for one fault she has kept on purpose.

Her gentle folk of the early eighteen hundreds speak plain modern English. In life, she says, high and low kept a Scots of their own, called court Scots. Two old ladies of her memory supplied her models for the sisters in the tale. The story is set on the east coast, by the estuary of the North Lour. An heir, a dovecote, and a looking glass open the family drama. Strife of tongues and plain speaking fill the middle books.
65820-the-bee-hunter:
George Harold Edgell wrote The Bee Hunter, printed at Cambridge in 1949 by Harvard University Press. The little treatise is part child of frustration and part of irritation, Edgell confesses at the start. At eighteen he wrote a first book with this title, submitted on Robert Chambers's advice, and saw it rejected by publishers.

Maeterlinck's Life of the Bee had lost money in English, the publisher tactfully explained to the young author. Irritation comes from articles by men who never could have found a bee tree by the methods they describe, Edgell charges. Fifty years a successful bee hunter, he writes the facts as bee hunting becomes a lost art. Burroughs came nearest truth. Woodsmen get the real craft.
65833-the-fire-flower:
The Fire Flower, a novel by Jackson Gregory, ran in the All-Story Weekly of March 3, 1917, from the Frank Munsey Company. Gregory had already written The Short Cut, Wolf Breed, and The Outlaw. His hero, Sheldon, rides north from Belle Fortune into country few men enter, and five days out he knows he has taken the wrong trail.

The land ahead is the Sasnokee-keewan, which the Indians call Bad Country and other men call No-Luck Land. It lies between Belle Fortune and the old Russian camp at Ruminoff Shanty, two hundred and forty miles apart. Gold camps stand at both ends, but the trails bend east or west around the iron mountains and lava rock between. Sheldon smokes his pipe in deep content at being lost. The tale is a northern adventure of the pulp years.
65839-the-stranger:
The Stranger is a science fiction story by Gordon R Dickson, taken from Imagination for May 1952. Its hook asks what an alien craft that is not a rocket ship can be, and whether the men who find one should look closer or run for their lives.

Jeff and Peter Wadley, son and father, bring their mining ship Emerald Girl down on an unnamed planet in the Buckhorn Cluster, five hundred and eighty-two days out of Arcturus Station. Only on the ground do they see the other ship, five hundred feet off against a cliff. Jeff beams the demand in Common Code: identify yourself. The demand crackles again and again, and no answer comes. Jeff wants to lift and report it to the Federal ships. His father says maybe it just landed, maybe it is in trouble, and they had better look into it.
6584-princess-polly-s-gay-winter:
Amy Brooks brings Princess Polly back for a gay winter at Avondale, where little Rose Atherton deems no spot lovelier in all the world. A summer at the shore gives way to school days, a sea nymph play, a new friend named Gwen, and a call that brings joy. Uncle John, Aunt Judith, and Aunt Rose all have parts in the fun.

Parties, a holiday frolic, and Gyp's small ambition fill the chapters with warm, home-like cheer. Brooks writes in a gentle voice for young girls, with manners, kindness, and play as the chief lessons. Princess Polly's Gay Winter is a cozy seasonal tale, bright with friendship and family love.
65844-the-flag-of-the-adventurer:
Sydney Grier wrote a novel of the modern east, printed at Edinburgh and London in 1921 with a front picture by A Pearse. Chapter one brings Eveleen Ambrose up a ships ladder after four days and nights of being tossed in a cabin. She begs pardon of a man she bumps, then laughs weakly at her own state.

Her husband Richard speaks sharply and sets her in a corner of the deck. Twenty five chapters follow, with a colonel named Bayard, a seal of Solomon, and the entry of the adventurer of the title. A contest of wits, deeds not words, and Brian to the rescue fill the later run.
65853-the-driver:
Garet Garrett wrote The Driver, a novel printed at New York in 1922, with a first printing in September and a second in October. Contents promise phantasma, a funk idol, Galt, an economic nightmare, Vera, a giant in baby sweat, daring the dark, low water, heyday, hearth notes, success, combat, and the heights.

Easter Sunday in Massillon, Ohio, opens the tale in 1894, fourth year of the soft Money Plague, with church bells remote and disapproving. The Army of the Commonweal of Christ will set forth on foot from the village in quest of the Economic Millennium, advertised in every newspaper. A railroad financier's rise drives Garrett's business epic onward. Finance readers get a period saga.
65861-the-mischievous-typesetter:
The Mischievous Typesetter, a science fiction story by Noel Loomis, ran in Imagination in July 1952. The blurb plays on a proud saying about man and machines. Man is the master of any machine he can devise, they say. Whoever coined the phrase did not know this linotype, a machine with a mind of its own.

The story opens in a courtroom, before a judge of strong views. In his opinion, a linotype operator stands near the bottom of the scale of humanity. Only the poet stands beneath him, the judge declares. His eyes turn on High Pockets, a gangling man seven feet tall. Threat hangs in the air of that comic start. Loomis builds a tall tale on a printing machine gone rogue.
6590-quotations-from-the-pg-collected-wo:
David Widger gathers striking lines from the collected novels of Gilbert Parker, for readers who want to find a favorite passage fast. His editor's note invites new tips from readers, and notes that web publication lets him fix and add lines with ease. Each quote can be traced back to its novel by a search for a short phrase.

The set spans Parker's tales of Canada and the wider world, in his own words, without added comment. It works best as a companion to the novels, not as a stand-alone book. Widger's Quotations gives Parker fans a quick path to lines they loved, and a prompt to read the full tales again.
65949-psychology-and-copper:
Tuttle wrote Psychology and Copper, a western story told in dialect round a campfire. Ike Harper, the narrator, climbs out of a gopher hole, fills his pipe, and delivers his doctrine. Scientific prospecting has its merits, he grants, but fool luck has uncovered more bonanzas than science. Jerry Sullivan's burro slid down a hill and uncovered the Silver Cross, making him a millionaire.

The talk turns to Magpie Simpkins, an elongated person nobody ever had the pleasure of knowing. Magpie was a scientific prospector who could read a rock like a book, and never made a strike. He was also loco on everything except work, beginning with hypnotism tried on a wildcat. Tuttle's tale connects Magpie, two claims on Plenty Stone Creek, and the defunct Copper King mine into one yarn of luck against learning.
65956-the-beachcomber:
Damon Knight wrote The Beachcomber, a tale from Imagination in December 1952. A front note sets up the clash in one line. Alice saw the Beachcomber as a fine hunk of man. Maxwell saw him as a super being from the future. In truth, the note says, he was both.

Maxwell and Alice start a weekend on Thursday in Venice. They go to Paris on Friday and to Nice on Saturday. By Sunday they are bored stiff. Alice pushes away insect eggs served at a vast price. Maxwell counts the cost of five rich days with dread. He writes scripts for a state news unit and bosses six gag men. The tale mixes a rich future with a strange guest.
65977-time-grabber:
Time Grabber, a science fiction tale by Gordon Dickson, ran in Imagination in December 1952. A blurb frames the puzzle: switching sixteen Romans from the first century to the twenty-seventh looked like sound research. But who was going to take their place? The tale unfolds in diary entries and memos that jump between eras.

A scholar of the year 2631 writes in his diary of February 16. He chafes under Croton Myers, the physicist who controls the time-grapple and will not let him use it. Myers warns of tearing the fabric of time and talks of twenty years of trials. The scholar's fame in sociomatics is at stake, and he vows to act without leave. A memo from ancient Rome then asks for Christians to fight gladiators. Dickson plays the swap for dry comedy.
6600-the-moccasin-maker:
Pauline Johnson's prose, gathered soon after her death in 1913, speaks from two worlds at once. The daughter of a Mohawk chief and a white mother, she lived for years on the Iroquois Reserve, and her tales carry that life in their bones. An introduction by Gilbert Parker and praise from Charles Mair frame the set.

Stories of her mother, of a red girl's reasoning, of a pagan in St. Paul's, and of Lillooet Falls move between reserve, town, and church. Johnson writes with pride, wit, and a clear eye for both peoples she belonged to. The Moccasin Maker is a warm, important record of a Native writer finding her voice in print.
66066-nat-the-trapper-and-indian-fighter:
Nat, the Trapper and Indian-Fighter is a frontier tale by Paul J Prescott, issued in New York by Beadle and Adams. The copyright entry dates the tale to eighteen seventy two under a prior publisher. Twelve short chapters carry the whole story in dime novel form. Chapter heads promise a ledge, a wild chase, and a lost girl named Marion.

A hole in a hill, a happy meeting, and a last hope mark the rising action. Toward noon on a June day a rider on a mustang crosses the plain as the tale opens. Beadle's cheap tales sold adventure to boys by the millions. Scouts, traps, fights, and rescues follow the house formula with pace.
66088-recollections-of-captain-wilkie-a-:
A Conan Doyle tells a railway tale of a practised criminal in a short story headed by his name. The narrator rides second class on the London and Dover Railway, bound for Paris gaieties.

He pulls his cap down and studies his companion under its brim. Who can he be? The narrator prides himself on spotting a man's trade by his look. He learned the art from a master of it. That teacher once told a patient his fingers played some curious instrument for a living. The man blew Rule Britannia on a coffee-pot, its spout pierced as a flute. The companion across the carriage seems vulgar, fairly opulent, and extremely self-possessed. He could out-chaff a bargee yet sit easy in middle-class society. Doyle builds the piece on close watching.
66112-purpose-in-prayer:
Purpose in Prayer is a devotional work by Bounds, published by Revell at New York in 1920. Bounds is named as author of Power through Prayer on the title page. A portrait of Edward Bounds fronts the volume for its readers in this edition. A sketch of his life in the book tells how the last seventeen years were spent.

He lived those years with his family in Washington, in Georgia, in the sketch account. Most of the time he was reading, writing, and praying in that retirement of his age. He rose at four in the morning each day for many years for his prayer. He was indefatigable in his study of the Bible, the sketch adds in praise.  Purpose is his word for the aiming of prayer at a mark, and this book presses that aim.
66138-guaranteed-forever:
Guaranteed Forever is a short tale of a fraud hunt gone strange. Frank Robinson wrote it for a pulp book of the year 1953. Its hero, Manning, has spent his life on mail fraud hunts. A new firm tops all the frauds he has met in his work.

The firm's goods are too good to be true, yet they stand real. The tale opens on a mean street just north of the town Loop. Cheap bars and cheap rooms line the walk of that old street. A host of trade trick men have their dens on that strip. Manning parks his car with a scratch to the paint at the start. A pain in his side, hid from his mate, ticks like a clock in him.
66154-the-music-master:
The Music Master is a science fiction story by F L Wallace, taken from Imagination for December 1952. Danny Tocar slips away from his mother after a concert and climbs onto the stage. The instruments left behind are heavy, solid, and silent.

The performers were robots, and the instruments are toys. Real music came from somewhere else, a harmony the boy remembers as synthony. One large instrument stands apart in a transparent case. Danny finds the hidden opening and gets inside. Its white markings are keys, and his fingers copy what he saw. Sound rolls out into the empty hall. Without knowing it, he has made the first human music in a hundred years. The blurb adds his ambition: robots can play but cannot write music. Danny wants to do both, even if it means facing the psych squad.
66176-earthmen-ask-no-quarter:
Earthmen Ask No Quarter is a science fiction story by Fox B Holden. It appeared in Imagination in December 1953. General Taylor of the New United Nations World Space Force faces the press. He is impossibly exhausted after a day and night of useless words. Foreign admirals and defence secretaries have come and gone. The promised ion-field cannon never arrived.

Taylor tells the reporters that the alien ship is hostile. Its hostility, he hopes, may be mollified. The ship is cigar-shaped, about three miles long. It circles Earth some two thousand miles out, passing the stations every forty-eight hours. Contact has been made, but the result is classified. Rumours say the 402nd Space Wing sent J-83 Lancers from Lunar Base and lost them. The blurb gives the story's turn. Taylor knew Earth could not resist, so he ordered surrender. One commander read the order otherwise, and fought.
66230-an-address-to-the-people-of-new-en:
An Address to the People of New England is a sermon pamphlet by Samuel Hopkins, pastor of a church in Springfield. It was printed at Boston in seventeen fifty three as a conclusion to memoirs on the Housatunnuk Indians. Its text from the Acts holds that God is no respecter of persons. The title states its whole argument in one long sentence.

Hopkins urges the great importance of attaching the Indians to the English interest, his title says. That must be done by treating them justly and kindly, he argues. It must also be done by proper efforts to settle Christianity among them. Mission, fairness, and frontier politics are bound together in a colonial pastor's plea.
66327-the-sun-of-saratoga-a-romance-of-b:
The Sun of Saratoga, a Romance of Burgoyne Surrender, by Joseph Altsheler, was published in New York in 1897. The novel opens on watch, with a general telling the narrator to guard a hollow and a hill. No soul is to pass north or south, and the fate of all the colonies may rest on his care.

The narrator feels the weight of that trust, with thirteen colonies and millions of folk behind him. Chapter heads move through a light in a window, a shot, Burgoyne camp, and a night under fire. Later come a pursuit, a chase, the taking of Chudleigh, a battle of the guns, and terms of surrender. Readers get a war romance of the American fight for freedom, told close to the ground.
66332-good-newes-from-new-england-or-a-t:
Good Newes from New England is an early account of the Plymouth colony by Edward Winslow, first printed in London in 1624. The hosted text follows the reprint of 1841, which adds many footnotes by its editor. Winslow signed himself only with his initials, and said he had borne a part in the troubles he tells.

The title page sets out the contents. The book shows the providence of God in the settlers' keeping, through many seeming deaths and dangers. It tells of the laws and customs, religious and civil, of the Indians who lived beside them. It lists the goods that the country could raise to keep the plantation up. A short account of the present state of Virginia is added at the end.
66381-messenger:
Messenger, a short science fiction tale by William Morrison, ran in Imagination in July 1954. A lone being who moves through space without a ship must find one planet in the vast universe and do a task there. The catch is sharp: a nova blast has wiped his memory of where to go and what to do.

He had grown careless after ages of travel and failed to note a white dwarf about to blow. The blast hit him with no shield, and he woke far past the star, rushing toward a cluster a thousand light years away. He slows, sure that cluster is not his goal. Dread and duty drive a spare tale of loss and search.
66431-the-missing-disclaimer:
Missing Disclaimer is a science fiction story by Sam Sackett. It first reached print in a magazine of science and fantasy in November nineteen fifty four, the hosted note says. Its headnote gives the hinge of the plot: an editor's error cost him his job. It also created a grave problem for a being called K seventeen. As an invader, had he walked into a trap, the note asks.

The tale opens in the office of a science fiction magazine. The publisher storms in waving the first issue and fires the editor on the spot. The contents page lacks the usual notice, he roars. That notice says the persons in the stories bear no likeness to real people. Without it, libel suits will ruin them, he insists. The scene then cuts to K seventeen with a copy of the magazine.
66506-observations-on-abortion-containin:
Observations on Abortion is an old med book on the loss of the unborn. John Burns, who taught the birth craft in Glasgow, wrote it. The book came out in London in the year 1806. He gives it to the men who sat in his class of 1802.

Burns sets out what the word means in the craft of his day. It is the loss of the womb's load too soon for the child to live. Such loss is rife, he says, and fraught with grief at the time. It can sow harm that shows its face at a late date as well. The book tells how the loss comes on and what brings it on. It ends with the means to ward it off or to ease its ills.
66618-the-pioneer:
The Pioneer is a science fiction story by Irving Cox Jr. It ran in Imagination in October 1955. Greg, its hero, is a pilot grown old at forty in a young space age.

Greg brings his worn ship down with skill that no new gear can match. He thinks with bitterness that he gave men the stars. In twenty years they have made him a museum piece. The young now hold a whole planet in their hands. Greg doubts they have the wisdom for such power. The tale turns on age, pride and being left behind. Cox keeps the tale short, sharp and sad at heart.
66629-historical-record-of-the-sixty-fir:
Historical Record of the Sixty-First, or the South Gloucestershire Regiment, stands in the great set of regimental histories made by order of the Horse Guards. A general order of January 1, 1836, set the pattern for the whole set. The King had charged that an account of the services of every regiment in the British Army be printed, under the eye of the Adjutant-General.

That order fixed what each record must hold: the raising of the regiment, its stations, and its battles and sieges. It also called for the names of men killed and wounded, and of those honoured with titles or medals for gallant work. This volume gives the Sixty-First that full, formal record.
66650-the-life-of-the-grasshopper:
Henri Fabre's essays on the grasshopper kind were gathered in English dress by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos and printed at London. The fable of the cicada and the ant opens the book. The cicada leaving the burrow, her change of skin, her music, and the laying and hatching of her eggs follow. The mantis at her hunting, love making, nest, and hatching takes four chapters.

The empusa, the white faced decticus, the green grasshopper, and the cricket at his burrow and song come next. Locusts, their work, sound organ, eggs, and last moult close the tale, with the foamy cicadella. Fabre watched insects for years in a dry Provence garden, and his patient eyes turned small lives into high drama for common readers.
6667-poems-of-power:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox explains her title in a note: the final word means the divine power in every human being, whose recognition is the secret of all success and joy. Many verses in the book try to show that idea at work. The Queen's Last Ride, The Meeting of the Centuries, Grief, Illusion, Assertion, and I Am lead the contents.

First issued in 1903 and reprinted again and again, the volume won Wilcox a wide, loyal audience. Her verse is plain, bold, and meant to stir the will. Poems of Power is a stirring set for readers who like poetry that urges them to stand tall and trust their own inner force.
66684-life-and-remarkable-adventures-of-:
The Life and Remarkable Adventures of Israel Potter is the true story of an American soldier of the Revolution, first printed in 1824. The hosted edition is a faithful copy of that printing, with an introduction by Leonard Kriegel. Potter's tale later served as the base of Herman Melville's novel of the same name.

Potter fought at Bunker Hill and took three wounds there. He was seized by the British and carried to England. For thirty years he kept himself and his family in London by crying old chairs to mend in the streets. He came home at last, old and infirm. Melville, in his dedication of 1854, calls the first printing a blurred record on cheap grey paper, sold by peddlers. The edition adds the last chapters of Melville's novel at the back.
66697-the-fighter:
The Fighter is a novel by Albert Payson Terhune, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York under a copyright of 1909. Its hero is Caleb Conover, the railroad magnate of Terhune's earlier Caleb Conover, Railroader. Terhune dedicated the book to his wife, his kindest and severest critic.

The cast list introduces Conover as a self-made man who glorifies his maker. Amzi Nicholas Caine, a young newspaper owner, stands against him, and Desirée makes plans of her own. The chapters follow Conover's combats: he wins, fights, explains, runs away, and storms a rampart. A battle, a peace conference, moonlight and mistakes, and forest madness follow, to the last fight. The opening portrait sets the type: he had always been fighting, and the square jaw and bull neck proclaim him of the battling breed.
66882-summer:
Summer is volume two of The Soul Enchanted, a long novel by Romain Rolland, turned from French by Eleanor Stimson and Van Wyck Brooks. Henry Holt printed it in New York in 1925. Volume one is Annette and Sylvie, and the heroine is Annette.

A stern motto heads the book, to strive, to seek, not to find, and not to yield. Fifty one chapters fall into three parts. The tale opens in a dim room with closed shutters, where Annette sits on her bed and smiles. Her washed hair, still loose, falls over her white gown. Waves of soft feeling pass through her rest. Rolland writes the inner life of a woman in fine, slow detail. Readers of deep character tales will find his art here.
67005-an-index-to-the-first-thirty-three:
An Index to the First Thirty-Three Volumes of the Yale Literary Magazine covers the magazine from February 1836 to July 1868. It was compiled by L H Bagg, of the class of 1869, and printed at New Haven in 1868. Only three hundred impressions were struck, and readers are urged to preserve their copies.

The index is sorted into prose, verse, memorabilia, illustrations, Yale Lit essays, DeForest orations, Townsend essays, and a list of editors. A note explains the volume-and-page references and the marks for second issues and deaths. Early prose entries run from Aboriginal Monuments of the Mississippi Valley to essays on Addison.
67038-the-radio-gunner:
A novel for young readers tracks Jim Evans from boyhood to war at sea. The book came out in Boston in 1924. It opens on a hot Memorial Day in a small New England town. Jim, age six, watches old Civil War men march past. His mother's tears pose a riddle he wants to solve.

Later chapters move through school, a storm cloud of war, and call-up. At sea Jim works with radio and joins a hunt for foe ships. A secret scout, a trap, and a big fight fill the last third. Four drawn plates show key scenes. The tale gives young readers both thrills and a feel for sea war in that age.
67051-carson-of-red-river:
Carson of Red River is a western novel by Harold Bindloss, published in New York by Stokes in 1924. In England it came out under the title The Lute Player. The list of the author's works at the front runs to more than thirty Canadian tales.

The hero Kit is marked out by music from the first chapter, called Blake's Piano. He works in a drawing office and plays for his supper on the road west. The chapters take him through a lost lake and a storm to his reward at the end. A fiddle is tuned, a cook keeps a musician, and a water cure is tried on the way. Bindloss mixes the hard life of the prairie farms with a love plot, in his usual plain style.
67075-a-whirl-asunder:
A Whirl Asunder is a novel by Gertrude Atherton, issued in 1895. Stokes published it in New York and London. Atherton had written The Doomswoman before it. A frontispiece by Frederick illustrates the tale. Clive comes to California to marry. He has crossed the ocean and the continent. Seven days at sea and six on the train have soured him. His betrothed waits in the northern redwoods.

At the sixth stop he leaves the narrow-gauge train. He will walk the rest of the way, he says. The road dives down slopes and swings over trestles. Brush scrapes the windows on the curves. Canyons drop five hundred feet below. Atherton sets her love tale in wild country. The title hints the match will not run smooth.
67077-barbara-hale-a-doctor-s-daughter:
Barbara Hale, A Doctor’s Daughter, a girls’ story by Lilian Garis, was copyrighted in 1926. Grosset and Dunlap of New York published the book. Pictures by Foster go with the tale. A front scene shows Babs gasping that she did not know, in mid surprise.

Sea Sands and Somersaults is the title of the first chapter. When the Day Arrived and Her Father’s Daughter follow in the contents. Garis wrote whole series of girls’ books in that age. Barbara Hale and Cozette stands as a companion volume in the list. A doctor’s daughter carries her father’s standards into school and society scrapes. Such books gave girl readers a heroine with work in her blood. The Hale tales mix beaches, boarding school, and family pride.
671-phil-the-fiddler:
Horatio Alger, Jr. writes of Italian street musicians in New York in this boys' tale. Phil, a twelve-year-old violin boy with a battered fiddle, sings Viva Garibaldi in uptown streets while a padrone profits from his play. A preface tells how Alger learned the trade's hard facts from Italian gentlemen and the Eco d'Italia, whose editor called such boys the White Slaves of New York.

Alger writes with plain, earnest prose, following Phil through ferries, barrooms, sieges, and escapes. The tale mixes adventure with a plea for the children. It endures as a vivid Alger story, where a fiddler's courage wins friends and freedom.
67154-the-laugh-maker:
The Laugh Maker is a story by James Oliver Curwood. Gayle Hoskins drew its illustrations. The hero is Bobby McTabb, a man of great weight and cheer. He weighed fourteen pounds at birth, the tale says. At thirty he tips the scales near two hundred and eighty. The story opens with a warning. You can laugh too much, it claims. You can look too long on the sunny side.

Kitty Duchene helps Bobby prove that warning true. Rumour says the fat newcomer is rich. Fawcettville wakes up at his arrival. Talk runs to railroads, factories, and oil. Bobby wears striped waistcoats and a rosy, laughing face. Curwood is known for tales of the north woods. This piece turns to a village comedy of money and love. Its moral hides inside the laughter.
67169-the-rival-trappers-or-old-pegs-the:
Lewis Carson wrote The Rival Trappers, a dime tale for Beadle and Adams. Old Pegs the mountaineer is its second title, from 1874. Contents open with Old Pegs and his treasure in the hills. Dave Farrell and bruin scouting follow in the heads. Whirlwind and a coward's deed come next.

A footstep comes up the canon in the first chapter. A man of strange appearance steps into view round the bend. At first glance he seemed a dwarf, it says. Broad shoulders and herculean arms never belonged to a dwarf, though. Scarcely five feet high, he had a giant's body on crooked legs. Hyar we come and hyar we go, he half-sang as he pegged along. A border battle crowds the contents. The heroine a captive closes the middle. Carson gives the frontier its bow-legged legend.
6718-cap-n-dan-s-daughter:
Joseph Lincoln sets Cap'n Dan's Daughter in Trumet Centre, where the Metropolitan Dry Goods and Variety Store opens for business in August. Sam Bartlett takes down shutters, sweeps, and dusts, then goes home for breakfast, having waited on no customers at all, for there were none. The store is ready, but trade is not.

August should bring city visitors, white duck hats, and oilskin coats for sailing, yet the town waits. Into that quiet shop world comes Cap'n Dan's daughter, with love and town talk in her wake. Lincoln writes with Cape Cod humor and warmth. Cap'n Dan's Daughter is a cozy, comic tale of a small town and its people.
6720-the-wentworth-letter:
Joseph Smith writes, at the request of John Wentworth, editor of the Chicago Democrat, a sketch of the rise, progress, persecution, and faith of the Latter-day Saints. Wentworth wanted the account for a friend writing a history of New Hampshire, and Smith asks only that it be printed entire, ungarnished, and without misrepresentation. The letter first ran in Times and Seasons in March 1842.

Smith tells of his birth in Sharon, Vermont, in December 1805, and of his family's move when he was ten. The sketch that follows is the founding statement of his faith. The Wentworth Letter is a short, historic document, central to Mormon history and to American religious life.
67218-the-conscript-mother:
Robert Herrick's short novel, published by Scribner in 1916, follows an Italian mother on a journey of dread. The narrator meets the signora at the tram station on a May morning, and they cross the flowering Campagna to a little town in the Albanian hills. Her son Maironi is stationed there with his regiment, and with luck and an indulgent officer she may see him for a few minutes.

War has been threatening Italy for months, and when a great dirigible rises over the road like a huge silver fish, the signora whispers that it is coming. The illustration shows her prize: five minutes at most with him by the side of the highroad. Herrick tells the story quietly, through a mother's fatalism in a country of conscription.
67302-the-summers-readers-first-reader:
The Summers Readers: First Reader is a school reading book by Maud Summers. Beatty's company published it in New York. Lucy Fitch Perkins and Marion Mahony drew the illustrations from original designs. The contents list short lessons for beginning readers. The Little Red Apple opens the book. The Wind and the Sun, The Three Bears, and Chicken Little follow. Classic fables like The Ant and the Dove appear early. The Fox and the Crow and The Lion and the Mouse are also included.

Little Red Riding Hood, The Three Little Pigs, and The Gingerbread Boy come later. Nature pieces treat the brook, the woodpecker, and maple sugar making. Work lessons include the carpenter, the miner, and the sawmill. Mary's Little Lamb and other rhymes give verse practice. An alphabet and a word list close the reader. The book teaches reading through story, fable, and song.
67343-the-engineer:
The Engineer is a science fiction story by Frederik Pohl and C M Kornbluth, first printed in Infinity Science Fiction in February 1956. Some combination of low temperature and high pressure has forced matter from seepage at the ocean bottom into a new compound. The impregnable armour around Subatlantic Oil's drilling chamber has found a weakness.

Muhlenhoff watches on a screen as water with the pressure of eighteen hundred meters behind it batters a bulkhead flat. Down more than a mile, he tells himself, little technical problems are bound to come. That is why the deep-sea oil wells are still there, waiting to be worked. He flicks off the screen and marches in to an Engineering Board waiting in flabby panic. The tale's proverb runs that the big wheels of tomorrow will be men who can see the big picture, but blowouts have small beginnings.
67374-caleb-conover-railroader:
Albert Payson Terhune wrote Caleb Conover, Railroader, published by Cupples and Leon in New York in 1907. Every chapter title carries the hero's name: Caleb Conover receives, makes a speech, regrets, listens and answers, makes terms, and fights. The novel opens at his mansion on Pompton Avenue. A line of carriages passes through a mighty white marble arch lit by electric light, bearing his name in letters a foot high.

A guest jokes that the poor man must think he is a cemetery. The arch sets the theme: Conover is a railroad magnate of vast wealth and vaster self-regard, whose road and whose pride dominate his town. Terhune, later famous for his dog stories, began as a novelist of business and adventure. This early book gives the American railroad king as hero and warning at once, in the years when such men stood at the centre of public argument.
67403-the-stuff-of-manhood-some-needed-n:
The Stuff of Manhood, some needed notes in American character, by Robert Speer, was copyrighted in New York in 1917. The talks were the Merrick Lectures for 1916-17, given at Ohio Wesleyan University in Delaware, Ohio, from April 1 to 5, 1917. Front ads list Speer's many books on missions, faith, and young men, most priced at a dollar or less.

Speer, a leading church and mission voice, asks what traits make a man sound and useful. His other titles, from Paul the All-Round Man to Young Men Who Overcame, show his bent: Bible study joined to daily duty. The lectures urge faith, grit, and clean habits as the base of national character in wartime.
67487-the-stilled-patter:
The Stilled Patter is a science fiction story by James E Gunn, first printed in Infinity Science Fiction in June nineteen fifty six. A teaser calls the battle of the sexes the deadliest battle of all. The narrator is Andrew Jones, and he states the tale's stakes at once. Because of him, he says, there will be no more Joneses, and no more anybody.

The end of the world did not come through fire or ice, he explains. Nor did it come from the sun or from atomic misuse, the usual fears of his decade.
