His flat denials build dread for the true cause, tied to birth itself in the title's stilled patter of small feet. Gunn tells extinction as confession.
67489-the-wreck-of-the-mail-steamer:
The Wreck of the Mail Steamer is a sea tale by Wilfred Grenfell, set on the northwest coast of Newfoundland. That shore runs straight and rock bound for eighty miles with no shelter, yet fishing craft crowd its cold waters for cod each spring. Women and children often sail with the men.

Uncle Joe Halfmast, a fisherman turned carpenter, has come north to build a church at Wild Bight. Fall storms delay the fish curing, and the one little mail steamer for three hundred miles of coast passes twice without calling. Winter ice closes in while the cove waits three weeks for its last chance to go south before Christmas.
67495-from-sea-to-sea-or-clint-webb-s-cr:
From Sea to Sea is a sea tale of Clint Webb on a windjammer. Bert Foster wrote it, with rights held in the year 1914. Donohue of Chicago published this Clint Webb volume for boy readers. Foster also wrote Clint Webb among the sealers and among the whalers. A front cry, You want us to lose this race, sets the tone.

Chapters open as Clint shields a friend and makes an enemy at once. He relates his history and stands up to a bully in chapter two. Captain Bowditch crowds on sail, and a ship sails in the sky. A ghostly visitation, a mid ocean race, and a prophecy follow fast. A captain's dog goes overboard in the race for home ports.
6754-the-tale-of-brownie-beaver:
Arthur Scott Bailey tells of Brownie Beaver in Pleasant Valley, near a village Farmer Green seldom visits, beyond Blue Mountain. Brownie must find a queer place to live, learn to fell a tree, and build with sticks and mud. A freshet, a dam in danger, and a happy thought test his skill and pluck.

Mr. Crow, Mr. Frog, Jasper Jay, and Grandaddy Beaver all have parts in the woodland fun. Bailey writes in simple, gentle prose for the youngest readers, with a new lesson in each chapter. The Tale of Brownie Beaver is a sweet, old-style animal book for small children.
67558-the-origin-of-property-in-land-wit:
Fustel de Coulanges wrote The Origin of Property in Land, translated by Margaret Ashley and published in London in 1891. An introductory chapter on the English manor, by William Ashley of the University of Toronto, stands before the essay. Fustel's piece first appeared in a French historical review in April 1889. The preface praises it as a brief statement of his case against primitive agrarian communism.

Chapter by chapter, Fustel answers scholars who claimed that early peoples held land in common. He takes up Maurer on the Germans, Viollet on the Greeks, and Mommsen on the Romans. A chapter on the comparative method and one on the Gauls follow. His conclusion denies that history shows a communal stage at the start of property. Ashley's introduction applies the argument to England and the origin of the manor. The small book remains a sharp salvo in a famous scholarly quarrel.
67571-the-black-tiger:
Patrick O'Connor wrote a tale of a young car man and a famed race car. The book came out in New York in 1956. He gave it to Bill and Steve Dredge and the race crew. Their hero grease men share that warm gift line. Woody Hartford, age seventeen, stands at the tale's start.

Woody sits in a shop and picks at a carburetor on a bench. He can build one back with no thought at all, the tale says. His true care is a far more fine ask than car parts. Work at the McNess Union post in Hermosa Beach grounds him. Race dreams and a black tiger car pull him on. Young speed fans get a keen shop tale.
67583-the-jazz-singer:
The Jazz Singer is a play by Samson Raphaelson. Brentano's published it in New York in 1925. Raphaelson based it on his short story The Day of Atonement. That story ran in a magazine in January 1922. A foreword thanks the director Albert Lewis and the cast.

A preface states the play's idea of America. American life in 1925, Raphaelson writes, consists of surfaces. He who would picture it must work like a kaleidoscope. Jazz is his chosen symbol of the nation's soul. Jazz is prayer, he insists, though prayer distorted and sick. The jazz singer stands lost between two worlds. One world is dead. The other is powerless to be born.
67671-metzerott-shoemaker:
Metzerott, Shoemaker is a novel copyrighted in 1889, given to the clergy and the workingmen of America. Its motto is that to labor is to pray. Three books divide the tale: Love, Altruism, and Flood and Fire.

Karl Metzerott, a shoemaker, counts himself fairly well off. His Socialist views, he says, do not grow from his own needs. When the commune comes, he expects to be among its givers, not its receivers. He bends ten hours a day over his lapstone in a poor quarter of a city the author will not place on any map.
67694-the-crater:
Robert Gore-Browne frames a tale of East Africa as a story told on shipboard. George H Doran Company issued the novel at New York in 1926. A note warns that no white character in it is drawn from life.

Ross tells the tale across a stifling night off the East Coast of Africa. A wind off the equator makes sleep impossible. Ross is a big man with a walrus moustache and few goods: a rifle or two and a green kit bag. He aims his cigar end at a glowing patch of sea. Her story, he says, was discreditable enough to be true. The woman and her husband, he claims, reduced the Decalogue to ribbons in three weeks. Gore-Browne writes in the clubman's mode, where Africa tests every code the English carried out.
67698-the-woods-rider:
Frank Lillie Pollock wrote The Woods-Rider for boys. The Century Company issued it at New York in 1922. H C Edwards and John Edwin Jackson drew plates. Pollock had written Wilderness Honey before. Eighteen chapters carry the tale. Wreck in the Woods opens the action.

Joe Marshall leans from his saddle in chapter one. A cup hangs on a turpentine tree before him. Bark stripped three feet high scars that pine. Two tin gutters feed the cup with gum. Old Dick's Bees and The River Orchard follow. Buried Treasure and Stolen Rosin build the plot. Bees and rosin mix through the whole tale. Pirates' Treasure and Under Fire raise the stakes. The Bee Raft and War on the River come late. The Harvest closes the woods work. Turpentine camp fiction is rare, and Pollock's tale smells of pine gum, river water, and bee smoke.
67706-the-story-of-a-lover:
Boni and Liveright printed this frank first person tale in New York in 1919. The narrator says he was thirty when he first saw her. They never spoke and were never introduced at that first sight. Yet he knew at once that he must meet her soon.

He says they have now been married fifteen years in one home. Still, he feels she has never truly seen him in that time. Boyhood dreams and youth adventures left him hungry and unsatisfied. Art and philosophy soothed, then inflamed, his search for deep union.
67834-the-adam-chaser:
Bower wrote The Adam Chaser as a western tale, printed in The Popular Magazine in 1925. John Abington, a young man who studies old remains, drives into a deep canyon in the Sonora hills of Arizona. His car blows its cap, boils dry, and stalls fast in sand and rock under fierce heat.

A note at the start says old records of early Indian towns drew Abington to the caves, and that fate makes him a judge of the fates of living men. Low on water, he waits in thin shade as a dust-caked roadster rolls down the grade toward him. Heat, thirst, and armed men shape a tense desert tale of chance and choice.
67890-the-thirteenth-letter:
Natalie Sumner Lincoln wrote a mystery printed at New York in 1924. Lincoln had written The Cat's Paw, The Meredith Mystery, The Red Seal, and The Unseen Ear. The book is given to Harriet Brownson Hussey in memory of happy hours. Lincoln thanks Alain Campbell White of Litchfield, Connecticut, for a clever stamp code used in the tale.

The events of a night open it, then caught in the web, complications, and the black crest. Sheriff Trenholm asks questions, the third hand appears, and blackmail and the denial follow. The folded note, the human eye, the spider and the fly, and the will of hate lead to the thirteenth letter itself. A doctor by a patient's bed shakes his head at the close of the shown scene. Letters and stamps hide the key.
67950-marcus-or-the-boy-tamer:
Walter Aimwell wrote a set of tales for boys and girls called the Aimwell Stories, each about three hundred pages in cloth with gilt backs at sixty three cents. Press notices at the front praise the set. The Boston Transcript says the Aimwell Stories rival the Rollo Books in the affections of the young. Marcus, or the Boy Tamer, is the fifth volume, now ready as the advert runs.

Oscar, Clinton, Ella, and Whistler come before it in the set, and Jessie follows. Each volume stands alone, yet characters and places link them in part. Under the guise of a story, Aimwell teaches a moral lesson, the notices say, mixing instruction with amusement. Marcus tames boys by kindness and firm character in a famed Sunday school style tale.
67971-getting-ready-to-be-a-mother:
Getting Ready to Be a Mother is a guide book for women expecting a child, issued by Macmillan. A painting by Gari Melchers, The Caress, serves as its frontispiece for the volume. It opens with a poem in which a baby asks its mother where it came from. The mother answers that the child was hidden in her heart as its desire.

That tender opening sets the tone for counsel that follows in the chapters ahead. Childhood dolls, household worship, and hopes and loves braid into the poem answer. The book treats motherhood as a long preparation of heart as much as body. Expectant readers of its day found both comfort and practical framing here.
6799-philosophical-letters-of-friedrich-:
Schiller's Philosophical Letters open with prefatory remarks on how reason, like the heart, passes through epochs and transitions, yet its growth is seldom portrayed. Writers show passions in extremes, aberration, and results, Schiller notes, without asking how closely they bind to a person's intellectual frame. Moral decay, he argues, roots in a one-sided, wavering philosophy that blinds the mind with a show of truth.

An enlightened understanding, by contrast, ennobles and steadies the soul. Letters on the theosophy of Julius and on the animal and spiritual natures in man follow. Philosophical Letters is a short, searching work of a poet thinking as a philosopher.
6800-the-works-of-frederick-schiller:
The Works of Frederick Schiller gathers his histories, plays, poems, philosophy, and a novel in one collected edition, translated from German and illustrated. History holds the Thirty Years' War in five books and the Revolt of the Netherlands in four. Plays run from The Robbers and Fiesco to Wallenstein and Wilhelm Tell. Don Carlos, Demetrius, and Mary Stuart also appear. Poems in three periods, aesthetical essays, philosophical letters, and The Ghost Seer complete the set.

A preface to the sixth edition calls this the best collected Schiller in English, with many corrections. For readers who want Schiller whole, this volume is the gateway. The Works of Frederick Schiller is a vast, essential shelf for any lover of German letters.
68018-the-peak-in-darien-with-some-other:
The Peak in Darien, subtitled An Octave of Essays, is a book of papers by Frances Power Cobbe, published at Boston in 1882. In her preface Cobbe says the volume is meant for her grown fellows in years. They face the darker problems of the time and ponder the great change of death. Some papers are new, and some first appeared in journals.

The essays ask whether denying God and life after death is truly a brave creed, as agnostics boast. They ask whether life is a curse, as some thinkers teach, and whether health is the highest good of all. One paper argues the fitness of women for the ministry of religion. The book closes with thoughts on entering the life after death at once.
68034-memories-by-admiral-of-the-fleet-l:
Lord Fisher, an admiral of the fleet, set down his memories in a book printed in London in 1919. A note at the front warns that Fisher had small faith in the printed word. Had he had his own way, the note says, there would have been no book at all.

The book rests on words taken down from his talk in September 1919, left much as he spoke them. Fisher states in his own opening that there is no plan nor order, just thoughts as they rose. A few chapters come from pieces he had printed for friends, and letters to Lord Esher from 1903 to 1912 fill some gaps.
68044-the-wanderings-of-an-elephant-hunt:
W D M Bell recounts a hunter's life in The Wanderings of an Elephant Hunter. Country Life and George Newnes of London and Charles Scribner's Sons of New York first published it in 1923. A front plate shows a native attack. The contents open with craft: hunting the big bull elephant, and the brain shot and body shot at elephant.

African medicine or witchcraft and its bearing on sport follows. Then the road runs wide: Karamojo, Dabossa, the Sudd of the Gelo River, the Lado Enclave, Liberia, and Buba Gida, the last African potentate. Buffalo, lions, rifles, and administrations close the book.
6809-the-doctor-s-daughter:
Vera, author of Honor Edgeworth, opens The Doctor's Daughter with a preface on prefaces themselves. Dickens, she notes, said prefaces, though seldom read, are continually written, and she likens them to soft explanations whispered when one person is introduced to another. Such a note, she suggests, can reconcile fastidious friends to a quaint, old-fashioned little body.

The tale that follows centers on a doctor's daughter, her home, her loves, and her trials, in the gentle style of Victorian domestic fiction. Vera writes with warmth and a touch of humor. The Doctor's Daughter is a pleasant, old-fashioned novel of family life and feeling.
68181-address-of-president-roosevelt-at-:
President Roosevelt spoke at Saint Louis, Missouri, on October 2, 1907, during a trip down the Mississippi, and the Government Printing Office at Washington issued the address the same year. This time he came by water, down the river highway that runs past its doors. His theme is that the nation has let its rivers decay while railways grew, and that the loss is neither healthy nor lasting.

Bulky goods, he argues, belong on the water, as the canal systems of the Old World show. The Great Lakes prove the point at home, and the commerce through the Soo Canal already passes the Suez Canal. The Mississippi and its tributaries cross too many states for any one state to fit them for their full use. Improving them, he insists, is a national task.
68205-john-jasper-the-unmatched-negro-ph:
William Hatcher wrote John Jasper, the Unmatched Negro Philosopher and Preacher, copyrighted in 1908. Jasper was a Richmond preacher, born a slave, who became a national character. The Richmond Dispatch, quoted here, called him a Richmond institution.

Chapters tell of his thrilling conversion, how he got his schooling, and his years as the slave preacher. His sermon asking where sin came from, and the famed sermon that the sun does move, fill the middle. Hatcher grants that the sun sermon made Jasper known, but credits also a strong personality and earnest conviction. Jasper took the Bible literally, the Dispatch says, and trusted it wholly.
68215-the-answer:
George Smith's The Answer ran in Astounding Science-Fiction in February 1947, with drawings by Orban. The tale opens in the office of Robert Hohmann, a dictator, who smiles with scorn at the man before him. That man is Greg Hammond of the United Nations, and he has come with a flat order.

Hohmann is not to attempt the building of a plutonium producing uranium pile. The United Nations makes no threats, Hammond says; it is the voice of the people, and the people will judge. Hohmann turns the point back on him: the person is secondary to the State, he thunders, and a state that gives orders is no better than a dictator. The talk is the tale's battlefield.
68223-the-fixer:
Fixer is a science fiction tale by Wesley Long of a woman on Telfu. The story ran in Astounding Science Fiction for May nineteen forty five. Kramer drew the pictures for this tale of Sandra Drake and tailoring. Sandra sits in her perfect flat on Telfu and swears at her needlework.

Her clothes are falling to pieces, and no good tailor stands within nine light years. Telfan tailors are good for Telfans, but not for Solarian cut and hang. Four breasted Telfan women differ too much from Sandra thin waisted figure. Telfans wear next to nothing for their pelt, but Telfu is too cold. Making over outsize Telfan dress is her one poor way out left.
683-the-compleat-angler:
Izaak Walton wrote this 1653 classic as a talk between friends on the art of fishing. Piscator, the angler, teaches Venator, the hunter, how to catch trout, pike, and other river fish, with lore on bait, tackle, seasons, and the habits of each kind. Songs, poems, and old sayings break up the lessons.

Walton praises angling as a calm, honest pastime, close to nature and far from the noise of town and court. The book is not just a manual: it is a plea for a quiet life, patience, and good company by the water. It has stayed in print for centuries as both a guide for anglers and a gentle piece of English prose.
68340-a-landscape-painter:
Henry James wrote A Landscape Painter, with three more tales, for Scott and Seltzer at New York in 1919. The other tales are Poor Richard, A Day of Days, and A Most Extraordinary Case. The title tale opens with gossip of a broken engagement, a dozen years past. Young Locksley, rich to a vast degree, had been set to wed Miss Josephine Leary. Her beauty was great, and her lover likened her to the Venus of Milo.

The narrator paints her gray eyes, auburn hair, and calm, sweet face. One flaw stands out: a want of life in her look. Locksley was short, dark, and plain, a match that raised surprise at the time. What drew him, past her beauty, the narrator never learned. James turns high-life talk into a fine study of wealth, art, and a love that failed.
68371-the-luckless-trapper-or-the-haunte:
William Eyster wrote this frontier tale, issued by Beadle and Adams of New York as a pocket novel in November 1876. The hero is Bill Blaze, called the luckless trapper and the haunted hunter. The first chapter, A Corpse in the Stream, opens with a rifle ball hissing past the trapper's head as he scouts in the bush.

Hiding in the brush, Blaze watches two men step into the moonlight across the stream and talk, unaware that he hears every word. One is tall, handsome, and quick on the trigger, with a hand raised to wave the other back. The second is short, broad, and built for strength, with a bold, resolute face. The scene sets the tone of the dime novel west: sudden shots, night meetings, and men whose talk reveals a plot the hidden hunter must unravel.
68377-let-s-get-together:
Isaac Asimov sounds an alarm in Let's Get Together, from Infinity magazine in February 1957, with drawings by Engle. A kind of peace has endured for a century, and people have forgotten what anything else was like. Worse, a kind of war has finally come, and no one quite knows how to react.

Elias Lynn, Chief of the Bureau of Robotics at Cheyenne, takes the news from a young Security officer, Ralph G Breckenridge, and answers with plain disbelief. The old cold war has long been a game with unspoken rules, played as We and They. That comfort is ending.
68447-recollections-and-impressions-of-j:
Recollections and Impressions of James McNeill Whistler is a memoir by Arthur Jerome Eddy. Lippincott issued it in 1903, the year of Whistler's death. Eddy also wrote Delight, a book on the soul of art. The contents run to ten chapters. The first asks why Whistler never returned to America. The tariff on art is among the causes weighed. His Valparaiso days are recalled there.

Later chapters trace his birth and schooling. Saint Petersburg, West Point, and the Coast Survey mark his youth. Paris and Venice days bring the etchings. Chelsea chapters treat the Mother portrait and Carlyle. The Peacock Room and the Ruskin suit fill the middle. Colour and music are joined in a late chapter. Eddy knew the painter and writes as a friend. The book is a first-hand portrait of a famous exile.
6845-the-whistling-mother:
Grace Richmond's Whistling Mother opens with a son's praise: he has the greatest mother on earth, five feet six, weighing just what she ought, and never still long enough to grow stout. She is game for any outing, awfully good company, and more like a vigorous girl than a mother in the usual sense. A picture caption adds that a boy with work to do is immortal till his work is done.

The tales that follow show that mother in home, town, and trouble, whistling her way through life. Richmond writes with warmth and humor. The Whistling Mother is a cheerful, loving portrait of a mother who stays young in spirit.
68453-the-summers-readers-primer:
Maud Summers wrote The Summers Readers Primer for Frank Beattys and Company in New York, with copyright in 1908. Lucy Fitch Perkins drew the pictures from original designs, and a Froebel motto calls the perfected family the model of all education. The little book teaches first reading through tiny sentences and rhymes.

Opening pages pair one verb at a time: sing, run, jump, hop, then combine them into short lines. A child narrator meets Rover the dog, Kitty, and a bird, asking what each can do and what the reader can see. Ball play with Baby follows, building words by steady repetition. A closing list names nursery rhymes such as Two Little Blackbirds, Rock-a-By Baby, and Little Boy Blue.
68474-nick-carter-stories-no-157-septemb:
Nick Carter Stories number 157, dated the 11th of September 1915, is a five-cent weekly issue from Street and Smith of New York. Its story is A Human Counterfeit, or Nick Carter and the Crook's Double, edited by Chickering Carter. The tale opens at dinner in a new and fashionable New York hotel.

Clayton, manager of the new Westgate hotel, tells Nick Carter and his assistant Chick of an experience he calls beyond words. He says most men's motives can be read in their acts, but in this case there was nothing to read. The act seemed to him like a horrid dream or the work of a dope fiend. He has come to ask the detective's opinion of the affair. Subscription terms and back-number prices fill the front pages, as in every issue of the series.
68483-the-time-raider:
Edmond Hamilton's The Time Raider ran as a serial in Weird Tales from October 1927 to January 1928. The narrator warns at the start that his tale has gaps, for it is only a record of his own meetings with the Raider. The science of the thing, he says, stands in Lantin's work on time-displacement and in their joint study.

The door into the affair is the Cannell Mystery, still in the newspapers of the day. Professor Ferdinand Cannell, one of the greatest living students of old ruins, had vanished in the jungles of Indo-China as if blotted out. Cannell, loosely tied to a great New York museum, roamed the world chasing proof for his startling theories. Where his road crossed the Raider's, the tale begins.
68488-the-voice-at-johnnywater:
The Voice at Johnnywater is a western novel by B M Bower, published at Toronto by McClelland and Stewart in 1923, with a frontispiece by Remington Schuyler. Bower's name stood behind a long shelf of range novels, from Good Indian and Lonesome Land to The Trail of the White Mule. The title page list shows how steady her output ran.

Patricia opens the tale, entertaining and explaining, then takes her stand. Gary goes on the warpath, does a little sleuthing, and rides out to Johnnywater, where a voice is heard that no one can place. Chapters promise a cat with a secret, millions in question, and Gary insisting he does not believe in spooks. Bower mixes the range mystery with her usual dry humor and horsemanship.
68514-the-little-country-theater:
Alfred G Arvold of North Dakota Agricultural College wrote an account of a rural theater he founded on February 10, 1914. The book came out in 1922. Early chapters treat raindrops, country folks, and the land of the Dakotas. A chapter then describes the little country theater itself, set in a remodelled chapel.

The theater seats two hundred people. A package library system forms part of the work. Later chapters cover the heart of a prairie, characteristic incidents, and the town of Larimore. Forty towns and Cold Spring Hollow close the story. Arvold quotes Victor Hugo calling the theater a crucible of civilization.
68544-st-cuthbert-s-tower:
Florence Warden wrote St Cuthbert's Tower, a novel printed at New York in 1889 as number nine in Lovell's International Series of modern novels at thirty cents. Warden also wrote The House on the Marsh, Scheherazade, and A Witch of the Hills. Series mates include Ouida's Guilderoy and tales by Sims and Macquoid.

Rishton Hall Farm was let at last after Lord Stannington held it long at lower and ever lower rent. John Oldshaw, careful tenant of Lower Rishton Farm, had expected the hall lease to drop into his hands for a trifling rent at last. His property throve under his hands, the village knew well. A new tenant upsets such quiet calculations. Sensation readers get a village mystery.
68545-a-second-reader:
Frank E Spaulding and Catherine T Bryce wrote A Second Reader, issued at New York in 1907 as part of The Aldine Readers. Spaulding led the schools at Newton and Bryce led its first grades. Margaret Ely Webb drew the pictures. Nathaniel L Berry helped plan the art.

Groups of tales and verse suit young school readers. Out of Door Neighbors holds beast tales such as The Proud Crow. Once Upon a Time holds Lambikin and more old tales. Songs of Life holds verse by Lucy Larcom, Mary Lamb, and more. With Nature's Children and In Story Land close the book. Short pieces and clear print help new readers build skill and love of tales.
68577-the-mother:
Pearl S Buck wrote a novel of a poor farm mother in China, issued in New York. The John Day Company held the rights in 1934. Buck was known for The Good Earth, Sons, and East Wind West Wind. The tale opens in a small thatched farmhouse kitchen at dawn.

The mother tends an earthen stove, feeding grass and leaves to the fire with deft hands. Near her sits a very old woman, half blind, wrapped in padded coats of red and blue. Work, want, and kin duty shape the days that follow. Readers get a close, spare tale of a woman who holds a home through loss.
68656-the-new-book-of-niagara-scenes-in-:
The New Book of Niagara was copyrighted in 1901. Reid published the picture book at Buffalo that year. A line from an oration by Carter heads it. Niagara, Carter said, is a symbol of infinite power and beauty. No contents page stands in the book; plates and captions carry it. A general view opens the set. Hennepin View and the new steel bridge frame it. The American Fall lies at the left, Luna Island beside it. Goat Island divides it from the Horseshoe Fall. The Maid of the Mist waits near her landing below. A second plate takes the Canadian Fall from that boat.

The run past the falls lends enchantment, the caption promises. Prospect Point gives most visitors their first sight. Winter plates show the ice bridge growing under frozen spray.
68713-a-history-of-the-administration-of:
Oppenheim wrote a history of how the Royal Navy was run, and of merchant shipping in its bearing on the navy. John Lane published volume one in London and New York in 1896. The book covers the years 1509 to 1660, with an opening part on the navy before that date. Its frontispiece shows a warship of Henry the Eighth.

Chapters follow each reign in turn. Henry the Eighth, Edward the Sixth, Mary, and Elizabeth fill the first half. James the First and Charles the First come next, with the seamen, the shipping, and the offices treated apart. The Commonwealth closes the volume. Oppenheim argues that no one king made the modern navy. Gun ports, new builds, and new offices grew by slow steps across the whole span. Lists drawn from old stores and a mutiny tale stand in the appendix.
68748-peacemaker:
Alan Nourse's story, from Science Fiction Adventures Magazine in February 1953, opens with Flicker bound to a pallet aboard an alien ship, fighting to lie still under a burning light.

Flicker can hear the aliens' thought patterns though their speech lies beyond his ears, and one of them demands that he be killed while they can. Others argue he is sedated and bound until they reach home. Flicker knows the aliens have drained and pillaged a dozen star-systems, and his mission depends on contact. Every tremor could end his chance, so he clings to stillness. The magazine printing carried pictures by Ebel.
68753-forgotten-danger:
William Morrison wrote the science fiction story Forgotten Danger, first printed in Science Fiction Adventures Magazine in February 1953, with pictures by Freas. The cover blurb sets the hook: a man called Crusoe can remember only one thing, that some deadly danger threatens him nearby. He does not know what it is, why he is in a swamp, or even his real name. Then, the blurb adds, he finds he can work miracles.

The story opens at night around a fire, where four men in ragged clothes eat stew from a great pot. Crusoe watches Angel, a huge man who does the cooking, and Professor, small and bald, without knowing any of them. When Professor asks if he recalls his real name now, he has to say he remembers nothing at all. Readers start with a lost man piecing himself together while an unseen danger waits.
6881-note-book-of-an-english-opium-eater:
Thomas De Quincey gathers short essays in this notebook, opening with a sequel to his famous piece on murder as a fine art. Three memorable murders leads a set that ranges widely, from the Bible and mere human science to the literary history of the eighteenth century and the Antigone of Sophocles. Later pieces weigh Wellesley, Milton against Southey and Landor, and the falsifying of English history.

Other essays touch suicide, shallow learning, English dictionaries, and Dryden and Pope at their sharpest. De Quincey writes with a playful edge even on gloomy themes, and he warns that readers who cannot meet gaiety halfway will miss his drift. The book reads as a cabinet of curiosities from a most restless mind.
68849-the-pretender-a-story-of-the-latin:
The Pretender is a novel by Robert W Service, published by Dodd, Mead and Company of New York in 1914. The subtitle calls it a story of the Latin Quarter. The hero tells his own tale.

J Horace Madden is rich, idle, and dreaming. His bank-book shows credits of more than twenty thousand dollars. In Maine he spent a paltry thousand and banked the rest like falling snow. He sees himself as two men at war. One is James H Madden, the man of affairs. The other is Horace, the dilettante and near-poet. The contents run in three books: The Challenge, The Struggle, and The Awakening. Manhattan gives way to the city of light, laughter, and love. Chapters promise an involuntary fiancé, the chewing gum of destiny, and the life and death of Dorothy Madden.
68913-the-iroquois-or-the-bright-side-of:
The Iroquois, or The Bright Side of Indian Character, is a book in defence of the native peoples of America by Minnie Myrtle. It was published in New York by Appleton in 1855. The author dedicates it to two men known as friends of the red man.

The contents promise a full picture of Iroquois life. Chapters treat national traits, homes, hospitality, and King Philip. The government of the League, the Long House, gets a chapter of its own. Later pages give the maple festival, thanks to the Great Spirit, and the guessing of dreams. One head states the thesis plainly: the Iroquois are not savages. The book answers the harsh tales of its day with scenes of courtesy and council fire order.
6893-in-the-quarter:
Robert Chambers opens this novel in Paris in May 1888, in the crowded Cafe des Ecoles of the Latin Quarter. Art students argue over Salon news, sing half mocking songs about masters and mistresses, and trade chalk and spoons across marble tables wet with beer. Elliott, Rhodes, Clifford, and Thaxton talk of who is in and who is out, while Rhodes nurses a drink and a grudge.

The Quarter itself is the true subject, a place where young painters live cheap, love lightly, and weigh art against money and family duty. Chambers follows their evenings, studios, and quarrels through sixteen chapters, catching the noise, humor, and restless hope of Americans and others learning to paint in Paris.
68931-colonel-crockett-the-texan-trailer:
Beadle and Adams issued Colonel Crockett, the Texan Trailer, as a dime novel in 1871. LaSalle wrote it, years after Crockett's death at the Alamo had made him a folk industry. The first chapter is Colonel Crockett on a bear-hunt.

Crockett dashes at full speed through the dense forest and bursts into a clearing. A big Dutchman sits on a log eating his dinner. Did you see a confounded big bear pass this way, stranger? The Dutchman, mouth crammed full, wants particulars: was the bear going by his legs, or flying with his wings? Dime novels sold this Crockett by the hundred thousand: the ring-tailed roarer of Tennessee, half horse, half alligator, and all comedy. The historical congressman is in there somewhere, under the coonskin.
68936-the-mate-of-the-vancouver:
The Mate of the Vancouver, by Morley Roberts, is a sea novel first published in 1892. Roberts had written King Billy of Ballarat. The catalog title is clipped to the ship's name, but the title page gives the full name.

The narrator, a sailor from a family of seamen, tells the story of one year of his life. His father commanded a China clipper, and his elder brother Will went to sea before him. The tale is told in five parts. It begins on board the Vancouver, moves to San Francisco and the north, and turns on a golden link, on love and hate. The final part reaches the Black Cañon. Will's love of drink, the narrator says, always set the brothers apart.
6903-miss-ludington-s-sister:
Edward Bellamy opens with a reflection on how happiness falls unevenly across lives, coming all at once to some and spread thin for others. For men, he says, the bright years often arrive in manhood or later, with a hard and successful career. For women, and most of all for women who do not marry, the bright years most often come in girlhood and young womanhood, before life grows lonelier.

Miss Ida Ludington, at twenty five, feels that truth take hold, as her interests narrow and her days grow quiet. The novel that follows traces what such a life can still hold, and what a sister's bond can mean when the spring of youth has passed. Bellamy writes with quiet care about time, loss, and the search for joy.
69072-the-haliburton-primer:
The Haliburton Primer, by M W Haliburton of the State Normal School at Farmville, Virginia, was printed in 1911. Haliburton made the book to teach small children their first reading steps. Each page pairs a new letter sound with short lines and a picture.

Early pages stay with two children, Alice and Frank, and a ball they pitch, catch, and chase. The same words come back again and again so new readers can learn them by sight. Sentences grow a bit longer as the book goes on, yet they stay short and clear. The primer shows the drill and repeat method used in many schools of its day to build first reading skill.
69091-the-pampas-and-andes-a-thousand-mi:
The Pampas and Andes tells of a thousand miles walked across South America. Nathaniel Bishop wrote the narrative. Lee and Shepard issued this third edition at Boston. The copyright entry dates to 1868. Edward Samuels wrote the introduction. Bishop dedicated the book to Spencer Baird of the Smithsonian.

A preface tells the book's odd history. Bishop made the trip at seventeen years of age. His publishers kept his boyish draft nearly untouched. They feared revision would spoil its freshness and truth. Bishop regrets his thin science. He carried no instruments for exact observation. He could not preserve specimens on the march. Still, he strove to make his notes truthful. A frontispiece shows the throwing of the lasso.
69124-the-hellflower:
George Smith wrote a novel that ran in Startling Stories in May 1952. The book had been thrown at Charles Farradyne. Then they had added the composing room, the printing press, and the final grand black smear of printer's ink. So when Howard Clevis found Farradyne working in the fungus fields of Venus four years later, Farradyne was a beaten man.

He no longer burned with resentment because he was all burned out. I am Howard Clevis, said the visitor, and Farradyne grunted at one of the few white shirts in a thousand miles. I have a job for you, Clevis says. Who do you want killed, Farradyne asks. A dumped ship, a fair trial that was not fair, and a hellflower drive a hard spaceman's comeback tale.
69127-bromoil-printing-and-bromoil-trans:
Bromoil Printing and Bromoil Transfer is a manual of the bromoil photographic process, by Emil Mayer, president of the Vienna club of amateur photographers. Fraprie, editor of American Photography, translated it from the seventh German edition. The American Photographic Publishing Company issued it at Boston in 1923. Chapters begin with making the bromide print: the choice of paper, development, and control of the image.

Then comes bleaching away the silver image and the middle drying. The inking up is the heart of the craft: the swelled relief takes greasy ink where water does not hold it. Brushes, inks, supports, and rollers each get their treatment. Later chapters cover after treatment of the print and the transfer methods, by which the inked image moves to a fresh sheet. Polychrome bromoils close the technical tale.
69128-the-making-of-a-mountaineer:
The Making of a Mountaineer is a climbing memoir by George Ingle Finch, first published at London in May 1924. Arrowsmith issued it, with seventy-eight photographs, a drawing, and two diagrams. Finch dedicates the book to his wife. A front picture shows climbers cutting steps across an ice slope on the Matterhorn's Zmutt ridge.

Twenty-one chapters run from early days to Mount Everest. Finch climbs in Corsica, takes the Wetterhorn and the Jungfrau, and skis the Bernese Oberland. He spends a winter's night on the Tödi and climbs Mont Blanc from the south. The tale begins twenty-two years back, on a spring morning in the Australian bush, chasing wallaby on a panting pony.
6915-in-camp-on-the-big-sunflower:
Lawrence Leslie sends a band of boys to camp on the Big Sunflower, opening with an alarm when Toby looks as if he has seen a ghost. Steve and Bandy-legs hold the camp while Max and his cousin Owen walk the river bank looking for fresh water clams. The contents promise treasure hunting, unknown shell gatherers, a puzzler for Max, and a great find from the river.

A new cook springs a surprise, danger waits on the trail, and Max plays the good Samaritan before the man trap is set again. At dead of night the mystery deepens, and the closing chapter solves it at last. Leslie writes a lively camp tale of boys, river craft, and a puzzle worked out in the open air.
69201-spiritual-vampirism-the-history-of:
C W Webber's Spiritual Vampirism, the history of Etherial Softdown and her friends of the New Light, was published at Philadelphia in 1853 by Lippincott, Grambo and Co. Webber had earlier written Old Hicks the Guide and Tales of the Southern Border, and this book grew out of a cabinet of papers left behind by a friend.

The introduction tells how the papers reached him. A man named Carter, called away suddenly on a yacht voyage, sent Webber a dark wooden escritoire banded with silver, with a sealed note on top. The cabinet had been left in Carter's charge by an extraordinary friend, not to be opened until six months after that friend's death.
69204-the-white-cipher:
The White Cipher, a novel by Henry Leverage, author of Whispering Wires, was copyrighted in 1919 and quickly reached a second edition. Chapter one, The Open Gate, opens in a prison at dawn. The prisoner stares through the bars of his door at the pearl grey light creeping over the barricade, changing from pearl to ruby and from ruby to gold.

He is C 45, better known in the international underworld as Chester Fay, alias Edward Letchmere, serving ten years at hard labor. His crime: opening a jeweller's strong box in Hatton Garden by means Scotland Yard never guessed. A bell clangs, keys grate, and an aged turnkey stops at his cell with a paper in trembling fingers. Get your clothes on, he says. You are going out. Fifteen chapters promise Scotland Yard, a cipher, passengers for Holland, and a house of lions.
6923-the-miser:
Moliere's Miser, first acted on September 9, 1668, appears here in Charles Heron Wall's English prose translation, with a short introduction and notes. Wall notes that Moliere borrowed from Plautus and imitated others, yet far surpasses them in handling his theme. Harpagon, the miser, loves money above all natural feeling, shuns family life, and treats his own children as natural enemies.

The cast sets Harpagon against his son Cleante and daughter Elise, both in love, with Valere, Marianne, and Anselme tangled in the plot. Master Jacques, cook and coachman both, and the valet La Fleche add comic edge. Moliere himself played Harpagon, and the play remains a sharp, moral comedy on greed.
69268-over-the-border:
Over the Border is a collection of sea stories by Morgan Robertson, issued by McClure's Magazine and Metropolitan Magazine. The title story stands among tales called The Last Battleship, Absolute Zero, The Fire Worshiper, and Kismet. The first piece opens near midnight on the battleship Argyll, stripped to bare steel.

The ship drifts with banked fires and a full head of steam, waiting for daybreak to discover the enemy. Wireless news has told of submarines, as yet unproved in war, and a telescope has sighted two small moving spots in the sky, airships of unknown side. No hammocks are piped that night; men sleep at their stations or talk. Officers off duty debate the future of warfare and the coming place of the battleship. The talk narrows to a wordy combat between the executive officer and a young torpedo lieutenant.
6927-the-white-feather:
Wodehouse sets The White Feather a year and a term after The Gold Bat, at the school of Wrykyn. His note jokes that the short stories bridging the two books kept away from his publishers, a painful show of the white feather itself. Sheen, the hero, faces home troubles, visitors with advice, and the charge of cowardice that gives the book its title.

Chapters follow Sheen's slow education, his progress under Mister Joe Bevan, a naval battle and its fallout, and a skirmish that ends in the rout at Ripton. Drummond retires, Seymour finds one success, and Bevan's counsel shapes the close. Wodehouse turns a schoolboy's fear into a light tale of pluck learned the hard way.
69352-the-x-bar-x-boys-on-whirlpool-rive:
The X Bar X Boys on Whirlpool River is a western novel for boys by James Cody Ferris. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York in 1926. It belongs to a series about the Manley brothers at the X Bar X ranch.

The story opens with Teddy and Roy finding bear tracks in soft earth. Chapters promise a fugitive, a night search, a chase, and the whirlpool itself. One brother is swept out of reach by the rushing current. Series books gave young readers a steady cast and fresh dangers each volume. Ferris kept the formula tight across many titles.
6937-a-biography-of-edmund-spenser:
John Hales writes the life of Edmund Spenser, revised in 1896 from the Macmillan Globe edition of Spenser's works. He opens with Latin verses on a life laid open like a votive tablet, then admits how little is known. Spenser's life, like Chaucer's, hides in obscurity, and like Shakespeare's it rests on meagre entries in official papers rather than on full records.

Hales therefore builds from documents, dates, and the poems themselves, tracing a poet whose great work outshines his paper trail. Footnotes mark each chapter's sources, and old spelling marks are explained for the reader. The biography serves as a compact, scholarly guide to the author of The Faerie Queene.
69385-nick-carter-stories-no-124-january:
Nick Carter Stories, number 124, for 23 January 1915, is a weekly detective number from Street and Smith. The tale is The Girl Kidnaper, or Nick Carter Up to Date Clew, in the heading. The stories are issued weekly and entered as second class matter at the New York post office. Single copies or back numbers cost five cents each in the terms.

Terms to mail subscribers are printed at the head of the number for its readers. Three months cost sixty five cents, and one year two dollars and a half, postage free, in that list. The Carter weeklies were the school of a generation of American boys in detection. Each number gave a complete case of the great detective for a nickel, and the girl kidnaper plot of this one follows the house pattern of clue, chase, and rescue.
69408-the-shoemaker:
Olive Harper wrote The Shoemaker, a story based on Hal Reid's play of the same name, with rights held from nineteen seven. It sold for twenty-five cents as a tale of strong feeling drawn from the stage. The tale is set in side streets off the Bowery, on the East Side of New York. Old fine houses there had sunk into poor shops and homes.

Morris Goldberg, a Jewish shoemaker, works in a cellar lit by grated panes. He fled the Kishineff killings with his wife and small girl, robbed of all else. A Hebrew aid group helped him start, and in a year of hard work he paid back the loan. His girl grows into the pride of the street, and the tale tracks the family's rise and trials.
69410-christina-alberta-s-father:
Christina Alberta's Father is a novel by Wells, the famed author of The Time Machine and The War of the Worlds. The front pages list his novels and romances by the dozen, from Kipps and Tono Bungay to Mr Britling Sees It Through. The tale itself, a note says, is the story of a certain Mr Preemby.

Preemby was a retired laundryman and widower, who gave up his active part in the Limpid Stream Laundry on his wife's death in 1920. The laundry stood in the parish of Saint Simon Unawares, near Woodford Wells. Some very remarkable experiences then came to him, the note promises. Wells turns from his early science romances here to a tale of a small man touched by great delusions and hopes. Christina Alberta, the daughter, gives the book its name and its counterweight. The novel mixes comedy, faith, and madness in Wells's late manner.
69432-david-thompson-the-explorer:
Charles Norris Cochrane wrote David Thompson, the Explorer, issued by Macmillan of Canada at Toronto in nineteen twenty four. The book is Number Two in Canadian Men of Action, edited by W Stewart Wallace of the University of Toronto. Cochrane taught ancient history at University College, Toronto. Maps of Thompson journeys aid the text. Eight chapters run from apprenticeship to last years.

Cochrane thanks J B Tyrrell in a prefatory note for use of material in Tyrrell edition of Thompson Narrative. Tyrrell, he says, first rescued Thompson name from undeserved oblivion. Chapter one opens on December thirtieth, seventeen eighty three, when Hudson Bay Company sought four boys trained in navigation from a London school. Thompson became a trader, surveyor, and explorer who crossed the Great Divide and raced to the sea. Young Canadians get a hero of maps and wilderness.
69440-letters-to-a-daughter:
Hubert Bland writes counsel to his daughter in letters gathered in a third and popular edition from T Werner Laurie, London. Bland wrote as Hubert of the Sunday Chronicle and had written With the Eyes of a Man before. The book goes to Rosamund, with a Shakespeare line on ruddy drops that visit his sad heart.

Fifteen letters run from On Life at Large to The Subtle Something at the close of the set. Heads treat churchgoing, being delightful, the glamour of the footlights, dress, flirtation's limits, and modern marriage in turn. A first letter dated Oct 17 opens to Alexa, who asked for long letters while away from home. Bland grants that ink may say what face-to-face talk left unsaid between father and grown daughter.
69443-the-kiss-to-the-leper:
François Mauriac wrote The Kiss to the Leper, a French novel of nineteen twenty-two turned into English by James Whitall. The English issue was first published in nineteen twenty-three. A note by the translator traces Mauriac's fast rise.

Mauriac printed his first poems in nineteen hundred and nine, at twenty-one, to praise from Maurice Barrès. Two novels came in nineteen thirteen and nineteen fourteen, and more after the war. The French press hailed this tale as a near masterwork at once. The translator grants its appeal is narrow, since its theme is a hard problem most readers shun. The tale's scenes can be painful, even grim.
69475-the-chinese-theater:
A E Zucker wrote The Chinese Theater, published at Boston in 1925 in a limited edition of 750 copies. Zucker taught comparative literature at the University of Maryland. He had earlier taught English at Peking Union Medical College. He dedicates the book to his wife, dated from Riverdale, Maryland, in December 1924. Contents open with early history.

Formal development under the Yuan dynasty follows, then the Ming dynasty with the Pi-Pa-Chi, and the drama under the Manchus and the Republic. Modern tendencies, the external aspects of the theatre, and its conventions come next. A chapter on Mei Lan-fang, China's greatest actor, stands near the end. Readers get the first full English survey of the Chinese stage.
69497-records-by-admiral-of-the-fleet-lo:
Records, by Admiral of the Fleet Lord Fisher, is a memoir in documents. Hodder and Stoughton issued the book in London, New York, and Toronto in nineteen nineteen. A first photo shows Fisher in eighteen eighty two as captain of Inflexible. The preamble calls this a second book, mostly records after nineteen o two.

Fisher says the war period of a man life is what readers want. No full biography is tried, since records speak for the facts best. Chapters run from early years and King Edward memories to Bible thoughts. Episodes, democracy, and public speeches fill the middle of the volume. The essentials of sea fighting close the naval lord case in print.
69535-planet-explorer:
Murray Leinster wrote Planet Explorer, first called Colonial Survey. Avon Publications issued it at New York in 1957. Astounding Science Fiction ran its parts in 1956. Gnome Press shared in the book's making. Leinster gave it to Austin Stanton with praise. Stanton trusts young men with real work, he writes.

Bordman serves as the tale's survey officer. He makes raw worlds fit for settlers to come. Lani Three is a glacier land warmed by man. Xosa Two is a desert made green. Loren Two is a beast inferno tamed by men. Solar Constant and Sand Dope head the contents list. Worlds and worlds wait in the book's proud open. Survey tales of one skilled man fixing planets gave space opera a working engineer for a hero.
69545-oliver-october:
Oliver October is a novel by George Barr McCutcheon, author of Beverly of Graustark. The New York edition was copyrighted in nineteen twenty two and twenty three. Contents run to twenty five chapters. Oliver is born in October heads the first. His relatives and neighbours and women in red shawls follow. His fortune, good and bad, and his temper take their turns.

Later heads bring him home from the war and through idle days. Old Oliver disappears, and a detective named Malone enters the list. The brewing of the storm and the hanging close the tale in the heads shown. Chapter one fixes his birth at seven in the morning on a vile October day in eighteen ninety. A band of gypsies camped at the town's edge drew more concern that day.
69546-together:
A travel and memory book by Norman Douglas. Robert M McBride published the New York edition in 1923. Douglas dedicates it to Archie and Robin, from their father. An epigraph from Ezekiel asks whether dry bones can live. The chapters bear place names from Vorarlberg, in western Austria. Bludenz and its valley form the home ground.

One chapter recalls the Brunnenmacher, the town's official water expert. He never saw the man, Douglas admits, only his son. The old man and Douglas's father were rival mountain maniacs. Both made first ascents across a then-virgin climbing province. Neither ever tried the Zimba, the noblest peak in view. The book mixes memoir, walks, weather, and ants into one meditation.
69579-adventures-of-the-comte-de-la-muet:
Adventures of the Comte de la Muette during the Reign of Terror is a novel by Bernard Capes, printed at Edinburgh and London by Blackwood in 1898. Capes also wrote The Mill of Silence and The Lake of Wine. The book is inscribed to the author's wife, his best counsellor and helpmate. Fifteen chapters and a set of notes make up the tale.

The last chapters pass through the quarries of Mont-Rouge to The Salad Course. The story opens in a lodging at La Bourbe. The narrator, a proscribed royalist, has taken shelter with his old friend Casimir Bertrand, now a deputy of the Revolution. Bertrand has passed through every party in turn: Lameth, Feuillant, Jacobin, moderate and extremist. He was always sincere and never consistent.
69636-salome-shepard-reformer:
Helen M Winslow wrote a novel copyrighted in 1893 and issued by the Arena Publishing Company of Boston. Salome Shepard drives her pony phaeton through factory precincts on a wet October day. She wonders why the crowd fills the street when workers should be at their benches. The narrow street is slippery, and the boardinghouses loom dingy in the gloom.

An hour before, the mill machinery shrieked and then, at ten o'clock, stopped all at once. Every man, woman, and child left the mills without a word. Salome had spent the morning in cosy talk of crochet and novels elsewhere. The stoppage confronts the mill owner's daughter with the grievances of the hands.
69664-the-law-of-the-road-or-wrongs-and-:
Law of the Road, or Wrongs and Rights of a Traveller, is a legal handbook by Vashon Rogers. It is volume four of the Legal Recreations series in its heading. Rogers was a barrister at law of Osgoode Hall, in Toronto, as the title page states. Sumner Whitney at San Francisco and Hurd and Houghton at New York published it, copyrighted in 1876.

A preface to the Canadian edition says the little work does not aspire to compete with the learned productions of the jurists. It aims to supply a want felt in this age of perpetual motion in its words. That want is a plain and brief summary of the rights and liabilities of carriers and passengers. The summary covers travel by land and by water in the book. Rogers writes railway law for the man in the seat, in the great age of the excursion ticket.
69704-the-case-of-oscar-slater:
The Case of Oscar Slater is a work of criminal advocacy by Arthur Conan Doyle, published in 1912. Hodder and Stoughton and Doran issued it. Oscar Slater was convicted at Edinburgh in May 1909. He stood accused of murdering Marion Gilchrist, an old lady of Glasgow. Doyle writes that no one can weigh the facts without deep dissatisfaction. The jury of fifteen split nine for guilty and five for not proven.

One juror voted not guilty outright. Under English law such a split would mean a new trial, Doyle argues. In Scotland Slater was condemned to death instead. He was reprieved two days before his execution. When Doyle wrote, Slater was serving life at Peterhead. The book retells the case in connected form for the reader's judgement. It is Doyle's most famous real life investigation.
69758-folly-corner:
Mrs Dudeney wrote Folly Corner, for Holt at New York in 1900. Holt holds the rights from that year, and the book is hers. She had written The Maternity of Harriott Wicken before it. A prologue and twenty-three chapters make the body of the novel. The prologue opens on a stifling London day of steam and haze.

Shrill cries of children loose from school cut the air. A train rushes across the bridge above Wood Lane, it says. Cyclists tinkle their bells down toward the Uxbridge Road. Costers vend dried fish and fruit from Portobello Road. A young woman stands still in a limp, hopeless attitude. Her face is turned on Wormwood Scrubbs. Her attitude is one of strong appeal, the tale says. As if despair might work a miracle, it adds. Dudeney opens a London novel of want and folly.
69762-hellflower:
Hellflower is a science fiction novel by George Smith. Abelard-Schuman first published it in 1953, and Pyramid Books reprinted it. The cover copy gives the book its lurid hook at once. A flower's perfume, it warns, can master any woman who breathes it.

The hellflower looks as innocent as a gardenia in that telling. Its scent arouses desires no ordinary passion can satisfy. Its victims are left burnt-out husks when the fever passes. Charles Farradyne knows that no woman can resist the bloom. Yet Carolyn, the girl he wants most, smiles as she inhales it. The tale opens with Farradyne ruined and working the fungus fields of Venus. The publishing world had thrown the book, the press, and the ink at him. Howard Clevis crosses half of Venus to offer the beaten man a job.
69763-kwasa-the-cliff-dweller:
Katherine Atherton Grimes wrote a school tale printed at Dansville, New York, in 1916 as number 257 of the Instructor Literature Series. Wilson drew the pictures. The game on the terrace opens it. It did, said Kwasa. It didn't, said Wiki. But I say there were three reds up, Kwasa insists, and Wiki holds that one of the dice came up white.

Well, Kwasa returns good humoredly, we will not quarrel about a game, I will throw again. He catches up the three small sticks of cane, painted red on the hollowed inner side and white on top, and tosses them deftly. Kwasa told the truth that it was a long way to the spring. The great rock built house stood three hundred feet up. Pueblo boy life is rebuilt for young readers.
69788-the-avenger:
The Avenger is a thriller by Edgar Wallace, printed at London by John Long. The copyright is 1926, and the hosted copy is the tenth edition. The front pages list Wallace's other novels, among them Room 13, The Face in the Night and The Man from Morocco. Forty two chapters tell the tale.

The first chapter is called The Head-Hunter. It opens with Captain Mike Brixan and his mild, innocent superstitions. At the bookstall of Aix la Chapelle station he buys a cheap novel. Later come The Mark on the Window, The Face in the Picture, The Cavern of Bones and Camera. A creature or servant named Bhag runs through the tale like a thread. Wallace packs the book with towers, caves, hidden marks and midnight visits, in his best breathless manner.
69809-for-whose-sake-a-sequel-to-why-did:
Southworth continues a hit tale in For Whose Sake, a sequel to Why Did He Wed Her. The book bears an 1884 copyright and came out in New York. The front pages list her famed tales, among them Ishmael, The Hidden Hand, and Self-Raised.

The tale opens on the ocean steamer Scorpio, bound from New York to Liverpool. Gentleman Geff rides in bliss with his queenly bride. He does not know his cast off wife is on the same ship, with his child. He thinks her dead in a pauper grave. Two sharp scenes from his past haunt him as the ship sails on.
69837-an-index-finger:
Tulis Abrojal wrote a book copyrighted in 1897, opening with a line that all the Sutras are but fingers pointing at the shining moon. A Walt Whitman passage follows, on being as lucky to die as to be born. The dedication honors those who follow their ideals through poverty and defeat. Such people, Abrojal says, pay any price for freedom of soul.

Chapters move from a child among her own people to where the road divides. Her story and fate, the end of the dream, and a butterfly follow. Later chapters treat death's narrow sea and the tongues of angels. The simple way closes the argument of the book.
69846-encaustic-or-count-caylus-s-method:
Encaustic is a treatise on painting in wax, written by Muntz and printed in London in 1760. The full title presents Count Caylus's method of painting in the manner of the ancients. A second method, for fixing crayons, is added at the end.

Muntz dedicates the work to Lord Edgcumbe, a patron who had seen his first trials in the revived art. The dedication admits the defects of language a foreigner must commit, and begs the patron's judgement as cover. Caylus invented the method, the author says, and the book offers it to the public under a great name. Encaustic had been lost since antiquity, and its recovery drew wide interest. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
69953-life-and-writings-of-amelia-bloome:
D C Bloomer wrote Life and Writings of Amelia Bloomer, a book put out at Boston in 1895. Portraits fill the book, and a new form ran in 1976. The writer was her spouse, and he gives the book to his wife. A first word calls her a scout in the cause some call the Woman Movement.

He says a record of her work should rest in a form that will last. He gives a brief tale of her life, then long scraps of her own words. One of her talks is printed in full, as the best proof of her thought. A full bound set of The Lily, her sheet of six years, rests in the state rooms at Albany.
69969-the-golden-whales-of-california-an:
The Golden Whales of California is a book of verse by Vachel Lindsay, issued by Macmillan in New York in 1920. Its subtitle calls the pieces rhymes in the American language. Lindsay lists his prose and verse works at the front, in the order he wishes them read.

The book is inscribed to Isadora Bennett of Springfield. She helped him write many of the pieces, the title poem among them. She also danced the Daniel Jazz, he says. Some verses had first appeared in Poetry of Chicago, The New Republic, and other magazines of the day. Lindsay's rhymes were made to be chanted aloud, with a beat drawn from hymns, parades, and street cries. The title poem takes the gold rush coast for its scene.
701-the-king-of-the-golden-river:
John Ruskin wrote this fairy tale about three brothers who live by a river in a rich valley, where gold seems to flow from the hills. Two brothers are greedy and cruel, and their selfish acts turn the valley barren. The youngest, kind and just, meets the King of the Golden River and faces a test of his heart.

Ruskin draws a clear moral: wealth kept by greed dries up, while wealth shared with care brings life back to the land. Mountain scenes, storms, and a touch of wonder carry the lesson without preaching it flat. The tale is unlike Ruskin's art writing, yet it shares its core belief that nature rewards right use and punishes abuse.
70106-dymer:
Dymer is a long narrative poem in nine cantos by Clive Hamilton, published in New York by Dutton in 1926. Hamilton was a pen name, used here for a work of romance and fantasy. A saying from the old Norse Havamal heads the book: Odin hung nine nights on the tree, wounded with the spear, an offering of himself to himself.

The poem opens by addressing the stranger who finds these words. Poet and reader, it says, begin a partnership and must hold the clue together. Then the marvel is named: in the city men called in scorn the Perfect City, Dymer could be born. There the gods seemed smothered and every hour charted in advance. A youth born in a world with no room for wonder or revolt is the seed of the tale. The cantos run to nearly a hundred pages of rhymed verse.
70131-how-he-won-her:
How He Won Her, a novel by Mrs Emma D E N Southworth, was entered for copyright in 1869 and sold by T B Peterson and Brothers of Philadelphia. The book is a sequel to her earlier novel Fair Play. Southworth was one of the most widely read American story tellers of her day. Her name fronts a long list of tales from the same house.

The title page pairs two mottoes, one from Shakespeare and one from Collins, both on love won through danger and courage. The sequel takes up the cast of Fair Play and carries their story onward. It belongs to the line of popular domestic novels of its time.
70168-up-the-ladder:
Mrs Madeline Leslie wrote a moral tale for the young, published at Boston in the eighteen-sixties, in her Leslie Stories. She inscribes it to her son William, just entering active life, hoping its hero's example will inspire the virtues that ensure success. Each chapter is headed by a text from Proverbs.

The hero is Harrison, met first with Ella, then in an oyster-saloon, then in trouble and affliction. Chapters warn that the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty, and that slothfulness casts into a deep sleep. Harrison becomes a merchant, gains a secret partner, and wins his reward. A sailor brother and a returned prodigal fill out the lesson.
70205-designs-for-crazy-daisy-winder:
Designs for Crazy Daisy Winder is an instruction booklet for a patented crochet gadget. It sold for seventy-five cents, with crochet time cut in half as its promise. The winder makes yarn daisies on a frame of twelve spokes. Step-by-step illustrations lettered from A onward guide the worker's hands.

The directions begin with holding the winder flat in the left hand. A thumb turn of the knob releases the spokes for the wrapping. Yarn is held across the centre, leaving an inch of end beyond it. It passes around the top spoke, then across to the spoke opposite. Spoke by spoke the wrapping continues around the whole frame in order. A single petal daisy wraps each spoke once in that fashion. The centre must be made before the daisy leaves the winder.
70222-meet-mr-mulliner:
Wodehouse opens a storyteller's shelf in Meet Mr Mulliner, first published in 1927. Jenkins made the first edition; Penguin reprint this copy in 1962, with later printings. Wodehouse gives the book to the Earl of Oxford and Asquith. Nine tales fill the contents, all under one roof of talk.

The truth about George leads, then a slice of life. Mulliner's Buck U Uppo, a tonic of family fame, follows. The bishop's move and came the dawn fill the mid run. The story of William and a portrait of a strict keeper of rules vary the cast. The romance of a bulb squeezer brings a photographer into love's way. Honeysuckle Cottage closes the book, a house tale with a sting. Mr Mulliner tells them all, a man whose kin stretch into every trade and trouble in England. Readers meet the family here at full length for the first time.
70261-tannha-user:
Tannhäuser is a mystical poem by Aleister Crowley, subtitled A Story of All Time. This new edition came from the Society for the Propagation of Religious Truth at Boleskine, Inverness, in 1907. It was priced at fifteen shillings net to the trade.

The etext opens in mid-flight, with numbered prose passages that play on Browning's Master Hughes of Saxe-Gotha. A dedication in verse then addresses a beloved the poet will not name as loved. Twin souls, it says, are bound to one star in heaven. Earthly bars divide them, and silence shields their rapture. Love's disdain is praised above love's glances. Crowley takes the old Tannhäuser legend of the knight and Venus and lifts it out of time. The poem mixes verse, prose meditation, and symbol. It belongs to his early Boleskine period.
70399-the-clammer:
The Clammer is a book of three tales by William John Hopkins, printed at Boston in 1906. The first and longest bears the book's title. Its narrator owns that many of his friends, and probably all his neighbours, think him erratic and peculiar. His friends remonstrate mildly, and he listens and makes no reply.

How can they know, he asks, things that must be born in a man? His neighbours stare and shake their heads because he chooses to go clamming. Goodwin the Rich has the palace on the hill above his favourite clam beds, and his automobiles cover the narrator's hedge with dust. The narrator does not like automobiles. He smiles and passes on, sure that what he knows passes their understanding. The other tales are A Daughter of the Rich and Old Goodwin's Wife. Hopkins writes quiet New England sketches of shore folk and their ways.
70404-the-negro-as-a-soldier:
Negro as a Soldier is an address by Christian Fleetwood on Black troops. Fleetwood was late sergeant major of the Fourth United States Colored Troops. He wrote it for the Negro Congress at Atlanta in November 1895. That congress met at the Cotton States and International Exposition there. George Cook published it at Washington, printed by Howard University in 1895.

A commission for the District of Columbia coloured exhibit fronts the pamphlet. Jesse Lawson heads that commission as its chief commissioner in print. A ladies' auxiliary committee, led by Mrs Bruce as president, stands listed. Fleetwood marshals the record of Black soldiers in American wars for proof. Congress delegates heard a veteran make the case from his own service.
70442-the-barnum-bailey-greatest-show-on:
A clown song book for the Barnum and Bailey Greatest Show on Earth holds songs sold at the circus in 1892. Frank Tousey held the rights to its songs and sold full sheet music by mail for twenty cents. The first song, by Felix McGlennon, praises a snug little home of your own above all the fashions and follies of life.

Worldly pleasures soon cloy, the song warns, but smiling faces round a home hearth give pure joy. Other songs tell of weary workers at day's close and the face waiting at the window. Sentiment, not sawdust, fills most pages. The songster shows what circus crowds took home to sing at the piano.
70455-angel-s-brother:
Eleanora H Stooke wrote a children's story for the Religious Tract Society, with colored pictures by W H C Groome. Angelica Willis, called Angel, is a slight, pale girl of about eleven. She sits alone in a shabby third floor sitting room in a London suburb. November sun shows up the worn furniture and tarnished mirror.

Chapters name the milkman's little account, an unexpected visitor, and the Mickle family. Gerald's jealousy and selfishness drive much of the plot. Uncle Edward makes an offer, and the family leaves London. Spring flowers, robins, and a quarrel follow. Gerald's repentance comes late, and a conclusion five months later ends the tale.
705-the-roadmender:
Michael Fairless wrote these short papers about a man who leaves town life to mend roads by hand in the English countryside. He sits by a white gate, breaks stone, and watches the seasons change. The papers first ran in The Pilot and were gathered in 1911, with three parts: the roadmender's own tale, a passage out of shadow, and a scene at the white gate.

The narrator finds peace in plain work, prayer, and the sights of hedge, field, and sky. His musings turn on faith, death, and the worth of a simple life. The book is quiet and devout, prized for its gentle prose and its belief that humble labour, done with love, can be a form of worship.
70571-earth-needs-a-killer:
Bryce Walton wrote this feature novel, printed in Future combined with Science Fiction Stories in 1950. Its pitch is spoken to Ray Berton: you are the man we need, a killer, but sane and rational, while those we fight are insane and will destroy humanity. The speakers have power but cannot use it for destruction; they can give it to him.

The story opens with a news broadcast from New York in September 1983. At five that afternoon, a man's body materialised out of thin air ten thousand feet above Manhattan. It smashed onto the plasticrete of a future Fifth Avenue. Readers get a pulp tale of a hired killer armed by pacifists.
70598-a-pet-reader:
Edith Wilhelmina Lawson, a primary teacher in Rockford, wrote a reader for young pupils dated 1926. Short pieces, grouped by kind of pet, open with notes on kindness to animals. Dogs come first, with tales of brave dogs, pet dogs, and a dog and a cat who live as friends.

Cats, hens, canaries, and wild birds each get a full group of short tales and rhymes. Horses, rabbits, and squirrels close the pet parade, with notes on food, care, and play. Each piece is brief and plain, made for new readers who love pets and want to treat them well and with care each day.
70640-third-base-thatcher:
Third Base Thatcher is a boys' baseball novel by Everett Scott, published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1923. Scott was the real shortstop of the New York Yankees, champions of the American League in 1922. Leslie Crump drew the illustrations. The book belongs to a series named for fielding positions.

Pitcher Pollock, Catcher Craig, and First Base Faulkner stand on the same shelf. The chapters open with a disputed foul and a fight in the dark. A cub reporter, a wreck, and a rescue carry the schoolboy plot. One hundred thousand dollars raises the stakes midway. Indoor practice, the scrub team, and a stiff schedule bring the season round. Ballplayer authors lent their names and trade knowledge to such series. Scott's volume teaches the hot corner while it entertains.
70668-needler:
Needler is a science fiction story by Randall Garrett, with pictures, printed in a leading science fiction magazine in June 1957. A Sherlock Holmes line stands at its head, on a case where the trouble was too much evidence. What was vital lay buried under what did not matter, the detective says. The tale opens after a space battle, with survivors brought back wrong.

They just did not give a damn, the first lines say of the first load of men fetched home. Brought back after the battle of a named star, they had been short circuited somewhere. They cared not two hoots whether they lived or died. The crew of another ship, found drifting after winning its fight, showed the same flat state. Fighting men in a half sleeping trance, while their foes burned, is the story's grim riddle.
70678-einstein-the-searcher:
Alexander Moszkowski wrote Einstein the Searcher, a book of dialogues with Einstein, translated by Henry Brose and published by Methuen in London. The translator's note, dated at Oxford in 1921, thanks the author for material about Einstein that would otherwise remain unknown. The book presents both the work and the man.

Chapters range over phenomena in the heavens, education, the discoverer, and different worlds. A full chapter gives Einstein's life and personality. The opening chapter treats the new mechanics: parallels with Leverrier, the planets Neptune and Mercury, and tests of relativity. The solar eclipse of 1919 and its curved ray of light come in for close attention. Moszkowski lets general readers ramble with Einstein beyond pure physics, into the thought of a great scientist.
70824-the-world-mover:
George Smith wrote a feature novel for a science fiction magazine of November 1950. Its headnote sets the hook. Les Ackerman, unbelievably alive after a nuclear explosion, finds himself sought by the denizens of three possible worlds. All contend that he alone can adjust the situation he has created. Only Les doesn't know what he's done.

Ackerman has spent months writing three hundred thousand words on a new transuranic element, its physical and chemical properties nearly complete. The nuclear properties are left to last, since bombardment defiles the sample. He loads deuterium ice and the sample into the cyclotron for a half-hour test, expecting the counters to record while he sleeps. A laboratory accident with cosmic consequences is the setup.
70866-recollections-of-the-eventful-life:
Recollections of the Eventful Life of a Soldier, by the late Joseph Donaldson, was issued in a new edition in London and Glasgow in 1859. Donaldson was a sergeant in the Ninety Fourth Scots Brigade. A Shakespeare motto heads the book: a round unvarnished tale of moving accidents by flood and field.

An introductory notice explains the form. The narrative first came out in three volumes: the recollections themselves, the war in the Peninsula, and scenes and sketches in Ireland. Those volumes succeeded, but their form kept them from most readers. Now they are collected into one volume, at a price within reach of all classes. The story runs to 1814, over about twenty one years. Fifteen relate to his boyhood, and six to his career in the army. Readers get a ranker memoir of the Napoleonic wars.
70884-french-without-a-master:
French Without a Master is a farce in one act by Tristan Bernard, translated by Barrett H Clark. Samuel French published it at New York in 1915 in the series The World's Best Plays. The editor's note sets Bernard beside George Cohan: in his comedies the amusing types of the society of the day are set forth with good humour and freshness.

Many of Bernard's plays are broad farces, the note says, but a vein of thought runs through them and lifts them above the merely theatrical. The farce here is Bernard's early play about English as it is spoken, adapted since English serves as the foreign tongue in the original. Its plot turns on the character of the interpreter. The piece has kept its place in the repertory of the Comedie Francaise for years.
70901-the-great-fraud-of-ulster:
Healy's The Great Fraud of Ulster, issued under the title Stolen Waters, is known here through the volume's own press notices, which open the book. The Morning Post welcomes Healy's treatment of a difficult and obscure episode in Ulster's history, calling him a historical detective of Sherlock Holmes ingenuity. The Athenaeum praises a romantic story woven from the dry material of official records and legal documents.

The Daily Telegraph calls it a wonderful effort in legal and historical research. The Outlook praises a lawyer of original genius, telling a tangled legal dispute with eloquence and a characteristic sting. Healy was a famous Irish member of Parliament, and the book unravels a net of intrigue by which, he argues, rights in Ulster were stolen. The Pall Mall Gazette notes the less favourable light the story throws on past Irish administration.
70953-the-model-prayer:
The Model Prayer collects expositions on the Lord's Prayer by J D Jones, issued in a third edition by James Clarke and Company of London. The talks began as Sunday morning lectures to his own congregation, printed because members found them helpful and wanted them in lasting form.

Nine chapters work through the prayer phrase by phrase, from the disciples' request and Our Father to daily bread, forgiveness, and temptation. Jones credits help from earlier expositions by Dods and Stanford and claims no originality for himself. Readers get a plain, pastoral walk through each petition, written for ordinary churchgoers rather than scholars.
70964-the-wrong-letter:
Walter S Masterman opens a detective tale with a calm phone call to Scotland Yard, in a novel with a preface by G K Chesterton. Superintendent Sinclair takes the call himself, since he is not to be disturbed for small matters. A woman's cool voice reports that the Home Secretary has been murdered at his own house.

Sinclair asks who speaks, hears a laugh, and is told it is the murderer, no one in particular. He sets his man Lewis to trace the call, then thinks to check where the Home Secretary truly is. Into the office walks Sylvester Collins, a barrister turned inquiry agent who hates being called a Sherlock Holmes. Readers get a crisp British mystery built on nerve, false scents, and close teamwork with the police.
71010-the-british-soldier:
