The British Soldier, His Courage and Humour, by the Reverend E J Hardy, was first printed in 1915. Hardy was a chaplain to the forces, now retired, and had written Mr Thomas Atkins. He gives the book to those who gave life or health to save the world from barbarism.

More than twenty chapters sort tales of the common soldier by theme, from courage and discipline to cavalry charges and grit and guns. Later heads treat men under fire, men in the trenches, and men in hospital, still not downhearted. A French lady letter at the front says the poor Tommies fight like lions and are very funny. Hardy writes to show the stock of the ranks in the Great War.
71019-the-summers-readers-second-reader:
Maud Summers made a second reader for schoolchildren, published at New York in 1909, with drawings by Lucy Fitch Perkins and Marion Mahony. Its contents march by the months of the school year, each month headed by a poet's name. September opens with Indian corn and Longfellow's coming of the corn, adapted.

October brings Hiawatha's canoe and the elves and the shoemaker. November keeps the first Thanksgiving, with Whittier and Lydia Maria Child. December has a birds' Christmas feast and Piccola. Franklin's kite, Stevenson's Singing, and Rossetti's boats sail on the rivers fill the spring. Stories are credited and adapted throughout, a child's library in one volume.
71068-the-rambler-club-on-the-texas-bord:
The Rambler Club on the Texas Border is a boys tale by Sheppard, writ and drawn by his own hand. It stands in a long run of club books: the club at sea, in a cold camp, in the hills, and on a ranch. Gold, a sky ship, and a house boat stand in that list.

It came out at Philadelphia in the year cut in Roman marks on its title page. Its rights were set that same year. A front print shows a crowd as it watches the law men at work. This trip takes the club of lads to the far south line of the land, for rides, hunts, and risks among ranch men, horse thieves, and the guards of the line.
71146-phronsie-pepper:
Phronsie Pepper is a children's story by Margaret Sidney of Boston. Sidney wrote Five Little Peppers and How They Grew and its sequels. Lothrop, Lee and Shepard issued this volume at its seventy first thousand. McDermott drew the illustrations of Phronsie and the children for it. Rights date to 1897 under the old Lothrop Publishing name.

A preface says Phronsie alone of the five had no grown up book. She was the youngest of the Five Little Peppers in the family. Readers who loved the Peppers thought that gap a little unfair, Sidney says. This volume gives the baby of the family her own chance to grow. Sidney dedicates it to her husband's memory with love and thanks.
71215-our-davie-pepper:
Margaret Sidney wrote a new Pepper tale of the lad Davie. The book stands last of twelve in the famed Pepper set. Alice Barber Stephens drew its plates for the young crowd. A front plate shows a hearth blaze praised for its fine look. My, hear the logs pop, is the cry in that warm scene.

Five Little Peppers and How They Grew leads the set's long list. Midway, Grown Up, and Phronsie Pepper stand in the roll of twelve. Polly's tales, Joel's trips, and school days fill the mid set. Abroad, friends, Ben, and the small brown house close the line ere Davie. Home love and brave poor days rule the whole set. Young hearts warm to it.
71319-clarissa-dormer:
Clarissa Dormer; or, The Advantages of Good Instruction is a children's moral tale of 1808. J Harris printed it in London, at the corner of St Paul's Church-yard. Harris succeeded E Newbery at the Original Juvenile Library. Clarissa's parents were natives of a West India settlement. The narrative describes their mixed descent with period frankness. Taught by example, they tyrannised over enslaved Africans, callous to their sufferings.

Clarissa, their only child, inherits vast possessions. From her first steps she is never contradicted. Every slave must serve her before any other business. Before five years old she is a tyrant. A governess is engaged from England at prodigious expense. The agent, Mr Franklin, chooses Miss Melville after long search. Melville lost her parents and much of her property through an unjust executor. Franklin lays the family's particulars honestly before her.
71346-the-young-ship-builder:
Sophie Swett wrote this tale of a young ship builder family. Penn printed it at Philadelphia in 1918, Betts drew plates. Contents open with We and the Aliens on Groundnut Hill, Palmyra. Cyrus sacrifices himself for the aliens sake in chapter two.

A little alien woes, the family disgraced, and Loveday mystery follow. A studio tea, business efforts, and a diplomatic effort fill middle. A luncheon with unbidden guests and a surprising announcement come late. Mother second marriage mixed two sets of children in the house. A chance meeting and a little journey into the world fill two more of the chapters.
71352-the-crimson-banner:
The Crimson Banner is a story of college baseball by William D Moffat, held under a 1907 copyright. Moffat had written A Schoolboy Honor and The County Pennant. A front plate shows a crack that rang over the whole field.

Thirty or more chapters open with a singular letter and a choice on joining the league. A new president, an intercepted letter, and open enemies stir the plot before the nine is even picked. Later heads name a night expedition, a prisoner, and a hearing before the faculty. Three games pace the back half, with a trip to Berkeley and a return to Belmont. One head has the boys burning the midnight oil. College sports fans get ball, honor, and school intrigue mixed.
71357-phemie-keller:
Phemie Keller, a novel in three volumes by F G Trafford, author of George Geith and City and Suburb, opens with volume one from Tinsley Brothers at London in 1866. The right of translation and reproduction is reserved.

Chapter one, Among the Hills, follows a traveller toiling under noontide heat up the defile from Grassenfel to Tordale. Stormy Skillanscar rises on one side and the peaks of Helbeck on the other, hemming him in like a prisoner. Round a bend of rock, Tordale church comes suddenly into view, with its waterfall and larch-shaded graveyard.
71358-phemie-keller:
Trafford wrote a Victorian novel in three volumes, and volume two came out in London in 1866. The story turns on Phemie Keller and on Captain Stondon, who comes home to his estate after a long absence. No crowd greets them, since the suicide of Montague Stondon has cast a shadow over the return.

Phemie first sees Marshlands, the red brick house she comes to love with deep feeling. Its gardens, park, and long belts of trees shut out views of the country beyond. Chapters named Basil, The Next Heir, Jealousy, and The Downward Road promise family tension and hard choices. Readers get a slow, rich picture of estate life, love, and rank in mid Victorian England.
71359-phemie-keller:
Phemie Keller is a novel by F G Trafford. Tinsley Brothers published it in London in 1866. This is the third of three volumes.

The final volume opens near the close of 1856. Letters from India arrive for Captain Stondon at Marshlands. They are written by Basil, who left nearly three years before. Phemie lives for those letters, the narrator says. She can give her husband duty but not love. Chapters move through sorrow, a meeting, and confessions toward the close. Three volume novels were the standard form for serious fiction then. Trafford builds the ending on long separation.
71374-the-dalehouse-murder:
Francis Everton writes a murder tale told in the first person in a novel with sixteen chapters and a tennis house-party. The narrator heads for Merchester at a friend's call in chapter one to open the tale. Stella Murdered stands as chapter three, and Detective Inspector Allport enters at chapter four in the contents.

A letter warns the narrator that his mixed doubles partner, Margaret Hunter, holds a devastating attraction for men. Stella Palfreeman, the prettiest girl he ever saw, will stay for the tournament week as well in that house. Kenneth, Ralph Bennett, and a locum called The Tundish fill out the party at the house. Heads promise a Chinese poison, a case-book, an inquest, and a close call in the run.
71428-rings-for-the-finger:
George Frederick Kunz wrote Rings for the Finger, a study of the ring. His other jewel books are advertised in the front pages here. The curious lore of precious stones is one of those volumes. The magic of jewels and charms and a Shakespeare stones book follow. A plate shows the Maharani of Sikkim in her royal ornaments.

She wears two gold rings, one set with a turquoise. The other of her rings is set with coral, the caption says. Her peculiar crown is of gold, turquoise, and coral together. From her amber necklace hangs a charm box set with rubies. Lapis-lazuli and turquoise share that charm box with the rubies. Kunz was the great American writer on gems of his day. The book gathers the history and lore of the ring on the hand.
71432-the-black-border:
Ambrose Gonzales wrote this story collection, The Black Border: Gullah Stories of the Carolina Coast, printed at Columbia, South Carolina, in 1922, with a glossary of the Gullah tongue at the back. He dedicates it to Robert Elliott Gonzales. A foreword discusses earlier tellings of coast tales by Colonel Jones of Georgia.

Contents list more than forty pieces. Hunting tales stand thick together: the lion killer, the raccoon hunter, the turkey hunter, and the gator hunter. Old Barney, Sam Dickerson, and Mingo the drill master get stories of their own. Two beast fables close the main set, and a version of the Tar-Baby story, as told by Jones and by Joel Chandler Harris, ends the volume before the glossary.
71441-mating-center:
Frank Belknap Long's The Mating Center was printed in the United States in 1961 as a Chariot Book. The prologue sets its cold creed in a seven-tiered hall, where a Guiding Specialist tells the crowd what love is. Love, he says, must be stripped of glamour and seen as a mere tool for breeding the race.

Its use, in that world, is kept to a picked few men and women whose sole task is to breed. Against this stands Teleman, who trembles as a lovely woman steps toward him on the travel strip. She is not free for sex, by her dress, yet she clings to him and whispers that the love instincts are coming back. The clash is the tale.
71449-meg-of-the-heather:
Evelyn R Garratt tells a girl's story in Meg of the Heather, issued by the Religious Tract Society in London. The contents promise storm and flight: The Storm, A Dream of Lions, Golden Chains, Sheila's Confession, and a last chapter named for Jem. A front plate shows Meg refusing wedlock for now: she wants to be free, she tells Jem dear.

The tale opens with Meg face down on the heath, worn out from walking, glad to be alone under a bright sun. A storm brews, thunder rolls, and then a voice calls her name and a hand grips her arm. Young readers get a wild start.
71486-the-kansas-university-science-bull:
Volume one, number six of the Kansas University Science Bulletin came out in Lawrence in September 1902. The number costs fifteen cents and holds two papers, both by Beede. The first tells of new fossils from the upper Carboniferous rocks of Kansas. A plate shows the forms.

Beede says the finds help complete the order of animal life in the topmost Carboniferous beds. One new crinoid has a surface of pustules and granules, a basin shaped calyx, and ten short massive arms. The second paper studies variation in the spiralia of a shell named Seminula argentia. Museum workers and fossil hunters get exact measures and close description for Kansas field work.
71501-the-kansas-university-science-bull:
Beede and Rogers study the fossils of the coal measures in this university bulletin of September 1902. Volume one, number seven, was published by the university at Lawrence, Kansas, at 25 cents. The paper treats the fauna of the Shawnee formation, by Haworth's earlier work, in its long title.

The Wabaunsee formation and the Cottonwood limestone get lists of their fossils too. Beede continues the lists Rogers published in the same journal before this number. Shells, corals and other sea life from Kansas coal-age rocks are named and ranged, the patient spadework on which geology's map of the plains was built.
71514-the-kansas-university-science-bull:
The Kansas University Science Bulletin holds one study in this count. The issue is the eighth of its first run, from September 1902. Its one piece is on the split of seed cells in a clan of hoppers. McClung wrote the piece, with four plates to show his finds.

He first sets out his tools and the names he will use for parts. He then tells what he saw in the glands of the male of the clan. Young cells, first and next seed forms, and ripe seeds are traced in turn. His close weighs the names and sets two hopper clans side by side. A strange spare part in the cell gets a part of its own in the study. A list of past works on the theme ends the piece in full.
71578-bonnie-scotland-and-what-we-owe-he:
William Elliot Griffis wrote Bonnie Scotland and What We Owe Her, published at Boston in October 1916. Griffis had written on Holland, Belgium, China, and Japan for young readers. He gives this book to three women friends who traveled Scotland with him.

Twenty-five chapters tour the land: Glasgow, Edinburgh, Melrose Abbey, Stirling, Iona, and the Orkneys and Shetlands. Griffis treats Burns and his teachers, John Knox, and Bonnie Prince Charlie. A closing chapter counts America's debt to Scotland. A time chart of Scottish history and an index end the book. Heather, Highland dress, and the old Highlands get chapters of their own.
71642-with-boone-on-the-frontier:
Captain Ralph Bonehill wrote 'With Boone on the Frontier; or, The Pioneer Boys of Old Kentucky,' copyrighted in 1903 and issued by Grosset and Dunlap. A frontispiece shows Long Knife taken fairly and squarely in the breast. Chapter I, 'Two Boys of the Wilderness,' opens with a gunshot: Harry Parsons and Joe Winship, out to bag a deer or two, hear a report where no one should be.

Joe levels his gun as four deer burst into view, but Harry stops him, fearing the Indians they met yesterday are after the game. Later chapters bring Daniel Boone himself on stage, leading the way and making his great shot. The boys settle at Boonesborough, rescue Jemima Boone, and endure a night raid, a forest fire, and an attack on the fort before the retreat of the Indians closes the tale.
71667-confessions-of-a-book-lover:
Confessions of a Book-Lover is a book of essays by Walters, with an introduction by Coulson Kernahan. Kelly published the first edition in London in 1913. The author dedicated it to the memory of his father. The contents list fourteen chapters of bookish confession. Humbly to Confess opens the volume. Books and Gardens and Books That Tempt follow in order. Books That Captivate and Personalities in Bookland come next. Second-Hand Books and the cult of the bookplate get chapters.

Bedside Books, Old Friends, and rose coloured spectacles fill the middle. With Nature and A Pilgrimage vary the bookish theme. Farewell closes the contents at the end. Kernahan's introduction recalls meeting the author as a boy. Part of the volume had appeared in Great Thoughts magazine. The essays celebrate buying, keeping, and loving books. Walters confesses a gentle vice in fourteen chapters.
71672-a-virginia-cavalier:
Molly Elliot Seawell wrote this historical tale, A Virginia Cavalier, copyrighted in 1896 and printed at New York and London in 1903 with pictures. A motto heads it: nature made Washington great, but he made himself virtuous. The frontispiece shows a sword's charge: never draw it in an unworthy cause.

A list of pictures tells whose youth this is. George is presented to Washington, bids Betty goodbye, takes his daily lesson in arms, and has a savage by the throat. Chapter one paints midland Virginia in late October 1746, in Indian summer. Great rivers roll through rich woodlands and corn-fields, the broad Rappahannock shimmers under an occasional grain vessel, and quiet homesteads bask in a musical silence of country sounds.
71691-the-modern-writer:
The Modern Writer is an essay by Sherwood Anderson, printed at San Francisco in 1925. The Lantern Press issued the small volume. Anderson asks why America was so long in gaining a national literature. Nations are not made in a short time, he answers. In a small old country, one people sings the same songs for centuries. The poet there rests on tales in the very air.

The American writer faces a unique and near impossible task. The country is vast, with many conditions of life and traditions. California is not Maine; Ohio is not North Carolina, Anderson insists. Americans are still strangers to one another, a little afraid of each other. Time alone can weld them into one people. Anderson classes himself among the Moderns, as the critics had labelled him. The essay is his account of their craft.
71748-joyce-kilmer:
Volume two holds the prose works of poet Joyce Kilmer, with letters. Holliday edited the set, printed by Doran in New York. A photo shows Sergeant Kilmer of the 165th Infantry in France. The shot is dated May 1918, months before his death.

Essays treat Holy Ireland, Christmas giving, and the inefficient library. Belloc poetry and Catholic poets of Belgium get full essays here. Letters run to fellow poets, priests, his mother, children, and wife. War songs, a short tale, and a one act play close the volume. A grave photo stands among the plates in the book.
71757-waves-and-ripples-in-water-air-and:
J A Fleming, professor at University College, London, gave a course of Christmas lectures at the Royal Institution on waves and ripples. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge issued this second, revised issue in 1912. Fleming notes that such lectures speak to a young crowd, yet welcome older hearers too.

Wireless telegraphy had made waves in the aether a hot topic, and Fleming uses that hook. He treats waves in water first, then sound waves in air, then aether waves. Tests with simple gear show each claim on the bench. A front plate shows his Christmas lecture on waves in the air, drawn from the Graphic. Clear talk, not hard math, carries the science.
71766-rachel-dyer:
John Neal prefaced his 1828 Portland novel with a long argument against the novelists of his age. They held, he says, that personal beauty and moral beauty are apportioned together. Godwin saw only a shadow of the fuller truth. Brown, Scott, and Byron made all their great men scoundrels, hypocrites, or banditti, while their good men stayed subordinate and destitute of energy.

Neal answers that a man may have a club-foot, a hump-back, or red hair and yet be good. He may even be great, and a dwarf of distorted shape may be a giant in goodness of heart. Rachel Dyer, issued by Shirley and Hyde, is the North American story built on that conviction. Neal had labored at the same proof before, in his earlier Errata.
71800-formula-for-murder:
Formula for Murder is a science fiction story by Lee Gregor, printed in the magazine Infinity in November 1957. Its blurb gives the hook. It is easy to get away with murder: just prove insanity. But make sure, it warns, you hide the method in your madness.

The first chapter opens in space. The figure of Professor Glover slips from the surface of a space station and twinkles away among the stars. Jim Britten stares as though his gaze could call the man back. He stands paralysed while the suited body falls toward the dazzling sun. In his hand is the radiophone antenna he ripped from Glover's back. The station is a vast doughnut, twenty-five miles across, floating a thousand miles above the earth. A death in the void, a torn antenna, and a plea of madness are the parts of Gregor's formula.
71889-chants-for-the-boer:
Joaquin Miller wrote poems in support of the Boers in their war with Britain, printed in San Francisco in 1900. A verse at the front says the fittest place for man to die is where he dies for man. Miller owns he holds no ill word for brave old England, whose folk were his first, best friends.

Her policy, her politicians, and her speculators he hates, he says. Poems speak to the Boers, to fighting lords of London town, to Oom Paul Kruger, and to Mother Egypt and India. A closing verse calls men to aid the right that needs assistance and resist the wrong. The small book captures American sympathy for a small farmer people at war.
71945-frank-merriwell-s-brother:
Frank Merriwell's Brother, also called The Greatest Triumph of All, is a tale by Burt Standish. Copyright in 1901, it was printed at Philadelphia by David McKay. Standish wrote many Merriwell tales, and this one turns from Frank to his brother Dick and the friends around both young men.

The book opens as thirteen men leap on Frank in his room, in what the first chapter calls a warm reception. Chapter heads promise a stolen message, a kidnapped girl, a foe named Anton Mescal, and a ball game won by one run to nothing. School sport, loyalty, and pluck drive the plot, in the brisk style that made the Merriwell name a byword for clean grit.
71948-an-elder-brother:
An Elder Brother is a religious tale by Eglanton Thorne, published in London by the Religious Tract Society. Its hero is Michael, a keeper of a second-hand book shop. The first chapter sings the pull of such a shop on a certain kind of man. Michael's shop lay below street level, down stone steps. Books filled its shelves from floor to top, its upper room, and its back parlour. They spilled onto a bench before the window and up the steps to the street.

The chapter heads map a tale of fault and repair. Little Margery's loss comes early. Michael makes a good bargain that proves unrighteous gain. Pain grips him, and the burden makes itself felt. Restitution follows, then confession shared with a friend. At the end his house becomes a home. The tale is a plain lesson in honesty, told through a bookseller's small world.
71949-geoff-s-little-sister:
Geoff's Little Sister, by Evelyn R. Garratt, is a story for young readers published at Ipswich in 1900. Garratt had written other tales for children, and Ernest Smythe drew the pictures for this one. A verse from Proverbs about ruling one's spirit stands at the front.

The chapters follow Geoff, who is charged with the care of his little sister, through scenes of family life. One chapter asks who broke the doll, and another prepares for Christmas. A chapter called Taking a City turns on the verse about mastering one's temper. The opening scene shows the boys of the house upset at the end of November, comforted by their nurse with a dish of oranges. The story closes with their mother's Christmas present.
71960-the-conquest-of-cancer:
Wright, a surgeon, argued in 1925 that the fight with cancer had passed out of the hands of doctors alone. Kegan Paul of London and Dutton of New York published his essay, with an opening note by Crookshank. The cure, Wright says, is now a task for teachers, writers, and law makers. He claims that seventy five per cent of cases could then be cured, with deaths under five per cent.

His figures give the claim its weight. In the United Kingdom, deaths ran at 466,000 a year, and 43,000 of them were due to cancer. Of those, 19,000 were men and 24,000 were women. In Great Britain in 1921, one in seven deaths over the age of thirty came from this disease. Wright holds that most of these cases could be stopped or cured if found in time. Folk, he says, must face the facts and seek help early.
71996-jack-derringer:
Jack Derringer: A Tale of Deep Water is a sea novel by Basil Lubbock. John Murray published it in London in 1906. Lubbock had written Round the Horn Before the Mast. Part one names its world in the first title: the Yankee hell-ship. The rule of the belaying-pin and the use of a sheath-knife follow.

Later chapters bring the fatal red lead and Studpoker Bob's malady. Part two goes adrift with the Ocmulgee. The burning of the South Seaman, the open boat, and the atoll fill its middle. A fight on the sands, a lynching, and the Black Adder lead to Papeete. The first chapter wakes Bucking Broncho in the foc's'le. Dawn shows men sprawled in drunken stupor among the bunks. A blood-stained figure breathes hoarsely on a chest below him. The forecastle's brutality is established before the ship even sails.
72032-china-under-the-empress-dowager:
Bland and Backhouse published China Under the Empress Dowager in 1910. The book is a history of the life and times of Tzŭ Hsi, compiled from state papers and the private diary of the comptroller of her household. A photograph from the portrait by Katharine Carl fronts the book.

The Empress Dowager ruled China for nearly half a century, through rebellion, foreign invasion, and the Boxer catastrophe. The book made her vivid to English readers: the holy mother of the Forbidden City, painted as cruel, shrewd, and magnificent. Later scholarship showed the comptroller's diary to be a fabrication. The volume is thus a double document: a portrait of the Dowager, and a famous case of a source too good to be true.
72038-captain-mary-miller:
Harriet Robinson wrote this drama, copyrighted in 1887 and printed at Boston. Its motto comes from Margaret Fuller, who held that women might fill any office, even sea-captains if they would. The cast centers on the Gandy family of Annisport: retired Captain Nathan Gandy, his wife Lorany, and their daughter Mary, with skipper William Miller and ship-owner Romberg.

Act one opens in the Gandy living room, where Lorany refuses to pick up money her husband dropped on the floor and swears she never will. Nathan sold the calf she counted as hers, and she has heard a lecture-woman quote the law's view that husband and wife are one, and that one is the husband. The quarrel sets the play's theme, a wife's claim to her own property joined to a daughter fit to command a ship.
7211-the-american-union-speaker:
Philbrick's American Union Speaker, entered in 1865, serves two ends at once. It meets the demand for new selections suited to the spirit of the hour, and it gathers standard pieces for elocutionary exercise on which time has set its seal. About one hundred extracts from recent work, by more than fifty authors, appear here for the first time in a speaker.

Old and new pieces stand side by side, chosen and prepared with care for reading aloud in school, hall, or home. The book belongs to a wartime moment when public speech carried unusual weight, and its selections mix fresh feeling with lasting eloquence. Readers get a portable stage for voice, memory, and civic pride.
72111-dick-s-retriever:
Stooke wrote a tale for young readers about a boy named Dick and his dog. The book came out in 1921 with Thomas Nelson and Sons. Stooke also wrote Tim and Jim and A Reformatory Boy. Dick is the eldest child of Widow Wilkins. Their small home stands near elm trees and the sea.

A storm at night brings a lost dog to their door. Dick runs errands, meets a bully, and seeks a ten-shilling prize. He talks with a colonel, faces hard times, and makes a brave rescue. A front plate shows his mother at a laid table. Good acts earn their due by the close.
72140-the-home-maker:
The Home-Maker is a novel by Dorothy Canfield, printed in New York in 1924. Canfield's earlier books listed here include Understood Betsy, The Bent Twig, and The Brimming Cup. The story opens on a wife scrubbing furiously at a line of grease spots leading from the stove toward the dining room door.

The spots came from a platter her son Henry tilted while carrying in the steak, though she has warned him a thousand times. Her children pay her no attention, the cleaning powder is on its second can this month, and the telephone rings at the worst moment. A sober little boy with a teddy bear watches her quivering back and slips away unseen.
72148-the-satellite-keeper-s-daughter:
Mark Reinsberg wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Fantastic Universe in December 1956. An editor's note calls it a quiet story of a susceptible space trucker who swore by a guidebook. Its opening line is flat: sex and space do not mix, and Mattapenny's Galactic Guidebook cannot be trusted.

Bill Brack hauls valuable deluplasm out of Dryod-7 and has twelve hours to kill before his convoy jumps off. The guidebook lists Corbie as a fuel station and gives the Hotel Eros two asterisks, plain but fairly comfortable. Brack finds no modern comforts there at all, and oxygen service costs ten per cent extra. The keeper's daughter waits beyond that grievance.
72164-a-scrap-of-paper:
Dillon wrote this inside history of German statecraft and its bid for world rule. The third edition came out in London in 1914 with Hodder and Stoughton. The title takes the German Chancellor sneer at a treaty with Britain. He called the pact on Belgium just a scrap of paper.

Chapters lay out a scheme, its steps, and how a quarrel was forced. Germany programme, Italy stance, and the twelfth hour get full parts. British neutrality and a famed infamous offer close the main text. An appendix on statecraft and the war rounds out the case.
72182-hannibal-s-daughter:
Andrew Haggard wrote this romance of Hannibal and ancient Carthage. The book came out in London in 1898 with Hutchinson. Haggard began the tale on the site of old Carthage itself. He wove its plot through feats told by Polybius and Livy.

Parts bear names like Hamilcar, Carthage, and Hannibal Vow at first. Later parts bring Elissa, Maharbal, and plots within the city walls. Cleandra cunning and warnings of risk drive the tale onward. The book mixes love, war, and lore of Rome and its great foe. Haggard asks readers who shun dry history to try this form.
72198-meleager:
Meleager is a tale of the strange by Vaughan, a fellow of a learned guild. A quote at its head, from a famed book on sad humours, asks how far the stars work on us. It was first set in print in the mid war years at London.

Its form is a found hand script, with a word at its front by its first hand. That word takes up the charge to print the tale. The script came to him, he says, by the kind hand of a great rover and hill man of the age. That man had chanced on it in the course of his work in far lands. A fore tale, two great parts, and a close word make its frame.
72202-the-life-trial-and-conversations-o:
The Life, Trial and Conversations of Robert Emmet tells of the leader of the Irish rising of 1803. It also prints his famed speech from the dock. This New York edition of 1850 was stereotyped from the last Dublin edition and published by Robert Coddington of the Bowery. A poem by Moore, bidding readers not breathe his name, stands at the front.

A second piece describes Emmet's uninscribed tomb. Emmet asked that his grave bear no lines until other times and other men could do justice to his character. The book gathers life, trial talk, and speech into one memorial volume for the young patriot hanged after his failed rising.
7224-within-you-is-the-power:
Henry Thomas Hamblin argues that a power lies hidden in every person, by whose use one may rise to higher and better things. His chapters move through infinite life and power, the overcoming of life's difficulties, and fate or free will. Cause and effect, success, health, and the secret of abundant supply follow, then turn to the subconscious and superconscious mind.

Character building, habit, happiness, and the right use and misuse of mental and spiritual powers follow, closing with the overcoming of limits and the awakening of inward powers. Hamblin writes in a calm, encouraging voice for readers seeking practical hope rather than abstract theory. The book offers plain counsel for a steadier, fuller life.
72247-answer-please-answer:
Ben Bova wrote this science fiction story for Amazing Stories of October 1962, illustrated by Schelling, with a headnote calling Bova an astronomer who draws on the facts of his field. Two drafted soldiers winter at the South Pole, where the thermometer reads fifty degrees below zero and the winter is just beginning.

The narrator runs a dome crammed with control consoles, computers, and weather sensors, transmitting memory tapes to McMurdo. His companion Rizzo, a drafted electronicist from the radio astronomy observatory at Greenbelt, jokes that they both have appendicitis and need replacements at once. The joke turns into discovery: Rizzo is an astronomer too, from Project Ozma, while the narrator worked at Lick Observatory with the 120-inch reflector. Two rival kinds of astronomer are thus trapped together for the long polar night.
7229-rujub-the-juggler:
G. A. Henty's Rujub, the Juggler is a historical tale for young and old set in the Sepoy Mutiny in India from 1857 to 1859, while Lord Canning held the reins of British rule. The publisher's introduction recalls chupatties passed from village to village and placards against British rule at Delhi. It also recalls the greased cartridges of the new Enfield rifle, rumoured to be smeared with forbidden pig's fat.

Fanatical feeling, the introduction says, soon brought the mutiny to a head, and Henty builds his story on that storm. A juggler's craft and a boy's courage thread through camps and sieges, giving young readers adventure with a history lesson inside it. Henty keeps the pace brisk and the loyalties plain.
72293-the-social-center:
Woodrow Wilson, then Governor of New Jersey, gave the address printed here as The Social Center, a Means of Common Understanding. He spoke before the First National Conference on Civic and Social Center Development at Madison on October 25, 1911. The University of Wisconsin issued the speech that December as a bulletin of its Extension Division, priced at five cents.

Wilson argues for the school house and like public rooms as meeting ground where neighbors can talk out shared concerns and reach a common mind. The bulletin around it lists the extension work of the university, from courses by mail to lectures and town reference help. It is a small relic of the civic center push of those years.
72389-utopia-never:
Utopia Never is a science fiction story by Thomas Disch, printed in Amazing Stories in August 1963. Its scene is New Katanga, a colony world whose guide insists it is a paradise. A stranger has accepted citizenship there willingly enough, yet he will not admit the place is perfect. The tag line adds that, little as he knew it, he was right.

The story opens in mid-argument. The visitor holds that there is always a fly in the ointment, that injustice is part of human nature and no society can do without it. The guide answers that these are special conditions, centred on the gobblers, creatures whose fleece, only on this world, is tough as iron and soft as silk. The prosperity of New Katanga, the visitor charges, rests on worlds that cannot raise gobblers. The debate sets the tale's question.
72391-star-chamber:
Star Chamber, by H B Fyfe, illustrated by Summers, first appeared in Amazing Stories in March 1963. There were no courts on the isolated world, the blurb says, but there was a Judge.

Quasmin's first impulse at the roar of landing rockets is to dash to the hilltop with his salvaged telescope. The wrecked ship near his shack was not his own, and the authorities might want to know what became of its original crew. A Terran-seeming spaceship settles half a mile away, by the wreck, and Quasmin creeps through the purplish scrub to watch its airlock open.
72501-alden-the-pony-express-rider:
Alden the Pony Express Rider, or Racing for Life, is a boys' tale by Edward Ellis. He was the hand of the deer foot books and of a set of the south west. Plates are by a named hand. The tale stands in a set of the road west books. It was put out with rights held in nineteen hundred and nine. Its list of parts runs to two and twenty.

A lead in heads the run. A clash, west bound, and a cloud of risk come next. On guard, the craft of the first folk, and just in time fill the first run. The charge, old friends met, and a hunt stand past them. A let down, a not rare turn, and a jest on the hero's way fill the mid run.
72512-ten-years-after:
Ten Years After, a reminder by Philip Gibbs, was published by Hutchinson and Company of London in 1924. Gibbs had been a war correspondent of the first rank. Ten years after the guns of August 1914, he looks back at the war and forward at the peace. Four parts make the book: the world war, the uncertain peace, the present perils, and the hope ahead.

Ten years ago, he opens, a spiritual tremor shook the souls of many peoples, as though the last trump were sounding. The most civilised nations on earth were hurled against each other with all their power, science, manhood, and wealth. Dynasties have fallen since, kings are in exile, and the maps are redrawn. Yet the deeper change, Gibbs argues, is in the minds of men and women, whose old securities and convictions lie in wreckage that will never be restored.
7252-the-women-who-came-in-the-mayflower:
Annie Russell Marble wrote this little book as a memorial to the women who came in the Mayflower. Their comrades followed in the Ann and the Fortune and kept high standards of home life in early Plymouth Colony. She makes no attempt at a genealogy of any family, and she admits frankly how much proof is lacking where accounts conflict.

Her aim is glimpses of communal life in 1621 to 1623, with silhouettes of single matrons and maidens whose influence reached into domestic life and schooling. Marble honours endurance, thrift, and care as public virtues, not merely private ones. The book keeps its scale small and its respect large.
72522-nightmare-tower:
Nightmare Tower, by Jacques Jean Ferrat, was produced from Fantastic Universe for June and July 1953. A head note calls Lynne a girl who disliked the man from Mars on sight. Yet, drawn by forces beyond her control, she let him carry her off to the Red Planet.

The magazine bills the story as launching a new name in science fiction. Lynne Fenlay had had a few headaches in her twenty four years, but never one like this. One came from a field hockey ball at twelve, another from a bottle of liqueur at seventeen. A third came from overwork. Each had a clear cause. This headache came out of nowhere, and showed no signs of going away. A health check booth gives her a stamped card. Readers get a Mars tale built on a mystery in a woman head.
72524-the-life-story-of-charlotte-de-la-:
The Life-Story of Charlotte de la Trémoille, Countess of Derby, is a biography by Mary Rowsell. Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner published it in London in 1905. A portrait of the countess, after the painting by Vandyke, stands at the front. Rowsell had written historical tales for the young before this life.

The contents open with birth, parentage, and a peaceful childhood at home. Huguenots and Catholics, a gallant soldier, and gathering storm-clouds surround her girlhood. A Rubens portrait and a naughty little girl enliven the first chapter's summary. The second takes her to The Hague and a marriage of convenience at sixteen. A lady-of-honour's duties and a firstborn child follow in that court. Straitened means at home — the Latin tag heads the third chapter. Lathom House, the Derby seat, anchors the fourth chapter's account of her married world.
72528-thicker-than-water:
Thicker Than Water is a western novel by Wilbur Tuttle, published in 1927. It is billed as a story of Hashknife Hartley, Tuttle's cowboy detective. The opening chapter, The Ace of Spades, sets father against son. Rance McCoy owns the Circle Spade ranch. His son Jack, called Angel, faces him across a lamp lit table. Angel wears a white silk shirt and smells of perfume.

Rance is a scarred fighter of about fifty, his face like jerked venison. The contrast between the two men drives the tale. Twenty two chapters carry the action through saloons, horse trades, and escapes. Lila's departure and return thread through the plot. A fire, a lost hat, and two suspects build the mystery. Hashknife at Work names the chapter where the detective takes hold. The finish comes at the JML ranch.
72585-the-viaduct-murder:
Ronald Knox wrote The Viaduct Murder, a detective novel built like a puzzle. The frontispiece is a map of the railway line between Paston Oatvile and Paston Whitchurch, with the viaduct, the golf links, and a railway timetable. A line from Gaboriau heads the book: suspect what seems probable, and believe first what seems incredible.

The first chapters gather at the Paston Oatvile dormy-house, the lodging of golfers, and move into the rough. A body at the viaduct is the crime the map prepares for. Piecing it together and endless clues name the middle chapters. Knox, a priest and a wit, helped set the rules of the fair-play detective story. Timetables, golf, and a railway line do the work. The reader is given the same map as the hunters and dared to beat them.
72642-dusty-answer:
Dusty Answer is a novel by Rosamond Lehmann, published by Holt in New York in 1927. A Meredith line about a dusty answer fronts the title page. The soul hot for certainties gets that answer in this life, it says. Lehmann dedicates the book to George Rylands. Part one opens when Judith is eighteen years old. The house next door, empty for years, is getting ready again. Gardeners mow and roll the tennis court back to life. They plant tulips and forget me nots in the stone urns.

The grey stone front is made prim and trim again. It seems the next door children must still be there, Judith feels. Those mysterious cousins dropped over the peach tree wall for tea. In truth all was changed, the chapter goes on to say. Lehmann's first novel made her name with Judith's growing up.
727-the-star-spangled-banner:
John A. Carpenter traced the history of the song that became the American national anthem. He starts in August 1814, when Admiral Cockburn threatened Washington in revenge for American raids in Canada, and follows the war that led Francis Scott Key to write his verses at Baltimore. The song's words, music, and early fame are set out in turn.

Carpenter adds the story of the flag, the fort, and the men who sang the song into public life. His account is short and factual, drawn from letters and records of the day. The book serves readers who want to know how a wartime poem grew into a national symbol, and what its first singers meant by it.
72705-tom-swift-and-his-great-oil-gusher:
Victor Appleton's Tom Swift and His Great Oil Gusher, or The Treasure of Goby Farm, was published in New York by Grosset & Dunlap under a copyright of 1924. The frontispiece shows the strike: the oil shot a hundred feet into the air in a huge black geyser. Chapter one is The Falling Airplane, and a second chapter heading begins Almost, cut off in this slice.

A publisher's list at the front marches the series past in order, from motor cycle and motor boat to airship, submarine boat, and electric runabout. The flying boat and this oil gusher itself close the run. The Moving Picture Boys series follows it, fourteen volumes deep, from the West and the coast to Panama and the war front.
72742-a-christmas-prayer:
James Foley wrote this Christmas prayer in verse for friends far away. Volland printed the gift booklet in 1918 with snow tree plates. Dear Lord, these friends of mine, where they may stray, it opens. Wilt Thou bear each Thy blessing on this day, he asks.

Yule logs burn and hearts grow kind as the season comes. If any weep, be kind, if any stray, find them, he prays. If some be far from home or wanderers on the way today. Give them my share of joy, let peace be theirs, he pleads.
72803-tracked-to-his-lair-or-the-pursuit:
Colonel Spencer Dair's Tracked to His Lair, or The Pursuit of the Midnight Raider, ran in the American Indian Weekly. It was volume one, number two, from the Arthur Westbrook Company of Cleveland in 1910. A cast list at the front gives away the whole plot in brief. The Midnight Raider is Scalping Louie, a chief who breaks from the reservation.

Sam Bowser of the Double Cross ranch in Arizona is roused by an eerie cry. He finds his cattle stampeded by a spectre over the corral, and trails the raider through a swamp that nearly sucks him down. Henry Hawks, whose ranch buildings burn, joins the hunt. Deadshot Pete, a cowpuncher, fires the shot that ends it, with an old scout's help.
72814-an-imperial-lover:
An Imperial Lover, a historical novel by Imlay Taylor, was published by McClurg and Company of Chicago in 1898. Taylor, the author of On the Red Staircase, sets the tale in Russia, and its frontispiece shows Pierre le Grand, Peter the Great.

The narrator, Guillaume de Lambert, returns to Moscow twenty years after a visit made memorable by his marriage. The chapters move through the Czar's court: a Livonian peasant girl, Catherine and the Czar, Mentchikof, an intercepted letter, a marriage of dwarfs, and at last a future empress. Lambert recalls that the king's favours to him had been conspicuous, and that obedience to the royal wish sent him on a second Moscow mission he did not want. The love story plays out against Peter's modernizing court.
72869-meet-the-tiger:
Leslie Charteris wrote Meet the Tiger, billed as the first Saint novel. Chapter heads promise a pill box, a naturalist, a little melodrama, and a social evening. Aunt Agatha is upset, the Tiger shows kindness, and the fun goes on. Patricia perseveres, Carn listens in, and the Saint returns before the Tiger is met at last.

The tale opens at Baycombe, a village on the North Devon coast so cut off that the summer holiday rush neglects it. Simon Templar has settled there for all of three days and fallen into regular habits. Templar, known in some parts of the world by his initials as the Saint, is twenty-seven, tall, dark, and keen-faced. His house was a war-time coast defence station, made fit to live in by workmen in thirty-six hours.
72908-the-cardinal-s-musketeer:
The Cardinal's Musketeer is a historical novel by Taylor, published by McClurg at Chicago in 1900. A portrait of Cardinal Richelieu, after Champaigne, fronts the book. The first chapter opens in a clockmaker's shop. The secret of a garret and a pastry shop on the Rue des Petits Champs follow.

Péron, the hero, wins his first victory in the ninth chapter. The cardinal's clock, the cardinal's instructions, and the cardinal's snare mark the rising plot. A house at Poissy, an inn at Amiens, and a greenwood tribunal carry the tale through France. Taylor writes a cloak-and-sword romance of Richelieu's Paris in the manner of Dumas.
72930-the-juggler:
Craddock, in truth Mary Murfree, wrote this Tennessee mountain novel. Houghton Mifflin printed The Juggler at Boston in 1897. Front lists name In the Tennessee Mountains and other tales at prices. Chapter one says mystery was not far to seek in the coves.

Great crags were moulded by heat from fires below in old ages. Waters once drowned the deep coves and ebbed long ago seaward. A split sandstone slab in the path holds worm trace fossils. Ripple marks on rock tell of the waters past being there. Fossil worm burrows in a path slab record life of remote ages in the cove.
72933-miss-devereux-spinster:
Agnes Giberne wrote Miss Devereux, Spinster, in a new edition from a London religious publisher. Giberne also wrote Sun, Moon and Stars and Sweetbriar. A motto bids us take no thought for aught save right and truth. Four books structure the novel.

Book one, In Childhood's Hour, opens with a middle-aged young lady and runs through Dear Aunt and Severely Smitten to an appeal and its results. Book two, After Seven Years, brings Mrs Kennedy's notions, mud and brambles, and a strife for the mastery. Book three is Action and Reaction; book four completes the design. Readers get a Victorian tale of a woman ageing unmarried, told across her whole life.
72945-mrs-harter:
Delafield wrote this novel, Mrs Harter, printed by Harper and Brothers with copyright in 1925. Delafield had written The Heel of Achilles and The Optimist before it. The book is given to Phyllida. The tale is set at Cross Loman, where folk have begun to forget about Mrs Harter and Captain Patch.

The narrator sets himself to rebuild the affair of last summer from slight facts. Mary Ambrey shares his talks and guesses, going by intuition more than knowledge. His wife Claire, who lives on the edge of a volcano by her own saying, saw Mrs Harter in yet another light. Diamond Harter, as the narrator calls her, struck each witness in a different way, and that puzzle drives the book.
72953-studies-of-trees-in-winter:
Studies of Trees in Winter is a guide by Annie Oakes Huntington, printed at Boston in 1902. Its subtitle describes the deciduous trees of northeastern America. Sargent, director of the Arnold Arboretum, wrote the introduction. Coloured plates by Morse and photographs by the author fill the book.

The first chapter teaches the winter marks of a tree: trunk, twigs, leaf scars, bundle scars, and buds. Then the kinds follow, from horsechestnut and the maples to ashes and walnuts. Birches, hornbeams, beeches, and oaks take their chapters. A front plate shows a swamp white oak. Huntington shows that a leafless tree still carries its name written on its twigs.
72985-the-tower:
The Tower, by Yeats, was published in London in 1928. The contents list twenty one poems and a set of notes. Sailing to Byzantium opens the book. In it an old man scorns a land fit only for the young. He sails to the holy city of Byzantium. There sages in gold mosaic are asked to school his soul. He hopes to be made into a gold bird set on a golden bough.

The title poem takes up age tied to a still wild fancy. Other poems include Leda and the Swan and Among School Children. Meditations in Time of Civil War and Nineteen Hundred and Nineteen face recent strife. A Prayer for My Son and All Souls' Night close the set on family and the dead.
73011-the-house-at-pooh-corner:
The House at Pooh Corner is a children's book by Milne, with decorations by Ernest Shepard. The New York edition was first printed in 1928 and reprinted many times over, the copyright page shows. A dedication in verse gives the book back to the mother who, the poet says, gave him Christopher Robin and breathed new life into Pooh.

An opening piece called Contradiction explains the book's place. Christopher Robin and his friends have already been introduced to readers, Milne writes. Now they are going to say good bye, so this opening is the opposite of an introduction. That farewell frame sets the tone for the last set of stories in the wood. The long line of printings listed up to 1951 shows how often the book was called for.
73032-the-reality-of-prayer:
The Reality of Prayer, by Edward Bounds, was edited by Homer Hodge for its readers. Bounds books on prayer are listed at the front in a publisher roll. The Possibilities of Prayer stands there at one dollar and twenty five cents in cloth. It is praised as a rich and helpful book on the place of prayer, there.

Heaven, a place, a city, a home, stands next in that list of his works. Purpose in Prayer and a book on Satan fill out the roll of titles. A full knowledge of scripture wins Bounds praise in the advertisement quotes. A Sunday School Times line praises his gift of insight and choice of words. Southern Methodist devotion to prayer speaks in these warm short books.
73040-the-pioneer:
The Pioneer is a novel by Geraldine Bonner, published in Indianapolis by Bobbs-Merrill in 1905, with illustrations by Harrison Fisher. Its subtitle calls it a tale of two states. Bonner had written Tomorrow's Tangle before it. The book is built in three parts: the country, the town, and the desert.

The contents trace a rising arc. The first book opens with a squatter, the Gracey boys, and a summons, and closes with prizes of accident. The town book turns to city life: feminine logic, danger signals, the great god Pan, and a chapter called business and sentiment. The desert book moves to Nevada. Old friends wear new faces, embers smoulder, and the tale runs to the edge of the precipice before the colonel comes back and the story ends at home. Bonner's West is one of land, money, and the women who must choose within it.
73043-jack-heaton-gold-seeker:
Frederick Collins wrote a boys' adventure novel in 1921, one of a series about Jack Heaton. Jack has also been a wireless operator and an oil prospector in other books. Here he heads for the gold country and outfits at Circle. Chapters follow dog teams, winter quarters, and life on the Arctic Circle.

Bill and Black Pete bring danger, and a cache of gold hidden in stones brings hope. Pictures show snowshoeing, a six gun fired at a great beast, and a boat pitching like a cork. Collins mixes trail craft, cold, and greed for gold. The tale aims at young readers who liked northern adventure.
7309-business-correspondence-vol-1-how-t:
Business Correspondence, Volume One, teaches how to write the business letter in twenty-four chapters on preparing to write, finding the proper viewpoint, opening, presenting a proposition convincingly, and making an effective close. Forceful style, originality, selling appeal fitted to different prospects, and getting orders by letter follow, with proved principles illustrated by extracts from two hundred and seventeen actual letters.

The book opens with what a postage stamp can do and the advantages of doing business by letter, treating the letter as a sales tool, not a formality. Its lessons stay practical throughout, showing real letters rather than preaching rules in the abstract. Clerks, salesmen, and managers get a working manual for the post.
73101-the-royal-banner:
Royal Banner, or Gold and Rubies, is a story for the young. Nelson and Sons published it in London in the year 1888. It forms part of the Little Hazel series of tales for youth. Its author wrote Little Hazel, the King's Messenger, and kindred books of faith. A hymn verse, Stand up for Jesus, stands as its rallying cry.

Chapters run from a wishing well and an old nurse to school life. A diadem of leaves, new friends, and an English home fill early pages. Climbing Schiehallion and a Highland field preaching give Scottish colour. Sought and found, the cousins, and a bridal day close the list. Young readers got faith, family, and highland scenery in one tale.
73144-lady-chatterley-s-lover:
Lady Chatterleys Lover is a novel by Lawrence, in the form of its third hand writ draft. That draft was first put out at Florence in the late nineteen twenties. A small press there made the first print. The copy at hand was set in America by a New York house. Leave for sale in Canada was held by an agent in London.

The first pages set its bleak key at once. Ours is a tragic age, the voice says. So we refuse to take it in a tragic way. The great crash has come, and men live in the ruins. They build small new homes and small new hopes. No smooth road runs to the years ahead. The tale then turns to its chief pair, a young wife and her man, wed in a short leave from the war.
73220-gangway-for-homer:
Gangway for Homer, a tale by George R Hahn with drawings by John Forte, first ran in Science Fiction Quarterly in spring nineteen forty two. The head note says the tale came from that magazine. A wild, pale woman cries out in the tale. She claims that a plain man near her is a great hero of old. She calls him Achilles Maravain.

The man is in truth John Smith, a name he has borne since he was a small child. He is of middle height, middle age, and plain looks in all ways. Yet the woman holds that his touch brings swift death and that no bullet, bomb, or blaster can hurt him. Folk listen with care but do not quite trust her words. The clash of plain fact and wild claim drives the tale.
7326-the-yeoman-adventurer:
George Gough's Yeoman Adventurer follows a hero through chapters on the great Jack, a sergeant of dragoons, Mistress Margaret Waynflete, a journey's start, an ancient high house, and his lord Brocton. Losing his Virgil, a conjurer's cap, a career as a highwayman, Sultan, a slip, and the guest-room of the Rising Sun carry him onward. Pharaoh's kine, war's risks, moorlands, and Bonnie Prince Charlie lie ahead.

Gough dedicates the book to A. D. Steel-Maitland in gratitude and admiration, and his tale mixes Jacobite adventure with rogue's comedy. A new hat, a double six, foppery, a council at Derby, and a brother who knows at last promise twists to the end. The novel reads as a brisk historical romp.
73271-essentials-of-prayer:
The Essentials of Prayer is a devotional book by Edward M Bounds. Homer W Hodge edited it for a series called The Spiritual Life Books. The opening pages advertise Bounds's other works on prayer.

Bounds wrote that prayer holds the central place in a believer's life. His books stress purpose, possibility, and the reality of prayer. Admirers quoted here praise his deep knowledge of Scripture. Bounds served as a minister and chaplain in the nineteenth century. His short books stayed in print long after his death. They shaped how many churches still teach private prayer today.
73273-the-frantic-master:
Douglas Pulleyne wrote this novel, published by Chapman and Hall in London in 1927. A saying of Sophocles from Plato's Republic gives the book its title and epigraph. Asked how he felt about love, the old poet rejoiced to have escaped it, as from a frantic and savage master, the epigraph quotes.

An incident of soldiers in a railway carriage, in essentials true, seeded the book. The author's note credits an editor of the Pioneer who first recorded it for him. A tale told to the Nicobarese, called 'Shoan and the Mermaid,' is also true in his note, in a novel of India and desire.
73283-the-bombardier-and-pocket-gunner:
Ralph Willett Adye wrote The Bombardier, and Pocket Gunner for young gunners. E Larkin printed this first American form at Boston in eighteen hundred four. Adye, a captain of the Royal Regiment of Artillery, made the book. He hopes for his senior officers’ good word as well as the juniors’.

Letter by letter, the pocket book packs a gunner’s whole need. Arms and shot for small arms lead its close set tables. Field guns split by battalion, park, and horse in the next part. Loads for each waggon and stores for each piece stand counted there. French scales of guns and shot close that first wide survey. Siege and fortress wants take their own full lettered spans. Ground works for guns, mortars, and howitzers fill the B part. Beds, boxes, and powder barrels end this chunk of the roll.
7334-with-buller-in-natal-or-a-born-lead:
G. A. Henty's With Buller in Natal, or A Born Leader, opens with a frank preface on the late war. A full, impartial history will take a long time, since even witnesses in different parts of the field differ widely. Until fuller details supplement the meagre military despatches, Henty writes, anything like an accurate history would be impossible. So he has reconciled the various narratives of fighting in Natal as best he can.

His hero, Chris, springs at the enemy in the book's illustration, and the tale follows Buller's campaign through Natal's battles with a boy's eye for action. Henty balances war story with an attempt at fair narrative, admitting gaps where sources clash. The novel gives young readers a campaign in vivid, careful form.
73365-the-chevalier-s-daughter:
The Chevalier's Daughter, or An Exile for the Truth, is a historical tale by Lucy Ellen Guernsey. It forms part of her Stanton-Corbet Chronicles. John F Shaw and Company published the new edition in London. The story is dated sixteen sixty, in the France of the persecuted Protestants.

The frame presents the narrative as memoirs written by the narrator's grandmother in old age. Her husband sat beside her, recalling each incident as she wrote. The note adds a hope about the young dauphin. Unlike his father, he might one day bring toleration to France's Protestants. Guernsey's chronicles retell seventeenth-century religious persecution as family history. The publisher's list praises this tale as a quaint old-world story in her known manner.
73375-30-day-wonder:
Richard Wilson wrote 30-Day Wonder, a novel issued at New York by Ballantine Books with a copyright of 1960. Sam Kent, the narrator, works for a wire service called World Wide, editing American news in the Times Building for relay to London. The story opens on an ordinary hot July morning, a Tuesday, when Sam gets off the long distance bus and walks to his desk.

The headnote tells the turn: the Monolithians, who cannot be harmed, have picked Sam, a good reporter and average man, to head their public relations program. They have a message, and everybody must be convinced, so he has no choice in the matter. Their rules run act peaceful, love thy neighbor, obey the law, and Wilson asks whether people could go mad living that way.
73378-the-war-maker:
The War Maker is a biography by Horace Smith, published by McClurg at Chicago in 1911. Its subtitle calls it the true story of Captain George Boynton. A note warns that Boynton was not the hero's real name. He carried the secret of his true name to his grave. He was born in New York in 1842, the note says. His father was a distinguished surgeon with an estate on Lake Champlain. The captain rarely talked of his remarkable life.

In his closing months he recounted his career to the author in detail. The note calls him a filibuster of a type often read of but rarely met. He was tall, bronzed, athletic, and broad shouldered. Fighters from Hongkong to Valparaiso knew the name of Boynton. He explored the sources of the Orinoco in his travels. The book is an adventure life told at its ending.
73394-the-virtues-of-common-water:
John Smith gathers praise of plain water in The Virtues of Common Water, here in a tenth edition printed at Dundee in 1799. Colvill and Son printed it for Milln, a bookseller, with material passed on by Ralph Thoresby and others. A verse motto calls the best physic the one that cures without apothecaries' bills.

Smith says he drew on eminent physicians, on word of mouth reports, and on his own trials from age thirty to seventy-four. He styles water a near universal remedy, cheap, easy to get anywhere men live, and fit to prevent or cure many distempers. Manwaring is quoted first, calling water the most wholesome drink, made for man in his best state. Rules for keeping health by diet are added.
73447-magazine-of-western-history-illust:
The Magazine of Western History, volume I number 1, launched in Cleveland, Ohio, in November 1884. Its terms were $4.00 per year in advance, or 50 cents a number. A portrait of Arthur St Clair fronts the issue. Col Charles Whittlesey leads with the discovery of the Ohio River by La Salle in 1669-70. The Northwest Territory, he notes, held perhaps three thousand white people in 1762.

C C Baldwin contributes a geographical history of Ohio. A description of Fort Harmar follows, with an illustration of the fort in 1788. Alfred Mathews writes on the Ohio Land Company and on Indian occupation. A portrait of Rufus Putnam illustrates the company article. William W Williams treats Arthur St Clair and the Ordinance of 1787. Walter Buell recalls Washington's first experience as a surveyor. Editorial notes, pioneer societies, and historical news close the number.
7359-indian-summer:
William D. Howells's Indian Summer opens midway on Florence's Ponte Vecchio, where Colville lounges against a jeweller's booth and stares at the Arno. It is a January afternoon that began bright and warm, then changed mood as clouds flew and rain threatened. A yellow torrent seethed below, fed by rain already fallen in the mountains.

From that bridge the novel follows middle-aged Americans in Italy, love renewed late, and the comedy of manners abroad. Howells writes with his usual gentle irony, letting talk and small choices carry feeling. The Florentine opening sets a mood of late light and second chances that the whole book keeps.
73595-try-to-remember:
Frank Herbert wrote Try to Remember, a science tale printed in Amazing Stories in October, nineteen sixty-one, with art by Finlay. A note at the start praises the science of language as a rich field for such tales. A spaceship has come out of the sky over Oregon. Its five green skinned, froglike crew have given Earth an ultimatum, and the headlines blare Talk or Die.

The visitors ask Earth to send its best minds in human speech to five rooms of their ship. There the teams must find a way to talk with them, or all thinking life on the planet will be destroyed. As proof of power, Eniwetok atoll was wiped flat and all sky satellites were combed away. The tale turns on a woman who goes back past Babel to older ways of meaning.
73612-the-murderer:
The Murderer is a horror story by Murray Leinster. It appeared in Weird Tales in January 1930. The opening puts the killer back in a dark room he fled. His hair lifts at the back of his neck as it begins. A crawling sensation spreads down his spine in the dark. There is something moving in the room with him. He had left the room half an hour before, maybe twenty minutes.

Then he remembered something he had left behind in that room. It was the only thing that could throw suspicion on him. So he came back to pick it up before dawn. The sound comes again, alive, furtive, and terribly playful in the dark. The thing is amused by his terror, he feels. He stands teetering on his toes against the wall. Leinster traps a murderer with an unseen playmate.
73649-ye-butcher-ye-baker-ye-candlestick:
Ye Butcher, Ye Baker, Ye Candlestick Maker, by Robert Seaver, is a book of sundry amusing and instructive verses for both old and young, adorned with numerous woodcuts. Houghton Mifflin printed it at Boston in 1908, and Seaver also designed and illustrated it.

Seventeen trades and callings get a poem each: housewife, baker, doctor, town crier, tythingman, pirate, pedagogue, chemist, merchant, printer, brewer, robber, tailor, chandler, student, husbandman, and jester. The housewife scours her pots, kneads her bread, and knits her goodman mitts of homespun yarn, blessed that the adversary has not yet made the modern servant. The baker's shop shows men of gingerbread with currant eyes, in days before the canner came with his fifty nine varieties. The doctor rides the country round with physic in his saddlebags, cupping and bleeding with good will, though the modern doctor now telephones an absent treatment.
73715-cudjo-s-own-story-of-the-last-afri:
Zora Neale Hurston wrote this account of Cudjo Lewis, printed in the Journal of Negro History in October 1927. Cudjo was a survivor of the Clotilde, the last known ship to bring enslaved Africans to the United States. Hurston sets the scene at African Town, a settlement above Mobile founded by the ship's captives, on land once held by the Meaher brothers.

The Meahers, Maine men with a mill and shipyard, owned the fast Clotilde and sent Captain Foster to Whydah for a cargo of people. Hurston tells how Dahomey's warriors, including women fighters, raided weaker peoples to stock the trade. Cudjo's own people in Togo farmed corn, beans, and yams and lived by the palm tree. The piece preserves, in print, the story of the last slaver as told by a man who had lived it.
73734-the-gray-wolf-s-daughter:
Gertrude Warden wrote The Gray Wolf’s Daughter, a tale of a Gypsy curse. The Federal Book Company issued the book in New York in eighteen hundred ninety four. A gypsy’s prophecy and a charm drive the dark plot along. The Romanys have not forgotten, one grim chapter warns the house.

Ernest Netherbridge, a young doctor, starts his work at Grayling in Surrey. His blunt truth telling to patients makes him few friends there. He lays fainting fits to ill temper and sighs to the liver’s faults. Then a grand coach from the Chase stops at his plain door. Sir Philip Cranstoun, rich and strange, begs his blunt word at once. A patient at the great house needs a man who speaks plain truth. Lord Carthew’s wooing, a mad bride, and a wedding eve fill the list. The Curse Fulfilled names the last of its fierce chapters.
73739-the-river:
Ednah Aiken wrote The River, a novel published in Indianapolis by the Bobbs-Merrill Company in 1914. Sidney Riesenberg drew the pictures. Aiken dedicated the book to Charles Sedgwick Aiken, and the chapter list runs long, to 42 chapters.

The headings draw the map of the tale: a desert hotel, a garden in a desert, chapters on the blessing of dryness, on the levee, and on the passing of the waters. The men at the center are Rickard, called Casey, Marshall, and Hardin. The first chapter has Marshall send for Rickard, whose dancing step carries him into an office as the clock strikes nine. Rivalry, betrayal, and a discovery wait down the list. Readers get a story of men fighting to make dry land bloom with river water.
73745-the-dark-mother:
Waldo Frank wrote The Dark Mother, a novel issued by Boni and Liveright in New York in nineteen hundred twenty. Frank gave the book to Margaret Naumburg. A line at the front calls the dark mother flesh that moves through flesh. Fourteen long chapters make up the tale.

A grown boy drifts in a canoe on a lake at dusk. Wind, waves, and trees all seem to lean toward a peak. Cloud hides the moon as night comes on. Woods roll dark on each shore of the lake. The boy wakes from a doze and paddles on with clear brow. Frank tells the tale in thick, dream-like prose. Sense and soul blur in each slow scene of the opening.
73843-a-voice-from-harper-s-ferry-a-narr:
A Voice from Harper’s Ferry, by Osborne Anderson, was printed for the author at Boston in 1861. Anderson was one of the number who followed Captain Brown in the raid. His preface states his sole purpose in publishing the narrative. It is to save from oblivion the facts of that movement, he says.

The movement aimed at the overthrow of American slavery, in his words. Anderson served under Brown’s orders on the sixteenth and seventeenth of October 1859. He calls himself the only man alive who was there during the entire time. Others had groped after these facts and failed to get them, he writes. His narrative gives the raid from inside, by a Black raider who escaped. Few documents of the war’s coming match its witness.
73850-frank-merriwell-s-danger:
Frank Merriwell's Danger is a number of the Medal Library, a weekly line of copyrighted stories for boys published at the turn of the century. The front matter is the publisher's own showcase: lists of books to come in January, February, and March, most of them new Merriwell tales by Burt Standish. The line also carried Horatio Alger and Oliver Optic, named as masters of fiction for boys.

Its Merriwell is praised there as a truly representative American lad, full of character and strong resolve to do right at any cost. The weekly numbers sold the hero as much as the tale: Frank at Yale, Frank's skill, Frank's champions, and here Frank in danger. The surviving head is mostly that promise, the shop window of the dime novel trade.
73937-i-gardener:
Allen Kim Lang wrote I, Gardener, a science fiction tale from Fantastic Science Fiction Stories in December 1959. A television producer flies to Boston to sign Axel Ozoneff, a professor of cryptochemistry, to a new fall show called Point of View. Ozoneff has written thirty-three books, appears in a dozen magazines, and works as a television personality of note.

At the hilltop house, a garden threatens to pullulate into unproper Bostonian jungle among flowering trees that hint at tigers. The gardener, a desiccated man tall and lean as a figure in a Navaho sand painting, blocks the brick path with hedge shears held like a short sword. The blurb asks if the great first law can fall. Satire and wonder mix.
7395-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
Grandmother's Story of Bunker-Hill Battle gives this volume its center. Holmes retells the Revolution as a grandmother told it to a child, with a grandson promising to come right back and staying away the live-long day. Around that fireside tale sit poems from 1874 to 1877. They include a memorial to Samuel Gridley Howe, a hymn for Governor Andrew's statue, and a welcome to the nations at Philadelphia on July 4, 1876.

The centennial year runs through the book, as Holmes, now an elder statesman of letters, looks back at the Revolution his grandparents' generation fought. Old Cambridge, family records, and the ship of state fill out the volume. It is Holmes in his late, public role: the survivor who speaks for the past to a nation celebrating a hundred years.
74012-janet-s-college-career:
Janet's College Career is a girls' novel by Amy Blanchard, printed at Philadelphia with copyright in 1904. Blanchard also wrote Two Maryland Girls and Thy Friend Dorothy. Twenty chapters follow Janet through a college year. The front picture shows her struggling with a heavy feather bed.

The tale opens with Janet at her window, deep in a problem of furnishing. She settles on two home-made spreads woven by her great-grandmother, blue and red. Chapters ahead promise fraternity girls, an initiation, and a Thanksgiving box. There are caramels and a cat, a studio tea, and a stolen feast. Blanchard closes with field day and partings, the full round of a college girl's year.
74038-the-call-of-the-night-rider:
Albert Lee sets The Call of the Night Rider in the days of William Tyndale, published by Morgan and Scott in London. Campbell drew the pictures, including a front plate of Herman carrying Tyndale toward a river bank. Lee had written The Key of the Holy House and other tales of peril.

Thirty chapters run from a man in a meadow through a printer's workshop, a search, and a night ride. Margaret Byrckmann opens the tale crossing a meadow at sunset, hoping to meet Herman and instead finding a dusty, worn traveller with a heavy wallet. Roye and the inquisitors, a cavern, a castle dungeon, and a mill in the forest follow. A ship rounding a bend and fingers closing round cell bars mark the danger around Tyndale's work.
74082-farmer-bluff-s-dog-blazer:
Florence E Burch tells a tale for the young issued by the Religious Tract Society in London, with pictures by Gordon Browne. The story opens with Dick Crozier, new to the neighborhood, chafing under his father's rules. He may not pass the common or go near the river until he can manage a boat.

Dick argues that no time is like the present, then submits outwardly and walks the other way, grumbling. The title dog, Blazer, belongs to Farmer Bluff, and chapter titles promise an inquest, an artist-detective, a runaway's story, and a rescue. A goose in the front picture rushes screaming at some intruder. Readers get a Victorian tale of boys, dogs, duty, and danger, with a moral edge kept in the Tract Society manner.
74086-the-invisible-master:
Edmond Hamilton wrote The Invisible Master, a tale from Scientific Detective Monthly in April 1930, illustrated by Ruger. The magazine defies any reader to guess the secret of the invisible master who broods over the city. Even the editorial staff claim they were astounded at the ending of the yarn.

A thousand alarms pour into police headquarters as the tale opens with a newspaper city room scene. Reporter Carton scoffs at an assignment to write of Howard Grantham, a super-physicist said to have found the secret of invisibility. Rival papers already rush men to the university on the tip. The editors call it the greatest scientific detective story of the year.
7410-the-minister-s-charge-or-the-appren:
William Dean Howells, author of The Rise of Silas Lapham, builds this novel around a minister's conscience. On the way home from boarding in the country, the Reverend Sewell is reproached by his wife: he had no right to give a poor boy false hopes about his poetry. To discourage the boy would have been kinder, she argues, if the verses were bad. Yet Sewell has taken the boy's case on himself.

The boy is Lemuel Barker, and the novel follows his apprenticeship to life under the minister's charge. Howells uses the small story to ask large questions: what do we owe the hopeful, and when does kindness become cruelty? Told with Howells's quiet realism, the book is a study of conscience, poetry, and the education of a young man.
74158-hemming-the-adventurer:
Hemming the Adventurer, a novel by Theodore Roberts, was published in London by Ward, Lock and Company in 1906. Roberts also wrote Brothers of Peril. Pictures by A G Learned go with the text. A warm dedication to the woman who restored his faith in his own stories opens the book, dated 1903.

Three parts follow Captain Hemming through a change of life. He resigns his commission, meets the men of a syndicate, and sails into intrigue in Pernambuco. Chapters bring a sporting president, a first shot, an attack, and a rescue by O'Rourke. The last part turns to love, restlessness, and sailing orders from a master not to be denied.
74161-or-darwin-if-you-prefer:
Mel Hunter, an artist known for science fiction magazine covers, made his first story with Or Darwin, If You Prefer, in Fantastic Universe in September 1954. The editor's note calls it no beginner's work, but sparkling and the product of a craftsman. The head note says Harbinger could not quite believe in the Mouth.

Harbinger is a chemist at the Cushman Chemical Company, sick of his job and of his own neat, orderly habits. One day he puts down his pencil in the middle of a set of chemical notations. He tells Cushman to take the titrations and jam them. He hangs up his spotless smock and walks out for the last time. At home his drab, proper room defeats him, and something else waits there. Readers get a quiet man's revolt with a strange turn.
74179-a-royal-son-and-mother:
Baroness Pauline von Hügel wrote this Catholic life of Prince Demetrius Gallitzin and his noble mother, reprinted from The Ave Maria. The book was copyrighted in 1902 and later tied to a memorial church at Loretto, Pennsylvania. Gallitzin founded that village and served as its first pastor, a pioneer priest of the Alleghenies.

The dedication honors Charles Schwab and his wife, who built the memorial, and others who kept Gallitzin's memory alive. Von Hügel also answers the strong dislike of the Catholic Church that she says was common in America. Her story joins a prince's birth to hard frontier mission work.
74189-guy-falconer:
L E G writes a tale of an old moat house in a Sunday School Union volume from London, in its third thousand. The author had written The Object of Life, Myra Sherwood's Cross, and Homes Made and Marred before. A sub-title calls the tale a battle of fortune in bold type.

Sixteen chapters run from Only a Stroke of the Pen to Clouds with Silver Linings at the close. Plates show the moat house, village politics, a meeting on the road, a plot, and wedding bells in the set. Chapter one finds an old man in bed, urged to sign papers while witnesses wait in the room. Geoffry swears he has quite decided and will not regret the stroke, come what may in time.
74195-the-fourth-progressive-reader:
The Fourth Progressive Reader is a school reader, carefully arranged for the use of schools and published in New York by O'Shea in 1871. It belongs to an illustrated progressive series, graded readers that carried a child from primer to literature. Such books were the core of the nineteenth-century classroom.

The preface states the method. The lessons were chosen to interest the young and to convey, each one, an instructive moral that would impress itself deeply on the pupil's mind. They also serve as exercises in reading aloud.
