New selections come from distinguished writers: Archbishop Spalding, Father Lacordaire, Doctor Newman, and others, several of them Catholic voices, which marks the book's intended schools. Short lives of the authors are appended. A graded reader of 1871 shows what the age thought children should read, and how it wished them to feel while reading it.
74210-the-moving-finger:
Natalie Sumner Lincoln writes a mystery in The Moving Finger, published by D Appleton and Company in 1918, with illustrations by Charles L Wrenn. She dedicates the book to Mr and Mrs Thomas E Newbold. Chapters move from visions and tragedy through testimony to Dorothy Deane, society editor, a black-edged card, a counterfeit bank note and a first shot. Detective Mitchell asks the questions in chapter twelve.

The opening chapter sets a nurse, Deane, against her patient, who refuses his medicine and orders the glass put down. His harsh voice and clutched bedclothes suggest he knows the woman at his bedside better than a stranger should.
74221-the-scientific-pioneer:
Nelson Bond wrote The Scientific Pioneer, a tale from Amazing Stories in March 1940. Horse-Sense Hank could answer all the problems of science and even apply logic to love, but turnips baffled him, the blurb jokes. The narrator's car dies where concrete gives way to macadam, then to a thin silver of bumpy dirt road.

He struggles with the hood, admires the innards' incomprehensible compactness, and jiggles wires to no effect under grey skies. A man leans on the worm fence across the road, shifting a billiard ball of tobacco between cheeks with drawling incuriosity. The nearest garage is two miles, maybe two and a half, northward. Do you swim good, the stranger asks. Pulp humour follows in dialect.
74239-dreams-of-an-astronomer:
Dreams of an Astronomer, by Camille Flammarion, in English by E E Fournier d Albe, was printed in New York by D Appleton and Company in 1923. Flammarion was the famed French star writer. The book opens with a voyage in the sky, in staged leaps outward.

The leaps run from two hundred and forty thousand miles from Earth to thirty seven million miles. Then come seven hundred and fifty million miles, two thousand five hundred million miles from the sun, and twenty five billion miles. Later chapters treat the world of long ago and the world to come. Venus the beautiful, the planet Mars, and the giant world of Jupiter follow. Heartbeats across space and ideas on talk between the worlds fill the close. Sky fans get a dream tour with a poet astronomer.
743-thoughts-on-man-his-nature-productio:
William Godwin gathered thirty-four years of reflection in this 1831 volume on man, his nature, his works, and his finds. The book grew from thoughts first aired in his earlier Enquirer, now given a fixed and lasting form. Godwin writes on mind, habit, genius, and the forces that shape human life.

Essays move from the growth of character to the value of books, the arts, and science, with personal notes on the author woven in. His tone is calm and inquiring, not fiery, though the views are bold. The volume gives readers Godwin the thinker at leisure, weighing what people are and what they may become.
74328-peter-pettigrew-s-prisoner:
Nelson S Bond wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Amazing Stories in July 1942. Peter Pettigrew captures a strange prisoner whose sabotage methods are unique. The man carries a weird dust in a bag. A picture shows him throwing a handful of dust into Pettigrew's face. Sergeant McCurdle lectures on delayed action bombs and incendiaries.

Pettigrew daydreams through the lecture, imagining himself halting a Nazi spy. The sergeant's voice snaps him back with a sharp Mister Pettigrew. Bond mixes home front defense training with fantasy. Pettigrew, a civilian volunteer, dreams of heroics while real danger hides in plain sight. The tale plays wartime vigilance for comedy and suspense.
7434-the-adventures-of-joel-pepper:
Margaret Sidney's Pepper books were beloved by generations of children, and this volume follows Joel Pepper, the family's irrepressible boy, through his own adventures. The contents promise mischief from the start: Joel and the snake, Deacon Brown's nail pile, the muffin man and the tramp, and a scramble on Bandy Leg Mountain. A birthday party, a fishing trip, and a bag of rye flour all turn into trouble.

Later chapters take Joel to Grandma Bascom's, onto the Boxford stage, and into a fight at Strawberry Hill, with Polly and Dave close at hand. Sidney writes with the warmth of the Pepper household itself, where scrapes are forgiven and courage counts. The book stands alone, but readers of the Five Little Peppers will greet old friends here.
74373-the-giant-sorcerer:
William Whitman the Third wrote The Giant Sorcerer, the adventures of Raphael and Cassandra, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1927. Frank Boyd drew the pictures. The frontispiece shows the Atlantic navy passing before the President.

Fifteen chapters carry the children through a war of machines and magic. Gaea the Earth Mother appears early. The sorcerer's castle and a visit to the President follow. Then the tale goes off to war, with eagles overhead. A council of the animals debates the crisis, and Raphael is captured. The giant announces his name in a caption: I am Mechanus, the Giant Sorcerer. His metal servants, the Mechanicos, swarm through the later chapters. Children of 1927 got a fairy tale with a machine giant for its ogre.
74409-blowing-weather:
John McIntyre wrote this tale of Anthony Stevens and blowing weather. Stokes printed it in New York, copyright 1923, Mabie drew colour plates. Chapter one sets Anthony on the Black Horse Tavern door stone. Second Street lies much changed since his boyhood years there.

Thick ribbed and confident, the street thrusts out store windows. Yet nothing stodgy sits in its new fatness, he notes gladly. It holds the readiness of a well mastered ship ordered deck. Autumn wind and sun touch the street with bright coolness. He had spun tops on its stones and raced its dust as a boy of town.
74441-the-sturgis-wager:
The Sturgis Wager, a tale of crime by Edgar Morette, was issued in New York with a 1899 imprint by the Stokes company. The book opens on a cold December night on Broadway, amid crowds, cabs, and bright shop fronts. A cab crosses the street against a warning hand, and the plot is soon under way.

The parts that follow name a wager, a bank head, an artist, and a portrait. One part is called Piecing the Evidence, and a later one A Reconstructed Drama. The bookkeeper owns up at one point, yet the trail is lost soon after. Late parts bring in Roentgen rays, an underground passage, a lead-lined vat, and a death chamber. The last part names the Murder Syndicate.
74489-a-royal-smuggler:
William Dalton wrote A Royal Smuggler, or the adventures of two boys in the Indian Archipelago, copyrighted in 1902 and printed at Chicago. The tale opens with a letter from Uncle Adam that shapes the fate of a father and his sons. A robbery and the taking of Marie drive the boys from home. They run away and take service with nest-hunters.

Chapter heads trace a voyage among nest-caves, where the boys know the nest-robbers again. A Dutch cruiser overhauls them, and they sell their nests, are taken prisoner, and outwit their captors. Later heads promise a big snake, widow-burning in Bali, a tiger hunt, and prison at Mojopahit as rebels. A tolerably happy ending closes the tale.
74582-the-wolf-slayer-margaret-kaurner:
Wolf Slayer and Margaret Kaurner is a pair of tales by Christoph von Schmid. The American Tract Society of New York issued the two stories in one volume. Schmid is named in brackets as the author of The Basket of Flowers. Margaret Kaurner is subtitled a story of gold and copper coins on the contents.

Her tale runs in letters between Margaret, her mother, and a George of the story. Winter opens the Wolf Slayer, with sharp winds scattering snowflakes over the land. Cozy warmth indoors grows doubly precious against the bleak scene outside the door. German moral tales in translation fed generations of American Sunday school readers.
74595-the-president-s-daughter:
Nan Britton wrote The President's Daughter, printed at New York in 1927 by the Elizabeth Ann Guild. Quotation from the book was restricted to three hundred words except by special permission of the publishers. Emerson's line heads the book: there is no such thing as concealment, from the essay on compensation.

A poem, Her Eyes, describes her child's eyes as sometimes deep sea-blue and calm as waters stilled at evenfall. In those eyes she sees not quite her child, but him whose soul shines through her, serene and unafraid. The eyes and smile, she insists, are her father's own, page after page of the verses. Britton claimed President Harding fathered her daughter. Scandal readers get the famous 1927 memoir.
74746-esther:
A tale of the Oregon Trail fills this book, named for its maid, Esther. It was printed at London by George Routledge and Sons. The list of parts maps the road west. Westward stands at its head. Names fill the road: Waltermeyer, a fine man of the wilds; an apostle; Claude and Ellen; and a man held by the Dacotahs. Thirst, the ride of a Mormon, and a fire on the plain mark the mid parts.

More turns of the road crowd the last half: a true heart, a sharp break, a lone ride, and a night storm in the hills. A camp of the Dacotahs, a revolt, a trial on the heights, and a duel in the wilds lead to a start of dread. The home road and the home end the tale.
74835-the-last-buccaneer:
Last Buccaneer is a tale by L Cope Cornford, author of Captain Jacobus. Its fuller title adds a line about the trustees of a Mrs A. The Philadelphia edition was published in October nineteen oh two. The book is dedicated to Rudyard Kipling. A verse prologue gives Captain Dawkins explaining himself. Some plunder large, some pilfer small, the verse begins.

The same remark fits them all, the verse holds: of buccaneering there is no end. The captain tells of a man he admired, ranging the seas of all the world. He laid East Indiamen and king's ships aboard in his day, the poem says. From pillaging a fairy hoard he turned to fill his hold with cod. The tale proper opens one dark winter afternoon in seventeen oh eight. The narrator meets an old schoolfellow in Bristol.
74840-the-circuit-rider:
Edward Eggleston wrote a tale of the heroic age of frontier preaching, printed in New York in 1874. Eggleston had written The Hoosier Schoolmaster. He gives the book to the brave, self sacrificing men he served with in a frontier ministry. A spinning wheel and rifle front the tale.

Corn shuckings, frolics, and going to meeting set the scene in a raw settlement. A preacher is treed by roughs, a sermon is preached by Kike, and Morton makes his retreat. Patty in the spring house and a conference at Hickory Ridge fill the mid tale. The circuit rider, who rode from cabin to cabin with the gospel, stands as hero of a hard and lively age.
74896-a-gentle-pioneer:
Amy Blanchard wrote A Gentle Pioneer, a story of the early days in the New West, published in 1903 in her Pioneer series. Ida Waugh made the illustrations. Blanchard also wrote tales of the Revolution and of the War of 1812 for girls.

The chapters open with emigrants on the move and a housewarming in the new home. A search, the unexpected, and a girl named Polly follow. Jeanie keeps a secret, an intruder appears, and Archie forms a plan. What the freshet brought changes things in the middle of the book. A visit ends, plotting begins, and Jeanie wedding day crowns the later chapters. The pioneer West here is seen through a family, with girls at the center of the work and the danger. Young readers got settlement life with a gentle hand on the rein.
74989-bill-porter:
Bill Porter is a drama by Upton Sinclair about the writer O Henry in prison. Sinclair published the play himself at Pasadena, California, in 1925. The scene is the state penitentiary at Columbus, Ohio, in 1899. Four acts pass between the prison hospital drug-store and the post office. Bill Porter works as night drug-clerk of the prison hospital there.

Biggins the pickpocket and Purzon the swindler stand among the convicts. Joe, a trusty, and Al Jennings the train-bandit fill the prison cast. Jimmie Valentine the cracksman and Raidler the Oklahoma terror join them. Margaret, Porter's little daughter, and Athol, his dead wife, appear too. Espiritu de la Vina stands as Porter's temptation in the play's list. Dulcie the little shop-girl closes the cast of Sinclair's drama. The Four Million names the play's frame at its printed head.
75002-the-golden-spider:
Francis Lynde wrote The Golden Spider, a boys adventure in the Dick and Larry series, published in New York in 1923. Lynde dedicated the book to Clarence Clark, his mineralogical mentor, whose library, specimen cabinets, and laboratory helped him write it. The tale mixes college boys with mining.

The opening chapter is set in Lost Canyon, though it starts in a handsome bank office. A frozen trail, short rations, and an ice cavern follow. Chapter titles promise the spider web itself, a notice to quit, and finders keepers as the prize is fought over. One picture caption has a boy asking whether the stuff in hand might be ore of some kind. The golden spider is a mineral prize, and claim jumpers want it. Dick and Larry must hold their find against scamps who bark up the wrong tree.
75034-bob-the-photographer:
Arthur Winfield's Bob the Photographer, or A Hero in Spite of Himself, came from the Stitt Publishing Company in New York. The copyright is dated 1902. Winfield also wrote the Rover Boys and Putnam Hall series for young Americans. The frontispiece shows Joel Carrow darting from a barn after scampering pigs. The story opens with Carrow berating his farm boy, Bob Alden, over a lost saw.

Bob insists he left the saw on its peg. Carrow threatens him with a tanning, and the boy stands his ground. Chapter titles promise an escape, an elephant, and a first customer. Bob becomes a travelling photographer and shows up a swindler. He takes a dive overboard, rides a freight train, and becomes a prisoner. The last chapter joins Bob with his mother and concludes the tale.
75067-the-boys-of-columbia-high-on-the-r:
The Boys of Columbia High on the River, or The Boat Race Plot That Failed, by Graham Forbes, was copyrighted in 1911 by Grosset and Dunlap of New York. Earlier books put the boys at school and on the diamond. This one opens with Frank Allen and Lanky Wallace marooned on Rattail Island in a leaking boat, two miles from home.

A stolen eight oared shell, a night alarm, and a plot against the great race drive the story. Even Lef, the series comic, gets his share in chapter thirteen. Forbes writes the clean, fast school sport tale that filled boys' shelves before radio.
75112-the-air-splasher:
Air Splasher is a pulp flying story by Rickard Howells Watkins, about a circus stunt pilot. A headnote calls its hero a daredevil of the clouds performing the most hair raising feat of his life. He does it to prove that he is a safe pilot in the paradox of the tale. Watkins is named as author of Full Throttle on the byline of the story.

Ladies and gentlemen, bawls Sam Smith, the barker, rotating his fat body on a creaking box in the text. The next feature will be an exhibition flight by King Horn, the wild man of the air, he announces. Horn has crashed no less than twelve ships as Ace of Deuces in his career, the barker boasts. The Tennant Flying Circus promises nothing, but watch him fly, the pitch goes on in the story of the barnstorming years.
75145-human-nature-and-the-social-order:
Charles Horton Cooley wrote Human Nature and the Social Order, printed in New York in 1902. Contents open with society and the single man. They are sides of the same thing, the head says, and it is a mistake to set them against each other. That mistake, in its many shapes, is the first theme.

Hint and choice take the second chapter: what the words mean, how they hang together, and how they work in children. The scope of hint is much underrated, Cooley holds, and set choice has narrow bounds in practice. Fellow-feeling takes the third head: talk with made-up persons and how children learn to read a face. The personal idea, he argues, is the social fact at hand, and society must be studied in the mind's eye. Fellow-feeling as a bond of society fills the fourth head.
75166-stories-told-by-the-miller:
Stories Told by the Miller is a book of fairy tales by Violet Jacob, published in London by John Murray in 1909. Jacob had earlier written Irresolute Catherine. The book is dedicated to her boy Harry, and it opens at a cottage by a mill pool.

Janet and little Peter live in the whitewashed cottage in the field. The tales they hear include the story of the water nix and the king of Growgland's crown. Master Bogey, the tree of pride, and farmyard Maggie follow in the contents. A fiddling goblin and a witch's cloak close the set. Illustrations show the miller's man meeting the nix and Maggie rocking a strange burden. Jacob, a Scots poet and novelist, gives the tales a country voice. The frame of children at the mill makes the wonders feel told aloud.
75184-political-fragments-of-archytas-ch:
Thomas Taylor translated from the Greek the Political Fragments of Archytas, Charondas, Zaleucus, and other ancient Pythagoreans, printed at Chiswick in 1822. The pieces survive because Stobaeus preserved them. Treatises on a republic, on sanctity, on law and justice, and on a kingdom fill the political half, drawn from Hippodamus, Diotogenes, Sthenidas, and Ecphantus.

Prefaces by Charondas and Zaleucus to their own laws stand out. Perictyone writes on the duties and harmony of a woman, and Phintys on a woman's temperance. Ethical fragments of Hierocles, on conduct toward gods, country, and parents, close the volume. The pieces are short, and each speaks with the voice of an old lawgiver or a king's adviser.
75217-in-the-camp-of-the-black-rider:
Capwell Wyckoff wrote a tale of adventure and mystery for boys of twelve to sixteen. Burt of New York copyrighted it in 1931. The first chapter opens at noon in the small inland town of Ridgefield. Factory whistles blow, and the men at Thorn's lumber yard lay down their work for their lunch pails.

Two clean cut young fellows lift a long plank at the far end of the yard. One is Ted Thorn, the owner's son. The other is Buck Dalton, his constant chum. The chapters ahead take the pair to a camp in the hills. They bring a prowler in the night, strange sounds, a grim find, and a mountain chase. One chapter gives the story of the Black Riders, and a mutiny tests the camp. By the last chapter the mysteries are cleared up, as the list of contents promises.
75351-won-over:
Nellie Hellis wrote a tale dated 1885 about Phil and Millie, a brother and sister who come to live in London. The first chapter finds Millie, flushed and out of breath, racing through heat near Drury Lane to meet Phil. She brings news that Miss Crawford, a kind friend from their past, has at last found where they live.

Phil hears the news with a stern, sad face, and warns his frail sister not to run in such heat. Chapter heads point to a word broke, a stay in hospital, and a bond said to be stronger than death. Want and care sit side by side in the tale of the two young lives.
75361-the-basket-maker:
Basket Maker is a manual training essay by Luther Weston Turner, issued at Worcester in 1909. The Davis Press published the piece, reprinted from The School Arts Book of its day. Turner was director of manual training at the Hill School at Pottstown, in Pennsylvania. His subject is basketry as a school craft for children in the classroom.

Basketry, he writes, has been called one of the fads of the newest education in his opening. It was one of the essentials of the oldest education, he answers in the same breath. It still holds a commanding position among the arts of men, even in civilized countries, he argues. Properly taught, it vitalizes certain periods in history for the pupil in his scheme. Turner essay belongs to the manual training movement, which put tools in schoolrooms to train the hand as a road to the mind in children.
75473-brazil-the-land-of-rubber:
Brazil, the Land of Rubber is an exhibition pamphlet issued by the Brazilian government. It describes the Brazil Court at the Third International Rubber and Allied Trades Exhibition, held in New York in 1912. The pamphlet was given away with the compliments of the government.

Brazil's court filled ten thousand square feet on the balcony floor. Archways bore the arms of the federal government, and an information bureau answered all enquiries about Brazilian rubber. The walls carried statistics and maps, and a kiosk served free Brazilian coffee. The great sight was the Rubber Colossus, a huge reclining figure overlooking the Amazon and its tributaries. Pictures twenty two feet by twelve gave a bird's eye tour up the river. A pyramid of caoutchouc, a mountain of rubber, and a single rubber ball weighing sixteen hundred pounds showed off the product.
7548-quotes-and-images-from-the-confessi:
Charles James Lever's Confessions of Harry Lorrequer is a rollicking Irish military novel. First published at Dublin in 1839, it is gathered here in quotations and images. The title page bore no author's name, though the work is generally attributed to Lever. Harry is a young officer in a British regiment stationed in Ireland in the early 1800s, and his confessions are misadventures in love and soldiering.

The edition's story is part of its charm. The first edition's pages were too stained and friable to scan, so a colleague typed the book out in the old-fashioned way for this eBook. The quotations catch Lever's high spirits. There is a set of raps, and curses at being in such quarters. Comrades smoke, sigh, and snore, and men who never prayed before pray for the route to Cork or Galway.
75508-life-the-interpreter:
Phyllis Bottome wrote Life the Interpreter, for Longmans in 1902. Three cities shared the edition of the novel. Having what we want is riches, it quotes. To be able to do without it is power, the text adds. The extraordinary thing is that it has happened, a lady opens.

She lay back in her chair as she said it. Black velvet slippers on a fender are a poem. Poor Muriel had everything in her favour once, the talk runs. Money, position, and looks were all hers. Earnestness ruined her, the ladies agree. Take up the church, she was often told. Too comfortable, it would crush her, Muriel answered. She has dropped out now, and nothing can be done, they sigh. Her Stepney club fills her time now. Bottome gives earnest poverty a drawing-room tribunal.
7553-quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of:
Gilbert Parker, the Canadian-born novelist of the North and of Egypt, is gathered here in short passages and pictures from his works. His novels move between frontier settlements and drawing rooms, and the passages sample both worlds. Characters recur in brief, vivid turns of speech. Each passage can be traced to its full scene, so a line never has to carry the whole story alone.

Read together, the passages sketch Parker's range: hard country, social codes, and people tested by both. Loyalty, pride, forgiveness, and the weight of a past act recur across them. The volume suits a reader who wants Parker's voice in small doses before choosing a novel. It is a compact way to meet a once-popular storyteller on his own terms.
75540-pieter-bruegel-the-elder:
Virgil Barker wrote a study of the Flemish painter Pieter Bruegel the Elder, issued in New York in 1926 by The Arts Publishing Corporation. Much of the text first ran in a special Bruegel number of the magazine The Arts. Barker notes that few hard facts about the painter's life survive beyond his signed and dated works.

The essay leans on Carel Van Mander, who wrote about Bruegel some thirty years after his death. It weighs doubts about his birth place near Breda and his birth year, most often set at 1525. Plates of works such as Hunters in the Snow help readers see the art while they read the life.
75564-the-puzzle-of-life-and-how-it-has-:
The Puzzle of Life, and How It Has Been Put Together, by Arthur Nicols, is a short history of the earth and its life for young readers. The hosted copy is the second edition, from Longmans of London, 1877. Nicols dedicates the book to the children of George du Maurier, and a mammoth fronts the volume.

Footnotes point readers to the very cases in the British Museum where the fossils and tools of the text can be seen. New matter covers chalk seas from the Challenger expedition, Ohio mound builders, and Easter Island. The first edition's preface says children took fire from the story of life, and the book feeds that fire plainly.
7557-quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of:
Charles Dudley Warner, the Hartford essayist and novelist, wrote about gardens, travel, and American life for a generation, and this volume gathers quotations from his writings. The contents list his range: Summer in a Garden, Backlog Studies, Baddeck, In the Wilderness, and Spring in New England stand beside Captain John Smith, Pocahontas, and Saunterings.

Being a Boy and On Horseback follow, with For Whom Shakespeare Wrote, Novel and School, and Their Pilgrimage. Later entries cover modern fiction, culture, equality, literature and life, literary copyright, and the education of the Negro. Nine short essays close the list, on truthfulness and the pursuit of happiness among them. The volume is Warner the companionable American, in his own best sentences.
75583-the-informer:
Liam O'Flaherty wrote The Informer, a novel published in New York in 1925. The tale is set in Dublin among criminal and pauperized circles. Its first page fixes the hour: three minutes to six on the evening of the fifteenth of March.

Francis Joseph McPhillip runs up the concrete steps of the Dunboy Lodging House and peers through its glass-panelled door. The House, as it is called, is a grey building of four stories in a maze of slum streets. Drizzle falls from a black bulging sky, and gusts drive hailstones dancing down the lane. The smell of food and scrubbed floors comes from the building, and the smell of crowded human beings fills the air around it. O'Flaherty writes the city as weather and hunger. His informer moves through it with a price on his soul.
75627-a-borrowed-sister:
A Borrowed Sister is a girls' story by Eliza Orne White, with illustrations by Katharine Pyle. Houghton Mifflin copyrighted it in 1906. Lois Page, an only child all her life, is to have a borrowed sister for a year or more, and the prospect fills her with keen delight.

The sister is Jessie Matthews, serene as a summer morning. Lois clears two bureau drawers for her and counts it the best part of the plan: someone to talk to at bedtime and on waking. Her friend Ellen Morgan, fonder of Jessie than she admits, calls the arrangement horrid and means the jealousy honestly. Chapters promise a witch kitten, a summer exchange, a storm at Hollisford, a vegetable tea party, and a Christmas tree.
75631-whither:
Whither came out at Boston and New York in 1915, from Houghton Mifflin. Rights were held that year by an Atlantic company and by Mifflin. It opens with a division of household goods among heirs. A quaint gray chest brings the writer a heritage of letters. They were tossed carelessly there with mouse-eaten diplomas, he says.

He reads them with difficulty, in old-fashioned handwriting on yellowed paper. What fullness of life is here, he pauses to marvel. What richness, what greatness, the letters hold for him. A mother writes to a little daughter at school in the city. An aged father writes from a visit to his clergyman son. Glad letters for marriages and solemn ones for death fill the chest. They reveal a deeper life and a profounder faith, he holds. The book asks where modern faith is drifting from theirs.
75666-hay-fever:
Noel Coward wrote Hay Fever, a light comedy in three acts, printed at London in 1925. The play was dedicated to Lorn Loraine, and the second impression followed within two months. Performing rights stayed with the author.

The Bliss family fills the cast: Judith, a retired actress, her husband David, and their children Sorel and Simon. Four guests, Myra, Richard, Jackie, and Sandy, join the house party at Cookham. Act one opens on a Saturday afternoon in June, in a comfortable, untidy hall. Simon cuts paper squares on the floor while Sorel lounges with a lurid book of poems, mocking its verses aloud.
75689-beth-s-wonder-winter:
Marion Ames Taggart wrote this girls' story, copyrighted in 1914, alongside her Six Girls series. It is dedicated to little Frances, with great love, and illustrated by William Stecher.

The contents move by moments: when the mail came in, when the train pulled out, the changeling, the fairy-land children. Later come the island day, pilgrims and strangers, tanagers and bluebirds, and a hospital on the heights. Kris Kringle's jingles and a Shrove night masque carry the winter, which melts in spring at the end. Chapter one opens on a torn apron: Beth Bristead, eleven, insists to her stern Aunt Rebecca that it tore itself, kind of, on the old Baldwin apple tree. Girls get a winter away from home.
75851-incidents-on-land-and-water:
Bates tells of four years on the Pacific Coast in Incidents on Land and Water, published for the author at Boston in 1860 in an eighth edition. The book, first entered for copyright in 1857, is dedicated to her mother and billed as a record of shipboard fires and land adventures.

Its centre is the burning of three ships, the Nonantum, the Humayoon and the Fanchon. The contents run from a fire on board the Nonantum at sea and a stop at the Falkland Islands to a second fire off Cape Horn. Later chapters reach Payta and Panama, the fire at San Francisco, hotel keeping in a canvas shanty at Marysville, an Indian rancheria, a mining spell and a visit to Sutter's home.
75899-tarka-the-otter:
Henry Williamson wrote Tarka the Otter, his joyful water-life and death in the country of the two rivers. E P Dutton published it at New York in 1928. Sir John Fortescue wrote the introduction. Williamson dedicated the book to William Henry Rogers. Its contents run backward in style: the last chapter is listed first, then the first year. The tale opens at dusk on meadow and water.

Old Nog the heron cries over the estuary, and the owl drifts above the reeds. Below Canal Bridge, twelve great trees stand with their roots awash. Thirteen stood there once; the book tells the lost oak's whole life. A swelled black acorn, a bullock's hoof, a fork that held two hundred years of rain, then frost and flood brought it down. Williamson writes an otter's life with great patience for the riverbank.
75905-the-king-s-messenger:
Marion Crawford wrote this tale of a strange dinner and a portrait that should not be there. Frank Snapp drew its plates. The King's Messenger is told in the first person, by a man come back to a house he knew long ago.

The dinner is dim, with sunset glow over the park trees at the west window. He had looked for a large party, but only a dozen sit at table. In old times, he recalls, thirty or forty guests filled that room. He knows some faces twice over: at the table and in the portraits on the walls. Worst shock of all, his own portrait hangs there, painted by Lenbach twenty years back, and he cannot recall sitting for it.
75909-the-double-dagger:
Nat Ridley the younger wrote this detective novel, published by the Garden City Publishing Company in 1926 as one of the Nat Ridley rapid fire detective stories. Ridley the detective keeps an office at Times Square, where Broadway meets Seventh Avenue, and his capable assistant is Berry Todd. Earlier cases named at the front include Guilty or Not Guilty and A Scream in the Dark.

The story opens with a telephone call that puzzles Ridley: Carl Lemberg, a rival sleuth, wants him to come in on one of his own cases. Twenty-five chapters follow under the sign of the double dagger, with another murder, a rope in the dark, a change of identities, and a trip off to Texas. A dungeon, a bomb, a black cave, and a deaf mute lead the trail over the line into Mexico.
76017-a-croatian-composer:
A Croatian Composer is an essay on Joseph Haydn by Hadow, a fellow of Worcester College, Oxford. Seeley published it in London in eighteen ninety seven as notes toward a study. Hadow builds the whole essay on the work of Doctor Kuhac of Croatia. Kuhac gathered South Slavonic folk songs and wrote a pamphlet on Haydn's roots.

On a visit to Croatia, Hadow got leave to use Kuhac's findings in full. He adds only fresh order, comment, and a few facts of his own. The claim is that Haydn drew his tunes from the folk music of his homeland. England, Hadow says, has somewhat forgotten Haydn and his debts of blood. To grant the claim rescues a musical nation from plain neglect, he argues. Critics who shun such prying behind the veil are answered in the preface.
76021-the-hardwood-finisher:
Fred T Hodgson gathers rules for finishing hardwoods in natural tints and antique styles in an Industrial Publication volume from New York dated 1892. Hodgson edited The Operative Builder and past trade papers on building and cabinet work. Rights were secured in 1892 by John H Phin, the title page adds.

A preface states that wood finishing touches each man who builds or trims a house, from architect to carver. Hodgson culled the best rules from many authorities and cut what his own trials proved useless or absurd. Filling, staining, varnishing, and polishing for mahogany, cherry, walnut, oak, and pine fill the core of the book. Side rules treat dyeing, gilding, and bronzing, while work on toys and instruments stays outside the plan.
76043-every-woman-her-own-flower-gardene:
Mrs Johnson, writing as Daisy Eyebright, wrote Every Woman Her Own Flower Gardener, a handy manual of flower gardening for ladies. This fourth edition was printed in New York in 1874. A verse at the front vows to compose a flowery crown of crocus, rose, narcissus, hyacinth, and violet. Contents open with the flower garden and its uses. The making of beds comes next, with beds in lawn, ribbon gardening, and rockeries.

Diagrams for laying out gardens go with that chapter. Annuals and their kinds fill the third chapter, with a list of the most fit for home gardeners. Hardy flowers and two-year flowers follow. One chapter treats geraniums and their kin, with the difference between the two plants. Bedding plants, the fuchsia, and the rose each take a chapter. Vines, shrubs, the carnation, and the paeony, phlox, and other lasting flowers close the run of heads.
76046-shoulder-to-shoulder:
Gordon Stables's Shoulder to Shoulder, a story of the stirring times of old, is kept here in a new edition from John Shaw of Paternoster Row. Stables, a surgeon of the Royal Navy, is billed by his other sea tales, On to the Rescue and Hearts of Oak among them. A Burns stanza stands as motto, and the frontispiece shows Sir John Moore crying, Hurrah, my lads, remember Egypt.

Book one is laid in the Highlands a hundred years ago. Its chapters name Auld-Da, then My Hero, Bonnie Prince Charlie, and the first act in a tragedy, with a wild and lawless man and Muirchie the dwarf. The Duke at Fontenoy and Culloden Moor stand in the chapter heads, with a cave and a brave Highland lassie. A long publisher's list of uniform copyright books fronts the volume, Stebbing, Everett-Green, and Meade among the authors.
761-a-v-laider:
Max Beerbohm wrote this short tale about A. V. Laider, a man who claims a strange power: he can see, in a flash, the future of those he meets. The narrator hears Laider's account with doubt, then with unease, as the tale turns on fate, chance, and the burden of knowing what is to come. Beerbohm tells it with dry wit.

The story is brief, but it lingers. Its charm lies in the talk between two men, one credulous and one sceptical, and in a twist that leaves the reader unsure what to believe. It shows Beerbohm's gift for the polished, uncanny tale, where a drawing-room chat opens onto mystery.
76105-a-spectre-of-power:
A Spectre of Power, a novel by Charles Egbert Craddock, was published in Boston in 1903. That pen name hid Mary Murfree, named in the copyright line. Murfree was known for tales of the Tennessee mountains. This novel opens long before, in the Cherokee town of Great Tellico. A Choctaw herald runs in bearing a great white swan wing marked with clay.

The headmen gather in the beloved square to greet the envoy. Eve, a Cherokee woman, watches from the river bank among the other women. The narrator blames her curiosity, then adds ambition and a greedy scheme. What looks like a small scene carries the seed of disaster. The tale blends frontier history with the inner life of its people.
76131-the-mark-of-the-monster:
Jack Williamson's horror novelette The Mark of the Monster appeared in Weird Tales in May 1937. Its narrator, Clay, comes home to the decaying village of Creston after seven years of fortune-hunting in the Orient. He carries his earnings and means to marry Valyne Kirk, the girl he left behind.

A letter from Doctor Kyle warns Clay against the marriage in riddling terms. Kyle, the old physician who adopted and raised him, hints at black venom flowing in his blood. He speaks of a stain no one else can see. The opening frames the mystery around a black altar on the hill-top above the village. It also asks whether Clay belongs to the monster his foster father fears he is.
76154-london-lavender:
E V Lucas wrote London Lavender, an entertainment, issued in New York by the Macmillan Company in nineteen twelve. Lucas had earlier written Over Bemerton and Mr Ingleside. A choice of mottoes heads the book, drawn from an optician catalogue, a stock exchange bulletin, and Dr William Osler. Certain characters from his earlier books would keep breaking into this one, he says.

Chapter one finds a new home, and determines the status of anthropoid apes. Chapter two gives the four gentlemen above their characters, and Primrose Terrace is rudely disturbed. Chapter three visits a red haired lady, and enumerates members of London foreign population. Chapter four forbids the narrator to be idle, so he finds congenial employment. Chapter five finds lovers of two kinds, and meets a poignant invention. Novel readers get a gentle London lodging house comedy.
76208-his-brother-s-keeper:
Tuttle wrote His Brother's Keeper, a Western tale set in the Bitter Water Valley. The place is always hot, its hills like rumpled yellow blankets. A dirt road runs from the town of Calor out to scattered ranches.

Mrs Jim Deming rides that road with Joe Mills, her husband's deputy, and frets over what she has done. Jim Deming, the sheriff, is known as Duty Deming for his hardness. The book's blurb tells that the sheriff rides into the bad lands after Red Cowan. Desert justice, not courtroom law, will settle the chase.
76289-the-breath-of-slander:
Ida Reade Allen wrote The Breath of Slander, Number 1124 in the New Eagle Series, sold for fifteen cents. The tale runs to thirty two chapters. It opens with a mountain storm and a mountain maid. Names in the chapter heads trace the plot from first love to late peace.

Heads name Lettie Allan, Clinton, Norine, Conway, Elwell, and Fanny Morain in turn. One head tells of a lost love and one of mixed joy. Later heads tell of divorce, a rise in public life, and a congressman elect. A bomb, a flight, and two widows mark the late turns. The book was sold as a love story for a wide home market.
76296-ralph-waldo-emerson-philosopher-an:
Alcott wrote this estimate of Ralph Waldo Emerson, philosopher and seer, in prose and verse, printed at Boston with copyright in 1882 and a second edition in 1888. Its full title promises an account of Emerson's character and genius. A letter from Emerson himself, dated at Concord on July 5, 1865, stands near the front.

Emerson thanks Mary Stearns for a birthday gift, a book about himself more beautiful, he says, than Aldus or Elzevir ever made. He confesses he suffered more than he enjoyed at first, since the praise ran so high he had to shade his eyes. Yet he came to admire its lyrical tone and the goodwill of the friends behind it, and learned to look at it with courage.
76480-sir-william-flower:
Sir William Flower, by Lydekker, was published in 1906. Dent issued it in London; Dutton in New York. The volume stands in a series on English men of science. Reynolds Green edited that series. Flower was born on November 30, 1831, at Stratford-on-Avon. His father's house, the Hill, was his birthplace. Eight chapters and an appendix make the life. A general sketch opens the book. Flower's years at the College of Surgeons museum come next. There he was conservator and Hunterian professor. The Natural History Museum, which he directed, takes a chapter. His presidency of the Zoological Society takes a short one.

Work on whales and on mankind fills two more. An appendix lists his books and memoirs. As a boy, Flower kept a museum in a cardboard box. He catalogued that first collection with care.
76539-the-life-eater:
Harold Ward wrote this terror tale, first printed in Weird Tales in June 1937. A headnote calls it a tale of much power, about the frightful wraith from Beyond. The wraith brought panic and death to a little town in the Louisiana swamplands. The first chapter, The Terror, opens on the village of La Foubelle at the edge of the great swamp.

Death has stalked there again and again, fattening the tiny graveyard until scarcely a house is not in mourning. The folk call it a sickness with no sickness. Victims are left shriveled and drained, their skin puckered into a thousand wrinkles. Jules Delatour, the village drunkard, swore he saw the horror over his dying mother: a black, transparent thing, smoke-like, with a beast's face. No one believed him. Doctor Lamontaine reads Cagliostro over Jamaica rum as the chapter closes.
76603-karl-grier:
Louis Tracy wrote Karl Grier, a novel published in New York in 1906 with the subtitle The Strange Story of a Man with a Sixth Sense. Tracy had already written The Wings of the Morning and The Pillar of Light. The tale opens with an affair at a tea garden.

Karl shares the stage with Constantine, who has visions, and with Maggie Hutchinson, whose own story fills a full chapter. A man called Steindal gives a public performance of the strange gift late in the book. Chapters move through hotels, garden courts, and a scene where blood is called a very peculiar juice. Readers get a tale of second sight, love, and danger told at a brisk pace.
76615-dick-chester:
Whitham's Dick Chester, a story of the Civil War, was published by Blackie and Son, with pictures by Paul Hardy. Its frontispiece, Dick answering the Roundhead messenger, dates the war: England's civil war, king against parliament. Twenty-three chapters carry his part in it, from Dick swims the moat to the end of John Dent.

Chapter one sets the castle's fall. Sir Reginald Chester is dead, killed in battle, and his cousin Captain Dent will not hold Dent Castle for the king. The servants have fled at news of the enemy; Master Purvis stays because he is too fat to run away, and Giles the stableman by Dent's orders. Dick, the late baronet's son, eleven years old, waits red-faced on the steps for his cousin. Out comes Dent in buff leather, steel breastplate, and crimson sash and plume, sword at his heels, and Dick springs forward to speak.
76622-the-story-hunter:
Ernest Suffling wrote The Story Hunter, or Tales of the Weird and Wild, published in London in 1896 with illustrations by Paul Hardy. Suffling had written Afloat in a Gipsy Van and Life on the Broads. A frontispiece shows a man speaking into the mouthpiece of a machine and asking, do you hear me?

In his preface Suffling recalls the reviews of his earlier Crusoe life in the Channel Islands. All but two were kind, and the flattery made him blush, he says, perhaps of modesty and perhaps of hope. One adverse critic, troubled in his liver, doubted his facts and ran amuck. The tales here hunt stories rather than game: strange machines, wild places, and corners of fact and fancy. East Anglia stands behind his work. The story hunter brings home wonders like fish.
76643-heu-heu-or-the-monster:
H Rider Haggard sends Allan Quatermain after a fabled monster in an African adventure issued in 1924. The tale is framed as one Quatermain told the editor years before his last, fatal expedition. The editor lost his notes, then found them again in an old hand-bag and set the story down.

Inside, chapters promise a picture in a cave, a legend of Heu-Heu, a black river, and a holy isle. A feast, a sacrifice, a sluice gate, and a race for life drive the plot to its close. Haggard adds a note linking his hairy wood-folk to fossil finds in Rhodesia reported after the tale was drafted. Readers get late Haggard in full form, with lost peoples, old gods, and Quatermain as guide.
76668-trial-by-water:
Sewell Peaslee Wright wrote this tale, Trial by Water, taken from a weekly story magazine of March 1929. A headnote sums its cast in one line: a son of the voyageurs tests the hearts of his young wife and of his debonair friend.

Jean Baptiste Chabrier listens to the roar of rapids he has lived beside for three years. In Cree the place is Assin-nebah, rocky water. His gaze rests on his wife Charlotte, seated in the middle of the canoe. Once she would have faced him; now she looks toward the bow, where big, blond, gay Les Walters rides. Jean Baptiste invited Les, who had never killed a moose, up to camp for the hunting season, and ten days have passed. Love, he thinks, is not blind: it sharpens the eyes, and he has seen his wife falling for his guest.
76692-hunger:
Knut Hamsun, the Norwegian writer, wrote Hunger, here in English by George Egerton. The Knopf edition came out in New York in 1920 and was printed three times that year. Edwin Bjorkman wrote the introduction. He calls Hamsun the foremost creative writer of the Scandinavian lands since Ibsen and Strindberg.

Bjorkman notes that fame in Russia matched Hamsun with Tolstoy and Dostoyevski. The novel itself follows a young writer with no food and no money in a city. Pride keeps him from begging while hunger clouds his mind. He pawns his goods, chases small sums, and swings between hope and shame. The book is famed for its close, raw look inside a starving mind.
76699-the-town-down-the-river:
Edwin Arlington Robinson published a book of poems in September 1910, dedicated to Theodore Roosevelt. The Master opens the volume, and a note marks it as a poem on Lincoln. A name once sneered at, the poem says, was soon everywhere, to be reviled and then revered. Lincoln came when days were perilous and hearts were sore beguiled.

The title poem follows, then An Island and a set on Calverly's. Leffingwell appears in three parts: the lure, the quickstep, and a requiescat. Later poems include Uncle Ananias, The Whip, and Miniver Cheevy. How Annandale Went Out and Doctor of Billiards show Robinson's town portraits at their sharpest.
76732-songs-and-rhymes-of-a-lead-miner:
Songs and Rhymes of a Lead Miner is a book of verse by Thomas Grierson Gracie of Wanlockhead. It came out at a Scots town press in nineteen twenty-one. Gracie was one of ten young of a lead mine man, born in eighteen sixty-one. His youth was spent in want, on a mine wage of a few coins a week.

Yet he calls that youth glad and free, with the glens and hills as his joy and school as his bane. The book stands in bands by kind, tales of place, notes for the dead, songs, and mixed bits. Mine shafts and pumps stand in the song list next to brides, curl games, and the war dead of his glen. Verse in broad Scots fills the whole.
76929-maugis-ye-sorcerer:
A burlesque romance copyrighted in 1898 by F Tennyson Neely claims to come from the ancient French, from the writings of a mad savant of the Maison Maugis in Mouzon. Its author signs as Lord Gilhooley, author of Yutzo. A picture shows a mysterious door. The dedication addresses the fools who compose the ethnographic society of Nancy, France. Neely published the book in London and New York.

The mock antique dress, with ye and olde throughout, signals a comic hoax. Maugis was a sorcerer of the Charlemagne romances. This version plays the matter for farce. Such nonsense books traded on the 1890s taste for whimsy and fake medievalism.
76935-walter-pater:
Walter Pater is a life book by Benson in the English Men of Letters set. A Macmillan house of New York and London brought it out in nineteen six. Parts treat first life, first works, and Oxford days in scheme rank. Marius the Epicurean gets a part of its own in that scheme. London life, late works, and the man cast close the book parts.

Small is known of Pater line stock, Benson grants at the start. A Dutch sea chief tale hangs on the name in kin lore. His kin dwelt at Weston Underwood near Olney in the past age. One of them crossed to America, where his sire was born there. That sire came home to heal the poor at Shadwell for small pay.
76955-nora-s-twin-sister:
Nina Rhoades wrote this tale for girls, printed by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard of Boston in August 1919. Nana French Bickford drew the plates. The book stands in her Brick House Books, sold at a dollar fifty each, whose brick house cover made girl readers happy at sight. A plate shows one girl crying to another that she is just like her.

Rhoades had written Marion's Vacation, Dorothy Brown, and The Girl from Arizona in the same line. Front pages tell a bedtime tale of Tommy, who trips down the kitchen stairs in a dream and wakes in his own bed. The main tale turns on Nora and a girl who mirrors her, as the title promises: a twin in face, if not in blood.
76993-an-independent-daughter:
An Independent Daughter is a girls' novel by Amy Blanchard. Lippincott of Philadelphia held the rights from 1898 and printed it in 1900. Alice Barber Stephens drew the pictures that stand through the tale. Blanchard had writ Two Girls, Betty of Wye, and Three Pretty Maids. Twenty chapters run from college-mates to a close called At Last.

Persis Holmes walks in her college gown as the tale opens here. A serenade, farewell to alma mater, and Lisa's wedding day follow on. Ruffled feathers, dear delights, and a coming shadow fill the mid list. The new teacher, a Christmas tree, and a sleighing party come next. Pitfalls and the house of the blacksmith darken the late chapters. A dream fulfilled and leave-takings lead to the final chapter's close. The front picture shows the new graduate hurrying to meet her friends.
76999-freston-tower:
R Cobbold, rector of Wortham, wrote a tale of the times of Cardinal Wolsey named for Freston Tower in Suffolk. The preface places the tower on the banks of the river Orwell, where it has stood for centuries. Every Ipswich sailor knows it, Cobbold says. Travelers sailing from Ipswich to Harwich see it towering above the trees.

Many guesses have been made about its origin and use. Cobbold promises a record of that origin tied to one of the most learned youths of his age, the boy bachelor of Oxford. The tale connects with the Reformation and with Wolsey's pride and fall. It is offered as a lesson against haughtiness.
77047-wings-of-silver:
Evelyn Gage Browne wrote a small book of verse held under a 1918 right, full of faith and flight. The lead poem, Wings, calls the force that stirs the bird to sing and bids it fly. That same urge breaks the grey cocoon and the seed shell, and calls the soul of man to rise.

Birds of Passage prays to learn from birds that keep their course through wind and change of clime. Faith holds that drop by drop, thought by thought, love shall beat hate and life shall beat death. Twelve short poems in all treat stars, doors, webs of dreams, and calls to the sky.
77051-the-defender:
Nicholas Kalashnikoff tells a Siberian tale in The Defender, printed in New York in 1951. Scribner made the book, with copyright the same year. Claire and George Louden the younger draw the plates. Kalashnikoff had writ Toyon, a dog of the north, and Jumper, the life of a Siberian horse. He gives the book to his daughter.

His foreword opens with a remembered saying. Everywhere there is life, and everywhere there are warm human hearts: the words of a school teacher, Ivan Pavin, from his boyhood in Siberia. The teacher took joy in his work and passed joy on to his pupils. Grown and gone north, the writer spent several years in the far north testing the truth of the saying. He found warm hearts in plenty, he says, but none warmer than that of Tim, of the Yakut tribe.
77111-the-mother:
Grazia Deledda, an Italian novelist, wrote The Mother, issued in English in 1923 in a version by Mary Steegmann. The tale is set in a remote hill village in Sardinia, and the whole plot runs in just two days. A mother who works as a servant watches her son Paul, a young priest, slip out at night in secret.

Fourteen parts trace her fear, his inner clash, and the tight pull of faith, duty, and human love. The note at the front calls the book a study of two minds under strain, close to Greek tragedy in its plain force. No church doctrine is argued. The clash is human, not formal.
77136-the-wilderness-hunter:
The Wilderness Hunter stands in the works of Theodore Roosevelt, in a grand set of fourteen books, from a copyright of 1889 held by G P Putnam's Sons. Verse by Joaquin Miller and Walt Whitman fronts it: storms with beards, herds spread on the plain, and a bear-skin bed. The first head takes the whole field: wilds of forest, plain, and peak, and the men who hunted them. Boone, Crockett, Houston, and Carson lead the roll of scouts.

Trappers, buffalo men, stockmen, and troops fill out the breed. Then the game: bison, moose, elk, caribou, and deer. Heads turn to ranch hunts for the blacktail, poor sport with the whitetail, and the pronghorn on the cattle range. Hunt fans get a president's own hard lore of the old wild West.
77147-on-the-frontier:
On the Frontier, by Charles Henry Pearson, is a set of western tales. The Massachusetts Sabbath School Society issued the book. Its copyright was entered in 1864. The title story opens on a western steamer. A party of travellers meets the dangers of the river and the border country.

Companion tales include Death on the Prairie. Another tells of a ride to a western wedding. Peril mixes with the manners of new settlements. Such books were made for Sunday school libraries, so the adventure carries a moral frame. Courage, honesty, and faith are tested in a land without settled law. Pearson's West is a frontier of scattered cabins and rough travel. He wrote for young readers in the East who knew that country mainly through stories.
77347-the-pony-express-rider:
Earl McCain's novel opens at the desert edge of Great Salt Lake, where a tired sorrel smells water and quickens toward Ross's Post. The post is the key station on the Pony Express route between Salt Lake and Placerville.

The newcomer is Dixie Rollins, five days past twenty one, come to ask Jim Slade for a rider's job. Slade, a power in the Express who can ride and shoot with any man under him, sizes him up across a table. Dixie admits his Kentucky horsemanship is better than his gun work and owns that his older brother Clint already rides the line. Slade hires him on the Express principle: a man starts with a clean page and writes his own record. The novel is built on that promise, a man's name to make on the hardest mail route in America.
77384-the-vagabond-lover:
Charlson Gray turned The Vagabond Lover into a novel from the scenario by James Creelman, with rights held from nineteen twenty-nine. The book prints scenes from the Radio Picture of the same name, starring Rudy Vallee. Its hero is Rudy Bronson, a slim, blond student with a dreamer's eyes. He sits in his dorm room and calls himself a failure.

A note from the registrar bars Rudy from the state university that fall for poor grades. He had spent his year at work on his saxophone, hoping to make the school band. The bandmaster heard his try-out and called his playing a little worse than rotten. Chapter heads promise a roadhouse, false colours, and the wings of song, as Rudy chases fame and love past his fall.
77440-encovragements-for-such-as-shall-h:
Encouragements is a promotional tract for a Scottish colony in America. It was printed at Edinburgh in 1625. The author signs himself Lochinvar. The tract urges undertakers to join the new plantation of Cape Breton. The colony is there called New Galloway.

The dedication addresses Sir William Alexander of Menstrie. He was the king's lieutenant for New Scotland. A letter to the adventurers follows. It argues that planting colonies is the universal policy of civil states. Adam and Eve began the work, the writer says. Noah's family began it again after the Flood. The confusion of tongues at Babel scattered colonies over the earth. Great princes gained dominion and revenue by planting. The tract presses Scots to follow that example.
77515-the-woodranger:
The Woodranger, a story of the pioneers of the debatable grounds, is a boys' novel by Waldo Browne. Page first held its copyright of 1899, and Wessels reissued it at New York in 1907. Bridgman drew the pictures. Browne inscribes it to his merry little son, hoping it will interest and instruct him. The contents open with the deer's leap.

Norman, the hero, meets his enemy early, faces a perilous predicament, and stands trial. A shooting match, an alarm, bad news at home, and the honour of the McNeils fill the middle chapters. To understand the scenes, Browne says, one must glance at the Merrimack River country in 1740. New England was then a narrow strip along the coast, in four provinces. His tale of forest law, deer reeves, and ranger work brings that border world to life. It mixes hunting craft with the quarrels of settlers and crown.
77621-magnolia-flower:
Magnolia Flower is a story by Zora Neale Hurston, printed in The Spokesman in July 1925. It opens in a moonlit Florida of brooks and rivers that talk. The brook laughs and sings, hurling its water in sparkling dance figures when it meets hard places in its bed. At last it dances into the bosom of the St Johns river, upsetting the whispering hyacinths.

The river, the Mighty One, wakes peevish and washes the feet of the palmetto palms. A palm cannot speak without wind, Hurston writes, and nature knows nothing of death. The river asks the brook why it hurries and chatters so. It has borne millions of lovers up and down and gathered infinite tears. At the brook's begging, it settles to tell a story of some of them.
77826-belchamber:
Belchamber is a novel by Howard Overing Sturgis, published by Constable in 1904. Sturgis had written Tim and All That Was Possible before this country house tale. The book is dedicated to William Haynes Smith in a brief front line. Chapter one calls Belchamber one of the most beautiful places in England.

The name, if not the house, dates from Norman French days at the court, it says. A king, some early Henry or Edward, praised the fair chamber in high good humour. Old world scandal hangs about the legend in the authorised form of the tale. A frail, gentle heir in a great house gives the novel its pathos.
77858-old-rough-the-miser:
Lily Wesselhoeft wrote Old Rough the Miser, a fable for children, for Roberts Brothers at Boston in 1891. Goodridge drew the plates for the book. It opens on a large farm, with meadows, fields, and many acres of woods. A crow, a water-rat, an owl, a frog, and a weasel all live there. Room seems ample, yet the tale starts with a feud. The water-rat claims a right to a cornfield near the brook, and the crow claims it too.

Chapters bring Old Rough at home, the counsel of Old Caw, and a declaration of war. A battle, a lost chick, and a spy named Flipwing raise the stakes. At last the beasts lay their case before the owl. Wesselhoeft uses beast talk to teach young readers how greed starts strife, and how law can end it.
77886-an-historical-account-of-all-the-v:
An Historical Account of All the Voyages Round the World, volume the first, was printed for F Newbery in London in 1774. The set ran to four volumes, faithfully extracted from the journals of the voyagers and dressed with maps, charts, and historical prints. The preface promises a copious store of rational entertainment in small compass.

The roster of English navigators starts with Drake in 1577 and Cavendish, runs through Dampier, Cooke, and Rogers, and ends with Byron, Wallis, Carteret, and Cook. Sydney Parkinson's voyage with Cook and Bougainville's French voyage are added, plus a North Pole appendix.
77912-campaign-diary-of-a-french-officer:
Campaign Diary of a French Officer is a war diary by Rene Nicolas. Katharine Babbitt rendered the French notes into English for American readers. Houghton Mifflin issued the book in Boston and New York in nineteen seventeen. Nicolas served as a junior lieutenant in the French infantry arm.

A friend preface warns that the true diary bears blood and mud stains. A hole from a steel shard pierces it from cover to cover. No change has been made, and the notes stand as set down at the front. Nicolas was a university student in letters when war broke out in France. He trained fast for a commission and went to the front young.
77984-harry-s-newspaper:
Stephen Cox wrote Harry's Newspaper, or The Young Publisher, published at Chicago with copyright in 1930 and illustrations by Willard Smythe. Twelve chapters follow Harry from being thrown on his own resources to the end of a year. The setting is Coalville, a mining town drawn at the book's front.

Chapters mark his progress: ready for business, the outlook encouraging, busy days, and then the Coalville News, volume one number one. A mass meeting, a mine disaster, and a fire test the young editor. Illustrations show the paper just off the press and an old army press at work. Readers get a boys' success story about a lad who prints his way up.
78003-the-captive-singer:
Marie Bjelke Petersen wrote a novel in three parts, printed in London with a front view of limestone caves at Launceston. The book opens in a hot house, moves into wild country, and then to a voice heard in a cave. A black horse and rider, a girl in a yellow gown, and a shrine all appear in the first part.

Part two brings Iris and Ralph, a man named Justin who goes away, and Captain Barton with a plan for a rescue. Field glasses show a key sight from a summit before a woman makes an offer. Part three turns on a visit from an earl, cables, and the pair reaching their goal at last.
78004-an-historical-account-of-all-the-v:
An Historical Account of All the Voyages Round the World is a gathering of sea journals, printed in London in 1774 for F Newbery. The title promises the voyages of English navigators, faithfully drawn from the journals of the voyagers. Drake leads the list, with his voyage of 1577 to 1580. Cavendish, Cowley, and Dampier follow in their turns. Cooke and Rogers, who sailed together, and Clipperton and Shelvocke fill the next names. Anson's great voyage stands near the end.

The second volume, from which this text comes, takes up Captain Cooke. The Manila galleon, rich with the goods of the east, was the prize all private men of the South Seas sought. Ships of war sought the return ship instead. A journal of a voyage to the North Pole, by Commodore Phipps and Captain Lutwidge, is bound with the set.
78019-an-historical-account-of-all-the-v:
An Historical Account of All the Voyages Round the World, volume three, gathers the great English circumnavigations. Newbery printed the set in London, with maps, charts, and historical prints. The accounts, the title page says, are faithfully drawn from the voyagers' own journals.

A roll of names and dates maps the age: Drake in 1577 to 1580 and Cavendish in 1586 to 1588 lead. Dampier, Cooke, and Rogers follow, then Clipperton, Shelvocke, and Anson. Byron, Wallis, and Carteret bring the tale to Cook's voyage of 1768 to 1771. Sydney Parkinson, draftsman to Joseph Banks on the Endeavour, has his own account in the set. Bougainville's French voyage stands alongside the English ones. An appendix adds a journal of a voyage to the North Pole under Phipps and Lutwidge.
78104-an-historical-account-of-all-the-v:
An Historical Account of All the Voyages Round the World by English Navigators, printed at London in 1773, gathers the great circumnavigations into one narrative. Its fourth volume moves from Drake in 1577 through Cavendish, Dampier, Anson and Byron, and reaches the recent voyages of Wallis, Carteret and Cook in 1768 to 1771. Bougainville's French voyage is added, along with an appendix on Phipps and the attempt toward the North Pole.

The specimen passage prints the Endeavour narrative of Sydney Parkinson, who sailed with Joseph Banks, and records the speech and customs of New Holland. Parkinson notes a language wholly unlike any other, and describes natives going naked, smeared with red paint, their weapons tipped with fish bones.
78126-the-weird-of-the-wanderer:
Prospero and Caliban produced The Weird of the Wanderer in 1912. William Rider and Son issued it at London. The book claims to print papyrus records. They tell of Nicholas Crabbe's previous lives. Domenico Comparetti receives the book in homage. His honors fill a full page of print.

Senator of the kingdom stands among those honors. Oxford, Athens, and Cracow gave him degrees. The Lincei academy counts him a national member. Turin and Naples list him as well. A Horace line bids men mix brief folly with counsel. The book is given to divert his leisure hours. Past-life tales in mock-old records gave Edwardian readers occult romance dressed in a scholar's seals and Latin tags.
78269-the-princess-and-the-tiger:
Goethe wrote a tale of a princess and a tiger, here as Little Blue Book Number 1458. E Haldeman-Julius edited the cheap set at Girard, Kansas, with rights held in 1929. Fog hangs over the castle courts on an autumn morning as the tale starts. Huntsmen, dogs, and horses stir for a day in the field.

The Prince lingers with his young wife, whose fond farewells hold him late. Both are lively, and each shares the joys of the other with delight. Court pomp and wild beasts set the poles of the coming plot. Pocket readers of the time got a famed German tale in a form that cost mere cents.
78323-dark-power:
Dark Power is a mystery novel by Elisabeth Sanxay Holding, printed in New York by the Vanguard Press under a 1930 copyright. A table of sixteen chapters runs from A Rescue to It Over. The tale turns on a young woman in a strange house.

Di goes through the house once more, finding all in neat order yet with the look of a place looted and left bare. Bureau tops are swept clean, and great gaps mark where Angelina flamboyant things had stood. Angelina own room is worse, a sad neatness where wild disorder reigned the day before. Her wedding had been a cyclone, and Di was whirled like a leaf in the gale. Reporters crowded the event, since Angelina exploits were famed. Later heads name a forbidden room, a white figure, and a will. Mystery fans get gloom.
7841-a-primary-reader:
E Louise Smythe's A Primary Reader offers old-time stories, fairy tales, and myths retold by children. It served first-grade readers in Santa Rosa schools. Its aim is threefold: give small readers sight-word texts, meet heroes of song and story early, and plant a desire for literature.

Following G Stanley Hall's call for true child editions, Smythe tested tales piece by piece. She cut and shaped them to children's minds, and let pupils retell them aloud before they appeared on blackboard or mimeograph. The result is a gentle first reader built from children's own words.
78411-a-warrior-who-fought-custer:
Thomas Marquis's A Warrior Who Fought Custer was published at Minneapolis in 1931 by the Midwest Company. Marquis interpreted the account; the telling is Wooden Leg's, a Northern Cheyenne who fought at the battle, and the frontispiece shows him holding a rifle a Cheyenne companion captured there. A passage from Custer's My Life on the Plains, printed in 1876, stands at the front.

Marquis states that the Indian story of Custer's last battle had never been told, apart from a few distorted interviews. No white man survived it to tell his side. Sixty-one years old and forty-one years in Montana, he had served as agency physician for the Northern Cheyennes, the Sioux's allies in the fight. He learned the plains sign-talk well enough to drop interpreters, hosted the old warriors at his home, and after a long siege won the whole story out of them.
7842-the-rise-of-iskander:
Benjamin Disraeli's The Rise of Iskander opens at sunset behind Athenian mountains, where the plain glows violet and olive groves stir. Turkish pennons twinkle over Piraeus harbor, women process to a fountain, horsemen throw javelins, and nightingales, grasshoppers, and violets fill purple air with music and scent.

On the Acropolis crag, amid Minerva's temple ruins, a lone figure gazes on columns and Caryatides that baffle modern proportion. That figure is Iskander, the Albanian hero also known as Skanderbeg, whose rise against Ottoman power the romance will trace through war, pride, and fate, in Disraeli's early ornate style.
78496-the-keystone-jacket-and-dress-cutt:
Charles Hecklinger wrote this treatise on jackets, dresses, and other garments for women, published at New York in 1895 and specially designed for self-instruction. Its preface promises the simplest and most reliable systems ever offered to the trade.

The index runs from taking measures and drafting the waist through forms stout, erect, and stooping. Jackets follow in every cut: Eton, bolero, cutaway, covert, frock coat, and riding jackets single and double breasted. Sleeves, vests, collars, capes, and an ulster get their own drafts, then dress skirts, a riding skirt, trousers, and breeches. The introduction answers years of inquiries for a reliable textbook on ladies' tailoring. Dressmakers get a complete drafting system.
78500-the-young-reporter:
The Young Reporter is a boys' tale of the press by William Drysdale. Charles Copeland drew the plates for the book, out in 1895. Its hero is Dick Sumner, a printer boy in a small town. The tale opens at half past three on a dark day in his shop.

Dick stands at his case and drops the type with a glum heart. He pulls himself up and works the faster for his low mood. The part heads show him rise to the post of a news man at last. A stole train, a wild night on the bay, and a chase fill the tale. Dick spurns a bribe and lands in far lands with a house in tow. A wrecked ship, a fight priest, and a cursed boat crowd the plot. The tale ends with Dick at work on a book of his own.
78508-the-hand-of-power:
Edgar Wallace wrote The Hand of Power, a mystery from the Mystery League at New York in 1930. This is the first edition of the book. Its contents run past fifty chapters of intrigue. The tale opens with the men of the moor, on the bare face of Dartmoor. Wind howls and shrieks over that ancient waste, above the roar of a motor. Betty Carew hears it as her car rattles on in the storm.

Laffin gives orders, Pawter serves, and Captain Harvey Hale takes the stage. A locked room, an initiation rite, and a priory full of proud sons add dread. The Grand Prior shows his hand at last, and a ship named Escorial bears the plot to sea. Wireless rooms and warships fill the close.
78664-the-adventures-of-pony-dexter:
Harriet Cheever wrote a tale for girls of a pony and its young owner. The book came out in Boston in June 1911. Diantha Marlowe drew its plates. Cheever wrote tales of Billy Trill and of Madame Angora. A front plate shows two who sped neck to neck a brief space.

Pony Dexter's deeds fill the book from race to romp. Girls' books by Laura Richards stand in its front ads. Those ads name the Margaret and Hildegarde sets of tales. Cheever's own world is one of pets and kind young folk. Short parts suit new readers at home or school. Warm fun and small perils rule the tale.
7870-tales-of-daring-and-danger:
G. A. Henty's Tales of Daring and Danger, published in 1890 by Blackie, opens with a merry party on a Poona bungalow verandah, where Colonel Hastings commands a brigade. Tiffin is served as officers and ladies lounge in cane chairs, before tales carry readers far from that calm.

Contents promise bears and dacoits in the Ghauts, the Paternosters, a pipe of mystery, white-faced Dick, and a brush with the Chinese. An illustration sights the wreck of a steamer. Through India, sea, and frontier, Henty gives boys brisk adventures of pluck, loyalty, and quick action.
78716-sport-and-science-on-the-sino-mong:
Sport and Science on the Sino-Mongolian Frontier, by Sowerby, was published at London by Andrew Melrose in 1918. A note says the book was written in 1913 and held back by the war. Sowerby, a fellow of the zoological and geographical societies, dedicates it to Major Robert Sterling Clark, his hunting partner.

Chapters cross the Ordos border and the Fen River basin, hunt argali and wapiti, and climb the Mongolian plateau. Later parts turn to pure science, the plant and animal life of the frontier. Kipling's explorer song stands at the front, and the book lives up to it.
78732-an-unmarried-father:
Floyd Dell wrote this novel, printed at New York under copyright in 1927. Norman Overbeck, a young lawyer in Vickley, a town on the Mississippi, has just joined his father's law firm. The elder Overbeck argues cases before the supreme court, while Norman feels himself the unworthy son, driving his father to the early train.

The book falls in three parts: The Discovery, In Exile, and The Dominant Sex. A letter, legal advice, and a post mortem on a dead romance open the tale, and a baby stands near its heart. Dell follows his hero through family breakfasts, flights, lost jobs, and hard talks about what a man owes to a child and to the woman he did not marry.
78766-the-shadow-shooter:
A western story by W C Tuttle featuring Hashknife Hartley. The headnote bills Hashknife as a wise, humorous adventurer of the open range. He rides over the hill again here. The opening scene, though, belongs to Soapy Weed. Soapy stands in the AH bunkhouse under two oil lamps. A mail-order suit has just defeated him completely.

The checked sleeves end far above his wrists. The trousers, inches too large, drop when he lets go. Cling Heffner, a giant on the bunk, surveys the disaster. You need suspenders, Soapy, is his whole diagnosis. Tuttle opens with pure bunkhouse comedy before the plot starts. His Hashknife tales mixed detection with range humour for the pulps.
78779-dark-hester:
Anne Douglas Sedgwick wrote Dark Hester, a novel printed at Boston in 1929. Monica Wilmott, living alone in Essex, catches herself saying aloud that she has hated Hester from the first moment she saw her. Hester, her son Clive's wife, sat once in a Chelsea window against the river, quiet and assured.

Monica fears the habit of thinking aloud, lest a said thing grow more real than it is and wall her in. Cold summer rain darkens the solitary afternoon in her cottage made from two old homes. Black brows and a thin black cloak lined with red fix Hester in memory. Readers get a fine study of jealousy and family strain.
78801-the-parlor-gardener:
Cornelia Randolph translated The Parlor Gardener from the French, at Boston in 1861. Tilton at 161 Washington Street published her American version. Its subject is the house culture of ornamental plants, the title says. A first figure shows a mantelpiece garden in flower. The author's preface asks who does not love flowers in our days.

Who does not like to do a little gardening, it adds warmly. The taste affords the greatest amount of elegant, harmless pleasure, it holds. Yet many deem that taste unfortunate, being unable to indulge it. Business forbids a country residence to one reader, the preface says. A young family ties a lady reader to the city in its pages. Want of health condemns others to a sedentary existence indoors. The book brings the garden to the parlor window and shelf. Randolph adapts French counsel to American rooms and winters.
78883-the-man-from-the-river:
The Man from the River is a detective novel by G. D. H. Cole and Margaret Cole. It is called a Wilson story, for its lead man of that name. The book came out in New York in 1928 from the Macmillan Company. The front pages list the Coles' other tales: The Blatchington Tangle, The Murder at Crome House, and The Death of a Millionaire.

The first chapter opens on a fine July morning. Michael Prendergast, a doctor and a rising Harley Street consultant, wakes at the Old Malting House, Steeple Tollesbury. His first thought is one of relief: thank goodness, Wilson is coming today. A picture at the front shows the steeple of Tollesbury, Loring Grange, and the country round. The tale is a mystery of the English riverside, opened through the eyes of a man glad of help.
78887-the-doctor-s-daughter:
The Doctor's Daughter is a novel by Catharine Shaw, in the Arundel Family series. Shaw and Company published it in London. Shaw also wrote The Gabled Farm and Nellie Arundel. A picture shows Ruth passing an astonished ayah. Thirty-three chapters run from Lonely through Arthur Arundel and Something to Live For.

A posted letter and a lost letter turn the plot. An angry elephant appears in India, and a parting and good news follow. The tale ends in a large family and a shaded room. Shaw wrote evangelical domestic tales, and this one joins an English family story to Indian scenes of service and faith.
78892-the-flying-buccaneer:
Flying Buccaneer is a novel of adventure in the skies by Jack Binns, issued at New York in nineteen twenty three. All rights, including stage and photoplay rights, are reserved on its title page. Chapter one opens with a cry of alarm in a Washington home. Something terrible has happened, a wife tells her husband. She thrusts a newspaper at him as he comes down the stairs.

Her husband is George Cowl, the Secretary of Air. A banner headline fills the front page of the paper. A transpacific mail airship has been destroyed by an aerial pirate in mid ocean, it says. The giant airship Langley was shot down midway between Honolulu and Manila. Survivors were picked up by a cargo steamer. A masked pirate escaped with the valuable cargo, the sub heads report.
78920-the-money-spider:
The Money-Spider is a novel by William Le Queux, published in Boston in 1911 by the Gorham Press. Le Queux was a prolific writer of mystery and intrigue, author of The Great God Gold and The Red Room. A frontispiece shows a man and woman staring at each other in defiance, even hatred.

The contents promise a tale of secrets and peril. Early chapters concern certain secrets, the end of the world, and the touchstone of misfortune. An allegation, strange matters of fact, and a captain's suggestion follow. The shadow is revealed, and the scene shifts to the Arctic wilderness. Love's shadow, faces in the mist, and four letters close the first part. The second part opens at a tryst and runs toward peril. Le Queux's readers expected hidden wealth, hidden enmity, and a chase across strange country.
78948-killer:
Killer is a science fiction story by James E. Gunn, published with illustrations by Freas. Its narrator is an alien who came to Earth from the stars. He tells the tale himself, in the first person, beginning with his arrival riding a tail of flame.
