Cream is most often skimmed from the top for churning. Some churn the whole milk at once. Churning breaks the oil sacs, and the freed fat joins to form butter.
britannica-1911-byles-mather:
Mather Byles, an American clergyman who lived from 1706 to 1788, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Boston in Massachusetts, he came on his mother side from John Cotton and Richard Mather. He graduated at Harvard in 1725 with high standing. In 1733 he became pastor of the Hollis Street church in Boston, a Congregational charge.

Byles held a high rank among the clergy of the province for his learned sermons and his ready wit. At the start of the War of Independence he spoke out boldly for the royal cause. After the British left Boston, his tie with his church was dissolved by the parish. He stayed in Boston all the same and was arrested in 1777. A sentence of exile was changed to confinement in his own house, and he was soon set free.
britannica-1911-calder:
Calder is an ancient district of Midlothian, in Scotland. This 1911 Britannica entry describes its parishes and industries. The district splits into Mid-Calder and West-Calder. East-Calder belongs to the parish of Kirknewton. Mid-Calder held 3132 people in 1901. West-Calder held 8092, and Kirknewton 3221. The district owes its prosperity to one great industry. That is the mineral oil trade, hugely developed there.

Coal-mining is also carried on widely in Calder. Sandstone and limestone are quarried as well. Paper-mills flourish in the district too. Mid-Calder town stands on the river Almond. It has an ancient church and a notable minister. John Spottiswood, the Scottish reformer, served there for years. His sons John and James were both born in the town. West-Calder is the district's chief centre. It stands on Breich Water, south-west of Edinburgh. At Addiewell, works make ammonia, naphtha and paraffin oil.
britannica-1911-calender:
Calender is a word with two quite separate meanings. This 1911 Britannica entry sets out both senses. The first is a machine used in cloth and paper making. It consists of two or more rollers in close contact. The rollers are often heated in use. Cloth passes between them under pressure. The process flattens the fibres of the fabric. It removes unevenness and gives a smooth finish. It can also leave a glaze on the surface.

Paper manufacture uses the same machine in its finishing. The second sense is a religious one. A calender was a member of an order of dervishes. The order split from the Baktashite order in the 14th century. Its members were vowed to perpetual travelling. The name appears in several other forms as well. Kalenderis and Qalandarites are among them. The entry points readers to the article on dervishes for more.
britannica-1911-california-lower:
Lower California is a long, narrow peninsula of Mexico. It is also called Baja California. It lies between the Gulf of California and the Pacific Ocean. This 1911 Britannica article surveys the territory. Its population was 42,245 in 1895. By 1900 it had risen to 47,624. The peninsula runs about 760 miles long. It is only 30 to 150 miles wide. Its area is 58,328 square miles.

A range of barren mountains runs the peninsula's full length. It slopes gently toward the Pacific side. Toward the Gulf it breaks down in steep faces. The land looks arid and desolate in general. Rain is too scant for most plants to grow. Volcanic remains add to the barren look. The north is hot and dry, like southern California. The south gets more rain and has fertile tracts. Orchil is the chief natural product named. With irrigation, farmers grow sugar cane, cotton and grapes.
britannica-1911-cancer:
Cancer, also called carcinoma, is treated in a 1911 Britannica article on a grave class of growths. The name comes from Latin and Greek words for an eating ulcer. Such growths occur in man and in most or all animals with backbones. The common term malignant disease is used in the text as a synonym.

The article lists traits that the many forms of cancer share. In structure, the growths are made of cells with nuclei and free nuclei. A milky fluid, called cancer juice, sits in a dense fibrous frame. The growths have no clear limits or edges. They spread into the tissue around them. For the wider study of tumours, the reader is sent to a companion article. The piece shows how doctors of that era framed a disease still feared today.
britannica-1911-caponier:
A caponier is a work built in the ditch of a fort. This short 1911 Britannica entry defines the term. The word comes from the French caponnière. That word properly means a capon-cote, or house. The work's fire sweeps the bottom of the ditch. Muskets, machine-guns and case shot can all fire from it. Its guns stop an enemy from settling in the ditch.

The term appears in military use by the late 17th century. In some bastioned systems the caponier had a second role. It served as a covered way to the outworks. The main parapet then defended the ditch by its own fire. The bastion trace made that plan possible. The whole notice is a short paragraph in the original. It gives the word's origin, the work's purpose, and its variant use. Readers get a plain definition of a fortification detail.
britannica-1911-carlyle-alexander:
Alexander Carlyle (1722–1805) was a Scottish divine. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. He was born in Dumfriesshire on 26 January 1722. He passed his youth at Prestonpans, in the east. There he witnessed the battle of 1745 as a young man. He was educated at Edinburgh, Glasgow and Leiden. From 1748 until his death he was minister at Inveresk.

Carlyle rose to high eminence in the Scottish church. He led the moderate, or “broad,” party within it. He was moderator of the General Assembly in 1770. In 1789 he became dean of the Chapel Royal. His striking looks earned him the name “Jupiter Carlyle.” His autobiography appeared in 1860, long after his death. It stops at the year 1770 in its narrative. Still, it pictures 18th-century Scottish life in rich detail. He remembered the Porteous Riots of 1736 in it. Adam Smith, David Hume and John Home were his friends.
britannica-1911-carrier:
Carrier is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the law that governs people who carry the goods of others for hire. In common speech the word covered the wagoners who hauled goods by road, a trade the railways had largely replaced. In law it covers all conveyers of property, by land or by water. The growth of world transit made the subject more important, not less.

The entry grounds the carrier's duty in Roman law. A praetorian edict, preserved in the Pandects, promised judgment against shipmasters, innkeepers, and stable-keepers who failed to return what they had received safely. From that short rule grew the principle that a carrier's promise to the public is a contract of indemnity. He must deliver what he took in, or pay its value. The entry traces how that simple Roman rule shaped commercial law across the civilised world.
britannica-1911-carrying-over:
Carrying over is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry defining a stock exchange term, also called continuation. It names the operation by which settlement of a bargain made for money, or for a given account, is put off from one settling day to the next. The delay is not free: the party who carries over pays a consideration for it. That charge is called a contango or a backwardation.

The entry explains the mechanics in terms of sale and repurchase. A continuation equals a sale for the day joined to a repurchase for the succeeding account, or a purchase for the day joined to a resale. The price used to adjust such deals is the “making-up” price of the day. The entry is brief and points readers onward to the articles on Account and Stock Exchange for the fuller treatment of how accounts and settlements worked.
britannica-1911-cartwright-peter:
Peter Cartwright (1785–1872) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an American Methodist Episcopal preacher born in Amherst county, Virginia. His father, a veteran of the War of Independence, moved the family to Kentucky in 1790. Peter had little schooling and gambled at cards and horse racing until 1801, when a sermon by John Page brought him into the church.

He was licensed as an exhorter in May 1802 and soon known as the “Kentucky Boy.” Ordained deacon in 1806 and presiding elder in 1808, he served districts in Kentucky and, from 1823, in Illinois, where he stayed until 1869. By 1856 he had preached some 14,600 times, received about 10,000 people into the church, and baptized about 12,000. The entry calls him a typical backwoods preacher, able and strong, and gives his death near Pleasant Plains, Illinois, in September 1872.
britannica-1911-cashier:
Cashier is a word article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica covering two different senses of one term. In the first sense, from the French word for the keeper of a money box, a cashier is the person charged with paying out or receiving money in a business house. The post can be a high one, like the chief cashier of the Bank of England, whose name appears on its notes.

The second sense is military, traced to Dutch use in the sixteenth century and Latin roots meaning to shatter. To cashier an officer is to dismiss him for grave offences. The Army Act of 1881 names it behaving in a scandalous manner unbecoming an officer and a gentleman. The penalty goes beyond loss of the commission: the man is barred for good from serving the state in any capacity.
britannica-1911-cato-marcus-porcius-phil:
Marcus Porcius Cato, a Roman philosopher who lived from 95 to 46 before Christ, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He is called Uticensis to set him apart from his great grandfather, the Censor. After his parents died, he was raised in the house of his uncle. He fought with honour against Spartacus in the year 72.

The entry says he became a military tribune and served in Macedonia, but never loved the soldier's life. On his return he became quaestor and ran the public accounts with such zeal that he won a post in Asia. He was sickened by the rot he met among public men. Yet he admired the strict order Lucullus had kept in the east and backed his claims. At the same time he opposed the vast demands of Pompey.
britannica-1911-cavalier:
Cavalier is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a word for a horseman. It meant in particular a horse soldier, or a man of gentle birth trained in knightly exercises. The word comes from French forms that go back to the late Latin caballarius, a horseman. That in turn comes from caballus, a pack horse. The same root gave French the word chevalier, the regular term for a knight.

In English the word took on a sharp political sense. It was first used with contempt for a swaggering gallant. Then it fastened to the Royalists, the supporters of Charles I against Parliament. Their opponents coined it as a reproach. The king's party soon adopted it as a title of honour. They answered with the name Roundhead for their foes. The court party kept the name at the Restoration, until the term Tory rose.
britannica-1911-cayenne-pepper:
Cayenne pepper, also called Guinea pepper, Spanish pepper, or chilly, is the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The spice is made from the dried fruit of several Capsicum plants. Those plants belong to a family that is quite distinct from the true peppers. All capsicum fruits share a strong, pungent taste. The plants bear greenish-white flowers and pod-like fruit that holds pulp and seeds.

About thirty species are known, all native to Central and South America. They are now grown in many parts of the world, for food and for show. The article gives plain growing notes for England, from spring sowing under glass to summer flowering. It notes which sorts are planted out in rich soil and which tender kinds need shelter in winter. Several species and forms are used to make the pepper.
britannica-1911-chafer:
Chafer is an insect article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In modern speech, chafer names the beetles of the family Scarabaeidae. The word is used above all for those kinds that feed on leaves as adults. It comes from an Old English word, ceafor.

The entry notes a German cousin of the word. The German Kafer is applied to beetles of every kind, not just this family. The scarab family itself is large and varied in its feeding. Some of its members feed on dung, and others on living plant tissue. The cockchafers and their kin form one subfamily of leaf eaters. The rose-chafers form another, bright beetles that haunt gardens. In both groups the grubs live long underground, devouring roots. Readers get a short guide to a family that farmers and gardeners know too well.
britannica-1911-charisius-flavius-sosipa:
Flavius Sosipater Charisius, a Latin grammarian, is kept in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He thrived near the middle of the fourth century of our era. Born in Africa by most accounts, he was called to Constantinople. There he took the chair of a famed gloss man on Terence. His grammar, in five books, was addressed to his own son.

That work has come down to us in a torn state. The start of book one and most of book five are lost. The book is a mere gathering from older hands, the entry says. Yet it keeps bits of lost grammar men found nowhere else. Palaemon, Romanus, and Cominianus are named in its pages by name. Keil's text of 1857 is called the best for study.
britannica-1911-charter:
Charter is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a key kind of legal writ. The word goes back through Latin to a Greek word for the stuff men wrote on. A charter was a writ that proved a grant of land, rights, or perks. The one who held it could show it as proof of lawful claim.

The entry traces charters from feudal times, when kings and lords granted them to towns and guilds. It links the word's fame to King John's Great Charter of 1215. Later, the name was used for basic laws granted by kings to their peoples. France in 1814 is one case the text names.
britannica-1911-chateau-gontier:
Château-Gontier is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of western France, capital of an arrondissement in the department of Mayenne. It stands on the Mayenne river, 18 miles south by east of Laval. Its population in 1906 was 6871. Of its churches, St Jean dates from the eleventh century and is a relic of the castle. The town has a tribunal, a communal college for boys, and a small museum.

Local work includes spinning wool and cotton. Serge, flannel, and oil are made there. The town is also an agricultural market, and chalybeate springs lie close by. Its name and origin come from a castle built in the first half of the eleventh century by Gunther, steward of Fulk Nerra of Anjou. The site had been a farm of the monks of St Aubin. Louis XI later gave the lordship to Philippe de Comines. The Vendeans occupied the town in 1793.
britannica-1911-cheffonier:
Cheffonier is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a piece of furniture, a sideboard like cabinet with doors closing its whole front. The hosted text begins in mid description, so the entry's opening lines are not present here. Its name comes from the French for a rag gatherer. That hints at its first purpose: a place for odds and ends. It now usually serves as a sideboard.

The entry judges it a remote and illegitimate descendant of the cabinet. It has rarely been elegant and never beautiful. The earliest cheffoniers date from the Empire period in England. They are usually of rosewood, with brass knobs and handles. A raised shelf with a pierced brass gallery often stands at the back. The doors are well panelled. The feet are pads, claws, or gilded bronze sphinxes. Cheap forms are still made in England in great number.
britannica-1911-cher:
Cher is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a department of central France. It takes in the eastern part of the old province of Berry. Loiret bounds it in the north, Allier and Creuse in the south, and Nièvre in the east. Its population in 1906 was 343,484. Its area is 2819 square miles. The south and east are elevated, one point reaching 1654 feet. A wide limestone table land fills the centre.

The Cher river becomes navigable where the Arnon and Yèvre join it. The Canal du Berry crosses the department from east to west. The climate is temperate and the rainfall moderate. Apart from the Sologne plain in the north, the soil is generally fertile. Wheat and oats are the main crops, with hemp, vegetables, and fruit. Vines flourish in the east, near Sancerre. Wide pastures support a strong trade in horses, cattle, and sheep.
britannica-1911-chichester:
Chichester is a city and municipal borough in Sussex, England, 69 miles south-south-west of London, lying in a plain at the foot of the South Downs. Its people numbered 12,224 in 1901, and it stands a mile from the head of Chichester Harbour. The cathedral church of the Holy Trinity was founded late in the 11th century, after the see moved here from Selsey in 1075. Fires in 1114 and 1187 kept building going for two centuries.

Norman work fills the nave and choir, while fine Early English work crowns the eastern parts, and the nave has rare double aisles. A detached campanile, unique among English cathedrals, stands beside the church, and the spire rises 277 feet. The market cross, town walls, St Mary's hospital and a grammar school founded in 1497 fill the town account. Cattle trade, farming trade, breweries and tanneries support the city.
britannica-1911-cipher: Cipher, also written cypher, comes from an Arabic word for void, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. At its first sense it is the symbol nought, or zero, the figure 0. From that sign the word spreads to name symbolic or secret writing of any kind. The entry sends readers to the text on cryptography for that art in full. The word can even stand for shorthand in loose use. In the schoolroom of old it named the doing of simple sums, called ciphering by teachers and pupils alike.
britannica-1911-cirencester:
Cirencester is an old market town in Gloucestershire, England, on the river Churn, 93 miles from London. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its urban district 7,536 people in 1901 and pictures its old houses round a fine parish church. The church is mainly Perpendicular, with a high battlemented tower and a famed south porch.

Two museums hold mosaics, inscriptions, and carved stones, for the town was the Roman Corinium, though little of it shows above ground beyond the amphitheatre and wall lines. An abbey founded by Henry the First in 1117 leaves a Norman gateway. West of the town stands Cirencester House, seat of Earl Bathurst, whose park the first lord planted with fake ruins. Pope and Swift both visited, and Pope designed a seat in the grounds. A mile away stands the Royal Agricultural College, chartered in 1845.
britannica-1911-clark-josiah-latimer:
Josiah Latimer Clark (1822-1898), an English engineer, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Great Marlow in Buckinghamshire, he first took an interest in chemicals. In 1848 he became an assistant engineer at the Menai Straits bridge under his elder brother Edwin. Two years later he followed his brother to the Electric Telegraph Company and in time took his place as chief engineer.

The article lists his range of work. In 1854 he patented a way to send letters and parcels between places by air pressure and vacuum. He helped build a large tube of that kind between the head post office and Euston station in London. He also tested how electric current moves in sea cables, and sat on the state panel of 1859 that weighed why so many such cable schemes had failed.
britannica-1911-clarke-john-sleeper:
John Sleeper Clarke was an American actor who lived from eighteen thirty three to eighteen ninety nine. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Baltimore, Maryland, he was educated for a life in law. He first acted in Boston in eighteen fifty one as Frank Hardy.

Clarke wed Asia Booth, daughter of Junius Brutus Booth, in eighteen fifty nine. He helped run theatres with his brother in law Edwin Booth then. In eighteen sixty seven he went to London and acted at Saint James theatre. His success was so great he stayed in England for life most. Parts like Toodles, Pangloss, and Ollapod ranked among his best loved roles.
britannica-1911-clever:
Clever is an adjective implying dexterous activity of mind or body, and ability to meet emergencies with readiness and adroitness. Its etymology and early history are obscure, and the earliest instance quoted comes from a Bestiary of about 1200. There the adder is called cof and the devil cliver on sins, quick to seize hold. That use would connect the word with cliver or clivre, a talon or claw, and the root seen in claw and cling.

Earlier uses seem confined to bodily dexterity, nimble and skilful use of the hands, as when a horse is called clever at his fences. Sir Thomas Browne listed the word among terms of common use in Norfolk but no general reception in English. A link with Old English gleaw, wise, has also been suggested through Scots gleg. The earliest dictionary use for mental quickness comes from Addison in 1716.
britannica-1911-clinker: Clinker is defined in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, with two groups of senses. In the first, from an old Dutch word tied to ringing, it means a hard paving brick or a brick with a glassy skin. It also means the hard waste left when coal burns in a grate or furnace, and a fused mass of lava. In the second sense, from a word for fastening, it names a way of building boats whose planks overlap, unlike carvel-built boats whose planks sit flush.
britannica-1911-cloister:
Cloister, from the Latin claustrum, now names the four-sided enclosure with covered ambulatories usually attached to conventual and cathedral churches, and sometimes to colleges. Originally the word signified the entire monastery, a sense frequent in earlier English literature and still used in poetry. The Latin word first denoted only the enclosing wall of a religious house. It then came to cover the whole building enclosed within that wall, as German Kloster still does.

In the common modern sense the cloister is the quadrilateral area round which the principal buildings are ranged. A covered way runs all round it, giving communication between the centres of ecclesiastical life without exposure to weather. Under the Benedictine arrangement, generally adopted in the West, the church forms one side. The refectory occupies the side opposite the church, so that worshippers suffer least annoyance from noise or smells at meals.
britannica-1911-clothier:
Clothier is a manufacturer of cloth, or a dealer who sells either the cloth itself or made-up clothing, the entry states. Those two trades, making and selling, share the one occupational name here. A dealer may sell the raw fabric to buyers, or sell garments already made up from it. No place, date or person is attached to the term in this notice, which is a trade definition only.

American use has shifted with time, and the entry records that shift as its second fact. In the United States the word formerly applied only to those who dressed or fulled cloth during manufacture. Fulling, the cleansing and thickening of woven cloth, was thus the clothier's work there. Now the word is used in the general sense given above, for makers and sellers alike, and the older narrow American sense has faded.
britannica-1911-clover:
Clover, in botany, is the English name for plants of the genus Trifolium, from Latin words for three and a leaf, after its three leaflets. Trefoil is its popular name, and it belongs to the family Leguminosae, with about three hundred species. Most species live in north temperate regions, though some grow on mountains in the tropics. The plants are small herbs with heads or dense spikes of small red, purple, white or rarely yellow flowers.

Eighteen species are native in Britain, and several are extensively cultivated as fodder plants, with red or purple clover the most widely grown. Sown alone or mixed with rye grass, it long formed the staple crop for soiling cattle. Its power to shoot again after repeated mowings and its bulk entitled it to that preference. Except on certain rich calcareous clay soils it has now become an exceedingly precarious crop.
britannica-1911-coco-de-mer:
Coco de Mer, also called the double coco-nut, is the subject of a short 1911 Britannica article. It is a palm, named in Latin Lodoicea Sechellarum. It is native to the Seychelles Islands. The male and female flowers grow on distinct plants, in huge fleshy spikes.

The fruits are among the largest known. They take ten years to ripen. A fleshy and fibrous coat wraps a hard, nut-like part. That part is most often two-lobed, like a large double coco-nut. The contents of the nut can be eaten, as with the coco-nut. Empty fruits, after the seed has sprouted, are found floating in the Indian Ocean. They were known long before the palm itself was found. That mystery gave rise to many tales of where they came from.
britannica-1911-codrington-christopher:
Christopher Codrington (1668–1710) was a British soldier and colonial governor, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his promise. He was born in Barbados in the West Indies in 1668. His father was captain general of the Leeward Isles before him. The young Codrington was educated at Christ Church, Oxford.

He was elected a fellow of All Souls College at Oxford. He then served with the British forces in Flanders. In 1695 he was rewarded with a captaincy in the Guards. That year he attended King William the Third on a visit to Oxford. In the absence of the public orator, Codrington was chosen to deliver the university oration. In 1697 his father died, and he succeeded to the command of the Leeward Isles. In 1703 he led a British expedition against Guadeloupe that failed.
britannica-1911-coffer:
Coffer, in building terms, is a sunk panel in a ceiling or vault. The word comes through French from a Latin term for a basket. It also names a casket or chest for jewels and rich goods. Large coffers held clothes instead. Form and use thus split in two.

One thread of the entry treats carved work. Marriage coffers in Italy stood out for rich carving and gilding. Great artists at times painted them. That fact lifts a storage chest into the rank of art. The entry stays short, with no list of makers or dates. A reader gains the two senses of the word and one note on Italian craft. The panel sense belongs to building, the chest sense to the home.
britannica-1911-colchester:
Colchester is a market town and river port in Essex, England, 52 miles north-east of London by rail. Its people numbered 38,373 in 1901. It stands on the river Colne, twelve miles from the open sea. Old buildings fill the town with points of note. First among them is the ruined keep of the castle.

That keep is the largest of its kind in England. It covers near twice the ground of the White Tower in London. Kings William I or William II raised it. Roman stone from the old town went into its walls. The Essex Archaeological Society keeps its museum there, rich in Roman finds. Ruins of Saint Botolph's priory add a second Norman sight. The entry also traces the borough's early growth. Domesday Book names 276 burgesses there. Roman walls and finds mark the site throughout.
britannica-1911-colden-cadwallader:
Cadwallader Colden is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Duns, Scotland, on the seventeenth of February 1688, he was a doctor and a colonial officer in America. He took his degree at Edinburgh in 1705 and crossed the ocean in 1708.

The article follows his long career in New York. After ten years of practice in Philadelphia he moved to New York. He became the first surveyor general of the colony in 1718. From 1761 till his death he held the post of lieutenant governor. As acting governor in 1765 he faced the fury over the Stamp Act. A mob burned him in effigy in his own coach. In science he was known for plant study and for a history of the Five Nations, printed in 1727.
britannica-1911-coldwater:
Coldwater is the subject of a city entry in the 1911 Britannica. The city lies in Michigan in the United States. It is the county seat of Branch county there. It stands on a stream that links small lakes near by. Counts are given across four census years in the entry. The count in 1910 was just under six thousand souls. A rail line of a lake shore road serves the city. A state school and home for children stands there.

That home took in children under twelve in need. The city sits in a fine farming region round it. Flour and grist mills lead its trades by weight. Works make cement, lumber, furniture, and shoes as well. The city owns and runs its water and light plants. It was settled in 1829 and named in 1833.
britannica-1911-collins-william-painter:
William Collins (1787–1847) was an English painter born in London, son of an Irish picture dealer and man of letters. He studied under Etty in 1807. In 1809 he showed his first works of note, Boys at Breakfast and Boys with a Bird's Nest. He became an associate of the Royal Academy in 1815 and a full member in 1820.

For sixteen years he showed work without pause. His fishermen, shrimp-catchers, boats and nets won wide love. His rustic children pleased most of all. On Wilkie's advice he went abroad and spent two years in Italy. In 1840 he became librarian to the Academy and first tried history painting. In 1842 he went back to his early themes. His last years brought his greatest fame. The entry calls him a good colourist and a fine draughtsman.
britannica-1911-commandeer: Commandeer is defined in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from the Dutch of South Africa, from a verb meaning to command. In its proper sense it means to force a man to do military duty in the field, above all in the Boer republics. It also means to seize goods for the needs of an army. From that use it spread to mean any high-handed seizure of goods for other ends.
britannica-1911-commander: Commander is a rank in the British navy. It is the second grade of captains in that service. A commander has charge of a small vessel, or is second in command of a large one. A staff commander is put in charge of the steering of a large ship. He ranks above a navigating lieutenant. In the navy of the United States, the officer next in rank to a captain has borne the name commander since 1838.
britannica-1911-commissioner:
Commissioner is an office article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a title used across British government. In general, a commissioner is an officer picked to do a set task, or a member of a commission. The title fits members of standing boards, such as the civil service and income tax boards. It also fits the heads of departments, such as customs.

In some British lands in Africa and the Pacific, the head of government is styled high commissioner. In India, a commissioner is the chief officer of a division made up of several districts. He stands midway between the local government and the district officer. The post is found in most provinces but not in Madras. There a board of revenue does the same work. The entry maps how one title shifts its weight from place to place.
britannica-1911-composite-order: The Composite order is a style of column in classical building. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica calls it a blend of the Ionic and Corinthian orders. Its mark sits in the capital, the carved column top. A double row of acanthus leaves, like those on a Corinthian capital, sits below the Ionic scrolls. Richer carved Ionic capitals had shown up earlier in the Erechtheum at Athens. The first known Composite capital stands on the arch of Titus at Rome. The beam work above was taken from the Corinthian order.
britannica-1911-condenser:
Condenser is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name is given to many kinds of apparatus that share one aim. Each gathers matter into a smaller space, or makes a force stronger. In chemistry the word names the device that cools a vapour back into a liquid.

The article sends readers to other entries for each trade's form of the tool. One form cools the spent steam of a steam engine. In woollen making, a condenser does a key step in working the wool. The word also tags pumps and syringes that squeeze air or vapour. In optics a condenser is a lens, or a set of lenses, that gathers light rays to a point for a lantern or microscope. In the science of static charge, it is a device for storing up a charge.
britannica-1911-connecticut-river:
Connecticut River is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a stream of New England. It rises in Connecticut Lake in north New Hampshire state. Its course runs about 345 miles to Long Island Sound. The basin it drains covers 11,085 square miles of land.

It forms the border between Vermont and New Hampshire as it flows south. Then it crosses Massachusetts and Connecticut on its way to the sea. The Farmington is named as its chief branch stream in the text. In its upper course the banks are wooded and the bed narrow. The fall there runs from fifteen to thirty-four feet a mile. In the south the vale broadens into rich farm land.
britannica-1911-cooper-alexander:
Alexander Cooper (died 1660) was an English miniature painter whose works are of great rarity. His chief works form a series of the king and queen of Bohemia and their children. Those pieces belong to the German emperor. Other fine portraits belong to the queen of Holland and to the king of Sweden. He was brother to Samuel Cooper, the famed miniaturist.

Which brother was the elder is not known for sure. Swedish sources put his birth in 1605, four years before Samuel, on slight proof. He lived in Holland before he came to Sweden in 1646. There he entered Queen Christina's service as her miniature painter. He held that post until she gave up the crown in 1654. Two years later he worked in Denmark for Christian IV. In 1657 he was back in Stockholm, where he died early in the next decade.
britannica-1911-cooper-peter:
Peter Cooper (1791–1883) was an American manufacturer, inventor and philanthropist born in New York city on 12 February 1791. His grandfathers and his father all served in the War of Independence. He had next to no schooling. He worked with his father at hat-making, brewing and brick-making in turn. At seventeen he was set to a coach-builder in New York.

On coming of age he made machines for shearing cloth at Hempstead. Three years later he set up in that trade for himself. He held the sole right to make such gear in New York state. The War of 1812 fattened the business, and peace thinned it. He turned to furniture, then to groceries for a short spell. Next came a glue and isinglass factory that ran for twenty-one years in Manhattan. His name clings most to the school he founded.
britannica-1911-cooper-thomas-writer:
Thomas Cooper (1805–1892) was an English Chartist and writer, son of a working dyer, born at Leicester on 20 March 1805. His mother ran a dyeing and box-making trade at Gainsborough after his father's death. The boy was set to a shoemaker. A hunger for knowledge drove him to Greek, Latin and Hebrew in his spare time. In 1827 he left cobbling to teach school.

Preaching and newspaper work followed, at Lincoln and then in London. In 1840 he joined the Leicestershire Mercury staff. His backing of the Chartists cost him that post. In 1841 he edited a Chartist journal instead. He rose to lead the extreme wing of the movement. For urging on the strike of 1842 he spent two years in Stafford gaol. There he wrote The Purgatory of Suicides, an epic in ten books. Later years turned to teaching and a sharp change of belief.
britannica-1911-cope-edward-drinker:
Edward Drinker Cope (1840–1897) was an American palaeontologist born in Philadelphia on 28 July 1840. His family came from Wiltshire and crossed the Atlantic about 1687. Natural history drew him at an early age. In 1859 he sent a paper on the Salamandridae to the Academy of Natural Sciences at Philadelphia. He studied in part at the University of Pennsylvania.

After more study and travel in Europe he became curator of that academy in 1865. He held the post until 1873. He taught natural science at Haverford College from 1864 to 1867. In 1889 he took the chair of geology and palaeontology at Pennsylvania. Fossil vertebrates of America held his chief zeal. He dug in Kansas, Wyoming and Colorado from 1871 to 1877. In time he made known at least 600 species new to science. He died in Philadelphia on 12 April 1897.
britannica-1911-copper:
Copper, symbol Cu, is a metal known and used by mankind from the most remote ages. Its alloy with tin, bronze, was the first metal compound in common use. That vast use gave a whole age its name, the Bronze Age. Greeks and Romans used one word for the metal and its alloys alike. Rome drew its chief supply from Cyprus, and the name cuprum grew from that source.

The metal shows a brilliant red colour of its own. A fresh fracture of the pure metal takes a pink or yellow tinge. With cuprous oxide in it the hue turns purple. Weight for its bulk runs near 8.9 times that of water. Ore dressing, smelting and refining fill great parts of it. One method wets broken ore in heaps with a mix of salts. The sheer scale marks it as a full trade treatise.
britannica-1911-coquet-river:
Coquet, a river of Northumberland in England, gets a course entry in the 1911 Britannica. It drains a fair valley about 40 miles long and rises in the Cheviot Hills. Winding east, it passes Harbottle, where Stone Age relics are seen. At Holystone, Bishop Paulinus is said to have baptized a great body of Northumbrians in the year 627.

Border forts of the middle ages crown the hills of the upper dale. The river dashes through a narrow gully called the Thrum, then passes Brinkburn priory, whose Norman church was restored in 1858. At Warkworth, with its fine castle, the dale stays rich in woods. The mouth lies in Alnwick Bay, with the port of Amble on the south bank, and salmon and trout draw anglers.
britannica-1911-coriander:
Coriander, the fruit of a plant grown for spice, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. The plant is native to the south of Europe and Asia Minor. It is grown in the south of England, where it also runs wild. Its name comes from a Greek word for a bug, from its rank smell when fresh.

The plant has a slim hollow stem one to two feet high, with fine cut leaves. Its small blooms are pink or whitish, set in flat heads. The round fruit has five faint ridges, and its halves do not part with ease. In medicine it serves as a scented aid to digestion. Its sharp taste makes it a pet part of hot curries and sauces, sweets, and drinks.
britannica-1911-cornelius-carl-august-pe:
Carl August Peter Cornelius (1824-1874) was a German musician and poet, and his life is traced in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Mainz, he was the son of an actor, the grandson of an engraver, and the nephew of a painter. As a boy he liked languages, but he also learned to sing and to play the violin.

The entry follows his brief start on the stage, his turn to music, and his hard study of theory in Berlin under Siegfried Wilhelm Dehn. It notes early trios, sonatas, a Mass, and French poem translations. It also covers his move to Weimar in 1852 and his link with Liszt.
britannica-1911-coroner:
Coroner is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on an old post in English law. Coke says the name comes from keeper of the pleas of the crown. When the post began is a point of much doubt in study. Some new writers date it from the year 1194 at first.

One writer has shown it must have lived before that date, though. The post was always filled by vote of the county freeholders. They met in county court to pick the man for the post. A statute of Westminster set a bar for who could serve. None but lawful, discreet knights were to be picked for it. One man was in fact removed for too small an estate.
britannica-1911-cover:
Cover, from a French word for covering, names that which hides, shuts in or hides from view. A lid to a box or vessel bears the name. So does the binding of a book or the wrapper of a parcel. As a hunting term it names the wood or brush that shelters game. Trade gives the word a sharper and more set sense.

It is a deposit lodged with a broker to keep him from loss if stocks fall against his client. The client must pay the difference if he can, and the deposit guards that gap. A court case of 1898 gives that sense in set words. Men who wish to cap their risk at a small sum use the mode most. Outside brokers, not members of the Exchange, run most of that trade in England.
britannica-1911-cracker:
Cracker is a word built on crack, a term for a sharp break or snap. It names, first, a firework made to pop with report after report. The piece jumps at each bang as it lies on the ground. It names, second, a roll of coloured paper with a snap strip inside. Sweets, cheap trinkets and paper caps fill that roll for party use.

Third, it names a thin, crisp biscuit. In America the word serves as the general name for a biscuit of any kind. A fourth sense carries a sting in the southern states of America. There cracker is a term of scorn for the poor or mean whites, most of all in Georgia and Florida. That use is old and runs back to the Revolution. Men trace it to the cracked corn that formed the staple food of that class.
britannica-1911-cratippus-philosopher:
Cratippus of Mitylene, a Peripatetic philosopher of the first century before Christ, was a contemporary of Cicero. He taught Cicero's son at Athens in his school. Cicero praises him in the De officiis as the greatest man of his school. Pompey counted him as a friend as well. After the battle of Pharsalia he shared Pompey's flight from the field.

Men said his aim in that flight was to sway Pompey to trust in providence. Brutus heard his lectures at Athens after the killing of Caesar. One work is laid to his name, a treatise on divination. In 44 before Christ the Areopagus asked him to head the school in place of Andronicus of Rhodes. Motion, sense and appetite, he held, cannot live apart from the body. Thought gains its peak when most free of the body's curb.
britannica-1911-credit-foncier:
The Crédit Foncier was a French body that lent money on mortgage of real property. It was created by a government decree of 28 February 1852. Its loans carried low interest, ran for long terms, and were repaid by yearly payments that included capital. It began in Paris as the Banque Foncière de Paris with a capital of 25,000,000 francs. Sister bodies at Nevers and Marseilles soon merged into it.

Under the name Crédit Foncier de France its capital rose, and the state named its governor and two deputies. It could issue bonds repayable in fifty or sixty years, some carrying prizes. Loans could not pass half the worth of the mortgaged property. It also lent to local bodies, and its charter was renewed in 1881 for ninety-nine years. A linked Crédit Agricole failed after heavy loans to Egypt, and the bank suffered with it.
britannica-1911-crofter:
A crofter is a tenant who rents and works a small holding of land, a use strongest in the Highlands and islands of Scotland. The word croft first meant an enclosed field. The Crofters' Holdings Act of 1886 fixes the legal sense. A crofter there is a tenant who lives on his holding, in a crofting parish, at a rent of not more than thirty pounds a year. Clearances in the 1800s stripped many tenants of such holdings.

Those clearances, made against what tenants claimed was an implied security of tenure, stirred long agitation. Royal commissions studied the grievances, and laws followed in some number. The entry judges that the Act of 1886, with its later amending acts, markedly improved the crofters' condition. Much of the agitation had died out by the time of writing. For the history of the crofter laws the entry sends readers to the article on Scotland.
britannica-1911-cromer:
Cromer is a watering-place in the northern division of Norfolk, England, 139 miles north-east of London by rail. Its urban district held 3,781 people in 1901. The town stands on high cliffs and has often suffered from the ravages of the sea. A wall and esplanade run along the cliff foot, with a fine stretch of sandy beach and a short pier. The church of St Peter and St Paul is Perpendicular, with a lofty tower.

On a three-acre site stands the convalescent home of the Norfolk and Norwich hospital, and the town has an excellent golf course. Herring, cod, lobster, and crab fisheries are prosecuted from the town. The village of Sheringham, lying to the west, also draws visitors. A so-called Roman camp on a height above the sea is, the entry notes, actually a modern beacon.
britannica-1911-cromwell-oliver:
Oliver Cromwell (1599–1658), lord protector of England, was the fifth and only surviving son of Robert Cromwell of Huntingdon. His grandfather was Sir Henry Cromwell of Hinchinbrook, and his line ran back to a nephew of Thomas Cromwell, Henry VIII's minister. Born on 25 April 1599, he was schooled under the puritan Dr Thomas Beard at Huntingdon. In 1616 he entered Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge. He married Elizabeth Bourchier in 1620 and settled at Huntingdon.

In 1628 Cromwell entered parliament for Huntingdon and spoke at once for puritan doctrine. The entry, a full-scale biography, follows him from those beginnings through the wars and governments of the next thirty years. It ends with his rule as lord protector. A detailed bibliography, arranged by period and topic, closes the long text. Works listed cover the legal side of his rule, the navy, the church, foreign relations, and the mission of Menasseh Ben Israel.
britannica-1911-cross-river:
Cross River is a river of West Africa, more than 500 miles long. It rises in the mountains of Cameroon and flows first north-west. A series of rapids marks its course, and below them the river is navigable for shallow-draught boats. At its most northern point it turns south-west and then south. It enters the Gulf of Guinea through the Calabar estuary.

The Calabar river runs parallel to the Cross, ten to twenty miles east of it, and the town of Calabar stands near its mouth. Cross, Calabar, Kwa, and other streams from the Cameroon Mountains form a large delta together. The Calabar and Kwa lie wholly within the British protectorate of Southern Nigeria. So does the Cross from its mouth up to the rapids. The upper course of the river lay in German territory.
britannica-1911-cross-springer: Cross springer is a term in architecture for the block from which the diagonal ribs of a vault spring or start. The top of that block carries its own name, the skewback. The hosted entry is a single sentence and gives no more than that definition and cross-reference. For the wider subject it sends the reader to the article on the arch. Nothing else, no history, use, or example, is stated in the entry as hosted.
britannica-1911-crowe-sir-joseph-archer:
Sir Joseph Archer Crowe (1828–1896) was an English consular official and art critic, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his two careers. He was born in London on the twenty fifth of October 1828. His father, Eyre Crowe, was a noted figure in the press world. The young Crowe showed an early gift for painting.

He entered the studio of Delaroche in Paris, where his father served a London paper. In the Crimean War he reported for the Illustrated London News. In the Austro Italian War he represented The Times from Vienna. He then served as British consul general at Leipzig from 1860 to 1872. A post at Düsseldorf followed, until 1880. He then became a commercial attaché, first in Berlin and then in Paris. In 1889 he acted as plenipotentiary, as the entry goes on to tell.
britannica-1911-crozier:
Crozier, or pastoral staff, is one of the marks of a bishop, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a short entry. The staff has a crooked, hooked head and is borne by bishops and archbishops alike. It most likely derives from the lituus, the curved staff of the Roman augurs. 

The word itself comes through old French and medieval Latin terms for the bearer of the bishop's crook. An older English form was confused in speech with the word cross, and the staff was called the crozier staff before the plain name crozier took hold in the early fifteen hundreds.
britannica-1911-cruden-alexander:
Alexander Cruden is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Cruden was the author of the famous concordance to the English Bible. He was born at Aberdeen in 1701 and educated at its grammar school and Marischal College. He meant to enter the ministry and took a master's degree.

A disappointment in love soon after disturbed his mind. After a term of confinement he recovered and moved to London. He worked as a private tutor at Eton Hall and at Ware. For some years he also served as a corrector for the press. In 1729 the earl of Derby employed him as reader and secretary. The entry traces a scholar whose life was marked by both brilliance and breakdown. His concordance, a full index of the Bible's words, outlived all his troubles.
britannica-1911-csoma-de-koros-alexander:
Alexander Csoma de Körös (about 1790–1842) was a Hungarian traveller and philologist born at Körös in Transylvania, of a noble family sunk in poverty. Educated at Nagy-Enyed and Göttingen, he split his study between medicine and Oriental languages. His youthful dream was to find the origin of his countrymen. In 1820, backed by a friend's promise of 100 florins a year, he set out for the East. He passed through Egypt and reached Tibet.

In Tibet Csoma spent four years in a Buddhist monastery, studying the language and its sacred books. The search for Hungarian origins gained nothing there, to his disappointment. In Bengal the Asiatic Society employed him for its Tibetan library of over 1,000 volumes. His Tibetan dictionary and grammar appeared at Calcutta in 1834, with an analysis of the Kah-Gyur. Early in 1842 he set out again on the quest. He died at Darjiling on 11 April 1842.
britannica-1911-cucumber:
The cucumber, Cucumis sativus, is a creeping plant of the order Cucurbitaceae, grown across the world. It likely began in northern India, where it may have been grown for three thousand years. It spread west to Europe and was known to the ancient Greeks. China received it two hundred years before the Christian era. The plant is an annual with a rough trailing stem, hairy lobed leaves, and branched tendrils for climbing.

Male and female flowers grow on the same plant, the female known by the swollen ovary below the bloom. That ovary becomes the fruit without fertilization. The entry sorts the many garden kinds into forcing and field varieties. Long pages give the hot-bed craft in full detail. A closing note describes a way of turning the pulp to a drink inside the fruit, and names the squirting cucumber as the source of the drug elaterium.
britannica-1911-cumberland-river:
Cumberland River is a great stream of the United States described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a south branch of the Ohio river. It rises in the high part of the Cumberland plateau in south-east Kentucky. After a winding course of six hundred and eighty-eight miles through Kentucky and Tennessee it flows into the Ohio near Smithland.

Its basin drains more than eighteen thousand square miles. Light steamers can work up it for about five hundred miles in good water, and to Nashville all the year round. At the Great Falls in Kentucky it drops more than sixty feet at a leap. Above the falls it is a mountain stream, small in dry months. It then runs in rapids through a fine gorge with cliffs three or four hundred feet high. Below Nashville it runs four or five hundred feet wide, with banks of rich soil.
britannica-1911-cunningham-alexander:
Alexander Cunningham was born about 1655 and died in 1730, a Scottish scholar. The 1911 Britannica life calls him a scholar of the classics and a critic. He was born in Ayrshire, but scant facts survive on his quiet life. He most likely finished his studies at Leiden or at Utrecht. He tutored the son of the first duke of Queensberry in youth.

Through that duke he won the chair of civil law at Edinburgh. In 1710 the town magistrates set his appointment at nought in a row. They named a new professor in his place, in spite of his tenure. Cunningham left for the Hague and lived there till his death. He is chiefly known for his edition of Horace in 1721.
britannica-1911-deer:
Deer are the members of the Cervidae family, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica defines them. The word first meant a wild animal in old English and in kin tongues. It then narrowed to the two British kinds, the red deer and the fallow deer. Now it covers all members of the family, both living kinds and most extinct kinds as well.

In brief, deer are set apart by a short list of traits in the text. Males bear antlers, or, when antlers are absent, the upper canine teeth are large and sabre like. The side bones of the foot are cut down to their lower ends alone in living kinds. Antlers rest on a pair of solid bony stems that rise from the skull. The piece then points the reader to full accounts of antlers and of the larger groups to which deer belong in the scheme of animal life.
britannica-1911-demeter:
Demeter, in Greek mythology, was a daughter of Cronus and Rhea and a sister of Zeus, goddess of agriculture and civilized life. Her name is read as grain-mother or as earth-mother. She is rare in Homer and not counted among the Olympian gods. The central fact of her cult is the story of her daughter Persephone, carried off by Hades from the Nysian plain with Zeus's connivance.

Demeter wandered the earth seeking her daughter, learned the truth from Helios, and came in an old woman's shape to Celeus at Eleusis. In her wrath she laid a great dearth on the earth until Zeus let Persephone spend two-thirds of the year above ground. Before leaving, she taught the rulers of Eleusis agriculture and her rites, the mysteries that promised a future life.
britannica-1911-ellsworth-oliver:
Ellsworth, Oliver (1745–1807), was an American statesman and jurist born at Windsor, Connecticut, on 29 April 1745. The hosted text breaks off mid-sentence, so only the opening of the article survives here. He studied at Yale and Princeton, graduating from Princeton in 1766. After a year of theology he turned to law and began to practise at Hartford in 1771.

From 1777 to 1785 Ellsworth was state's attorney for Hartford county, and he won great success at the bar, amassing a large fortune for his day. He represented Windsor in the general assembly of Connecticut from 1773 to 1775. In the latter year he joined the important commission called the Pay Table, which watched over the colony's spending. The hosted text ends at that point, mid-sentence, and the rest of his career is not present in the record.
britannica-1911-elmsley-peter:
Elmsley, Peter (1773–1825), was an English classical scholar educated at Westminster and Christ Church, Oxford. Having inherited a fortune from his uncle, a well-known bookseller, he gave himself to the study of classical authors and manuscripts. In 1798 he was appointed to the chapelry of Little Horkesley in Essex, which he held until his death. He travelled widely in France and Italy.

In the winter of 1818 Elmsley examined the manuscripts in the Laurentian library at Florence. In 1819 he was commissioned, with Sir Humphry Davy, to decipher the papyri found at Herculaneum, but the results proved insignificant. In 1823 he became principal of St Alban's Hall, Oxford, and Camden professor of ancient history. He died at Oxford on 8 March 1825. The entry remembers him chiefly for collating the manuscripts of the Greek tragedians. He edited plays and scholia of Sophocles and Euripides.
britannica-1911-emmons-ebenezer:
Emmons, Ebenezer (1800–1863), was an American geologist born at Middlefield, Massachusetts, on 16 May 1800. He studied medicine at Albany and practised for some years in Berkshire county. In 1824 he helped Professor Chester Dewey prepare a geological map of Berkshire county.

Emmons joined the Geological Survey of New York in 1836 and in 1842 grouped the local strata into the Taconic and the overlying New York systems. In 1844 he first gained fossils in his Taconic system, unlike all then-known Palaeozoic forms, and they were taken to represent the oldest group of life. Jules Marcou called him the founder of American palaeozoic stratigraphy. Later opinion, the entry notes, went against his Taconic system as a whole, since its fauna proved to cover only the lower part of Sedgwick's Cambrian. Emmons was state geologist of North Carolina from 1851 to 1860 and died at Brunswick in that state on 1 October 1863.
britannica-1911-ems-river:
Ems is a river of Germany, rising on the south slope of the Teutoburger Wald at 358 feet and flowing north-west and north through Westphalia and Hanover. The hosted file holds several articles together; this entry is the river article within it. It reaches the east side of the Dollart, just south of Emden, and its length is 200 miles. Past the Dollart the stream splits around the island of Borkum to the North Sea.

Between 1892 and 1899 the river was canalized along its right bank for 43 miles. As part of the same plan, the Dortmund-Ems Canal was dug to link the river at Münster with Herne in the Westphalian coal-field. A huge lift carries vessels over a 46-foot gap between two branches. The canal runs 169 miles, was built for boats up to 220 feet and 750 tons, and cost £3,728,750 in all.
britannica-1911-erskine-ebenezer:
Erskine, Ebenezer (1680–1754), was a Scottish divine and the chief founder of the Secession Church, born on 22 June 1680, most likely at Dryburgh in Berwickshire. His father Henry, a minister ejected in 1662, later held the parish of Chirnside. Ebenezer studied at Edinburgh and became minister of Portmoak in Kinross-shire. There he stayed twenty-eight years before moving to the West Church, Stirling, in 1731.

A sermon he preached against lay patronage in 1733 brought fresh charges, and the general assembly confirmed his rebuke. In November that year he and three fellow ministers, Wilson, Moncrieff, and Fisher, were suspended. They protested and formed a separate court, the associate presbytery. Erskine joined the “burgher” side when the body split in 1747 and became its professor of theology. He preached at Stirling until his death on 2 June 1754.
britannica-1911-eschweiler: Eschweiler is a town of Germany in the Prussian Rhine province, on the river Inde. It lies about eight miles from Aix la Chapelle, on two rail lines. Its people numbered twenty thousand six hundred forty three in nineteen o five. The town has one Protestant church and four Roman Catholic churches. It also has a gymnasium school and an orphanage. Iron and steel goods are made there in large amounts. Other trades include zinc wares, tanning, distilling, and brewing. Rich coal mines lie in the country round the town.
britannica-1911-esher:
Esher is a township in Surrey in England, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies by rail south-west of London, on high ground above the river Mole, three miles from where that stream joins the Thames. The wider urban district held 9,489 people in 1901. The whole place is in large part a home district for folk who work in town.

To the north-west lie the grounds of Esher Place. Of the great house built by Bishop Waynflete about 1450, in which Cardinal Wolsey lodged for some weeks after his fall in 1529, the gatehouse alone stands. It is known as Wolsey's Tower. To the south stands Claremont Palace, built by Lord Clive in 1769. Princess Charlotte lived there and died there in 1817. The ex-king of the French, Louis Philippe, lived there from 1848 to his death. Sandown Park, by the station, holds great race meetings.
britannica-1911-esker:
Esker, a local Irish name for long mounds of ice age gravel, is explained in a 1911 Britannica article. In Sweden the same forms are called asar. They wind from side to side across land once covered by ice. They seem to have been formed by streams that ran in or under the ice sheet.

When large streams cut tunnels in the ice, the tunnels can fill in part with wash. When the ice melts, those filled paths stand out as long ridges of gravel and sand. Like ridges may form in cuts through the ice from top to base. The piece notes that streams on top of the ice are too swift to drop much load. Eskers are set apart from kames.
britannica-1911-espalier: Espalier, a frame for training fruit trees and climbers, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes through French from an Italian term for a thing to rest the shoulder against. An espalier is a lattice or row of stakes, first made about shoulder high. Fruit trees, shrubs, roses, and creepers are tied to it and trained flat.
britannica-1911-ether:
Ether, (C2H5)2O, the Aether of pharmacy, is a colourless, volatile and highly inflammable liquid. It boils at 35 degrees and freezes near minus 117 degrees. It dissolves in ten parts of water and mixes with alcohol in all proportions. Its vapour mixed with air or oxygen is violently explosive. Making ether from sulphuric acid and alcohol was known by about the 13th century. Frobenius named the drug in 1730, and Valentine Rose showed around 1800 that it held no sulphur.

Manufacture distils five parts of 90 per cent alcohol with nine parts of concentrated sulphuric acid at 140 to 145 degrees. A steady stream of alcohol feeds the still, and lime and calcium chloride purify the distillate. Williamson explained the reaction in 1850. Sprayed on skin, ether evaporates fast and chills the part into local numbness.
britannica-1911-ewing-alexander:
Alexander Ewing, Scottish divine born in Aberdeen on 25 March 1814, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came of an old Highland family. In October 1838 he was admitted to deacon orders. After a return from Italy he took charge of the Episcopal flock at Forres. He was ordained a presbyter in the autumn of 1841.

In 1846 voters picked him as first bishop of the newly restored diocese of Argyll and the Isles. He discharged that post till his death on 22 May 1873. Oxford gave him a high degree in 1851. A frail body hampered him all his life. Yet he worked in a spirit of bright cheer at all times. Charm of manner and wide sympathy raised him to a leading place. In debate on faith he pled for broad tolerance.
britannica-1911-exchequer:
The hosted text of the Exchequer article opens part-way through the subject, its first portion not present. What stands here treats the medieval machinery of the king's revenue. Grants from chancery, called first contrabrevia and later originalia, fixed the rents and fines owed. Estreats from the justices settled the profits of justice. The court sat first at Winchester, where the treasury was, then usually at Westminster.

The Angevin exchequer described by Richard the Treasurer stayed the model throughout. Under Henry II the great officers already attended by deputy. In Henry III's reign the chancellor's clerk gained the title chancellor of the exchequer. The ordinance of 1323 split the two remembrancers' work. The king's remembrancer charged the casual revenue, and the lord treasurer's chased the fixed. By the end of the 14th century three offices had hardened into separate departments. The article runs on to later reforms and authorities.
britannica-1911-faber:
Faber, the pencil house of Nuremberg, is traced in a trade entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Kaspar Faber founded the work at Stein in the year 1760. His son and then his grandson kept the firm in the family. In time it fell to Johann Lothar von Faber, the founder's great-grandson. Some twenty hands then worked the shop in the old slow way.

French crayons had cut the whole Nuremberg trade to a low ebb. Johann brought in new machines and sharp ways of work and time. His plant rose to the best of its kind in the land. Shops in New York, Paris, London, and Berlin spread his name. In 1856 he won sole rights to Siberian graphite mines in full. Paints, inks, slates, and fine tools joined the pencil line.
britannica-1911-fall-river:
Fall River is a city in the state of Massachusetts, set on a bay at the mouth of a river south of Boston. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its counts at four dates, which show fast growth across twenty years. It ranked as the third city of the state in size.

The entry dwells on who its folk were. Near half of the town count was born abroad, and most of the rest had a parent born abroad. French folk from Canada formed the largest bloc, then folk from England, Ireland, and other lands. Rail and boat lines link the city to great ports, and the famed Fall River Line boat run serves those who ride between New York and Boston. Its port is large, deep, and easy to reach.
britannica-1911-fallow-deer:
Fallow deer is a mid sized deer known for its flat branched horns. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its coat, range, and kin. Its name sets it apart as the dun deer beside the red. Bucks bear broad palmed antlers with no low tine.

The coat shows white spots in summer and turns plain in winter. The tail is long, black above and white below. Parks in Britain keep the kind in a half tame state. Wild herds live in west Asia, north Africa, and south Europe. Bucks and does live apart outside the rut. Does drop one to three fawns at a birth. The deer love horse chestnuts and knock branches to get them. A huge fossil kin, the Irish elk, may belong to the same line.
britannica-1911-farah-river: Farah is a very short place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a river in Afghanistan that rises on the south slopes of a range by Herat. The river flows south west for about two hundred miles to a salt lake basin. At the town of Farah it runs wide but shallow in the dry season, with a clear and swift stream. In flood it can block all travel for weeks. Its lower valley is rich and well farmed.
britannica-1911-farnese-alexander:
Alexander Farnese (1545–1592), duke of Parma, was Spain's governor-general of the Netherlands under Philip II. He was born at Rome on 27 August 1545. His father was Ottavio Farnese, and his mother Margaret of Austria, a natural daughter of Charles V. Raised partly in Spain with Don Carlos and Don John of Austria, he married Maria of Portugal at Brussels in 1565. He fought with distinction under Don John at Lepanto in 1571.

Sent to the Netherlands in autumn 1577 with reinforcements, he won Gemblours in 1578 by a prompt decision. On Don John's death he took the government himself. He played Catholic against Protestant and Walloon against Fleming with persuasion and bribery. The treaty of Arras in January 1579 brought the Walloon provinces back to the king. He died at Arras on 3 December 1592, feeling his services ill repaid. His son Ranuccio succeeded him.
britannica-1911-father:
Father means the begetter of a child, the male parent. The word is common to the Teutonic languages and, like mother, brother, son, sister and daughter, appears in most Indo-European tongues. Its Old English form is faeder, matched by German Vater, Dutch vader, Greek pater and Latin pater. It also serves for remoter male ancestors, and for ancestors in general.

Transferred uses fill much of the entry, and many are religious. God is Father of Jesus Christ and Creator, the orthodox name for the First Person of the Trinity. Early Christian writers are the Fathers of the Church, a spiritual parent is a father, and the pope is the Holy Father. Founders are fathers too, from the Pilgrim Fathers to the Father of the House, the longest-serving member of parliament.
britannica-1911-feather:
Feather is a horny outgrowth of the skin of birds, matching the scale of the reptile. Feathers form the body-covering of birds without exception. By that trait alone birds can be told from all other animals. A perfect feather has a long tapering rod fringed on both sides by slender rods called barbs. Those barbs form the vane. The axis divides into a hollow quill set in the skin and a solid shaft.

The long article works through feather structure in fine detail, with many figures. It treats kinds of feathers, their colours, moulting and growth. It also explains the pattern in which feathers are set on the body. Later sections turn to human uses. Soft feathers and down are prepared for stuffing. Quills served for writing, the main writing tool from the sixth century until steel pens arrived.
britannica-1911-fender:
Fender, a metal guard for a fireplace, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its name comes from its work as a defence for the hearth. When the open hearth gave way to the closed grate, the fender was devised for smaller fireplaces. It also guards against cinders dropping on the wooden floor, now much nearer the fire.

Fenders are usually of steel, brass, or iron, solid or pierced with openings. Brass fenders of the late 1700s and early 1800s are by far the most elegant and artistic, the entry says. They usually had three claw feet. The lyre and other motifs of the Empire style were much used in their day. The modern fender is much lower, often little more than a kerb. It is now not seldom made of stone or marble, fixed to the floor.
britannica-1911-fever:
Fever is the subject of a medical article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word covers all states where body heat rises well above normal for some length of time. The Latin root links it to burning. When heat reaches a set high point, the text uses a special term for excess fever. Such heat, held for long, is a sign of danger and can end in death.

The article looks at how fever starts in the body. Each rise comes from a fault in the heat control system. The skin plays the chief part in letting heat out. Heavy exercise can lift heat for a short time when the skin cannot keep up. Lasting fever can come in three main ways. Nerves can be disturbed, heat loss can be blocked, or poisons can act on the body. Named fever diseases are treated under their own headings.
britannica-1911-fitz-osbern-roger:
Fitz-Osbern, Roger is a short life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Norman earl in the years after the Conquest. Roger took the earldom of Hereford and the English estate of William Fitz-Osbern in 1071. He did not stay on good terms with William the Conqueror. In 1075, against the king's ban, he wed his sister Emma to Ralph Guader, earl of Norfolk.

That wedding, the famed bridal of Norwich, sparked a revolt of the two earls. Roger was to bring his force from the west to join Ralph. Bishop Wulfstan and the Worcestershire fyrd held him in check at the Severn. When the rising fell apart, Roger was tried before the Great Council. He lost his lands and earldom and was jailed for life. He was freed, with other state prisoners, at the death of William the First in 1087.
britannica-1911-flower:
Flower is the subject of a long botanical article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The hosted text opens in mid-article, in a discussion of inflorescence, the ways flowers are grouped on a plant. It treats heads of flowers such as the capitulum of the dandelion and daisy. It also treats the hollow receptacle of the fig, where small flowers line an inner surface. Compound inflorescences come next.

From grouping, the article moves through the flower's structure and life. Its later pages reach fertilization: the pollen-tubes, the changes in the ovule that turn it into a seed, and the growth of the ovary into the fruit. In gymnosperms the pollen-tubes pause in the tissue of the nucellus, sometimes for nearly a year. Fruit and seed, the entry notes, have an article of their own. The botanist Alfred Barton Rendle signs the piece.
britannica-1911-fortescue-sir-john-lawye:
Sir John Fortescue, an English lawyer who lived from about 1394 to about 1476, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the second son of a Devonshire knight and was born at Norris in Somersetshire. He was educated at Exeter College in Oxford. Under Henry the Sixth he was three times a governor of Lincoln's Inn.

In 1441 he became a king's serjeant at law, and the next year chief justice of the king's bench. As a judge he won praise for wisdom, gravity, and upright conduct. He held his post to the end of the reign and stayed true to Henry in all his woes. For that he was charged with treason under Edward the Fourth. In exile with Queen Margaret he wrote his famed book in praise of the laws of England for the young prince.
britannica-1911-fournet-joseph-jean-bapt:
Joseph Jean Baptiste Xavier Fournet (1801-1869), French geologist and metallurgist, was born at Strassburg on 15 May 1801. He was educated at the Ecole des Mines at Paris. After wide experience as a mining engineer he was appointed professor of geology at Lyons in 1834. He was a man of broad knowledge and much research. His memoirs covered chemical and mineral subjects, eruptive rocks, the structure of the Jura, the changing of rocks in the Western Alps, oolitic limestones, kaolin and mineral veins.

On metallurgy Fournet was an acknowledged authority, and he published observations on the order in which metals take sulphur, known as Fournet's law. His chief books were studies of metalliferous deposits in 1834 and a history of dolomite in 1847. He died at Lyons on 8 January 1869. The notice stands in a shared file, where his entry precedes that of the typefounder Pierre Simon Fournier.
britannica-1911-fraser:
Fraser is the chief river of British Columbia, Canada, running 740 miles from the Rocky Mountains to the Gulf of Georgia. It rises in two branches and flows north-west for about 160 miles. Then it turns south past the Cariboo Mountains for over 400 miles to Hope, and bends west for 80 miles to its mouth at New Westminster.

Its chief tributaries are the Stuart, the Quesnel, the Chilcotin, and the Thompson, the largest, which joins at Lytton. The river is a fast mountain stream, in many parts not passable even by canoes. It cuts deep canyons through the Coast Range linked with gold-rush tragedies in the Cariboo district. From Yale, 80 miles inland, it becomes navigable. With its branches it drains nearly the whole province.
britannica-1911-frater: Frater, also Frater House or Fratery, is an architecture term for the hall where monks or friars met for meals. The word is the same in origin as refectory. Older forms such as freitur and fraytor show it came from Old French fraitour, a shortened form of refraitour, from the medieval Latin refectorium. Because the word looks like frater, a brother, it has sometimes been limited to the dining hall of a friary, while refectory is used of a monastery. The entry is a brief word study.
britannica-1911-french-daniel-chester:
Daniel Chester French (1850- ), American sculptor, was born at Exeter, New Hampshire, on 20 April 1850, son of a lawyer who served in the treasury. After a year at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and a month in the studio of John Q. A. Ward, he took commissions young. At twenty-three the town of Concord ordered his Minute Man statue.

The Minute Man was unveiled on 19 April 1875, one hundred years after the battle of Concord, after French had spent a year in Florence with Thomas Ball. His best-known work, Death Staying the Hand of the Sculptor, a tomb memorial in Boston, won a medal of honour at Paris in 1900. Other works named include the colossal Statue of the Republic at Chicago, Alma Mater at Columbia University, and statues of John Harvard and Rufus Choate. He joined the National Academy of Design in 1901.
britannica-1911-freshwater:
Freshwater is a watering place in the Isle of Wight, England, 12 miles west of Newport by rail, with 3306 people in 1901. The scattered township lies on the peninsula at the western end of the island. Freshwater Gate fronts the English Channel along a low strip between two lines of cliffs.

The peninsula rises to 397 feet in Headon Hill, and its cliffs are grand. Alum Bay cuts the north side of the western point. The detached rocks called the Needles stand off it. Farringford House in the parish was for a time the home of Alfred, Lord Tennyson. A tablet in All Saints church and a great cross on the downs mark him. Golf links lie on the downs. The hosted file also holds the neighbouring Frescobaldi and Fresnel entries.
britannica-1911-fugger:
Fugger is the name of a famous German family of merchants and bankers of Augsburg. The founder was Johann Fugger, a weaver of Graben whose son settled in Augsburg about 1367. Of the next line, Ulrich, Georg, and above all Jakob (1459-1525) built the fortune. They banked for the Habsburgs and worked silver mines in Tirol and copper mines in Hungary.

Jakob built the Fuggerei at Augsburg, 106 dwellings let cheaply to the poor, which still stand. His money helped elect Charles V in 1519. His nephews Raimund and Anton farmed Spanish mines and revenues for the emperor. They gained county rank in 1530 and the right to coin money in 1534. Anton died worth a reported 6,000,000 florins. The entry follows the later branches, their church patronage, and the records left in Augsburg.
britannica-1911-fusilier:
Fusilier was at first the name of a soldier armed with the fusil, a flintlock musket, and it survives as a regimental title. In the English civil war the word firelock set these weapons apart from the matchlock. Firelocks mattered near artillery, where open powder barrels made lighted matches dangerous, so escort companies guarded the guns and watched the gunners. From these companies grew the fusiliers of Louis XIV's wars, and Vauban's Royal Fusiliers of 1671 became the model for Europe.

Once every army took the flintlock and dropped the pike, fusiliers lost their special duties and were much used as light infantry. The Royal Fusiliers was raised on the French model in 1685. British fusiliers wear a fur cap like the Foot Guards' but smaller. In Germany the name belongs to infantry regiments and to one battalion in each grenadier regiment.
britannica-1911-gabel-kristoffer:
Gabel, Kristoffer (1617–1673), a Danish statesman, was born at Glückstadt on the 6th of January 1617. When his master, Duke Frederick, became king of Denmark as Frederick III, Gabel followed him to Copenhagen as private secretary and man of business. His veiled manner hid real financial skill, and he gained great influence over the irresolute king. He served on secret missions to Sweden and acted as chief go-between in the intrigues that made the crown absolute in 1660.

Gratitude made him rich and noble, and in 1664 he became governor of Copenhagen, remaining the greatest person at court until 1670. When Frederick died that year, Christian V dismissed him on the 18th of April, and no one pitied the man who had grown rich while others found it hard to live. He died on the 13th of October 1673.
britannica-1911-gabelentz-hans-conon-von:
Gabelentz, Hans Conon von der (1807–1874), a German linguist and ethnologist, was born at Altenburg on the 13th of October 1807.
