At school and at Leipzig and Göttingen he studied Arabic and Chinese on his own account. He entered the Altenburg public service in 1830, sat in the Frankfort parliament of 1848, and briefly headed the Altenburg ministry before resigning in 1849. From 1868 he gave up public life for research, dying at Lemnitz on the 3rd of September 1874.

Gabelentz is said to have learned eighty languages and to have spoken thirty of them fluently. His Manchu grammar appeared in 1832, and with Julius Löbe he edited Ulfilas's Gothic Bible between 1843 and 1846. His studies ranged over Finno-Ugrian, Swahili, Samoyede and many other tongues. His chief work, on the Melanesian languages, was completed in 1873 and showed their kinship with the Polynesian class.
britannica-1911-gachard-louis-prosper:
Gachard, Louis Prosper (1800–1885), a Belgian man of letters, was born in Paris on the 12th of March 1800. He joined the staff of the royal archives in 1826 and became director-general, a post he held for fifty-five years. In that long tenure he reorganized the service, enriched the records with copies gathered from other European collections, and kept up a wide correspondence with archivists and scholars. He also edited and published many collections of state papers, 246 publications in all by the printed list.

His best-known historical writings include Don Carlos et Philippe II of 1867 and a history of Belgium at the opening of the 18th century, published in 1880. His chief editorial works are the acts of the states-general of the Netherlands for 1576 to 1585 and the reports of the Venetian ambassadors on Charles V and Philip II. He died in Brussels on the 24th of December 1885.
britannica-1911-gadsden-christopher:
Gadsden, Christopher (1724–1805), an American patriot, was born at Charleston, South Carolina, in 1724, the son of the collector for that port. Schooled near Bristol, he returned in 1741, worked in a Philadelphia counting house, and became a merchant and planter at Charleston. He sat in the South Carolina legislature almost without break from 1760 to 1780. He represented his province in the Stamp Act Congress of 1765 and the Continental Congress of 1774 to 1776, already urging separation from Britain.

In February 1776 Gadsden took command of South Carolina's forces and in October became a brigadier-general in the Continental service, resigning in 1777 over a clash of state and federal authority. As lieutenant-governor in 1780 he was taken when Charleston surrendered, and for refusing a second parole he lay 42 weeks in a dungeon at St Augustine. Elected governor in 1782, he declined as too old and infirm. He died at Charleston on the 28th of August 1805.
britannica-1911-gambier:
Gambier is a village in Ohio, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry records it as the seat of Kenyon College. The village stands in Knox county on the Kokosing river, five miles east of Mount Vernon. Its count fell from 751 in 1900 to 537 in 1910. The Cleveland, Akron and Columbus railway serves the village.

Alongside the college sits its seminary, Bexley Hall, and a girls boarding school called Harcourt Place. The college dates to 1824, when it was set up as a seminary of the Protestant Episcopal Church in Ohio. Its first classes met at Worthington, in the home of Bishop Philander Chase. Funds for the school had been raised in England, with Lords Kenyon and Gambier as chief donors. The first lasting building rose on Gambier Hill in 1827.
britannica-1911-gardiner:
Gardiner is a city in Kennebec county, Maine, on the Kennebec river. Its city entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands where the Cobbosseecontee river joins the Kennebec, below Augusta. Counts put its people at about fifty five hundred in nineteen hundred.

The site lies just above sea level, and large ships reach the city. Falls on the Cobbosseecontee give strong water power for mills in town. Paper, machine shop goods, and shoes are its chief manufactures there. Large amounts of lumber and ice are shipped out each year too. Sylvester Gardiner founded the town in seventeen sixty on that site.
britannica-1911-gardner:
Gardner, a township of Worcester county in Massachusetts, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its people grew from 8424 in 1890 to 14699 in the census of 1910. Of those in 1900, 3449 were born abroad. The town covers 21 square miles of hill country, well watered with streams and ponds.

Three villages sit inside it, Gardner, South Gardner, and West Gardner. A state colony for the insane and a memorial hospital serve the town. Its library honours Levi Heywood, a local chair maker who devised chair making machines. Chairs rule its trade above all else. That work dates from 1805, and in 1905 the town held the largest chair factory in the world. Toys, baby carriages, silver ware, and oil stoves add to the output.
britannica-1911-gastric-ulcer:
Gastric Ulcer, the 1911 Britannica medical entry on ulcer of the stomach, calls it a grave disease. It is commonest in women, the entry says, and above all in anaemic domestic servants. The cause given is a clot in a small blood vessel of the stomach wall, linked to poor blood, vessel disease, or long indigestion.

Once the blood supply to a patch is cut off, the stomach juices digest that patch, and an ulcer forms. The entry puts its usual size at a silver threepence or sixpence, and its usual place on the back wall near the pylorus. Healing may leave little trace, or may pinch the stomach into an hour-glass shape. The great danger is a hole through the stomach wall, often fatal unless an operation is done fast. Symptoms are pain after food, tenderness, and vomiting.
britannica-1911-gawler:
Gawler is a town of Gawler county, South Australia, on the Para river, about 24 miles by rail north-east of Adelaide. The 1911 Britannica entry calls it one of the most thriving places in the colony. The town itself held 1,996 people in 1901, while town and wide suburbs together numbered about 7,000.

Its strength is the large wheat-growing district around it. The entry lists engineering works, foundries, flour-mills, breweries and saw-mills in the town. It also notes gold, silver, copper and lead found in the hills nearby. The notice is a brief gazetteer entry: position, population, farm trade and local works, in a handful of lines.
britannica-1911-gay-walter:
Walter Gay (1856- ) was an American artist, born at Hingham, Massachusetts, on 22 January 1856. The 1911 Britannica entry says he became a pupil of Leon Bonnat in Paris in 1876. His work then won steady notice in Europe: an honourable mention at the Salon of 1885 and a gold medal in 1888.

More awards followed at Vienna, Antwerp, Berlin and Munich through the 1890s. He was made an officer of the Legion of Honour and joined the Society of Secession at Munich. The entry places his pictures in the Luxembourg, the Tate Gallery in London, and the Boston and Metropolitan museums in New York. His subjects are mainly figures, portraying French peasant life. The notice is a compact record of training, prizes and where his work hangs.
britannica-1911-geber:
Geber is the name long given to the author of Latin treatises on alchemy, among them the Summa perfectionis magisterii and the Liber fornacum. The 1911 Britannica entry explains that these works were generally taken as translations from the Arabic of Abu Abdallah Jaber ben Hayyam, said to have lived in the 8th or 9th century.

About that man, the entry stresses, there is deep uncertainty. The Kitab-al-Fihrist of the 10th century lists some 500 treatises under his name, yet reports claims that he wrote only one book, or never existed at all. Its writer rejects those claims. Other details conflict too: his home is given as Kufa or Khorasan, his master as one Ja'far or another. The entry weighs these tangled reports without settling them.
britannica-1911-geddes-alexander:
Alexander Geddes (1737-1802) was a Scottish Roman Catholic theologian, born at Rathven in Banffshire on 14 September 1737. The 1911 Britannica entry traces his training at the seminary of Scalan and the Scottish College in Paris, where he studied biblical languages and theology. He served as a priest at Dundee, then lived with the earl of Traquair, studying in the earl's library.

His free dealings with Protestant neighbours drew his bishop's rebuke. For hunting, and for attending a friend's parish church at Cullen, he was stripped of his charge in 1779. He moved to London in 1780 and spent his life there, backed by Lord Petre in a scheme for a new Catholic Bible version. In 1786 he published a prospectus of that translation, with support from scholars such as Kennicott and Lowth.
britannica-1911-george-v-of-hanover:
George the Fifth, king of Hanover who lived from 1819 to 1878, gets a long life entry in the 1911 Britannica. The only son of Ernest Augustus and a grandson of George the Third, he was born in Berlin. His youth passed in England and Berlin till his father took the Hanover throne in 1837. He lost one eye to illness as a child and the other in 1833, and was wholly blind.

George took a high, autocratic view of royal power and fell into the hands of poor advisers. From his accession in 1851 he fought his parliament in dispute after dispute. In 1866 he backed Austria and refused Prussia's demand for a neutral Hanover. Prussian troops took his land at once, and Hanover was annexed that September. He died at Paris in 1878, never reconciled to Prussia.
britannica-1911-gerardmer:
Gerardmer is a town of north-eastern France, in the department of Vosges, 33 miles east-south-east of Epinal by rail. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the town 3,993 people in 1906, and the commune 10,041. It stands 2,200 feet up, at the eastern end of the small Lake of Gerardmer, among forest-clad mountains.

The entry calls it the chief summer resort of the French Vosges and a centre for excursions. Named trips run to the Hohneck, the Schlucht pass toward Germany, and the defile of Granges with its Saut des Cuves waterfall. The town weaves cloth, bleaches, saws wood and makes wooden goods, and trades in the geromes cheeses of the district. Its name is traced to Gerard of Alsace, first duke of Lorraine, who built a tower by the lake in the 11th century.
britannica-1911-gerrymander:
Gerrymander is an American word for the drawing of election districts to give one party an unfair edge. The 1911 Britannica article gives both the sense and the tale of its birth. In 1812 Elbridge Gerry was governor of Massachusetts. The ruling party in the state house redrew the senate districts to boost its own seats. One district in Essex county took a strange, twisting shape on the map.

A painter saw the map in a Boston print office and added a head, wings, and claws. He called the beast a salamander. The editor shot back that it was a gerrymander, joining the governor's name to the beast. The name stuck at once. The article notes the trick was older than the name. It was first used in Virginia in 1788 against James Madison.
britannica-1911-ginger:
Ginger is a plant entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes the hot root stock of a reed like plant grown in warm lands. The plant stands three or four feet high, with leaves and blooms on split stems. It is thought to come from the warm parts of Asia.

The entry traces the spice trade in the root from old times to the middle ages. Greek and Roman buyers thought it came from Arabia by the Red Sea. Tax lists in port towns show how much of it moved each year. In England it ranked next to pepper in worth for a long time. Three trade grades known to Italian merchants are also named.
britannica-1911-glacier:
Glacier, in the 1911 Britannica, is a mass of compacted ice that begins in a snow-field. The article, adopted from the French word for ice, starts from the snow-line: the level above which ground stays snowy all year. That line forms an uneven shell round the earth, touching sea level near the poles and rising to 15,000 or 18,000 feet over the tropics.

Above the line, snow barely evaporates and so it piles up, each year's fall burying the last. The article follows what happens to those buried layers: how snow hardens into ice, how the mass begins to move, and how a glacier behaves as it travels. Later parts take up glacier motion, the work glaciers do on the land, and their kinds and distribution. It is a full physical account of ice in motion, built step by step from the snow-field down.
britannica-1911-glaser-christopher:
Christopher Glaser was a pharmaceutical chemist of the 17th century, a native of Basel. The 1911 Britannica entry is short: he became demonstrator of chemistry at the Jardin du Roi in Paris, and apothecary to Louis XIV and to the duke of Orleans.

His name rests on his Traite de la chymie, printed at Paris in 1663. It went through some ten editions in about twenty-five years, and was translated into both German and English. The entry then notes a darker claim: that Glaser was an accomplice in the poisonings carried out by the marchioness de Brinvilliers. The extent of his part, it says, is doubtful. He appears to have died some time before 1676. The salt called sal polychrestum Glaseri, normal potassium sulphate, was his preparation, used in medicine.
britannica-1911-gloucester:
Gloucester, a city and port on the river Severn in England, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The city is the county town of Gloucestershire and sits 114 miles west north west of London. The count for 1901 gave it 47,955 people. Rail lines and the Berkeley Ship Canal link it to Sharpness Docks on the Severn estuary.

The entry sets the city on a low rise above the river. The Cotteswolds shelter it on the east, with the Malverns to the west. Much space goes to the cathedral in the north of the city. Its roots lie in an abbey of St Peter founded in 681. The present church was begun under Abbot Serlo in the late eleventh century.
britannica-1911-goatsucker:
Goatsucker is the name of a bird long held, with no truth, to suck goats. That old belief lives in the bird's names in many tongues, from Greek and Latin to French, Spanish, and German. The common goatsucker, Caprimulgus europaeus, is the type of a clear family, the Caprimulgidae. The birds of that family have flat heads and huge, wide mouths. They also have large eyes and soft, pencilled plumage.

Members of the family range in size from a lark to a crow. Their place in the bird order has been set in more than one way by scholars. Linnaeus put all the kinds he knew among the Passeres. Huxley later grouped the family with the swifts and the humming-birds in one division. The article also notes two ways of fixing the family's bounds, one of which takes in the genus Podargus and its kin.
britannica-1911-godmanchester:
Godmanchester is a borough in Huntingdonshire in England, on the right bank of the Ouse. It stands one mile from Huntingdon, on a branch of the Great Eastern railway. Its people numbered two thousand and seventeen in nineteen o one. It has a fine church of Saint Mary in the later Gothic style. Its trade is in farming goods, with flour mills in the town.

A Romano British village once held the site of Godmanchester town. The town belonged to the king before the Conquest and at the survey of Domesday. In twelve thirteen King John granted the manor to the men of the town. Later kings confirmed that grant in charters of their own reigns. Richard the Second added freedom from toll and other dues in his charter. James the First gave a charter of incorporation in sixteen o five.
britannica-1911-goes-hugo-van-der:
Hugo van der Goes, a painter of Ghent who died in 1482, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. For a long time he was known by one large work in Florence. That work was ordered by Tommaso Portinari, an agent of the Medici firm at Bruges. Tommaso had a chapel in the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova at Florence.

The work is a vast triptych with figures of life size. At its centre the Virgin kneels in worship before the new born Christ, with shepherds and angels near. On the wings Tommaso and his sons pray on one side, and his wife and daughters on the other. Saints stand guard over each group. The text praises the work more for true likeness in its faces than for ideal beauty, and notes the harm done by decay and repair.
britannica-1911-goffer:
Goffer means to give a fluted or crimped look to a thing, most of all to linen or lace frills. The 1911 Britannica article says the work is done with hot irons of a set shape, called goffering tongs. The French term gaufrage is used of the wavy edge on some porcelain. It names as well the stamped trim on the edges of a book binding. A heated iron does for cloth what a stamp does for those goods.

The word came from a French term for a thin cake marked like a honeycomb, a wafer. That cake word is Teutonic in root, as Dutch and German forms for waffle show. The root sense goes back to weaving, since the cells of a honeycomb look woven. A quote from 1433 shows the phrase for a cake iron in old French books.
britannica-1911-goldsmith-oliver:
Oliver Goldsmith, born in seventeen twenty eight, was an English poet, playwright, and novelist. He came of a Protestant family long settled in Ireland. His birthplace is disputed, with Pallas in Longford the usual claim. New study points to a house at Elphin in Roscommon instead. His father Charles lived at Pallas on small means from church and farm work.

While Oliver was still a child, his father gained a better living at Kilkenny West. The family moved to a large house on a busy road near Lissoy. There a kinswoman taught the boy his letters at home. At seven he went to a village school kept by an old soldier. That teacher professed to teach reading, writing, and sums alone. Yet he held an endless fund of tales of ghosts and fairies for the boys.
britannica-1911-goltz-colmar-freiherr-vo:
Colmar von der Goltz, a Prussian soldier and military writer, was born in East Prussia in eighteen forty three. He entered the Prussian infantry in eighteen sixty one as a young man. In eighteen sixty four he entered the Berlin Military Academy for staff training. He was pulled out in eighteen sixty six to serve in the Austrian war. In that war he was wounded at the battle of Trautenau.

In eighteen sixty seven Goltz joined the map section of the general staff. At the start of the Franco German War he served on a prince's staff. He took part in the battles of Vionville and Gravelotte and the siege of Metz. After Metz fell he served in the campaign of the Loire. In eighteen seventy one he became a professor at the military school at Potsdam. His books on the war were praised as fair in their judgments.
britannica-1911-goniometer:
Goniometer is an instrument article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A goniometer is a tool for measuring the angles of crystals. Its name joins two Greek words, for angle and for measure. The entry sorts the instruments into two kinds and traces their history.

The story starts with Nicolaus Steno in 1669. He found the face angles of quartz by cutting sections across the crystal's edges. The first true instrument was the contact goniometer, devised by Carangeot in 1783. It is built of two metal rules hinged over a graduated semicircle. The user sets the tool square to an edge of the crystal. The rules are then brought to rest against the two faces. Their spread on the scale gives the angle between the faces. A reflecting form of the instrument is also named. Readers learn how a simple hinged rule opened the exact study of crystal form.
britannica-1911-gopher:
The gopher of the 1911 Britannica entry is a land tortoise of the south east parts of the United States. It ranges from Florida north to a great river that parts the states there. Its shell is long, flat, and grooved, in a yellow brown tone, and the front of its lower shell bends up past the upper one.

The entry says the beast haunts woods most, but strays to open plains where it can harm potato crops, on which it feeds. It hides by day in a deep burrow and comes out at night to eat. Its eggs, five in a clutch, lie in a side pit near the mouth of the hole. The piece ends by noting that the name gopher more often means a small burrowing rodent.
britannica-1911-gordon-alexander:
Alexander Gordon (about 1692 to about 1754) was a Scottish antiquary from Aberdeen. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that little is known of his early life. He shone in classics at Aberdeen and taught languages and music at first. Travel abroad as a tutor likely filled his young years as well.

His great work, Itinerarium Septentrionale, came out in 1726. It made his name as a student of old remains in the north. He later served as secretary to learned societies in London. In 1741 he sailed to South Carolina with Governor James Glen. There he gained land and held posts as registrar and justice.
britannica-1911-gossamer:
Gossamer is the fine, thread like film spun by small spiders. It is seen on stub fields and gorse in the fall. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that it also floats in the air in clear weather at that season. By shift of sense, any light, frail, or flimsy thing is called gossamer.

The entry adds two trade uses of the word from past days. A thin gauze cloth for trims and hats bore the name. It was much like the sheer cloth of today. In the hat trade of a past reign it meant silk hats of very light weight. The root of the word is dim, the entry says. It seems to join goose and summer, since the threads show most in warm late fall days when geese are in season.
britannica-1911-gouffier:
Gouffier names a great French family traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The house held the estate of Bonnivet in Poitou from the fourteenth century. Guillaume Gouffier served as chamberlain to Charles the Seventh. He was a sworn foe of Jacques Coeur and gained his fall and then his property.

Guillaume had a great number of children, and several shaped the course of events. Artus taught the young count of Angoulême, who became Francis the First. On that king rise, Artus led the royal household and took a large part in rule. He was set to make the treaty of Noyon in 1516. Roanne and Boisy were raised to a duchy for him just before his death. Adrien became a bishop and grand almoner of France.
britannica-1911-gower:
Gower is a district and old lordship in Glamorgan, Wales, by the sea. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it between the Tawe and Loughor rivers. In Welsh it was called Gwyr, an old commote linked to Ystrad Tywi. In common speech Gower often means just the southern peninsula near Swansea.

Coast caves there hold rich stores of animal remains. Paviland cave and Bacon Hole hold the clearest traces of early people. Later waves shaped the area in turn. Norsemen raided the coast, and Norman lords took the land around 1100. English and Flemish settlers then filled the south while Welsh life held in the north.
britannica-1911-graham-sylvester:
Sylvester Graham is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an American diet reformer. He lived from 1794 to 1851. He was born in Suffield, Connecticut, in 1794. He studied at Amherst College in his youth. In 1826 he was ordained a Presbyterian minister. He seems to have preached but little in that role. 

He held that a flesh diet caused abnormal cravings. His last years were spent in quiet retirement. He died at Northampton, Massachusetts, in September 1851. His name lives on through unbolted Graham flour. He is also the originator of Graham bread. But his reform reached much wider than bread. He urged education in how the body works. His Science of Human Life of 1836 set that out. The entry calls that book an exhaustive text on the subject. He planned a full regimen of life in detail.
britannica-1911-grant-sir-alexander:
Alexander Grant, who lived from 1826 to 1884, was a British scholar and school reformer. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his work in India and Scotland. He was born in New York in September 1826. Childhood in the West Indies came before Harrow and Oxford.

Grant made Aristotle his chief study while a fellow at Oxford. His edition of the Ethics became a standard school text. In 1859 he went to India as a schools inspector. He rose to lead a Bombay college and its university. Back in Scotland he became head of Edinburgh University in 1868. He drove the founding of its medical school almost alone. His history of the school first three hundred years came out in 1884.
britannica-1911-grasshopper:
Grasshopper is an insect article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a group of jumping insects. The name covers two families of the straight winged order. They are famed for two powers, their leaps and their song.

The article sets the two families side by side. One bears very long, thread like feelers and lays its eggs with a long tool. Its ears sit on the first pair of legs. The other bears short, stout feelers and a short egg tool. Its ears sit on the first ring of the body. All grasshoppers feed on plants, the text notes. They grow by steps, with no resting stage, so their harm runs from birth to death. Green kinds blend with the grass they live in. Some bear bright under wings that flash in flight.
britannica-1911-grenadier:
A grenadier was originally a soldier whose special duty was to throw hand-grenades. The 1911 Britannica entry dates the organization: in 1667 four men per company in the French Regiment du Roi were trained with grenades at the siege of Lille. Grenadier companies followed in that regiment and some thirty others by 1670.

Evelyn's Diary records the new sort of soldiers at Hounslow on 29 June 1678, dexterous in flinging hand-granades, and England copied France quickly. Grenadiers also carried axes, for the assault of fortresses. Chosen as the most powerful men, they kept their elite place after the grenade itself vanished: the crack company of each battalion, taking the right of the line. Napoleon grouped such companies into whole brigades and divisions. The entry ends with their dress, from the pointed embroidered cap to the tall bearskin of the British Guards.
britannica-1911-grenville-sir-richard-na:
Sir Richard Grenville (c. 1541-1591) was a British naval commander, born of an old Cornish family about 1541. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that his grandfather was marshal of Calais under Henry VIII. His father commanded the Mary Rose and was lost with her in 1545. Young Grenville is supposed to have fought the Turks in Hungary under Maximilian.

He sat for Cornwall in 1571 and 1584 and served on the Dover harbour works. In 1585 he commanded the seven ships that carried Raleigh's colonists to Roanoke Island, capturing a Spanish vessel on the way home. In 1586 he brought provisions, found the colony deserted, and left a few men to hold it. The entry calls him a man of much pride and ambition, of undoubted bravery. In 1591 he sailed as second in command against the Spanish treasure fleet. The article closes with the Revenge's last fight, the stand that made his name immortal.
britannica-1911-grenville-sir-richard-so:
Sir Richard Grenville (1600-1658) was an English royalist, third son of Sir Bernard Grenville and grandson of the famous seaman Sir Richard. The 1911 Britannica entry has him serving in France, Germany and the Netherlands. Favour with the duke of Buckingham brought him into the Cadiz, Rhe and La Rochelle expeditions. Knighted, he sat for Fowey in 1628.

His marriage to the wealthy widow Mary Fitz made him a baronet in 1630 but ruined him. The entry blames his violent temper: lawsuits with his wife and her kinsman the earl of Suffolk left him imprisoned. He escaped in 1633, spent six years in Germany, and returned to fight the Scots. In Ireland he won fame as governor of Trim. Sent to the parliamentary army in 1643, he changed sides instead. The article follows his stormy royalist career in the west.
britannica-1911-grocer:
A grocer is literally one who sells by the gross. The word means a wholesale dealer. It comes through Old French from the medieval Latin grossarius. Early usage attached the word to a commodity. Writers spoke of wholesale dealers in wine or fish. The word later settled on one trade. It named the dealer in tea, coffee and cocoa. Dried fruits, spices and sugar joined that list.

That settled meaning grew from the Grocers' Company of London. The company is one of the twelve great livery companies. Pepperers and spicers joined in 1345. They formed the Fraternity of St Anthony. The name grocers appears in company records in 1373. A first charter followed in 1428. The company won rights to search and inspect spices. It also sold drugs and medicines for many years. The apothecaries separated from it in 1617.
britannica-1911-haggard-henry-rider:
Henry Rider Haggard, born in 1856, was an English novelist. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica links his fame to African romance. He was born at Bradenham Hall in Norfolk in June 1856. At nineteen he sailed to South Africa as a governor secretary.

Haggard served in the Transvaal through its first annexation and fall. Back in England he read for the bar, then turned to books. A defense of a chief policy came first in 1882. Novels followed, but King Solomons Mines in 1886 made him popular. She, a year later, scored a still greater hit. Its sequel came out in 1905 to eager readers. Allan Quatermain tales kept the African scene alive for him. Later he wrote on farm loss and land settlement with zeal.
britannica-1911-halleck-henry-wager:
Henry Wager Halleck (1815–1872) was an American general and jurist. He was born in Oneida county, New York. He graduated from West Point in 1839 into the engineers. Defence works at New York employed him for years. In 1845 the government sent him to inspect European military establishments. His lectures became Elements of Military Art and Science in 1846. Volunteer officers used that book widely in the Civil War.

He served in California during the Mexican War. There he helped frame California's state constitution in 1849. He resigned in 1854 for a successful law practice. The Civil War recalled him as major-general. He took supreme western command in November 1861. His administrative skill brought order from chaos. The victories of 1862 belonged more to Grant, Buell and Pope. His slow advance on Corinth drew heavy criticism. Washington later made him chief of staff.
britannica-1911-hanaper:
A hanaper is properly a case or basket. It held a hanap, a stemmed drinking goblet. Antiquaries still use hanap for medieval stemmed cups. The Royal Gold Cup in the British Museum is one. In the English chancery, hanaper named a wicker basket. Writs and documents were kept in that basket. The basket then gave its name to a department.

The clerk of the hanaper received fees for sealing charters and patents. Certain writs under the great seal issued from his office. The English department is now abolished. In Ireland the clerk of the crown and hanaper survives. His office issues writs for parliamentary elections there. The modern word hamper descends from hanaper. The verb to hamper, meaning to hinder, is probably a different word. Icelandic and German roots for restraining are suggested.
britannica-1911-hardt-hermann-von-der:
Hermann von der Hardt was a German historian and scholar of eastern tongues. He lived from sixteen sixty to seventeen forty six, and his entry is in the nineteen eleven Britannica. Born at Melle in Westphalia, he studied at Jena and at Leipzig. In sixteen ninety he took the chair of eastern tongues at Helmstedt.

Hardt held that chair until he resigned it in seventeen twenty seven. He lived at Helmstedt for the rest of his life after that. The entry lists his many works on Luther, councils, and tongue studies. They include guides to Hebrew, Syriac, and Chaldaic speech and writing. He left a past of the Reformation in draft at his death.
britannica-1911-harrison-thomas-alexande:
Thomas Alexander Harrison (1853- ) was an American artist, and this 1911 Britannica entry records his training and honours. He was born in Philadelphia in January 1853. He studied at the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts and then at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, where he went in 1878. Before that he had served with a government survey party on the Pacific coast.

Chafing under the rules of the schools, he settled in Brittany, at Pont Aven and Concarneau, and turned to marine painting and landscape. In 1882 he sent a figure piece to the Salon, a fisher boy on the beach, which drew notice. Honours followed in a stream: the Temple gold medal in 1887, a first medal at the Paris Exhibition of 1889, and medals at Munich, Brussels, Ghent, and Vienna.
britannica-1911-hatton-sir-christopher:
Sir Christopher Hatton (1540–1591) was lord chancellor of England. He was also a favourite of Queen Elizabeth. Holdenby in Northamptonshire was his family's home. St Mary Hall, Oxford, educated him. Handsome and accomplished, he danced elegantly. That grace first caught the queen's notice. He became a gentleman pensioner in 1564. He captained her bodyguard in 1572. Estates and profitable offices flowed to him.

Mary queen of Scots charged him with being Elizabeth's lover in 1584. He was probably innocent of that charge. Parliament knew him as the queen's spokesman. He prosecuted Stubbs and Parry in her interest. He sat on the court that tried Babington. He also helped condemn Mary herself. In 1584 four hundred kneeling members repeated his prayer for Elizabeth. The lord chancellorship came to him in 1587.
britannica-1911-head-sir-edmund-walker:
Sir Edmund Walker Head (1805–1868) was an English colonial governor and art writer. His father was the Rev. Sir John Head, rector of Rayleigh. Winchester and Oriel College, Oxford, educated him. First-class honours in classics won him a Merton fellowship. He succeeded as 8th baronet in 1838. Poor-law work came first: assistant-commissioner, then commissioner in 1841. That service earned him New Brunswick in 1847.

In 1854 he passed to the governor-generalship of Canada. He retained Canada until 1861. A civil service commissionership followed his return home. The Privy Council took him in 1857 and a K.C.B. in 1860. His only son died in 1859, so the baronetcy died with him. His writings range widely for a governor. A Handbook of Spanish and French painting appeared in 1845. Shall and Will treated future auxiliary verbs. His Viga Glum's Saga translation came in 1866.
britannica-1911-hebel-johann-peter:
Johann Peter Hebel (1760–1826) was a German poet and popular writer. He was born at Basel on 10 May 1760. His father died when he was little over a year old. Poverty marked his upbringing at Hausen in the Wiesental. Kind friends funded his schooling and theology at Erlangen. Private tutoring came first after university. Then he taught at the Karlsruhe gymnasium. Its directorship followed in 1808.

Hebel is among Germany's most widely read popular poets. His tales and lyrics are written in the Alemannic dialect. Goethe said they rusticise the whole universe most attractively. Fidelity, naïveté and humour mark his descriptions. Die Wiese is called the pearl of German idyllic poetry. His Schatzkästlein prose (1811) ranks with Germany's best stories. Vilmar rated it above a cartload of novels. Memorials stand to him at Karlsruhe, Basel and Schwetzingen. He died at Schwetzingen in 1826.
britannica-1911-heddle-matthew-forster:
Matthew Forster Heddle (1828–1897) was a Scottish mineralogist. He was born at Hoy in Orkney on 28 April 1828. The Edinburgh Academy gave him his early education. He entered Edinburgh as a medical student. Chemistry and mineralogy studies followed at Klausthal and Freiburg. His M.D. came in 1851, and he practised about five years. Medicine held little attraction for him, though.

He became assistant to Professor Connell at St Andrews. In 1862 he succeeded Connell in the chemistry chair. A South African gold-mine report took him abroad in 1880. On return he devoted himself wholly to mineralogy. Personal exploration across Scotland built one of its finest collections. Those specimens now sit in the Royal Scottish Museum. His great Mineralogy of Scotland appeared posthumously in 1901. J. G. Goodchild edited it from his manuscripts. He died on 19 November 1897.
britannica-1911-heifer:
A heifer is a young cow that has not calved. The word descends from the Old English heahfore or heafru. That older word is of obscure origin. Bede's History, about AD 900, already shows the form heahfore. Many later forms intervened before the modern spelling. One suggested derivation joins heah, high, with faren, to go. That would make the animal a high-stepper.

Another suggestion derives it from hea, a stall, and fore, a cow. Neither derivation is presented as certain. The entry is one of the shortest word studies in its band. It gives the definition in its first sentence. The rest is pure etymology and doubt. No farming practice or breed detail appears. The word's history, not the animal, is the whole subject here.
britannica-1911-helst-bartholomaeus-van-:
Bartholomaeus van der Helst was a Dutch painter who died at Amsterdam in 1670. His birth date and place are both uncertain. Tradition gives Amsterdam in 1613. Competent authority doubts even that. A Haarlem family bore his name from 1607. Pictures there might show he learned from Frans Hals. No proof has traced him among Severijn van der Helst's children. His first great picture shows civic guards at a brewery.

That canvas, dated 1639 or 1643, still adorns Amsterdam's town-hall. Portraits of the burgomaster Bicker followed in 1642. Portraiture alone filled his whole later career. In 1654 he helped found Amsterdam's painters' guild. He married Constance Reynst of a patrician family. His Peace group celebrates the treaty of Münster. Critics praise his life-like heads and admirable hands. Careful finish, not central thought, is his limit. Galleries across Europe hold his numerous portraits.
britannica-1911-hemy-charles-napier:
Charles Napier Hemy (1841– ) was a British painter. He was born at Newcastle-on-Tyne. The Newcastle school of art trained him first. The Antwerp academy followed in his education. Baron Leys's studio in Belgium completed it. He produced some figure subjects and landscapes. Marine painting is what he is best known by. Those marines are called admirable in quality. Honours accumulated steadily in his later career.

The Royal Academy elected him associate in 1898. The Royal Society of Painters in Water Colours took him earlier. He became its associate in 1890 and full member in 1897. Two paintings hang in the National Gallery of British Art. Pilchards dates from 1897. London River dates from 1904. The entry is a short gallery-style notice. Training, specialty and honours are its whole content. No prices, patrons or personal detail are given.
britannica-1911-henderson-alexander:
Alexander Henderson (1583–1646) was a Scots churchman. He was born at Criech in Fife in 1583. St Andrews gave him his degree in 1603. In 1610 he took a chair of rhetoric there. Soon after, the living of Leuchars was given him. Archbishop Gladstanes forced him on a parish that did not want him. His love of bishops made his start hard.

He changed his views in time, and fully. He became a Presbyterian in faith and church rule. Men came to hold him in high esteem. He spoke out early against the five acts of Perth. The forced prayer book and canons met his protest too. On 1 March 1638 men began to sign the National Covenant at Greyfriars. The final form of that bond was chiefly his work. In November the great Glasgow Assembly met. It chose him as its head by acclaim. His works are speeches, sermons and tracts of the day.
britannica-1911-henderson-ebenezer:
Ebenezer Henderson (1784–1858) was a Scottish divine. He was born at the Linn near Dunfermline in November 1784. He was an agricultural labourer's youngest son. Three years of schooling preceded watchmaking and shoemaking apprenticeships. Robert Haldane's seminary received him in 1803. In 1805 he was chosen to accompany John Paterson to India. The East India Company blocked British missionary passage. Denmark became their waiting place instead.

Preaching in Copenhagen changed the plan entirely. He became pastor at Elsinore in 1806. Bible distribution across Scandinavia occupied him until about 1817. He visited Sweden, Lapland and Iceland in those years. He formed Sweden's first Congregational church in 1811. Russia called him in 1818 and again in 1822. Prince Galitzin engaged him for the Russian Bible Society. Twenty years of foreign labour preceded his English settlement. He died at Mortlake on 17 May 1858. Iceland and biblical criticism books carry his name.
britannica-1911-henry-i-the-fowler:
Henry I (c. 876–936), called the Fowler, was a German king, son of Otto the Illustrious, duke of Saxony. His first marriage, to Hatburg, was ruled illegal by the church, as she had taken the veil after a former husband's death. In 909 he married Matilda, said to descend from the hero Widukind, and in 912 he became duke of Saxony.

Conrad I, whom he had resisted, on his deathbed in 918 urged the nobles to choose Henry. The Franks and Saxons elected him at Fritzlar in May 919, and he refused church sanction for the choice. By talks more than war he won over Bavaria, Swabia and Lorraine. He beat Slav tribes, took Brennibor, and held both banks of the Elbe. A ten-year truce with the Hungarians, bought in 923, ended in his victory over them in March 933. He died at Memleben on the 2nd of July 936, and Otto the Great succeeded him.
britannica-1911-herne-the-hunter:
Herne the Hunter, a ghostly huntsman of Windsor Great Park, is the subject of a short legend entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was said to haunt the park at night, most of all round an old tree known as Herne's oak. That tree, said to be near 700 years old, blew down in 1863, and Queen Victoria had a young oak planted there. In France the Grand Veneur fills a like role.

Herne shows up in The Merry Wives of Windsor and in Ainsworth's Windsor Castle. Nothing firm is known of the tale's source. One guess ties it to the life of some keeper of the forest. A stronger guess makes it a form of the Wild Huntsman myth of folk lore. Tylor, cited here, held that such myths are the late form of a very old storm myth.
britannica-1911-hero-and-leander:
Hero and Leander is a myth article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about two lovers famed in the ancient world. Hero was a priestess of Aphrodite at Sestos. Leander, a youth of Abydos, saw her at a feast of the goddess and fell deeply in love. Her post and her parents barred any marriage.

So the two met in secret. Each night Hero set a lamp at the top of her tower by the sea. Guided by that light, Leander swam the dangerous Hellespont. One stormy night the lamp blew out, and Leander drowned. When Hero found his body on the shore next morning, she threw herself into the waves. The article notes the tale in Virgil, Statius, and Ovid. A small epic by Musaeus tells it in full, and Marlowe and Chapman made it into an English poem.
britannica-1911-hero-the-younger: Hero the Younger is the name given, without good reason the entry admits, to a Byzantine land surveyor who wrote about the year 938 after Christ. The 1911 Britannica entry explains that his treatise on land surveying was modelled on the works of Hero of Alexandria, above all on the Dioptra. It then points readers to the modern printed study of that Byzantine text by Vincent at Paris in 1858. A further study by Martin in academy papers of 1854 is also named for those who want more.
britannica-1911-hexameter:
Hexameter is the earliest and most important form of classical verse, in dactylic rhythm. Each line holds six feet: the last a spondee, the one before it a dactyl. A spondee may stand in the fifth foot for effect, making a spondaic line; the other feet may be spondees or dactyls. All the great epic verse of Greek and Roman poets uses this metre, finest in Homer and Virgil.

Varied cadence and caesura keep it from monotony: the usual breaks fall mid-third foot (penthemimeral) or mid-fourth (hepthemimeral). English tries include Longfellow's Evangeline and Clough's Bothie of Tober-na-Vuoilich, but the metre does not truly suit English. English lacks real spondees and runs on accent, not long and short syllables; German fits it better. The article sits inside a larger hosted file holding neighbouring entries.
britannica-1911-heyden-jan-van-der:
Jan van der Heyden (1637–1712) was a Dutch painter of buildings and town views, born at Gorcum. A contemporary of Hobbema and Ruysdael, he had a second string they lacked: he improved the fire engine. He died at Amsterdam in 1712 as superintendent of lighting and director of the firemen's company. Till 1672 he painted in partnership with Adrian van der Velde.

Heyden mastered linear perspective and painted brick houses, churches, canals and moated granges. He travelled to The Hague, Ghent, Brussels and Cologne, copying the cathedral tower again and again. His gift was minute painting that kept its breadth: bricks in sun, steeples in moving shadow. But he could draw neither man nor beast, nor ships nor carts. Velde filled that gap with lively figures, and their joint work is delicate and full of glow.
britannica-1911-heylyn-peter:
Peter Heylyn (1600–1662) was an English historian and controversialist, born at Burford in Oxfordshire. He entered Hart Hall, Oxford, in 1613, moved to Magdalen College, and in 1618 began lecturing on cosmography as a fellow there. His lectures, as Mikrokosmos, were printed in 1621, and many editions followed. Ordained in 1624, he drew the notice of William Laud, and in 1630 he became chaplain to Charles I.

The king made him a prebendary of Westminster, and in 1637 treasurer of Westminster Abbey. By then he was known as an able high-church controversialist. He disputed with John Prideaux, answered Bishop Williams in pamphlets such as A Coal from the Altar, and opposed the Puritans. He helped William Noy build the case against Prynne over the Histriomastix. When the Long Parliament met he retired to Alresford, and in 1642 he joined the king at Oxford. There he edited Mercurius Aulicus, a sharp royalist news-sheet.
britannica-1911-holbein-hans-the-elder:
Hans Holbein the elder (c. 1460–1524) belonged to a famed family of painters at work in Augsburg and Basel from the late 15th century. Augsburg then followed Flemish art, under the schools of Bruges and Brussels. Hans first appears at Augsburg as partner to his brother Sigismund, leading the partnership and signing all its pictures. His early style matches Memlinc and the Brussels-Brugeois school, tempered by study of the Cologne masters.

Between 1499 and 1506, as his custom grew, Holbein leaned more on direct observation of local passion plays. Most of his early works take Passion subjects, marshalled with the shallow grouping of the stage. After 1500, Italian example began to soften South German painting, and at Augsburg that tempering of Flemish and German art with Italian elements was Holbein's work first of all. His sketch-books picture Augsburg life at the century's turn, Maximilian and the Fuggers among the sitters.
britannica-1911-holbein-hans-the-younger:
Hans Holbein the younger (1497–1543) was a German painter, the favourite son of Hans Holbein the elder, probably born at Augsburg about 1497. He doubtless learned art from his father. About 1515 he left Augsburg with his elder brother Ambrose to seek work illustrating books at Basel. His first patron is said to have been Erasmus, for whom he sketched in pen and ink an edition of the Encomium Moriae.

At Basel Holbein's chief work was drawing title-blocks and initials for new editions of the Bible and classics from Froben and other presses. Yet the portraits of Jacob Meyer and his wife, one dated 1516, are already wonders of workmanship, hard to credit to his nineteenth year. Neither brother could join the Basel guild at first; Ambrose entered it in 1517. Hans wandered in Switzerland, painting at Lucerne, then returned to Basel in 1519, joined the guild, and, it is thought, married.
britannica-1911-holster: A holster is a leather case to hold a pistol, used by a horseman and properly fastened to the saddle-bow, though sometimes worn in the belt. The word came into English from Dutch. Its root is hel- or hul-, to cover, seen in the Old English heolster, a place of shelter or concealment, and in hull, a sheath or covering. The German word for the same thing, holfter, is said to come from a different root. The entry is a short definition with the word's history.
britannica-1911-holy-water:
Holy water is, technically, the water with which Christian believers sign the cross on their foreheads on entering or leaving church. By the edict of Gratian it must be exorcized and blessed by the priest and sprinkled with exorcized salt. The rite stands in the Gelasian, Gregorian and other sacramentaries. In the East the water was blessed once a month; in the Latin Church it is now blessed every Sunday.

The long account traces the rite's slow growth. In the early church, water was not expressly consecrated for baptisms: Tertullian held water pure in itself, the first abode of the divine Spirit. The Canons of Hippolytus, about A.D. 250, give no prayer for blessing fonts. Rituals for consecrating water arose late in the 3rd century. Behind them lay an older world of belief in water-sprites, naiads, kelpies and river-gods, grim reality to the generations that shaped the rites.
britannica-1911-honey-eater:
Honey-eater, or honey-sucker, is a name used loosely for many birds, but here it is kept for the family Meliphagidae, leaving out the sun-birds and the genera Promerops and Zosterops. Even so bounded, the family is hard to fix, for want of material. It holds some of the most characteristic birds of the Australian region; only one species is said to occur outside its limits.

All these birds have a long tongue that shoots out and ends in a brush-like tip, unlike that of any other bird. The tongue can form a tube to suck honey from the nectary of flowers. Yet the insects drawn by that honey feed many species chiefly, and others eat fruit as well. The birds are mostly small, never bigger than a missel thrush. They fall into more than 20 genera with above 200 species, most ranging over very small ground.
britannica-1911-hulke-john-whitaker:
John Whitaker Hulke (1830–1895) was a British surgeon and geologist. He was born on 6 November 1830, the son of a known doctor at Deal. He was schooled in part at a boarding school in England. He also spent two years at the Moravian College at Neuwied, where he learned German well. Visits to the Eifel district there woke his love of geology. He then went to King's College school in London.

Three years later Hulke began work at the hospital and took his first rank in surgery in 1852. In the Crimean War he gave his service as a helper in surgery at Smyrna and then at Sebastopol. Back home, he taught at his old hospital and rose in his field. He served at the Royal Ophthalmic Hospital at Moorfields, first as a helper and then as surgeon.
britannica-1911-hume-alexander:
Alexander Hume (about 1557-1609) was a Scottish poet, the second son of Patrick Hume of Polwarth in Berwickshire. He was most likely born at Reidbrais, one of the family houses, about 1557. He is thought to be the Alexander Hume who entered St Mary's College, St Andrews, in 1571. He took his degree there in 1574.

In a letter in verse Hume tells the tale of his own youth and its lost hopes. He spent four years in France, then read law for three years in the courts at Edinburgh. He left the law in disgust and sought a post at court. Still unmet in his hopes, he took orders. In 1597 he became minister of Logic, near Stirling, and lived there till his death on 4 December 1609. His best known work is his Hymns, or Sacred Songs, printed at Edinburgh in 1599.
britannica-1911-hunter-william-alexander:
William Alexander Hunter (1844-1898) was a Scottish jurist and politician from Aberdeen. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his schooling at Aberdeen and his call to the English bar. He was called in 1867 but soon turned mainly to teaching law. Chairs in Roman law and legal theory at London followed in turn.

His book Roman Law in the Order of a Code set his name in the field. A smaller guide for students shared that wide use as well. In 1885 he entered parliament for Aberdeen as a Liberal. He was first to urge old age pensions in that house. Poor health forced him out of politics in 1896.
britannica-1911-hutchinson-john-soldier:
John Hutchinson, a Puritan soldier, is followed in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1615, he was a Nottinghamshire knight's son of Owthorpe. Schools at Nottingham and Lincoln and Peterhouse, Cambridge, formed him. In 1637 he entered Lincoln's Inn to learn the law of England. When the great revolt broke out he took the side of parliament.

In 1643 Hutchinson took charge of Nottingham Castle as its governor. He held that post through raids from foes and strife within. In 1646 the shire sent him to sit in parliament at London. He signed the death warrant of the king in that hard age. Cromwell's later course drove him from public life in cold disgust. Seized in 1663 on a plot charge, he died in gaol.
britannica-1911-hutchinson-john-writer:
Hutchinson, John is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English theological writer. He was born at Spennithorne in Yorkshire in 1674 and died in 1737. He served as steward in several great houses. The duke of Somerset at last got him a quiet post worth about two hundred pounds a year.

In 1700 he met Dr John Woodward, a physician and writer on the earth's history. Hutchinson gave him a large set of fossils he had gathered, plus a mass of notes, to arrange and print. A quarrel grew over how the work should be handled. That quarrel drove Hutchinson to print his own Moses's Principia in 1724. In it he mocked Woodward's book and hinted darkly at his conduct. He also made a serious attempt to refute Newton's doctrine of gravity.
britannica-1911-hypsometer:
A hypsometer is a tool for measuring heights by the boiling point of a liquid, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains how it works. The name joins two Greek words, for height and for measure. The tool rests on a plain fact of nature. A liquid boils at a lower heat when the air pressure falls. Air pressure in turn drops as the place of viewing rises.

The tool is a round vessel where water is boiled. A jacketed column stands above it. Steam moves in the outer parts of the column. A thermometer sits in the central part. To turn a boiling point reading into a height, the user needs two known links. One joins boiling point to pressure, and the other joins pressure to height.
britannica-1911-iller: The Iller is a river of Bavaria, described in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It rises in the south-west corner of the kingdom, among the Algaeuer Alps, and flows north for a total length of 103 miles. It leaves the mountains at Immenstadt and passes Kempten, from which point rafts can use it. For part of its course it forms the border between Bavaria and Wuerttemberg. It then joins the Danube on the right bank, just above the city of Ulm.
britannica-1911-imperial-chamber:
The Imperial Chamber is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a high court. Its German name is given as Reichskammergericht in the text. It was the supreme court of the Holy Roman Empire. It sat from 1495 to the end of the Empire in 1806. Before it stood an older court, the Hofgericht. In that court the emperor sat in the chair himself.

By the emperor sat a body of assessors, at least seven in count. In grave cases their count could be much higher. The old court hung on the man of the emperor. It stopped when he was abroad, and it died with him. As respect for emperors sank, trust in that court sank too. The reign of Frederick the Third struck its death blow. It ceased to sit after 1450, and a new court took its place.
britannica-1911-inn-and-innkeeper:
Inn and innkeeper are taken up in a long article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. An inn is a house where wayfarers are fed and lodged for pay. The word is an old form of in or within, and the Inns of Court in London keep that sense. In the Bible the word means a lodging place for the night.

In the East, welcome for the traveller has long been a sacred duty. On crowded roads, rich men built khans and caravanserais at their own cost. Such a house was a square ring of rooms round a court, with space for beasts and bags. Guests bought their own food and fended for themselves. Greeks held inns and their keepers in low repute, the entry says. In Rome a thing like the modern inn grew up on the great roads.
britannica-1911-inn-river:
Inn is a river entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a major stream of Europe that feeds the Danube from the right. The stream rises in a small lake high in the Swiss Alps. It flows through a long high vale and then quits Swiss soil.

The entry follows its rush through a deep gorge into Austrian lands. Side streams swell it as it runs north east past walled towns. Boats can work its flow from one town down stream in its course. At one pass it cuts through hard rock beds to a broad flat. It meets the Danube with a flow as great as that river own.
britannica-1911-interloper:
Interloper is a word article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. An interloper is one who interferes in affairs that are not his concern. The word first appears at the end of the sixteenth century. It arose in trade, among the chartered companies and their rivals.

Unauthorized traders kept breaking into the monopolies of the Russia Company and the East India Company. Such men were called interlopers, and their act was interloping. The entry quotes the New English Dictionary for early uses of the word. One comes from Hakluyt's Voyages, where Dutch interlopers supply the Muscovites. Another comes from East India Company minutes of 1615. A dictionary of 1658 defines interlopers as those who intercept a company's trade without legal right. The piece shows how a word born in trade disputes spread into common speech.
britannica-1911-james-the-pretender:
James Francis Edward Stuart, who lived from 1688 to 1766, was the son and heir of James the Second of England. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born at Saint James's Palace on the tenth of June 1688. A false tale that he was a smuggled-in child has been fully disproved. As a baby he was sent to France when his father fled. He grew up at the court of Saint Germain.

On his father's death in 1701, Louis the Fourteenth named him king of England. His friends called him James the Third, while his foes called him the Old Pretender. A French fleet took him to the Firth of Forth in 1708, but the plan failed. After the Peace of Utrecht he left French soil. In 1715 his backers rose in the Scottish Highlands and raised his standard at Mar.
britannica-1911-joinder:
Joinder is a term of English law with more than one use, explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In its first sense it is the joining of more than one claim in a single action. A plaintiff may as a rule join such claims with no leave from the court. Suits to win back land are one bar to that free right.

Claims of husband and wife may join with claims of each one alone. Claims by an executor in his office may join with his own claims if both touch the same estate. A second sense is the point in a plea where both sides join on one issue and put the cause to trial. A third sense is the joining of parties in one suit. Folk who could sue apart on the same deal may be joined as plaintiffs in one action.
britannica-1911-jones-ebenezer:
Ebenezer Jones, a British poet, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Islington, London, in January eighteen twenty, he was of Welsh descent on his father's side. His father was a strict Calvinist. Ebenezer was taught at a dull middle class school, the entry says plainly.

His father's death forced him to become a clerk in a tea merchant's office. Shelley and Carlyle were his guiding spirits, and he spent all spare time in reading and writing. His style grew overblown, a flaw the entry links to gaps in his schooling. The cold reception of his first book deepened a bitter life.
britannica-1911-joseph-father:
Father Joseph, born François Leclerc du Tremblay (1577–1638), was a French Capuchin monk and the close confidant of Richelieu, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens his story. He was the eldest son of a president in the parlement of Paris. As a boy he had a careful training in the classics. In 1595 he made a long tour of Italy.

Joseph came home to take up the career of arms. He served at the siege of Amiens in 1597, then went with an embassy to London. In 1599, known at court as Baron de Mafflier, he renounced the world. He entered the Capuchin monastery at Orleans. He took to the religious life with great ardour. He became a noted preacher and reformer, and in 1606 aided a work of reform among nuns.
britannica-1911-juba-river:
The Juba, or Jub, is a river of East Africa more than 1000 miles long. It rises on the southeast border of the Abyssinian highlands and flows south across the Galla and Somali lands to the sea. Three streams join to form it, all rising in the range northeast of Lake Rudolf.

Of the three headstreams, the Web, the Ganale, and the Daua, the Ganale counts as the true upper course. Its far branch rises at about 7500 feet and runs at first over rock with swift water and rapids. Lower down it cuts a narrow valley far below the level of the land, then crosses a broad grass plain. The Web joins it from the east, and the Daua enters ten miles below. The entry follows the river reach by reach in close survey detail.
britannica-1911-juggler:
Juggler, from the Latin joculator, a jester, means in the modern sense a performer of sleight-of-hand tricks and neat feats of skill in tossing balls, plates, knives, and the like. The term is in practice one with conjurer. The joculatores of old were the mimes of the middle ages.

The French jongleurs, a faulty form of the same word, included the singers known as trouvères. The humbler English minstrels of that kind passed in time into strolling jugglers. From their shows the term spread to cover loosely any act of tumbling, dumb show, and sleight of hand. In ancient Rome such performers went by sharper names. The ventilatores were knife-throwers, and the pilarii were ball-players. The entry is brief: a word, its path through medieval showmen, and the Roman terms that split the trade by act.
britannica-1911-kalir-eleazer: Eleazer Kalir was a Hebrew liturgical poet whose hymns, or piyyutim, fill the festival prayers of the German synagogue rite. His segment sits in a hosted file shared with the Kalisch entries. The age in which he lived is not known. Some, resting on Saadiah's Sefer ha galuy, place him as early as the 6th century, while others put him in the 10th. His style is powerful but involved: a Hebrew Browning. Fine renderings of his poems appear in the Davis and Adler Festival Prayers.
britannica-1911-kanker: Kanker was a feudatory state of India within the Central Provinces. Its segment sits in a hosted file shared with Kangra and Kanishka material. The state covered 1429 square miles and held 103,536 people in 1901, with a revenue put at £10,000. It is a hilly tract that holds the headwaters of the Mahanadi. Its wide forests have lately been made profitable by the opening of a branch railway. The raja, of an old Rajput family though ruling over Gonds, lives at the town of Kanker, which held 3906 people.
britannica-1911-keep-robert-porter: Robert Porter Keep (1844–1904) was an American scholar, born in Farmington, Connecticut, on the 26th of April 1844. He graduated at Yale in 1865 and taught there for two years. He was consul at the Piraeus from 1869 to 1871, then taught Greek at Williston Seminary from 1876 to 1885. From 1885 to 1903 he was principal of Norwich Free Academy, a school that owed its prosperity largely to him. In 1903 he took charge of Miss Porter's school at Farmington, founded by his aunt Sarah Porter. He died at Farmington on the 3rd of June 1904.
britannica-1911-kidderminster:
Kidderminster, a market town in Worcestershire in England, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies north west of London and north of Worcester by rail. It stands on the river Stour and on a canal that joins two shires. Its count in nineteen hundred and one was twenty four thousand six hundred and ninety two.

The parish church stands well above the river. It is a fine work in two old styles, with a late part added in a third. Chief halls hold a town hall, the town board rooms, and a school of science and art with a free book house. A free school of the old type was set up in sixteen thirty seven. A park for play was opened in eighteen eighty seven.
britannica-1911-kingfisher: Kingfisher is the bird known to science as Alcedo ispida, as the 1911 Britannica entry states where its own text begins. The hosted text opens with the tail of the King-crab article, and only the first lines of the bird entry are present. Those lines call the kingfisher one of the most fair and best known of European birds. They add that it is found across the region, though nowhere in great numbers.
britannica-1911-kipper:
Kipper, in its first sense, names the male salmon at a stage of the breeding season, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. At that time the male grows a sharp beak of gristle. That beak is called the kip, and the fish name is said to come from it.

Old uses of the word are not clear, and the root is in doubt. Some uses seem to cover salmon of both sexes. Writers used the term for fish in and after spawning. Breeding salmon were often said to be poor food. Split, salted, and smoke dried fish took the same name in time. Herrings cured that way are the best known case, while a bloater is cured whole.
britannica-1911-kuban-river:
The Kuban is a river of southern Russia. It rises on the west slope of Elbruz in the Caucasus, 13,930 feet up, and races down the north face as a mountain torrent. On reaching the steppe south of Stavropol it turns north-west at 1075 feet, then west, and enters the Gulf of Kyzyl-tash on the Black Sea, near the Straits of Kerch. Its whole length is 500 miles, and its basin covers 21,480 square miles.

In its lower course the river runs through marshes. At flood time it spreads from its normal 700 feet to over half a mile wide. Steamers can use it for 73 miles, as far as the meeting with its branch the Laba, which is 200 miles long. Its other branches, the Byelaya, Urup and the Great and Little Zelenchuk, all join it from the left. The Kuban is the ancient Hypanis and Vardanes.
britannica-1911-l-estrange-sir-roger:
Sir Roger L'Estrange (1616–1704) was an English pamphleteer of the royalist side in the Restoration age. He is chiefly marked as the first English man of letters of any standing who made journalism a trade. He was born at Hunstanton in Norfolk on the 17th of December 1616. In 1644, in the civil war, he led a plot to seize Lynn for the king and was condemned to death as a spy. After four years in Newgate he escaped abroad, and in 1653 Cromwell pardoned him at his own plea.

At the Restoration L'Estrange became licenser of the press. He ran the office as a zealous cavalier, harsh in censorship. In 1663 he began the Public Intelligencer and the News, from which the London Gazette grew in 1665. His Observator of 1679 defended the court against the charge of secret popery. Yet in 1687 he shut the Observator rather than back James II's Edict of Toleration.
britannica-1911-lacquer:
Lacquer is a general name for coloured, often opaque varnishes laid on certain metal objects and on wood. The word comes from the resin lac, the base of lacquers properly so called. In the West, lacquering means coating polished metals such as brass, pewter and tin with prepared varnishes that give them a golden, bronze-like or other lustre.

In the East Indies lacquered wood is everywhere: large pieces of household furniture, small boxes, trays, toys and papier-mâché objects are decorated in bright, varied colours. The Eastern lacquer is generally coloured sealing-wax, applied, smoothed and polished hot, and worked by various devices into marbled, streaked and mottled designs. The lacquer work of Japan stands quite apart from all these.
britannica-1911-langtoft-peter:
Peter Langtoft (died about 1307) was an English writer of history who took his name from a Yorkshire village and served as a canon at the priory in Bridlington. His Chronicle, written in French verse, covers England from its earliest times down to the death of Edward I in 1307.

Three parts hold about 9,000 rhyming lines in all. Early sections lean on Geoffrey of Monmouth and other writers. For Edward's reign Langtoft wrote as a man of the time, and that part holds real worth, above all for the north of England and for Scotland. Robert Mannyng turned the last part into English verse about 1330, and the Chronicle was later printed in the Rolls Series.
britannica-1911-langton-walter:
Walter Langton (died 1321) climbed from the royal chancery to become bishop of Lichfield and treasurer of England under Edward I. He joined the suit over the Scottish crown in 1292, went to France on royal business, took the treasury in 1295, and gained Lichfield the next year.

Charges of murder, adultery, and misuse of church wealth brought suspension and a trial path through Rome, yet the archbishop who heard the case found him not guilty in 1303. Edward stood by him to the end and named him chief executor. Under Edward II his luck broke: arrest, seized lands, and long prison years followed. Freed in 1312, he served again as treasurer, sat on the council, and died in November 1321.
britannica-1911-lauder:
Lauder is a royal burgh in Berwickshire, Scotland, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a short gazetteer entry with a dark tale. The burgh stands on the Leader river, twenty nine miles south east of Edinburgh. It held 719 people in 1901, and a branch rail line ends there. The burgh is said to date from the reign of William the Lion.

Its charter was granted in 1502, long after its founding. In 1482 King James the Third rested at Lauder with his court and army. The king was on his way to raise the siege of Berwick. While the nobles met in the church to air grievances, a royal favourite sought entry. That man was Robert Cochrane, newly made earl of Mar. Archibald Douglas seized him at the door, and he was dragged off to Lauder Bridge.
britannica-1911-le-daim-olivier:
Olivier Le Daim, favourite of King Louis the Eleventh of France, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born of humble parentage at Thielt in Flanders. Seeking his fortune at Paris, he became court barber and valet to the king. His gift for pleasing Louis raised him fast and far.

In 1474 the king ennobled him, and three years later made him Count of Meulant. Sent to Burgundy to sway the heiress of Charles the Bold, he was mocked and driven from Ghent. He answered by seizing Tournai for France. His enemies said he could be counted on for the king's baser designs. He grew rich, it was charged, by oppression and force. When Louis died, the lords he had slighted struck back. He was tried at Paris and hanged at Montfaucon in May 1484.
britannica-1911-ledger:
Ledger is a word of many uses, traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. At root it names a book that stays put in one place. So the great Bibles and service books kept in a church were called ledgers. A quote from a chronicle of 1538 bids curates keep such a book for the flock to read.

Trade took the word for the chief book of accounts in a house of business. Off that stem, more uses grew in time. A ledger is also a flat run of timber in a scaffold, laid along the face of a wall. It is a flat stone laid over a grave, and a fixed rig of hooks and bait used by anglers. In the form lieger it once named an envoy who lived at a court for good.
britannica-1911-leicester:
Leicester is a borough and the county town of Leicestershire, England. It stands on the river Soar, a south branch of the Trent. Its people numbered 174,624 in 1891 and 211,579 in 1901. The Midland railway puts it 99 miles north-north-west of London. Other lines and the Leicester canal also serve the town. Leicester was the Roman Ratae, and Roman remains of high note are kept there.

Those remains include a piece of Roman wall known as the Jewry Wall and floors found in the ground. The museum holds a milestone from the Fosse Way, set two miles from Ratae. St Nicholas church is a good case of early Norman work, built in part with Roman bricks. St Mary de Castro shows Norman parts and rich Early English work in its tower. The article goes on to the town's other old churches, such as All Saints and St Martin's.
britannica-1911-lely-sir-peter:
Sir Peter Lely is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English painter. He lived from 1617 to 1680. He was born at Soest in Westphalia in 1617. His father was a Dutch military captain by birth. The family name was at first van der Vaes. He studied two years under Peter de Grebber at Haarlem.

Charles the First's patronage of art drew him to England. He removed there in the year 1641. At first he painted historical subjects and landscape. He soon rose so high in his profession that Charles employed him. He afterwards portrayed Cromwell in the same role. At the Restoration, Charles the Second favoured him greatly. The king made him state painter and later knighted him. He formed a famous collection of art in his life. It held drawings, prints, and paintings by the best masters.
britannica-1911-leo-brother:
Brother Leo (died about 1270) stood closest to St Francis of Assisi. He served the saint as disciple, secretary, and confessor. In the last years of Francis he belonged to the small trusted circle. Birth dates and the date he joined the order are not known.

After the saint died, Leo fought Elias and his plans. He smashed the marble box Elias set up for gifts at Assisi. Elias had him scourged for that act. The blow hardened the revolt and brought Elias down. Leo led the early fight to keep strict poverty in the order. His voice shaped the Spirituals and their tale of Francis. He sat at St Clara's deathbed in 1253. He died at the Portiuncula, very old.
britannica-1911-letter:
Letter carries more than one sense, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sorts them out in a short entry. At its base a letter is a sign for one basic sound in a spoken word. It is one part of an alphabet. The word comes through French from the Latin word littera.

The same word also means a note sent from one person to another. In the plural it covers formal legal papers such as letters patent. It can also mean learning or books in a broad sense. Readers get a clear map of how one short word grew several linked uses.
britannica-1911-lightfoot-joseph-barber:
Joseph Barber Lightfoot, an English theologian and bishop of Durham who lived from 1828 to 1889, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Liverpool, the son of an accountant, he was schooled at King Edward's school in Birmingham under James Prince Lee. There he had as school fellows Westcott and Benson, both later famed churchmen.

In 1847 Lightfoot went up to Trinity College at Cambridge and read for his degree beside Westcott. He graduated as senior classic and was elected a fellow of his college. From 1854 he edited a journal of classical and sacred philology for five years. In 1857 he became a tutor, and his fame as a scholar grew fast. He was made Hulsean professor in 1861, and soon chaplain to the Prince Consort and to the queen. His sermons were not marked by eloquence. Their solidity and clear speech won hearers.
britannica-1911-logan-john-alexander:
John Alexander Logan (1826-1886) was an American soldier and leader in politics. Jackson county, Illinois, was his birthplace on 9 February 1826. No schooling came till age fourteen. Three years at Shiloh College and Mexican War service followed. Law study in an uncle's office led to a Louisville law degree in 1851.

County clerk, state house seats, and a prosecutor's post built his start. Congress took him as a Democrat in 1858 and 1860. He fought at Bull Run with no post held. Then he quit his seat and raised the 31st Illinois. Vicksburg's fall saw his men first inside the town. High command in the Army of the Tennessee came at Atlanta. Peace turned him Republican. House years ran 1867 to 1871. Senate years ran 1871 to 1877 and 1879 to his death at Washington on 26 December 1886.
britannica-1911-lycurgus-spartan-lawgive:
Lycurgus, in Greek history the reputed founder of the Spartan constitution, is the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Plutarch opens his life of Lycurgus by warning that no statement about him goes unquestioned. His family, travels, death, and above all his laws are all variously recorded. Even his date is disputed. Modern criticism, the article says, has reached no certain results.

Many scholars suppose Lycurgus was in truth a god or hero. A temple and cult of Lycurgus existed at Sparta in the time of Herodotus. The Delphic oracle seems to call him more god than man. Yet most modern historians accept him as a real person, while differing widely about his work. Spartan tradition made him a member of the Agiad house. On his brother's death he became regent and guardian of his young nephew. Other accounts give a different line.
britannica-1911-lysander:
Lysander, the Spartan sea lord, is weighed in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son of Aristocritus, he may have had a helot mother, tales say. Plutarch makes him a Heraclid, though not of a royal house. How he rose is not known till he took the fleet in 407. That year he won the ear of Cyrus the Younger of Persia.

His sea win off Notium and his clash with his heir mark 406. In 405 he struck the great blow at Aegospotami creek. Athens fell to siege and gave up with his hand in it. By 404 he stood as the strongest man in Greece. He set bands of ten to rule towns in place of free rule. Kings and ephors grew jealous and called him home.
britannica-1911-macdonald-sir-john-alexa:
Macdonald, Sir John Alexander is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the first premier of the dominion of Canada. John Alexander Macdonald was born in Glasgow on the eleventh of January 1815 and died in 1891. His family crossed to Canada in 1820 and settled at Kingston, Ontario. At fifteen he entered a law office.

He was called to the bar in 1836 and set up practice in Kingston, with success from the first. He began his career at a tense time, the year before the rising of 1837. The whole land was unsettled, split by race and party strife that seemed hard to heal. During the rising the young lawyer served as a volunteer, though his soldiering went no further than drill and marching.
britannica-1911-macdowell-edward-alexand:
Edward Alexander MacDowell, an American composer, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica.
