Born in New York City in eighteen sixty one, he was the son of an Irishman from Belfast. His music training was broad, first with Spanish American teachers. He then studied in Europe, at Paris, Stuttgart, Wiesbaden, and Weimar.

The entry names Joachim, Raff, and Liszt as key guides in those years. From eighteen seventy nine he lived in Germany, teaching, studying, and playing as a solo pianist. He wed Marian Nevins in eighteen eighty four. Back in America he settled in Boston, then became professor of music at Columbia in eighteen ninety six.
britannica-1911-mackennal-alexander:
Alexander Mackennal, who lived from 1835 to 1904, was an English free church minister. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Truro in Cornwall. His father was a Scot who had settled there. The family moved to London when the boy was thirteen. Glasgow and Hackney College trained him for the Congregational ministry. Pastorates at Burton, Surbiton, and Leicester followed in turn.

From 1877 he held the church at Bowdon in Cheshire until his death. In 1886 he chaired the Congregational Union. The first world council of his church group, held in London in 1891, grew from that trip. He served as its secretary. Later he led the push to join the free churches in one federation. The plan sought joint work and worship where it could be had. Anglicans alone stood apart from the scheme.
britannica-1911-mackenzie-alexander:
Mackenzie, Alexander, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a Canadian statesman. Born in Perthshire, Scotland, on the 28th of January 1822, he was a builder's son. He crossed to Canada in 1842 and worked as a stone-mason. Later he set up as a builder at Sarnia with his brother.

In 1852 his zeal for reform made him editor of a Liberal paper. That post brought him to the front of public life fast. In 1861 he won a seat in the Canadian assembly as a member. He rose to lead the Liberal side against the government in time. In 1873 the fall of Macdonald's ministry gave him his chance. He formed a new government as first Liberal premier of Canada.
britannica-1911-malou-jules-edouard-xavi:
Jules Edouard Xavier Malou (1810-1886) was a Belgian statesman and a leader of the clerical party. He was born at Ypres on 19 October 1810. He was a civil servant in the justice office when his home town chose him for the Chamber of Deputies in 1841. He served for a time as governor of Antwerp. In 1844 he was minister of finance in a joint ministry.

In 1846 Malou formed a Catholic cabinet with de Theux. It fell in the Liberal win of 1847, and Malou moved to the senate. His party came back to the fore only in 1870. After grave riots in Brussels, Malou was the true head of the milder clerical rule that ran from 1870 to 1878. He kept the finance post in his own hands. He also kept his party clear of loud support for German Catholics in the Kulturkampf fight.
britannica-1911-manometer:
A manometer is a tool for gauging the push of gases and vapours. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica starts from a plain U shaped tube of liquid. If the push on both arms is equal, the liquid stands level. If one side pushes harder, that side sinks. The gap in height tracks the gap in push. It also shifts with the weight of the liquid used.

Two forms are in use, the entry explains. In the open tube form, one arm meets the open air. The other arm's push is read off a scale behind the tube. Mercury is the liquid most often used. In the closed tube form, the test push is set against trapped air. That trapped air is squeezed as the push grows. The maths for the closed form is harder, since the air's own push changes too.
britannica-1911-map-walter:
Walter Map, also called Mapes, died about 1208 or 1209 and was a church wit. The 1911 Britannica life hails him as author and court jester of note. Much prose lore of King Arthur was once laid at his door. He thrived in the late 1100s and the first years of the 1200s. No firm facts survive on his birth or on his parentage.

Map himself hints that his parents held some rank at court. He studied at Paris under Girard la Pucelle in his youth. By his own book he was at the court of Henry the Second before 1162. His work life mixed church posts with royal service at court. He served as clerk of the royal household and as a travelling judge.
britannica-1911-marlowe-christopher:
Christopher Marlowe, an English dramatist who lived from 1564 to 1593, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The article calls him the father of English tragedy. It also names him the founder of dramatic blank verse. He was the eldest son of a Canterbury shoemaker.

Marlowe was born at Canterbury in February 1564, weeks before Shakespeare's birth year. He was christened at St George's church in that city. At the King's School he sat beside boys who later rose high in Ireland and letters. He won a scholarship to Cambridge and took his first degree in 1584. A master's degree followed three or four years later. A college tutor burned for heresy may have shaped his bold views on religion.
britannica-1911-martello-tower:
Martello Tower is a fortification article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a kind of tower once used in English coast defence. The name is a worn form of Mortella. The tower came in after an event of the French revolutionary wars. In September 1793 a British squadron moved to aid Corsican rebels.

First it had to take a tower on Cape Mortella that commanded the one safe anchorage in the Gulf of San Fiorenzo. The tower mounted one twenty-four-pounder and two eighteen-pounders on its top. Frigates shelled it for a short time. Its small garrison then left, and a landing party took it. The French later retook the tower from the Corsicans. Up to that point, the article says, it had done nothing to earn its later fame. A fresh attempt in 1794 changed that story.
britannica-1911-martin-francois-xavier:
François Xavier Martin, who lived from 1762 to 1846, was an American judge and author born in Marseilles, France. The 1911 Britannica article traces his path from France to Martinique and then to North Carolina. There he taught French, learned English, and worked as a printer. He read law and joined the North Carolina bar in 1789. He also sat in the state assembly in 1806 and 1807.

Most of the article deals with his long work in Louisiana law. Martin served as a judge in the Orleans Territory and then on the state supreme court until 1846. He wrote case reports and a digest of local laws. The text says he won the name of father of Louisiana law, since the law there mixed French, Spanish, and new American rules.
britannica-1911-martin-luther:
Luther Martin, an American lawyer born in New Jersey in seventeen forty eight, led his college class. He graduated at the college of New Jersey in seventeen sixty six at its head. He then moved to Maryland, teaching at Queenstown until seventeen seventy. He was admitted to the bar in seventeen seventy one and practised in Virginia. Back in Maryland he rose to lead the bar of that state.

Martin served as attorney general of Maryland from seventeen seventy eight to eighteen o five. He sat in the Continental Congress and in the Constitutional Convention of seventeen eighty seven. There he opposed the constitution and refused to sign it at the close. He later joined the Federalists and fought Jefferson in politics. His fame rests in part on two great defences in court. He defended Judge Samuel Chase and Aaron Burr in famed trials.
britannica-1911-matthew-of-westminster:
Matthew of Westminster is the name of a man who in truth never was. For long he was held as the hand past a Latin tale of English deeds. A knight in eighteen twenty-six first showed the fault in that view. A peer in time proved it past doubt.

The name seems made from that of a famed Paris tale man, whose great work was the source of the first part. The last part takes the name of the abbey where part was writ. The tale spans from the make of the world to the year thirteen twenty-six. Its worth is held as slight past one reign.
britannica-1911-mcclernand-john-alexande:
John Alexander McClernand, an American soldier and lawyer who lived from 1812 to 1900, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Kentucky, he was admitted to the bar in Illinois in 1832. He served as a volunteer in the Black Hawk War that year. In 1835 he founded a Democratic newspaper, which he then edited.

McClernand sat in the Illinois house and then in Congress for two spans. In his second span he was a strong Unionist and moved a pledge of men and money in July 1861. He gave up his seat, raised a brigade in Illinois, and became a brigadier general. He fought at Belmont and at Fort Donelson, and led a division at Shiloh. Friction with Grant and his peers marred his Vicksburg campaign. Grant relieved him of command in June after a breach of orders.
britannica-1911-mcclure-sir-robert-john-:
Sir Robert John le Mesurier McClure is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English Arctic explorer. He was born at Wexford in Ireland in 1807. He died in 1873, the heading notes. His father, an army captain, died before his birth. His godfather, a general, raised and schooled him for the army. He chose the navy instead and joined in 1824. His first Arctic work came twelve years later.

He sailed as mate of the Terror in 1836 and 1837. That voyage was led by Captain George Back. On return he gained his rank as lieutenant. He served on the Canadian lakes in the next two years. He then served in North America and the West Indies till 1846. In 1848 he joined the search for Franklin's lost ships. He sailed as first lieutenant of the Enterprise. A new command, the Investigator, came his way next.
britannica-1911-meer-jan-van-der:
Jan van der Meer, better known as Vermeer of Delft, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He lived from 1632 to 1675 as a Dutch painter. The Dutch biographers tell us little of his life. He was born at Delft and learned painting under Carel Fabritius.

In 1653 Vermeer married and entered the guild of St Luke at Delft. Twice he headed that guild. He died at Delft in 1675, leaving a widow and eight children. He left twenty-six pictures unsold, and his widow sought the court's protection. For more than two centuries the painter was almost wholly forgotten. His works sold under the names and forged marks of greater favourites. An exiled French critic first recalled the art world to his worth.
britannica-1911-merganser:
Merganser, a group of fish eating ducks, is explained in a nature entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name was coined by Gesner in 1555 and long served as the group name in English. These ducks dive with great power. They have a long, narrow bill with a small hook at the tip.

Both edges of the bill carry rows of horny teeth, which earn them the name saw bill. All kinds wear a crest or tuft on the head. Three kinds range across the north of the Old World, and two of those also live in North America. The goosander is the largest, near the size of a small goose. Its adult male in breeding dress has a dark green head and a salmon breast. The red breasted merganser is smaller, and the smew is smallest of all.
britannica-1911-merimee-prosper:
Prosper Mérimée, who lived from 1803 to 1870, was a French writer of tales. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica ranks him among the great masters of French style. He was born in Paris in 1803. His father was a painter of good name. He was trained for the bar but chose state service. The romantic wave shaped his youth, though he joined no school.

His first fame came from two bold hoaxes. In 1825 he issued plays said to be by a Spanish lady, Clara Gazul. The tale of how he found them was pure invention. In 1827 came La Guzla, songs said to be rendered from Illyrian verse. There was no such source book at all. The fake fooled real Slav scholars and the poet Pushkin. His stock of that tongue was a handful of words.
britannica-1911-messager-andre-charles-p:
Andre Charles Prosper Messager, a French musician born in 1853, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was born at Montluçon in December 1853 and studied at Paris. In 1874 he became organist at St Sulpice. For some time he was a pupil of Saint-Saëns. In 1876 he won the gold medal of the Société des Compositeurs with a symphony.

In 1880 Messager was made music director at a Paris church. He completed another man's comic opera in 1883 and produced his own operettas in 1885. His ballet Les Deux pigeons reached the Paris Opéra in 1886. His comic opera La Basoche, staged in 1890, fixed his reputation. Tuneful light operas followed, among them Véronique in 1898, a great success in London. He also conducted at the Opéra Comique and at Covent Garden.
britannica-1911-meuse-river:
Meuse, called Maes in Flemish and Maas in Dutch, is a river rising at Pouilly in the French department of Haute Marne, as this 1911 Britannica article describes it. After passing through a great part of Belgium and Holland it flows into the Waal channel of the Rhine at Fort Loevenstein. Some miles below Gorinchem the river splits into two branches.

The northern branch flows almost due west, joins the Lek above Rotterdam, and enters the North Sea at the Hook of Holland. Sea-going steamers for Rotterdam use the New Waterway, a little north of the Meuse. The southern branch turns south through the marsh of Biesbosch and reaches the sea by arms called Haringvliet and Krammer. The Meuse is nearly 560 miles long, of which 360 are navigable, and its traffic is likely beaten only by that of the Rhine.
britannica-1911-mews-peter:
Peter Mews, an English royalist and divine who lived from 1619 to 1706, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Caundle Purse in Dorset in March 1619. He was schooled in London and at St John's College in Oxford, where he was scholar and fellow. When the Civil War broke out in 1642 he joined the king's army.

He rose to captain and was taken at Naseby, but was soon freed. In 1648 he fled to Holland and grew close to the king's secretary. His gift for disguise made him of great use to the royal cause under Cromwell, and he made two secret trips to Scotland. At the Restoration he won back his fellowship and piled up church posts. In 1672 he became bishop of Bath and Wells, and in 1684 bishop of Winchester. He held that see till his death in 1706.
britannica-1911-michel-francisque-xavier:
Francisque Xavier Michel, a French antiquary who lived from 1809 to 1887, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Lyons, he became known for his editions of French works of the middle ages. The French government, seeing their worth, sent him to England in 1833 and to Scotland in 1837 to carry on his searches there.

In 1839 he was made professor of foreign writing at Bordeaux. Between 1834 and 1842 he issued editions of many works from the eleventh to fourteenth centuries. They were in French, English, and Saxon, and included noted poems of the age. Later he published French versions of Goldsmith, Sterne, Shakespeare, and Tennyson. His own works range over cursed races in France and Spain, trade in the middle ages, and Scots in France.
britannica-1911-miller-william-engraver:
William Miller is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Miller was a Scottish line engraver who lived from 1796 to 1882. He was born in Edinburgh and studied in London under a noted teacher. He returned to Edinburgh and cut plates after Scottish landscape painters. His chief works were his copies of the paintings of Turner.

The article lists the great book projects that used his plates. Among his larger Turner plates are scenes of Venice, the Rhine, and the Tower of London. Turner himself valued Miller's art warmly. Ruskin judged him the most successful translator of Turner into line. Late in life he turned to water colours, then took up his tool again for a last set of small plates. He died in 1882.
britannica-1911-miller-william-soldier:
William Miller, a British soldier who lived from 1795 to 1861, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He took a leading part in the South American wars of liberation. He entered the British artillery in 1811 and served with Wellington in the Peninsula until 1814. That year he joined the ill fated expedition to New Orleans.

After the general peace he travelled in Europe for two years, then went to South America. War to expel the Spanish was just breaking out there. He took command in the Chilean artillery and later led marines on a famed warship. In 1821 he landed in Peru to aid San Martin. Made a general, he grew close to Bolivar. His regiment won glory at the decisive victory of Ayacucho in 1824.
britannica-1911-milo-of-gloucester:
Milo of Gloucester was lord of Brecknock and earl of Hereford, and he died in eleven forty-three. He was the son of Walter of Gloucester, a sheriff of that shire. Milo took his fathers posts and served King Henry the First with trust. He held the roles of sheriff and judge for his shire at once.

When Henry died, Milo at first stood with Stephen. He then switched to the cause of Matilda when she came in eleven thirty-nine. He gave her the town of Gloucester and sacked Worcester for her sake. She made him an earl, and he stayed true to her through her loss at Winchester.
britannica-1911-monier-williams-sir-moni:
Sir Monier Monier-Williams, a British orientalist who lived from 1819 to 1899, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a colonel who was surveyor-general in the Bombay presidency. He was born at Bombay in November 1819. He went to Oxford in 1837 but left on a post in the civil service of the East India Company.

His mother, who had lost a son in India, won him back from that path. He went to Oxford once more and gave himself to Sanskrit, and he won the Boden prize in 1843. He taught eastern tongues at Haileybury and then at Cheltenham. In 1860 he was picked as Boden professor of Sanskrit at Oxford, after a famed fight with Max Muller that drew wide note. His works in Sanskrit are praised as first rate, among them word books of Sanskrit and English both ways.
britannica-1911-monster:
Monster is a science article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin term tied to warning, since a monster was seen as something dire or portentous. In zoology, monsters or monstrous births fall under a branch of study that treats departures from normal growth of the embryo. The entry sets that study's scope at the start.

It draws a line between two stages of early life. The embryo is the unborn young in its first three months, while rudiments of form are still forming. The foetus is the same being in later months, growing on lines already laid down. Most departures that show as monstrosities at birth begin in the first stage, the article says. Slight early flaws can grow with the body into grave defects, often barring life outside the womb.
britannica-1911-montdidier:
Montdidier is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Montdidier is a town of northern France, in the department of Somme. It stands on a rise above the right bank of the Don. The town dates from Merovingian times and may take its name from a Lombard king held prisoner there.

The article is chiefly a tour of its old buildings. The church of St Pierre holds fonts from the eleventh century and a count's tomb. The church of St Sepulcre is known for its Holy Sepulchre work inside. The law court, once the castle, keeps fine tapestries from the seventeenth century. A statue honors Antoine Parmentier, born in the town in 1737. He is linked with the start of potato growing in France. The entry suits readers who like small towns with long memories.
britannica-1911-montgomerie-alexander:
Alexander Montgomerie was a Scottish poet who lived from about 1550 to about 1610. His life is told in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the second son of Hugh Montgomerie of Hessilhead in Ayrshire. Part of his youth was spent in Argyll, and a time at Compston Castle in Galloway. He served the regent Morton and then the king, James the Sixth.

In 1583 the crown gave him a pension, made sure by grant. Three years later he set out on a tour of France, Flanders, and other lands. He seems to have got in trouble, been held in prison abroad, and lost the king's grace and his pension for a time. No record of his last years stands. His chief poem is The Cherry and the Slae, first printed in 1597. It was printed again and again in the next two centuries and twice put in Latin dress.
britannica-1911-montpelier:
Montpelier is a city in Vermont, the state capital, and the seat of Washington county. It stands on the Winooski river, forty miles by rail from Burlington. Its people numbered seven thousand eight hundred fifty six in nineteen ten. Two rail lines serve the city. Barre granite is mined much in the area near it. The city makes marble and granite goods, flour, lumber, and saddlery hardware.

The chief building is the state house, topped by a figure of Agriculture. It was first used in eighteen thirty six and was near destroyed by fire in eighteen fifty seven. The town was granted in seventeen eighty and first settled for good in seventeen eighty seven. It was chosen as state capital in eighteen o five. The law makers first met there in eighteen o eight.
britannica-1911-montpellier:
Montpellier is the subject of a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Montpellier is a town in southern France, chief town of the Herault district. It lies a few miles from the sea, on a plain near the small river Lez. By 1906 its people numbered near sixty six thousand. It held a university and a famed medical school.

The article walks through the main squares and streets. It notes the Peyrou terrace, with its wide view and its arch for King Louis the Fourteenth. It describes the cathedral, once a monastery church, hurt in the wars of religion. It also notes the old botanic garden, the law courts, and the Fabre museum. The museum holds rich groups of French and foreign paintings.
britannica-1911-montreuil-sur-mer:
Montreuil-sur-Mer, a town of northern France in the department of Pas-de-Calais, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands 24 miles south of Boulogne by rail. Its people numbered 2,883 in 1906. The town, with its old citadel and ramparts largely due to Vauban, sits prettily on a rise. It stands on the left bank of the Canche, ten miles from the Channel.

The chief buildings are the church of St Saulve, of mixed date, and a hospital founded in 1200, with a fine Flamboyant chapel. Buildings of the old abbey of Ste Austreberthe also remain. Montreuil is the seat of a sub-prefect and has a court of first instance. The town owes its origin to a seventh-century monastery founded by St Saulve, bishop of Amiens.
britannica-1911-mortimer:
Mortimer is a family history in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, tracing the Mortimers of Wigmore. They became earls of March and Ulster in later days. The stock was akin to the dukes of Normandy and to great houses of the duchy. Their ancestor Hugh was bishop of Coutances in the year 990.

Hugh's son Roger took his name from Mortemer in the Pays de Caux. At the battle fought in his own village, Roger helped beat the French. Yet he freed a foe of his duke, and for that act lost his castle. The castle went to his nephew, William of Warenne. The Conqueror drove Roger from Normandy and never gave the place back. Still the family kept the surname drawn from that lost seat. Their arms, like Warenne's, plainly show the common root of the two houses.
britannica-1911-mowat-sir-oliver:
Sir Oliver Mowat, a Canadian judge and statesman who lived from 1820 to 1903, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of John Mowat, who fought in the Peninsular War under Wellesley. He was born at Kingston in Ontario in July 1820 and taught at home. In 1836 he began the study of law under John Macdonald.

He joined the bar in 1841 and soon led as a counsel in chancery. He entered parliament in 1858 as a Liberal and became postmaster-general in 1863. He took a chief part in the Quebec Conference of 1864, which set the terms for the union of the provinces. That year he was made vice-chancellor of Upper Canada. In 1872 he became premier of Ontario and held the post until 1896. His laws were copied by other provinces and by states of the union.
britannica-1911-musk-deer:
Musk Deer is a beast entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a small odd deer of the high hills of Asia. Both sexes lack the crown of horns worn by most deer kin. The males bear long tusk teeth that jut below the chin.

The entry gives its height at the shoulder as less than a roe deer. Long hind legs and free hoof joints suit its leaps on crags. Its coat is long, coarse, and prone to snap like dry pith. Grey brown hues with pale flecks mark most of the herd. The deer haunts high woods and is rare below a great height in summer.
britannica-1911-neumunster:
Neumunster is a town in the north of Germany, set on both banks of a small river. The 1911 Britannica entry calls it, after one port town, the chief work town of its province. Rail lines meet there to ports, to the Danish border, and to the coast.

The entry lists its two churches and its schools, then its trades at length. Large cloth works lead, with shops for leather, cotton cloth, wadding, rugs, paper, machines, beer, and sweets. Its trade is brisk as well. The name came from a house of monks founded by a famed mission man of Holstein, first writ as a new monastery in an old deed. Mill folk who moved there in a past age set its work life in train.
britannica-1911-north-roger:
Roger North, an English lawyer and biographer who lived from 1653 to 1734, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was the sixth son of the fourth Baron North. He built up a good practice at the bar. His elder brother Francis helped him on that path. Francis became lord chancellor and was created Baron Guilford.

In 1684 North became solicitor-general. The Revolution, though, stopped his rise. He retired to his estate of Rougham in Norfolk. He grew his fortune by marrying the daughter of Sir Robert Gayer. He collected books and was constantly busy with writing. He is best known for his Lives of the Norths. Those lives came out after his death, with his own autobiography. The text calls that work a classic authority for the period. He died at Rougham, as the article goes on to tell. A stopped career left England a family chronicle.
britannica-1911-notker:
Notker, a name borne by more than one church man of the Middle Ages, is treated in a 1911 Britannica article. The first, Notker Balbulus, lived from near 840 to 912 in north Switzerland. He taught for years at the school of Saint Gall. He made a book of martyr lives and other works.

Balbulus is famed most for his work for church music and for the sequences he composed. He was made a saint in 1513. The second man, Notker Labeo, died in 1022 and also taught at Saint Gall. He rendered many works into Old High German. His texts list the Psalms, works of Aristotle, and the Consolation of Boethius. They hold great worth for the study of tongues.
britannica-1911-oder:
Oder is a river of Germany that rises in Austria, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Its source sits high on a Moravian table land. From source to its mouth in the Baltic, the river runs five hundred sixty miles. Boats and barges can use most of that length.

The river drains a vast area of more than forty thousand square miles. Its first stretch lies in Moravia, then it forms a border for a short way. The rest belongs to Prussia, through Silesia, Brandenburg, and Pomerania. It flows south east at first, then turns north west. Near its mouth it splits into many arms and forms islands. It then widens into a lagoon linked to the sea by three channels.
britannica-1911-odoacer:
Odoacer was the first barbarian ruler of Italy after the Western empire fell. He lived from about four thirty four to four ninety three. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born near the middle Danube, in lands once held by Rome.

German tribes such as the Rugii, Scyrri, Turcilingi, and Heruli tore at that region. All four groups later claimed Odoacer as one of their own kin. The entry weighs proof for his birth and leans toward the Scyrri. It also tests claims about his father and finds them in doubt. A tale tells of a tall youth in skins who sought a blessing from Severinus.
britannica-1911-ohio-river:
Ohio River is a geography article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the chief eastern tributary of the Mississippi river in the United States. The Ohio forms where the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers join at Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, and flows 967 miles to the Mississippi. No branch of the Mississippi pours in more water, and only the Missouri beats it in length and basin size.

The steepest drop comes at Louisville, where the stream falls near 24 feet in just over two miles over a mass of limestone. Great branches feed it from both sides, among them the Muskingum, Scioto, Miami, and Wabash from the north and the Kentucky, Cumberland, and Tennessee from the south. Sudden floods can lift the river 30 to 50 feet.
britannica-1911-old-deer:
Old Deer, a Buchan village with a lost book, is placed in a site entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the South Ugie Water in Aberdeenshire, Scotland. Peterhead lies ten miles east of the village by the road. In 1901 the parish held over four thousand folk in count. Distilling, brewing, and woollen work give trade to the place.

Columba and his nephew Drostan founded a cloister there in old times. No trace of that sixth century house stands on the ground now. In 1857 a small Gospel book of its monks came to light. It had slept in the Cambridge library since the year 1715. Gaelic notes in it rank among the oldest Scots Gaelic we have. John Stuart brought it out in print in the year 1869.
britannica-1911-osier:
Osier is the common name for the willow species and hybrids used in making baskets, and this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article describes them. The word comes through French from a late Latin term for a bundle of willow twigs. The chief species in cultivation are named, with the common osier first. That species, with some forty varieties, long formed the staple basket material in England.

The common osier crops heavily and can reach thirteen feet on low-lying soils. Being pithy, it serves mainly for coarse work as brown stuff. Harder kinds, called stone osiers, are raised on drier soils, peeled, and used for fine work. Another species is used by market gardeners for tying up greens. Demand for finer work has lately turned growers to tougher species.
britannica-1911-oyster:
Oyster is the common name for a group of shell fish that live fixed in one place. Their life of rest has worn down parts that free kin still keep. The foot is all but gone, and one great muscle shuts the shell. The two shells are not alike in size or shape.

The left shell is big, thick, and curved, and the beast rests on it. The right shell is flat and thin. The entry maps the nerves and heart in fine terms. It shows how loss of the front parts reshaped the whole frame. Growth and rest on the sea bed drive each change.
britannica-1911-oyster-catcher:
The oyster catcher is a shore bird, and a natural history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica begins with its name. The name does not seem to occur in books until 1731. In that year Catesby used it for a species in Carolina. He saw the bird thick on oyster banks left bare at low water. He believed it fed mainly on those shellfish.

In 1776 Pennant applied the name to the kindred British species. English writers had called that bird the Sea Pie for near two hundred years. The new name won general approval, though the entry calls it a misnomer. In England, at least, the bird does not feed on oysters. In books the new name has all but wholly replaced the old one. The entry then turns to the bird of Europe itself.
britannica-1911-palmer:
A palmer was a pilgrim who, as a sign that he had made the trip to Palestine, bore a palm branch on his staff. More oft he wore a cross of two strips of palm leaf pinned to his hat. The word is oft used as a plain twin for pilgrim as such.

The name is given to a host of hairy caterpillars as well, the 1911 Britannica entry says. One of them is the young of a pest moth that harms fruit trees. The name may come from the use of palm for the soft bloom of the willow, which such grubs much look like. It may come from their roam, like that of a pilgrim on the road. Fake flies for fish sport, clad in stiff hairs, bear the same name in the trade.
britannica-1911-pamphilus-teacher:
Pamphilus was a great friend of learning in the early church, born of a good house in Phoenicia. The 1911 Britannica entry places his birth in the last half of the third century. He studied at Alexandria under a pupil of Origen, then was made a priest at Caesarea in Palestine.

There he set up a school for the study of the faith and urged students on with warmth. He founded, or much enlarged, the great store of books at Caesarea, to which later church writers owed a deep debt. He copied out the Scriptures and the works of church men with his own hand, above all Origen. Jailed in a time of torment for the faith, he wrote a defense of Origen with a dear pupil, and was then put to death.
britannica-1911-pannier:
Pannier is an article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It traces one word through several linked meanings. The first sense is a broad, flat basket for carrying bread or other food. Such baskets were often slung in pairs across a mule, pony, or ass.

The article then turns to dress. A pannier could be an overskirt, or the stiff frame of whalebone or steel worn under it. It also describes the pannier man, an old officer at the Inns of Court in London. That office was abolished at the Inner Temple in 1900. Readers get a short lesson in how one word can spread across trade, dress, and custom.
britannica-1911-passionflower:
Passionflower, Passiflora, is the type genus of the order that bears its name, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The flower's name comes from marks read as signs of the Passion: the corona as the crown of thorns, other parts as the nails or wounds. Its five sepals and five petals were taken for the ten apostles, leaving out Peter and Judas.

Most kinds are natives of western tropical South America, and most are climbers with woody stocks. Tendrils from the stems let the branches hold themselves up at small cost. A few kinds grow into trees with broad leaves like the magnolia's. The flower rises from a cup or tube bearing sepals, petals, and the corona, its showy crown of threads. That coronet is the most striking part of many kinds, the piece by which gardeners know the plant.
britannica-1911-passover:
Passover, the Hebrew spring feast kept by Jews, is explained in a long entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The feast recalls the exodus from Egypt. It is marked by a family meal at home on the first evening. For seven days no leaven is eaten. Old tradition links the first Passover to a command given through Moses.

Detail follows on how the lamb was chosen, killed, and eaten in haste. Blood was placed on the door posts so that homes would be passed over. The entry then weighs many views on where the feast came from. Some writers saw a spring rite or a rite of cleansing behind it. Newer study, based on close reading of the first five books of the Bible, is given the most weight at the end.
britannica-1911-pausanias-spartan-comman:
Pausanias, a Spartan regent and commander, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He lived in the fifth century before Christ and came from the Agiad family. He was nephew of Leonidas, the hero of Thermopylae. When Leonidas died, his young son became king and Pausanias became regent.

He first won fame as commander of the combined Greek forces at the victory of Plataea. In the next year he was appointed admiral of the Greek fleet. He reduced much of Cyprus, called the key of the Levant. He also captured Byzantium from the Persians, the entry relates.
britannica-1911-pausanias-traveller:
Pausanias was a Greek traveller and land writer of the second century. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places him in the age of Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius. He was most likely a native of Lydia in Asia Minor. His tours reached far past his home coast. Before Greece he had seen Antioch, Joppa, and Jerusalem. His great work walks the reader through Greece site by site.

The entry praises his eye for the land itself. He notes pines on the sandy shore of Elis and boars in oak woods. One river he calls the fairest of all, the Ladon. Tall reeds, wild strawberries, and date palms all catch his notice. Love of old Greek glory drives the whole tour. He grieves for the ruin that fell on the land at Chaeronea. His best pages treat the sacred art of Olympia and Delphi.
britannica-1911-payne-peter:
Peter Payne, an English Lollard and Taborite who lived from about 1380 to 1455, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a Frenchman by an English wife and was born near Grantham. He was educated at Oxford, where he took up Lollard views. He took his master's degree before October 1406.

From 1410 to 1414 he was principal of St Edmund Hall, and in those years he crossed swords with Thomas Netter, a defender of the old faith. In 1414 he was forced to leave Oxford and taught for a time in London. In the end he had to flee England and found haven in Bohemia. Prague took him in in 1417, and he soon led among its reformers. He joined the band called the Orphans.
britannica-1911-peisander:
Peisander of Camirus in Rhodes was a Greek epic poet of old times. He is thought to have thrived in about six forty before Christ. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He wrote a Heracleia, a poem on the hero Hercules and his deeds.

Peisander gave Hercules a lion skin and club in place of old Homer arms. He is also said to have fixed the labours of Hercules at twelve. Critics at Alexandria placed him in the epic canon for that work. Clement claimed the poem was copied from Pisinus of Lindus, a charge noted here. His home town raised a statue in his honour, Theocritus tells us.
britannica-1911-pepper:
Pepper, a name used for a set of hot spices, is treated in a 1911 Britannica article. Black pepper is the dried fruit of a climbing shrub from the woods of Travancore and Malabar. The vine climbs tree trunks by roots, like ivy. It is one of the first spices known to man.

For ages pepper was a chief trade good between India and Europe, the piece shows. Alaric took three thousand pounds of it as part of Rome's ransom in 408. Its high price in the Middle Ages helped spur the search for a sea road to India. When that road was found in 1498, the price fell hard. Most of the crop then came from Penang and near lands.
britannica-1911-perceval-spencer:
Spencer Perceval, prime minister of England from eighteen hundred and nine to eighteen twelve, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London in seventeen sixty two, he was the second son of John, second earl of Egmont. He was schooled at Harrow and at Trinity College, Cambridge, and called to the bar in seventeen eighty six.

A strong speech in a famed forgery case brought him quick fame at law. He led on the Midland circuit and entered Parliament for Northampton in seventeen ninety six. He backed the Pitt government in speech. He then rose to solicitor general and then to attorney general. The entry also marks his firm stand against Catholic relief. It gives a clear path from court room to high office.
britannica-1911-periander:
Periander, the second tyrant of Corinth, is the subject of an ancient history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He ruled from 625 to 585 before Christ and was the son of Cypselus, who founded the line. Old tales paint him as a cruel despot who crushed his city. One famed tale has him cut the tallest ears of corn as a hint on rule.

The entry warns that those tales came from rich foes who had cause to smear him. A fair sifting of the proof points the other way. His rule was firm and so sound that direct taxes could be dropped. He backed crafts and trade, curbed idleness and excess wealth, and found work for the poor. New colonies and busy sea trade on both coasts are also credited to him.
britannica-1911-permeameter: Permeameter is a short tool entry in the 1911 Britannica. The tool gauges how well iron or steel lets force pass. It does so fast and with fair truth for trade use. The name was first used for a tool from 1890. A man named Thompson made that first tool himself. It shows the pull force needed to free a test piece. That piece sits as the core of a straight magnet. When that force is known the rate can be worked out.
britannica-1911-perron-pierre-cuillier:
Pierre Cuillier Perron is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French soldier of fortune who rose high in India. Born in seventeen fifty five, he was the son of a cloth merchant. He sailed to India as a sailor and then slipped away from his ship.

The entry tracks his climb from ranker to chief of a great Indian army. He won a famed battle for his master and then led all of that force. In a later war he held back aid and lost his master trust. He fled to the British camp as his own troops were crushed. He went home to France with a large fortune and died there.
britannica-1911-peter: Peter is the subject of a short name article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Peter is a man's name found in many tongues, from Pierre in French to Pedro in Spanish. It derives from the surname Christ gave his apostle Simon. The words ran, thou art Peter, and upon this rock will I build my church. The name has thus been very popular in Christian lands. Yet no pope has ever taken it, out of respect for the first bishop of Rome.
britannica-1911-petofi-alexander:
Alexander Petofi, a Hungarian lyric poet who lived from 1823 to 1849, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born in Pest county on New Year's Day 1823. He changed his family name, Petrovics, to the pure Magyar form Petofi. He learned Latin well as a boy and taught himself French.

Petofi began verse at age twelve and loved the stage, which angered his stern father. Cast off in 1839, he lived three hard years as a wandering player. He served as a common soldier to escape hunger. At college in 1842 he met Jokai and placed a poem in a top review. By 1844 he had settled at Pesth, living by hack writing.
britannica-1911-pewter:
Pewter, a name for a set of metal mixes with tin as the chief part, is treated in a 1911 Britannica article. The word is thought to come from spelter, changed in each land that bought the ware. Roman pewter, the oldest known, was made of tin and lead alone. Its mixes cluster round two set shares of each metal.

In the Middle Ages lead stayed the main second part, the piece shows. Town rules set how much lead could go in each grade of ware. Montpellier used four parts of lead to ninety six of tin for most goods. France in the 1700s capped lead at fifteen parts in a hundred. Such caps guarded food and wine ware.
britannica-1911-phalanger:
Phalanger is an animal article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a family of marsupials of the Australasian region. The name is a book name for the more typical members of the diprotodont marsupials. Among them are the cuscuses of the Moluccas and Celebes and the so called opossums of Australia.

By day phalangers seem dull and sleepy, but at night they wake and move. Several bear flying membranes between fore and hind limbs and make long sailing leaps like flying squirrels. Yet the membrane is no true mark of kinship, since skull and teeth bind the flying kinds to plain climbers. The ring tailed phalangers of Australia, Tasmania, and New Guinea, some ten species with naked tipped grasping tails, appear the most generalized of the group.
britannica-1911-philo-philosopher:
Philo, often called Philo Judaeus, was a Jewish thinker of Alexandria, and this 1911 Britannica entry covers his life and his standing in thought. He seems to have spent his whole life in that city, where he was likely born some twenty to ten years before Christ. His father held a high tax post, from which the entry takes his family to have been rich and well placed. Almost nothing of his life can be dated with care.

One event can: in the year forty he led a Jewish embassy to Rome to beg the emperor Gaius not to demand divine honours from the Jews. Though his life is dim, his many surviving writings show his views of the world and of life in full. The entry calls him the most important voice of Hellenistic Judaism.
britannica-1911-pilaster:
Pilaster, in architecture, is a shallow pier built into a wall, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains its use through the ages. It stands out slightly from the wall face, to break up and adorn a surface or to answer a column. Pilasters carry bases and capitals, and are often fluted like columns.

The entry cites an early case, about 100 BC, in the gateway at Priene in Asia Minor, where the form tapers toward the top. The Romans liked half-columns better, yet used pilasters in the upper story of the Colosseum. In the classic revival, above all in Italy, builders spread a network of pilasters over every storey, inside churches as well as out.
britannica-1911-pioneer: Pioneer, properly, is a foot soldier who goes before an army with spade and axe, as a brief word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica records. The word comes through Old French from a Medieval Latin term for a foot man, kin to the word pawn. He clears roads, digs trenches, and readies camps. By transfer the word covers all who first open a new country or a new field of inquiry.
britannica-1911-plaster: Plaster, in the 1911 Britannica, is a short word entry covering three uses of one name. In building it is a mix of lime, hair, and sand used to cover rough walls and lath work. A fine white kind made of gypsum is known as plaster of Paris. In medicine the word, also spelled plaister, names sticky mixes laid on the body to guard hurt skin, brace weak parts, or soothe pain. The name traces to a Greek word for a daubed on medical mix.
britannica-1911-pliny-the-elder:
Pliny the Elder, whose full name was Gaius Plinius Secundus (about 23-79), is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He wrote the great Roman work on nature known as the Natural History. The entry is firm on his birthplace: he was born at Comum, not at Verona, as some had supposed. His father took him to Rome before the year 35.

The article traces his schooling in Rome. A poet and army commander who was a friend of his father taught him and filled him with a lifelong love of learning. In that man's library he saw writings in the own hand of the Gracchi, two centuries old. He studied plants in the garden of an aged expert and saw fine old lotus trees on land once held by Crassus. He later wrote the life of his teacher.
britannica-1911-pliny-the-younger:
Pliny the Younger (about 61 to about 113 AD) was a Latin author of letters. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives his full name as Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus. Born at Como, he lost his father young and leaned on his uncle. The Elder Pliny adopted him by will and gave him his name.

At fourteen he wrote a Greek tragedy as a school exercise. He trained in speaking under Quintilian and pled cases from age eighteen. His famed letter to Tacitus tells how his uncle died at Vesuvius. Senate posts under Domitian began a long public career in Rome. His Letters and a speech for Trajan anchor his fame.
britannica-1911-plunder: Plunder is a short word history in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word, meaning to rob or pillage above all in war, came into English straight from German during the Thirty Years' War. The German noun behind it meant household stuff, bedclothes, and clothing. Thomas May, writing in 1647, said the word was first used in England of Prince Rupert's raids, borne in from Germany. The Swedish Intelligencer of 1632 gives the earliest known quotation.
britannica-1911-plunket-oliver:
Oliver Plunket, an Irish Catholic divine who lived from 1629 to 1681, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Loughcrew in county Meath. He was schooled in part at Rome, where he went in 1645. From 1657 he taught theology there for twelve years.

In 1669 the pope made him archbishop of Armagh and primate of Ireland. He reached his see in 1670 and set up a Jesuit school in Dublin. His pay was scant, yet his zeal for his church was vast. Hard laws after the Test Act bore on him, and he spent six weeks in Dublin Castle. Charged in the scare of the Popish Plot, he was tried in London for a plot to land a French army. A jury found him guilty on wild proof, and he was hanged at Tyburn.
britannica-1911-poker:
Poker, a card game played for stakes, is treated in a 1911 Britannica article. Most writers trace it to an Italian game of the 1400s, by way of French and Spanish kin games. One proof shows it came to Louisiana from France, its name a garbled form of the French Poque. It was played on Mississippi steamboats as early as 1830.

At first just twenty cards were used, and the full pack of fifty two came later. Draw poker, added near 1860, is the most liked form of the game. Two to seven people play it with a full pack. Chips of set worth serve as the stakes, sold by a banker or split among the players. The piece then sets out the deal and play.
britannica-1911-poole-paul-falconer:
Paul Falconer Poole (1806-1879) was an English painter born at Bristol in 1806. He taught himself, yet his feel for colour, his poetic touch, and his dramatic power won him a high place among British artists. He first showed work at the Royal Academy at age twenty-five. The work was The Well, a scene set in Naples. After a gap of seven years came Farewell, Farewell in 1837.

Poole's place was made safe in 1843 by Solomon Eagle and by a prize in the Cartoon Exhibition. He became an associate of the Royal Academy in 1846 and a full member in 1861. His work falls into two kinds, the calm and the dramatic. May Day of 1852 shows the calm kind well.
britannica-1911-powder:
Powder, a word from the Latin for dust through French, is treated in this 1911 Britannica article in its broad sense. It names the small loose grains into which solid matter is broken by grinding, crushing, or pounding. Hence it covers any preparation that takes that loose form, the most familiar example being gunpowder.

Many powders serve in medicine, some keeping the name of their maker, such as Gregory powder, a compound powder of rhubarb named for a Scottish doctor. Others serve for the toilet. In the days of powdered hair and wigs, houses had a special powdering room set apart for the task. The article ends with a use in birds: in herons, some down feathers break into a fine dust as fast as they form, making patches known as powder-down.
britannica-1911-privateer:
Privateer is an armed ship owned by a private man and hired for war. Its sea law entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. A state at war grants the ship a paper called letters of marque. British subjects are barred from taking such work by an act of eighteen seventy.

The Declaration of Paris in eighteen fifty six said privateering stays abolished. That pledge binds only states that signed it or joined it later. The United States and Spain never joined, yet both kept the rule in eighteen ninety eight. Privateers sit between warships and merchant ships in law and in use. New Hague rules in nineteen o seven set how merchant ships may turn warship.
britannica-1911-procter-bryan-waller:
Bryan Waller Procter (1787–1874) was an English poet who wrote as Barry Cornwall, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry tells his story. He was born at Leeds on the twenty first of November 1787. At Harrow he was a schoolmate of Lord Byron and Sir Robert Peel. He then trained for the law, first in a solicitor office at Calne in Wiltshire.

Procter came into a small property when his father died in 1816. He began to write verse in earnest around 1820, under his pen name. He was called to the bar in 1831. The next year he took a post as a commissioner of lunacy, and he held it for near thirty years. The entry notes that most of his verse was written from 1815 onward.
britannica-1911-quimper:
Quimper is a town in France and capital of the Finistere department in Brittany. A 1911 Britannica entry sets it in a lovely vale ringed by high hills. Two streams, the Steir and the Odet, meet above the town and form a channel. Ships of one hundred and fifty tons can reach the sea eleven miles down.

Old town walls of the 1400s survive in parts by the palace and college. The town is the seat of a bishopric in the province of Rennes. Its cathedral, built from 1239 to 1515, honours Saint Corentin as patron. A fine front from about 1425 bears heraldic carvings in hard granite stone.
britannica-1911-radiometer:
A radiometer is a device built to show how radiation can push on a fine, free body. Observers had long noted that bodies hung in a partial vacuum seem to be pushed by rays. Sir William Crookes took up the question in full. He had found that fine weighings in vacuum were spoiled by this effect. A black face, which soaks up rays, is pushed more than a bright face.

Crookes built a light mill with a upright axle inside a glass bulb emptied of air. The axle bore vanes set at equal gaps, each black on one side and bright on the other. Sunlight, candle light, or heat rays set the vanes turning. Speed rose, then held steady when friction and thin air balanced the push. The steady speed might serve as a rough measure of the rays.
britannica-1911-raleigh-sir-walter:
Sir Walter Raleigh (about 1552-1618) was a British explorer, poet, and writer of history. He was most likely born in 1552, though the date is not quite sure. His father was Walter Raleigh of Fardell, near Plymouth, a country gentleman of old stock but small means. The father wed three times in his life. Sir Walter was the child of the third match.

His mother was Catherine Champernown, a widow with three sons by her first marriage. The boys John, Humphrey, and Adrian Gilbert were thus his half-brothers. The family had to give up its own house at Fardell. Sir Walter was born in a farmhouse at Hayes, on the Devon coast between Exmouth and Sidmouth. Even the spelling of the name shifts from man to man in the family. The form Raleigh, used by his widow, is the one now in common use.
britannica-1911-ralph-de-guader:
Ralph de Guader is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Norman earl of Norfolk. He was active near 1070 and was the son of a Norman who held high posts in East Anglia under Edward the Confessor. Ralph fought on the Norman side at Hastings. William the Conqueror made him earl of Norfolk.

In 1075 the king refused to allow his marriage to the sister of Roger, earl of Hereford. That refusal drove the two earls to revolt, and they were easily beaten. Ralph sent to Denmark for ships and went there himself to fetch them. He lost his English lands and took refuge in Brittany, on his wife's estate. He and his wife joined the first crusade in 1099 and died on the road to Palestine.
britannica-1911-ramsay-allan-painter:
Allan Ramsay, a Scottish portrait painter who lived from 1713 to 1784, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Edinburgh, eldest son of the poet who wrote The Gentle Shepherd. His gift for art showed early. At twenty he was studying in London under the Swedish painter Hans Huyssing.

In 1736 Ramsay went to Rome and worked three years under Italian masters. Back in Edinburgh, fine portraits of Scots notables drew him notice. He moved to London and won patrons among the great, aided by his charm and wide culture. In 1767 he became principal painter to the king. Royal portraits, sent as gifts to ambassadors and governors, kept him so busy that he used many aides. An accident that dislocated his right arm broke his health. He finished the king's likeness he had in hand, then left for his beloved Italy.
britannica-1911-rappoltsweiler:
Rappoltsweiler is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town in Alsace-Lorraine, in Germany. In French it is Ribeauville. The count of 1905 gave it 5,986 people. It lies at the mouth of the Strengbach valley, under the east slope of the Vosges. Old walls still ring part of the town.

It has many pretty medieval houses and two old churches, Saint Gregory and Saint Augustine, both fine Gothic works. The town hall holds a valued set of antiquities. A salt spring, the Carolabad, had great fame in the middle ages and was found again in 1888. That find made the town a watering place. Its trades are the spinning and weaving of cotton and wool, printing, dyeing, and tanning. There is also a brisk trade in wine.
britannica-1911-register:
Register, a book of facts kept for look up, is set out in a long word and rite entry in the 1911 Britannica. The word comes through French from Latin words for things set down. It names both the act of entry and the book that holds the list. The man who kept such a book was long called a register as well. That post name lives on in a Scots state post and in use in America.

Church lists of births, weddings, and deaths fill the rest of the shown text. Thomas Cromwell set them up in England by an order in fifteen thirty eight. Spain had such lists first, at Toledo in fourteen ninety seven. Rules in fifteen ninety seven called for skin bound books and copies on the same stock. A copy had to go to the bishop each year.
britannica-1911-rensselaer:
Rensselaer, a city in New York state, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the east bank of the Hudson River, opposite Albany. Three bridges link it to the capital across the water. The census of 1910 counted 10,711 people there.

Two railways, the New York Central and the Boston and Albany, keep shops in the city. Rensselaer was first called Greenbush, and was settled in 1631. Its site formed part of the great tract bought from the Indians for Killian van Rensselaer. That estate was known as Rensselaerwyck, and the city keeps the family name. A speculator laid out a square mile of lots in 1810, and growth followed. The village was chartered in 1815 and became a city in 1897, taking the name Rensselaer. Its factories make knit goods, felt, and cloth from remade wool.
britannica-1911-retainer:
Retainer is a word with more than one sense in law and old custom, as a 1911 Britannica entry shows. At base it means the act of keeping, or a thing that keeps. In past use it meant a follower of a great house, above all an armed man in a baron train. One old gloss calls such a man a servant who bore his lord name but did not live in his house.

The entry then turns to retainer of counsel, the fee that binds a barrister to a client case. Once paid, counsel must give that client first call on his work in the matter. Such fees may be general, for all a client suits, or special, for one case alone.
britannica-1911-reynolds-walter:
Walter Reynolds (died 1327) was archbishop of Canterbury, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry tells how royal favour raised him. He was the son of a Windsor baker. He became a clerk in the service of Edward the First. He held several church livings in those years.

Reynolds became a prime favourite with the prince of Wales, the future Edward the Second. His skill as an actor may have helped that rise, the entry hints. Just after the prince became king in 1307, Reynolds was made treasurer of England. In 1308 he became bishop of Worcester, and in 1310 chancellor. When Archbishop Winchelsea died in May 1313, the king pressed the pope to name his favourite. Walter was enthroned at Canterbury in February 1314. His private life, the entry warns, was far from a model.
britannica-1911-rhone-river:
One of the great rivers of Europe, the Rhone earns a full study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The river rises high in the Swiss canton of Valais. It flows past the Bernese Alps, spreads into the Lake of Geneva, and bends round the Jura hills. At Lyons it takes in its chief feeder, the Saone. From there it runs south through France to the Mediterranean Sea.

The entry gives the river a length of just over five hundred miles. Its basin covers close to thirty-eight thousand square miles. The course falls into three parts, split by the lake and by Lyons. The first part is a pure Alpine stream in a deep trough.
britannica-1911-rice-paper: Rice paper is explained in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name is a mistake, since the stuff is not made from rice at all. It is the pith of a small tree that grows in the swampy forests of Formosa. The round core of pith is rolled on a hard flat surface against a knife, cutting it into thin sheets with a texture like ivory. Dyed in many colours, the sheets are used for false flowers. Plain white sheets serve local artists for water colour work.
britannica-1911-rive-de-gier:
Rive-de-Gier is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a town in east central France, in the department of Loire. The town lies fourteen miles east north east of Saint Etienne, on the railway to Lyons. Its population in 1906 was 15,338. It stands on the river Gier and on a canal.

The entry says the town rests chiefly on the coal trade, and gives its name to a coal basin linked to that of Saint Etienne. Its glass works were famed for the fine, pure sand found by the Rhone and the Saone. Iron and steel works made iron goods of many kinds. The article also notes Gallo Roman remains, mosaics, and coins, and says coal working had raised the place by the time of Henry the Fourth.
britannica-1911-river:
A river is any large stream of water flowing in a set channel. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with that plain definition. It sends the reader elsewhere for how rivers form and carve valleys. Those questions belong to its articles on geography and geology. The entry itself is spent on the word's own history. River comes from an Old French word, rivière. That word descends from a Latin term for a river bank.

Rivulet, by contrast, comes from rivus, the Latin for a stream. The two words are thus distinct in origin, the entry insists. Yet the sense of rivus likely coloured the later Latin form of river. Scholars dispute the roots of both rivus and ripa. Some trace them to a root meaning to drop or flow. Others link ripa to a root for tearing, as in a broken cliff or steep bank.
britannica-1911-roanoke-river:
The Roanoke river of Virginia and North Carolina is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. With the Staunton, which rises in the Appalachian Valley, it forms one river. It flows in a general south-east course across the state line. It then crosses just above the Fall Line and empties into Albemarle Sound. The river is nearly 400 miles long. Its drainage area covers 9,237 square miles.

The article gives the state of work on the channel at the time. In 1871 the United States adopted a plan to clear a channel. It was to run five feet deep at low water from the mouth to Weldon. By 1909 the work was about four-fifths done. Boats drawing four feet could then reach nearly to Weldon. The Weldon Canal, opened in 1829, was given up in 1850.
britannica-1911-roger-of-wendover:
Roger of Wendover (died 1236), an English chronicler, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was most likely a native of Wendover in Buckinghamshire. At some unknown date he became a monk of St Albans. He was later made prior of a small house that answered to the abbey, but lost the post for wasting its funds.

His last years passed at St Albans, where he died in May 1236. The article calls him the first of the great chroniclers who worked in the writing room of that house. His Flowers of History runs from the creation of the world to the year 1235. Only from 1202 does it hold worth as his own work. Some critics think he copied an older gathering for the years up to 1189, but the entry calls the proof weak.
britannica-1911-rogers-john-preacher:
John Rogers, an English preacher, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Messing in Essex in sixteen twenty seven, he was the second son of a royalist clergyman. He became a student of medicine at King's College, Cambridge. As a youth his deep religious despair led him to attempt to take his own life.

He then joined the extreme sect of the Puritans, the entry tells. Driven from home, he walked to Cambridge and nearly starved there. School posts in Huntingdonshire and at Saint Neots kept him alive. He became known as a preacher and gained posts that followed from that fame.
britannica-1911-ross-alexander:
Alexander Ross lived from 1699 to 1784 and was a Scottish poet. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Kincardine O'Neil in Aberdeenshire. He was born there in April 1699 and schooled at Marischal College, Aberdeen. He then tutored the children of Sir William Forbes of Craigievar. In 1732 he became schoolmaster of Lochlee in Angus for life.

There the rest of his days were spent in quiet school work. For years he wrote verse for his own joy in spare hours. In 1768, at the urging of James Beattie, he published a poem. The Fortunate Shepherdess is a pastoral tale in the Scots tongue. It copies Allan Ramsay's Gentle Shepherd in form and plan.
britannica-1911-rudolph-glaber:
Rudolph Glaber, or Rudolph the Bald, was a French tale man who died about the year ten fifty. He was born in Burgundy about nine eighty-five. He dwelt in turn in three church houses, then joined the famed house of Cluny. He was a monk past the year ten thirty-nine and seems to have gone to Italy.

His chief work claims to tell the tale of the world from nine hundred to ten forty-four. In truth it is a loose tale of deeds in France and Burgundy. He held with force that the end of the world was near. A life of a saint by him also lives.
britannica-1911-russell-john-painter:
John Russell, a British portrait painter who lived from 1745 to 1806, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Guildford in Surrey, he entered the studio of Francis Cotes at an early age. From Cotes he gained his training in art, and in 1767 he set up a studio of his own. Russell was a man of marked religious character.

He was a devout follower of Whitefield, and from 1766 he kept a full diary in shorthand. In it he recorded his own state of mind and his religious exercises at length. Only now and then does it give news of his sitters, the entry notes. He won a gold medal for figure drawing in 1770 and showed work at the Royal Academy until 1805. His fame rests on pastel work, called the finest England produced.
britannica-1911-sampler:
Sampler is a model or pattern to be copied, above all a small cloth worked in needle stitches. A 1911 Britannica entry gives its roots in French and Latin words for an example. Girls once worked a sampler as a test and proof of beginner skill. The piece taught the stitches while it showed what the child had learned.

Samplers most often held the alphabet, the worker name, the date, and Bible texts. Verses, mottoes, and a stock border design filled out the cloth as well. Work from the 1600s is still found and hunted by collectors today. The oldest known sampler dates to 1643 and rests in a London museum.
britannica-1911-satterlee-walter:
Walter Satterlee, an American painter of figures and scenes, was born in Brooklyn in eighteen forty four. He graduated at Columbia University in eighteen sixty three. He studied at the National Academy of Design and with Edwin White in New York. In eighteen seventy eight he went to Paris to study under Leon Bonnat. He first showed work at the National Academy in eighteen sixty eight.

Satterlee was elected an associate of the Academy in eighteen seventy nine. He won its Clarke prize in eighteen eighty six for his work. He belonged to the American Water Color Society and the New York Etching Club. The entry also calls him an excellent teacher of art. His favoured subjects were Arab life and figures in colonial dress. He died in Brooklyn on the twenty eighth of May nineteen o eight.
britannica-1911-scarlet-fever:
Scarlet Fever is a health entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a sharp catching ill with high heat and sore throat. A red flush spreads wide across the skin in the course of the ill. A famed doctor first set the ill apart in clear terms in old times.

The entry tells how germ hunts of the age chased its true cause. One germ drawn from the throat was named for the fever itself. Blood tests show signs that tie it to kin germs of foul wounds. Seed like specks found in skin cells drew note as a fresh clue. The ill spreads from case to case by close touch and breath.
britannica-1911-scavenger-s-daughter: Scavenger Daughter is the name of a tool of torture used in England in the 1500s, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. The name is a worn form of Skevington Daughter, for its maker, Sir William Skevington. He was lieutenant of the Tower under King Henry the Eighth. The tool was a wide iron hoop that was screwed tight round the body of the victim. The squeeze forced blood from the nose and ears, and at times from the hands and feet as well.
britannica-1911-september:
September is treated in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on the month. Its name comes from the Latin word for seven. It was the seventh month of the old Roman year. It kept thirty days in that calendar. In the Julian calendar it became the ninth month. It kept its old name and its count of days.

The article notes the feasts and names tied to the month. The great games in honour of Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva began on the fourth. Church feasts fall on the eighth, fourteenth, twenty-first, and twenty-ninth. Charlemagne's calendar called it the harvest month. The Anglo-Saxons called it the barley month, for that crop was then cut. In Switzerland it is still called the harvest month.
britannica-1911-shoveler:
Shoveler is a duck with a broad, spoon shaped bill, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name once meant the bird now called the spoonbill, but in the late 1500s it passed to this duck. Its long bill plates set it apart from the common duck group. The drake would rank among the most fine looking of ducks but for the clumsy look of that bill.

His colours are set out in rich detail in the text. He has a gold eye, a dark green head, and a breast of pure white. Rich bay covers his lower parts and sides, with a deep brown back. Pale blue wing patches and a glossy green wing bar edged with white add to the show. Few of his kin match him for bright and mixed hues.
britannica-1911-shushter:
Shushter is a district and town in the province of Arabistan in Persia, south of Dizful. The 1911 Britannica article gives the district a count of about 40,000 souls. That count takes in the town and twenty-two villages, plus near 3,700 nomad families of four tribes. Its fields yield grain, opium, cotton, and wool. Its limes give a juice that is made into a green extract. The extract is shipped out in small earthen jars.

The town itself holds some 15,000 people. It stands where the river Karun splits into the Gerger canal and the Shutait stream. A citadel on a sandstone hill guards its north-east corner. Above the town a great dike of hewn stone blocks the Gerger. It was known as the Caesar's Dike, and was rebuilt by a prince in the early nineteenth century.
britannica-1911-sigalon-xavier:
Xavier Sigalon, who lived from 1788 to 1837, was a French painter. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica stresses his power and his poverty. Born at Uzes, he was the son of a poor village schoolmaster. Hard struggle marked his road to a Paris studio.

Studio teaching missed his needs, so he studied alone in the Louvre. A Young Courtesan shown in 1822 won instant notice. Bigger canvases on grim tales proved his force in the 1820s. His Vision of Saint Jerome in 1831 was his most personal work. The Legion of Honour cross came to him that same year. Yet charm of color was not his gift, and sales lagged. Portraits at times were all that kept him fed. A state task copying the Sistine Last Judgment saved him late.
britannica-1911-simplicius-philosopher:
Simplicius is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a thinker from Cilicia and one of the last of a late Greek school. He learned from two masters of that school in his youth. When the Athens school was shut by law, he fled east with six peers.

The entry tells how a Persian king gave the group a warm welcome at court. Life among strangers still wore on them, and they soon went home. A peace treaty wrote in their right to live free in faith. Back home he wrote long notes on the works of Aristotle. Those notes keep scraps of lost old thought that scholars still mine.
britannica-1911-sin-eater:
A sin-eater was a man who, for a small fee, was thought to take on the sins of a dead person. He did so by means of food and drink. The custom was once common in many parts of England and in the Scottish highlands. It lived on into late years in Wales, Shropshire, and Herefordshire. Villages had their own sin-eater. Word was sent to him as soon as a death took place.

The sin-eater came to the house and sat on a stool by the door. He was given a coin, a crust of bread, and a bowl of ale. When he had eaten and drunk, he stood and spoke words of ease and rest for the dead. In an older form, bread was laid on the breast of the corpse first. The sin-eater then ate it in the room with the dead.
britannica-1911-sinter:
Sinter, a porous mineral deposit, is explained in a geology entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from German and is kin to the English word cinder. Two main kinds are known. One is rich in silica, the other in lime. Each forms where mineral waters lay down crusts over time.

Silica sinter forms round hot springs and geysers as crusts, mounds, or terraces. Study at Yellowstone showed that algae in the hot waters help lay it down. Lime sinter is best seen in travertine, the chief building stone of Rome. Springs in limestone lands coat objects left in their flow. Moss and plant bits that rot away leave holes in the crust. In caves the same lime deposit forms stalagmite. A like term is at times used for bog iron ore.
britannica-1911-skram-peder:
Peder Skram, a Danish senator and sea hero born about fifteen hundred, came from his father's estate near Horsens in Jutland. He first served in the Swedish war of Christian the Second. At one battle in fifteen eighteen he fought, and two years later he saved the life of a standard bearer. For this work he won an estate in Norway. There he settled for a time with his wife Elsebe Krabbe.

In the Count's War the Danish state sent Skram to help Gustavus Vasa build a Swedish fleet. He blocked the Hanseatic fleets that backed the other side. He took a whole Lubeck squadron off Svendborg and kept food from reaching Copenhagen by sea. Christian the Third knighted him and gave him rich estates.
britannica-1911-slocum-henry-warner:
Henry Warner Slocum (1827-1894) was an American general, and his career is traced in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Delphi, New York, he graduated from the United States Military Academy in 1852. He resigned in 1856 to practise law at Syracuse and sat in the state Assembly in 1859.

The entry follows his Civil War rise: colonel in May 1861, major-general of volunteers by July 1862, fighting from Bull Run to Gettysburg, where he commanded a corps. He joined the Tennessee campaign, the Atlanta campaign, and Sherman's march to the sea, leading the left wing. After the war he served two spells in Congress as a Democrat from Brooklyn.
britannica-1911-smart-christopher:
Christopher Smart, an English poet who lived from 1722 to 1771, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Shipbourne, Kent, in April 1722. His father was steward for the Kentish estates of Viscount Vane. The boy was schooled first at Maidstone, then at Durham grammar school.

Part of his holidays were spent at Raby Castle. His gifts as a poet won him the backing of the Vane family. The duchess of Cleveland granted him a pension, paid until her death in 1742. The article also quotes a warning from Thomas Gray. Writing in 1747, Gray told a friend to keep quiet about Smart's faults. Word of them, he feared, might reach the ear of his patrons. The piece paints a talent that lived on the goodwill of the great.
britannica-1911-smith-william-sonneteer: William Smith was an English sonnet writer who flourished in fifteen ninety six. In that year he published a set of sonnets naming Chloris, the complaint of a scorned shepherd in love. Smith was a follower of Spenser, and the first two sonnets and the last are addressed to Spenser. He signed with initials only, as W Smith. He has at times been confused with a playwright of a like name.
britannica-1911-solder: Solder is a brief word article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It traces the name through French to the Latin soldare, to make firm. Solder itself is an alloy that melts with ease and is used to join two metal faces, joints, or edges, working much like a cement made of metal. For the craft side the entry sends the reader on to the article on brazing and soldering. The piece thus serves as a short definition and a pointer rather than a full treatment.
britannica-1911-soter: Soter is a brief church entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on an early pope. Soter held the papal office from about the year 167 to about 174. He wrote to the church of Corinth and sent it aid. His letter is named in the reply sent back by Dionysius, bishop of Corinth. Harnack holds that the letter can be matched with the second of the writings that go under the name of Clement's letters to the Corinthians.
britannica-1911-spencer:
Spencer is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a township in Worcester County, Massachusetts. It stands about eleven miles west of Worcester and covers some thirty-four square miles. The census showed its people falling: 8,747 in 1890, 7,627 in 1900, and 6,740 in 1910. Rail and electric lines serve it.

The Richard Sugden Public Library, founded in 1889, held twelve thousand books in 1908. Parks honour Samuel Bemis, the first settler. The town's trades are boots and shoes, woollens, muslin underwear, wire, and boxes of wood and paper. Spencer was part of the Leicester grant and was first settled in 1721. It became a township under its present name in 1753. One house in town was the birthplace of Elias Howe, who devised the sewing machine, and of his inventive uncles.
britannica-1911-spherometer:
