Spherometer is a term entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains a fine tool for measuring the curve of a ball or lens. The tool can also gauge the thickness of a thin plate. Its core is a fine screw that turns in a nut on a small three leg stand.

The entry tells how the screw head is split into fine marks for close reads. A side scale counts the whole turns of the screw as it moves. To test a plate, the user sets the tool on a flat face and takes a read. The plate is then slipped in and a second read is taken. The gap between the two reads gives the depth of the plate.
britannica-1911-st-dizier:
St Dizier, an iron town of north-east France, is set down in a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Marne River and a canal in Haute-Marne. Chaumont lies forty-five miles to the south-east by rail from it. In 1906 the town held over ten thousand people in count. The wider commune held close to fifteen thousand at that count.

Foundries, forges, and machine works make the town an iron hub. Grain and timber add their share to its trade by rail. The town dates from the third century of our era. Relics of Bishop Didier were brought there from ruined Langres. That bishop's name lives on in the name of the town. In 1544 the town held out through a famed siege by Charles.
britannica-1911-st-riquier:
St Riquier is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town in northern France, in the department of Somme. It stands eight miles north-east of Abbeville, by rail. The count of 1906 gave it 1,158 people. The town was first called Centula and was famed for its abbey.

Riquier, son of the town's governor, founded that abbey near the year 625. King Dagobert enriched it, and it thrived under Angilbert, son-in-law of Charlemagne. The abbey buildings of the eighteenth century now house a church seminary. The church is a grand work of flamboyant Gothic from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Its west front is rich with carving under a square tower. Inside, the article praises the vaulting, the font, the carved stalls, and the treasury with its relics.
britannica-1911-star-chamber:
Star Chamber was the name of an English court of high power. The 1911 Britannica entry dates its work to the 1400s, 1500s, and 1600s. The name may come from stars painted on the roof of its room. In Latin the room was called the camera stellata, the entry notes. A rival tale links the name to a Hebrew word for a bond.

That tale says the room once held the bonds of the Jews. Jews were cast out of England by Edward the First in that age. The true roots of the court are dim, the entry admits. It grew from the old curia regis of the 1100s in part. The crown kept a top right to judge through its council.
britannica-1911-stavanger:
Stavanger is a seaport of Norway and capital of the county of the same name, as this 1911 Britannica article describes it. It lies on the south side of the Bukken Fjord, with a harbour well sheltered by islands, and had 30,541 people in 1900. The town is one of the oldest in Norway, founded in the 700s or 800s, though narrow winding streets and wooden houses give the modern town an old look.

It became the seat of a bishopric in the 1200s, and its Romanesque cathedral of St Swithun still stands, rebuilt after a fire in 1272. The article calls it, after Trondhjem, the most notable stone church in Norway. Trades include canning of foods and making of woollens and linens, and the fisheries for herring, mackerel, cod, and salmon are of great weight. Fish is the chief export.
britannica-1911-stevens-alfred-painter:
Alfred Stevens, who lived from 1828 to 1906, was a Belgian painter of fashion. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica praises his finish and grace. He was born in Brussels in May 1828. His father, an old officer, loved pictures and fostered his gift.

Stevens trained in Brussels, then in Paris under a family friend. Early works tried soldiers, grief, and tales of murder. A small piece called At Home in 1855 found his true path. From 1857 he painted graceful women of fashion almost alone. At the Paris show of 1867 he sent eighteen choice works. Lady in Pink and other hits fixed his manner for the age. Show after show in Paris and Brussels crowned that path. A great writer called his pains with finish immense and rare.
britannica-1911-stillwater:
Stillwater is the subject of a city article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Stillwater is a city in Washington County in Minnesota. It stands at the head of Lake Saint Croix, on the west bank of the Saint Croix River. It lies northeast of Saint Paul. By 1910 its people numbered just over ten thousand, down from earlier counts.

The article notes rail lines and a street car link to Saint Paul and Minneapolis. The city sits on bluffs with fine views over the river. Public buildings include a library, city hall, court house, and hospital. The city holds the state prison, set up in 1851, with a school and library inside. In trade it is a centre for lumber and a shipping point for grain. Water power drives its varied factories.
britannica-1911-stirling-william-alexand:
William Alexander, called earl of Stirling, was an American soldier born in New York City in seventeen twenty six. He was the son of James Alexander, a noted colonial lawyer of his day. His father had been barred for a year over the defence in the Zenger trial. William served first as commissary, then as aide to Governor Shirley. That service came at the start of the French and Indian War.

In seventeen fifty six Stirling went with Shirley to England on service. There he was urged to claim the earldom of Stirling for himself. An Edinburgh jury declared him nearest heir to the last earl in seventeen fifty nine. He returned to America and took the title, though the Lords forbade its use. He settled in New Jersey and joined its council as a member. At the war's outbreak he backed the colonial cause with warmth.
britannica-1911-stowe-harriet-elizabeth-:
Harriet Elizabeth Beecher Stowe is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an American writer. She was also a philanthropist in her work. She lived from 1811 to 1896. She was the seventh child of Lyman and Roxana Beecher. She was born at Litchfield, Connecticut, in June 1811. Her father was the Congregational minister of the town. Both parents descended from founders of New Haven colony.

The community of her childhood was among the most intellectual in New England. At her mother's death in 1815, her sister's influence grew. Catherine, her eldest sister, was eleven years her senior. She soon set up a school at Hartford. Harriet went to that school first as a pupil. In 1832 her father accepted a new post in the west. That post was the presidency of Lane Theological Seminary.
britannica-1911-stranraer:
Stranraer is a royal burgh and seaport in the south west of Scotland, at the head of a sea loch. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its town count at the turn of the age, about six thousand souls. A mail boat sails each day to a port in Ireland across the channel, a short sea run off.

The town first bore the name of a saints chapel, then rose by steps to burgh rank and at last to royal burgh rank. At its heart stand the ruins of a castle of the middle ages, held for a time by a famed stern lord who served as sheriff of the shire. The entry lists its halls, court house, school, and poor house. Dairy tools are made there, among other trades.
britannica-1911-strathpeffer:
Strathpeffer is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a village and spa in Scotland. It lies in the county of Ross and Cromarty. Dingwall stands five miles to the east by rail. A count from 1901 gives the village 354 people. It sits in a valley two to four hundred feet high. Hills shelter it on the west and the north. That shelter gives it a dry and warm climate.

Several sulfur springs rise in and near the village. One is saline, and one is strong with sulfur gas. They are held in great repute for gout and rheumatism. Skin, liver, and kidney complaints are also treated there. A fizzy iron water draws guests with anaemia. A peat bath, like those in Bohemia, has been set up. The season runs from May to October each year. The pump room and pavilion stand mid village.
britannica-1911-stuyvesant-peter:
Peter Stuyvesant was a Dutch chief of a new land, who lived from fifteen ninety-two to sixteen seventy-two. He was born in Friesland, the son of a church man. He went to war in the west isles as a youth and ran an isle post for ten years. A wound past a strike cost him a leg.

He wore a wood leg bound with bright bands from that day. In sixteen forty-five he was picked to run the New Netherland post. He came to its chief town to great cheer two years on. Calls for self rule met his harsh hand, and strife grew fast.
britannica-1911-suger:
Suger was a French churchman, statesman, and writer of history in the early middle ages. Born of poor parents, in a place the sources do not fix for sure, he entered the great abbey of St Denis as a boy. There and at a priory school he was taught, and first met the prince who would be King Louis the Sixth.

The 1911 Britannica entry follows his rise in church and court. He served as scribe to the abbot, then as provost of towns in Normandy and the Beauce. Sent to the pope on the kings work, he spent years in Italy. Home again, he was made abbot of St Denis. He split his time between the affairs of the realm and the reform of his abbey, and rode with the next king to his royal match.
britannica-1911-sumter:
Sumter, a city in South Carolina, gets a brief place entry in the 1911 Britannica. It is the county seat of Sumter county, 42 miles by rail east of Columbia. Its count rose from 5,673 in 1900 to 8,109 in 1910. Lines of the Atlantic Coast and Southern railways serve the city. It is the seat of St Joseph's Academy, a Roman Catholic school for girls.

The region round it yields tobacco, vegetables, and cotton, and the city has varied manufactories. Sumter was founded in 1800 and named in honour of General Thomas Sumter. It was first chartered as a city in 1887. The entry is short, in the gazetteer style of its day. In a few lines it fixes the town's rail place, its school, its farm belt, and the source of its name. That compact record is all the piece sets out to give.
britannica-1911-sunflower:
The sunflower is a tall annual plant grown for seed, oil, and show. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its home as the western United States. Its rough hairy stem runs from 3 to 12 feet high. Broad toothed leaves line that stem. Flower heads span 3 to 6 inches in the wild. Grown kinds can stretch a foot or more across. Double forms with globe shaped heads are also raised.

The plant earns its keep in many ways. Its leaves serve as fodder for stock. Its flowers yield a yellow dye. Its seeds hold a sweet yellow oil held equal to olive oil. The pressed cake feeds stock and poultry, with Russia a large exporter. The genus holds about fifty kinds, chiefly North American. Gardens raise several of them with ease in fair soil.
britannica-1911-surrender:
Surrender in law, as a way to pass land rights, is set out in a 1911 Britannica law entry. Lord Coke is quoted for the core sense of the term. A man gives up a life hold or a term of years to the next holder. That next holder holds the right that waits in line. The act is the flip side of a release, the text says.

For copyhold lands, surrender was the stock way to pass the hold. The gift went to the lord, who then let the buyer in by roll entry. A will could pass such land by surrender in the past as well. A law of eighteen thirty seven eased that path. Since eighteen forty five the act must be by deed, save for copyholds and cases set by law.
britannica-1911-taillefer:
Taillefer, the bard who struck first at Hastings, is kept in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His true name and birthplace are not known to the record. He crossed to England with the Norman army in 1066. William let him strike the first blow of the great battle. He fought with spirit and fire, the old accounts agree. He was killed on the field of Hastings that same day.

Two early writers name Taillefer and his bold deed at Hastings. His prowess also shows in the Bayeux tapestry of the conquest. Wace adds that he rode first, singing of Roland and Charlemagne. That song note counts large for the early tale of Roland. It hints that a Roland song lived well before the fight.
britannica-1911-tancred-crusader:
Tancred, a crusader who died in eleven twelve, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. He was nephew of Bohemund and grandson of Robert Guiscard through his mother. In ten ninety six he took the Cross with Bohemund and marched to Constantinople.

There he refused to swear an oath to the emperor Alexius. He slipped across the strait dressed as a peasant. After Nicaea fell, he gave his oath like the other princes. In Asia Minor he left the main host and struck into Cilicia. He made himself master of Tarsus, then lost it to a stronger force. He went on to take Adana and Mamistra. He rejoined the main army at Antioch and played a great part in its siege.
britannica-1911-tandy-james-napper:
James Napper Tandy (1740-1803) was an Irish rebel, and his political life is traced in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son of a Dublin ironmonger, he began as a small tradesman, then joined the Dublin corporation. He won favor by attacking corruption in the city and by urging a boycott of English goods.

The entry follows his clash with the Dublin volunteers, his work on a reform committee in 1784, and his place in the Whig club of Grattan. With Theobald Wolfe Tone he helped found the Society of the United Irishmen in 1791 and became its first secretary. His fierce views, shaped by French revolutionary ideas, soon drew the eye of the government.
britannica-1911-tangier:
Tangier is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a seaport of Morocco. Its local name is given as Tanjah. It stands on the Straits of Gibraltar. Cape Spartel lies about fourteen miles to the west. The town nestles between two hills at a bay's end. Its people number about forty thousand in all. From the sea it presents a picturesque appearance. It rises in the form of an amphitheatre.

The citadel and the remains of the English mole stand to the right. York Castle is named among those remains. The commercial quarter fills the central valley of the town. A track to Tetuan runs along the beach to the left. Its streets are narrow and crooked in the old town. A sanitary body has had them repaved and cleaned. New roads have also been made outside the town. Rivalry between European powers delayed many public works there.
britannica-1911-tannhauser:
Tannhäuser was a German Minnesinger of the thirteenth century, and a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his wanderings. He lived for a time at the court of Frederick the Second, duke of Austria. After the death of that duke, he was received at the court of Otto the Second of Bavaria. He was of a restless bent, the entry says.

Tannhäuser wasted his fortune and spent much time wandering about Germany. He also went as a Crusader to the Holy Land. His poems belong to the decline of the Minnesang, the old German love song. They mix a show of learning with scenes of peasant life, in a somewhat coarse tone. His wild life led the popular mind to link him with a knight of legend. That knight comes at last to the Venusberg, the hill of Venus near Eisenach.
britannica-1911-taylor-john-pamphleteer:
John Taylor, an English pamphleteer who lived from 1580 to 1653, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was commonly called the Water-Poet. He was born at Gloucester in August 1580. He was apprenticed to a waterman in his youth.

In 1596 he served in the fleet of Essex. He was present at Flores in 1597 and at the siege of Cadiz. On his return to England he became a Thames waterman. At one time he collected the fees exacted by the lieutenant of the Tower. He was an expert in the art of self-advertisement. He won fame by a run of eccentric journeys. With a companion, he rowed from London to Queenborough in a paper boat. Two stockfish tied to canes served as oars. His Pennyles Pilgrimage told of a walk made without money. The piece delights in a showman of the river and the road.
britannica-1911-temper: Temper is a word of many senses, all traced from a Latin verb in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The root verb means to mix in due proportion, to qualify, rule, or regulate, and so to be moderate. From that base the word serves for blending by mixing, and hence for restraint and calm. One special use is for bringing steel to the right hardness and spring. As a noun for a frame of mind, used alone it has come to mean a hasty, passionate temper.
britannica-1911-tender:
Tender is a word study article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, setting out several senses of the word. As an adjective it means soft, in body or in feeling, and comes through French from a Latin word for soft. The entry traces that root to an older idea of stretching out thin.

As a legal term, a tender is an offer made for acceptance. Most often it is an offer of money to meet a debt or to carry out a contract. The phrase legal tender is sent to another article for full treatment. The word also covers an offer to do a set piece of work or supply goods at a set price. Large works are often put out to tender to gain the lowest price, the entry explains.
britannica-1911-terpander:
Terpander, of Antissa in Lesbos, a Greek poet and song man, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Near the time of a great war in the south of Greece, he settled in Sparta. Some tales say a voice from the shrine at Delphi sent for him. He was to soothe strife that had grown between ranks in that state.

At Sparta he won the prize in the song games of a great feast. He is held as the true founder of the set music of Greece and of the lyric ode. Our facts on his new steps in the art are thin. One Greek holds that he raised the strings of the lyre from four to seven. A shard of his own verse may mean a like change in the parts of the ode in its stead. The entry holds both reads in view with care.
britannica-1911-tiber:
The Tiber is the subject of a river entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a river of central Italy, known in Italian as the Tevere. It rises in the Tuscan Apennines and flows through a chain of ravines. It then skirts the Sabine hills and crosses the Roman Campagna through Rome itself.

It reaches the sea by two arms at Ostia and Fiumicino, one of them artificial. Its chief tributaries are named as the Paglia, the Nera, and the Anio. Boats could travel up it as far as the meeting with the Nera. The entry follows the full course from mountain source to the coast.
britannica-1911-ticino-river: Ticino is a river of Switzerland and northern Italy, also called Tessin in German. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces it from the Gries Pass west of Airolo. Its upper valley, the Val Leventina, carries the Saint Gotthard road and railway. The river flows through Lago Maggiore and leaves at its south end. From there it runs south to join the Po below Pavia. The river gives its name to the Swiss canton of Ticino.
britannica-1911-tiger-flower:
Tiger-flower is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a group of bulbous plants. In botany the group is known as Tigridia. It belongs to the iris order, Iridaceae, in the text. Its plants are natives of Mexico and Central America. They also grow wild in Peru and in Chile. Long, narrow leaves spring straight from the bulb. Those leaves are veined in neat pleats along their length.

A stem bears two or three smaller leaves above. A few flowers emerge from a spathe at its top. The flowers are spotted, which gives the plant its name. Each flower has segments that spring from a tube. The three outer segments are large and spread wide. The three inner ones are much smaller and more erect. One kind bears large blooms of gold and orange. White and yellow forms of it are also noted.
britannica-1911-tiglath-pileser:
Tiglath-Pileser was the name of several kings of Assyria, and the numbering of them is not fixed. The 1911 Britannica article deals first with Tiglath-Pileser the First. He came to the throne about 1120 BC and ranks among the great Assyrian conquerors. His first wars drove foes from Assyrian lands on the Upper Euphrates. He then overran lands to the east and pushed into the hills south of Lake Van.

Westward, he took Malatia and reached the sources of the Tigris three times. He held the road to the great sea by taking Pethor, and at Arvad he got gifts from the king of Egypt. The article notes his love of the hunt and his building work at Assur. A later king of the name reigned about 950 to 930 BC, but next to nothing is known of him.
britannica-1911-timber:
Timber is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on wood cut and shaped for building, or growing wood fit for that use. The word appears in many forms in Teutonic tongues. At first it meant material to be used for building. Its root is seen in Greek and Latin words for building and for a house.

The wood used in building comes from trees that grow by adding a layer of new wood each year. A cross cut of such a tree shows three clear parts, the entry explains. At the centre sits the pith, around it the wood in near rings, and outside the bark. The wood near the pith is hard and close in grain and is called heart wood. The softer, younger wood outside it is treated next.
britannica-1911-tinker: Tinker, the name for a wandering mender of kettles and pans, is explained in a brief word entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name means one who makes a tinkling sound as he mends the vessels. In the sixteenth century the form tinkler was in use. From early times tinkers were looked on as vagabonds. An act of Elizabeth against vagrancy classed them as such by law.
britannica-1911-tordenskjold-peder:
Tordenskjold, Peder is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Danish naval hero. He was born at Trondhjem on the twenty-eighth of October 1691 and died in 1720. He was the tenth child of an alderman of Bergen, in Norway. As a boy, named Wessel, he was wild and unruly and gave his pious parents much trouble.

At last he ran away, hidden in a ship bound for Copenhagen. There the king's chaplain took pity on the friendless lad. He fed the boy's love of the sea with a voyage to the West Indies and won him a cadet's place. After voyages to the East Indies, Wessel became a second lieutenant in 1711. Soon he held a little four-gun sloop and cruised the Swedish coast, gathering news of the enemy. In June 1712 he was raised to a twenty-gun frigate.
britannica-1911-torrey-reuben-archer:
Reuben Archer Torrey, born in 1856, was an American evangelist whose life is summed up in a 1911 Britannica entry. He was born at Hoboken in New Jersey and trained at Yale for the church. He became a Congregational minister in 1878 and then studied in Germany for a year. In 1889 he joined Moody in his church work in Chicago.

He later led the Chicago Avenue Church and then ran the Moody Bible Institute there. From 1902 he preached across much of the English speaking world. With a singing partner he led revival meetings in Britain for two years. He then ran a like tour of cities in America and Canada.
britannica-1911-towcester:
Towcester is a market town in Northamptonshire in England, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands eight miles south-west of Northampton, on two rail lines. The small river Tove runs by it on its way to the Ouse. Its people numbered 2,371 in 1901. The church of St Lawrence shows work of three old styles and has a fine west tower.

The town has a fair trade in farm goods and a trade in boots and shoes. A Roman town or village once stood here on Watling Street, and the site has yielded many relics. In the tenth century a fort was kept here against the Danes. A mound called Burg Hill marks the place of both the Roman post and the fort. The district saw much of the fighting of the Civil War.
britannica-1911-tower:
A tower is a tall building first designed for defence, as part of the walls of a city or castle. The word comes from the Latin turris, with kin forms in French, Italian, and German. Towers seem not to have existed in Egypt, the entry says. In Mesopotamia they form the chief feature of city walls from the earliest times. Assyrian palace carvings at Nimroud show them in that role.

The earliest picture of a tower may be a plan cut on a tablet held by a priest king. It shows a walled circuit with gates, bastions, and towers. Towers found in that region stood about forty feet square. They jutted sixteen to twenty feet in front of the walls. They stood about eighty feet apart, though later ages spaced them wider. Faster missiles are given as one cause of the wider gap.
britannica-1911-treguier: Treguier is a port in western France, described in a brief place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in Cotes du Nord, where two streams join to form the Treguier river. About two thousand six hundred people lived there in 1906. Fishing and a small coastal trade support the town. The cathedral, from the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, is noted for three towers. A statue marks Ernest Renan, a native of the town.
britannica-1911-trencher:
The 1911 Britannica article on the trencher describes an old form of platter. It was a flat piece of wood. The earliest ones were square. Later ones were round. Food was carved and served on them. The word comes from a French term for a place to cut up food.

The article explains what came before and after. Thick slices of coarse bread served as trenchers first. Soaked in gravy, they were eaten or given to the poor. Pottery and then porcelain plates ended the wooden trencher. Winchester College still uses old square beechwood ones. Flat earthenware plates of the seventeen hundreds were called trencher plates. Small salts by each diner were trencher salt-cellars. Great standing salts were a separate, showy kind.
britannica-1911-trenck-franz-freiherr-vo:
Franz, Freiherr von der Trenck (1711-1749), was an Austrian soldier, born of a military family, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. Educated by the Jesuits at Oedenburg, he entered the Imperial army in 1728 but resigned in disgrace three years later. He then married and lived on his estates for some years.

On his wife's death in 1737, Trenck offered to raise an irregular corps of Pandours for service against the Turks. The offer was refused, and he entered the Russian army instead. After a short time fighting the Turks as a cavalry officer he was accused of bad conduct, brutality, and disobedience. He was condemned to death, though the sentence was cut by Field Marshal Münnich to loss of rank and imprisonment. Back in Austria he fell out with everyone and even took sanctuary in a convent in Vienna.
britannica-1911-trent-river:
The Trent is the subject of a river entry in the 1911 Britannica. The Trent is the chief river of the midlands of England. Only the Thames and the Severn run longer in the land. It rises in the north of Staffordshire. It flows through the Humber out to the North Sea. Its full course runs to about one hundred and seventy miles. Its basin spans just over four thousand square miles.

The course is traced town by town from the source. It skirts the Potteries and passes Stoke at the start. It then turns south east and takes in side streams. The Sow, the Penk, and the Tame join it in turn. The Dove, Derwent, and Soar feed it in swift order. It passes Nottingham and Newark on its way north.
britannica-1911-trier:
Trier is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an ancient city of Germany. In French the name is given as Treves. The city was once capital of an archbishopric and electorate. It is now seat of a Roman Catholic bishop. It is also chief town of a government district in Prussian Rhine land. Counts put its people at 46,709 in 1905. Most of them were Roman Catholics, the text says.

The city stands on the right bank of the Moselle. It lies in a rich valley shut in by vine clad hills. Red sandstone buildings of the old town mix with orchards. Gardens follow the line of the old medieval walls. The Roman city once spread much farther south and east. Trier holds more key Roman remains than any place in northern Europe. Some bridge piers may be the oldest of those remains.
britannica-1911-tumbler:
Tumbler is traced as a word with many lives in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. At root it means that which tumbles, that is, falls or rolls over or down. The entry links the Old English form to Dutch and German kin words for stagger and fall. French tomber, to fall, is also said to be of the same stock.

As a word for a person, a tumbler is an acrobat. He shows his skill by turning head over heels or walking on his hands. Old texts even call the girl who danced before Herod by this word. The entry then moves to the plain glass cup that bears the same name. Readers get word roots, stage use, and home use in one short piece. It shows how one plain word can spread wide.
britannica-1911-twysden-sir-roger:
Sir Roger Twysden, an English antiquary and royalist writer who lived from 1597 to 1672, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He came of an old Kentish family, and his father was a courtier and scholar of note. Roger was schooled at St Paul's in London and at Emmanuel College, Cambridge. He entered Gray's Inn in 1623 and took the baronetcy on his father's death in 1629.

For years he stayed at Roydon, building, planting, and studying old records and the law. The king's rule without parliament offended him, and he refused to pay ship money. He sat in the Short Parliament of 1640 but not the Long one. As war neared he backed the king in words, not in the field. His Kentish petition of 1642 brought arrest, the Tower, fines, and seized rents, till he compounded in 1650.
britannica-1911-typewriter:
Typewriter, a machine that prints letters like a press, is given a history in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word also names the person who works such a machine. The article starts with a British patent granted to Henry Mill in 1714. Mill claimed a method for printing letters one after another, as neat as print itself.

The piece then moves through a chain of early designs in France and America. Burt's American typographer of 1829 left no records, lost in a fire at Washington. Progrin's French machine of 1833 worked on the type-bar plan. Thurber's chirographer used a wheel that turned the wanted letter into place. A machine for the blind and Foucault's rod design, shown at the Great Exhibition of 1851, close this early survey.
britannica-1911-typhus-fever:
Typhus fever is a sharp spread ill that lasts about two weeks. Its name comes from a Greek word for smoke or mist, for the daze it brings. Great loss of strength, hard nerve signs, and a odd rash on the skin mark the ill. It has borne scores of names in past days.

Old English books give the best tales of its raids on towns. Courts were struck when ill men from gaols were brought in to face trial. Crowds and want are named as the chief soil for the ill. It struck the poor of big towns and hosts in the field most hard.
britannica-1911-urswick-christopher:
Christopher Urswick is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English envoy born in Lancashire in fourteen forty eight. He served as chaplain to the mother of a future king. She used him to push her secret plans to win the throne for her son.

The entry tells how he crossed the sea with that son and stood at the great battle. Church posts and honours then came to him in fast order. He ran talks in Spain for a royal match and in France for a peace pact. He was a close friend of two famed scholars of the age. A chapel at Windsor still bears his name today.
britannica-1911-usher:
An usher is, in root, an official who guards the entrance to a building. The word comes through French from a Latin term for a door keeper. Such a servant lets in those with a right to enter and keeps strangers out. Ushers also lead guests to their seats or to those who receive them. They keep order and silence in the room as part of their work.

Ushers of a law court are the best known officials of this kind. The British royal household holds several gentlemen ushers on its staff. The four chief orders of knighthood each style one of their officers an usher. The best known is the gentleman usher of the Black Rod, an officer of the Lords. A fading use of the word names an under master at a school.
britannica-1911-usk-river:
Usk is a river entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a river of Wales and England that runs to a great channel. The stream rises high on the flank of a Welsh beacon peak. Its course runs for some seventy miles from spring to sea.

The entry follows its flow east through a vale shut in by high hills. Walled towns of old stand on its banks at each broad turn. For a short stretch the stream forms the Welsh border with England. Canals that trace its vale carry a small trade up to a hill town. The stream is famed far and wide for its salmon and trout sport.
britannica-1911-vener:
Lake Vener, the great lake of Sweden, is measured in a lake entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the largest lake in that land and third in Europe. Its waters spread over more than two thousand square miles. It runs eighty-seven miles long and forty-four miles wide at most. Its deep point sounds at two hundred and ninety-two feet.

The Klar River feeds it most from the north woods of Sweden. The Göta River drains it south to the Cattegat sea arm. Two points of land and a knot of isles split it in two. The west half of the lake bears the name Lake Dalbo. North shores rise high, rocky, and clad in dark woods. Sea beasts left in its waters tell of a drowned past age.
britannica-1911-viper:
Viper, in the 1911 Britannica, is a snake entry on a family of Old World poisonous snakes. Vipers bear a pair of poison fangs set in short, movable jaw bones. The entry covers the true vipers only, those with no pit between eye and nose. Pit vipers and rattlesnakes are sent to their own articles. About nine genera and forty species make up the group.

The entry sorts them by head and tail shields. Echis, a desert kind, shuffles into sand with keeled side scales and makes a rustling sound by rubbing them. Cerastes, the horned viper of North Africa, buries itself till only eyes and horns show. Bitis holds the puff adder, a thick and deadly snake of near all Africa, four or five feet long.
britannica-1911-voltmeter:
Voltmeter is an instrument for the measure of electric force, as an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. It reads the gap in electric potential between two points in the unit called a volt. That unit is named for Volta. A volt is the gap that, laid across a resistance of one ohm, drives a steady current of one ampere through it.

A voltmeter is a form of electrometer, but the name is kept for the tool that reads at once in volts on a scale. Such tools fall in two classes, those that work by static force and those that work by current. In the first class two conductors at unlike potentials draw to each other with a force that grows as the square of the gap. One plate is fixed and one can move, held by a spring or by weight, and its shift gives the reading.
britannica-1911-walmer:
Walmer is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a sea resort town in Kent in England, south of Deal. The town forms part of an old port league town by the coast. The part most used by guests runs north to meet its neighbour town.

The entry gives a count of more than five thousand souls in the district. A castle by the sea was built as a shore fort by a Tudor king. That fort became the home of the wardens of the port league. Great men held that post and left their mark on its rooms. One famed duke died in that house in the mid last century.
britannica-1911-walsh-peter:
Peter Walsh, an Irish statesman and church voice born about sixteen eighteen, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Mooretown in county Kildare, he studied at Louvain. There he joined a great order of friars. In sixteen forty six he went to Kilkenny.

That town was then held by the rebel league of Irish church men. Walsh stood against the envoy of the pope in that camp. He urged peace with the royal deputy, and in time he helped win it. From that hour the hard line backers of the pope claims hounded him. He was at times in risk of death for his stand. When Cromwell won Ireland, Walsh lived in dim state in London and abroad.
britannica-1911-water:
Water is a 1911 Britannica article on the most common of substances, read by the chemist's light. Strictly speaking, water is the oxide of hydrogen. Its formula is usually stated as two parts hydrogen to one part oxygen. In popular use, the term covers a wide range of substances.

All of those, the text says, are the chemist's water changed by impurities. In ordinary waters, used for daily purposes, the impurities are very small by weight. As a rule they come to less than a tenth of one per cent. Of all natural stores of water, the ocean is by far the most abundant. From it, all other water may be said to derive. A steady stream of vapour rises from its surface into the air. There it condenses again in colder regions. The article opens the water cycle as science then told it.
britannica-1911-webster:
Webster was a township in Worcester county in the state of Massachusetts, set on the French river south west of the city of Worcester. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its counts at three census dates, its land area, and its rail and tram links. A fine lake of about two square miles lies in the township.

The entry names cloth and boots and shoes as its chief trades, with the worth of its mill output for a set year. It then tells how the town began: a mill builder raised cotton mills there early in the eighteen hundreds, then woollen mills, on land that had been near empty. The township took its name in honor of a famed statesman of that age.
britannica-1911-webster-alexander:
Alexander Webster, a Scots minister of numbers, is noted in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Edinburgh in 1707, he was a covenanting minister's son. He rose as a minister in the Church of Scotland in time. In 1742 he put forth a plan for widows of ministers. That plan would pay set sums to such widows for life.

Webster drew tables from returns sent by all Scots presbyteries. His sums rested on how long men and wives might live. Insurance firms in later times used much the same reckoning. In 1755 the state set him to count the folk of Scotland. That count was the first census of the land in full. He led the General Assembly as its moderator in 1753.
britannica-1911-weir-robert-walter:
Robert Walter Weir is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an American painter. He lived from 1803 to 1889. He was born at New Rochelle, New York. He painted portraits and historical scenes in his career. He was a pupil of the painter Jarvis. In 1829 he was elected to the National Academy of Design. He taught drawing at West Point for many years.

He was teacher of drawing there from 1834 to 1846. He then held the professor's chair till 1876. He died in New York City in May 1889. His best known work shows the Pilgrims setting sail. That canvas hangs in the rotunda of the Capitol. Other works show Hudson's landing and the Crucifixion. He painted Columbus before the Council of Salamanca. Portraits by him are held at West Point itself. His son John became a painter and sculptor too.
britannica-1911-welser:
Welser is the name of a famed family of German merchants, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. Members held office in the city of Augsburg as early as the 1200s. The family rose to weight in the 1400s, when the brothers Bartholomew and Lucas Welser traded with the Levant and beyond. They had branches in the chief trade centres of south Germany and Italy, and in Antwerp, London, and Lisbon.

Antony Welser, a son of Lucas, was among the first Germans to use the sea route to the East found by Vasco da Gama. The family also took part in mining ventures and amassed great wealth in trade. His son Bartholomew lent large sums to the emperor Charles the Fifth. Bartholomew and his brother are chiefly known for backing a voyage that seized land in the New World in 1528.
britannica-1911-wendover:
Wendover, a market town in Buckinghamshire, England, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town lies north west of London on a joint rail line. Its count in nineteen hundred and one was two thousand and thirty six. The entry sets it in a shallow gap in the Chiltern Hills.

Wendover is drawn as a quiet town of no great bustle. Its church of Saint Mary is mainly in the Decorated style, and a few old houses remain. The past runs deeper. The town stands on the Upper Icknield Way, an old British road, and traces of a British settlement have been found nearby. The king held the manor in ten eighty seven. The entry blends scene, church, and long past in a compact town portrait.
britannica-1911-weser:
Weser is one of the chief rivers of Germany, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows its course to the sea. It is formed where the Werra and the Fulda join at Münden in Hanover. From there it flows generally north and enters the North Sea below Bremerhaven. The mouth lies 170 miles from Münden, but the winding course runs to 270 miles.

From the source of the Werra the whole stream measures 440 miles. Nearly all of the course lies in Prussia, though the river touches Brunswick and Lippe and flows through Bremen. Between Münden and Minden it runs through a pretty valley flanked by broken ranges of hills. It then breaks out of the hills by a narrow pass called the Porta Westfalica. Below that the land opens, and the river widens toward its estuary.
britannica-1911-west-chester:
West Chester is a borough and the county seat of Chester county, Pennsylvania. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it some 20 miles west of Philadelphia. Its count grew from 8,028 in 1890 to 11,767 in 1910. Two rail lines and an electric line link it to the great city. The town sits some 450 feet above the sea in rolling country.

Schools form a proud part of the life of the borough. A state normal school there dates from the year 1871. A seminary for girls was founded in 1851 by Smedley Darlington. Friends schools for boys and girls add to the list of seats of learning. Fine plant gardens fill Marshall Square for all to enjoy in town.
britannica-1911-westminster:
Westminster is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the London district that holds the Abbey, the Houses of Parliament, and the offices of government. Strictly it is a city in the county of London, bounded east by the City, south by the Thames, and west and north by Chelsea, Kensington, Paddington, Marylebone, and Holborn. It was formed into a borough under the London Government Act of 1899 and made a city by royal charter in October 1900.

The city covers 2,502 acres from Fleet Street to Kensington Gardens and takes in Buckingham and St James's palaces and the National Gallery. The article turns at length to Westminster Abbey, the church of St Peter, raised on Thorney isle in the Thames marshes.
britannica-1911-wilson-john-writer:
John Wilson, a Scottish writer born in seventeen eighty five, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Readers knew him best as Christopher North of a famed magazine. Born at Paisley, he was the son of a rich gauze maker who died when John was eleven. He was the fourth child but the eldest son, with nine brothers and sisters.

He entered the town university at Glasgow at age twelve. He stayed six years in its classes, most of that time in the home of his tutor. In those years he built skill in study and in sport alike. He also fell in love with a girl named Margaret, who held his heart for years. In eighteen hundred and three he went on to Oxford as a gentleman commoner. The entry traces how a bright, bold youth became a lead voice in print.
britannica-1911-winchester:
Winchester, a city and borough of Hampshire in England, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies about sixty six miles south west of London by rail. The count in 1901 was 20929 people. The city holds a hilly and pretty site in and above the valley of the Itchen, mostly on the left bank.

Chalk downs ring the town, while the valley floor is well wooded. The entry sets aside legends of a church founded there in the second century. It dates the making of Winchester as a bishop seat to the late seventh century. The West Saxon see moved there from Dorchester on the Thame. Its first bishop was Hedda, who died in 705. The modern diocese takes in nearly all of Hampshire.
britannica-1911-winter-peter:
Peter Winter was born about 1755 and died in 1825, a German composer. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Mannheim, where he was born. He had some lessons from the Abt Vogler but taught himself most. He played in the court band of the Elector Karl Theodor. In 1776 he took charge of the court theatre at Munich.

When Mozart staged Idomeneo at Munich in 1781, Winter grew bitter. He conceived a fierce hate for the younger man, the entry says. Yet of more than thirty operas he wrote, few failed on stage. His best loved work was staged at Vienna in the year 1796. Two more works there spun on from Mozart's Magic Flute tale.
britannica-1911-wren-sir-christopher:
Sir Christopher Wren, an English architect who lived from 1632 to 1723, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at East Knoyle in Wiltshire, the son of a clergyman. He entered Wadham College, Oxford, in 1646 and took his degree in 1650. At Oxford he stood out in geometry and applied mathematics, and Newton praised his work highly.

In 1657 Wren became professor of astronomy at Gresham College, and in 1660 he took the Savilian chair at Oxford. Yet he is best known as an architect, a path opened by the great fire of London. The fire gutted the old Saint Paul's Cathedral and most city churches. Just before it, Charles the Second had asked Wren for a scheme to restore Saint Paul's. His plan kept only the choir and rebuilt the rest in a Roman manner, with a high dome.
britannica-1911-yeats-william-butler:
William Butler Yeats (1865-) is an Irish author born at Sandymount, Dublin, on 13 June 1865. His father, J. B. Yeats, was a noted Irish artist. At nine the boy went to live with his parents in London and went to school at Hammersmith. At fifteen he moved to a school in Dublin. He later studied painting for a short time but soon turned to writing.

Yeats sent poems and pieces to Irish journals in his youth. In 1888 Oscar Wilde urged him to try his luck in London. There in 1889 he brought out his first book of verse, The Wanderings of Oisin. Its fresh and romantic touch struck keen critics and lit new interest in the Celtic movement. He also made a gathering of Irish folk tales for a popular series.
britannica-1911-yellow-fever:
Yellow fever is a sharp tropical fever spread by a mosquito. The 1911 Britannica entry names the germ and its winged carrier. The Stegomyia fasciata, a house mosquito, bears the germ from man to man. The ill is native to a few set tracts of the hot world. Those tracts span the West Indies, Mexico, and Central America in part.

The west coast of Africa and Brazil round out its home range. The first sure report comes from Bridgetown in Barbados in 1647. There it was hailed as a new pest of unknown source and cause. A local historian tied its coming to the arrival of ships in port. Like outbreaks struck Guadeloupe and St Kitts in those same early years.
brother-and-sister:
Josephine Lawrence's Brother and Sister opens the Morrison family at breakfast on a rainy morning. Brother will not drink his milk because rain stops outdoor growing. His brother Ralph promises a birthday present next week, if Brother is tall enough by Wednesday. Louise, the older sister, calls him silly.

Twenty-two short chapters follow Brother and Sister through party preparations and presents. Dick's buttons, a haunted house, and a very sick doll supply the adventures. Mickey Gaffney, a poorer neighbour boy, needs plans and finally owns up. Lawrence wrote the first of her Brother and Sister series for young children. The episodes are gentle, funny, and exact about family life: spilled treats, small jealousies, and making up. Grandma Hastings and Miss Putnam keep the grown-up world kindly in view.
browning-as-a-philosophical-and-religiou:
Henry Jones, professor of philosophy at Glasgow, wrote a study of Robert Browning as a teacher in thought and faith. Eleven chapters line the frame. First comes the need of a life philosophy. Browning's place in English verse holds the third place. Hope as his ruling note holds the fourth.

Hope and morals clash in the fifth chapter, and that clash is worked out in full. Love as a rule of life holds the sixth. Idealism and its grounds hold the seventh. The hard case of evil gets its own long eighth chapter. Where knowledge fails holds the ninth. Heart and head, love and reason, meet in the tenth, and a close sums the whole. A Hegel line fronts the start: a great man lays on the world the task of making him plain. Jones takes up that task for the poet.
bucky-o-connor-a-tale-of-the-unfenced-bo:
William MacLeod Raine dedicates Bucky O'Connor to his brother Edgar. The Denver letter is dated March 1910. It offers the tale of the unfenced border as a companion for a long northern winter. Sheriff Bucky O'Connor of Arizona enters with Bear-Trap Collins in chapter one. Taxation without representation and a called bluff follow in the contents.

Bucky crosses into revolutionary Mexico and survives the hold-up of the M C P flyer. He pursues a kidnapped girl and stolen money, through stone walls that do not a prison make. He climbs stairs three at a time to meet brown eyes after the night's hazards. Raine, a Colorado schoolteacher turned Westerner, writes clean action with a romantic shine.
bull-hunter:
Max Brand wrote a western novel that opens on hard stump work in high woods. Two men have cut through side roots thick as branches. Small roots below gave way as well. One great taproot in the core still holds the stump fast. Their hole is too tight for a free axe swing.

Blows fray the root but cannot cut it clean. Both men haul at it with a grunt till wood tears. Still the stump holds and up it will not come. Too tired to swear, they stop and gaze down the slope. Trees tell them the height of the place. Strength spent on one root sets the book's scale: big land, big men, and work that fights back. The title's bull hunter waits past this first scene, in the tale's own good time.
burnham-breaker:
Homer Greene wrote a coal-town tale, signed at Honesdale, Pennsylvania, in September 1887. The book is given to his father, whose grey hairs and manhood he praises in warm lines. Twenty-four chapters line the frame. Scranton and its breaker yards set the stage, as the first chapter's screen-room scene shows.

A strange guest and a bright scheme open the run. A hunt for a mother and the breaking of news fill the early heart. Rhyming Joe brings the light touch. Court bar, proof in the case, and a bought lie raise the stakes hard. A writ of habeas corpus and tales told to a jury fill the law run. Back to the breaker, fire in the shaft, and a hard passage in the dark lead to dawn at the close. Boy work, law, and mine risk drive the whole.
business-correspondence-vol-1-how-to-wri:
An anonymous manual, Business Correspondence, Volume One: How to Write the Business Letter, teaches the art of selling and persuading by post. Its twenty-four chapters draw proved principles and practical schemes from extracts of 217 actual letters.

Early chapters prepare the writer: what a postage stamp can do, the advantages of doing business by letter, and gathering talking points. Later parts show how to open a letter, present a proposition convincingly, close effectively, and acquire a forceful, original style. The volume adapts selling appeal to different prospects and aims at orders by letter. Modern readers will find it a vivid record of early twentieth-century salesmanship.
cabin-fever:
B M Bower named Cabin Fever for the malady her first chapter diagnoses: the restlessness that snow, isolation, and a failing marriage breed in a northern cabin. Bud, a young rancher, quarrels with his wife Marie and heads south with ten dollars and a job. The contents promise deserts, barren months, and cabin fever in its worst form.

Bud partners with the older Cash, whose sourdough loaves and silence steady the partnership through mining disappointments. A child, Lovin Child, enters the tangle, and Marie takes a desperate chance of her own. Bower resolves the fever with facts faced and a cure complete. Her Westerns ground romance in work, weather, and money, and this one adds a rare honest look at marriage.
campaign-of-the-indus-in-a-series-of-let:
T. W. E. Holdsworth's letters from the Indus war stand here in a print of 1840, framed by his father A. H. Holdsworth. The son served with the Bombay division. His home letters, writ for kin alone, form the book. Few copies were struck, for friends who cared, the front word owns.

An English army had cut into Central Asia, through lands no European troops had crossed since Alexander. That fact drives the print, the father holds. The son saw the Bombay part at first hand, and his word holds good where his eyes went. Plain home style is owned and left as is. March, camp, and fight in a strange land fill the letters. A proud father's hand, not a trade press plan, gave the tale its book form.
can-you-forgive-her:
Anthony Trollope wrote a long novel that first ran in monthly parts in 1864-1865, at a shilling each. Chapman and Hall put out the book form in two volumes, 1864 and 1865. Phiz drew the plates for the first volume. Trollope disliked that work, an editor's note owns, and Miss E. Taylor drew the rest.

Mr. Vavasor and his kin open the contents in view. A balcony at Basle fronts the book as its first plate. Orley Farm, Doctor Thorne, and Framley Parsonage head Trollope's past work on the title page. The title's own ask — can you forgive her — sets the book's moral test in four words. Love, cash, and kin pride in high life form the ground such a frame in Trollope's hands would work, and the part-issue dress marks its first readers' pace.
cap-n-dan-s-daughter:
Joseph C. Lincoln's Cap'n Dan's Daughter is a Cape Cod story set in the village of Trumet Centre, where the Metropolitan Dry Goods and Variety Store opens for business with no customers at all. August should bring city visitors hunting white duck hats, oilskin coats, post cards and chocolates, but the shop stands quiet.

Lincoln peoples his village with shopkeepers, sailors and summer folk, telling their doings in the dry, affectionate dialect humour that made his Cape Cod books famous. The daughter of the title, Cap'n Dan's own girl, stands at the centre of the village's hopes and gossip. Readers who enjoy gentle American local-colour fiction, with salt air and small-town comedy, will feel at home in Trumet.
cape-cod-and-all-the-pilgrim-land-june-1:
Cape Cod and All the Pilgrim Land comes here as one monthly number: June 1922, volume six, number four. Lemuel C. Hall ran the sheet as editor, with Charles L. Gifford on the trade side. The Cape Cod Publishing Company at Hyannis put it out. Its aim, by the masthead, is the good of south-east Massachusetts.

Dancing on the sands fronts the plates. Portal of the Cape opens the reads, by Hall's own pen. Where to spend a break, Wellfleet town, and a squeak for a life fill the first run. Cape trout streams and sea trips by Emma M. Pray spread the net. E. M. Chase gives proof and phone tales. Falmouth's inner port and Bass River get their takes. Cape notes, a late letter, and a tale of a million quarts of strawberries close the list in view.
carmen-s-messenger:
Harold Bindloss published his novel in New York in 1917, opening at Gardner's Crossing in North Ontario, a mill town on the edge of the northern woods. Jake Foster, waiting at the station, is drawn into his friend Featherstone's troubles and makes a promise that sends him travelling with a packet he must deliver and protect.

Thirty-two chapters carry Foster between Canada and northern England, along drove roads and waste ground, past poachers and false trails. A man named Daly works against him, letters and a glove become clues, and Carmen waits at the heart of the errand. Bindloss mixes mystery, pursuit, and quiet romance, with hard outdoor travel doing much of the work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-deer:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Deer describes a once-famous Scottish monastery on the Ugie in Buchan. Celtic legend tells how St. Columcille, with his disciple Drostan, founded a missionary centre there on lands given by the local chief, whose son Columcille's prayers had healed.

Columcille soon moved on, leaving Drostan as abbot until his death about 606, and Aberdour's veneration of Drostan supports the legend. In 1219 the Earl of Buchan founded the Cistercian abbey of New Deer two miles west, granting it part of Old Deer's lands. Later a titular abbot held the lands in commendam, and the flourishing monastery fell prey to the troubles of the age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-dorc:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Dorchester describes an abbey founded in 1140 by Alexander of Lincoln for Augustinian canons, or Black Canons. Dorchester, a Roman city of Mercia nine miles from Oxford, had held a bishopric from 634, when St. Birinus arrived, until the see moved to Lincoln in 1085.

The abbey, dedicated to Peter, Paul and Birinus, drew rich gifts from the old bishopric's lands and tithes, with twelve parishes subject to it. Its first abbot appears to have been Alured, and its last, John Mershe, elected in 1533, subscribed to the king's supremacy and took a pension of twenty-two pounds a year. Henry the Eighth kept much of the property for a college of his own founding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abner:
Abner, son of Ner and cousin of Saul, served as commander-in-chief of Saul's army. After Saul and three of his sons fell at Mount Gelboe, Abner made Isboseth, Saul's fourth son, king over all Israel except Judea, which held to David. For seven and a half years he fought for Isboseth's throne, and near Gabaon he reluctantly slew Asael, brother of Joab, who pursued him hotly.

That killing embittered Joab, who counted himself his brother's avenger. When Isboseth rebuked Abner for marrying Respha, a concubine of Saul, Abner angrily opened talks with David, restored Saul's daughter Michol to him as demanded, and reached a full understanding. Joab then called him back and killed him at the city gate, and David mourned him and charged Solomon to avenge the murder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adalbert-stif:
Adalbert Stifter was a poet and pedagogue born at Oberplan in Bohemia on 23 October 1805. He died at Linz on 28 October 1868; his father had been a linen weaver and flax dealer. The boy's first stimulus came from his mother and grandmother, tellers of fairy tales, stories, and legends. School proved him apt, with talent for music and drawing. After his father's sudden death in 1817, his grandfather placed him at the Benedictine school at Kremsmunster.

In 1827 Stifter went to Vienna University, moving from philosophy and law toward mathematics and natural science. He supported himself by private lessons among leading families, gaining a wide circle including Metternich's family. He wished to teach natural science and passed the written examination with honour in 1830, though not the oral one. At thirty-two, still a teaching candidate, he married, and his later writing and school work made him a noted Austrian author.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-heinrich:
Adam Heinrich Muller was a publicist and political economist, and a convert, born at Berlin on 30 June 1779. He died at Vienna on 17 January 1829. Meant for Protestant theology, he gave himself from 1798 at Gottingen to law, philosophy, and natural science. Back in Berlin, his friend Gentz persuaded him to take up political science. After serving in the Kurmark chamber and travelling in Sweden, Denmark, and Poland, he went to Vienna.

There he entered the Catholic faith on 30 April 1805, then lived at Dresden from 1806 to 1809, tutoring a Saxe-Weimar prince and lecturing on literature, drama, and political science. In 1808 he edited the periodical Phoebus with Heinrich von Kleist. In 1813 he became imperial commissioner and major of the Tyrol rifle corps in the wars of liberty, then a government counsellor reorganizing the country.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-tanner:
Adam Tanner was a controversialist born at Innsbruck in 1571 who died at Unken on 25 May 1632; he joined the Jesuits in 1589, teaching first Hebrew, apologetics, and moral theology. When a Catholic-Lutheran debate was arranged at Ratisbon in 1601, Tanner aided his fellow Jesuit Gretser. Together they argued the Bible's dead word could not be faith's supreme arbiter, and Tanner published an account of the proceedings in 1602.

In 1603 Bavaria's duke called him to Ingolstadt's scholastic theology chair. There he exposed the fallacies of the Augsburg Confession in his work of 1613. He defended Communion under one species and the sacrifice of the Mass against the Utraquists. He also vindicated church freedom against Venice in 1607. After fifteen years at Ingolstadt he moved to Vienna, published his great Universa theologia scholastica, and became Prague's chancellor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adelaide-anne:
Adelaide Anne Procter was a poetess and philanthropist born in London on 30 October 1825. She died there on 2 February 1864. Eldest daughter of Bryan Waller Procter, the poet Barry Cornwall, and Anne Benson Skepper, she showed precocious intelligence as a child. She gained French, German, and Italian, as well as music and drawing, and she read widely. Brought up amid literary leanings, she began writing verses early, contributing to the Book of Beauty at eighteen.

In 1851 she and two sisters became Catholics without disturbing the domestic circle's harmony. In 1853, under the pseudonym Mary Berwick, she sent a short poem to Household Words. It so pleased Charles Dickens that he accepted it and invited more. Only late the next year did Dickens learn his unknown correspondent was Barry Cornwall's daughter. Her poems and charitable work made her a beloved Victorian voice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adele-bayer:
Adele Bayer, nee Parmentier, was the eldest daughter of Andrew Parmentier. She was born in Belgium on 4 July 1814 and died in Brooklyn, New York, on 22 January 1892. Her father, a horticulturist and civil engineer born at Enghien in 1780, reached New York in 1824 en route to the West Indies. Persuaded to stay, he bought land near Brooklyn for a horticultural park.

His park soon became famous, and his skill was sought far and wide. He shaped American landscape gardening more than any other practitioner of his day. He introduced the black beech tree and several shrubs, vegetables, and vines, and helped found St. James's, Brooklyn diocese's first Catholic church. After his death in 1830, his daughter Adele and her mother carried on. During the Civil War Madame Bayer took up caring for sailors at the Brooklyn Navy Yard, a task she pursued for thirty years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adolf-pfister:
Adolf Pfister was an educationist born at Hechingen in Hohenzollern on 26 September 1810, who died at Ober-Dischingen in Wurtemberg on 29 April 1878. He was educated at Hechingen's Latin school, the Lyceum of Rastatt, and Sasbach, then studied theology at Strasburg's Grand Seminary. Ordained priest on 25 May 1833 at Freiburg, he served as curate at Sasbach and assistant at Freiburg Cathedral.

From 1835 to 1838 he was curate at Steinhofen, then pastor at Dotternhausen, Rosawangen from 1839, and Risstissen from 1841, also serving as school inspector at Ehingen from 1851. In 1857 he founded the Rottenburger Kirchenblatt, and from 1860 he edited Catholic school weeklies. His most valuable work was editing with Rolfus the Real-Encyclopadie of education on Catholic principles, four volumes from 1863 to 1866, with a second edition to 1874.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-advocates-of-:
Advocates of St. Peter are a body of jurists chartered by Leo XIII's brief of 5 July 1878. As the name indicates, their main object is defending the Holy See's rights and privileges, in both the spiritual and temporal order. Members bind themselves to refute calumnies against the church, whether from distortions of history, jurisprudence, or dogma.

Above all they devote their legal knowledge to defending church rights before civil tribunals. The society formed in 1877, on the Golden Episcopal Jubilee of Pius IX, with Count Cajetan Agnelli dei Malherbi of Rome as first president. Pius IX warmly approved the undertaking and desired its wide extension, since church immunities need defence everywhere and under every government. Branches spread rapidly across the Catholic world, with colleges in Italy and England, Austria and France, Spain and Germany, Canada, and South America, each affiliated to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aer:
Aer, Greek aer, the air, is the Greek church's largest, outermost chalice-and-paten covering. It matches the Latin rite's veil, slightly larger than that veil and is embroidered in the style and colour of the priest's vestments. Its name comes either from its former light material or from the priest holding it high in the air during the Nicene Creed.

During the Creed the priest waves it slowly toward the chalice. Its use, like the veil's, was first to cover the chalice and keep anything from falling in before consecration. It is first named in a sixth-century explanation of the liturgy and as the so-called aer in Constantinople's council acts. In the Greek church the veil rests on the deacon's shoulders at the great entrance, a rite kept in Greek Catholic practice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alabaster:
Alabaster, from Greek alabastros and Latin alabaster, of uncertain origin, is commonly fine-grained gypsum, calcium sulphate, much used for vase and ornament making. Oriental alabaster, the alabastrites of old writers, is a translucent marble formed from dripstone deposits. Because its banded structure is like onyx, it also goes by onyx marble, or simply, though wrongly, onyx.

From remote times it won high esteem for decoration. Among the ancients Oriental alabaster often held unguents in vases, believed to preserve them. Hence alabasters named the vases even when made of other materials. The sinful woman's alabastrum unguenti, anointing the Saviour, in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, was such a one. The vase, though probably of alabaster, need not have been of that material, as the English alabaster box of ointments seems to imply.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alain-chartie:
Alain Chartier, French poet of Bayeux, was born about 1390, who died between 1430 and 1440. He is believed to have studied at Paris, as did his brother Guillaume, later Bishop of Paris. In life he counted an eminent writer, and a century later men of letters still called him a noble poet and the father of French eloquence.

He is best known by the story of Margaret of Scotland, said to have kissed his sleeping lips to honour the mouth that spoke so many virtuous words. The story is only legend: Margaret came to France only in 1436, when Chartier was already dead by the best authorities. His love poems include Le debat de reveille-matin and Belle dame sans merci. Praised then, they seem to modern readers lifeless and pedantic. His Breviaire des Nobles codes the perfect knight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alban-butler:
Alban Butler was an English Catholic historian born at Appletree in Northamptonshire in 1710, who died at St-Omer in France in 1773. Schooled first at Dame Alice's School in Lancashire and then at the English College at Douai, he was ordained a priest in 1735. He ranked with Bishop Challoner as a leading Catholic scholar of England. The first half of the eighteenth century was a bleak time for English Catholics.

Butler gave nearly thirty years to his great work, Lives of the Fathers, Martyrs and Other Principal Saints, published between 1756 and 1759 and reprinted many times since. He finished it during his years at St-Omer, where he became president of the English College in 1766. He had earlier travelled with the Earl of Shrewsbury and his brothers in 1745. His other writings include letters on Bower's Lives of the Popes and a life of Mary of the Holy Cross.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albrecht-dure:
Albrecht Dürer was a celebrated German painter and engraver, born at Nuremberg in May 1471 and dead there in April 1528. He left his native city only three times. After his apprenticeships to his goldsmith father and to the painter Wohlgemut, he travelled through Germany. In 1505 to 1507 he spent time in Venice, and he travelled again in 1520 to 1521. Nuremberg itself was then famous for commerce, learning, and art.

The entry divides his work into three periods. Before 1505, he set up his own studio in 1494 after early portraits, Madonnas, and landscape sketches. From 1505 to 1520, his Festival of the Rosary, painted in Venice for German merchants, rivalled the Italian colourists. From 1520 to 1528, his diligence shows in newly found sketches for St. Jerome with the Skull. Dürer emerges as a master of both painting and engraving, rooted in Nuremberg's commerce, learning, and art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-bau:
Alexander Baumgartner was a Swiss poet and writer on the history of literature, born at St. Gall in June 1841 and dead at Luxemburg in September 1910. His father Gallus Jakob Baumgartner was a noted statesman. At the abbey school of Maria Einsiedeln, where he began higher studies at fourteen, the poet and scholar Father Gall Morel shaped the boy's mind. His bent was confirmed at the Jesuit school at Feldkirch.

Baumgartner joined the editorial staff of Stimmen aus Maria-Laach and wrote for it for thirty-six years, scarcely a number appearing without something from him. His fame rests on his writings on literary history, including studies of Lessing, Longfellow, and Joost van den Vondel, gathered toward his larger History of World Literature. He also travelled widely, visiting Iceland, Scandinavia, and St. Petersburg in 1883 and Denmark, Sweden, and Norway three years later, trips recalled in his Northern Journeys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alma-redempto:
Alma Redemptoris Mater, Kindly Mother of the Redeemer, opens one of four antiphons sung at Compline and Lauds honouring the Virgin through the seasons. This antiphon is assigned to the part of the year between first Vespers of the first Sunday in Advent and Compline of 2 February. It ceases then even if the Feast of the Purification is transferred. Six hexameter verses in strict prosodial form make it up, followed by versicle, response, and a seasonal prayer.

Hermannus Contractus, or Hermann the Cripple, who died in 1054, gets the credit for the hexameter verses. The antiphon must have been popular in England both before and after Chaucer's Prioress's Tale. The tale rests wholly on a legend about its recitation by the little clerk. Professor Skeat first thought the Alma Redemptoris in Chaucer was the sequence, but corrected the error in Modern Philology in April 1906.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloisius-edou:
Aloisius Edouard Camille Gaultier was a priest and schoolmaster, born at Asti about 1745 to French parents, dead at Paris in 1818. He studied first in France, then in Rome, where he was ordained. Returning to France in 1780, he devoted himself to education. In 1786 he opened a Paris school instructing children while amusing them. The Revolution drove him to England, where former pupils of the French nobility joined his London course for refugees.

Oxford and Cambridge admired his principles and commended his methods. He returned to France in 1801, teaching and publishing. A later London journey studied Bell and Lancaster's monitorial system for French schools. During the Hundred Days, Carnot named him to the public instruction commission. Later he helped found the Society for Elementary Instruction. His textbooks cover every branch of primary instruction, applying his instructive plays. The plays are questions and answers, with credits gained and lost stimulating interest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloys-karl-oh:
Aloys Karl Ohler was an educationist, born at Mainz in 1817 and dead there in 1889. He attended Mainz gymnasium, read theology at Giessen, then took orders at Mainz in 1839. First chaplain at Seligenstadt, he helped Moufang found and teach at the Progymnasium. He directed Mainz's St. Rochus Hospital in 1845, pastored at Abenheim near Worms in 1847. In June 1852 he became director of Bensheim's Hessian Catholic teachers' training college.

For fifteen years there, encouraged by Bishop von Ketteler, Ohler laboured for a better spirit in Hesse's teaching body. In April 1867 he became a Mainz cathedral canon, took charge of education, and lectured in pedagogy and catechetics at the seminary. He held the post until the seminary closed during the Kulturkampf in 1878. His chief work, Textbook of Education and Instruction (Mainz, 1861; tenth edition 1884), holds that Catholic youth should be educated on Catholic principles, Church and school cooperating. It was meant for clergy and teachers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloys-senefel:
Aloys Senefelder, inventor of lithography, was born at Prague in 1771, died at Munich in 1834. His father, a Munich Royal Theatre actor, played at Prague at his birth. Young Senefelder studied at Munich on a 120-florin diligence scholarship, then jurisprudence at Ingolstadt. His father's death in 1791 forced him to quit his studies, supporting his mother and eight siblings.

His experiments led to chemical printing. The design is marked on stone with greasy soap, wax, and lampblack, then washed with water soaking the unmarked parts. Printing ink adheres only to marked places, water protecting the rest, yielding many impressions, with no etching needed, since grease and water do not mix. His improvements won English, Bavarian Polytechnic, and Bavarian Crown medals. Despite financial difficulties, he stayed devoted to high ideals, hoping his invention would benefit mankind, never misused. His Complete Textbook of Lithography (Munich and Vienna, 1818) was translated into French, English, and Italian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alphons-huber:
Alphons Huber was an historian, born in October 1834 at Fügen in the Zillerthal, Tyrol, dead in November 1898 at Vienna. After humanities at Hall and Innsbruck, he studied history under Ficker at Vienna University. Very young, Annegarn's history interested him deeply. In 1859 he became Innsbruck history lecturer, professor in 1863, Academy of Sciences Corresponding Member in 1867, and full member in 1872. In 1887 he became Vienna University professor, succeeding Ottokar Lorenz.

Under Ficker he learned critical accuracy, purity of style, and strictly impartial investigation, and diplomatics, the study of documents. His training showed in his writing and life: sober, opposed to claptrap, liberal in politics, but deeply religious. His earliest writings, on the Austrian Freiheitsbriefe and the forest cantons Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden, deal with territorial history. For Austria and Tyrol's union anniversary in 1864 he wrote its history, with a sequel on Duke Rudolf IV in 1865.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosiaster:
Ambrosiaster names the unknown author of a commentary on all St. Paul's Epistles except Hebrews, usually printed among St. Ambrose's works. Each epistle opens with a short prologue on purpose and context, the text given by sections with a natural, logical explanation for each portion. Modern scholars call it excellent, some the best of its kind before the sixteenth century. The commentary's section-by-section method keeps Paul's argument clear for readers following epistle by epistle.

Published in Migne's Patrologia Latina, volume seventeen, columns 45 to 508, it stands as a patristic landmark. The name itself marks the work's long misattribution to Ambrose, corrected by modern study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce:
Chester held a bishop and a cathedral only at intervals before the Reformation. The title Bishop of Chester appears even before the Norman Conquest, for prelates better called bishops of Mercia or Lichfield. After the Council of London in 1075 ordered sees moved into cities, Peter, Bishop of Lichfield, moved his seat to Chester. He took Saint John the Baptist as his cathedral.

His successor moved the see to Coventry for its rich monastery, keeping the palace at Chester. Saint John's still ranked as a cathedral, with its own dean and chapter of secular canons, down to the Reformation. The chief foundation in the city was its Benedictine monastery. Henry VIII created the see anew in 1541, but Rome recognized it only during Queen Mary's reign. One later bishop was sent to the Tower, escaped to the Continent, and died at Louvain in 1564.

Worcester was created in 680, when the Synod of Hatfield under Archbishop Theodore split the great Mercian diocese into five sees. Tatfrith, a monk of Whitby, was named bishop but died before consecration, and Bosel, a fellow monk, was consecrated in his place. The diocese then ran a singularly uneventful course, fortunate above all in never staying vacant long, with an unbroken line of bishops from 680 to 1565.

Mercian kings lavished gifts on the cathedral church, first dedicated to Saint Peter and later to Our Lady. Secular canons served it until Saint Oswald replaced them with Benedictines in the tenth century and rebuilt the church, finishing in 983. Danes burned city and cathedral in 1041, and Saint Wulstan rebuilt it between 1084 and 1089. Fires struck again in 1113, 1180, and 1202. King John was buried there in 1216, between the shrines of Oswald and Wulstan, and the restored cathedral was consecrated two years later before king, prelates, and nobles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Stavanger, in Norway, covered Stavanger, Lister and Mandal, and Nedenes. It was formed early in the twelfth century from southern Bergen, which had till then held all western Norway. Reginald, an Englishman, was its first bishop. With money King Sigurd Jorsalefarer gave him in 1128, for allowing the king to marry Cecilia during Malmfrid's lifetime, Reginald began the cathedral and founded the chapter.

Harald Gille had Reginald hanged at Bergen in 1135. He had refused to impoverish his see by paying fifteen marks of gold to a king who suspected him of hiding royal treasures. His successor John Birgersson moved to Trondhjem in 1152, as did Eric Ivarsson in 1188. Bishop Arne, from 1276 to 1303, quarrelled with his chapter from 1294 to 1303.
