Thomas Lister, also known as Thomas Butler, was an English Jesuit writer born in Lancashire about 1559. He trained at Douai and in Rome, and joined the Society of Jesus in 1582 or 1583. He came back to work on the English mission, and was arrested in 1598, years after an earlier long spell in prison.

His name lives on through a sharp pamphlet, Adversus factiosos in ecclesia. It damned English priests who refused the new archpriest, George Blackwell, as schismatics. The tract, passed around in manuscript, fanned a bitter clergy dispute. It drew an appeal of thirty-three priests to Rome, and was at last suppressed by a papal brief in 1601, with Blackwell rebuked for backing it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgical-us:
Water in worship goes well beyond holy water for blessings, foot washing, and the baptismal font. It has a set place in every Mass and in pontifical rites that involve washing, and the entry traces each use and the meanings attached to it.

Wine mixed with a little water in the chalice recalls both Christ joined to his people and blood and water flowing from his side. Water also washes the chalice after Communion, and communicants once drank water, or wine and water, as a purification after receiving. Greek practice adds hot water to the chalice before Communion, a custom Latins never shared.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lord-s-prayer:
The Lord's Prayer, the Our Father, is the prayer Christ taught his disciples, named for its teacher rather than for his own use of it. In medieval England it was said in Latin, even by the unlearned, and was known as the Pater noster.

Today's Catholic The English text owes nothing to the Rheims Testament; it follows a version fixed under Henry VIII and used in the prayer books of 1549 and 1552. It differs from that form only in who art for which art and on earth for in earth. The entry compares Matthew's fuller form with Luke's shorter one, and traces the prayer's use across centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenz-kellne:
Lorenz Kellner was a German educationist, born at Kalteneber in 1811 and dead at Trier in 1892. His father, a pupil of Pestalozzi, had opened the first teacher-training courses in Catholic Eichsfeld, and the son grew up inside that reforming world.

Kellner taught at Erfurt, helped run his father's seminary, and served Prussia's school boards at Marienwerder and then Trier. At Trier he founded seminaries for men and women teachers across twenty-nine years. His books tied grammar teaching to the reading book, gathered 178 essays on school and home training, and gave the first Catholic history of education.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-charles:
Louis Charles Couturier was abbot of Solesmes and head of the French Benedictine congregation, born at Chemille in 1817 and dead at Solesmes in 1890. He taught history at Combree, entered Solesmes in 1854 under its restorer Gueranger, and became master of novices within a month of profession.

Elected abbot on Gueranger's death in 1875, he kept Solesmes famed for piety and learning despite state persecution. The government expelled the monks in 1880 and again in 1882, yet the community lived on in three town houses, using the parish church as its abbey church. Couturier raised Marseilles to an abbey, restored deserted houses, and cheered the scholars among his monks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-honore-:
Louis Honore Mercier was a French-Canadian statesman, born at Iberville in 1840 and dead in 1894. Schooled by Montreal Jesuits and trained for the bar, he edited Le Courrier de St-Hyacinthe at twenty-two and at first opposed confederation as a blow to French-Canadian sway.

Rouville sent him to federal Parliament in 1873, and St-Hyacinthe to Quebec's assembly in 1881. Outrage over Louis Riel's execution let him found the National Party in 1885, blending Liberals and Conservatives. As premier from 1887 to 1892 he settled the Jesuit Estates Bill, paying the Society for lands seized by the Crown, and Leo XIII knighted him for it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucifer:
Lucifer, from Hebrew helel, first meant the morning star, the planet Venus in its brilliance. The Vulgate uses the word for morning light, for zodiac signs, and for dawn. In metaphor it crowns the king of Babylon, the high priest Simon, heaven's glory, and Christ himself as true light.

Jerome, following the Syriac and Aquila, traced helel to a verb meaning to lament. He made Lucifer the chief fallen angel mourning lost glory bright as the morning star. Christian tradition kept that sense, yet Fathers insist Lucifer is not the devil's proper name, only the shining state from which he fell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ludwig-babens:
Ludwig Babenstuber was a German Benedictine philosopher and theologian, born in Bavaria in 1660 and dead at Ettal in 1726. Slow to shine at first, he won vast learning by sheer industry and came to be called a man complete in every kind of doctrine and probity.

He taught philosophy at Salzburg from 1690, then theology at Schlehdorf, and returned to Salzburg in 1695 for twenty-two years as professor of moral, dogmatic, and exegetical theology. Vice-rector for three years and vice-chancellor for six, he stood as a staunch Thomist in dogma and a bold defender of probabilism in morals, while barring it wholly from faith. He retired to Ettal in 1717.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ludwig-von-sc:
Ludwig von Schwanthaler was founder of modern Romantic sculpture in Germany, born at Munich in 1802 and dead there in 1848. Schooled in Greek and Latin, he modelled wax as a boy. Love of country led him to paint battle scenes, and with Pocci he planned a march of knights to a tourney.

King Maximilian I and then Louis I of Bavaria gave him work in floods. He carved Glyptothek reliefs of Greek gods and Pinakothek artist statues. He made a 143-foot Bacchus frieze and Walhalla pediments of Germania and Arminius. His colossal Bavaria, 62 feet high, stands above Munich's Hall of Fame. Haste from patrons bred too much work, yet his inventive mind never repeated itself, fresh and lively in every monument.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-magnoald-zieg:
Magnoald Ziegelbauer was a Benedictine historian of Swabia. He was born at Ellwangen in 1689 and died at Olmutz in 1750. He took vows at Zwiefalten in 1707. Ordination came in 1713. He then taught theology in his own house, until friction with less learned monks drove him away.

Reichenau took him in next. A mission to the Vienna court followed around 1730. He taught moral theology at Gottweig in 1732 and 1733. Then he returned to Vienna for literary work. In 1734 he became tutor to the young Barons von Latermann. From 1747 he served as secretary of the learned Societas incognitorum at Olmutz. His chief book, a literary history of the Benedictine Order, came out after his death in four volumes in 1754. It remains the standard work on its subject.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manchester:
Manchester was a diocese in New Hampshire, suffragan to the Archdiocese of Boston. It was erected on 4 May 1884 by splitting the Diocese of Portland, which had held both Maine and New Hampshire. Much of its early story therefore lies in Portland's records, where it had spent twenty-nine years.

Its first bishop was Denis Mary Bradley, born in County Kerry in 1846 and dead in 1903. John Bernard Delany, born at Lowell in 1864, followed him and died in 1906. George Albert Guertin, born at Nashua in 1869, was the third bishop and the incumbent in 1910. The diocese counted 118 secular and 19 regular priests. Its charities included four hospitals, seven orphan asylums holding 710 orphans, an infant asylum, refuges and homes for girls and aged women, and a home for old men.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manharter:
The Manharter were a Tyrolese politico-religious sect of the early nineteenth century. Its founder was Kaspar Benedict Hagleitner, a priest of Aschau. He alone among Brixenthal clergy refused the oath of allegiance set by Napoleon's edict of 30 May 1809. He held that priests who swore it stood excommunicated along with Napoleon.

Supporters soon rallied from Austrian patriots in Westendorf, Brixen im Thal, Hopfgarten, Itter, Worgl, and Kirchbichl. The schism peaked at Easter 1815, when Manzl and his household first refused sacraments from their parish vicar. Thenceforth the Manharter took Hagleitner as the only priest with power to confess and give communion. They shunned public worship and held their own meetings. Visits by Salzburg's administrator in 1819, counsel, and civil penalties all failed, and they pressed to send a deputation to Rome for the pope's own ruling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marian-dobmay:
Marian Dobmayer was a Benedictine theologian, born at Schwandorf in Bavaria in 1753 and dead at Amberg in 1805. He first joined the Jesuits, and after their suppression in 1773 entered the Benedictines at Weissenohe, professed in 1775 and ordained in 1778.

He taught philosophy at Neuberg from 1781 to 1787, and church teaching and history at Amberg from 1787 to 1794. He also taught church teaching and study of the Fathers at Ingolstadt from 1794 to 1799. When Ingolstadt was reorganised in 1799 he returned to Weissenohe until its state closing, then taught theology at Amberg to his death. In 1789 he published a Conspectus of dogmatic theology at Amberg. His chief work, the Systema Theologiae Catholicae, came out after his death in eight volumes from 1807 to 1819, praised as very learned and free of harshness in controversy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marian-wolfga:
Marian Wolfgang Koller was a scientist and educator, born at Feistritz in Carniola in 1792 and dead of cholera at Vienna in 1866. Schooled first at home, he spent nine years at Laibach in classical, philosophical, and scientific studies, then took higher mathematics at Vienna. From 1814 to 1816 he tutored a family at Steinbach.

There the Benedictines of Kremsmunster drew him in, and he entered their novitiate in 1816, taking Marian for his baptismal Wolfgang. Ordained in 1821, he taught natural history and physics at Kremsmunster after parish work at Sippachzell. In 1830 he became director of its observatory, raising its repute across Austria over seventeen years. Called to Vienna in 1847, he served the university and the rebuilding Department of Education, overseeing Realschulen and polytechnic, nautical, and astronomical schools. The emperor gave him the Cross of the Order of Leopold in 1859 for organising the Realschulen, and his chief work, on periodic natural phenomena, appeared in 1850.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-marthe-:
Marie-Marthe-Baptistine Tamisier, called Emilia by friends, began the international Eucharistic congresses. She was born at Tours in 1834 and died there in 1910. From childhood she loved the Blessed Sacrament deeply. A day without Communion she called a real Good Friday.

She studied four years with Sacred Heart sisters at Marmoutier from 1847. Three tries at religious life failed, the third at Father Eymard's Perpetual Adoration house, where he told her she still belonged to the Lord in the Sacrament. In 1871 she settled near St John Vianney's tomb at Ars, and under Abbe Chevrier of Lyons found her calling, contemplative and active for the Eucharist. With bishops Segur and Richard, pilgrimages to miracle shrines began, and congresses grew from them. At Lourdes she was hailed as the Joan of Arc of the Sacrament, though her name stayed hidden until after her death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-bucer:
Martin Bucer, also called Butzer, was a leader of the South German Reformation, born at Schlettstadt in Alsace in 1491 and dead at Cambridge in 1551. He entered the Dominicans at fifteen in 1506, studied at Heidelberg from 1517, admired Erasmus, and turned Luther's disciple after hearing him dispute at Heidelberg in 1518.

Driven from Weissenburg in 1523, he reached Strasburg and became its chief reformer, active in many religio-political events. At first he backed Zwingli against Luther, then sought to mediate between them, offering vague formulas for unity that even his skill could not secure. After Luther and Melanchthon he ranked most influential among German reformers. He forms a link between German and English Reformations, and only one of his planned ten folio volumes appeared, the English volume at Basle in 1577.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-de-ber:
Martin de Bervanger was a French priest and founder of charitable institutions, born at Sarrelouis in 1795 and dead at Paris in 1865. After serving as assistant pastor at home, he helped found the Association Royale de Saint-Joseph in 1822 and later the Oeuvre de Saint-Henri. 

To reach that end better, he opened in 1827 a boarding school where poor boys gained manual, intellectual, religious, and moral education: the Oeuvre de Saint-Nicolas. It began with seven children in poor Faubourg Saint-Marceau quarters, then moved to Rue Vaugirard. The 1830 Revolution killed the first two institutions, but Saint-Nicolas survived. Scarce funds, hard-to-find teachers, and government suspicion of political plots brought vexatious inquiries, yet Bervanger overcame all obstacles and the house prospered. A branch rose at Issy. In 1859 he handed the institution to Cardinal Morlot, Archbishop of Paris, who gave its direction to the Christian Brothers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-deutin:
Martin Deutinger was a philosopher and religious writer, born at Langenpreising in Bavaria in 1815 and dead at Pfafers in Switzerland in 1864. Ordained in 1837, he taught philosophy at Freising in 1841, Munich in 1846, and Dillingen from 1847 to 1852. Like Baader and Anton Gunther before him, he tried to build a philosophy mediating Catholicism and Germany's ruling idealism, wedding faith truths to reason's demands.

His system rests on trilogies, with anthropology at centre. Starting from universal methodical doubt, he finds the Ego revealed in that doubt, then builds ternalities of nature, spirit, and personality with insight but much artificiality and mistiness. He failed chiefly by breaking with tradition to build his own house, boasting he cared not for other builders' form or material. Still, his rich mind, soaring imagination, and love of beauty mark his writings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-dobriz:
Martin Dobrizhoffer was a missionary, born at Graz in Styria in 1717 and dead at Vienna in 1791. He joined the Jesuits in 1736 and twelve years later sailed for South American missions, labouring eighteen years among Guaranis and Abipones. On Jesuit expulsion from Spanish lands in 1767 he returned home.

His three-volume Historia de Abiponibus of 1783 to 1784, on Paraguay's equestrian warlike nation, holds great ethnological worth. Seven years in four Abipone colonies let him watch manners, customs, superstitions, military discipline, slaughters given and received, and political and economic rules at close hand. He claims a candid, accurate account from eighteen years among Paraguayans, Indians, and Spaniards, across forests, mountains, plains, and broad rivers. He often refutes false claims about Paraguay Jesuits and calumnies that ruined their houses. Sara Coleridge, Samuel Taylor's daughter, made the 1822 English version, long ascribed to Southey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-kromer:
Martin Kromer was a distinguished Polish bishop and historian, born at Biecz in Galicia in 1512 and dead at Heilsberg in 1589. Son of a substantial citizen, he studied philosophy at Cracow, then theology at Bologna and Rome. Back in Poland he served as secretary to Bishop Gamrat of Cracow and to Prince Sigismund August, who made him a nobleman in 1552.

From that work came his thirty-book De origine et rebus gestis Polonorum, published at Basle in 1555, covering Poland to 1506 with keen criticism and polished Latin. His two-book Polonia of 1577, on Poland's land, peoples, customs, and government, remains a key source for contemporary Poland. He fought Protestantism with Polish sermons, polemics, and a catechism in plain style. Named Ermland coadjutor in 1570 by Cardinal Hosius, he succeeded as bishop in 1579 and held the see till death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-luther:
Martin Luther was leader of Germany's sixteenth-century religious revolt, born at Eisleben in 1483 and dead there in 1546. At eighteen he entered Erfurt University to study law at his father's wish, then joined the Augustinian monastery on 17 July 1505.

Ordained in 1507 and sent to Wittenberg in 1508, he wrestled with scrupulosity and God's anger, finally resting on justification by faith alone. On 31 October 1517 he posted ninety-five theses on indulgences to Wittenberg's castle church door, drawing Tetzel's reply and a papal hearing at Augsburg in 1518. The Leipzig disputation of 1519 fixed his break with Rome, and his 1520 manifestos made the religious agitation a political rebellion. Excommunicated and outlawed at Worms in 1521, he hid at the Wartburg, translating the New Testament into German. He married Katherine von Bora in 1525, finished his whole German Bible in 1534, and died at Eisleben in 1546.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-schong:
Martin Schongauer, also called Schon, was a German painter and engraver, born at Colmar between 1445 and 1450 and dead probably at Breisach in 1491. Son of Caspar Schongauer, a Bavarian goldsmith settled at Colmar about 1445, he had four brothers, Ludwig a painter and Caspar, Georg, and Paul goldsmiths. 

Almost all else about him comes from dates on drawings and engravings. His masterpiece, Virgin in the Garden of Roses, hangs in Colmar's St Martin church. Some call him Rogier van der Weyden's pupil, on a letter's authority, but though Rogier's influence shows, his studio entry stays doubtful. Few paintings can be proved his, and engravings signed M.S. rest on acceptance rather than documents. Still, in line-engraving technique he stands unsurpassed in his period, practically Durer's equal, with about a hundred plates surviving.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-waldse:
Martin Waldseemuller, Graecised Ilacomilus, was a learned humanist and celebrated cartographer, born near Fribourg about 1475 and dead as a St-Die canon probably early in 1522. He plainly studied theology, applying in 1514 as a Constance cleric for a St-Die canonry, which he won.

His great 1507 publication, Cosmographiae introductio with Vespucci's four voyages and a world map, drew wide attention on rediscovery as at first printing. Only a thousand copies of the map issued, and a single copy survived, found in Prince von Waldburg-Wolfegg-Waldsee's Wolfegg castle library. Twelve wood-engraved sections, each 18 by 24.5 inches, covered about thirty-six square feet in a modified Ptolemaic projection with curved meridians, a wholly new type of grandeur. With Ringmann he then made a new Latin Ptolemy, adding twenty modern maps, called the first modern world atlas. His 1516 Carta marina rivalled the 1507 map in size and worth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-agnes-ti:
Mary Agnes Tincker was a novelist, born at Ellsworth, Maine, in 1833 and dead at Boston in 1907. She began teaching in public schools at thirteen, saw her first literary work printed at fifteen, and became a Catholic at twenty, sharing sufferings from Know-Nothing bigotry even among Protestant kin. In 1863 she served as a volunteer war nurse in Washington until illness struck.

Short stories appeared in early Catholic World numbers, where her first novel, The House of Yorke, ran as a serial in 1871 to 1872. Grapes and Thorns followed in 1873 to 1874 and Six Sunny Months in 1876 to 1877, first fruit of her Italian stay from 1873 to 1887. These three struck a distinctly new note in Catholic letters, the highest ever struck by an American Catholic novelist. Later books, mostly reflecting Italy's beauty, won great fame as real art, though a lapse from religious practice shadowed a few.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-anne-mad:
Mary Anne Madden Sadlier was an authoress, born at Cootehill, County Cavan, Ireland, in 1820 and dead at Montreal in 1903. Her merchant father Francis Madden, a man of fine tastes, encouraged her writing, and her first efforts appeared in a London magazine while she was still young. After his death she emigrated to Montreal in 1844.

During fourteen Montreal years she wrote most of the books that made her famous, then moved to New York; her husband died there nine years later. Her stories and translations topped sixty volumes, popular among Irish-Americans in their constructive period and powerful in shaping their character. The Blakes and Flanagans treated the school question, Bessy Conway the immigrant girl's trials, and Aunt Honor's Keepsake New York's destitute Catholic children. Irish history fed The Red Hand of Ulster, The Confederate Chieftains, and Maureen Dhu.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-joseph-b:
Mary Joseph Butler was first Irish abbess of the Irish Benedictine Abbey of Our Lady of Grace at Ypres, Flanders. She was born at Callan, County Kilkenny, in December 1641 and died at Ypres in December 1723. 

She professed at Boulogne's English Benedictine convent on 4 November 1657 at sixteen. In 1665 Ghent founded Ypres under Dame Beaumont as abbess, but the house languished, and on Beaumont's death in 1682 it became a national foundation for Irish Benedictine nuns from Ghent houses. Dame Butler was sent to Ypres in 1683 and resumed convent life in extreme poverty with only a few lay sisters. The bishop urged her to sell the house and retire, but she held firm. By 1700 new subjects, including two Irish ladies from the French court, restored choir and observance, and she governed wisely till death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mater:
Mater was a titular bishopric in Byzantium province, named a free city by Pliny as Matera. Toulotte cites only two occupants of the see: Rusticianus, dead shortly before 411, and Quintasius, his successor. Gams lists four: Rusticianus, Cultasius for Quintasius, Adelfius in 484, and Victor about 556.

Mater is now Mateur, a small town of 4,000 people, largely Christian, in Tunis. The modern town is ringed by a wall with three gates and stands on the Tunis to Bizerta railway, not far from the lake that takes its name. Its ancient bishops, though few and sparsely recorded, link a Roman free city to a living Tunisian town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matter:
Matter, in the broad sense used here, means the stuff out of which a thing is made or put together. The Greek word hyle first meant woodland, then cut timber. The Latin materia likewise meant building timber rather than firewood. Paired with form, matter is the side of a thing that can take shape, as bronze takes the shape of a statue or leather takes the shape of a shoe.

Laid out in the scholastic manner, the entry walks through secondary matter in surface change and first matter in deep change. It then treats the nature of first matter, privation, its lasting presence, and its unity. Later sections cover its role in making each thing distinct, its causal work, and rival views. A reader who wants the classic Catholic philosophy of stuff and change will find the whole doctrine set out step by step.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthaeus-sch:
A Swiss churchman and diplomat, Matthaeus Schinner was born near Muhlbach in Valais about 1470 and died of plague at Rome in 1522. Taught by his uncle, later Bishop of Sion, he rose through parish and cathedral posts to that same see in 1499. His skill in talks and his pull over the Swiss cantons made him a trusted arm of two popes. Julius II and Leo X relied on him in their drive to free Italy from France.

Schinner brokered the Swiss alliance of 1511, won the cardinal's hat and the see of Novara, and led Swiss and Venetian troops to retake Milan in 1512. He beat the French at Novara in 1513, lost at Marignano in 1515, and kept plotting leagues against France until exile and court life filled his last years. His career shows a bishop who wielded armies as readily as pastoral staffs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthew-of-we:
No such man ever lived: Matthew of Westminster is an imaginary author born from a copyist's slip. A late manuscript of the chronicle Flores Historiarum calls it the book of Matthew, monk of Westminster. The scribe merely guessed, seeing that its later part was written at Westminster while its bulk followed Matthew Paris. Archbishop Parker printed the work under that name in 1567, following Bale and Joscelin.

In fullest form the chronicle runs from Creation to 1326, though many copies stop at 1306. From 1259, where Matthew Paris ends, it holds real worth as history. It was compiled at St. Albans to 1265 and then at Westminster to 1325 by several hands. Luard's Rolls Series edition of 1890, with a full inquiry into how the work grew, remains the standard guide to untangling the error.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthew-rader:
Matthew Rader, a Tyrolese Jesuit philologist and historian born at Innichen in 1561, taught the humanities for twenty-one years after joining the Society of Jesus at twenty. He wrote school dramas, but his fame rested on learned editions. In 1599 he published an improved, cleaned-up Martial, and in 1628 one of Quintus Curtius. His edition of the Acts of the Eighth Ecumenical Council joined a great collection of council acts.

His edition of the works of St. John Climacus, published in 1614, was reprinted by Migne in his Greek Patrology. His two rarest books, Bavaria Sancta and Bavaria Pia of 1628, celebrate Bavaria's saints and pious folk and were reprinted at Dillingen and Augsburg in 1704. Rader died at Munich in 1634, leaving scholarship prized by Catholics and non-Catholics alike for its care with ancient texts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthias-fabe:
Matthias Faber, a German writer and preacher born at Altomunster in 1586, died at Tyrnau in 1653. He served as parish priest of St. Maurice at Ingolstadt and professor at its university, winning fame as a sacred orator before joining the Society of Jesus at Vienna at the age of fifty. His Latin sermons, published in many editions, are prized for sound doctrine and wide learning.

Faber preached as a controversialist first and an orator second: his chief aim was to win over heretics or shield Catholics from Reformation teaching. He packed his sermons with Scripture texts after the fashion of his day, which makes them instructive but hard going. Readers seeking Counter-Reformation pulpit work in its classic Latin dress will find Faber a telling example.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthias-tann:
Bohemian Jesuit Matthias Tanner (1630-1692) spent most of his life at Prague. There he taught humanities, philosophy, theology, and Scripture, served as rector of the imperial university, and led the Bohemian province of his order for six years. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1646 and longed to match the apostles and martyrs of his order, a longing that shaped his writing.

To fire his brethren with the same zeal, he wrote lives of Jesuit martyrs and of Jesuits famed for heroic deeds across the world. He also prized reverence at Mass, celebrating, his biographer says, with a piety that drew the faithful like a lodestone to his altar. Two further works urged that reverence: an explanation of Christ's bloody sacrifice in the unbloody sacrifice of the Mass, re-edited three times, and a pamphlet against desecrating holy things.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthieu-peti:
Benedictine scholar Matthieu Petit-Didier (1659-1728) was born at Saint-Nicolas-du-Port in Lorraine and joined the Congregation of St-Vannes in 1675. He taught philosophy and theology from 1682. He was elected Abbot of Bouzonville in 1699 but barred from taking it by the Duke of Lorraine. He won Senones in 1715 only after a long dispute. He led his congregation from 1723 and became Bishop of Acra in 1725.

His reward followed his Traite sur l'autorite et l'infaillibilite du pape of 1724, a book banned in France and Lorraine yet translated into Italian and Latin. The pope prized it all the more because Petit-Didier had once appealed against the constitution Unigenitus. His other work includes sharp remarks on Dupin's church library and historical dissertations, marking him as a learned, combative defender of papal power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurus-corker:
Maurus Corker, an English Benedictine born James Corker in Yorkshire in 1636, died at Paddington in 1715. He took the name Maurus on entering the order and vowed at Lamspringe Abbey near Hildesheim in 1656. He returned to England as a missionary in 1665. Accused by Titus Oates in the Popish Plot, he was jailed in Newgate but acquitted of treason in July 1679.

Arraigned instead for being a priest, he was sentenced to death in January 1680, then reprieved through powerful friends and kept in Newgate. There he reportedly reconciled over a thousand Protestants to the faith. He befriended Archbishop Oliver Plunket in prison and prepared him for martyrdom in June 1681. Freed under James II in 1685, he served at court for the Elector of Cologne and built a convent at Clerkenwell, wrecked by a mob in 1688.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michel-cornei:
Michel Corneille the Elder, a French painter, etcher, and engraver born at Orleans about 1601, died at Paris in 1664. He studied with Simon Vouet, the celebrated master whose despotic sway over the French school stamped his personality on every pupil. Corneille gave himself to historical painting and ranked among the Royal Academy's twelve founding members in 1648, becoming its rector in 1656.

He was an excellent colourist, more Venetian than French in this, and his early manner resembled Vouet's. Later his work bore all the merits and faults of the post-Raphaelite, or decadent, sweet school of Italian art, showing the Carracci's far reach. Long employed decorating Paris churches, his masterpiece was St. Paul and St. Barnabas at Lystra, painted for Notre-Dame. His etched and engraved work, chiefly reproductive and close to the Carracci and his sons, includes the Murder of the Innocents after Raphael.

Michel Corneille the Younger, a French painter, etcher, and engraver born at Paris in 1642, died at the Gobelins manufactory in Paris on 16 August 1708. Son of the artist Michel Corneille of Orleans, he is sometimes called the younger Michel, but more commonly the elder Corneille, to set him apart from his brother Jean-Baptiste, also a painter. His father taught him first and hardest; Mignard and the famed Lebrun also taught him.

Wholly devoted to historical painting, Corneille won the Academy Prize and went to Rome on the king's pension. Feeling his genius cramped by the prize's rules, he gave up the money to study the antique his own way. Falling under the powerful Eclectics, he studied with the Carracci and modelled his manner on theirs. Returning to Paris in 1663, he joined the Royal Academy with Our Lord's Appearance to St. Peter after His Resurrection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michel-le-tel:
Michel Le Tellier, born 16 October 1643 to a peasant family, not at Vire as often said but at Vast near Cherbourg, died at La Fleche on 2 September 1719. Schooled at Caen's Jesuit college, he entered the order at eighteen and became professor, then rector of Louis-le-Grand College. He helped found the Journal de Trevoux and fought Jansenism in three works of 1672, 1699, and 1705.

In 1687 he joined the debate on Chinese ceremonies, publishing Defense des nouveaux chretiens et des missionaires de la Chine, du Japon, et des Indes. Rome disliked its tone, but the Jesuit General defended it before the Holy Office. Highly esteemed by the Jesuits, Le Tellier, after Father Petau's death, was charged with finishing his De theologicis dogmatibus. As Paris provincial, he became Louis XIV's confessor when La Chaise died in 1709, chosen through Chartres's bishop and St-Sulpice's rector.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-minister:
Minister has long been appropriated in a distinctive way to the clergy. Passages such as 1 Corinthians 4:1-2, Hebrews 8:2, and Matthew 20:26 must have helped familiarize the thought. Those charged with spiritual functions in the Christian Church were called to be servants, ministri, of their brethren. Even before the Reformation the word was occasionally used in English for clergy actually taking part in a function.

It then meant the celebrant as distinguished from the assistants, but it was not used alone to designate an ecclesiastic. That employment dates from Calvin and the Reformed churches, which made minister the ordinary title for their clergy. The article traces the term from its Latin root through medieval liturgical use to its modern Protestant sense.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montpellier:
Montpellier is a French diocese covering the department of Herault and suffragan to Avignon. It was re-established by the Concordat of 1802 with the Tarn added until Albi's creation detached it in 1822. Since 1877 its bishops may style themselves bishops of Montpellier, Beziers, Agde, Lodeve and Saint-Pons, recalling the sees now joined in it.

The original diocese was Maguelonne, whose apostolic origin legend names Simon the Leper landing with Lazarus, though the chronicler Arnaud de Verdale knew nothing of it. Its first certain bishop, Boetius, attended the Council of Narbonne in 589. After Saracen wars wrecked Maguelonne the see moved to Substantion and then to Montpellier itself, whose university and churches the entry traces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moritz-hohenb:
Moritz Hohenbaum van der Meer, born near Belgrade on 25 June 1718, was a Benedictine historian. He died at Rheinau monastery in Switzerland on 18 December 1795. He entered Rheinau as a student in 1730, took vows in 1734, and was ordained in 1741. He taught from 1744, served as prior from 1758 to 1774, and kept the monastic archives from 1759 until his death.

He also spent his last nineteen years as secretary of the Swiss Benedictine Congregation. He declined the bishopric of Lausanne when the pope offered it. His seventy-six treatises, mostly historical studies of his own and other monasteries, include a history of the Swiss Benedictine Congregation from 1602 to 1785 and a life of Saint Fintan. Nearly all remain in Latin manuscript, filling fifty-nine folio and twenty-three quarto volumes now largely at Zurich.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moriz-lieber:
Moriz Lieber, born at Blankenheim castle in the Eifel on 1 October 1790, was a politician and publicist. He died at Kamberg on 29 December 1860. He was a man of eminent ability, great learning and high culture, a faithful son of the Church and a fearless champion of her rights from youth to death. His earliest literary work translated leading Catholic books from foreign tongues. He fought the enlightenment and rationalism rampant in Germany since Joseph II.

He published de Maistre's three chief works in five volumes between 1822 and 1824. Then he translated Milner's End of Religious Controversy and Thomas Moore's Travels of an Irish Gentleman in Search of a Religion. Answering an anonymous attack on priestly celibacy, he wrote Vom Colibat in 1831. As a member of Nassau's Lower Chamber he defended church interests in print. He later helped found Catholic political organisation in Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-muenster:
Munster is a diocese in the Prussian province of Westphalia, suffragan to Cologne. Its earliest name was Mimegerneford, later Mimigardeford, and from 1076 Monasterium. First mentioned in 795, when Saint Ludger founded a monastery there and made it his see on becoming bishop, it already mattered. It held great estates apparently given by Charlemagne.

The entry follows the bishopric's growth into a prince-bishopric, its cathedral chapter and collegiate churches, and the Anabaptist rising of 1534 with its bloody suppression. It covers the Thirty Years' War and the Peace of Westphalia negotiated there. It ends with the diocese's later fortunes under Prussia, its parishes, schools and religious orders into modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-horn:
Nicholas Horner, layman and martyr, was born at Grantley, Yorkshire, and died at Smithfield on 4 March 1590. Working as a tailor in London, he was arrested for harbouring Catholic priests. Long confined in a damp, foul cell, he contracted blood poisoning in one leg, which had to be amputated. During the operation he reportedly received a vision that eased his sufferings.

Freed afterwards, he was again found harbouring priests, convicted of felony, and condemned for refusing to conform to the established Church's public worship. On his execution's eve he saw a crown of glory hanging over his head, filling him with courage. He told that story to a friend, who relayed it by letter to Father Robert Southwell on 18 March 1590. Horner was hanged, drawn and quartered for relieving Christopher Bales, a seminary priest martyred the same day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-sand:
Nicholas Sander, an English Catholic exile who became a leading voice against Elizabethan religious policy, fills this entry from the 1913 encyclopedia. Born in Surrey in 1530 and trained at Oxford, he fled abroad, took a doctorate at Rome, and advised cardinals on English affairs.

After teaching theology at Louvain, Sander argued against Bishop Jewel and wrote works on the Lord's Supper, images, and the visible rule of the church. Later he sailed for Ireland in support of a Catholic rising and died there in 1581. The entry closes by tracing his Irish mission and his death there in 1581.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-sylve:
French theologian Nicolas-Sylvestre Bergier, born in Lorraine in 1715, spent his maturity answering the philosophes in print. After a doctorate at Besançon and parish work there, he became canon of Notre-Dame in Paris in 1769 at the archbishop's call.

Asked to correct articles of the Encyclopédie, Bergier found he must write them afresh, and they grew into his Dictionary of Theology. Books against deism, Voltaire, and d'Holbach, plus studies of early languages and pagan gods, fill a career that ended at Versailles in 1790. He also wrote on the primitive elements of languages and the origin of pagan gods.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolaus-ferb:
Franciscan controversialist Nicolaus Ferber, born at Herborn in 1485, fought Lutheran teaching across northern Europe. As provincial of Cologne and vicar-general of the Cismontane Observance, he visited friaries in England, Germany, Spain, and Belgium for reform and discipline.

Summoned to Copenhagen by Danish bishops, he wrote a 1530 refutation of Danish Lutheranism that earned him the nickname Firebrand. His handbook of commonplaces against the heresies of his day, printed at Cologne in 1528, remained his chief work until his death at Toulouse in 1534. His Lenten Gospel explanations, preached in German and printed in Latin at Antwerp in 1533, complete the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nigel-wireker:
English satirist Nigel Wireker, a monk of Christ Church, Canterbury, around 1190, skewered monastic ambition in Latin verse. He knew Thomas Becket personally, served as precentor, and in 1189 joined monks pleading with King Richard against Archbishop Baldwin.

His Speculum Stultorum, or Mirror of Fools, follows an ass named Brunellus hunting a longer tail, a figure for the restless monk chasing promotion. Hugely popular in manuscript and early print, the poem reached Chaucer, who cites Daun Burnel the ass in the Nun's Priest's Tale. He claims to have known Saint Thomas of Canterbury personally, placing his monastic start before 1170.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nilus-the-you:
Calabrian monk Nilus the Younger, born at Rossano in 910, carried Greek monastic life into Latin Italy. Married for a time, he turned to the monk's life after sickness, lived as a hermit, and founded or restored houses under the rule of Saint Basil.

Nilus opposed the antipope Philogatos, then rebuked Gregory V and Otto III for torturing him. His chief foundation, the Greek monastery of Grottaferrata near Frascati, counts him its first abbot, and he died there in spirit in 1005, honored on 26 September. He spent his final years partly at Grottaferrata and partly as a hermit at Valleluce near Gaeta.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notker:
Notker, a name borne by several monks of Saint Gall, belongs chiefly to Blessed Notker Balbulus, the Stammerer, who died in 912. Schooled at Saint Gall beside Tuotilo, he served as librarian and master of guests, taught with taste, and wrote poetry, a martyrology, and a verse life of Saint Gall.

He is widely accepted as the monk of Saint Gall behind the legends of Charlemagne's deeds, and he brought the sequence into Germany by fitting Latin words to the long Alleluia melody. A collection dedicated to Bishop Liutward of Vercelli between 881 and 887 shows the new lyric form at work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-sain:
The Order of Saint Sylvester is a purely honorary papal title, neither monastic nor military, created by Gregory XVI on 31 October 1841. A fabulous Constantinian order claiming Sylvester's approval had usurped authority at Rome since the seventeenth century, and Gregory ended the abuse with a genuine title.

Its numbers run to 150 commanders, 300 Roman knights, and unlimited foreigners besides. It rewards service to the church with no privilege beyond wearing its decoration, a gold enamelled Maltese cross bearing Sylvester and the words 1841 Gregorius XVI restituit. Gregory created the title to end abuse by a fabulous Constantinian order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paolo-segneri:
Paolo Segneri the Elder was an Italian Jesuit preacher, missionary, and ascetical writer, born at Nettuno on 21 March 1624 and dead at Rome on 9 December 1694. He studied at the Roman College and joined the Society of Jesus in 1637, despite his father's opposition. Oliva guided his early religious life, Sforza Pallavicino taught him theology, and he lectured on humanities before ordination in 1653.

Steeped in Scripture, the Fathers, and Cicero's orations, he readied himself for the pulpit, his lifelong pull. He sought foreign missions, but Tuscany, the Papal States, and Italy's chief cities became his field. After cathedral preaching he gave popular missions for twenty-seven years, from 1665 to 1692, with eloquence matched only by holiness. Innocent XII, who had admired his Lenten sermons, called him to preach at court and made him theologian of the Penitentiaria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-passover:
Passover is the Jews' great yearly feast, awaited as eagerly as Christians await Christmas. Apart from Temple sacrifices, observance differs little from Christ's time. Law fixed the rules in Exodus and after the Exile they were kept with exactness. The feast runs from the fourteenth to the twenty-first of Nisan, a lunar month spanning late March and early April.

Houses undergo thorough spring cleaning, and the Saturday before, called Great Sabbath, announces the coming feast day. Utensils are cleansed of leaven and made kosher, with special sets kept for the feast. Later pages follow the seder meal, its four cups, bitter herbs, unleavened bread, and Haggadah reading, and the feast's keeping in Temple times, in exile, and in modern Jewish homes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-bened:
Patrick Benedict Zimmer was a philosopher and theologian born at Abtsgmuend in Wuerttemberg on 22 February 1752 and dead at Steinheim near Dillingen on 16 October 1820. He studied humanities and philosophy at Ellwangen, theology and law at Dillingen, and was ordained on 1 April 1775. He taught canon law at Dillingen's Saint Jerome College from 1777 and dogmatic theology at its university from 1783.

Dismissed from the faculty in 1795, ostensibly for living away from his Steinheim parish but truly for extreme idealism, he took dogmatic theology at Ingolstadt in 1799. He moved with the university to Landshut. He fought Kantian rationalism at Ingolstadt with courage and success, yet himself embraced Schelling's idealist pantheism without bending his Catholic practice. In 1819 he became university rector and deputy to Bavaria's Second Chamber.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patritius-spo:
Patritius Sporer was a moral theologian born at Passau in Bavaria and dead there on 29 May 1683. In 1637 he joined the Friars Minor at his home town's convent, then in the Strasbourg province. He taught theology for many years, earned the title Lector Jubilatus, and served as theologian to Passau's bishop.

His books include Love of God Above All of 1662, and a treatise on conscience as the immediate rule of human acts of 1660. His three-folio Moral Theology of 1681 was reissued at Salzburg, Venice, and Paderborn into the twentieth century. Ranked among his age's best moralists and still prized today, he is often quoted by Alphonsus Liguori. He followed probabilism, and between Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus he backed Scotus, drawing often on his own wide experience as a director of souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-pelisson:
Paul Pelisson-Fontanier was a French writer born at Beziers in 1624 of Protestant parents and dead at Versailles on 7 February 1693. He finished classical studies at eleven at Castres, read philosophy at Montauban and law at Toulouse, and at nineteen published a Latin translation and commentary on Justinian's Institutes, book one. His 1653 History of the French Academy won him election to that body.

Secretary to Superintendent Fouquet from 1652 and master of accounts at Montpellier in 1659, he stood faithfully by Fouquet at his fall. He spent four years in the Bastille from 1661, writing three memoirs in his defence. Freed in 1666, Louis XIV named him royal historian. In 1670 he abjured Protestantism, took minor orders and subdiaconate, gained the abbey of Guieont, and managed funds for needy converts. The tale that he refused last sacraments is false; he kept his religious duties to the end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pescennius-ni:
Pescennius Niger was a rival Roman emperor in 193 and 194, chosen by the legions of Syria. A central Italian who had held back German invasions under Marcus Aurelius and Commodus and crushed a rising of Jews and Saracens in 192, he took his chance when Pertinax fell. While Britain backed Albinus and the Danube backed Severus, Syria's soldiers proclaimed their governor emperor at Antioch.

Severus marched first on Rome, removed Didius Julianus, and made Albinus his partner before turning east. Niger closed Asia's ports, fortified the Taurus passes, and garrisoned Byzantium under his chief of staff, Asellius Aemilianus. Severus's advance guards were repelled at Perinthus, but his main army crossed the Bosporus, killed Aemilianus near Cyzicus in 194, and beat Niger himself near Nicaea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-faber:
Peter Faber was a Savoyard priest and one of the first Jesuits, born at Villaret in 1506. A shepherd boy who taught catechism to other children on Sundays, he went to Paris in 1525. He lodged at Sainte-Barbe with Francis Xavier and took his master of arts with him in 1530. There he met Ignatius of Loyola, was ordained in 1534, and received the first companions' vows at Montmartre that August.

Ignatius sent him to lead the group to Venice in 1536, and his later journeys carried him through Germany, Portugal, and Spain. At Louvain and Cologne he planted vocations and fought heresy, at Lisbon and Valladolid he strengthened souls, including Francis Borgia's. Worn out by walking journeys at forty, he reached Rome in July 1546 and died in Ignatius's arms on 1 August.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-george-:
Peter George Niger was a Dominican theologian and preacher of the later fifteenth century, born at Kaaden in Bohemia in 1434. He studied at Salamanca, Montpellier, and other universities, entered the order at Eichstätt in 1452, and wrote his first work, on preaching, at Leipzig in 1457. A brilliant defence of theses at Freiburg in 1459 sent him to Bologna for advanced theology and canon law.

Teaching posts followed at Cologne, Ulm, Eichstätt, Ratisbon, and Ingolstadt, where he became professor of Old Testament exegesis in 1478. King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary then made him rector of his new academy at Buda. To the king he dedicated his Clypeus Thomistarum of 1481, defending Aquinas against Scotists and Nominalists. A keen Thomist, he ranked among his age's foremost preachers. He died between 1481 and 1484.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-hasslac:
Peter Hasslacher was a German Jesuit preacher who reawakened Catholic life after the revolutions of 1848. Born at Coblenz in 1810, he studied medicine at Bonn and joined the student movement of 1831, paying for it with seven years' confinement at Berlin, Magdeburg, and Ehrenbreitstein. Prison turned him: reading the Church Fathers stirred his mind toward theology, and on release he entered the Jesuit novitiate at St. Acheul in 1840.

Ordained in 1844, he preached with success at Strasbourg cathedral until popular missions swept Germany in 1849. Delicate health barred him from mission tramping, so he made the conference his field, speaking in the great cities of the Rhine and Westphalia. Failing strength sent him in 1863 to the St. Joseph mission for German Catholics in Paris, where he died in 1876.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-michael:
Peter Michael Brillmacher was a Cologne Jesuit famed for eloquence and controversy, born in 1542. He entered the Society in 1558, studied under Maldonat at Paris, and returned to Cologne, where diplomatic skill served German princes and preaching drew crowds. His sermons cut so deeply into reformers' ranks that, the entry says, they resolved on his death and poisoned his food at a feigned debating banquet.

Controversy was his element. When the Cologne curate Stephen Isaac, a converted Jew, preached on the Eucharist in ways that weakened the doctrine, Brillmacher answered. His Controversiarum de Eucharistia Dialogi exposed Isaac until he openly avowed Calvinism. Further works against John of Münster followed in 1592 and 1593, winning back many the entry calls deceived. He died at Mainz in 1595.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-reichen:
Peter Reichensberger was a German jurist and parliamentarian, born at Coblenz in 1810. He studied at Bonn and Heidelberg, then climbed the bench from Coblenz councillor in 1843 to Cologne's appeal court in 1850 and Berlin's supreme court in 1859. From 1848 he sat in parliament after parliament. His seats included the Prussian Diet, the Erfurt Volkshaus, the second chamber, the North German Reichstag, and the Customs Parliament. In the German Reichstag he held one district from 1871 to his death.

Beside his elder brother August, the pair were called the Dioscuri, defending constitutional monarchy against radicalism and religious freedom against bureaucratic control. Less versatile than August, Peter surpassed him in legal sharpness and depth. His writings attacked the income tax, defended the Rhenish legal system, and treated the land question from economics, politics, and law. He died at Berlin in 1892.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-schoffe:
Peter Schöffer was a Mainz printer and publisher, born at Gernsheim about 1425. In minor orders, he copied manuscripts at Paris in 1451, then appeared at Mainz in 1455 as a witness for Fust against Gutenberg. He married Fust's daughter Christine, partnered Fust until 1466, and printed on his own until his death in 1503. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry firmly denies him any share in inventing or improving type.

His press kept the technical excellence of his predecessors without advancing it, and its late books even deteriorated. Conservative in management, he printed almost only civil law, canon law, and theology, ignoring smaller formats and popular books his rivals adopted. His real service was commercial, building trade beyond Germany's borders. By his death, printers in Germany and Italy had long surpassed him. His son John carried the firm to 1531.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-vischer:
Peter Vischer was a Nuremberg sculptor and bronze founder, born about 1460. His father Hermann, an immigrant founder, cast fonts and memorial brasses whose Gothic forms already showed a new naturalness. The son pushed that freedom further without leaving the Gothic manner, later absorbing Renaissance ideas. How far the sons shared in works after 1505 remains disputed, since the father often cast others' designs.

Vischer's standing beside Stoss and Krafft still holds. His tombs range from plain engraved brasses to richly ornate monuments. Three Bamberg bishops' tablets date from about 1490. Princely tombs at Meissen and episcopal tombs at Breslau and Magdeburg followed, one with a carpeted, perspective backdrop, another with the body set upright beneath a canopy. From 1505 he laboured on his masterpiece, the shrine of St. Sebaldus at Nuremberg. He died in 1529.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-faber:
Philip Faber, also called Fabri, was an Italian Franciscan theologian and commentator on Duns Scotus, born at Spinata di Brisighella in 1564. He joined the Conventual Franciscans at Cremona in 1582, taught in monastic schools, and became professor of philosophy at Padua in 1603 and of theology in 1606, winning fame as a lecturer. In 1625 his order elected him provincial.

Back in the professor's chair, he expounded Scotus with ability and judgment, dropping the superlative style of other commentators. His chief works spread Scotus's natural philosophy into theorems, commented on all four books of Sentences, and treated predestination, restitution, extreme unction, and holy orders. Works on Peter's primacy and Aristotle's Metaphysics appeared after his death through his friend Matthew Ferchius. He died at Padua in 1630.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-fisher:
Philip Fisher, whose real name was Thomas Copley, was an English Jesuit missionary in Maryland, born at Madrid about 1595. Eldest son of an exiled Catholic family of Gatton, he reached Maryland in 1637 and took charge of the mission, a post then needing businessmen more than preachers. His executive ability made him, in Hughes's judgment, the most distinguished of the fourteen Jesuits who worked in Maryland.

In 1645 he was seized and carried in chains to England with Andrew White, founder of the English mission in America. Released after hardships, he boldly returned in February 1648 to find his flock flourishing above their plunderers. That March he wrote to the Jesuit general of a new forest road to Virginia, planning to unite both missions and visit Virginia's governor. No record of that visit survives. He died in Maryland in 1652.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippe-andr:
Philippe André Grandidier was an Alsatian priest and historian, born at Strasbourg in 1752. At eighteen Cardinal de Rohan made him archivist of the diocese, and by twenty-five he belonged to twenty-one learned societies in France and Germany. Critical investigation was his forte, but intense application broke his health, and he died at thirty-four at Lucelles Abbey in 1787.

His two volumes on Strasbourg's church and prince-bishops, published in 1776 and 1778, carry Alsace's early church history to 965, and Liblin continued them from his manuscripts in six volumes. Pius VI admired the work and urged him on, though slighted fellow canons opposed his methods and even questioned his faith. Undeterred, he published essays on Strasbourg Cathedral in 1782 and a full Alsatian history in 1787, the year of his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pichler:
The Pichlers were a renowned Austrian family of gem-cutters who lived and died in Italy. Antonio, born at Brixen in 1697, was a merchant's son turned artist in Naples, working with a goldsmith and engraver before moving to Rome in 1743. Copying antiques, he won excellence and fame, though want of early design training narrowed his range.

His son Giovanni, born at Naples in 1734, surpassed him. Painter, gem-cutter, and experimenter in encaustic and mosaic, he learned from his father and Corvi, painted for Franciscans and Augustinians, then gave himself wholly to intaglio. His gems of great beauty and finish so matched the classic manner that Winckelmann reportedly took them for antiques. Hercules, Leander, Sappho, and portraits of Pius VI and Joseph II number among his works. His son Giacomo cut gems at Milan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pier-paolo-ve:
Pier Paolo Vergerio the Elder was an Italian humanist, statesman, and canonist, born at Capodistria in 1370. He studied rhetoric at Padua, canon law at Florence and Bologna, taught logic at Padua and Florence, and tutored the Carrara princes at Padua's court. After 1406 he served at Rome as secretary to Innocent VII and Gregory XII, became canon of Ravenna, and attended the Council of Constance in 1414.

In 1415 he joined the fifteen delegates who followed Emperor Sigismund to Perpignan to press Benedict XIII to resign. From 1417 until his death he served Sigismund as secretary, and in July 1420 he led the Catholic side at the Hussite disputation in Prague. Never married and probably in minor orders, he was no priest. His printed works include a plea for church reunion, a history of the Carrara princes, a life of Petrarch, and a treatise on liberal studies. He died at Budapest in 1444 or 1445.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-antoin:
Pierre Antoine Berryer was a French advocate, orator, and statesman, born at Paris in 1790. Schooled by Oratorians at Juilly, he weighed a church vocation, then chose the law, leaving college to Jena's cannon fire. Bonapartist verses in 1810 gave way to monarchism by 1812, after study of the Constituent Assembly's reports, and he held that the king stands above party for life. At the Restoration he helped defend Marshal Ney and won acquittal for General Cambronne.

Later causes defended Lamennais in 1826, the Jesuits against Thiers in 1845, and carpenters combining for a work stoppage, asserting labour's right to combine decades before French law recognized it. Liberty of association for all and state respect for the Church's autonomy formed his lifelong principle, crowned by his return to religious practice under Père de Ravignan. He never wrote his speeches, meditating instead until words came unforced. He died at Augerville in 1868.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-bereng:
Pierre Bérenger was a twelfth-century French writer and disciple of Abelard, flourishing about mid-century. His second name hints at Poitiers as his birthplace. He is famed chiefly for a vigorous defence of his master, written to St. Bernard after Abelard's condemnation at Soissons in 1141. The letter's tone runs intemperate, and its famous tale of bishops primed for Bernard's side the night before the council deserves little weight as history.

Hunted, as he puts it, not by wild beasts but by the faithful of Mende who backed Bernard, he wandered the Cévennes. He wrote the Bishop of Mende retracting his attack on the man of God, excusing the earlier letter as an inconsiderate youth's ardour. A letter against the monks of the Grande Chartreuse also survives, and a lost treatise on the Incarnation is mentioned. Migne prints the three letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-bouche:
Pierre Boucher was a Canadian pioneer and founder of Boucherville, born at Lagny near Mortagne in 1622. He sailed to Canada with his joiner father in 1634, served the Jesuits' Huron missions at eighteen, and soldiered at Quebec. In 1645 he became interpreter of Indian languages at Three Rivers, and in 1648 commissary-general of its trading station. As militia captain he repelled an Iroquois attack in 1653 and held command of the town until 1658.

Sent to France in 1661 to plead the colonists' needs, he returned as governor of Three Rivers in 1662 and resigned in 1667 to found the seigniorial parish of Boucherville opposite Montreal. His 1664 Histoire véritable et naturelle, on New France's customs and products, was printed at Paris and later reprinted several times, with an English translation in 1883. He stands as the model Canadian landed proprietor, pious, upright, and honourable. He died in 1717.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-joseph:
Pierre-Joseph Pelletier was a Paris pharmacist and chemist whose work on plant medicines gave the world quinine in usable form. He was born in Paris in 1788 to a pharmacist father. He turned to materia medica, the study of healing substances, and to the alkaloids, the active chemicals found in plants.

With Joseph Caventou he isolated quinine, the fever drug from cinchona bark. He published the result openly instead of keeping it secret for profit. He won the Montyon prize in 1827 for the discovery. He also helped identify strychnine, taught at the Paris school of pharmacy, and joined the Academy of Sciences in 1840.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-vernie:
Pierre Vernier was the French mathematician and official who invented the fine scale that still bears his name. He was born at Ornans about 1580 and taught science by his father. He became captain and castellan of Ornans castle for the king of Spain. He also served as director of coinage in the County of Burgundy.

His 1631 treatise described a movable scale that lets a reader measure fractions of a degree. The reader sees which of its lines lines up with a line on the main scale. The device is now fitted to sextants, barometers, and other graduated instruments. It owes its name to Lalande, who showed that the older term nonius belonged to a different contrivance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pirkheimer:
Charitas Pirkheimer was the abbess of Saint Clara's convent at Nuremberg and sister of the humanist Willibald Pirkheimer. She was born at Nuremberg in 1466 and formed in the cloister from the age of twelve. She was chosen abbess in December 1503 after serving as teacher and perhaps mistress of novices.

For twenty years she lived in contemplative peace, reading Latin authors and the church fathers, above all Jerome, with her brother as guide. Her later years were stormed when Lutheran doctrines reached Nuremberg and the peace of the convent ceased. She defended her house with learning and firmness, and the entry draws on her letters and friendships with humanists such as Celtes, Scheurl, and Dürer until her death in 1532.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-placidus-fixl:
Placidus Fixlmillner was an Austrian Benedictine astronomer who directed the observatory at Kremsmünster Abbey. He was born near Kremsmünster in 1721 and joined the Benedictines at sixteen. He showed early talent for mathematics and, after publishing a theological treatise in 1756, returned to mathematics when the transit of Venus in 1761 rekindled his interest.

As observatory director he rebuilt its instruments and fixed the latitude and longitude of the site. He amassed observations of great variety until his death in 1791. He was among the first to compute the orbit of Uranus after Herschel's discovery, and his many observations of Mercury helped Lalande build tables of that planet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-christop:
Pope Christopher reigned in 903 and 904, a figure some call antipope and others accept as true pope. Once Cardinal-Priest of Saint Damasus, a Roman and son of Leo, he took the papacy by forcibly dethroning Leo V and imprisoning him, seemingly about October 903. As Leo soon died in prison, Christopher may count as pope from his death.

His name stands in contemporary catalogues of popes. His portrait hangs among the popes at Saint Paul Outside the Walls. Leo IX, confirming Corbie Abbey's privileges, cited grants of Benedict and Christopher. That Corbie privilege is the only act of his that survives. A Greek document claims he first stated in his profession of faith to Constantinople that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son. No Patriarch Sergius then existed, however.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-porter-doorke:
Porter, also called doorkeeper, comes from the Latin ostiarius, a door-keeper. Among Romans the porter was the slave guarding a house entrance. Better houses all had one, though the duties ranked very low. From the late second century, as Christian communities owned houses for worship and business, church ostiaries appear, at least in larger cities.

Cornelius's letter to Fabius of Antioch in 251 counts Rome's clergy: forty-six priests, seven deacons, seven subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, and fifty-two exorcists, lectors, and ostiaries. The Liber Pontificalis says an ostiary named Romanus was martyred in 258 with St Lawrence. In Western Europe the ostiary was the lowest minor order. A 377 law of the Theodosian Code gives ostiaries personal immunity among Italian clergy. Gelasius wrote in 494 that clergy candidates must be able to read; a man without that could at most become an ostiary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prayer:
Prayer, from Greek euchesthai, Latin precari, and French prier, means to plead, to beg, to ask with earnestness. It is an act of the virtue of religion, asking fit gifts and graces from God. In a wider sense it is the mind's turn to Divine things, as a road to union with God. The Fathers call it the mind's lift to God, converse with God, and plain talk with God.

It voices our wants to God, not to school or steer Him, but to plead His goodness. Church use opens and closes the day with prayer. Morn and eve prayer bind no strict duty, yet long neglect counts more or less as sin, by its cause, most oft sloth. Prayer divides as vocal or mental, private or public. Vocal prayer joins an outward act, most oft words, to the inward act found in all prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prosper-louis:
Dom Prosper Guéranger, Benedictine monk and prolific writer, was born at Sablé-sur-Sarthe on 4 April 1805 and died at Solesmes on 30 January 1875. Ordained priest in 1827, he left parish work in Paris, returned to the Mans region, and in December 1832 bought the priory of Solesmes, then up for sale. There he set out to plant Benedictine monastic life again in France after the Revolution had wiped it out.

Guéranger's long campaign pushed the Roman liturgy in place of the many local French uses, and he lived to see that effort win across the country. He also battled Gallican and Jansenist leanings, arguing that error must be replaced rather than merely attacked. His books ranged from early political pamphlets to liturgical studies, a life of Saint Cecilia, and rules for Benedictine novices, closing a career that reshaped French Catholic worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quimper:
The Diocese of Quimper covers the Department of Finistère. This encyclopedia entry explains that the Concordat of 1802 rebuilt it from a large part of Quimper, also called Cornouailles. It added the whole Diocese of Saint Pol de Léon, and small parts of Tréguier and Vannes. From 1802 to 1859 it answered to Tours, and since 1859 it has answered to Rennes. Two bishop lists survive, from Quimperlé in the twelfth century and Quimper in the fifteenth.

Both name Saint Corentinus as first bishop, though his biography is very late. Some suppose Martin ordained him in the fourth century, others place him in the sixth. Later pages praise Albert Le Grand, whose Lives of the Saints of Brittany of 1636 fed a revival, and Maunoir, founder of Breton philology with his Breton dictionary. Quimper Cathedral's cornerstone was laid in 1424, and Alexander the Sixth's grant of Jubilee indulgences at last funded its completion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rafael-ferrer:
Rafael Ferrer, Spanish missionary and explorer, was born at Valencia in 1570 and died at San José, Peru, in 1611. This encyclopedia entry tells that his father meant him for a soldier's career, but he entered the Society of Jesus and was sent to Quito, Ecuador, in 1593. In 1601 he entered the land of the Cofanis, a hostile tribe. Within three years religion had so civilized several villages that the surrounding country lay open to colonists.

In 1605, at the viceroy of Quito's command, Ferrer travelled among the uncivilized tribes of the River Napo. He journeyed two and a half years and 3,600 miles into the interior. He returned with a chart of the Napo basin, a map of the explored country, and a herbarium. His grammar of the Cofani tongue survives, with his translations of the catechism and Sunday Gospel readings, though his longer manuscript was lost and never fully published.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raoul-glaber:
Raoul Glaber, Benedictine chronicler, was born in Burgundy before 1000 and died at Cluny about 1050. This encyclopedia entry paints a wayward boy, so mischievous that his uncle, a monk, forced him into Saint-Léger de Champeaux at twenty to keep him safe. Glaber took only the monastic habit. Pride made him resist and disobey his superiors and quarrel with his brethren, until he was expelled.

He then entered Notre-Dame du Moutier and Saint-Benignus at Dijon. Abbot William of Dijon, valuing his literary gifts, befriended him and took him to Susa in Italy in 1028. Yielding again to a roving temper, Glaber slipped away to Saint-Germain d'Auxerre, sure his learning would win him refuge anywhere. His chronology and geography fall short, yet his work stays interesting and useful, opening a window on the customs and morals of an age when continental Christianity had sunk low.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reform-of-a-r:
Reform of a religious order means restoring an order from mitigated, relaxed observance to its primitive rule's rigour. This encyclopedia entry first allows that mitigations may be lawful. They may come by the Holy See's authority, or by decree of the order's superiors within their power. Established prescription or custom may also allow them, so long as relaxations do not touch the vows. Obligations springing directly from vows cannot be changed by custom or prescription.

Abolishing abuses in vow matters is therefore not reform in the proper sense of the word. Where a rule's mitigation came about through authority, reform may be set on foot by the Holy See or by the order's superiors, the entry notes. They work through the channels the order's constitutions allow. Pellizzario, Schmalzgrüber, Bouix, Bachofen and Aichner supply the canon-law sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-dow:
Religious dower, the Latin dos religiosa, takes its name by analogy from the dower a bride brings her husband. It is the money or property a nun brings into her convent for her own maintenance, set apart for her support after profession. It is neither a gift to the convent nor the payments for a postulant or novice before profession. The custom was unknown in the ancient Church and came in only gradually for nuns under solemn vows.

The convent gained no possession of the dower until profession itself, and a novice who left beforehand recovered it, as the Council of Trent laid down. Dispensation from solemn vows was almost unheard of, so no rule covered restitution when a professed religious left; equity, not law, supplied the answer. The decree Perpensis of 3 May 1902 changed this, requiring three years under simple vows before solemn profession.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-remi-ceillier:
Remi Ceillier, patrologist, was born at Bar-le-Duc on 14 May 1688 and died at Flavigny on 26 May 1763. Schooled at the Jesuit College of Bar-le-Duc, he entered the monastery of Moyen-Moutier in the Vosges in 1705, a house of the Benedictine congregation of Saint-Vannes and Saint-Hydulphe. He taught there as professor for six years, became dean of Moyen-Moutier in 1716, and prior of Saint Jacques de Neufchâteau in 1718.

In 1724 he became assistant to Dom Charles de Vassimont at the priory of Flavigny-sur-Moselle, succeeding him as prior on his death in 1733. Under his wise rule the monastery flourished materially, spiritually, and intellectually. His first great work, begun while professor at Moyen-Moutier, defended the morals of the Fathers. Charges of Jansenism against him find no support in his writings, as Benedict the Fourteenth's treatment of him shows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-francois:
René-François Rohrbacher, ecclesiastical historian, was born at Langatte in the present Diocese of Metz on 27 September 1789 and died in Paris on 17 January 1856. After a few months' study at Sarrebourg and Phalsebourg, he had finished his classical studies by seventeen. He taught three years at the college of Phalsebourg, entered the seminary at Nancy in 1810, and was ordained priest in 1812.

He served briefly as assistant priest at Insming, then moved to Lunéville after six months. A mission he preached at Flavigny in 1821 led to a diocesan mission band, and he later joined the Congregation of Saint Peter founded by Félicité and Jean de La Mennais. From 1827 to 1835 he directed the philosophical and theological studies of young churchmen preparing to assist the two brothers. His great history of the Church crowns a life of teaching and preaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-chall:
Richard Challoner, Bishop of Debra and Vicar Apostolic of the London District, was born on 29 September 1691 and died on 12 January 1781. The leading figure of English Catholicism through most of the eighteenth century, he was no cradle Catholic: his father was a Presbyterian wine cooper of Lewes. After his father's death his mother kept house for the Catholic Gages at Firle. The boy entered the Church at about thirteen, at Warkworth, seat of the Catholic Holman family.

Challoner's Bible became the groundwork of nearly all English versions. Its Old Testament appeared in 1750, a third edition in 1752 carried over two thousand text and note changes, and an American edition followed at Philadelphia in 1805. In 1753 he published his Meditations for Every Day of the Year, many times reprinted and translated into French and Italian. His spiritual and controversial works carried that leadership into print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-franc:
A wandering Franciscan preacher known only as Richard appears in the record for a few crowded years, 1428 to 1431. His birthplace and nationality are unknown. He is linked by guesswork to the followers of Bernardine of Siena and Vincent Ferrer. Like them, he promoted devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus and warned that the end of the world was near. From the Holy Land he reached France and preached at Troyes and Paris.

Crowds flocked to his long morning sermons. Listeners burned dice and finery after hearing him. Threatened by the Paris theology faculty, he left the city. He met Joan of Arc at Troyes, helped bring that town over to Charles VII, and served as Joan's confessor and chaplain. Differences over a visionary woman cooled the friendship. After preaching Lent at Orleans in 1431, he was barred from preaching. No trace of him survives after that year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-of-ci:
Richard of Cirencester was a Westminster monk whose chronicle covered English kings from 447 to 1066. Almost nothing is known of his life beyond a pilgrimage to Jerusalem in 1391, his presence at Westminster in 1397, and a spell of sickness in the infirmary around 1400. His four-book Speculum Historiale de Gestis Regum Angliae is judged of little historical value, though it preserves several charters granted to Westminster Abbey.

His name gained a stranger fame centuries later. In the eighteenth century, Charles Bertram forged a work on Roman Britain and passed it off under Richard's name. The forgery fooled leading antiquaries, including Stukeley and Lingard, and was only exposed in 1866-67. The entry also lists two further works ascribed to Richard, neither of which survives today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-riemenschneid:
Tilman Riemenschneider was one of the most important sculptors of Franconia, working in Wurzburg from 1483 until his death in 1531. Born at Osterode am Harz in or after 1460, he joined the Guild of St Luke at Wurzburg and never left the city. His early tomb work still followed the Gothic manner. His carvings for the Marienkapelle moved toward the Renaissance style, keeping traces of older art.

He excelled at character and at female saints. The Marienkapelle holds his famed Adam and Eve and his larger-than-life Christ, Baptist, and apostles. Graceful figures of Dorothea and Margaret stand there too. His masterpiece is the tomb of Emperor Henry II at Bamberg Cathedral, with ideal recumbent figures and lively scenes from the couple's lives on its sides. Other works, including Lamentations over Christ and a suspended rosary Madonna at Volkach, survive across Germany. Faults in some pieces are blamed on apprentices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-joseph:
Robert Joseph Pothier was a French lawyer whose treatises shaped the Code Napoleon. Born at Orleans in 1699, son of a petty-court judge, he later held his father's judgeship and a professorship of French law at Orleans, both from 1750. His quiet life of teaching and judging was marked by austerity, modesty, and deep religion.

His chief early work rearranged the texts of Roman law in the Pandectae Justinianeae of 1748-52, under Chancellor d'Aguesseau's patronage. He then wrote on the customs of Orleans and a long series of treatises, collected in 1781. They covered duties, sales, rents, exchange, hiring, leases, contracts, marriage, community, dowry, possession, and title. Jurists drafting the new French Civil Code kept his clear, well-planned works in hand and owed them much, especially on duties and contracts. From a religious angle, his treatise on the marriage contract sets out Gallican doctrines in full. He died at Orleans in 1772.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-stephe:
Robert Stephen Hawker was a Cornish poet and antiquary who spent forty years as vicar of the wreck-strewn parish of Morwenstow. Born at Plymouth in 1803, son of a doctor turned vicar of Stratton, he was schooled at Liskeard and placed with a Plymouth solicitor. The law disgusted him, so an aunt paid for Cheltenham Grammar School, where he published Tendrils in 1821.

At Pembroke College, Oxford, from 1823, he married Charlotte I'ans, a Cornishwoman twenty years older. He won the Newdigate Prize for a poem on Pompeii in 1827 and took orders in 1831. As vicar of Morwenstow from 1834, he restored church and parsonage, founded a school, held synods as rural dean, succoured shipwrecked sailors, and buried drowned bodies. His poems and essays drew on Cornish history and legend. Finest among them is the Quest of the San Graal; most famous, the Ballad of Trelawney. Tractarian in views, he died at Plymouth in 1875.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rochester:
Rochester is the oldest and smallest of the suffragan sees of Canterbury, founded by St Augustine in 604. Augustine consecrated St Justus as its first bishop. The diocese covered roughly western Kent, divided from the rest of the county by the Medway, though its bounds did not follow the river closely. Its cathedral, founded by King Ethelbert and dedicated to St Andrew, was served by secular priests and endowed with land called Priestfield.

After the Conquest, Bishop Gundulf began a new cathedral. He replaced secular chaplains with Benedictine monks, and enshrined St Paulinus in a silver shrine that drew pilgrims. His nave is the oldest in England, and the cathedral has a Norman crypt. Consecrated in 1130 amid a great fire, it gained a rebuilt choir and central tower from offerings at St William of Perth's tomb by 1343. The right to nominate bishops passed from Canterbury archbishops to the cathedral monks in 1148.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roger-bishop-:
Roger, Bishop of Worcester, was a loyal friend of St Thomas of Canterbury. Younger son of Robert, Earl of Gloucester, he was schooled with the future Henry II, ordained priest, and consecrated Bishop of Worcester by Thomas on 23 August 1163.
