Adolphus William Ward wrote this life of Geoffrey Chaucer for the English Men of Letters series, a set of short literary biographies. Ward, a Cambridge scholar, built the account on public records and the Chaucer Society's research. He warns readers that many dates in the poet's life stay uncertain. Documents, not legend, set the limits of his story.

Four chapters divide the work, covering Chaucer's times, his life and writings, his character as a poet, and a short epilogue. Ward traces a courtier, soldier, customs official, and member of Parliament who also wrote the Canterbury Tales. He weighs which poems are truly Chaucer's and which later hands added. A glossary and index close the volume for student use. Readers who want a compact, careful Victorian life of the first great English poet, with the evidence shown, will find this volume serviceable and clear.
cheerfulness-as-a-life-power:
Orison Swett Marden, editor of Success, copyrighted his booklet in 1899, and it reached a tenth thousand with Thomas Y. Crowell. His foreword calls cheerfulness a lubricant. Human machinery, like inert machinery, wears out without oil. The hurrying, grasping age, he argues, needs a daily habit of good humour, not a Sunday dose.

Anecdotes carry the argument. Vanderbilt paid for twelve laughs from the actor Coquelin at Constantinople. A laugh cure and a cheap medicine open the chapters. Americanitis — nervous hurry — gets its own cure. Business machinery is oiled, fun is taken daily, and a don't-worry society is praised. Charles Lamb, John B. Gough, and Phillips Brooks model the sunshine temper in short lives.
child-songs-of-cheer:
Evaleen Stein published her verses for children at Boston in 1918, with illustrations by Antoinette Inglis. Her opening letter calls the poems a flock of little birds brought to sing to young readers. Dandelions front the book, shining through the dew. Kings can keep their cloth of gold, the first poem says.

Some seventy short songs follow the seasons round. Puppies, a lost balloon, a circus procession, and May-baskets fill the spring pages. Fireflies, fairy rings, a wren-house, and a rain song suit the summer. First snow, sleigh-bells, Christmas candles, and a Christmas-tree song close the year. Stein writes in short rhymed lines meant to be read aloud, cheerfully and often.
choice-specimens-of-american-literature-:
Prof. Benj. N. Martin of the University of the City of New York edited a school reader of American writing, in an enlarged second edition dated 1874. His preface explains the plan. The first edition, a supplement to Shaw's English specimens, had grown too cramped. Extracts are now longer and more coherent, and great authors get more room.

Franklin, Jefferson, Webster, Irving, Cooper, and Hawthorne head his list of the enlarged. Channing, Beecher, Prescott, Emerson, Poe, Bryant, and Lowell follow. Early chapters reach back to colonial sermons, Powhatan's rule, and Pocahontas in England. Franklin's kite and his motion for prayers appear among the specimens. A lively life of Baron Steuben, cursing his militia in three languages, shows the historical selections at their best.
cicero-de-officiis-miller:
Cicero wrote On Duties in late 44 BC, in the last months of his life, as a letter of advice to his son Marcus. Walter Miller's English translation is the text here. The old statesman, shut out of power after Caesar's murder, turned to teaching his son how to live in public life.

The three books weigh what is honorable, what is useful, and what to do when the two seem to clash. Cicero insists the useful and the honorable are one in the end. He treats justice, kindness, courage, and the duties of rulers and citizens. The book trained Europe's gentlemen and statesmen for two thousand years.
clotel-or-the-president-s-daughter:
William Wells Brown, who had escaped slavery himself, published Clotel in 1853, and it is often called the first novel by an African American author. The title figure is Clotel, daughter of Currer, an enslaved woman who had kept house for Thomas Jefferson and borne him two daughters. When Jefferson leaves for Washington, Currer and the girls are sold at auction in Richmond.

Brown follows Clotel and her sister Althesa through sales, separations, and escapes, mixing their story with speeches, songs, and newspaper matter against slavery. The president's daughter of the title ends as property in the republic her father helped found. Brown meant the irony to burn, and the novel still works as abolitionist argument in story form.
clover:
Clover, by Susan Coolidge, author of What Katy Did, continues the story of the Carr family in a Boston edition of 1907, illustrated by Jessie McDermot. Katy and Clover Carr open the book on their doorsteps in late April. The air holds nest-building birds, wisteria, and the smell of white violets under the parlor windows.

The contents promise change. The first wedding in the family comes early, then two long years in one short chapter. The scene shifts west: Car Forty-Seven, St. Helen's, High Valley, and a pass to cross. A house at No. 13 Piute Street shelters the later chapters. The last of the clover leaves closes the sisters' story.
consolations-in-travel-or-the-last-days-:
Consolations in Travel; or, the Last Days of a Philosopher, by Humphry Davy, is the dying work of the great chemist, here prefaced by a life of its author. Davy was born in Cornwall on December 17, 1778, and died at Geneva on May 29, 1829. He was apprenticed in 1795 to Dr. Borlase, a Penzance surgeon, after a Quaker saddler's electrical machine first turned him toward experiment.

The editor's preface says the dialogues were composed during bodily indisposition and concluded at the invasion of the last illness; the speakers are ideal, and incidents serve the doctrines. Geology fills the sampled talk: diluvian gravels and water-worn stones, and a new continent raised in the southern hemisphere by volcanic fire.
cowboy-dave-or-the-round-up-at-rolling-r:
Cowboy Dave, or the Round-Up at Rolling River, by Frank V Webster, is a western for boys from a writer whose list fills a page of ranch and school stories. Webster, author of Only a Farm Boy, Bob the Castaway, and Comrades of the Saddle, sets his hero among cattle at the season when herds are gathered, counted, and branded. The round up of the title is the year's hardest and most public work.

Dave's proving ground is that work itself: riding, roping, and judgment under the eyes of older hands. Missing cattle, disputed ownership, and the river country around Rolling River supply the friction that boys' westerns require. Webster wrote to a formula his readers trusted. A young rider's honesty is tested against rustlers and accidents. A reputation is made the way a brand is set. It is done in the open, and for good.
cowper:
A life of the poet William Cowper by Goldwin Smith fills this London book of 1880. Eight chapters trace him from early life to his close. Smith calls Cowper the most important English poet between Pope and the group led by Wordsworth, Byron, and Shelley.

The Huntingdon and Olney years, with the Unwins and Mr Newton, take the middle chapters. Then come the moral satires, The Task, short poems, translations, and the famed letters. Smith credits Cowper with calling verse back from stiff forms to nature. He also links him to the great religious revival of his age. The book is a short, clear life for readers who want the poet placed in his time.
cyclopedia-of-telephony-and-telegraphy-v:
A general reference work on the telephone and telegraph fills this first of four volumes, issued at Chicago in 1919 by the American School of Correspondence. A portrait of Alexander Graham Bell, the inventor of the telephone, stands at the front. More than two thousand engravings fill the set.

Named experts wrote the parts, among them Kempster B. Miller of Chicago and George W. Patterson of the University of Michigan. Chapters treat substations, party lines, switchboards by hand and by machine, and power plants. Building, running, and mending lines all get space, as do wireless forms of both arts. The book taught the wire trades by post. It is a thick snapshot of phone craft in 1919.
dangers-on-the-ice-off-the-coast-of-labr:
A penny tract, number 556 from the Religious Tract Society of London, tells of two Moravian missionaries on the Labrador coast. The brethren Liebisch and Turner set out on March 11, 1782, from Nain to Okkak, a trip of one hundred and fifty miles. Five men, one woman, and a child made the party, on sledges drawn by dogs.

Fine weather and smooth ice let them run six or seven miles an hour at first. Danger on the frozen sea soon forced them into a snow house, where Liebisch, hurt in the throat, sat at the door wrapped in skins. The tract adds notes on the native people of the coast. It praises the pair's safe keeping as a sign of God's care.
daniel-webster:
A life of Daniel Webster by Henry Cabot Lodge fills this volume in the American Statesmen line. Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York issued it, with dates of 1883 and 1911 on the title page. Lodge says he read all the printed matter on Webster, a vast mass, much of it worthless.

Ten chapters run from a New Hampshire childhood to the last years. The Dartmouth College case shows Webster as a lawyer. The reply to Hayne, the fight with Jackson, and the Ashburton Treaty fill the centre. The Seventh of March speech stands near the close. Lodge dwells on Webster's sheer presence, which awed a room before he spoke. The book is a statesman's life by a statesman.
de-la-salle-fifth-reader:
A school reader for the fifth year fills this volume of the De La Salle series, in a revised edition of 1922. The Brothers of the Christian Schools made it at their normal institute at Pocantico Hills, New York. A portrait of President William McKinley stands at the front.

Contents list a hymn to St La Salle, then tales, poems, and lessons in set order. Columbus at the convent, Carlyle on two laborers, and James Whitcomb Riley's Brook Song appear early. Louisa M. Alcott, Cardinal Newman, and Thomas Moore all give pieces. Definitions and a guide to pronunciation serve the class. Later pages treat the Old Law given on Mount Sinai. The reader mixes faith, letters, and morals for Catholic schools.
death-and-after:
What comes after death, in Theosophical teaching, fills this small manual by Annie Besant. It is number three of the Theosophical Manuals and stands in its twentieth thousand. The Theosophical Publishing Society of London and Benares issued it in 1906 at one shilling.

Besant says the manuals aim at the busy reader, not the eager student. Theosophy, she holds, is for all, not for the learned alone. The text treats Devachan, the state after death, and warns that to call it a mere dream is to give up the esoteric doctrine. Planes of gross matter and finer states are set in order. The book is a plain, cheap door into Theosophical thought for Edwardian readers.
delia-blanchflower:
A novel of a young Englishwoman fills Mrs Humphry Ward's Delia Blanchflower. Ward had won fame with Lady Rose's Daughter. The tale opens in a Tyrolese hotel, where an Englishman scans a crowd of South Germans, Austrians, Russians, and Italians after the mid-day meal.

Delia stands at the centre of the book, drawn between a stale country life and a great cause in London. An older friend urges her to come up to town, where the big meetings catch one again and show what it all means. The flat is not yet ready, and Delia runs down in health and spirit in the backwater. Ward writes of women's public work and private ties in her grave, full manner.
denzil-quarrier:
George Gissing set Denzil Quarrier in suburban London and a provincial town hungry for politics. Lilian Quarrier keeps a tasteful home on the edge of Clapham Common and waits each evening for her husband. Denzil is rich, restless, and eager for a public career. Their quiet domestic life opens the book in autumn dusk.

Quarrier's ambition draws the couple toward an election contest and the bargaining that surrounds it. Gissing watches how money, newspapers, and local pride shape a candidate's rise. Lilian's devotion is tested as public success demands ever more compromise. The novel asks what a man may hide, and what he may sell, to win a seat and a name. Its pleasures lie in sharp social observation and a marriage watched under growing strain.
doe-osti-1605921-micropower-thermoelectr:
Final report for a cooperative project, CRADA number CRD-16-607, closes work between the National Laboratory of the Rockies and MicroPower Global. David Ginley was the laboratory contact, and the report was issued in February 2026. Its subject is thermoelectric modules, devices that turn a heat difference into electric power.

Lab staff built a calibrated test system that could hold varied modules and track their heat, electric, and strength traits. Modules were run at set hot and cold side temperatures to find a best floor temperature. Single devices showed good conversion, but results did not repeat well. Many devices failed, proved brittle, and could not reach the wanted heat levels, so the team judged the design not workable at larger scale.
doe-osti-17010307-nsls-ii-backup-storage:
David Bergman of Brookhaven National Laboratory wrote this project report in August 2026 on a backup power supply for the NSLS-II light source. The storage ring dipole magnets run from two main supplies in series, each near 410 volts. Until this project, failure of that supply was a single point that could stop the whole ring.

Builders combined store bought water cooled converters with custom filter stages and custom controls in a compact rack layout. The finished unit supplies about 400 kilowatts with high precision. Its regulated current stayed stable over 120 hours, with spread measured at 1.9 parts in a million, giving the ring a redundant main supply.
doe-osti-17076224-smartgiscavp-builder-d:
Deployment and user guide ORNL/TM-2026/4956, by Jose Tupayachi and Xiao-Ying Yu of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, documents the SMARTGISCAVP Builder. The builder is a self contained prototype that turns plain language requests into multi page React dashboards, the web interfaces used to display data. It ships as a Docker image that bundles the interface, an API, and a retrieval based generation engine.

Guide sections cover setup needs, quick start commands, health checks, configuration, image rebuilding, and troubleshooting. A live example builds a dashboard with an interactive map, summary statistics, a chart, and a synced data table. The prototype runs offline except for calls to an outside language model service that writes the code.
doe-osti-2571932-from-structured-solvent:
Final report DE-SC0022214, led by Burcu Gurkan of Case Western Reserve University with co-investigators at Oak Ridge, Texas A&M, and Ohio State, covers September 2021 to March 2025. The program designed solvents and hybrid materials that grab carbon dioxide straight from air and then let it go on demand. Release is triggered by electromagnetic fields or moisture swings, rather than by plain heating.

The team made functionalized ionic liquids and deep eutectic solvents, tuning their hydrogen bond networks to control how carbon dioxide binds. Best solvents held as much as five moles of carbon dioxide per kilogram at one bar and 25 degrees Celsius. Performance stayed strong at air-like conditions, 400 parts per million carbon dioxide at 40 percent humidity. Solvents were also sealed into polymer capsules and other supports, forming layered interfaces for capture and release.
doe-osti-2572202-desert-urban-system-int:
Science plan DOE/SC-ARM-25-015, issued March 2026 and led by Allison Aiken of Los Alamos National Laboratory with twenty co-investigators, lays out the DUSTIEAIM field campaign in the American Southwest. For sixteen months from June 1, 2026, the first ARM Mobile Facility will sit on the Arizona State University West campus in the Phoenix metro area. Phoenix is one of the fastest-growing and most heat-stressed urban regions in the country.

The plan targets the meeting point of desert, city, and farmland in the Sonoran Desert. Instruments will track how storms, rain events, and airborne particles interact across that sharp landscape contrast. The campaign quantifies the region's two-season water cycle, winter rains and summer monsoon, plus surface energy budgets at the urban, rural, and farm boundary. Data from a related Southwest urban field project on extreme heat feeds into the same questions.
doe-osti-2583548-thermal-evaluation-of-c:
An August 2025 NREL study, led by Isaac Tolbert with Saroj Shinde, Marco Gaxiola, and peers, put EV charge adapters on a heat test bench, and most of them failed. Staff from EVgo, Amphenol, and Electrify America helped. As the field shifts to the NACS plug, adapters bridging CCS and NACS carry full fast-charge current. Hot connectors must warn, then shut down, just as SAE J3400 and UL 2252 say.

Five adapters were tested, two NACS-to-CCS and three CCS-to-NACS, after base work on inlets and a reference device. Only two adapters gave the heat warning properly; two more managed it in part. None fully met the shutdown rule, and one adapter never warned or shut down at all. None fully met UL 2252 heat limits either. For a part drivers will trust at high amps, the results are a to-do list for the whole adapter market.
doe-osti-2584244-artificial-intelligence:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise and NREL teamed up to teach data centers to watch themselves. Report NREL/TP-2C00-95486, dated December 30, 2024, closes CRADA CRD-19-00804, with Hilary Egan as the laboratory's contact. Exascale computing centers are too big and too fast for human operators to run by instinct. NREL had already built live data collection and streaming in its ESIF computing center, gathering metrics from machines, racks, rooms, and utility feeds into one research dataset.

The collaboration added artificial intelligence to that stream, and to HPE's own monitoring technology for exascale systems. Models trained on past behavior work on live data to predict trouble and tune operations: cooling, power, and workload choices that waste energy or court failure. The point of AIOps is a facility that flags its own problems before they become outages, at a scale where no team of operators could watch every signal by hand.
doe-osti-2584688-development-of-a-wester:
Workshop report by Maria L. Sushko, Chris K. Ajemian, Christopher J. Keane, and colleagues records an October 23, 2024 meeting on a Western U.S. fusion energy commercialization hub. The Fusion Energy Sciences program sponsored the workshop across four states: Washington, California, Colorado, and Nevada. Its premise: fusion's supplier base, workforce, and customers cluster regionally, so support should too. Seattle Fusion Week, the CleanTech Alliance conference running since 2021, showed the ecosystem already gathering on its own.

Much of the report mines Sematech for lessons. That chip consortium launched in 1987 with fourteen firms and split industry-DARPA funding. By 1993 it had reversed America's slide against Japan, largely by strengthening the supply chain rather than co-developing products. Its later fade, as members drifted and support waned, is also instructive. The hub applies those lessons to fusion: regional workforce, shared technology, and growth, in support of the Energy Department's public-private fusion plans.
doe-osti-2584963-code-coverage-status-of:
Kalin Kiesling and Micheal Smith of Argonne National Laboratory report on the code coverage of PERSENT in report ANL/NSE-25/50. PERSENT is part of the Argonne Reactor Code system used for fast reactor design. It generates reactivity coefficients for safety analysis and can compute sensitivity coefficients and uncertainty estimates from cross section errors.

The authors assembled a set of test problems and measured which parts of the PERSENT source code those tests actually exercise. Because PERSENT treats the DIF3D solver as an external program, the assessment focuses on the PERSENT code itself and a fraction of the connected library modules. Tables record, module by module, what is covered, what is only partially covered, and what no test touches. The work shows where verification effort should go next.
doe-osti-2587940-small-scale-assessment-:
J Gesualdi, E Schneiderlochner, Y Liao, J Rojas, and W Ebert of Argonne National Laboratory wrote this assessment, ANL/CFCT-25/15, dated September 10, 2025. It tests a simpler way to make the glass-bonded sodalite ceramic waste form, which locks chloride salt waste from pyroprocessing inside a stable solid. The work supports the Department of Energy's Materials Recovery and Waste Form Development Campaign.

The direct method just mixes zeolite 4A, chloride salt, and sodium borosilicate binder glass and heats the blend. It skips pre-setting the zeolite's moisture and skips occluding the salt into the zeolite first, and it tolerates larger crushed particle sizes. Most test materials were heated at 925 degrees Celsius for two hours in an argon glovebox; variants ran four hours, or two hours at 880 degrees. In every product, sodalite formed and became microencapsulated by the glass, with uniform microstructures throughout.
doe-osti-2588295-hazard-and-operability-:
Melissa Louie, Marina Miletic, and Brian Ehrhart of Sandia National Laboratories wrote this hazard and operability analysis, SAND2025-10986, printed September 2025. It examines fuel cell electric buses across their whole working life: driving, refueling with hydrogen, and maintenance. A HAZOP works node by node, asking what can deviate from design intent and what follows if it does.

Hydrogen's hazards frame the study: wide flammability, invisible flames, and high-pressure storage. One device gets close attention, the thermally activated pressure relief device that vents a tank in a fire. Lower-risk hazards in the analysis involve its timing, or ignition of the hydrogen it releases. Unlikely, the team notes, since the device might fail to open at once, or released hydrogen might ignite. Either path can still end in a high-consequence outcome. Recommendations for safeguards close each hazard thread, giving operators a mitigation checklist.
doe-osti-2588817-metaheuristic-feature-s:
Natalie Rouse of Los Alamos National Laboratory wrote this report, LA-UR-25-29285, dated August 5, 2025, with Nathan Gibson and Benjamin Whewell as mentors and co-authors. Neutron transport codes do not track every neutron energy. They bin energies into groups, and the bin edges, the group structure, quietly control accuracy. This project automates the search for better edges.

The method frames group selection as binary feature selection and hands it to metaheuristic algorithms in the MEALPY library. Candidate structures are scored on flux error across test problems. The best found structures beat the standard LANL30 structure on overall error while trading differently in the uranium-235 and plutonium-239 resonance regions. The report reads that trade as either more physically relevant placement or more error cancellation. An algorithm comparison closes the study, ranking which search strategies found the strongest structures.
doe-osti-2589496-develop-a-simulation-fr:
Cooperative project CRD-20-17273 for CHZ Technologies closes with National Renewable Energy Laboratory final report NREL/TP-2C00-96555. Technical contact Hariswaran Sitaraman built a simulation framework for the company's plastic thermolysis process, which uses heat to break waste plastic into gas, oil-like tar, and char. Operators need to know how settings change those yields before scaling up.

Models follow the physical and chemical steps inside the reactor and were checked against measured runs. In one comparison at about 773 to 780 kelvin, measured syngas yield was 20.5 percent against a simulated 22.7 percent, and tar was 71.7 percent against 68.9 percent. Agreement that close lets the company test new feedstocks and settings on screen first. The framework also points to where better measurements would most improve the model.
doe-osti-2998144-autonomous-synthesis-of:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report, by Sebastian Mergelsberg, Maxim Ziatdinov, Shawn Kathmann, and John Loring, dated September 2025, automates the making of short-lived materials. Many useful solids pass through a metastable phase, a temporary structure that decides the final product, then vanish. Catching those phases in a mixed-flow reactor takes patient, exact control that trial-and-error supplies slowly.

The team built a modular reactor steered by a theory-informed learning algorithm. Sample handling was automated down to motor indexing, so the system finds each sample and sets detector distances by itself, using the open-source pyFAI library for the geometry. Targets named in the report span energy storage, carbon mineralization, and recovery of critical elements. Chemists gain a machine that hunts fleeting phases methodically instead of by luck.
doe-osti-2998669-ldrd-abbreviated-report:
Yohann Dudouit's abbreviated report LLNL-TR-2012009, from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in October 2025, closes out a laboratory-directed research project on radiation transport computing. Transport codes follow particles or radiation through matter in many directions and energies at once. Such runs are costly, and the discrete ordinate method can leave ray effects, false streaks like those described in ray-effect studies.

The project built GenDiL, a software library designed first for graphics processors, the chips that speed up heavy computing. It uses high-order discontinuous Galerkin methods, a way of solving equations piece by piece, and matrix-free steps that save memory. Mesh size and accuracy can rise only where the problem needs them. A local refinement feature joins simple low-dimension models to full kinetic models through stable links. The aim is detailed transport inside fluid flow simulations without the cost of random-sampling methods.
doe-osti-2999814-institute-for-quantum-m:
Collin Broholm of Johns Hopkins University leads the final technical report for the Institute for Quantum Matter, an Energy Frontier Research Center funded under award DE-SC0019331, covering 2022 to 2024. Quantum materials show odd collective behaviour, superconduction, magnetism and the like, that could reshape energy and information technology. The centre paired many investigators across universities, mixing crystal growth, spectroscopy and theory on shared questions.

Work ran in three interlocking thrusts. One chased quantum entangled magnets, whose atomic moments never settle into a fixed pattern. A second engineered superconductivity out of correlated and topological matter, including metals with unusually light electrons. The third built new functions from magnetic topological materials, notably the Mn3X compound family. There, magnetic domains could be switched electrically and read through the anomalous Hall effect. The report gathers the centre's discoveries and argues they are conclusive answers, not loose ends, on the questions chosen.
doe-osti-2999981-flow-enhanced-electroch:
William Doniger, Timothy Kim, Nora Shaheen and Nathaniel Hoyt of Argonne National Laboratory report in ANL/CFCT-25/27, dated 30 September 2025, on sensors that watch molten salt fuel as it flows. In a liquid-fuel molten salt reactor, the nuclear material is dissolved in the coolant itself, so there are no fuel items to count. Inventory shifts as fuel burns and breeds. Safeguards accounting therefore needs chemistry measured live, inside the pipe.

Two sensor families are covered. Flow enhanced electrochemical sensors sit in the flow conduit, while multielectrode array voltammetry sensors work in still vessels. With new voltammetry methods, the team measured uranium chloride concentrations accurately in salts up to 72.3 percent by mass. Flow sensors were tested in salts holding up to 43.4 weight percent uranium chloride. Trials also ran at partner reactor institutions under rough real-world conditions, lifting the sensors' readiness for deployment.
doe-osti-3002317-model-card-for-wavedeno:
Chengping Chai, Derek Rose, Scott Stewart, and colleagues publish a model card, ORNL/LTR-2025/3955, dated August 2025. A model card is a standard disclosure sheet for an artificial intelligence model: what it does, what data trained it, how well it works, and where it should not be trusted. This one covers WaveDenoiser, a deep learning model for cleaning noise out of seismic waveforms.

Cleaner waveforms make earthquake and explosion monitoring more reliable, since analysts and automatic pickers both read the arrivals. The card sits in a family of Oak Ridge seismic AI work that includes PickerXL, a large model for timing arrivals in noisy signals. A trust calibration framework cited in the card guides how performance claims are stated. The card's audience is any team weighing WaveDenoiser for monitoring duty.
doe-osti-3005575-geant3-simulations-for-:
Sophia Florence Dellmann, René Reifarth, Andrew Leland Cooper, Aaron Joseph Couture, Caroline Harrington, and Ingrid Knapova simulate a neutron source part in Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-31426, issued November 20, 2025. The Neutron Target Demonstrator will make neutrons by spallation, slow them in a moderator, and use them to measure reactions on short-lived nuclei for astrophysics.

The existing moderator is an 80-centimeter carbon block. The proposed design puts a beryllium core, built from pieces already at Los Alamos, inside the carbon. GEANT3 simulations with 800 MeV protons striking a tungsten target show the beryllium core raises the moderated neutron density in the central beam pipe by roughly a factor of four. Layer-by-layer assembly steps for the beryllium pieces close the report.
doe-osti-3005784-results-and-lessons-lea:
A multi-institution team presents lessons in a slide deck from a June 2024 machine learning meeting in Norfolk, Virginia. The project, funded through the SciDAC program, applied machine learning to radio-frequency modeling for fusion plasmas. RF waves heat tokamak plasmas and drive current in them. The full-wave codes that model the waves can take tens to hundreds of CPU-hours per run.

Surrogate models cut that to milliseconds. Teams from MIT, Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Lawrence Berkeley, and San Francisco State paired physics codes with Gaussian process regression and other learners. One result: learned profiles reproduce the CQL3D code's current profiles even in the worst test case. Fast surrogates plug into integrated modeling and real-time feedback, where the slow codes could never sit. The deck reports what worked after three years plus an extension.
doe-osti-3005838-aerosol-acidity-across-:
Christopher J. Hennigan of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Akua Asa-Awuku, Peter F. DeCarlo, and Brook Nault report a field campaign in ARM report DOE/SC-ARM-25-029, dated November 2025. The CoURAGE campaign measured aerosol acidity across seasons in the Baltimore region. Acidity steers how particles form, grow, and deposit in lungs, and it shifts between city and countryside.

The rural comparison site, called S2, sits amid farmland, which complicated the record. At times its coarse particle levels ran four to ten times the urban site's, and the team traced many of those spikes to tractor activity on the surrounding farm. Events were classed as probable, unlikely, or unclear farm influence, and the flags were shared with the whole campaign team in June 2025. Honest site bookkeeping like this keeps later analyses from mistaking a tractor for a city plume.
doe-osti-3005884-rapids2-a-scidac-instit:
Wei-Keng Liao of Northwestern University reports his team's year in the RAPIDS2 SciDAC institute, in a final report for DOE award DE-SC0021399 dated December 2, 2025. The period covered is September 2024 to September 2025. RAPIDS2 exists to help Office of Science application teams beat computer science and data bottlenecks on the department's supercomputers.

Northwestern's contributions center on parallel input and output and on machine learning software. Faster parallel I/O shortens the time big analysis and training jobs spend waiting on storage, which the report frames as time taken directly off scientific discovery. The institute model pairs computer scientists with application teams rather than tossing tools over a wall. This short report is one partner's slice of the institute's year, filed in the standard award format.
doe-osti-3006191-investigating-spatial-v:
ARM campaign report DOE/SC-ARM-25-031, by E. J. T. Levin of Handix Scientific, dated December 2025, covers SAIL-Net, a six-node sensor network run during SAIL in Colorado's East River Watershed. SAIL's two main sites sat on Crested Butte Mountain and at Gothic. From October 2021 to July 2023 the nodes filled in the terrain between and around them. Each node measured aerosol particles from 140 nanometers to 3.4 micrometers with a portable optical spectrometer, plus cloud condensation nuclei and ice nucleating particles.

One site cannot speak for complex terrain: representation error grows with rough topography and drags model accuracy down. The report tracks seasonal swings in aerosol counts across the six sites and data completeness at each. Its guiding questions ask how aerosol varies in time and space, and what particles at cloud base look like. It also asks how future networks should be designed to catch aerosol-cloud interactions in mountains.
doe-osti-3007900-resolving-the-discontin:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2025/4013, by Jordan McDonnell, Iyad Al-Qasir, Jesse Brown, C. W. Chapman, and Dorothea Wiarda, dated September 2025, fixes a seam in nuclear data libraries. Neutron cross sections are computed with thermal scattering physics at low energy and fast-region physics above it, and the two treatments can disagree at the join.

Three causes get separate treatment: Bragg edge data that ends too early, the thermal cutoff set inside processing codes, and grids too coarse for double-differential cross sections. In the SCALE code system the cutoff sat near 5 electron volts before version 6.3. An appendix shows corrected cross sections, including beryllium metal from the ENDF/B-VIII libraries.
doe-osti-3010944-catalysis-driven-by-con:
Confined hot carriers at a liquid, metal, and zeolite interface drive catalysis in a final report by Wei Wang of the University of Oklahoma for award DE-SC0020300. The project period ran from September 2019 to August 2025. Plasmon excitation at the interface changes the chemistry on palladium particles held inside the zeolite environment.

The central finding is a switch in reaction path. Plasmon induced reduction of hydrogen coverage on palladium can move phenylacetylene conversion away from hydrogenation and toward homocoupling. The report, dated December 29, 2025, presents that carrier driven coverage change as the lever that selects between the two products.
doe-osti-3011779-rapid-t-cell-engineerin:
Functional CAR proteins made without cells are put into T cells on nanodiscs in a Lawrence Livermore report by Claire Robertson under LDRD project 22-DR-001. Cell-free protein synthesis produced chimeric antigen receptor proteins set in nanolipoprotein particles, making the membrane protein soluble. The work gave the first functional CAR proteins shown outside a cellular context.

Uptake into T cells and other immune cell populations was very high. Treated T cells bound CD19 protein in line with dose and killed CD19-positive Raji tumour cells at a one-to-one ratio, measured on days one and three. Refolded particles dosed from 0 to 50 micrograms of CAR per millilitre kept high uptake and cell survival.
doe-osti-3013930-characterization-of-inl:
Jason Wilkes of Southwest Research Institute led this final technical report for award DE-EE0009813, covering August 2022 to July 2025, on inlet guide vane performance for a supercritical carbon dioxide compressor. The compressor serves a pumped heat energy storage system, charging by compressing CO2 and discharging through expansion. Near the CO2 dome, where liquid and vapor blur, compressor behavior turns tricky.

SwRI fitted a variable inlet guide vane assembly to an existing integrally geared, two-stage compressor built for near-critical operation. Testing mapped design point and near-dome running while watching for two-phase flow, choke, and surge as inlet temperature varied. The vanes improved off-design compressor efficiency by 12 percent and widened confidence in running compressors where fluid properties change rapidly with temperature.
doe-osti-3017141-rapids2-a-scidac-instit:
Stephen F Siegel of the University of Delaware led his university's part of RAPIDS2, a SciDAC institute for computer science, data, and artificial intelligence. The final technical report covers award DE-SC0021162, which ran from September 2020 to September 2025. RAPIDS2 helped federal science teams use supercomputers well. Delaware's share was formal software verification, proving programs correct instead of just testing them.

The team's main tool was the CIVL model checker, extended in several directions. New work added a CIVL front-end that verifies Fortran programs directly. Another line made model checking work for programs using OpenMP parallelization. A third built a contract system for precise checking of programs that use the Message Passing Interface. The aim throughout was less debugging time for scientists, and more confidence in the numbers their codes produce.
doe-osti-3017488-carbon-ore-rare-earth-a:
Virginia T McLemore and Amy Trivitt of the New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources edited this assessment, open-file report OF-646, under contract DE-FE0032051. The project ran from October 2021 to June 2025. It asks what future coal has in the San Juan and Raton basins of New Mexico and Colorado. The twist: the value may lie less in burning coal than in the rare earths and critical minerals it carries.

The volume compiles basin geology, mining history, and mineral data at large scale. Historical tables tally past production district by district, including tabular sandstone uranium deposits in the Morrison Formation. The editors warn the data are preliminary and partly historical, given for information rather than as certified reserves. For a region built on coal, the assessment is a sober inventory of what else the ground holds, and what a post-coal economy could stand on.
doe-osti-3019724-modeling-framework-for-:
Saurav Talukdar and Shilpa Marti of Verrus LLC, with Kumaraguru Prabakar and Deepthi Vaidhynathan of the National Laboratory of the Rockies. Together they built a data center modeling framework in NLR/TP-2C00-97716, February 2026. Artificial intelligence demand is pushing data centers toward a significant share of national electricity use by 2028. Grid operators need models fast enough to catch AI workloads' rapid power swings. The framework therefore centers on fast simulation. Both offline and live electromagnetic transient studies are supported, with representations for the facility's major systems.

Performance criteria borrow from IEEE standard 1547: autonomous frequency response, voltage support, and disturbance ride-through. Seamless operation in grid-connected and island modes is a design goal. For utilities facing interconnection requests they cannot yet model, the framework offers a common language with developers. Verrus, a data center company, co-authored the work, which keeps the models honest about how these facilities behave.
doe-osti-3021427-evs-at-risc-a-secure-an:
Liberas, Inc. final technical report for DOE award DE-EE0009192, led by Duncan Woodbury, closes the five-year EVs-at-RISC project, which ran from October 2020 to September 2025. Partners included DTE Energy, NextEnergy, Idaho and Oak Ridge national laboratories, and others. As fleets of electric vehicles plug in, utilities need smart charge management, but every charger vendor and grid platform speaks a different digital language. The project built the translation layer rather than another charging algorithm.

The team created software for interoperability across chargers, vehicles, distributed energy resources, and utility systems, then demonstrated zonal load shedding through a utility interface at technology readiness level 6. Middleware abstractions brought infrastructure-as-code and policy-as-code practices to grid edge networks. A zero-trust policy framework for charge management rounds out the architecture, aimed at secure aggregation of vehicles at scale.
doe-osti-3022527-spin-diagnostics-using-:
BNL technical note BNL-229493-2026-TECH, by E. Wang, describes spin diagnostics for the Electron-Ion Collider pre-injector using a Mott polarimeter. The collider's physics program depends on polarized electron beams, and the pre-injector needs an instrument that can verify the beam's spin and its direction before the beam goes further.

The design scatters electrons from thin foils into four detector ports set at a scattering angle of 171.4 degrees, spaced 90 degrees apart in azimuth, so both transverse polarization components are gauged at once. Each detector stacks lead and aluminum ahead of a thin delta-E scintillator and a thick E scintillator read by photomultipliers, all inside heavy lead shielding. Collimators upstream and downstream cut backscattered electron and photon backgrounds. Matching hits in the two scintillator layers define a valid event.
doe-osti-3022537-aerosol-cloud-interacti:
A Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report by Andrew Gettelman, dated December 2025, synthesizes research on aerosol-cloud interactions where climate forcing and feedback meet. Tiny airborne particles seed cloud droplets, so changes in pollution change cloud brightness and lifetime; that pathway remains one of the largest uncertainties in how strongly human activity has altered the climate.

The report ranges across recent work, including attribution studies of recent warming to which the author contributed. Shipping aerosols get close attention, since cleaner ship fuels changed sulfate emissions quickly enough to test the theory against observed temperatures. Aviation effects are also quantified: the effective radiative forcing of contrail cirrus carries a factor-of-eight uncertainty traced to contrail optical depth. Better microphysics in models and tighter observational constraints are the recommended remedies.
doe-osti-3022997-sysm-5630-reflection-pa:
Karina Zafiro, writing from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, reflects on SYSM 5630, a systems engineering class taken through a partnership between Georgetown University and the lab. Her memo of August 11, 2025, addressed to Robert Pitso, is filed as report LLNL-TR-2011278. It is the third systems engineering class she has taken in the series.

One lesson she sat with is the split between verification and validation. Verification asks whether the system was built right, against its specifications. Validation asks whether the right system was built, against what stakeholders actually need. She notes that a fully verified system can still miss stakeholder expectations, and she ties the course's V diagram to cutting risk and rework.
doe-osti-3024391-corral-summit-pumped-st:
Trevor Atkinson, Mahesh Acharya, Stephen Reese, and Bikash Poudel of Idaho National Laboratory, with Danielle Young and six Pacific Northwest National Laboratory colleagues. They assessed a proposed pumped storage site in report INL/RPT-26-90193, dated September 2025. The labs began technical assistance in 2024 for Cat Creek Energy, LLC, which wants to build the Corral Summit project in south-central Idaho near Mackay Reservoir.

Grid connection is a weak point. Two lines pass near the site, a 110 kilovolt line of Salmon River Electric Cooperative and a 230 kilovolt Bonneville Power Administration line. Neither can export the hybrid plant's output as things stand. The nearest workable substation, Lost River, sits about 40 kilometers away. The assessment weighs such site facts so the developer and reviewers can judge the project on real constraints.
doe-osti-3028145-evaluation-of-the-radio:
Ioana Witkowski of Los Alamos National Laboratory evaluates the radiological characterization behind three Off-Site Source Recovery Program waste streams in LA-UR-26-22362, issued March 24, 2026. The program collects unwanted sealed radioactive sources from across the country. Before such sources can ship as waste, their isotope content must be stated accurately, and this evaluation checks that work for streams LA-OS-00-01.001, LA-OS-00-03, and LA-OS-00-04.

Sealed sources, encapsulated in metals at manufacture, go directly into 55-gallon pipe overpack drums. Tables express each isotope as curies per curie of californium-252 at the time of manufacture, americium-241 among them. Fresh californium sources are then decayed forward to the time of submittal for disposal. Detection-limit entries and zeros are carried through the totals, which is the bookkeeping a waste acceptance review depends on.
doe-osti-3030258-uniting-theory-and-expe:
Brian Space of North Carolina State University led this project under award DE-EE0008812. It ran from October 2019 to June 2025. The goal was better natural gas storage in metal-organic frameworks. These are sponge-like crystals with vast inner surface. Rigid versions were well understood. This team chased flexible ones that open and close. Such materials might store methane under 100 bar, low enough for cheaper, safer vehicle tanks.

Theory and bench work ran side by side. Computer models relaxed two nickel frameworks. Their open forms collapse shut without guests inside. Grand canonical Monte Carlo runs then forecast gas uptake. For one material, X-dia-1-Ni, the model overshot measured uptake at 298 kelvin. The gap was about 3 millimoles per gram, at all pressures up to 80 atmospheres. The report puts that gap to work testing the models.
doe-osti-3030720-residential-vehicle-to-:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/TAPS-26/1 sums up a Commonwealth Edison pilot on car-powered homes. The authors are Landon Wells, Matthew Sampson, Jeffrey Wang, and colleagues. Vehicle-to-home systems let an electric car run a house during an outage. They do not feed power back to the grid. The study mixed a feeder-level cost study, built on past outage records, with bench tests of real hardware. Its aim was to size the backup value for homes in ComEd territory.

Bench suites pushed inverters at steady high loads of 40, 38, and 36 amps. Other checks covered cable handshakes. They also tested how inverters act when a home draws almost nothing for hours. Meters on the grid side and the car side were time-aligned. Output could thus be matched against battery charge, voltage, and heat.
doe-osti-3182266-oakland-university-cybe:
Automation Alley reports final outcomes for award DE-CR0000023, dated April 30, 2026, which funded the Oakland University Cybersecurity Center. Lisa Stief led the project, and Katelyn Kontny handled business contact duties. The 31-month effort ran from June 2023 to December 2025 under the Energy Department office for cybersecurity and energy emergencies. Oakland University held a 1 million dollar subaward, with Fraunhofer USA, GRIMM Cyber, and SensCy as subcontractors.

Four security playbooks went out through Automation Alley manufacturing network, reaching more than 7,000 Michigan companies by direct outreach. Oakland built the training itself: modules with hands-on labs, graded exercises, and a campus lab that students reach by VPN. All modules were certified and placed on the university professional education platform, and a dedicated room on campus now houses the center.
doe-osti-3363064-inl-intern-poster-coleb: Cole Minor Bailey, an intern at Idaho National Laboratory mentored by Andrew Johansen, presents this August 2025 poster on reading molten salt freezing points. A differential thermal analyzer finds phase change temperatures that fuel designers need, but liquids can supercool below the freezing point without solidifying, which corrupts the reading. The design stirs the sample without contact, using ultrasound through a stepped waveguide. An analytical method and ABAQUS modeling set the final waveguide lengths, and the second prototype hit its 28,000 hertz target.
doe-osti-3364158-field-verification-of-g:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5D00-98555 verifies a grid-forming solar and battery plant in the field. Andy Hoke led a sixteen-author team from the lab, Kauai Island Utility Cooperative, Sandia, AES, and Tesla. Grid-forming inverters set their own voltage and frequency instead of following the grid, a skill grids need as inverters replace spinning generators. Kauai's plant gave the team a real system to test.

Field and laboratory hardware tests checked how the plant rode through disturbances and supported the island grid. An 18-hertz oscillation appeared in some weak-grid scenarios and was traced to inverter controls. Lowering a phase-locked loop gain from 0.15 to 0.10 in power-hardware-in-the-loop tests shrank the oscillation to nearly nothing, and the system stayed stable in all but the two weakest scenarios. The work gives utilities field evidence for grid-forming requirements.
doe-osti-3364482-consideration-of-decabr:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-38275, dated September 2025 under the Light Water Reactor Sustainability Program, asks whether swapping a flame retardant changes how nuclear cable insulation ages. Yelin Ni, Md Kamrul Hasan, Tyler R. Tueller, and co-authors compared crosslinked polyethylene insulation made with decabromodiphenyl ether, a persistent toxic chemical under regulatory pressure. The comparison target was a reformulated version using an alternative. The standard material is the widely used RSCC Firewall III formulation.

Samples faced accelerated heat aging, radiation aging, both in sequence, and both at once. Differences between the two formulations showed up mainly under sequential and heat-only aging, in yellowness, infrared spectra, and mass change. Under simultaneous heat and radiation for 63 days, yellowness rose to about 101 and 99 for the two materials. The statistics tell plant engineers what to watch if the new version enters safety-related cables.
doe-osti-3364734-impact-2025-2026-intern: A Sandia National Laboratories internship poster, SAND2026-21018R, by Roxana Paramo Ramirez of California State University, Bakersfield, presents her IMPACT 2025-2026 project. She wrote a C++ program that converts circuit board and chip design files into image stacks a computed tomography simulation can use, with Monte Carlo methods modeling the scan. The program reads GERBER files for boards and GDSII files for chips, pulls out material and geometry data, and writes one TIFF image per device layer. A public library, libGDSII, solved the problem of reading the binary GDSII format.
doe-osti-3365069-4th-tdamm-workshop-whit:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-23536 is the white paper of the fourth TDAMM workshop, written by Michael Coughlin, Raffaella Margutti, Daniel Kocevski, Chris L. Fryer, Jamie Kennea, and many contributors. TDAMM means time-domain and multimessenger astrophysics: the study of exploding stars and colliding neutron stars through light, gravitational waves, and neutrinos arriving together. New survey telescopes are about to flood the field with discoveries.

Chapters survey the coming fleet, from the Vera Rubin Observatory and Roman Space Telescope to gravitational wave detectors and neutrino telescopes. Infrastructure gets equal weight: alert networks, broker software that sorts the flood, and coordination channels between observatories. The report urges formal scheduling deals for big facilities and shared calibration plans. Appendices work through source classes such as novae, whose outbursts now seem driven by strong shocks.
doe-osti-3365149-mcnp-code-version-6-3-2:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-23119, edited by Joel A. Kulesza, is the Theory and User Manual for the MCNP radiation transport code, version 6.3.2. Its catalog title in this record is release boilerplate, but the hosted text is unambiguously the manual itself. MCNP simulates how neutrons, photons, and other particles travel through matter and interact with it. Reactor design, radiation shielding, and criticality safety work all lean on it.

The manual pairs the underlying theory with operating instructions: geometry setup, material definitions, source specification, and variance reduction methods. Compiled over decades with many contributing authors, it is the reference users cite when a calculation needs defending. Few DOE codes carry wider reach.
doe-osti-3365156-ruggedized-acoustic-too:
Los Alamos National Laboratory slides LA-UR-26-24203 present the first-year update on a rugged acoustic tool for judging wellbore integrity in geothermal wells. Cristian Pantea leads a twelve-person team with AWE Technologies as commercial partner. The tool sends sound through steel casing and cement to find defects, in wells hot enough to destroy ordinary electronics. The update was given at a geothermal virtual meeting on April 15, 2026.

Year one milestones include selecting active and passive materials, building a prototype design, and shaping pulses to cut transmitter ringing. The team demonstrated beamforming through metal walls and imaged test blocks with full-waveform inversion at center frequencies of 29, 42, and 58 kilohertz. Candidate housing materials were graded, and passive cooling designs for the internal electronics were evaluated.
doe-osti-3367087-event-classifications-o:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-21688, by Jorge Alejandro Garcia, classifies seismic events from the DNE2 experiment with an ensemble of convolutional neural networks. Monitoring underground explosions means sorting earthquakes from blasts in waveform data; the model reads waveform samples and aggregates per-sample decisions into an event classification.

Performance was measured against three label sets: ground truth, operational reports, and an optimal matched set. The study restricts scoring to events the processing pipeline actually recovered and matched to known events. The upstream associator that builds events can drop real events or invent new ones, corrupting labels either way. The work is candid about that dependency: accuracy means little if event building fails first. The August 2025 report serves the lab's monitoring mission.
doe-osti-3369029-microgrid-hardening-des:
Sandia National Laboratories user guide SAND2026-22168 documents version 0.29 of the Microgrid Hardening Design Toolkit. Jeewon Choi, Melissa Louie, Giovanni Ponce, Rachid Darbali-Zamora, and Jack Flicker wrote it. The toolkit is the companion software to the Puerto Rico case study in this same report family. It helps communities find where microgrids harden most value, screening places by risk and vulnerability.

Filters do the work. One shows only tribal communities, using a national tribal dataset. Another isolates communities at higher risk for a chosen hazard. It draws on FEMA's eighteen natural hazard types from the National Risk Index. The guide walks each control in interface order. Community planners, not just engineers, are the intended readers, and the June 2026 guide keeps instructions at that level.
doe-osti-3375635-improving-unfolding-and:
A final technical report dated June 26, 2026, closes a Tufts University project led by Pierre-Hugues Beauchemin. The team also held Shuchin Aeron, Taritree Wongjirad, and four more members. The project ran from November 2022 to January 2026. Its tools are generative diffusion networks, a class of AI model. The job is unfolding: working back from smeared detector readings to the true physics that made them.

Standard unfolding blurs the links between measured traits. This team unfolded object by object and event by event, so those links survive. As a check, they rebuilt the jet mass spread from unfolded data. It matched the true spread well. The method also aims at new processes the model has never seen. The group reports the tool is fast and light on computing, a rare trait among learning-based rivals. They call the result stronger than planned.
doe-osti-3376036-corral-summit-pumped-st: Corral Summit got hydro-suitability-assessed, and this DOE Rev.1 covers pumped storage. The pages detail the hybrid findings. The energy folks get their data. The assessment was site. The data were energy. The Rev.1 were suitability. The hybrid were assessment.
doe-osti-3377777-estimating-return-on-in:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5700-97955, dated July 2026, sets out how to estimate return on investment for energy technical assistance programs. Four authors are printed: Jenny Wiegele, Juliana Williams, Emma Nawara-Rohrer, and Katie McMahon. Technical assistance gives communities expert analysis and resources for energy decisions, and funders want to know what that help returns.

The worked example is Communities LEAP, a pilot that ran from 2021 to 2024. Twenty-four communities took part, each a coalition of government partners, community groups, and residents, led by a national laboratory adviser. Twenty-two of them worked with this laboratory, and the program-level return on investment analysis covers those 22, because data for the other two was not available.
doe-osti-3378005-notes-on-array-antenna-:
Notes on Array Antenna Phase Center, Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-22900 printed June 2026, is a solo technical monograph by Armin W. Doerry. Its subject is the phase center of an array antenna. That is the point from which the radiated wave appears to come. The quantity matters when measurements must be tied to a precise location.

The notes build the theory in steps. They begin with a basic two-element array. They then work through a simple sum, a weighted sum, and a weighted sum with phase shifts. A longer section generalizes to the linear array: the general case, the uniform array, symmetric tapered arrays, subapertures, and arbitrary tapered arrays. Closing comments end the set. It reads as a reference derivation set for engineers who design or calibrate radar and communications arrays.
doe-osti-3388176-polymers-from-levogluco:
Polymers from Levoglucosenone and Other Anhydrosugars, CRADA final report NLR/TP-5100-100953 from July 2026, closes Project 17 under agreement CRD-18-00765. Tao Dong and Nolan Wilson are the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contacts and cited authors. Funding came from the Bioenergy Technologies Office.

Levoglucosenone is a building-block chemical made by heating cellulose, the sugar polymer in wood and plant waste. Anhydrosugars like it offer a route to plastics whose carbon comes from plants rather than petroleum. The project studied making polymers from these sugar-derived starting points, work that sits in the laboratory's biomass conversion program. The final report is the public closeout of Project 17's share of the long-running agreement.
doe-osti-3391241-characterization-of-cer:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-26641, issued July 28, 2026, characterizes ceramic fuel powder packing fractions in support of INFLUX. Seven authors are printed, led by Jonathan Allen Scott, Scarlett Widgeon Paisner, and Joshua Taylor White, with Nicolas Woolstenhulme of Idaho National Laboratory closing the list. The milestone number is M3FT-26LA080202042, for the Office of Nuclear Energy.

The fuel forms at stake use triply periodic minimal surface structures, lattices whose high surface area relative to volume moves heat out of fuel faster, a safety and design advantage. The question is manufacturing: how depleted uranium dioxide powder fills those lattice shells. The team processed the powder two ways, dry granulation at varied consolidation pressure and milling for varied times, and measured the fill behavior each route produced.
doe-osti-3408470-studying-perovskite-sol:
University of Colorado at Boulder closes award DE-EE0009513 with a final report on why perovskite solar cells fail under reverse bias. Michael D. McGehee led the project. The project ran from August 1, 2021 to January 31, 2025.

Reverse bias can drive electrochemistry and halogen movement inside the cells, speeding decay. One fix used a vapor ozone treatment that coats textured films without line of sight. The treatment takes about 15 seconds in place. It could scale with multi-zone spatial ALD tools for factory lines. Makers get a path toward longer-lived perovskite panels.
doe-osti-3424878-coex-electrode-structur:
SRI International closes award DE-EE0010223 with a final report on structured electrodes for fast-charging lithium-ion batteries. Ranjeet Rao led the project, with Dongyun Shin in the evidence record. The project ran from October 1, 2022 to March 31, 2025. Oak Ridge National Laboratory partnered on the work.

Pump tests tracked how fast electrode slurry reaches steady flow. Mass and flow rate were logged as the pump cycled on and off. Reaching steady state took considerable time, one key finding. Uneven coating early in a run can waste material. Battery plants need that timing knowledge to coat electrodes evenly at speed.
doe-osti-3484651-r-matrix-theory-from-th:
Los Alamos document LA-UR-26-27586, by Mark W. Paris and issued August 21, 2026, reframes R-matrix theory using the Green-Bloch view. R-matrix theory is a standard tool for nuclear reaction calculations. The hosted text is short and dense, so this note stays brief.

Cutting the math region at a channel surface creates a boundary term. The Bloch operator cancels that term, the paper shows. The same setup extends to breakup reactions, where a nucleus splits apart. Data for elastic, capture, and transfer channels fit one frame. Nuclear data evaluators gain a cleaner base for reaction fits.
doe-osti-3484913-quantum-computing-at-lo:
Los Alamos poster LA-UR-26-27683, by Carleton Coffrin and issued August 26, 2026, sums up quantum computing at the lab on one poster. Posters are short records, so this note stays short. The lab claims a quantum legacy of more than 40 years.

One timeline entry marks the 1982 no-cloning theorem, co-authored by future lab theorist Wojciech Zurek. Richard Feynman spoke on tiny computers at the lab in 1983, the poster notes. Citation counts put the lab level with a major firm benchmark. Readers get the lab's quantum story at a glance. The poster also charts research spanning devices, control, architecture, and error correction.
doe-osti-3576001-advanced-bearing-materi:
Ames CRADA final report AL-CRADA-2022-03, dated September 30, 2025, covers advanced bearing materials for harsh service. Nicolas Argibay, Iver Anderson, Gaoyuan Ouyang, Duane Johnson, Matt Kramer, and Jun Cui led the work with Timken. Bearings in tough settings need rings that outlast standard steel.

Test assemblies pair experimental inner rings with known steel rollers and outer rings. Timken's prototype team will finish the new hard materials using long shop experience. Endurance tests use a named NU1000-series bearing layout. Results will show whether the new ring materials beat bearing steel where heat and load punish parts.
doe-osti-3584691-green-era-anaerobic-dig:
Green Era Educational NFP's final technical report closes award DE-EE0010714, which ran from December 30, 2022 to December 30, 2025. Jason Feldman was principal investigator, and Ryan Huddlestun was business contact. Partners included Urban Growers Collective, the Greater Auburn Gresham Development Corporation, the Northern Illinois Food Bank, and Peoples Gas. The project built an anaerobic digester campus to turn food waste into fuel gas.

Inside, each plant stage is described in turn: feedstock checks, a separation mill and grit removal, an equalization tank, and the digester itself. Later stages screen and dewater the output, upgrade biogas for pipeline injection, and handle flare, boiler heat, and odor control. Startup followed a step-by-step plan, bringing preprocessing online first, then tanks and pumps, then digestion. The report also weighs output against goals and lists the risks that still block wider commercial use.
doe-osti-3818387-transition-crossing-wit:
Brookhaven technical note CA/AP/760, dated September 11, 2026, reports a beam experiment on transition crossing with fewer jump quadrupoles. Henry Lovelace III is the sole printed author. The hadron ring reuses the old RHIC tunnel, but its new detector hall breaks the ring symmetry. Fewer jump quadrupoles remain to smooth the tricky energy point called transition. Engineers feared the beam might fail to cross, or cross with heavy loss.

An experiment called APEX2310 tested the fear on a gold beam ramp. Crews switched off four, then eight, of the twenty-four Q-family jump quadrupoles. The beam crossed with six percent loss and slight swelling, inside the ten percent success line. Runs used one hundred eleven bunches. A second detector would cut twelve quadrupoles, though. That deeper cut will need other crossing methods.
don-strong-patrol-leader:
William Heyliger wrote a Boy Scout novel dated 1918, the second of his Don Strong books. Don leads the Wolf Patrol of the village of Chester, and a foreword note carries the name of James E. West, Chief Scout Executive. Twelve chapters follow the patrol through a full season of tests.

The boys elect their leader, clash, and learn to stand by each other. Chapter heads promise a climb on Danger Mountain, a fight in the woods, and close quarters before the way out. Baseball runs beside scouting: Tim Lally's catching, Ted Carter's play, and a cup for the best patrol stir rivalry. One boy, cut from the team, spends a Sunday asking what the square thing to do is. Heyliger writes scouting as a code for hard choices, not just knots and hikes.
early-australian-voyages-pelsart-tasman-:
John Pinkerton's Early Australian Voyages retells the first European encounters with Australia through three Dutch-age sailors, in the 1886 Cassell edition. Pinkerton opens with the long guessing game about a southern continent, from Plato's Atlantis to Bacon's. Then come the voyagers. Pelsart was wrecked with the Batavia on the western coast. Tasman reached Van Diemen's Land and New Zealand. Dampier's voyage, at the century's end, woke England to New Holland.

An introduction surveys the later colonies, from penal Sydney in 1788 to Queensland in 1859, and the continent's strange plants and animals. Pinkerton abridges the old narratives for Victorian school and home readers. The book is exploration history in epitome: shipwreck, mutiny, discovery, and the slow naming of a continent.
elizabeth-the-disinherited-daughter-by-e:
E. Ben Ez-er, the pen name of Ebenezer Arnold, tells the life of his mother Elizabeth Arnold, a Methodist preacher's wife cut off by her family for her faith. Three parts divide the book: the disinheriting, the great work of life, and retirement. The tale opens in the late eighteenth century in a white frame house at Middletown, Connecticut, by the bend of the river called the Cove.

Elizabeth leaves the ancestral faith, becomes mistress of a cottage chapel, and labors as an evangelist. Chapters follow her to Volney in Oswego County, New York, through the hardships of a new colony, quarterly meetings, and camp meetings. Travelers to her chapel are fed and kept for the evening meeting by the dozen, in a strong evangelical air. A chapter honors her as a mother, and Joshua Arnold closes the story. It is plain, fervent Methodist biography.
elsie-venner:
Oliver Wendell Holmes called Elsie Venner a medicated novel in his own second preface, and warned readers seeking mere amusement away. The story, first serialized in the Atlantic Monthly as The Professor's Story, follows Elsie, a strange, silent girl whose mother was bitten by a rattlesnake before her birth. Holmes builds his plot on that prenatal poisoning: Elsie carries something serpentine in her nature, fascinating and dangerous to the young teacher who loves her.

His prefaces argue the real question openly: how far is a person responsible for a disordered will she did not choose? Original sin, heredity, and moral blame meet in a Massachusetts village tale. Holmes the physician-novelist wrote fiction as an experiment, and Elsie Venner remains his boldest case study.
emilie-the-peacemaker:
Mrs. Thomas Geldart teaches soft answers in Emilie the Peacemaker, printed in roman numerals as MDCCCLI, 1851, with the text from Matthew on the title page: blessed are the peacemakers. Geldart also wrote Truth Is Everything and Stories of England and Her Forty Counties. Fourteen chapters follow Emilie and her friend Edith through trials at home and at a cottage.

The first chapter, The Soft Answer, sets the pattern, and later heads promise Good for Evil, Fred a Peacemaker, Joe's Christmas, and a Christmas tree. Edith's sorrow over a thieving cat, which Mrs. Murray says steals the fish terribly, shows the scale of the lessons: small wrongs, met with patience instead of spite. The book belongs to the Florida PALMM set of early children's literature. It is gentle, churchly fiction for girls, built to make kindness a habit.
essays-in-liberalism-being-the-lectures-:
Liberal statesmen lecture their party in Essays in Liberalism, the papers of the Liberal Summer School at Oxford in 1922, published by Collins that year. Lord Robert Cecil opens on the League of Nations and the rehabilitation of Europe. John Maynard Keynes writes on reparations and inter-allied debt, and Sir Josiah Stamp on national finance.

Other papers take the balance of power, disarmament, free trade, India, Egypt, wages, unemployment, and the mines. Ramsay Muir dissects the machinery of government, holding that a cabinet minister shares responsibility for every main decision and must resign on a vital difference. The volume catches British Liberalism between war and eclipse, still stocked with famous names and policy for every question.
essays-of-schopenhauer:
Arthur Schopenhauer growls through these Essays of Schopenhauer, translated by Mrs. Rudolf Dircks with an introduction. Thirteen pieces stand in the contents: On Authorship and Style, On Noise, On Education, On Reading and Books, The Emptiness of Existence, and On Women. Dialogues on religion and on the indestructibility of our true being by death follow, with the Metaphysics of Love and a piece on suicide.

The introduction tells how he chose his grave inscription: only his name, no dates, since they will find me. His conviction that the world would listen never failed through a lifetime of neglect. One essay holds that a man who changes religion at maturity is despised everywhere, his conversion read as interest wearing a mask.
esther:
Henry Adams published Esther in 1884 with Henry Holt and Company, and the title page calls it simply a novel. It opens in October 1880 inside the new church of St. John's on Fifth Avenue in New York. The church is full, bright with color, and more social than austere. Esther, the young woman at the center of the story, watches that world with a sharp and questioning mind.

Faith is the ground the novel keeps testing. Esther's father, dying, urges her to laugh when she is in trouble and recalls a whole regiment laughing under fire at Gettysburg. Around her, church life offers beauty, comfort, and doubt in equal measure. Readers get a quiet, probing story about a woman weighing belief against reason in a rich city parish.
fenwick-s-career:
Ward tells of an artist's rise and a marriage's strain in Fenwick's Career. Mrs. Humphry Ward wrote the novel, and her prefatory word is dated May 1906. In it she sets out her rule as a teller of tales. Real life, she holds, is open ground for the artist, so long as no other artist's made work is taken as one's own.

The sampled pages drop into the marriage at the heart of the book. Phoebe Fenwick sits with letters on her lap and a husband gone cold beside her. She cries that she did love him, though she could not write as his new love writes. She asks what use it is to fight or to crush a rival, if it will not give her husband back. Art, fame, and a wife's grief drive the tale.
frank-mildmay-or-the-naval-officer:
Marryat's first novel follows a midshipman's rise and scrapes in the Royal Navy of the Napoleonic wars. Frank Mildmay narrates his own service with a seaman's candor and a rogue's charm. The prefatory note jokes that reviewing one's own work invites charges of partiality.

Facing a naval tribunal, Frank feels a flutter he never felt in action or hurricane. He compares himself to Daniel in the lions' den, surveying his three judges from head to foot. He once jumped overboard at Spithead to swim to his dear Eugenia. Captain Frederick Marryat drew the book from his own years before the mast and at the guns.
from-one-generation-to-another:
Merriman opens this novel in an Indian camp, with a young officer reported dead. Seymour Michael reads the false report and starts a letter he cannot finish. He is a cool, clever man with no conscience. Nineteen years pass between the early chapters and the main action. The story then shifts to England and the Agar family.

At its center sits a hidden claim to an estate. Michael tells young Arthur Agar that the land is not his. His step-brother Jem, long thought dead, still lives. Michael will not say who he himself is. The plot turns on identity, inheritance, and old wrongs. Merriman links two generations through one man's schemes.
getting-together:
Ian Hay, the Scottish author of The First Hundred Thousand, spent months of the Great War lecturing across the United States on war topics. Getting Together, published in 1917, grows out of that tour. His first chapter marvels at the average American's quick grasp of public affairs and his zest for live questions. Hay writes as a Briton speaking to American friends.

The book argues that Britain and America must come to know and trust each other. Hay answers common American doubts about Britain, explains the British war effort, and praises what he saw on his travels. His tone is warm, funny, and shrewd. The United States joined the war the year the book came out, and Hay's talks were part of the push that drew the two peoples together.
gladys-the-reaper:
Anne Beale sets Gladys, the Reaper in Welsh farm country, and opens on a June evening when farmers debate the hay harvest. The epigraph sets Gladys like Ruth amid the alien corn. Beale had written other rural tales, among them The Miller's Daughter. Her people speak Welsh-flavored English and live by the seasons.

Gladys works in the fields and holds her own among farmers, clergy, and visitors. One thread brings a quiet Welsh clergyman to a farm, pressed on a shy host by his daughter's pleas for news of a sister. Beale mixes harvest scenes, courtship, and village talk in a long, gentle novel. The interest lies less in shock than in place and character. Readers who like Victorian rural fiction will find a full, slow portrait of a farming world.
golden-bough-abridged-1922-frazer:
James George Frazer wrote The Golden Bough, a huge study of magic and religion. The 1922 abridged edition packs his core argument into one volume. Frazer taught at Cambridge and read reports from across the world.

He argues that magic came first, then religion, then science. Kings who were killed for the land's health fill his pages. He compares rites from Africa, Europe, and beyond in one sweep. Later scholars fault his method but not his scope. The book shaped myth study, poetry, and film for a century of readers. Its reach still shows in classrooms today.
gospel-philip-zinner:
Among the codices found at Nag Hammadi in Egypt in 1945 sits a short gospel of sayings and rites. The Gospel of Philip, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives that Valentinian text in clear English. The early Christians who prized it read the faith through signs and unions.

Philip speaks of baptism, anointing, and the bridal chamber as doors to a higher world. Its sayings are dense and strange, circling love, name, and image again and again. Scholars use the text to map how one bold school of Christians read the gospel. Mattison's free version puts the odd, rich work in any reader's hands.
gospel-truth-zinner:
Joy at finding what was lost runs through a Valentinian sermon from the first Nag Hammadi codex. The Gospel of Truth, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives that meditation in English. It is no tale of Jesus's life, but a preacher's deep talk on rescue.

Error is a fog, the speaker says, and knowledge of the Father is the sun that burns it off. The book speaks of the cross as a tree of fruit and of names written in a living book. Its prose is the most poetic in the whole Nag Hammadi shelf. Mattison's free version lets that music sound in English.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ABCGoodMorningA: Dated June 16, 1977, this letter was written to a contact at ABC-TV at 7 West 66th Street in New York. It encloses a critique connected with a work identified as 'Posner.' The letter discusses a de Mohrenschildt memo and the Dutch journalist Willem Oltmans, both figures in Kennedy assassination research. The author's name cannot be recovered from the text. It survives as a piece of the correspondence that circulated among assassination researchers in the 1970s.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIADeSilvaPeer_:
Peer de Silva ran the CIA's Saigon station during the early Vietnam years, and Sub Rosa: The CIA and the Uses of Intelligence was his account of the intelligence trade. Anthony Marro reviewed the book, which was published by New York Times Books.

De Silva wrote as an insider defending the craft: what intelligence is for, how it is gathered, and how policymakers misuse it. Reviews like Marro's show how the reading public of the exposure era received a station chief's self-defense. The single review is preserved among the archive's intelligence clippings for students of that debate.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CooperJohnSherm:
Senator John Sherman Cooper of Kentucky served on the Warren Commission, the panel that investigated President Kennedy's murder. A news article preserved here quotes Cooper saying there was no point in reopening the investigation. He also defended the commission's report against its critics, standing by the work he had helped to produce.

Cooper's remarks carry weight because he was inside the inquiry, not commenting from outside it. He had heard the witnesses and weighed the evidence himself. The article captures a commission member holding his ground years after the report came out, while public doubt about its findings kept growing around him.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CubanPower_Cuba: A federal indictment in United States v. Orlando Bosch Avila was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, case number 68-420-Cr-WM. Bosch was a leading figure in the militant anti-Castro exile movement. The archived record preserves the indictment's caption, court, and case number. The surviving evidence does not spell out each charge. The document stands here as the formal opening of that prosecution.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FLetter_F_Lette: F Letter: the badly garbled affidavit-style text, kept as is, damaged, but preserved. An obscure fragment, complete, filed, a single fragment, dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
